Original Gondola: Step inside one of the original 1960s gondola cabins. Looking at the tiny, brightly colored bubbles makes you realize just how far mountain technology has come compared to the massive Peak 2 Peak cabins of today.

Olympic Bid History: Whistler tried to get the Olympics many times before succeeding in 2010. The museum tracks this journey, showcasing the original bid books and torches. It’s a fascinating look at the persistence required to bring the world to the valley.

Toad Hall Photo: Ask to see the famous Toad Hall poster. It’s a legendary piece of Whistler history featuring a group of 1970s ski bums posing naked in front of their shared house. It perfectly captures the rebellious, fun-loving spirit of the early days.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Chat with the Staff: The people working here are often local history buffs with a wealth of off-the-record stories. If you want to know where a specific old cabin used to be or the best place to find historical markers in the forest, just ask.

Combine with the Library: The museum shares a courtyard with the award-winning Whistler Public Library. Grab a coffee, visit the museum, and then head to the library’s fireside lounge for a perfect, low-key afternoon.

Check the Speaker Series: The museum frequently hosts Museum After Dark events or guest speakers. These are fantastic for hearing first-hand accounts from the athletes and pioneers who actually lived through the events you see in the exhibits.
Admission by Donation: The museum operates on a by donation basis. It is one of the most affordable activities in the Village, making it a great stop for budget-conscious travelers.
Family Friendly: There are plenty of tactile exhibits for kids, including vintage costumes they can try on and old-school skis they can touch, making it a hit for all ages.
Hours of Operation: They are typically open daily, but hours can shift during the shoulder seasons (May and October). It’s always worth a quick check of their website before you walk over.

places.name: 6. Whistler Public Library
body: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:WhistlerPublicLibrary.JPG

The Whistler Public Library—affectionately known as the Whistler Cabin—is far from your typical quiet book depository. It is an architectural masterpiece and the community’s favorite living room. Designed with high vaulted ceilings, massive Douglas Fir beams, and floor-to-ceiling windows, the building captures the essence of a modern mountain lodge. It was built to the "LEED Gold" environmental standard, making it as sustainable as it is beautiful.

What makes this spot a must-visit isn't just the books; it’s the atmosphere. Whether the snow is dumping outside or the summer sun is hitting the Olympic Plaza next door, the library offers a warm, peaceful sanctuary with some of the best mountain views in the Village. It’s where locals come to remote-work, travelers come to recharge their devices, and families gather for some low-key downtime between adventures.

Location & Access: You’ll find the library at 4329 Main Street, right in the heart of the Village. It sits directly across the courtyard from the Whistler Museum and overlooks the open greenspace of Whistler Olympic Plaza.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Fireside Lounge: Head to the back of the library to find the cozy armchairs surrounding a modern fireplace. It’s arguably the best place in town to wait out a rainstorm or rest your legs after a long morning on the slopes.

Wonder Gallery: If you’re traveling with kids, this dedicated children’s area is a lifesaver. It’s packed with toys, puzzles, and books, and features giant windows that look out toward the mountains, keeping the little ones entertained in a safe, indoor environment.

Local History Collection: While the museum next door has the artifacts, the library has the records. Dive into their Whistler Collection to find rare books on local mountaineering, pioneer journals, and the development of the ski resort.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Free Wi-Fi: If you’re a traveler needing to upload 4K GoPro footage or hop on a quick Zoom call, the library offers the most reliable free Wi-Fi in the Village. There are plenty of workstations with power outlets, but they fill up fast during the après hours.

Check the Events Calendar: The library isn't just about silence; it hosts everything from Lego clubs for kids to evening workshops on local ecology and photography. Most of these events are free and open to visitors.

Quiet Secret: If the Village Stroll feels a bit too chaotic, the library’s outdoor patio (open in summer) is a hidden gem. It’s a peaceful spot to sit with a book and enjoy the fresh mountain air without the crowds.

Guest Memberships: Even if you’re just visiting for a week, you can get a temporary library card for a small fee. This gives you access to their physical collection and even their digital library of movies and magazines.
Printing & Scanning: If you need to print a travel permit or scan a document, the library provides public computers and printing services for a very nominal cost.

Opening Hours: The library has great hours, usually open 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM (and later on some weeknights), but they are closed on statutory holidays. Always check their board out front for the day's schedule.

places.name: 7. Whistler Art Galleries
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/view-of-sign-the-plaza-galleries-building-in-whistler-village-gm1299706782-392245918

Whistler’s art scene is a vibrant, mountain-town mix of high-end luxury and rugged, local creativity. While the big museums get the headlines, the private Whistler Art Galleries scattered throughout the Village are where you can actually get your hands on a piece of the Pacific Northwest. These spaces range from sleek, modern showrooms to cozy mountain studios, featuring everything from hyper-realistic landscape paintings to massive bronze sculptures and traditional Indigenous carvings.

The variety is what makes gallery-hopping here so engaging. It’s a culture of mountain-inspired art that reflects the scale of the peaks and the textures of the forest, offering a sophisticated way to experience the valley when you’re off the slopes or trails.

Location & Access: Most galleries are clustered along the Village Stroll, in the Upper Village (inside the Fairmont Chateau Whistler), or tucked into the Hilton and Westin resort lobbies. They are all easily reachable on foot within a 15-minute walk of the main gondola base.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Gallery Row Stroll: Start at the north end of the Village near Olympic Plaza and work your way south. Places like Fathom Stone Art (where you can watch artists carving local soapstone) and The Plaza Galleries offer two very different perspectives on mountain aesthetics.

Indigenous Excellence: Make sure to visit galleries that specialize in Northwest Coast art. Look for authentic Argillite carvings, cedar paddles, and intricate silver jewelry. These pieces aren't just art; they are thousands of years of storytelling rendered in physical form.

Fairmont Walk: The galleries located within the Fairmont Chateau Whistler are world-class. Even if you aren't staying there, the lobby and hallways act as a public art circuit featuring some of the most prestigious landscape artists in Canada.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Go During Wine Walk Season: If you’re in town during October or June, keep an eye out for the Whistler Wine Walks. You can purchase a ticket that allows you to wander from gallery to gallery, sipping local BC wines and chatting with the artists. It’s easily the most social way to see the scene.

Ask About the Artist: Many gallery staff are incredibly knowledgeable and can tell you exactly which local ridge or secret spot inspired a particular painting. Don't be afraid to ask—Whistler’s art community is surprisingly approachable.
Ship It Home: If you fall in love with a 6-foot-tall bronze bear, don't sweat the logistics. Most major galleries in Whistler are experts at international crating and shipping.
Admission is Free: Unlike the museums, entering these private galleries is completely free. It’s one of the best ways to spend a low-spend afternoon in the Village while still soaking up the culture.

Varying Hours: Most galleries open around 10:00 AM and stay open until 6:00 PM or 8:00 PM to capture the après-ski crowd. However, some smaller studios might have more sporadic hours during the shoulder seasons.
Etiquette: While photography is usually fine, it’s always polite to ask before snapping photos of original works. Some artists have specific copyright preferences for their newer collections.

places.name: 1. Lost Lake
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/lost-lake-in-whistler-canada-gm1355318032-429837946

Lost Lake is the local’s favorite sanctuary, offering a serene escape just minutes from the high-energy pulse of Whistler Village. Nestled within 525 acres of pristine parkland, the lake is a tranquil mirror reflecting the surrounding Douglas firs and the peaks of Blackcomb. In the summer, it’s the go-to spot for sunbathing on sandy beaches and swimming in the calm, crisp water; in the winter, it transforms into a world-class Nordic center with groomed cross-country ski and snowshoe trails that look like something out of a holiday card.

What makes Lost Lake truly special is its accessibility. You don’t need a mountain pass or a rugged 4x4 to get here—just a pair of sneakers or a cruiser bike. It’s a place that balances wild and convenient perfectly, allowing you to go from a morning coffee in the Village to a secluded lakeside forest trail in under 15 minutes.

Location & Access: You can reach Lost Lake via a flat, scenic 1.5-km (0.9-mile) walk along the Valley Trail starting from the Village. During the summer, a free shuttle bus (Route #8) runs regularly from the Village Gate Boulevard to the lakefront.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Floating Docks: There are several wooden docks scattered around the lake. Swimming out to one and lying in the sun while the water laps against the wood is a quintessential Whistler summer experience.

Nature Trail Loop: Instead of sticking to the main wide path, take the nature trail that hugs the shoreline. It’s a bit narrower and more rugged, offering better vantage points for photography and a more intimate forest feel.

Winter Nordic Skiing: When the snow falls, Lost Lake becomes a paid-access Nordic park. The trails are lit up at night, offering a magical night ski experience through the trees that feels incredibly peaceful compared to the daytime bustle.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Toad Crossing: If you visit in late summer, keep your eyes on the ground. Thousands of tiny Western Toads migrate from the lake to the forest. The park staff often close certain trails to protect them—it’s a fascinating natural event to witness (from a distance).

Early Morning Reflection: If you’re a photographer, get there at sunrise. The lake is usually glass-still, providing a perfect mirror reflection of Blackcomb Mountain before the first swimmers or dogs arrive to break the surface.

Avoid the Mid-Day Crowds: On hot Saturday afternoons, the main beach can get very busy. To find your own slice of peace, walk halfway around the lake to the far side where the small rocky outcrops provide more secluded spots to sit.
Dog Policy: The main beach at Lost Lake is no-dogs-allowed. However, just a short walk away is Canine Cove, a dedicated off-leash dog beach where your pup can swim and play to their heart's content.

No Parking: There is no public parking at Lost Lake Park. You must walk, bike, or take the free shuttle. This keeps the park quiet and the air fresh, but it requires a little bit of planning for your gear.

Wildlife: This is prime black bear territory, especially in the spring and fall. Keep your food securely packed, never feed the wildlife, and give any bears you see plenty of space—they are usually just there for the clover and berries.

places.name: 2. Valley Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/family-bike-on-the-valley-trail-gm1902687507-554359792

The Valley Trail is the scenic, car-free artery that connects the entire Whistler valley. Stretching over 46 kilometers (28 miles), this paved network links every major neighborhood, five shimmering lakes, and countless parks. While the mountains get all the glory, the Valley Trail is where the real Whistler happens. It’s a place where you can glide past golf courses, cross rushing glacial rivers on wooden bridges, and wind through ancient cedar groves without ever having to worry about traffic.

It’s a multi-seasonal gem; in the summer, it's a highway for cruiser bikes and skateboards, while in the winter, many sections are cleared or groomed, allowing for a unique perspective of the snow-covered valley floor.

Location & Access: The trail has entry points throughout the town, but the most popular hubs are in Whistler Village (near the Olympic Plaza), Upper Village, and Creekside. You can pick up a trail map at the Visitor Centre or simply follow the yellow directional signs located at every major junction.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Three Lakes Loop: For a perfect afternoon, rent a cruiser bike in the Village and head south. You can hit Alta Lake, Nita Lake, and Alpha Lake in one easy loop. Each lake has a completely different vibe, ranging from the busy docks of Rainbow Park to the quiet, mirror-like waters of Nita.

River Crossing Views: Make sure to cross the bridge over Fitzsimmons Creek between the Village and the Upper Village. It’s the perfect spot to see the power of the glacial runoff and get a great shot of both Whistler and Blackcomb mountains towering above.

Art in the Wild: Keep an eye out for public art installations along the trail. From stone sculptures to interpretive signs about the local flora and fauna, the trail serves as an outdoor museum that tells the story of the valley’s ecology.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Keep to the Right: The Valley Trail is a shared space. Whether you are walking, biking, or ebiking, always stay to the right and use your bell or a friendly on your left when passing others. It’s the local unwritten rule that keeps everything flowing smoothly.

E-Bike the Distance: If you want to see the whole 46km but aren't looking for a massive workout, rent an e-bike. It turns the slight inclines between Creekside and the Village into a breeze, allowing you to explore the further reaches of the trail like the Emerald neighborhood.

Bear Etiquette: It is very common to see black bears grazing on the clover alongside the trail, especially in the spring. If you see one, do not stop for a selfie. Keep moving at a steady pace and give the bear at least 100 meters of space.
Navigation: The trail is well-marked with Wayfinding maps at most intersections. Look for the You Are Here markers to help navigate the various loops and spurs.

Safety: While the trail is paved and relatively flat, some sections have steep grades, especially heading toward the north end of the valley. Ensure your bike's brakes are in good working order before you set off.

Lighting: While sections near the Village are well-lit at night, much of the trail through the woods is not. If you’re planning an evening ride to a dinner spot in Creekside, make sure your bike has a good headlamp and you have a reflective layer.

places.name: 3. Alexander Falls
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/alexander-falls-whistler-british-columbia-gm1332397942-415258103

Alexander Falls is the quiet giant of the Whistler area—a spectacular, multi-tiered waterfall that drops a sheer 43 meters (141 feet) into the Madeley Creek valley. While Brandywine Falls gets the highway crowds, Alexander Falls offers a more serene, off-the-beaten-path experience. The water cascades over three distinct steps of volcanic basalt rock, creating a wide, curtain-like effect that is especially thunderous during the spring snowmelt.

What makes it a standout is the viewing experience. Unlike many falls where you have to hike for miles to get a glimpse, Alexander Falls features a large, paved viewing platform located right at the top of the canyon. It provides a perfect, straight-on perspective of the water’s plunge against a backdrop of dense old-growth forest. It feels grand, wild, and incredibly peaceful, making it a favorite for those who want a big mountain view without the big mountain effort.

Location & Access: The falls are located in the Callaghan Valley, about a 20-minute drive south of Whistler Village. To get there, turn off Highway 99 onto Callaghan Valley Road (follow signs for Whistler Olympic Park). The parking lot for the Alexander Falls Forest Service Site is located on the left side of the road, just before you reach the main gate of the Olympic Park.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Main Overlook: The viewing platform is just steps from the parking lot. It’s the best spot for a panoramic photo of the falls. In the morning, you can often catch a rainbow forming in the mist at the base of the drop.

Winter Ice-Climbing: If you visit in the depths of winter, the falls often freeze into a massive, shimmering blue ice wall. It’s a surreal sight, and you’ll occasionally see professional ice climbers tackling the frozen pillars.

Picnic with a View: There are several picnic tables located right at the edge of the canyon. It’s one of the most scenic spots in the valley to grab a sandwich and listen to the roar of the water echoing through the trees.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Secret Base Hike: While the main view is from the top, there is a rugged, unofficial trail that leads down to the base of the falls. It is steep and can be very slippery, so only attempt it with proper hiking boots and a bit of a sense of adventure. Standing at the bottom and looking up makes the 141-foot drop feel twice as high.

Bear Watching: The road to Alexander Falls is legendary for bear sightings. Because the Callaghan Valley is quieter than the main highway, black bears are often seen foraging in the clover along the roadside. Keep your camera ready, but stay in your car for safety.

Combine with Olympic Park: Since you’re already in the Callaghan, spend the rest of your morning at Whistler Olympic Park. It’s just two minutes further up the road and offers great hiking and Nordic skiing depending on the season.
No Cell Service: The Callaghan Valley is a bit of a dead zone for cellular signal. Make sure you’ve downloaded your maps or told someone where you’re going before you head off the main highway.
Free Access: Unlike some provincial parks, there is currently no fee to park or view Alexander Falls, making it one of the best free high-value attractions in the region.

Seasonal Road Conditions: While the road is plowed for access to the Olympic Park in winter, it can be very icy. If you’re driving a rental car between November and April, ensure it has proper winter tires (look for the snowflake or M+S symbol).

places.name: 4. Cheakamus Lake Trailhttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/scenic-photo-of-the-calm-cheakamus-lake-gm168257954-16867159
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/couple-paddle-sup-boards-across-mountain-lake-whistler-gm2167626761-587682425

The Cheakamus Lake Trail is the perfect antidote to the steep, leg-burning climbs usually associated with Whistler. Located within the magnificent Garibaldi Provincial Park, this trail winds through some of the most impressive old-growth forests in the valley, featuring massive Douglas firs and ancient cedars that dwarf everything in their path. The payoff is a stunning, 7-km long lake filled with vivid, turquoise glacial water, framed by the dramatic, snow-capped peaks of the Fitzsimmons Range.

What makes this hike a local favorite is its accessibility and high reward for low effort. The trail is relatively flat, making it one of the few places in the region where you can experience true backcountry wilderness without a 1,000-meter vertical climb.

Location & Access: The trailhead is located at the end of Cheakamus Lake Road, a forest service road that begins just south of the Cheakamus Crossing neighborhood. It’s about a 15-minute drive from Whistler Village. The final 6 km of the drive is on a gravel road that can be bumpy, but it is typically manageable for most standard vehicles.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

First Beach Lookout: Just 3 km into the hike, you’ll hit the first clearing at the lake’s edge. This is the perfect spot to stop if you’re short on time. The view looking down the length of the lake toward the far-off glaciers is one of the best bang-for-your-buck vistas in BC.

Lunch at Singing Creek: If you have the energy, continue to the 7-km mark to reach Singing Creek. There’s a beautiful, pebbled beach here where a cold glacial stream enters the lake. It’s the ideal spot for a backcountry picnic before heading back.

Trail Running: Because the elevation gain is so minimal (less than 100 meters), this is widely considered the best trail-running route in Whistler. The soft, pine-needle-covered ground is easy on the joints and allows for a great flow through the forest.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Go Early for Parking: Even though it’s a wilderness trail, it is incredibly popular. The parking lot at the end of the forest service road fills up early on summer weekends. Aim to be at the trailhead by 8:30 AM to secure a spot.

Pack a Hammock: There are plenty of sturdy old-growth trees near the lake’s edge at the first few campsites. Bringing a lightweight travel hammock is the ultimate way to spend an hour soaking in the silence of the park.

Bring a Filter: While the water in the lake looks tempting and pristine, it is still untreated glacial meltwater. If you plan on drinking it, bring a portable water filter or purification tablets to stay safe.

Day-Use Passes: Just like Joffre Lakes, Cheakamus Lake is part of Garibaldi Provincial Park. In 2026, you will likely need to reserve a free BC Parks Day-Use Pass online starting at 7:00 AM two days before your visit.

No Dogs Allowed: Because this is a Provincial Park and a sensitive wildlife corridor, dogs are strictly prohibited on the Cheakamus Lake trail. Please respect the local ecology and leave your furry friends at home.

Biking the Trail: Mountain biking is permitted on this trail, but only as far as the first 3 km (up to the park boundary). It’s a great way to reach the lake quickly, but be mindful of hikers and keep your speed in check on the corners.

places.name: 5. Alta Lake Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/people-are-enjoying-boating-and-swimming-in-alta-lake-whistler-bc-canada-gm1328815978-412754428

Alta Lake is the historical heart of Whistler and its largest body of water. Long before the first ski lift was ever bolted into the mountainside, this was a summer retreat for fishing and lodge life. Today, it serves as the valley’s ultimate aquatic playground, framed by panoramic views of both Whistler and Blackcomb mountains. Unlike the glacier-fed lakes that stay bone-chillingly cold, Alta Lake’s shallower waters warm up enough in the summer to make it the go-to destination for swimming, paddleboarding, and kayaking.

Alta Lake is unique because of the different personalities found along its shores. It features three distinct parks—Rainbow, Lakeside, and Wayside—each offering a different view of the valley. Whether you want a sandy beach for a family barbecue, a quiet spot to launch a canoe, or a chance to see historic pioneer cabins, the lake provides a great escape from the busy Village.

Location & Access: Alta Lake is located about 2 km (1.2 miles) west of Whistler Village. It is most easily accessed via the Valley Trail, a scenic 20-minute walk or 10-minute bike ride. Each park has its own small parking lot, but these fill up quickly on sunny days.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

River of Golden Dreams: Start at Lakeside Park and rent a kayak or canoe to paddle toward the north end of the lake. You’ll find the entrance to the River of Golden Dreams, a winding, lush waterway that feels like a hidden jungle in the middle of the mountains.

Rainbow Park’s Heritage: Visit the western shore to see the site of the original Rainbow Lodge. You can explore the interpretive signs and restored cabins that tell the story of Whistler’s early days as a trout fishing destination in the early 1900s.

Floating Docks: Swim out to the large wooden docks anchored in the middle of the lake. They are the perfect spot for sunbathing or watching the floatplanes take off and land against the backdrop of the alpine peaks.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Go for the Golden Hour: Alta Lake faces east toward the mountains, meaning the late afternoon sun illuminates Whistler and Blackcomb in a stunning golden glow. It is hands-down the best spot in town for a sunset picnic or a quiet evening paddle.

Rent at the Source: Don't worry about hauling gear from the Village. Both Lakeside and Wayside Parks have on-site rental shops (Whistler Eco-Tours) for paddleboards, kayaks, and canoes, making it incredibly easy to get on the water.
Quiet Side: If Rainbow Park is too crowded, head to the smaller Wayside Park on the south end. It’s often overlooked by tourists but offers great swimming docks and a much more peaceful, local vibe.

Dog Etiquette: Like Lost Lake, the main sandy beaches are dog-free zones. However, Rainbow Park features a fantastic dedicated dog beach called Barking Bay, where your pup can swim off-leash with a view of the mountains.

Wind Patterns: The lake can get quite breezy in the afternoons, which is great for the local sailors but can make paddling back to the docks a bit of a workout. Try to head out in the calm, glassy conditions of the morning if you want an easy glide.

Water Temperature: While warmer than the glacial lakes, it’s still mountain water. In early June, it can be refreshing, but by August, it’s arguably the most comfortable swimming hole in the Sea to Sky corridor.

places.name: 6. Cheakamus River
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/family-hiking-adventures-gm1440877737-480733689

The Cheakamus River is the powerful, bright teal lifeblood of the Whistler valley. Fed by melting glaciers, the river shows off the raw beauty of the Pacific Northwest. It thunders through deep canyons and flows under giant, moss-covered trees. Its striking color comes from fine rock dust ground down by glaciers, making the water look like it is glowing against the dark forest.

Depending on where you are, you might see calm, quiet pools or crashing whitewater rapids. It is a perfect spot for everyone, from brave rafters and kayakers to hikers looking for a peaceful riverside walk.

Location & Access: The river runs south of Whistler Village. The best access points are in the Cheakamus Crossing neighborhood, via the Whistler Train Wreck trailhead, or from the Cheakamus Lake Road parking areas. Many sections are easily reached by a 10-15 minute drive from the main Village.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Suspension Bridge: Cross the bridge near the Train Wreck site for a bird’s-eye view of the river’s power. Watching the churning rapids from the swaying bridge is a heart-pounding way to appreciate the scale of the canyon.

Whitewater Rafting: For a true in-the-thick-of-it experience, book a guided rafting trip. These tours take you through the lower reaches of the river, offering a mix of splashy fun and a unique perspective of the towering rock walls you can't see from the trails.

Riverside Fishing: The Cheakamus is a legendary spot for catch-and-release fishing. During the right seasons, you can find anglers casting for Bull Trout and Rainbow Trout in the calmer eddies where the water slows down.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/aerial-view-of-a-river-flowing-through-a-temperate-rainforest-gm1329251224-413053904?clarity=false
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Mist Walk: Visit the riverside trails on a rainy or foggy day. The mist gets trapped in the canyon and hangs over the water, creating a moody, cinematic atmosphere that feels like a scene from a fantasy movie.

Stay on the Trails: The river banks can be incredibly steep and the rocks are often greasy with moss. To avoid an accidental (and very cold) swim, stick to the well-marked paths that overlook the water.

Look for the Salmon: If you are visiting in the autumn, keep an eye on the shallower pools. You might catch a glimpse of spawning salmon fighting their way upstream—a vital part of the local ecosystem that often attracts eagles to the treetops.
Water Temperature: Even on a 30°C summer day, the river is dangerously cold. It is direct glacial meltwater; hypothermia can set in within minutes, so it is not recommended for casual swimming.
Safety First: The current is deceptive and much stronger than it looks. Always keep children and pets a safe distance from the water's edge, as the banks can be undercut and unstable.
Leave No Trace: The Cheakamus River is a sensitive habitat for fish and wildlife. Ensure you pack out everything you bring in to help keep the water pristine and the bear-habitat clean.

places.name: 7. Wedgemount Lake
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/wedgemount-lake-in-summer-bc-canada-gm1161315240-318172367

Wedgemount Lake is often called the ultimate Whistler hike—a tough, steep climb that leads to a dramatic, otherworldly landscape. Located high in Garibaldi Provincial Park, the lake is a bright, milky turquoise and sits right at the base of the massive Wedgemount Glacier. This is not a casual walk; it is a rugged ascent through thick forests and rock fields that brings you face-to-face with the edge of a glacier.

The scenery here is legendary. Once you finish the final, difficult climb, you are rewarded with views of jagged mountain peaks. The area is incredibly quiet, with the silence only broken by the sound of moving ice or waterfalls crashing down the rocks. It is a place of extreme beauty that requires great effort, perfect for those who want to see the wild side of the mountains.

Location & Access: The trailhead is located about 13 km (8 miles) north of Whistler Village. You’ll turn off Highway 99 onto a gravel forest service road. While most cars can make it to the lower parking lot, a 4x4 is recommended for the final stretch to the upper lot.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Touch the Glacier: Follow the rocky path along the shore to the far end of the lake. Here, you can get incredibly close to the Wedgemount Glacier. You’ll see icebergs floating in the water and can witness the birth of the lake’s vibrant color firsthand.

Tupper Lake Extension: If your legs still have some life in them, continue upward toward Tupper Lake. It’s a smaller, higher alpine tarn that offers a birds-eye view of Wedgemount Lake below—it’s the best perspective for showing off the scale of the glacier.

Stay at the Hut: There is a small, basic emergency shelter (the Wedge Hut) at the top. While most people day-hike, those with overnight permits can stay here or camp at the designated platforms for a sunset that turns the glaciers a fiery pink.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Knee-Saver Strategy: The descent is just as hard as the ascent because it is so steep. Many locals swear by trekking poles for this hike; they will save your joints on the 1,200-meter drop back to the car.

Hydration is Key: There is very little water available on the trail until you reach the top. Bring at least 2–3 liters per person, and if you plan to refill at the lake, ensure you have a high-quality filter to remove the heavy glacial silt.

Start Before Dawn: To avoid hiking in the midday heat—especially on the exposed final scramble—try to be on the trail by 6:00 AM. This also ensures you have plenty of buffer time to enjoy the summit before the sun starts to dip.
Day-Use Passes: In 2026, Wedgemount Lake requires a free BC Parks Day-Use Pass during peak season. These are released online two days in advance and are mandatory for all hikers.

Physical Intensity: This is a Black Diamond hike. You will gain approximately 1,200 meters (3,900 feet) in just 7 km. It is physically demanding and requires a good level of fitness and proper mountain experience.

Pack for Four Seasons: Even if it’s a scorching 30°C at the trailhead, the wind coming off the glacier at the lake can be freezing. Always bring a tuque (beanie), gloves, and a down jacket, regardless of how the weather looks in the Village.

places.name: 8. Ancient Cedars Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/hiking-ancient-cedars-gm664853762-121068439

The Ancient Cedars Trail is a journey back in time, leading you to a hidden grove of giants that have stood for over 900 years. While much of the valley was logged in the early 20th century, this pocket of old-growth forest remained untouched. Walking among these massive Western Red Cedars—some measuring over 3 metres in diameter—is a humbling experience.

What makes this trail a standout is the atmosphere. The air is noticeably cooler and richer here, filtered by a canopy of prehistoric-looking trees and thick hanging moss. As you reach the grove, the forest opens up to reveal these ancient sentinels, their gnarled bark and sprawling roots telling a story of survival through centuries of coastal storms and mountain winters. It’s a short but impactful trip into the real wild BC that many visitors miss.

Location & Access: The trailhead is located on the far side of Cougar Mountain, about a 15-minute drive north of Whistler Village. You’ll turn off Highway 99 onto Sixteen Mile Creek Forest Service Road. The road is gravel and can be bumpy; while most cars can make it in the summer, a vehicle with higher clearance is definitely a plus.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Giant’s Hug: Once you reach the main grove, take a moment to stand next to the largest trees. It often takes four or five adults linking arms just to reach around the base of a single trunk. It’s the ultimate perspective-shifter for your vacation photos.

Waterfall Spur: On your way up to the cedars, there is a short side-trail that leads to a beautiful, cascading waterfall. It’s a perfect spot to stop, catch your breath, and listen to the sounds of the mountain runoff before entering the silent grove.

Lookout Views: Shortly before the forest thickens into the ancient grove, the trail offers a fantastic clearing with views looking back toward the Soo Valley and the jagged peaks of the Rainbow Range.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Mist Aesthetic: Don’t let a cloudy day stop you. This trail is actually more magical in the rain or fog. The moisture makes the moss glow a vibrant neon green and the clouds caught in the treetops add to the primeval, Jurassic Park feel.
Morning Light: If you do go on a sunny day, aim for mid-morning. The way the god rays of sunlight filter through the high canopy and hit the forest floor is a dream for photographers.

Footwear Choice: Even though the hike is relatively short (about 5 km round-trip), the trail is full of roots and can be quite muddy after a rainstorm. Wear boots with good ankle support to navigate the wooden stairs created by the cedar roots.
Bear Country: Cougar Mountain is a very active area for black bears. Always hike in groups, make plenty of noise to avoid surprising a bear, and ensure you pack out every scrap of food or trash.

Summer Access: This trail is typically accessible from late June through October. Because it sits on the cooler, northern side of the mountain, snow can linger on the access road and trail well into the spring.
No Cell Service: You will lose signal once you start driving up the Forest Service Road. Make sure you’ve noted the turns and the trailhead location before you leave the highway.

places.name: 9. Green Lake
body: Green Lake is Whistler’s most striking body of water, acting as a massive, emerald-colored mirror at the north end of the valley. Its namesake color is so vivid it looks artificial—a result of rock flour (fine glacial silt) suspended in the water that reflects light in a brilliant turquoise-green. As the largest and deepest lake in Whistler, it sits at the base of the mountains, providing a dramatic, cold, and majestic backdrop that feels worlds away from the busy Village Stroll.

What makes Green Lake truly unique is its role as the valley’s high-alpine airport. Because of its size, it is the primary base for floatplanes, where you can watch de Havilland Beavers and Otters skim the emerald surface against a backdrop of snow-capped peaks. While other lakes in Whistler are for swimming, Green Lake is for the big views—it’s a place of thundering glacial runoff, dramatic winds, and some of the most iconic photography spots in British Columbia.

Location & Access: Green Lake is located about 4 km (2.5 miles) north of Whistler Village. You can reach it via a scenic bike ride along the Valley Trail, or by a 5-minute drive north on Highway 99. The best viewing areas are found at Nicklaus North Golf Course or the Green Lake Boat Launch.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Watch the Floatplanes: Head to the docks at the Nicklaus North clubhouse. Watching a floatplane take off or land on the lime-green water with Wedge Mountain towering in the background is a quintessential Whistler moment.

The Valley Trail Boardwalk: Walk or bike the section of the Valley Trail that runs along the eastern shore. Much of it consists of raised wooden boardwalks over the wetlands, offering incredible views of the lake and a chance to spot nesting ospreys and eagles.

Table Nine Kitchen: For a meal with a view, grab a seat on the patio at Table Nine (located at Nicklaus North). It sits right on the water’s edge and offers the best front-row seat to the emerald expanse of the lake.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Reflection Shot: For the best photos, visit at sunrise. The water is usually at its calmest, and the Alpenglow hits the surrounding peaks, reflecting perfectly in the green water before the afternoon winds pick up.

Look, Don't Leap: Unlike Alta Lake or Lost Lake, Green Lake is extremely cold year-round because it is fed directly by glacial meltwater. It’s also quite windy. Unless you’re a seasoned "polar bear" swimmer, stick to kayaking or paddleboarding rather than a casual dip.

Winter Transformation: In the deep of winter, Green Lake often freezes over completely. While you should never walk on the ice without local knowledge, the snow-covered lake creates a massive, flat white plain that is stunning to see from the highway viewpoints.

Water Activities: There are no on-site rentals directly at the public boat launch, so you’ll need to bring your own gear or book a tour. Many guided kayak tours through the River of Golden Dreams end right here at Green Lake.

Wind Safety: Because of the valley’s geography, Green Lake can experience sudden, strong gusts of wind. If you are out on a paddleboard, stay close to the shoreline so you don't get caught in the choppy water in the middle of the lake.
Parking: Public parking at the boat launch is limited. If you’re visiting during a busy summer weekend, biking via the Valley Trail is much faster and saves you the hassle of hunting for a spot.

places.name: 10. Callaghan Lake Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/callaghan-lake-in-whistler-canada-gm1454079915-489836221

Callaghan Lake Provincial Park is a raw, high-alpine sanctuary that feels like a secret hidden in plain sight. While the crowds gravitate toward the Village, this park offers a rugged top of the world experience without the need for a gondola ticket. The lake itself sits in a sub-alpine basin at 1,370 metres (4,500 feet), surrounded by dramatic cirque glaciers, wildflower meadows, and jagged peaks that remain snow-capped well into August.

What makes Callaghan Lake truly special is its unpolished, wilderness character. This is a non-motorized paradise where the only sounds you’ll hear are the wind through the sub-alpine firs and the splash of a paddle. Because it sits so high in the valley, the park is a snow magnet, often holding onto its winter coat longer than anywhere else, which keeps the landscape lush, the water crystal clear, and the atmosphere feeling like a true backcountry expedition.

Location & Access: The park is located at the end of Callaghan Lake Road, about a 30-minute drive from Whistler. After turning off Highway 99, you’ll pass the Olympic Park and continue onto a 8-km gravel forest service road. This road can be rough and riddled with potholes; a high-clearance 4x4 vehicle is strongly recommended to reach the lakeshore.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Paddle to the Far Shore: Since motorboats are prohibited, the lake is a mirror for the surrounding mountains. Launch a kayak or paddleboard and head to the northern end to get a closer look at the cascading waterfalls and the hanging glaciers of the Solitude Range.

Wildflower Photography: In late July and August, the meadows surrounding the lake explode with color—Indian Paintbrush, Heather, and Arnica. It’s one of the most accessible places to see alpine gold without a strenuous 4-hour hike.

Conflict Lake Trail: From the main parking area, you can hike the relatively flat 5-km trail to Conflict Lake. It leads you through a high-elevation plateau that feels like a miniature version of the Swiss Alps, offering views of the iconic black volcanic spire of Mount Fee.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Bug: Because the park is so lush and stays damp from snowmelt, the mosquitoes and black flies can be intense in early summer. Bring heavy-duty bug spray and wear long sleeves if you plan to visit in July.

Go for the Reflection: Arrive just after sunrise. Because the lake is sheltered by high ridges, the water is often perfectly still in the morning, creating a flawless double-image of the mountains that is a dream for landscape photographers.

Check the Gate: The road to Callaghan Lake is only open during the snow-free months (typically late June to October). Outside of this window, the road is not plowed and becomes part of the Nordic ski trail network.

Self-Sufficiency: There are very limited facilities here—just a basic pit toilet and no running water or cell service. You are truly off the grid, so bring everything you need and be prepared to pack out all your trash.

Camping: There are a handful of rustic, first-come-first-served campsites at the lake’s edge. They fill up fast on weekends, so arrive early on a Friday if you want to snag a spot with a lakeside view.
Bear Safety: The Callaghan Valley is prime grizzly and black bear habitat. Keep your food locked inside your vehicle and never leave a cooler unattended on the beach or at a campsite.

places.name: 1. Scandinave Spa
body: The Scandinave Spa is Whistler’s ultimate sanctuary for digital detox and physical recovery. Tucked into a sprawling three-acre grove of old-growth cedars overlooking Lost Lake Park, this open-air spa feels like a secret Nordic village. It is dedicated to the ancient practice of hydrotherapy—a cycle of hot, cold, and relaxation designed to soothe sore muscles, improve circulation, and settle the mind after a high-output day on the mountains.

What sets Scandinave Spa apart is the total silence. It is a strictly quiet space where talking and electronics are not allowed. Instead, you only hear the sound of outdoor fires, waterfalls, and the wind in the trees. Whether you are soaking in a hot pool while it snows or resting in a hammock during a summer sunset, it offers a level of peace you won't find in the busy Village.

Location & Access: The spa is located at 8010 Mons Road, about a 5-minute drive or a 20-minute walk via the Valley Trail from Whistler Village. While there is plenty of parking, many guests prefer to take a local taxi or the public bus to fully lean into the relaxation.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Hydrotherapy Cycle: To get the full benefits, follow the circuit: 15 minutes of Hot (eucalyptus steam room, wood-fired sauna, or hot bath), 15 seconds of Cold (plunging into the icy Nordic pools or under a cold waterfall), and 15 minutes of Relaxation (by a fire pit or in a solarium).

Solariums: These glass-walled relaxation rooms offer floor-to-ceiling views of the forest and mountains. They are heated and filled with comfortable loungers—arguably the best place in town for a mid-afternoon nap.

Massage Therapy: For the ultimate indulgence, book a Swedish or Deep Tissue massage. Your massage booking includes full access to the thermal baths, allowing you to prep your muscles in the heat before your treatment.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Embrace the Plunge: The cold plunge is the hardest part, but it’s where the magic happens. It triggers an endorphin rush that leaves you feeling incredibly energized. The trick is to breathe deeply and submerge all the way to your shoulders.

Visit at Night: The spa is beautifully illuminated after dark with soft lanterns and the glow of fire pits. Visiting in the evening—especially during a light snowfall—is a surreal, cinematic experience that feels world’s away from the Après party scene.

Mid-Week Hack: To avoid the weekend warrior crowds, try to visit on a Tuesday or Wednesday morning. You’ll often find you have the saunas and steam rooms nearly to yourself, enhancing the feeling of total seclusion.
Silence Rule: They take the silence policy very seriously. If you’re traveling with a group of friends, be prepared to communicate only through nods and smiles until you reach the changing rooms.
Age Requirement: To maintain the peaceful environment, the spa is a 18+ facility. No children or infants are permitted on site.

What to Bring: You are provided with two towels and a locker. You’ll need to bring your own swimsuit and sandals (flip-flops). While robes are available for rent, they are often included in massage packages.
Digital Detox: Phones and cameras are strictly prohibited in the bath area. Plan to leave your devices in your locker and take a mental photo of the views instead.

places.name: 2. Vallea Lumina
body: Vallea Lumina is a nighttime walk that turns the forest of Cougar Mountain into a glowing wonderland. Created by the famous Moment Factory studio, this experience uses high-tech lights, beautiful sounds, and detailed sets to tell a story about two lost hikers. It is a mix of technology and nature that makes you feel like you have stepped into a magical version of the wilderness.

What makes it truly amazing is how the forest itself is used as a canvas. Trees seem to whisper, the ground glows with light, and the giant cedar trees are lit up to show their massive size. It is a journey that captures the mystery of the mountains at night, making it a perfect evening activity for families and couples looking for magic away from the Village.

Location & Access: The experience is located at The Adventure Group (TAG) base on Cougar Mountain, about a 10-minute drive north of Whistler Village. While you can drive yourself, the most convenient way to get there is via the complimentary shuttle that picks up guests from several designated locations throughout the Village.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Musical Grove: One of the most iconic sections of the trail features singing tools and lanterns that pulse in time with a catchy, campfire-style soundtrack. It’s a great spot to pause and appreciate the synchronization of the lights and music.

Stardust Bridge: As you cross the suspension bridge, look down at the forest floor. The light projections create the illusion of flowing stardust and celestial energy moving through the undergrowth—it’s arguably the most Instagrammable moment of the night.
S'mores at the Base: Before or after your walk, hang out at the base camp. There are fire pits where you can roast marshmallows and grab a hot chocolate, which perfectly sets the mountain camp mood.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Book the Earliest Slot: Especially in the winter, the first time slots allow you to see the transition from twilight to total darkness. However, for the most immersive lost in the woods feeling, a later slot ensures the forest is pitch black, making the projections pop with maximum contrast.

Dress for a Hike: Even though it’s a multimedia show, it takes place on a real mountain trail. The path is roughly 1.5 km (0.9 miles) long and includes some steep staircases and uneven terrain. Leave the heels behind and wear sturdy, comfortable walking shoes or boots.

Silence Your Flash: To fully appreciate the artistry, keep your camera flash off. The projections are designed to be seen in low light; a bright flash will wash out the effects and ruin the atmosphere for you and the hikers behind you.

Tickets: Vallea Lumina is a ticketed event with timed entry. It is extremely popular and often sells out days in advance, especially during the winter holidays and summer weekends, so pre-booking is essential.

Mood of the Season: The experience runs year-round. In the summer, you’re walking through a lush, misty rainforest; in the winter, the snow acts as a brilliant reflective surface, making the lights appear even brighter and more crystalline.
Duration: Expect to spend about 45 minutes to an hour on the trail itself, plus extra time for the shuttle and the base camp festivities.
Accessibility: Due to the natural terrain of Cougar Mountain—including stairs and narrow forest paths—the trail is not wheelchair or stroller accessible.

places.name: 3. Peak to Creek
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/skier-descends-mountain-in-fresh-powder-snow-gm2207161786-624421721

The Peak to Creek is Whistler Mountain’s legendary marathon run, famous for having the longest consistent vertical drop in North America. Starting at the very top of Whistler Peak and ending at the valley floor in Creekside, this groomed run covers 11 kilometers and drops over 1,500 meters. it is a true test of stamina and a "must-do" for intermediate and advanced skiers.

What makes Peak to Creek so iconic is how the scenery changes. You start in the high-mountain peaks with views of the vast wilderness before skiing down into the thick evergreen forests. On a clear day, the run feels endless—a long, exciting journey that shows off the massive scale of the mountain in a way few other ski runs can.

Location & Access: The run starts at the top of the Whistler Peak Express chairlift. To get back to your starting point after finishing at the base, you’ll take the Creekside Gondola back up the mountain.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Summit Photo: Before you drop in, walk over to the inukshuk at the Peak. It’s the highest point of the resort and offers the most unobstructed view of Black Tusk. It’s the perfect calm before the storm moment.

North vs. South Choice: The run is actually split into two sections: North and South Peak to Creek. Both are groomed to perfection, but South is often slightly quieter, giving you more room to carve wide turns as you descend.

Après at Dusty’s: There is no better way to celebrate finishing the run than at Dusty’s Bar & BBQ at the Creekside base. It’s a Whistler institution, and their legendary nachos taste significantly better when you’ve just conquered 5,000 vertical feet.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Check the Grooming Report: The Peak to Creek is only a dream run when it’s freshly groomed. Because of its length, if it hasn't been touched by the snowcats, it can become a field of massive moguls. Check the morning grooming map to ensure it’s corduroy before committing.

Stop and Breathe: Don't try to straight-line the whole 11 kilometers unless you have Olympic-level quads. Stop at the midway point near the bottom of the Big Red Express. The view of the valley lakes from here is spectacular, and your legs will thank you.
Mind the Clouds: Sometimes the Peak is in the sun while the valley is shrouded in fog (an inversion). Be prepared for visibility to change drastically as you descend through different climate zones.

Skill Level: While the run is rated as a Blue (Intermediate), its sheer length makes it a physical challenge. It is not recommended for beginners or those who aren't comfortable with sustained steep pitches.

Operational Status: Because the lower part of the run is at a much lower elevation, it requires a deep snowpack to stay open. It typically opens in mid-winter and may close earlier in the spring than the high-alpine runs.

Creekside Trap: Remember that this run ends in Creekside, not Whistler Village. If your hotel is in the main Village, you’ll need to take a shuttle, a taxi, or ride back up the gondola and ski across the mountain to get home.

places.name: 4. Bubly Tube Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/chair-lift-with-skiers-at-whistler-blackcomb-ski-resort-in-winter-gm1286445418-382948537

The Bubly Tube Park is Whistler’s premier destination for high-speed, gravity-fed fun without the need for skis or a snowboard. Located on Blackcomb Mountain, this massive snow-sliding arena features multiple lanes ranging from gentle to steep, allowing riders to zoom down groomed icy chutes at thrilling speeds. It is the ultimate family-friendly adrenaline rush, offering the simple, nostalgic joy of sledding but dialed up to a world-class resort scale.

What makes the Tube Park a standout is the sheer ease of the experience. After screaming your way down the 1,000-foot lanes, you don't have to worry about the grueling hike back up; a state-of-the-art conveyor lift whisks you and your tube back to the top in comfort.

Location & Access: The park is located at the Base II area on Blackcomb Mountain. You can reach it for free by taking the Excalibur Gondola from Whistler Village and getting off at the first stop (Base II). Alternatively, you can drive and park directly in Lots 7 or 8, which are just a short walk from the ticket booth.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Group Link: If you are traveling with friends or family, ask the attendants if linking is allowed. They often let you hold onto each other’s tubes to create a multi-person tube train, which adds extra weight and sends the whole group flying down the lane even faster.

Night Tubing: The park is fully illuminated with powerful floodlights. Sliding under the stars while the Village lights twinkle far below is a completely different experience than during the day—plus, the friction on the lanes often changes as the temperature drops, making for even faster rides.

Warm Up at the Fire Pit: There is a cozy outdoor seating area with fire pits near the base of the lanes. It’s the perfect spot for parents to watch the action or for sliders to take a quick break with a hot chocolate between runs.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Go for the Icy Lanes: The lanes on the far edges often stay a bit firmer and slicker than the middle ones. If you are a true speed demon, look for the lanes that have just been refreshed by the staff—they offer the least resistance and the most air time over the humps.

Mid-Week Twilight: The park can get very busy on weekend afternoons. For the shortest wait times at the conveyor lift, aim for a weekday evening slot. You’ll get significantly more laps per hour than you would on a Saturday morning.

Weight Distribution: For the fastest possible descent, sit deep in the tube and lift your feet up. Reducing the drag from your boots against the snow will help you maintain momentum all the way to the finish curve.

Height Requirements: To ensure everyone’s safety, children must be at least 36 inches (91 cm) tall to ride. Children between 36 and 41 inches are restricted to the specially designated Mini-Lane at the bottom of the park.
Tickets: You can purchase tickets for 1-hour or 2-hour sessions. It’s highly recommended to pre-book online, as the park has a maximum capacity and can sell out during peak holiday periods.

Clothing: You are on a mountain in the winter. Wear waterproof snow pants, a warm jacket, and gloves. High-speed sliding creates a lot of snow spray, and you’ll want to stay dry to enjoy your full session.
Helmets: While not mandatory, helmets are strongly recommended for children. If you don't have your own, you can usually find them available for use at the park.

places.name: 5. Forged Axe Throwing
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/axe-throwing-at-targets-gm949727612-259247631

Forged Axe Throwing is Whistler’s premier indoor lumberjack experience, offering a high-energy, satisfyingly tactile break from the mountain elements. Located in the hip, industrial neighborhood of Function Junction, this venue leans into the town’s rugged heritage, allowing guests to hurl professional-grade axes at wooden targets. It’s a place where technique beats brute strength, and the distinct thwack of a blade sinking into timber provides a unique brand of mountain-town catharsis.

What makes Forged a standout is the atmosphere of competitive camaraderie. It isn’t just about throwing sharp objects; it’s a fully hosted experience where expert axe masters guide you through the safety basics before leading your group into trick shots and tournament-style games.

Location & Access: Forged is located at 1208 Alpha Lake Road in Function Junction, about a 15-minute drive south of Whistler Village. You can easily reach it by car, taxi, or by taking the #10 or #20 public bus from the Village. For the adventurous, it’s also a scenic 30-minute bike ride along the Valley Trail.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Big Axe Challenge: Once you’ve mastered the standard hatchet, ask your host to try the Big Axe. It’s a much larger, two-handed beast that requires serious focus and provides an even more thunderous impact when it hits the bullseye.

Trick Shot Mastery: Don’t just settle for the basics. Your instructors can teach you how to throw two axes at once or even underhand. Perfecting a trick shot is the ultimate way to earn bragging rights for the rest of your trip.

Function Junction Brewery Crawl: Make a day of it. Forged is located steps away from Whistler Brewing Co. and Coast Mountain Brewing. After your session, head next door to sample some of the best local craft beers in the province.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Listen to the Axe Masters: Axe throwing is all about the rotation, not the power. Pay close attention to the footwork and release timing your instructor demonstrates; most people find that a lighter, more controlled throw is what actually makes the axe stick.

Book a Private Lane: If you have a group of four or more, booking a private lane ensures you get the maximum amount of throws per hour. It also allows your group to run your own custom tournament bracket.

Capture the Slow-Mo: Set your phone to Slow Motion video mode. Capturing the moment the axe leaves your hand and rotates through the air before hitting the target makes for incredible footage that really shows off the physics of the sport.

Closed-Toe Shoes: This is a strict requirement for safety. You will not be allowed to throw in sandals or flip-flops. If you forget, the venue often has a few pairs of shoes of shame to borrow, but it's best to bring your own sturdy sneakers or boots.

Age Limits: Forged is generally open to ages 10 and up, making it a great family activity. However, children must have the physical strength to throw the axe safely, and parental supervision is mandatory.
Pre-Booking: Especially on rainy days or during peak Après hours (4:00 PM – 7:00 PM), lanes fill up fast. Use their online booking system to secure your spot at least a few days in advance.

Waivers: Like most Whistler adventures, you’ll need to sign a digital liability waiver before you can pick up an axe. Doing this on your phone before you arrive will get you to the throwing line much faster.

places.name: 6. Coast Mountain Brewing
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/close-up-shot-of-a-variety-of-beers-also-known-as-a-beer-flight-as-served-in-a-gm1057666228-282652788

Coast Mountain Brewing is the soulful, independent heart of Whistler’s craft beer scene. Tucked away from the neon lights of the main Village, this boutique brewery is where the locals go to toast a successful day in the alpine. The space is a masterclass in mountain industrial design—think warm wood accents, views of the brewing tanks, and a cozy, bustling tasting room that smells faintly of fresh hops and malt.

What makes Coast Mountain a standout is their uncompromising focus on quality over quantity. Known for their Hope You’re Happy IPA and a rotating list of complex sours and stouts, they brew in small batches to ensure every pint reflects the rugged, adventurous spirit of the Coast Range.

Location & Access: Located at 1212 Alpha Lake Road in the Function Junction neighborhood, it’s about a 15-minute drive south of Whistler Village. You can hop on the #10 or #20 public bus, or better yet, take a leisurely 30-minute bike ride down the Valley Trail to earn your brew.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Tasting Flight: If you can’t decide (and you shouldn't have to), order a flight. It allows you to sample four different brews, letting you explore everything from their crisp, easy-drinking lagers to their bold, experimental seasonal releases.

Sunny Patio: During the summer months, their outdoor patio is one of the best spots in town to soak up the afternoon sun. It has a laid-back, neighborhood block party vibe that makes it easy to lose an entire afternoon.

Take the Mountain Home: They offer a wide selection of 4-packs and unique tall cans with locally designed art. It’s the perfect way to stock your fridge back at the hotel or grab a souvenir that tastes like Whistler.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Axe & Ale Combo: Since Coast Mountain is located right next door to Forged Axe Throwing, many visitors pair the two. Spend an hour throwing hatchets, then head over to the brewery to cool down with a pint—just remember to do the axes before the ales.

Check the Cask Days: Occasionally, the brewery will tap a special cask conditioned ale. these are one-off, unique flavor profiles you won't find anywhere else and often sell out within hours of being tapped.

Talk to the Staff: The team here lives and breathes beer. If you aren't sure what you like, tell them what flavors you enjoy (citrus, chocolate, pine), and they will guide you to a pour that fits your palate perfectly.

Food Options: While they don't have a full kitchen, they offer high-quality snacks like locally made pepperoni and pretzels. For a full meal, you can often find a local food truck parked nearby, or you can grab a world-famous Purebread treat just a few doors down.
Family & Dog Friendly: The tasting room and patio are welcoming to well-behaved dogs and children, making it a popular stop for families returning from a day at nearby Cheakamus Lake.
Peak Hours: Because it is a local favorite, Friday and Saturday afternoons can get very busy. If you prefer a quieter experience to chat with the brewers, aim for a mid-week visit around 2:00 PM.

places.name: 7. Harmony Lake Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/harmony-lake-on-whistler-mountain-in-summer-gm506037254-84008711

The Harmony Lake Trail is the perfect introduction to Whistler’s high-alpine beauty, offering a greatest hits reel of mountain scenery without requiring an elite level of fitness. Starting right from the bustling hub of the Roundhouse Lodge, this loop trail descends into a spectacular alpine bowl filled with vibrant wildflowers, weather-beaten krummholz trees, and its namesake—the serene, crystal-clear Harmony Lake.

What makes this trail so rewarding is the immediate immersion into the wilderness. Within minutes of leaving the gondola, the sounds of the resort fade away, replaced by the whistle of marmots and the wind rushing through the Harmony Horseshoes (the jagged rock ridges above). The trail features a series of well-maintained boardwalks that protect the delicate alpine ecosystem, allowing you to walk directly over marshy meadows and rugged terrain while keeping your eyes fixed on the panoramic views of the Overlord Glacier and the Fitzsimmons Valley.

Location & Access: The trailhead is located just below the Roundhouse Lodge on Whistler Mountain. You reach it by taking the Whistler Village Gondola from the main village. The trail is a 2.5-km (1.5-mile) loop that typically takes about 60 to 90 minutes to complete.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Harmony Lake Lookout: Before you head down to the water, stop at the designated lookout point. It offers a perfect bird’s-eye view of the lake’s turquoise hue tucked against the grey limestone cliffs.

Wildflower Season: If you visit in late July or August, the meadows surrounding the trail erupt in a kaleidoscope of colors. Look for the bright red Indian Paintbrush and the deep purple Alpine Lupines that carpet the basin.

Connect to High Note: For those feeling ambitious, the Harmony Lake Trail serves as the gateway to the High Note Trail. You can start with the lake loop and then continue onto the more rugged path that skirts the back of the mountain for views of Cheakamus Lake.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience
Go Clockwise: Most hikers find that tackling the loop in a clockwise direction provides the most dramatic reveal of the lake and the surrounding peaks as you crest the small ridges.

Marmot Spotting: The rocky slopes of the Harmony Bowl are prime real estate for Hoary Marmots. Keep your ears open for their distinct, high-pitched alarm whistle and look for them sunning themselves on the large boulders near the boardwalks.
Morning Calm: Aim to be on one of the first gondolas up in the morning. The water in Harmony Lake is usually glass-still before the afternoon alpine breezes
Tickets: You will need a valid Whistler Blackcomb Sightseeing Pass or a Summer Lift Ticket to access the gondola that leads to the trailhead.

Footwear: While the trail is well-marked and features boardwalks, there are still sections with loose rock and uneven dirt. Sturdy walking shoes or hiking boots are much better than flip-flops or smooth-soled sneakers.

Stay on the Path: The alpine tundra is incredibly fragile; a single footstep can kill plants that take years to grow in the short summer season. Always stay on the gravel paths or the wooden boardwalks.

Weather Shifts: Even on a sunny day, weather at the 1,800-meter level can change in an instant. Clouds can roll in quickly, dropping the temperature significantly, so always have a light waterproof layer in your pack.

places.name: 8. Whistler Village
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/whistler-winter-village-at-dusk-gm615822482-106945019

Whistler Village is a pedestrian-only heart of the valley. It was designed to look like a modern alpine fairy tale, inspired by the winding streets of European mountain towns. The Village is a car-free maze of world-class restaurants, shops, and lively outdoor patios. It serves as the base camp for both mountains, where wild mountain energy meets a stylish, modern atmosphere.

What makes the Village special is the "Village Stroll"—a walking path that lets you go from the Olympic Plaza to the gondolas in just a few minutes. Whether you are watching mountain bikers in the summer or walking through sparkling lights in the winter, the Village always feels exciting. It is the social center of the region where people gather to share their mountain stories over great food and local drinks.

Location & Access: The Village is located at the base of Whistler Mountain. It is divided into the Main Village, the Village North, and the Upper Village (at the base of Blackcomb). Everything is connected by the pedestrian Stroll and the Valley Trail, and a free shuttle bus (the Upper Village Loop) connects the two main base areas.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Whistler Olympic Plaza: This is the community's living room. In the winter, it features a massive outdoor skating rink and a Snow Zone for kids; in the summer, it hosts free outdoor concerts with the mountains as a backdrop. Don't forget to grab a photo with the iconic Olympic Rings.

Cultural Connector: Follow the yellow banners for a scenic walk that connects the Audain Art Museum and the Squamish Lil’wat Cultural Centre. It’s the perfect way to spend a morning soaking in the region’s deep Indigenous history and world-class fine art.

Après-Ski on a Patio: No trip to Whistler is complete without an après" session. Head to the Garibaldi Lift Co. (GLC) or Longhorn Saloon at the base of the mountains to watch skiers or bikers finish their day while you enjoy a drink in the sun.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Early Morning Serenity: The village is at its most magical at 7:00 AM. Before the shops open and the crowds arrive for the gondolas, you can enjoy a quiet coffee at Mount Currie Coffee Co. or Purebread and watch the alpenglow hit the peaks in total peace.

Hidden Short-Cuts: During peak season, the main Stroll can get very crowded. Use the back-way trails along the Fitzsimmons Creek or the forested paths behind the Audain Museum to move between the Village and Upper Village more quickly and quietly.

Dinner Reservations are Essential: Whistler’s dining scene is top-tier (think Bearfoot Bistro or Araxi), but tables disappear fast. In 2026, booking 2–4 weeks in advance for weekend dinners is a must if you want to snag a spot at the town's most popular tables.
Pedestrian Only: Once you enter the village, cars are non-existent. There are several large underground parking lots (Lots 1 through 5), but be prepared for daily parking fees.
Walking Distance: While the village is compact, you will do a lot of walking. Even if you aren't hiking the mountains, comfortable shoes are your best friend on the cobblestone streets.
Weather Prep: The village sits in a temperate rainforest. Even if the sun is shining, a Whistler mist can roll in at any time. Carry a light waterproof shell, especially in the autumn and spring.
Safe Drinking: Whistler has a strict no open alcohol policy in public spaces like the Stroll or Olympic Plaza. Keep the drinks to the licensed patios to avoid a fine from the local patrol.

places.name: 9. Crankworx Whistler
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/whistler-crankworx-joyride-mountain-bike-event-gm1146110235-308724466

Crankworx Whistler is the Super Bowl of mountain biking, a ten-day festival that makes Whistler the world capital of dirt and speed. Every summer, the world’s best riders come to the valley to compete in events featuring massive jumps, high speeds, and incredible tricks. The energy in the Village is electric, and the air is filled with the excitement of mountain bike culture.

Even if you don’t ride, the event is amazing to watch. The base of the mountain becomes a giant stadium where thousands of fans cheer as riders perform backflips off ramps as tall as a three-story building. It is a huge outdoor party and a celebration of the daring spirit that defines Whistler.

Location & Access: Most major events take place at the base of Whistler Mountain and within the Whistler Mountain Bike Park. The Village Stroll acts as the festival hub, with "Expo Way" stretching from the Olympic Plaza to the Skier’s Plaza. Access to the main spectator zones at the base is completely free.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Red Bull Joyride: If you only see one thing, make it this. It is the flagship event of the festival—a slopestyle showdown where riders are judged on style and technicality. The final drop into the finish corral is one of the most iconic sights in all of action sports.

The Expo Walk: Wander through the Village to see the massive vendor booths. You can demo the latest high-end mountain bikes for free, meet professional riders for autograph sessions, and grab limited-edition Crankworx "swag" from the world’s biggest bike brands.

Dirt Diaries: Head to the Olympic Plaza in the evening for this cinematic event. Local filmmakers and athletes team up to produce short mountain bike films that are premiered on massive outdoor screens under the stars.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Boneyard Hike: Don't just stay at the bottom fence. Hike up the side of the lower mountain trails (like the Joyride course) during practice sessions. Standing just feet away from a rider mid-air gives you a terrifyingly real perspective of how fast and high they are actually going.

Secure Your Patio Spot: During the big events like the Pump Track Challenge or Joyride, patios at the GLC or Longhorn Saloon are prime real estate. You’ll need to arrive hours early—or book a VIP table—to have a seated view of the action with a cold drink in hand.

Bring a Cowbell: It’s a mountain biking tradition. The louder the crowd, the faster the riders go. If you don't have a cowbell, an old bike rim and a wrench work just as well to join in the Whistler salute.

Crowds: This is the busiest ten days of the summer in Whistler. Accommodation is usually booked out months in advance, and the Village Stroll will be packed with people and bikes. Give yourself extra time for everything.

Bike Security: If you bring your own bike, be hyper-vigilant. Professional bike thieves unfortunately target the festival. Use the free Bike Valet services provided by the festival—never leave an expensive bike unattended on a rack, even with a lock.

Dust and Heat: Summer in the valley can be dusty and hot, with temperatures often hitting 30°C. Wear sunscreen and bring a bandana or buff to cover your face if you’re hanging out near the finish line where the dirt clouds are thick.
Tickets: While watching from the base is free, some premium events (like the Deep Summer Photo Challenge) or VIP viewing decks require paid tickets, which sell out rapidly online.

places.name: 10. Blackcomb Ascent Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/single-mother-hiking-with-daughters-in-moutnains-gm1314273191-402535802

The Blackcomb Ascent Trail is the ultimate vertical challenge for those who prefer to earn their mountain views one step at a time. Designed as an uphill only hiking route, this trail system masterfully weaves through the lush rainforest of Blackcomb Mountain, climbing from the valley floor all the way to the alpine. It is a grueling yet rewarding journey that gains a staggering 1,200 meters (3,937 feet) of elevation over a total distance of 6.2 kilometers (3.9 miles).

What makes the Ascent Trail so unique is its tiered structure, divided into three distinct sections: Little Burn, Big Burn, and Heart Burn. As the names suggest, the hike gets progressively more challenging, but the environment changes beautifully along the way—shifting from the massive Douglas firs of the lower mountain to the thinning sub-alpine meadows where the burn in your legs is matched by the jaw-dropping views of the Coast Range across the valley.
Location & Access: The trail begins in the Upper Village, right next to the base of the Blackcomb Gondola. You look for the trailhead signage near the bottom of the Wizard Express chairlift area.
Recommendations: What to Do & See

Full Vertical: For the ultimate bragging rights, hike all three sections in one go. It takes most fit hikers between 2 and 3 hours to reach the Rendezvous Lodge at the top. Once you arrive, you can treat yourself to a cold drink while watching the Peak 2 Peak Gondola glide overhead.

Lower Burn Loop: If you’re short on time or energy, just do the Little Burn. It’s a 0.8-km introductory loop that gives you a taste of the steep terrain and the beautiful forest floor without committing to the full-day climb.

Wildflower Sightings: In the final stretch of Heart Burn, the forest opens up into the sub-alpine. During August, these meadows are often filled with wildflowers and are a prime spot for seeing Blackcomb’s famous resident black bears from a safe distance.
Information & Tips for the Best Experience

Ride Down for Free: The best part of the Ascent Trail? You don't have to walk back down. Once you reach the top of the Blackcomb Gondola, you can download (ride the gondola down) for free. It’s the perfect knee-saver after a morning of heavy climbing.

Beat the Heat: Because the trail is mostly south-facing and heavily forested in the lower sections, it can get very humid and hot by midday. Start your hike before 9:00 AM to stay in the morning shade and reach the cooler alpine air before the sun hits its peak.

Pace Your Heart Burn: The final section, Heart Burn, is the steepest and most technical. Save at least half of your water for this stretch; the switchbacks are tight, and the elevation gain is relentless until you see the lodge peek over the horizon.

Uphill Only: For safety reasons and to protect the trail’s integrity, hiking down the Blackcomb Ascent Trail is strictly prohibited. You must be prepared to reach the gondola station at the top to return to the valley.

Gondola Hours: Always check the last download time for the Blackcomb Gondola before you start. If you reach the top after the cabins have stopped running, you’ll be looking at a very long, unauthorized walk down a service road.
Footwear: The terrain is often rooty, rocky, and steep. Sturdy hiking boots or high-traction trail runners are essential.
Wildlife: You are hiking through active bear habitat. Make noise, especially when moving through dense brush, and never leave food or trash behind.

places.name: 1. Ride the Peak 2 Peak Gondola
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/friends-ride-on-gondola-in-summertime-whistler-gm2260162845-673048308
The Peak 2 Peak Gondola is one of Whistler’s top summer experiences. It connects Whistler Mountain and Blackcomb Mountain and gives huge views of forests, valleys, peaks, and alpine terrain.

This is one of the best things to do if it is your first time in Whistler. You get the mountain experience without needing to hike from the village. Once you are up high, you can walk short trails, take photos, visit viewpoints, eat at mountain restaurants, or continue into longer alpine hikes if trails are open.
Best for: First-time visitors, families, views, photography, non-hikers, alpine sightseeing.
places.note: Mountain weather is often cooler than the village, so bring a jacket or warm layer even on sunny days.

places.name: 2. Go Mountain Biking
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/couple-on-a-mountain-bike-vacation-gm1355319390-429839006

Whistler is one of the best mountain biking destinations in the world, and summer is the main season for it. The Whistler Mountain Bike Park is known for lift-access downhill trails, flow trails, technical terrain, jump lines, lessons, rentals, and a strong bike culture.

If you are new to mountain biking, Whistler can still work well, but do not jump straight into advanced trails. Book a lesson, rent the right bike, and start on beginner-friendly routes. If you are experienced, this is one of the best places to spend several full days riding.
Best for: Mountain bikers, adventure travelers, teens, adults, bike park riders, summer sports trips.
places.note: The bike park is different from casual biking. Wear proper protective gear and choose trails that match your skill level.

places.name: 3. Hike in the Alpine
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/friends-hike-in-alpine-below-glaciated-mountain-peak-whistler-gm2260162872-673048324#
Summer is the best time for alpine hiking in Whistler. Gondola access makes it easier to reach high mountain trails without climbing all the way from the valley.
