If you visit at night, local astronomers suggest avoiding the use of bright white flashlights or car high-beams. Using a red-light filter on your phone or flashlight helps preserve your night vision and respects other stargazers.

Because the point juts out into the ocean, it is exceptionally exposed to the elements. Even on a warm summer evening, the wind coming off the water can be biting; always bring a windbreaker or a warm blanket if you plan to stay for the stars.

This is a premier location for long-exposure night photography. The lack of streetlights near the water's edge allows photographers to capture the stars reflecting in the tide pools or the lights of the San Juan Islands shimmering in the distance.
The park is home to several rare and endangered plant species, including the Garry Oak ecosystem. Stay on the designated rocky paths or the paved areas to avoid trampling the sensitive native flora.
Best Time to Visit
For Stargazing: New moon phases or during major astronomical events like the Perseid meteor shower in August. Check a clear sky forecast specifically for Oak Bay before heading out.
For the Blue Hour: The 30 minutes after sunset, when the sky turns a deep indigo and the lights of the Trial Islands Lighthouse begin to blink, creating a magical atmosphere for walkers.
For Storm Watching: During winter southeasterly gales, the waves at Cattle Point are some of the most dramatic in the city, frequently washing over the lower parking areas.

There are two distinct parking loops with ample space. Parking is free, but note that the park technically has a 10:00 PM closure time for vehicles, though stargazers are generally welcome if they remain quiet and respectful.
There are no public washrooms or water fountains directly at the point. The nearest facilities are located a short two-minute drive away at Willows Beach.

The upper parking loops provide excellent views for those who wish to stay in their vehicles. However, the paths down to the rocky shoreline are uneven and can be slippery, making them less suitable for those with mobility aids.

places.name: 6. Save-On-Foods Memorial Centre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/save-on-foods-memorial-center-gm458949839-19451899

Save-On-Foods Memorial Centre is a state-of-the-art 7,000-seat facility that serves as the heartbeat of the city’s major event scene. Built on the site of the historic Victoria Memorial Arena (the Barn on Blanshard), this modern venue is the home ice for the Victoria Royals of the Western Hockey League. It offers a high-energy, electric atmosphere where fans gather for everything from heavy-hitting hockey games and world-class concerts to figure skating championships and community trade shows.
What to See & Do

Victoria Royals Hockey: Experience the city's sporting passion firsthand. The arena provides superior sightlines, ensuring there isn't a bad seat in the house to watch the fast-paced action of WHL hockey.

Lion's Den Restaurant: For a more refined evening, visit this fine-dining establishment located within the arena. It offers a unique dinner and a show perspective, allowing you to enjoy a meal while overlooking the event floor.

World-Class Concerts: The venue has hosted legendary acts from Rod Stewart (who opened the arena in 2005) to Elton John and Aerosmith. Its acoustics are designed specifically to handle large-scale touring productions.
Public Skating: On select dates, the arena opens its doors to the public. You can lace up your skates and take to the same ice used by the pros, often accompanied by music and special lighting.
Tips & Key Info
As of early 2024, the venue has moved to a cashless system. Ensure you have a debit or credit card ready for all concession and merchandise purchases.

Like many major venues, the Memorial Centre has a strict no-entry policy. Once you scan your ticket and enter, you cannot leave and return, so make sure you have everything you need from your car before heading to the gates.
Avoid bringing large bags. To speed up security, only small purses are permitted; backpacks and oversized bags will be turned away at the door and must be returned to your vehicle.

Security requires all water bottles to be emptied before entry. While there are limited refill stations (primarily near Gate 3), you can often ask for a cup of water at quieter concession stands to stay hydrated during a long event.
Best Time to Visit
For Hockey Season: Between September and March, when the Victoria Royals play their home games. Friday and Saturday night games offer the most vibrant local atmosphere.
For Major Concerts: Check the seasonal schedule for big name tours. The venue often serves as the only Vancouver Island stop for major international artists.
For Victoria at Dusk: During the Family Day weekend in February, the area around the arena often becomes a hub for city-wide light festivals and illuminated art walks.

The on-site lot is managed by Robbins Parking and typically charges a flat rate of $15.00 during events. It fills up very quickly; many locals prefer to park in the nearby North Park residential area or use the parkades downtown and walk the 10 minutes to the arena.
All entrances and washrooms are fully wheelchair accessible. Elevators are located at Gates 1 and 3 to provide access to the club lounge and suite levels.
The venue offers upgraded, complimentary bike parking behind the arena near Gate 3, making cycling one of the most efficient ways to beat the post-game traffic.

places.name: 8. The Bay Centre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/bay-centre-shopping-mall-entrance-with-the-fountain-in-victoria-british-columbia-gm2163533079-583876514

The Bay Centre is Victoria’s premier urban shopping destination, an architecturally striking multi-level mall that occupies an entire city block in the heart of the central business district. This center is a sophisticated vertical experience, blending a modern retail environment with the historic charm of Government and Douglas Streets. It offers a climate-controlled sanctuary for over 7 million guests a year, providing a diverse atmosphere where international brands like Hudson’s Bay and Winners coexist with unique local boutiques and one of the city's most scenic food terraces.
What to See & Do

Urban Architecture: Take a moment to look up. The mall is famous for its soaring glass atriums and open-concept design that allows natural light to flood all four levels. The bridge-like walkways between stores offer great interior views of the bustling retail floors.

Victoria Market Collective: Located on the second level, this is the premier spot for those looking to shop local. It features a curated selection of handmade goods from over 100 Vancouver Island artisans, ranging from botanical skincare to West Coast art.

Food Terrace Patio: Head to the fourth floor for more than just a quick bite. The newly redesigned Food Terrace features an outdoor patio that offers rare, elevated skyline views of downtown Victoria—a perfect, affordable spot for an alfresco lunch.

Festival of Trees: If you visit during the holiday season, the hallways are transformed into a sparkling forest for the annual BC Children's Hospital Festival of Trees. It is a beloved local tradition where dozens of uniquely decorated trees are put on display for charity.
Tips & Key Info

Before you start shopping, stop by the Guest Services desk on the lower level. They offer a complimentary Visitor Savings pass that provides exclusive discounts and deals for out-of-town guests at dozens of participating retailers.

Because the mall spans a full block, there are entrances on Government, Douglas, View, and Fort Streets. The Government Street entrance is often the most festive, while the View Street entrance provides the most direct access to the parkade.

The Bay Centre Parkade offers the first hour of parking for free on Saturdays and is often free after 4:00 PM on weekdays. This is widely considered the best parking hack for anyone running quick errands in the downtown core.

For those driving electric, the parkade features several free charging stations. They are popular and operate on a first-come, first-served basis, so aim for an early morning arrival if you need a boost.
This is the city's go-to spot when the Victoria mist turns into a downpour.
Between 11:30 AM and 1:30 PM, the Food Terrace is the social hub for downtown office workers, providing a high-energy, authentic local atmosphere.

Visiting during holidays from late November through December is non-negotiable. Between the Festival of Trees and the elaborate window displays at the Hudson's Bay department store, it is arguably the most festive indoor space in the city.
The entrance to the underground parkade is located on View Street. Note that the parkade typically closes at 10:00 PM, so ensure you retrieve your vehicle before the gates lock for the night.

High-quality public washrooms, baby-changing stations, and nursing rooms are located on the fourth floor near the Food Terrace. There is also a Service Canada office located on the upper level for those needing federal services.

The mall is fully equipped with multiple elevators and escalators, making all four levels easily accessible for wheelchairs, walkers, and strollers. Designated accessible parking spots are located near the parkade elevators.

places.name: The Inner Harbour
places.section: Best places to kayak in Victoria
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/inner-harbor-activity-in-victoria-bc-gm586043782-100542005

This is the classic starting point and the easiest answer for travelers searching where to kayak in Victoria. Perfect for those who want to see the city from a different angle. Launching here gives you immediate views of the Legislature, the Empress, marinas, and floating homes, all from water level.

places.name: Gorge Waterway
places.section: Best places to kayak in Victoria
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/aerial-view-of-the-gorge-waterway-gm2175713470-595248429

Gorge Waterway, is a sheltered tidal inlet with calm, lake-like conditions. The Gorge is one of the best choices for beginners or anyone who wants calmer water and a more relaxed pace. Excellent for birdwatching, with frequent sightings of herons and other local waterfowl along the shorelines. You can paddle several kilometers inland toward Portage Inlet, passing under various historic bridges along the way.

places.name: Brentwood Bay & Tod Inlet
places.section: Best places to kayak in Victoria
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/tod-inlet-kayakers-gm1035886368-277298519

Located about 30 minutes north of downtown, this is a favorite for nature lovers. The waters are exceptionally calm, and a paddle into Tod Inlet offers a serene escape with lush forest shorelines and the chance to spot jellyfish, seals, and eagles.

places.name: Oak Bay & Cadboro Bay
places.section: Best places to kayak in Victoria
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/kayaking-in-haro-strait-oak-bay-gm2262158741-674957002

For a more coastal feel, these areas offer beautiful sandy beaches and views of the Trial Islands. It is a great spot to explore rocky islets and kelp beds, though it is more exposed to wind than the harbor.

places.name: Thetis Lake & Elk Lake
places.section: Best places to kayak in Victoria
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/thetis-lake-victoria-british-columbia-canada-gm1284143575-381370165

If you prefer freshwater, these local lakes are ideal for a relaxing afternoon. They are devoid of large boat traffic and ocean currents, making them the safest possible environment for your first time in a boat.

places.name: Fisherman’s Wharf and the Outer Harbour
places.section: Best places to kayak in Victoria
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/tourists-kayaking-at-fishermans-wharf-a-popular-marine-destination-in-victoria-canada-gm2223464669-639664812
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/water-sport-in-the-harbor-gm1092032676-292974868

This is a good option for travelers who want a little more character and wildlife without committing to a major open-water route. Serves as an iconic launching point right in the heart of the city, offering immediate access to the bustling Victoria Inner Harbour. Ideal for paddling past the historic houseboats and watching the seaplanes take off and land. It is important to note that this requires vigilance as you share the water with significant marine traffic and seaplane taxi lanes.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/people-kayaking-in-victoria-gm1194781791-340340574

Victoria’s climate is one of the big reasons kayaking is so popular here. Temperatures typically range from roughly 37°F to 66°F over the year, with the best warm-weather window for outdoor activities generally falling from mid-July to late August.

For most visitors, late spring through early fall is the best overall time to kayak. Summer brings the warmest, driest conditions and the longest daylight, while spring and early fall can be excellent if you prefer fewer crowds. Winter paddling is still possible with guided operators, but it is better suited to people comfortable with colder, wetter conditions.

Peak Season (May–September): This is the ideal window for most paddlers. The weather is warm, and the afternoon thermal winds are predictable. Most rental shops are in full operation during these months.

Shoulder Season (April & October): The water is quieter, and the wildlife—especially seals and migratory birds—is often more active. However, the water remains very cold, so dressing for immersion is crucial.

Year-Round Potential: Thanks to Victoria’s mild climate, you can technically paddle year-round. Winter days can be stunningly glassy, but you must be prepared for cold shock and wear a drysuit or heavy-duty wetsuit.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/people-kayaking-in-victoria-gm1194781698-340340474

Yes, in many cases it is. Victoria’s combination of sheltered water and guided options makes it one of the more beginner-friendly paddling cities on the BC coast. No experience is necessary and some operators offer everything from three-hour introductory tours to multi-day trips.

That said, not every launch point is equally easy. The Inner Harbour and Gorge are generally the better choices for beginners, while more exposed coastal areas can be more weather- and wind-dependent.
Guided tours vs rentals
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/kayakers-enjoy-cruising-on-the-water-gm585479996-100392073

If you are new to paddling, a guided tour is usually the best choice. It removes the stress of route planning and lets you focus on the experience. Ocean River, Victoria Kayak, and Kelp Reef Adventures all offer guided options in and around Victoria.

Rentals make more sense if you already have some paddling experience and want flexibility. Ocean River’s downtown location offers hourly rentals and harbour tours, and Victoria Kayak also offers rentals from the Inner Harbour.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sea-kayak-paddling-in-the-pacific-ocean-gm1340573051-420611247

Kayaking in Victoria is not only about paddling. Even short outings can include views of working harbours, marinas, seabirds, and marine life. You have the chance to see local marine wildlife from a unique vantage point, and sunrise or sunset tours can add another layer of atmosphere.
Here is what you are likely to encounter:
Marine Life
Harbour Seals: The most frequent companions; they often pop their heads up to watch paddlers or sunbathe on rocky outcrops.
River Otters: Common near the Gorge Waterway and houseboats, typically seen playing along the shoreline.
Harbour Porpoises: Small, fast-moving fins visible in more open waters like Oak Bay.
Jellyfish: Large clusters of translucent Moon Jellies often appear in Tod Inlet during late summer.
Coastal Birds
Bald Eagles & Ospreys: Often seen perching in tall Douglas firs or circling above the water.
Great Blue Herons: Patient hunters frequently spotted in the shallow mudflats and kelp beds.
Kingfishers & Cormorants: High-activity birds that dive for fish or dry their wings on nearby rocks.
Important Tips
Keep at least 100 meters from seals and sea lions to avoid disturbing them.
Drift quietly to see otters and herons; splashing often scares them away.
Feeding wildlife is strictly prohibited and disrupts their natural behavior.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/victoria-clipper-fast-ferry-in-victoria-canada-gm1091719142-292892007
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/float-plane-in-the-inner-harbor-gm1186917799-335065537
A little preparation can make your time on the water much more enjoyable, especially if you are new to kayaking in Victoria.

Dress for the water, not just the city. Even on a pleasant day downtown, it can feel much cooler once you are out on the water. Avoid cotton, which stays wet and cold, and choose quick-drying synthetic or wool layers instead.
Choose your route based on your confidence level. Beginners will usually have a better experience in the Inner Harbour or Gorge Waterway than in more exposed coastal areas.
Book ahead in summer. This is the busiest season for warm-weather activities in Victoria, so tours and rentals can fill up quickly.
Try to get on the water by 9:00 AM. Winds often pick up in the early afternoon, which can make paddling back more tiring for beginners.

Check the tides before you go. In places like the Gorge Waterway or the narrower channels around Oak Bay, tidal currents can be stronger than expected. It is always worth checking a local tide table or asking your rental shop about current conditions.

Carry the required safety gear. You should have a PFD (life jacket), a whistle, a buoyant heaving line, and a manual bailing device on board. Most rental shops include these as part of the rental fee.

Be extra careful in the Inner Harbour. This is an active waterway shared with other traffic, including floatplanes. Stay within designated paddling lanes near the shore and do not cross the middle of the harbour without checking carefully for incoming or departing aircraft.

Respect marine wildlife. Victoria’s waters are an important habitat for marine life, so it is best to observe animals from a respectful distance. Try to stay at least 100 metres away from seals and sea lions to avoid disturbing them.

Consider a guided tour if you are new to kayaking. A short guided trip with operators can be a worthwhile introduction, especially if you want help with basic paddling technique and safe entry and exit.

If you are wondering whether kayaking in Victoria is worth it, the answer is yes. It is one of the easiest and most scenic ways to experience the city from a different angle. With its mild climate, convenient launch points, and mix of harbour and coastal routes, Victoria is one of the best urban kayaking bases on Vancouver Island.

places.name: Top-Rated Tour Operators
places.section: Best whale watching tours in Victoria
body: Eagle Wing Tours is a carbon-neutral industry leader known for its high-performance catamarans and strong educational focus. Their tours typically last 3 to 3.5 hours, though they also offer extended Wildlife Safaris during peak season. Vessel options include open-air catamarans for a more immersive experience and semi-covered boats for added protection from the elements. Onboard naturalists provide detailed scientific insight into the local ecosystem and marine conservation, and guests are given access to high-end optics and binoculars.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/whale-watching-victoria-inner-harbor-gm1093062044-293329700

Prince of Whales is a long-established operator that received a Viator Experience Award in 2023. It features the Salish Sea Eclipse, a custom-built, environmentally friendly catamaran with three viewing levels. Tour options include the standard 3.5-hour whale-watching trip as well as full-day Ultimate Day Tours connecting Victoria and Vancouver. Guests can choose between high-speed Zodiacs for a more thrilling ride or large, stable catamarans with multiple viewing decks. A complimentary professional photo package is often included, featuring high-quality images from the specific trip. Their flagship vessel is designed for both environmental efficiency and passenger comfort across all age groups.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/whale-watching-tour-boat-gm1432420653-474673521

Orca Spirit Adventures is known for offering both high-speed Zodiac adventures and comfortable covered boat tours. The company is carbon-neutral and includes a hydrophone on its Zodiac tours, allowing passengers to listen to whale calls in real time. Tours usually last around 3 hours, with both morning and afternoon departures, as well as seasonal sunset tours during the summer. Their fleet includes open-air Zodiacs and large heated cruisers with indoor seating and washrooms. Covered boat options also make them a comfortable choice for winter excursions.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/transients-gm1023250912-274649066

SpringTide Whale Watching & Eco Tours offers a more boutique-style experience, with 3-hour tours focused on speed, comfort, and maximizing viewing time. The company specializes in high-speed cruisers that can reach sightings quickly while still providing a smooth ride. In addition to whale-watching trips, they also offer dedicated eco-tours that highlight seals, sea lions, and local birdlife. Their smaller-group approach allows for more personal interaction with the captain and onboard naturalists, giving the experience a more intimate and informative feel.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/whale-watching-victoria-inner-harbor-gm1093062060-293329702
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pleasure-boat-killer-whales-gm95795419-2234293

A typical whale-watching trip from Victoria is more than just looking for whales. The outing usually includes scenic cruising through the Salish Sea, views of islands and shoreline, and a chance to spot a range of marine life even before any whales appear. The overall experience is part wildlife tour and part coastal sightseeing trip.

Conditions on the water can change quickly, even in summer. It almost always feels cooler offshore than it does in the city, especially once the boat is moving. That is why dressing warmly is important and expect changing weather.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/southern-resident-killer-whale-k33-gm623523446-109394017
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/whale-watching-boat-tour-british-columbia-canada-gm171554693-2234248

Whale watching in Victoria comes with important wildlife-protection rules. Boats must keep minimum approach distances from marine mammals. Current federal guidance includes staying 100 m from most whales, dolphins, and porpoises, 200 m from killer whales in Pacific Canadian waters, and 200 m from whales, dolphins, and porpoises when they are resting or with a calf. There are also stronger protection measures in southern BC waters for Southern Resident killer whales.
That matters because the Salish Sea is not just a tourism zone. It is also important habitat, including for endangered populations such as the Southern Resident killer whales.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/humpback-whale-breaching-off-the-coast-of-victoria-british-columbia-gm1214792587-353590222

Book ahead if you are visiting in peak season, especially from late spring through summer. The most popular months can fill up quickly. Morning tours often experience calmer sea conditions, while sunset tours offer spectacular lighting for photography and a more serene atmosphere.
Dress in layers, even on sunny days. A light day in Victoria can still feel cold once you are out on the water.
Choose your boat style carefully. If you want comfort, go with a covered vessel. If you want a more thrilling ride, zodiac-style tours may be a better fit.

Bring binoculars if you have them, and do not rely only on your phone camera. Whale sightings can happen at varying distances, and sometimes the overall moment matters more than trying to capture the perfect photo. Several companies (like Prince of Whales and Eagle Wing) have professional photographers on board who share a high-quality photo gallery of your specific trip for free, allowing you to focus on the experience rather than your camera.
Final word

Whale watching in Victoria is popular for good reason. It combines wildlife, scenery, and a real sense of being on the west coast in a way that few other activities do. Whether you choose a covered cruiser or an open zodiac, go in summer or shoulder season, or see humpbacks, orcas, or simply a mix of marine life, it is the kind of experience that often becomes one of the highlights of a Vancouver Island trip.

places.name: 14. Cold Water Diving
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sea-anemone-gm1368270399-438299160

Known as one of the top cold-water diving destinations in the world, Campbell River sits on the edge of the Discovery Passage, where massive tidal currents act as a nutrient-rich conveyor belt for marine life. The result is a vibrant, emerald sea teeming with giants.
What to See and Do

Meet the Friendly Giants: This is one of the best places to encounter the Giant Pacific octopus and the prehistoric-looking Wolf eel. Despite their intimidating appearance, Wolf eels are often curious and will peek out from rocky dens to watch divers.

Explore the HMCS Columbia: Dive a 366-foot decommissioned destroyer escort sunk as an artificial reef. It sits in a protected bay, making it accessible even when the Discovery Passage currents are too strong.
Drift Diving at Steep Island: Experience the rush of a drift dive along sheer underwater walls covered in a carpet of strawberry anemones, yellow sponges, and purple Northern Feather Duster worms.

Snorkel with Salmon: From August to September, you can don a thick wetsuit and float down the Campbell River itself. You’ll be surrounded by thousands of Pink salmon, and you may also see Chinook salmon making their way upstream as well.
Sea Lion Encounters: In the winter and spring, Steller and California sea lions congregate here. They are famously playful (and mischievous), often darting around divers and nibbling on fins.
Tips & Key Information
Water temperature ranges from 7°C (45°F) in winter to 12°C (54°F) in late summer. Exposure protection (drysuit or very thick 7mm+ wetsuit) is mandatory.
Best in the winter months (up to 30m / 100ft) when the plankton blooms settle. Summer visibility is lower (approx. 10m) but the marine life is at its most active.

Most local sites can only be dived during slack tide—the brief window when the current stops moving. Attempting to dive mid-tide in the Discovery Passage is dangerous due to currents that can exceed 15 knots.
Shops like Abyssal Diving Charters and Oceanfix offer specialized boats equipped with elevators or sturdy ladders to help with heavy cold-water gear.
While you can dive in a thick wetsuit in summer, you will be much more comfortable (and able to do multiple dives) in a drysuit. Most local shops offer Cold Water Orientations.
Because you’ll be wearing more lead weight than you would in the tropics, mastering your buoyancy is critical—especially around the delicate, slow-growing sponges and corals on the reef walls.
Even in high visibility, the emerald water filters out light quickly. A good dive light is essential to reveal the neon pinks, oranges, and yellows of the anemones.

places.name: 13. Discovery Passage Aquarium
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/discovery-passage-aquarium-building-and-the-parking-lot-covered-in-snow-on-a-cold-gm1467920568-499588975

The Discovery Passage Aquarium is a very special catch-and-release aquarium located right on the Pier. Unlike most aquariums where the fish stay forever, the creatures here are collected from the local waters every spring and then safely returned to the exact same spot in the ocean every fall. This means the animals you see are the same ones swimming right under your feet.
What to See & Do

Touch Tanks: This is the best part for kids. You can gently touch colorful sea stars, prickly sea urchins, and squishy sea cucumbers. Knowledgeable staff are always there to explain how these creatures live.
Local Wonders: See amazing animals from the Discovery Passage, including camouflage-expert octopuses, tiny grunt sculpins, and bright stinging anemones.

The Big Release: If you visit in late September, you might get to help with the big release. This is a community event where everyone helps carry the buckets of fish and crabs back to the ocean to say goodbye.
Learn About the Ocean: The aquarium has great displays about how to protect our oceans and keep the water clean for the salmon and whales.
Tips & Key Information
Since the aquarium is right at the entrance to the Discovery Fishing Pier, it is easy to visit both on the same afternoon.
The staff are usually young students who are experts on marine biology. They love to tell you cool facts about the animals in the tanks.
If you plan on using the touch tanks, wear a shirt with sleeves you can easily roll up.
Sometimes they have feeding times or guest speakers who talk about sharks or shipwrecks.
There is a small entry fee (about $8–$12 for adults, with discounts for children and families).
The aquarium is seasonal. It is usually open from May to September. It is closed during the winter months while the fish are back in the wild.
Look for the colorful building right next to the Discovery Fishing Pier parking lot.
It is a small, cozy aquarium. You can usually see everything in 45 to 60 minutes.
The building is on one level and is wheelchair and stroller-friendly.

places.name: 12. Maritime Heritage Centre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/maritime-heritage-centre-gm1318722210-405774120

Just a short drive from the Tyee Spit, the Maritime Heritage Centre (MHC) serves as the cultural anchor of Campbell River’s waterfront. Housed in a former fish processing plant, it preserves the gritty, salty history of the "Salmon Capital of the World."
What to See and Do

The BCP 45: This is the crown jewel of the centre. It is a beautifully restored 1927 wooden seine fishing boat that was famously featured on the Canadian five-dollar bill from 1972 to 1986. You can actually walk onto the deck and explore the cabin.
The Rotary Sea Walk: Use the centre as your starting point for this 6 km paved scenic walk along the shoreline.
Hand-On Exhibits: Explore displays on local shipwrecks, the history of commercial fishing, and the evolution of diving gear used in the treacherous Discovery Passage.
Model Ships: View intricate, large-scale models of historic vessels that once patrolled these coastal waters.
The Gift Shop: Browse local Indigenous art, maritime-themed books, and unique coastal souvenirs.
Tips & Key Information
Located at 621 Island Highway, Campbell River, BC (right next to the government wharf).
Typically open Monday to Friday, 10:00 AM – 4:00 PM (Summer hours often extend to weekends).
Modest entry fee (usually around $5–$10), which goes directly toward vessel restoration and community programs.
The main floor and the BCP 45 viewing area are fully wheelchair accessible.
On-site washrooms, meeting rooms for rent, and a large parking lot that accommodates RVs.
Many of the staff are retired fishers or shipwrights. They have incredible firsthand stories about life on the BC coast that aren't on the placards.
The centre is right next to the Discovery Pier. Grab an ice cream at the pier and then walk over to the Maritime Heritage Centre for a perfect afternoon.
The centre often hosts "Wednesday Night Speaker Series" or local craft fairs during the shoulder season.
If you're a mechanical geek, the restored heavy-duty marine engines are a must-see—they are massive, polished, and historically significant.

places.name: 11. Tyee Spit (Dick Murphy Park)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/campbell-river-waterfront-gm1495963277-518791827

Located at the mouth of the Campbell River on Vancouver Island, Tyee Spit (and the adjacent Dick Murphy Park) is a unique geographical finger of land that offers a front-row seat to the region's maritime culture and natural beauty.
What to See and Do
Watch the Tyee Club Tradition: From July 15 to September 15, see anglers in classic wooden rowboats attempting to catch a 30+ lb Chinook salmon using only traditional, non-motorized methods.
Spot Marine Wildlife: Keep an eye on the Discovery Passage for humpback whales, orcas, and harbor seals. The currents here often bring marine life very close to the shore.
Go Birdwatching: The estuary is a haven for bald eagles, great blue herons, and trumpeter swans. Bring binoculars for the best views.
View Driftwood Art: Walk the shoreline to discover temporary sculptures and driftwood huts built by locals and visiting artists.
Watch Floatplanes: The Spit is a secondary runway for seaplanes; you can watch de Havilland Beavers and Otters take off and land just meters away.
Catch the Sunset: Visit the viewing platform on the estuary side for some of the best golden hour views of Quadra Island and the Coastal Mountains.
Tips & Key Information
Located at 3200 Spit Road, Campbell River, BC.
Open daily from 6:00 AM to 10:00 PM.
Paved, flat loop trails in Dick Murphy Park are wheelchair and stroller-friendly; the far end of the Spit is gravel/sand.
Ample free parking is available at the Dick Murphy Park lot and along Spit Road.
Seasonal public washrooms, picnic shelters, benches, and a small playground.
The area was originally known as ʔuxstalis (pronounced Oox-sta-lease) by the Liǧʷiłdax̌ʷ people.
Massive Alaska-bound cruise ships pass through the Discovery Passage frequently in the late afternoon/evening.
Even in mid-summer, the wind coming off the water can be significantly colder than it is in town. Bring a windbreaker.
Pets are welcome but must be on a leash to protect the sensitive nesting grounds in the estuary.
At high tide, the beach area disappears. If you plan to walk to the very tip of the Spit, check the tide charts to avoid getting a soaker on the way back.
If you are kayaking or boating during Tyee season, stay clear of the Tyee Pool to maintain the silence required for the traditional rowers.

places.name: 10. Quadra Island
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/quadra-island-old-historical-lighthouse-at-cape-mudge-vancouver-island-canada-gm2083049139-565365295

Just a 10-minute ferry ride from downtown Campbell River lies Quadra Island. It is the largest and most populated of the Discovery Islands, but it still feels like a quiet, magical world. Known for its vibrant artist community, hidden beaches, and deep Indigenous history, it is the perfect place to spend a full day exploring.
What to See & Do

Rebecca Spit Marine Provincial Park: This is the most famous spot on the island. It is a long, thin strip of land with sandy beaches on both sides. It’s perfect for a walk, a picnic, or looking for colorful sea glass and unique driftwood.

Cape Mudge Lighthouse: Built in 1898, this beautiful white and red lighthouse still helps guide ships through the dangerous waters. It is a great place to take photos and watch the massive cruise ships pass by.

Nuyumbalees Cultural Centre: Located in the village of Cape Mudge (Yaculta), this center holds a world-class collection of "Potlatch" regalia. You can see ancient masks, robes, and carvings that were returned to the Kwakwaka’wakw people.

Hiking to Chinese Mountains: If you want a bit of a challenge, this hike offers the best views on the island. From the top, you can see all the way across the ocean to the mountains of mainland British Columbia.
Kayaking and Paddleboarding: The water around Quadra is crystal clear. Many people rent kayaks at Heriot Bay to explore the tiny islands and look for sea stars and seals.
Tips & Key Information

You can take your car on the ferry, but if you only want to see the shops and the harbor near the ferry dock (Quathiaski Cove), you can walk on for a much cheaper price. However, to get to Rebecca Spit, you will need a car or a bike.
The ferry runs roughly every hour, but it can get very busy in the summer. Arrive at the terminal at least 30 minutes early to make sure you get a spot.
The Heriot Bay Inn is a historic hotel with a great restaurant overlooking the water. It’s a very "island-style" place to have lunch.
Many painters, potters, and carvers live on Quadra. Look for the yellow "Studio" signs along the road—many artists welcome visitors to come in and see their work.
You catch the ferry at the terminal in downtown Campbell River (near the Coast Discovery Inn).
You pay for a round-trip ticket. It is about $10–$15 per person and more if you bring a vehicle (around $30–$40).
The crossing is very short—only 10 minutes.
Quathiaski Cove (where the ferry lands) has a grocery store, a gas station, and a few cute cafes, so you can stock up on snacks when you arrive.
Dogs are welcome on the ferry and at all the provincial parks on the island.

places.name: 9. Quinsam River Salmon Hatchery
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/salmon-swimming-upstream-gm2178150539-597506752

To truly understand why Campbell River is the Salmon Capital of the World, you have to visit the Quinsam River Salmon Hatchery. Located just 5 kilometers west of downtown, this large facility helps millions of salmon start their lives before they head out to the Pacific Ocean. It is one of the best places on Vancouver Island to see the incredible life cycle of fish up close.
What to See & Do

The Interpretive Centre: Start your visit at the visitor center. It has cool 3D models you can touch, underwater photos, and even a microscope where you can look at the tiny bugs that baby salmon eat.

Fish Eye View: Walk through the facility to see the indoor and outdoor tanks. Depending on the time of year, you can see tiny "fry" (baby fish) swimming around or massive adult salmon waiting to spawn.
Salmon Spawning: In the fall, the river next to the hatchery turns silver and pink as thousands of salmon swim back home. You can watch them jump and splash as they move upstream.
Nature Trails: Follow the beautiful Canyon View Trail or the river walk. These paths wind through the forest and have great spots for photos and birdwatching.
Bear Watching: Because there are so many fish, black bears are very common here in the fall. It’s not unusual to see a bear sitting by the river having a salmon lunch.
Tips & Key Information
The hatchery gates open at 8:00 AM and lock promptly at 3:30 PM. Don't get your car locked inside—set a phone alarm for 3:15 PM just in case.
Wear polarized glasses. They help you see through the glare on the water so you can spot the fish moving below the surface.
Since bears live here, always make noise while walking the trails so you don't surprise them. Never approach a bear or try to feed it.
While the hatchery is interesting all year, September and October are the most exciting months because that is when the most fish and bears are active.
Visiting the hatchery and the trails is completely free.
Best Times for Salmon:
September: Pink Salmon (the most fish).
October & November: Chinook and Coho Salmon.
Year-round: Tiny baby salmon in the tanks.
Most of the hatchery area is flat and easy to walk on, making it great for strollers.
There is a large free parking lot right at the entrance (4217 Argonaut Road).

places.name: 8. Strathcona Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/cream-lake-alpine-lake-vancouver-island-gm1388800224-446322146

Established in 1911, Strathcona Provincial Park is the oldest provincial park in British Columbia. This massive 250,000-hectare wilderness is the backyard of Vancouver Island, featuring rugged, snow-capped peaks, alpine meadows, and crystal-clear lakes. It is a true haven for hikers, photographers, and anyone looking to escape into the wild.

While Strathcona is the backyard of Campbell River, it is actually located outside the city limits. To reach the main park entrance, you will drive west on Highway 28. It is roughly a 45 to 60-minute drive (about 48 km) to the Buttle Lake area.

Even though it requires a bit of travel, it is considered a must-do for anyone staying in Campbell River for more than a couple of days. Most visitors use the city as their base camp, heading into the park for the day to see its world-famous waterfalls and alpine scenery before returning to town for dinner.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/buttle-lake-at-strathcona-provincial-park-near-campbell-river-bc-canada-gm2191511364-609829781
What to See & Do

Waterfall Hopping: The park is famous for its accessible waterfalls along Highway 28. Don't miss Lady Falls (a 20-minute walk through old-growth forest) and Lower Myra Falls, which features stunning multi-tiered cascades flowing into a turquoise pool.

Buttle Lake: This 23-km long lake is the heart of the park. It’s perfect for swimming, kayaking, and fishing for Cutthroat and Rainbow trout. There are numerous pebbly beaches along the shore for a scenic picnic.

Paradise Meadows: Located at the Forbidden Plateau entrance, these sub-alpine meadows feature easy-to-walk boardwalks that are famous for vibrant summer wildflowers and birdwatching (keep an eye out for the Vancouver Island Marmot).
Alpine Hiking: For those seeking a challenge, trails like Crest Mountain or Flower Ridge offer staggering views of the Golden Hinde, the highest peak on Vancouver Island.
Winter Sports: In the colder months, the Paradise Meadows area becomes a hub for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, often with some of the deepest snowpacks in North America.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/young-woman-exploring-strathcona-provincial-park-gm913554228-251470733
Tips & Key Information
There are no gas stations or services once you leave Campbell River until you reach Gold River. Make sure your tank is full before you head into the park.
You will lose cell signal shortly after leaving Campbell River. Download your maps for offline use and let someone know your expected return time.
The weather in the mountains changes rapidly. Even if it’s hot at the beach in Campbell River, it can be chilly and rainy at Buttle Lake or Forbidden Plateau. Always bring a rain shell.
This is active Black Bear and Cougar country. Carry bear spray, travel in groups, and make plenty of noise on the trails.
Entry to the park is free. There are fees only if you are staying overnight at a designated campground (like Buttle Lake or Ralph River).
There are two main entrances from Campbell River:
Buttle Lake Area: Drive 45 minutes west on Highway 28.
Forbidden Plateau (Paradise Meadows): Drive 40 minutes south/west via Mount Washington.
Best Season: July through September for snow-free hiking; December through March for winter sports.
The Centennial Loop at Paradise Meadows is a barrier-free boardwalk, making it accessible for wheelchairs and strollers.
Dogs are allowed but must be on a leash to protect the sensitive alpine environment and local wildlife.

places.name: 7. Ripple Rock Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/ripple-rock-trail-on-vancouver-island-gm902740632-248998663

The Ripple Rock Trail is the most famous hike in Campbell River. It is an 8-kilometer round-trip trail that leads you through a beautiful forest to a high cliff. From the top, you can look down at the Seymour Narrows, a skinny piece of ocean where the water moves as fast as a river.
What to See & Do
The Big View: The best part of this hike is the lookout at the end. You can see for miles over the ocean and the mountains of Vancouver Island and the mainland.
Whirlpools and Rapids: Look down at the water below. Because the ocean is squeezed between the land, you can see massive whirlpools and white water, especially when the tide is changing.

History Under Your Feet: This trail overlooks the spot where the world’s largest non-nuclear explosion happened in 1958. Scientists used 1,200 tons of explosives to blow up an underwater mountain called Ripple Rock that was sinking too many ships.
Forest Magic: The trail takes you through mossy trees, over small bridges, and past big ferns. It feels like a scene from a movie.
A Great Workout: The trail goes up and down, so it’s a fun way to get some exercise while enjoying the fresh air.
Tips & Key Information
Pack water and snacks. The hike takes about 2.5 to 3 hours to finish. You will definitely want a drink and a granola bar when you reach the top.

Check the tide table. If you want to see the biggest whirlpools and fastest water, try to reach the lookout when the tide is running (moving in or out) rather than at high or low tide when the water is still.
Parts of the trail can be muddy or have loose rocks. Running shoes are okay, but hiking boots are much better for your ankles.
The cliffs at the top are very high and do not have fences. Stay back from the edge and keep a close eye on children and pets.
It is free to hike and free to park at the trailhead.
The trail’s length is About 8 kilometers (5 miles) total, going there and back.
Difficulty level is moderate. It has some steep hills, but most people who walk regularly can do it.
The parking lot is about 15 minutes north of Campbell River on Highway 19. Look for the large "Ripple Rock Trail" sign.
Dogs are allowed but should be kept on a leash, especially near the steep cliffs at the lookout.

places.name: 6. Museum at Campbell River
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/campbell-river-museum-gm458986081-19998519

The Museum at Campbell River is widely considered one of the best local museums in Canada. It isn't just a building full of old things; it is a storytelling center that brings the wild history of the coast to life. From the spiritual traditions of the First Nations to the dangerous days of early logging and fishing, this museum is a must-see to truly understand the spirit of the town.
What to See & Do

The Mask Gallery: Enter a stunning, darkened room filled with ceremonial masks carved by the Kwakwaka’wakw people. The masks are beautiful and sometimes a little spooky, representing spirits from the sea and sky.
The Ripple Rock Explosion: Watch a short, exciting film about the 1958 blast that blew up an underwater mountain. It was so big it was broadcast live on TV across the country.

Step Back in Time: Walk through a real 1920s float house (a house built on logs that floats on the water) and a vintage steam donkey used for logging. You can see exactly how people lived and worked 100 years ago.
The Gift Shop: This is one of the best places in town to find authentic Indigenous art, jewelry, and books about local legends and wildlife.
The View: The museum sits on a hill overlooking the ocean. After your tour, walk out to the gardens to see the totem poles and look for whales in the passage below.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/first-nations-totem-pole-gm2217346230-633939451
Tips & Key Information
Most people think they can finish in 30 minutes, but there is so much to see. Plan for at least 1.5 to 2 hours.
Ask the front desk when the Ripple Rock movie starts so you don't miss the beginning of the big bang.
If the weather turns sour and you can't go hiking, the museum is the perfect cozy place to spend an afternoon.
During the summer, the museum often hosts "Puppet Theatre" for kids and historic boat tours for adults. Check their website to see if anything special is happening during your trip.
There is a small admission fee (usually around $10–$12 for adults, with lower prices for kids and seniors).
Opening Hours:
Summer: Open daily from 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM.
Winter: Hours are shorter (usually Tuesday to Sunday), so check before you go.
Located at 470 Island Highway—it’s the big, beautiful building on the hill just south of downtown.
The museum is fully accessible for wheelchairs and has elevators to help you get between floors.
There is a large free parking lot right in front of the building.

places.name: 5. Rotary Seawalk
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/man-walking-his-dog-in-a-park-during-summer-gm1188043394-335847564

The Rotary Seawalk is a beautiful, paved pathway that stretches for 13 kilometers along the edge of the ocean. It is the favorite place for locals to walk their dogs, go for a run, or simply sit on a bench and watch the waves. It connects the southern part of the city all the way to the downtown area.
What to See & Do
Walk, Bike, or Blade: The path is wide and flat, making it perfect for a long bike ride or a slow stroll with a stroller.

The Big Rock: Along the way, you will see a massive boulder sitting on the beach. Local legend says it was once a giant grizzly bear that was turned to stone by the Great Spirit. It is a famous spot for a photo.
Whale Watching from Shore: Keep your eyes on the water. Because the ocean passage is narrow here, it is very common to see Humpback whales or Orcas swimming just a few meters away from the shore.
Art and Totems: Look for beautiful First Nations carvings and modern art statues placed at different points along the walk.
Beachcombing: When the tide goes out, you can hop off the paved path and onto the pebbly beaches to look for colorful sea glass, shells, and interesting pieces of driftwood.
Tips & Key Information
You don't have to walk all 13 kilometers. The section near Willow Point is great for cafes, while the section near the Fishing Pier is best for seeing big ships.
There are many picnic tables and benches along the route. Grab a sandwich in town and enjoy a lunch with a million-dollar view of the mountains.
The Seawalk faces east, so it is the best place in town to watch the sunrise. If you aren't an early bird, the blue hour just after sunset is also very peaceful.
Since people use the path for biking and walking, remember to stay on the right side so others can pass you safely.
It is completely free to use.
The Seawalk is open 24 hours a day and is well-lit in many areas.
The entire path is paved and flat, making it 100% accessible for wheelchairs and strollers.
There are several free parking lots located along the highway (Highway 19A) that give you direct access to the path.
You can find clean public bathrooms at Willow Point Park and near the Discovery Pier.

places.name: 4. Fishing Charters
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/trolling-for-salmon-gm1011971660-272641381

Dubbed the "Salmon Capital of the World," Campbell Riveroriginally became famous for its Tyee salmon derby in rowboats . It is not the place it was 50 years ago but there are certain times in the summer when you can catch salmon.
What to See & Do

Target the Big Five: Depending on the season, you can fish for all five species of Pacific Salmon: Chinook (King), Coho (Silver), Pink, Sockeye, and Chum. The Chinook is the ultimate prize, often reaching weights of over 30 lbs. The numbers of fish here are not what they once were but you can still have a shot at a Chinook salmon or every second year Pinks (smallest of the Pacific salmon) can be caught. In October its possible to catch Chum salmon.
Expert Guiding: Your charter includes a professional local guide who knows the secret spots, the best lures to use, and how to read the complex tides of the Passage.
Wildlife Sightings: While you wait for a bite, it is very common to see Humpback whales, Orcas, porpoises, and bald eagles. It’s essentially a fishing trip and a wildlife tour rolled into one.
The Tyee Experience: Some charters specialize in the traditional Tyee Club style—fishing from a classic wooden rowboat to catch a Chinook salmon over 30 lbs using strict, eco-friendly rules.
Catch Processing: Most charters will help you clean and bag your fish. Many local businesses can even flash-freeze, smoke, or ship your catch home for you.
Tips and Key Information
Even if it’s a sunny day in town, the temperature on the open water is significantly colder. Wear a windbreaker, a warm base layer, and waterproof shoes.
Book in advance. The best guides often book up months in advance, especially for the peak summer run (July and August).
The waters in the Discovery Passage are generally sheltered and calmer than the open ocean, but if you are prone to motion sickness, take a preventative an hour before boarding.
Bring a camera as you’ll want proof of your big catch. The views of the Coast Mountains from the water are also equally worth capturing.
Prices vary by boat size and duration.
You must have a valid British Columbia Tidal Waters Sport Fishing License with a Salmon Conservation Stamp. You can buy these online before your trip.
Most charters provide the boat, fuel, high-end fishing gear (rods, reels, bait), and safety equipment (life jackets).
Best Season:
May – June: Great for early Chinook
July – September: Peak season for all salmon species.
Winter: Quiet but excellent for feeder Chinook.
Most boats depart from Discovery Harbour Marina, Fisherman’s Wharf, or private docks at resorts like Painter’s Lodge.

places.name: 3. Discovery Fishing Pier
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/fishing-pier-in-campbell-river-vancouver-island-british-columbia-canada-gm114423325-10035023

Canada’s first saltwater fishing pier is a favorite spot for both locals and visitors. Stretching 180 meters out into the deep waters of Discovery Passage, it feels like you are walking right into the middle of the ocean without ever leaving the land.
What to See & Do

Catch a Big One: You don't need a boat to go fishing here. People catch huge Chinook and Coho salmon right from the pier. If you didn't bring gear, you can rent a rod and buy tackle at the pier office.
The Famous Ice Cream: Almost everyone who visits the pier stops at the concession stand. They are famous for serving massive soft-serve ice cream cones that are sometimes bigger than your head.

Marine Life Watching: Look straight down into the clear water to see bright orange starfish, sea anemones, and schools of tiny fish. Sometimes, curious seals or sea lions swim right past the pier looking for a snack.

Enjoy the View: On a clear day, you can look across the water to Quadra Island and the snowy peaks of the Coast Mountains. It is the best place in the city to watch cruise ships sail by during the summer.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/locals-and-tourists-enjoying-the-magnificent-view-form-the-fishing-pier-at-sunset-gm830504168-135499999
Tips for Your Visit
Bring a jacket. Even if it is a warm day, the wind blowing over the cold ocean water can be quite chilly on the pier.
If you plan to fish, remember that you still need a tidal water fishing license. You can usually buy a one-day license online or at local shops.
The pier is open 24 hours a day. It is a magical place to visit at sunset when the sky turns pink and orange over the water.
Even if you don't fish, it is fun to hang out and watch the local experts.
Key Information
It is free to walk on the pier. There is a small fee if you want to fish (usually around $2–$3 for the day).
The pier is open 24 hours a day, but the rod rentals and ice cream shop are usually open from May to September.
The pier is completely flat and wheelchair accessible, making it easy for everyone to enjoy.
There is plenty of free parking right at the entrance to the pier and along the street.
No bikes or skateboards are allowed on the pier to keep it safe for walkers and fishers.

places.name: 2. Whale & Wildlife Discovery Tours
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/whale-watching-vancouver-gm2157693186-578368672

Campbell River is one of the best places in the world to see marine giants. Because the city sits right next to narrow ocean passages filled with fish, it acts like a highway for hungry whales and other amazing animals.
What to See & Do
Whale Watching: Look for massive Humpback whales splashing and Orcas (Killer Whales) hunting in pods. You might even hear them sing if your boat has an underwater microphone called a hydrophone.
Dolphin Encounters: Pacific White-Sided Dolphins often travel in huge groups. They love to jump and play in the wake behind the tour boats.
Grizzly Bear Expeditions: In late summer and fall, you can take a boat deep into the inlets to see grizzly bears catching salmon right out of the river.
Island Exploring: These tours take you through the beautiful Discovery Islands, where you can see sea lions sunbathing on rocks and bald eagles watching from the treetops.
Choose Your Ride: You can pick a Zodiac (a fast, open-air rubber boat) for an exciting, bumpy ride, or a covered vessel with a heater and a bathroom for a more relaxing trip.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/humpback-whale-breach-strait-of-georgia-campbell-river-british-columbia-canada-gm2242677604-656976873
Tips for Your Visit
Even if it is a hot summer day on land, the wind on the ocean is very cold. Bring a warm jacket, a hat, and gloves.
Book for the morning trip. The ocean is usually calmer in the morning, which makes it easier to spot fins and blowholes in the distance.
Don't forget sunscreen. The sun reflects off the water and can give you a sunburn even on a cloudy day.
Bring binoculars. While the boats get as close as they safely can, binoculars will help you see the tiny details of a bear’s fur or an eagle’s nest.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/black-bear-on-the-rivers-edge-fishing-for-salmon-during-spawning-season-campbell-gm1176155862-327800944
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/humpback-whale-tail-fluke-sutil-channel-campbell-river-british-columbia-canada-gm2242677468-656976727
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sea-lions-of-campbell-river-gm2161364329-581816169
Key Information
The best time to see whales is from May to October. Grizzly bear tours usually run from late August to October.
Most tours last between 4 and 7 hours, so plan for a half-day or full-day adventure.
Most boats allow children ages 2 or 3 and up, but always check with the tour company before booking a Zodiac ride.
Many companies offer a "Whale Guarantee." If you don't see a whale, they might give you a free ticket to come back another time.
Most tours depart from the marinas in downtown Campbell River or near the famous Painter’s Lodge.

places.name: 1. Elk Falls Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/waterfall-in-elk-falls-provincial-park-near-campbell-river-vancouver-island-bc-gm1160475437-317660863

Just a ten-minute drive from downtown, Elk Falls Provincial Park is the most popular nature spot in Campbell River. It is famous for its massive trees, a rushing river, and a world-class suspension bridge that gives you a bird's-eye view of a thundering waterfall.
What to See & Do
The Suspension Bridge: Walk 60 meters across a deep canyon. It hangs high above the Campbell River and offers a thrilling view of the falls.
The Waterfall: Watch the water drop 25 meters down into a rocky gorge. It is loudest and most powerful in the spring when the snow melts.
Old-Growth Forest: Hike through giant Douglas fir trees. Some of these trees are hundreds of years old and are incredibly tall.
Wildlife Spotting: Keep your eyes peeled for bald eagles and deer. In the fall, you might even see black bears near the river looking for salmon.
Hidden Falls: If you have extra time, follow the forest trails to find Moose Falls and Deer Falls nearby.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/elk-falls-provincial-park-gm1319890580-406620049
Tips for Your Visit
This park is very popular. Visit in the early morning or late afternoon to have the bridge all to yourself.
The trail is mostly flat and easy, but the metal stairs leading to the bridge can be slippery when it rains.
Look for the cantilevered viewing platform. This is a deck that sticks out over the canyon for the perfect picture of the falls.
Near the parking lot, there is a free Discovery Centre where you can learn how the river creates electricity for the city.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/elk-falls-waterfall-vancouver-island-bc-canada-gm973540042-264905207
Key Information
It is free to enter the park and use the parking lot.
The park is open year-round during daylight hours.
It is an easy walk. It takes about 15–20 minutes to reach the bridge from the car.
The main trail to the first viewpoint is flat and gravel, but there are stairs to reach the actual suspension bridge.
Dogs are allowed but must be on a leash at all times to protect the wildlife.

places.name: 1. Province House National Historic Site
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/charlottetown-prince-edward-island-canada-gm172463993-23637220

Province House National Historic Site is the centerpiece of Charlottetown’s historic district and the Birthplace of Confederation. This grand neoclassical building is where the 1864 Charlottetown Conference took place, setting the stage for the creation of Canada. As of 2026, the site is entering the final phases of a massive, multi-year conservation project to preserve its 180-year-old sandstone walls and heritage interior.
What to See and Do

The Neoclassical Exterior: Even while the interior is being finalized, you can admire the stunning architecture from Queen Square. The building features a majestic symmetrical design, Greek and Roman influences, and massive sandstone blocks that have been meticulously restored stone-by-stone.

The Story of Confederation Exhibit: Since the main building is currently closed, head next door to the Confederation Centre of the Arts. This immersive exhibit features a replica of the Confederation Chamber, where you can sit at the same table as the Fathers of Confederation and watch the film A Building of Destiny.

Province House Virtual Reality: Experience the building's interior through a cutting-edge VR tour available at the Confederation Centre. It allows you to walk through the Legislative Assembly and the historic library as they will look once fully reopened.

Memorials and Statues: Wander the grounds of Queen Square to see the Charlottetown Veterans Memorial (honoring those lost in the World Wars) and the Boer War Memorial. Don't miss the tiny statue of Eckhart the Mouse, a favorite for children based on the beloved local books.

Imagine a Country Activity: If visiting in July or August, participate in this interactive experience on the upper plaza. It encourages visitors to share their own visions for Canada’s future, echoing the debates that happened inside Province House in 1864.
Tips and Key Information

Province House is currently closed to the public for the final stage of an extensive conservation project. It is scheduled to officially reopen later in 2026 with brand-new interpretive exhibits and modernized accessibility features.
When it reopens, the building will be fully accessible for the first time in its history, featuring a new elevator, universally accessible washrooms, and braille signage.

While the Halifax City Hall clock marks the 1917 explosion, Province House is the oldest building in Canada still used for a provincial legislature, having housed the PEI Legislative Assembly since 1847.

The best angle for a photo is from the bottom of Great George Street. Standing there allows you to capture the building’s portico framed perfectly by the historic rows of Victorian buildings leading up from the waterfront.
Situated at 165 Richmond Street, in the heart of downtown Charlottetown. It is the natural starting point for any walking tour of the city.
Once reopened, Province House typically requires a small admission fee, though it is often included for those holding a Parks Canada Discovery Pass.

places.name: 2. St. Dunstan's Basilica
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-facade-of-st-dunstans-basilica-in-the-downtown-of-the-city-of-charlottetown-in-gm2157671170-578347664

St. Dunstan’s Basilica is a stunning masterpiece of French Gothic architecture and a defining silhouette of the Charlottetown skyline. As the only Roman Catholic basilica in Prince Edward Island and a National Historic Site of Canada, this Stone Cathedral is a place of profound beauty, resilience, and quiet reflection. Rebuilt in 1919 after a devastating fire, its soaring twin spires and 200-foot peaks serve as a beacon for visitors entering the city.
What to See and Do

Admire the Twin Spires: Before entering, look up at the two massive spires, each topped with a 10-foot-high cross. They are among the highest points in the city and are beautifully illuminated at night, casting a serene glow over Great George Street.

The High Altar: Step inside to see the centerpiece of the basilica—a stunning 37-foot-high altar adorned with 23 statues of saints and angels. It is framed by a magnificent 14-foot-wide rose window that bathes the sanctuary in colorful, ethereal light.

Spot the 300 Angels: Throughout the interior, look for representations of angels tucked into the stained glass, carved into the pillars, and featured on the light fixtures. There are roughly 300 in total watching over the congregation.

The Relics of Bishop MacEachern: Visit the dedicated shrine to see the original mass kit, snowshoes, and a restored horse-drawn vessel used by Bishop Angus Bernard MacEachern, the Apostle of PEI, to travel across the rugged island in the late 1700s.

The Casavant Pipe Organ: Located in the loft, this historic organ features over 4,600 pipes. If you time your visit during a service or a free chamber music recital, the acoustics of the vaulted ceiling make for an unforgettable auditory experience.
The Holy Trinity Doors: Notice the intricate carvings on the main entrance doors, which feature depictions of the four Gospel writers: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.
Tips and Key Information
The Basilica is generally open to the public daily from 8:00 AM – 5:00 PM. Admission is free, though donations are welcomed to help maintain the historic structure.
As this is an active place of worship, please maintain a quiet demeanor. Photography is permitted, but visitors are asked to refrain from taking photos during active Mass services.
For a deeper dive into the history and symbolism, look for the QR codes at the entrance to access a self-guided audio tour on your smartphone. Using headphones is highly recommended.

Regular weekday Mass is typically held at 12:05 PM in Glastonbury Hall (the basement) during colder months to conserve energy, while weekend services are held in the main cathedral at 4:00 PM (Saturday) and 10:30 AM (Sunday).
Situated at 65 Great George Street, it is perfectly positioned between the Charlottetown Waterfront and the Confederation Centre of the Arts.
The basilica is wheelchair accessible through the side entrance on Dorchester Street, which leads to both the main sanctuary and the lower Glastonbury Hall via elevator.
Metered street parking is available on Great George and Dorchester Streets, though it can be busy during the summer. Many visitors find it easier to walk from the nearby waterfront parking lots.

places.name: 3. Government Househttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/government-house-in-charlottetown-prince-edward-island-canada-gm642058040-116356541
body: Government House, often called Fanningbank, is a stunning National Historic Site that serves as the official residence of the Lieutenant Governor of Prince Edward Island. Built in 1834, this white-shingled Georgian mansion overlooks the entrance to Charlottetown Harbour. It is more than just a home for the King's representative; it is a living piece of history that has hosted royalty, delegates of the 1864 Charlottetown Conference, and generations of Islanders.
What to See and Do

Guided Summer Tours: During July and August, the doors of Fanningbank swing open for free guided tours. You can explore the grand Main Hall with its impressive 15-foot Doric columns and the State Dining Room, home to an original 1834 mahogany table that still seats 24 guests for official functions.

The Royal Suite: Visit the second-floor apartments where Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip stayed during their 1959 visit. The rooms are preserved with period elegance, offering a rare glimpse into the vice-regal lifestyle.

Fanningbank Grounds: While the house is a private residence, the 10-acre estate's grounds are often open to pedestrians from 8:00 AM to 8:00 PM. Walk the tree-lined paths and formal gardens that offer a commanding view of the harbor and the passing cruise ships.

The New Year’s Levee: If you are visiting on January 1st, join the long-standing tradition of the New Year’s Levee. The Lieutenant Governor opens the house to all citizens to mark the start of the year with light refreshments and community spirit.

Architecture Appreciation: From the outside, admire the Greek-Revival and Palladian influences, including the massive gabled portico. The building was designed by Isaac Smith, the same architect responsible for the nearby Province House.
Tips and Key Information

Free guided tours are available Monday to Friday (10:00 AM – 3:00 PM) from early July through late August. No booking is required for small groups, but be aware that tours may be canceled on short notice for private functions or official ceremonies.

While walking the grounds, you might hear locals mention the Halifax Explosion connection. While this house is in PEI, it shares a heritage sibling bond with the Government House in Halifax; both are among the oldest vice-regal residences in North America.

As this is a private residence and working government office, a smart casual dress code is recommended for interior tours. Photography is generally allowed in public areas, but always check with your guide first.
The house is located at 1 Terry Fox Drive, directly adjacent to Victoria Park. The best way to reach it is via a 15-minute scenic stroll along the waterfront boardwalk from downtown.
There is no public parking on the Fanningbank estate. Use the metered parking on Kent Street or the large, free public parking lots at the entrance of Victoria Park.
The main floor of the residence is wheelchair accessible via a ramp. If you have specific mobility needs, staff at the front gate are available to assist with entry to the tour route.

places.name: 4. Charlottetown City Hall
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/view-of-the-charlottetown-city-hall-in-the-city-of-charlottetown-prince-edward-island-gm2157490244-578171195

Charlottetown City Hall is a grand Victorian landmark that has stood at the corner of Queen and Kent Streets since 1888. A striking example of Romanesque Revival architecture, it is the oldest municipal hall in Prince Edward Island and was designated a National Historic Site in 1984. With its red brick facade, heavy stone arches, and soaring corner tower, it remains the active seat of local government and a proud symbol of the city's late-19th-century prosperity.
What to See and Do

The Romanesque Architecture: Admire the building’s exterior character-defining elements, including the massive rounded arches over the windows and doors, the high square corner tower with its pyramidal roof, and the decorative Nova Scotia freestone bands that contrast with the red brick.

The Historic Bell: Look for the large, historic bell located on the Kent Street side of the building. It serves as a reminder of the era when the ground floor housed the city's fire hall and horse stables.

Council Chambers: On the upper floors, the Council Chambers continue to be the site where pivotal municipal decisions are made. While primarily a working space, the interior reflects the pride and confidence of the Victorian era.

Public Meetings: For those interested in local politics, the City Council and various committees hold regular public meetings. In March 2026, meetings are often live-streamed, but the public gallery provides a front-row seat to civic engagement in a historic setting.

Memorial Photos: The building serves as an incredible backdrop for photography, especially in the late afternoon when the sun highlights the texture of the brickwork and the intricate carvings around the main entrance.
Tips and Key Information
The administrative offices are open Monday to Friday.
Winter Hours (October – May): 8:00 AM – 4:30 PM.
Summer Hours (June – September): 8:00 AM – 4:00 PM.
Situated at 199 Queen Street, right in the heart of the historic downtown. It is the only 19th-century building left on its specific block, making it an easy landmark to find.

The first floor houses the Parks and Recreation administrative office, making it a great stop if you need information about local community programs, trail maps, or public skating schedules for the 2026 season.
City Hall is fully wheelchair accessible, with the main administrative entrance designed to accommodate all visitors.
Metered street parking is available on both Queen and Kent Streets. If you're attending a longer meeting, the Pownal Parkade is just a few blocks away and offers more reliable long-term parking.
The building is a major stop for T3 Transit, making it easily reachable from the University of Prince Edward Island (UPEI) or the outlying areas of Charlottetown.

places.name: 5. Victoria Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/people-in-victoria-park-gm697426834-129322037

Victoria Park is Charlottetown’s crown jewel—a sprawling 40-acre waterfront oasis that serves as the city's primary playground and scenic escape. Established in 1873 on former government farmland, the park gracefully balances its role as a historic military site with its status as a vibrant hub for families, athletes, and anyone seeking a breathtaking sunset over the harbor.
What to See and Do

The Waterfront Boardwalk: Stretching for 1.2 km along the harbor’s edge, this wide wooden promenade is the heart of the park. It’s the city’s favorite spot for a sunset stroll, offering unobstructed views of the water, the Brighton Beach Range Light, and the harbor entrance.

Prince Edward Battery: Located on the park’s southern bank, this historic fortification features a row of massive 19th-century cannons and a restored stone magazine. It’s a tangible link to the Napoleonic Wars and the War of 1812, providing an open-air museum feel with spectacular vantage points for watching cruise ships.

The Splash Pad & Pool: A summer must-visit for families. The park features a large, supervised outdoor swimming pool and a modern splash pad with interactive water sprayers. Best of all, admission to both is completely free for the public.

The Kiwanis Dairy Bar: No trip to Victoria Park is complete without a stop at this iconic seasonal hut. Grab a classic soft-serve cone or a deep-fried hot dog and enjoy it on one of the many benches overlooking the Narrows.

Dead Man’s Pond: Tucked away in the forested interior of the park, this tranquil (despite its name!) pond is surrounded by wooded walking trails. It’s a favorite spot for birdwatching and finding a quiet moment away from the breezy waterfront.
Tips and Key Information

Following the completion of the major Shoreline Protection Project, the park's sea wall is more resilient than ever. Look for the newly reinforced sandstone sections that protect the boardwalk from high-tide surges.
The outdoor pool and splash pad typically operate from late June through late August.
Hours: Sunday–Thursday (11:00 AM – 6:00 PM), Friday–Saturday (11:00 AM – 8:00 PM).
The park is located at the southern tip of the city, with the main entrance at 100 Victoria Park Roadway. It is a 15–20 minute walk from the Confederation Centre of the Arts.
The park is a primary hub for the city’s Bike Bus pilot program and features expansive bike racks and repair stations near the tennis courts.

While there is a large free parking lot near the ball diamonds, it fills up fast on sunny weekends. Many locals prefer to park on Brighton Road or near Beaconsfield Historic House and walk onto the boardwalk from the eastern end.

The boardwalk is entirely flat and wide, making it perfect for wheelchairs and strollers. The newer playground structures are also designed with inclusive play in mind, featuring rubberized surfacing and accessible ramps.
Keep an eye out for the PEI Marathon in October, which uses the park's scenic loop as a highlight of the race route.

places.name: 6. Victoria Row
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/downtown-victoria-row-charlottetown-pei-canada-gm854143298-140427521

Victoria Row is the vibrant, beating heart of downtown Charlottetown’s social scene. Located on Richmond Street between Queen and Great George Streets, this historic block features a stunning row of Victorian-era red brick buildings. During the warmer months, the street is closed to vehicles, transforming into a bustling pedestrian-only thoroughfare where live music, artisan shopping, and alfresco dining create a festive European-style atmosphere.
What to See and Do

Alfresco Dining: The Row is famous for its expansive outdoor patios. Grab a seat under a signature blue umbrella at The Cork & Cast or John Brown Richmond Street Grille to enjoy fresh PEI mussels and local craft beer while soaking in the street's energy.

The Victoria Row Stage: During the summer, a public stage hosts local musicians and performers daily. From jazz and folk to traditional fiddle music, the soundtrack of the city is best enjoyed from a nearby bench or cafe window.

Artisan Shopping: Browse unique Island-made goods at boutiques like Northern Watters Knitwear (famous for 100% British wool sweaters) or Kuriosities, an open jewelry studio where you can watch pieces being handcrafted.

Receiver Coffee Co. (The Brass Shop): Visit this local institution for a pour-over coffee and house-made pastries. The interior features high ceilings and industrial-chic decor, making it a favorite office away from home for locals.

Architectural Photography: Capture the intricate Italianate and Romanesque details of the Cameron Building (built in 1888). The contrast of the red brick against the leafy green trees and colorful umbrellas makes it one of the most photographed spots in PEI.
Tips and Key Information

Victoria Row is scheduled to be fully pedestrian-only starting Monday, June 22, 2026, through the end of September. Outside of these dates, cars are allowed, but the sidewalks remain wide and welcoming.

The street is at its most magical at night when the string lights are glowing and the patios are packed. If you want a prime dinner spot on a Friday or Saturday night, reservations are highly recommended.

The Row is located directly across from the Confederation Centre of the Arts. It's the perfect place for a pre-theatre drink or a late-night dessert after a performance of Anne of Green Gables – The Musical.
Located at 146 Richmond Street. It is a central hub that links the legislative district (Province House) to the shopping core of Queen Street.
Most of the Row is covered by the city’s free public WiFi, allowing you to stay connected while you lounge.

The street is paved with flat, even cobblestones and brick, making it highly accessible for wheelchairs and strollers. Most patios have ramp access, though some of the historic shop interiors have small steps at the entrance.
While you can’t park on Victoria Row in the summer, the Pownal Parkade and Queen Street Parkade are both less than a 3-minute walk away.

places.name: 7. Peake's Wharf
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/peakes-quay-charlottetown-gm697413688-129321975

Peake’s Wharf is the bustling heart of Charlottetown’s historic waterfront. Once a center for the city’s industrial shipping, it has been transformed into a picturesque pedestrian village where colorful boutiques, floating marinas, and salty sea air create the ultimate Island summer vibe. It is the go-to spot for those looking to experience the maritime pulse of the city, complete with live music and world-famous treats.
What to See and Do
