Peake’s Wharf Boat Tours: Hop on a Transport Canada-approved vessel for a harbor cruise. These tours are famous for their Lobster Trap Hauls, where you can see a live trap pulled from the water and even hold a lobster. Sunset and seal-watching cruises are also top-rated for 2026.

Live Music at the Quay: Every afternoon and evening during the summer, the Peake’s Quay outdoor stage features local musicians. From traditional East Coast fiddling to acoustic indie sets, it’s the perfect place to sit back and enjoy the atmosphere.

Canada's #1 Ice Cream: A visit isn't complete without a stop at COWS Ice Cream. While there are several locations, the Peake's Wharf shop is iconic. Grab a cone of Wowie Cowie or Gooey Mooey and walk the docks to see the luxury yachts.

Shopping at the Merchants: Browse over 20 unique shops in the historic warehouses. Must-visits include Amos Pewter (where you can watch artisans at work), PEI Dirt Shirt (clothing dyed with the island’s famous red soil), and MaiYa Pearls for unique maritime jewelry.

Floating Dining: Enjoy a meal at Peake’s Quay Restaurant & Bar, which boasts the largest patio in Charlottetown. For something unique, look for the Sol Paddle Tavern, a solar-powered cycle-boat where you can pedal through the harbor while enjoying a drink with friends.
Tips and Key Information

Peake’s Wharf is a seasonal destination. While the boardwalk is open year-round, most shops and boat tours operate from early May through late October, with the highest energy occurring during the peak summer months (July–August).

If you're visiting in late summer, mark your calendar for August 29, 2026, for the Charlottetown Dragon Boat Festival. The wharf area becomes a hub for spectators as teams race across the harbor to support the Make-A-Wish Foundation.
As the sun goes down, Peake’s Quay transforms into one of the city’s most popular nightclubs, featuring DJs and dancing. If you're looking for a quieter evening, stick to the earlier patio sets.
Located at the bottom of Great George Street (1 Great George St). It is just a short 5-minute walk from Province House and the Confederation Centre.
he Peake’s Wharf Parking Lot at 3 Prince Street is the most convenient spot. In 2026, rates are approximately $2 per hour (max $14/day) from June to September.

The entire wharf and boardwalk area are flat and made of wood or pavement, making it very accessible for strollers and wheelchairs. Most boat tours have accessible boarding options—just call ahead to confirm for specific tides.
Walk to the very end of the floating docks for a perfect skyline"shot of Charlottetown, featuring the spires of St. Dunstan’s Basilica and the colorful buildings of the wharf framed by the harbor.

places.name: 1. Confederation Centre of the Arts
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/performance-in-front-of-confederation-centre-of-the-arts-in-canada-gm513293337-47819210

The Confederation Centre of the Arts is Canada’s National Memorial to the Fathers of Confederation and the premier cultural hub of Prince Edward Island. Occupying an entire city block in the heart of Charlottetown, this brutalist-inspired landmark is a massive complex that brings together musical theatre, visual arts, and heritage learning.
As of March 2026, the Centre is in the midst of a historic $65 million renovation project, but it remains a buzzing hive of activity with its art gallery and theaters fully operational.
What to See and Do
The Charlottetown Festival: This is the jewel in the Centre's crown. In Summer 2026, the festival features a historic double-header of Canada's most successful musicals:
Anne of Green Gables – The Musical™: The world's longest-running annual musical returns to the Sobey Family Theatre from June 25 – September 5, 2026.
Come From Away: The global sensation about Gander, Newfoundland, makes its long-awaited Island debut, running from July 2 – September 26, 2026.

Confederation Centre Art Gallery: Spanning several floors, the gallery houses over 17,000 works of Canadian art. Current 2026 exhibitions include Sarah Maloney’s Pleasure Ground (a feminist take on the natural world) and the sweeping historical collection Together With Time.

The Story of Confederation: While Province House next door is being restored, the Centre hosts an immersive exhibit featuring a stunning replica of the Confederation Chamber, where you can learn about the 1864 meetings that built the nation.

Live @ The Centre: Throughout the spring of 2026, the Sobey Family Theatre hosts national touring acts. Highlights for this month include The Rock Orchestra by Candlelight (March 5), the PEI Symphony Orchestra (March 15), and Canada's premier party band, Dwayne Gretzky (March 28).
Mavor’s Lounge: A perfect spot for a pre-theatre drink or a casual lunch. It often hosts Arts Mixers where you can rub shoulders with local artists and performers.
Tips and Key Information

Construction is ongoing through Fall 2026. A safety partition is currently in place on the Victoria Row side (expected to remain until May), but all theater entrances, the gallery, and the box office remain open and accessible.
From now until June 2026, the Art Gallery operates on an Admission by Donation basis, making it one of the best budget-friendly cultural stops in the city.

Tickets for Come From Away are the most requested in the Festival's history. If you are visiting this summer, it is highly recommended to book your seats as soon as they go on sale to the general public.

Despite the construction, the Centre remains fully accessible. In 2026, new street-level entrances on Victoria Row are being finalized to make the transition from the pedestrian street to the art gallery even smoother.
Located at 145 Richmond Street. The building is connected to the pedway system, allowing you to walk indoors to the Confederation Court Mall and the Holman Grand Hotel.

places.name: 2. Beaconsfield Historic Househttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/historic-beaconsfield-house-in-charlottetown-prince-edward-island-canada-gm642055728-116356529
body: Beaconsfield Historic House is a stunning yellow-and-white masterpiece of Victorian architecture that serves as a testament to the Golden Age of Charlottetown. Built in 1877 for wealthy shipbuilder James Peake Jr., it was once the most modern home on the Island, featuring cutting-edge luxuries like running water, central heating, and gas lighting. Today, it is a National Historic Site and the headquarters of the PEI Museum and Heritage Foundation.
What to See and Do

The Grand Tour: Walk through 25 meticulously restored rooms filled with original period furniture. Don't miss the Double Drawing Room, featuring ornate plasterwork, porcelain chandeliers, and eight unique marble fireplaces that showcase the opulence of the merchant class.

The Peake Window: Look for the stunning stained-glass window above the grand staircase. It features the initials of James Peake Jr., designed to be perfectly illuminated as you ascend the stairs—though locals joke the banisters were built low more for style than for safety.
The Belvedere: Look up at the very top of the house to see the small rooftop observatory. From this vantage point, Peake could watch his fleet of ships entering and leaving the Charlottetown Harbour.

The Carriage House: Located just behind the main mansion, this space once housed horses and carriages. Today, it’s a cultural hub hosting intimate concerts, heritage lectures, and seasonal events like the popular Victorian-era Séance reenactments.

Victorian Gardens: Stroll through the heritage gardens that offer some of the best unobstructed views of the harbor and the entrance to Victoria Park. It is a favorite spot for wedding photography and quiet afternoon picnics.
Tips and Key Information
The house is open year-round, but operates on reduced winter hours.
Admission is $10.00 + HST for adults, $8.00 + HST for seniors and students, and free for children aged 4 and under. National Trust for Canada members also receive free admission.
Situated at 2 Kent Street, on the corner of West and Kent. It sits right at the transition point between the historic West End residential district and the start of Victoria Park.
This is one of the best spots in the city for high-quality, locally made gifts, including traditional pottery, Island-authored books, and unique heritage-inspired jewelry.

While the grounds and the Carriage House are accessible, the historic house itself features several flights of stairs and narrow hallways. Those with mobility concerns can view a digital tour of the upper floors in the main hall.

Learn the moving story of the home’s second owner, Henry Cundall, a philanthropist who willed the house to become a residence for young women coming to the city to study—a role it served for decades as a nurses' residence.

places.name: 3. Great George Street Historic District
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/colorful-buildings-on-great-george-st-charlottetown-canada-gm636812676-113209689

The Great George Street Historic District is one of the most significant and visually stunning streetscapes in Canada. Spanning six blocks from the waterfront at Peake’s Quay up to the front steps of Province House, this National Historic District is a living museum of architectural history. It is the very path the Fathers of Confederation walked in 1864 when they arrived to debate the birth of a nation.
What to See and Do

The Great George Heritage Walk: Follow the bronze footsteps embedded in the sidewalk that mark the historic route of the 1864 delegates. Along the way, you'll find four interpretive panels that use archival photos to tell the story of the street’s evolution.

Architectural Time Travel: The street is a masterclass in 19th-century styles. On one side, you’ll see perfectly preserved Georgian wooden row houses (1820s–1860s), while across the street, the massive stone towers of St. Dunstan’s Basilica represent the peak of High Victorian Gothic design.

The Row Houses (58–70 Great George): These are the most photographed buildings in PEI. Look for the Scottish dormers (five-sided windows) on the roofs, a unique maritime architectural feature. The Wellington Hotel (1811), built from logs, was the social hub of the city for politicians in the 1800s.

The Two Fathers Statue: At the corner of Great George and Richmond Streets, look for the life-sized bronze sculpture of two delegates engaged in a heated debate. It’s a favorite spot for travelers to join the conversation for a photo.

The Customs House (40 Great George): Admire this imposing brick Italianate building, originally built in 1867 as the Bank of Prince Edward Island. Its rounded arch windows and freestone casings are classic examples of the era’s pride and prosperity architecture.
Tips and Key Information
Stand on the top steps of St. Dunstan's Basilica and look down toward the water. You’ll get a perfect perspective of the symmetrical row houses framed by the harbor in the distance.

If you want the full experience, The Great George Hotel isn't just one building—it’s a compound of 17 meticulously restored heritage buildings along this street. Even if you aren't staying there, you can walk through the lobby to see the historical photos.

The street features a gentle, steady incline from the water up to Province House. The sidewalks are wide and made of modern pavers or cobblestones, making it highly accessible for strollers and wheelchairs, though some historic shop entrances have single steps.
Avoid trying to park on Great George Street itself, as spots are limited and metered. Instead, park at the Peake's Wharf lot or the Pownal Parkade and walk the historic ascent.

places.name: 4. All Souls’ Chapel
body: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Interior_of_All_Souls_Chapel.jpg

All Souls’ Chapel is a small but beautifully detailed stone chapel located beside St. Peter’s Cathedral in Charlottetown. Designated a National Historic Site in 1990, it is widely considered one of the finest examples of High Victorian Gothic Revival architecture in Canada. It was built in 1888 as a labor of love by two of the Island's most famous brothers: architect William Critchlow Harris and artist Robert Harris.
What to See and Do

The Harris Collaboration: Experience the unique harmony between the chapel’s structure and its art. While William designed the rust-red PEI sandstone exterior and the intricate wood-and-stone interior, his brother Robert—famed for painting the official portrait of the Fathers of Confederation—created the eighteen mural paintings that adorn the walls.

The Murals of the Faith: Look closely at the eighteen canvases that depict scenes from the life of Christ and the early Church Fathers. A local secret: Robert Harris used his friends, family members, and parishioners of St. Peter's as models for the biblical figures, making the art a literal snapshot of 19th-century Charlottetown.

The Ascending Christ: Above the altar, you’ll find the chapel’s most famous icon, a circular painting of Christ ascending into Heaven. It is framed by a stunning sandstone arch and a carved reredos featuring statues of the apostles.

Intricate Carvings: Admire the detailed woodwork in oak and walnut, carved by local artisans like Caleb Whitlock. The craftsmanship is so precise that the flowers, leaves, and fruits depicted in the panels appear almost lifelike.

Encaustic Tiles & Stained Glass: Look down at the floor to see the beautifully patterned encaustic tiles, then look up at the three recessed, hooded stained-glass windows imported from England, which cast a soft, reverent light over the sanctuary.
Tips and Key Information
The chapel is an active place of prayer and is generally open to the public for quiet reflection and self-guided tours daily from 9:00 AM – 5:00 PM (unless a service is in progress).
Look for the QR codes at the entrance to access a high-quality audio tour on your phone. It provides a station-by-station guide to the history of the paintings and the architecture.
Entry is free, though donations are gratefully accepted to help with the ongoing preservation of the murals and the historic sandstone exterior.
Tucked away at 7 All Souls Lane, overlooking the beautiful Rochford Square. It is a 5-minute walk from the Confederation Centre of the Arts.

Because of its small size and heavy stone walls, the chapel is incredibly quiet. It is widely regarded by locals as the best place in the city to escape the noise of the downtown core for a few minutes of peace.

While the exterior can be admired by all, the interior of the chapel is accessed via a few steps. If you have mobility concerns, the main St. Peter's Cathedral (next door) is fully accessible and offers a different, but equally impressive, perspective on the community’s heritage.

places.name: 5. The Mack (Theater)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/downtown-charlottetown-gm930692662-255140246

The Mack (officially the MacKenzie Theatre) is the Confederation Centre’s intimate, cabaret-style venue. Located just across the street from the main complex at 128 Great George Street, it offers a completely different vibe from the grand Sobey Family Theatre. With its small tables, licensed bar service, and 200-seat capacity, it’s the place to go for high-energy kitchen parties, stand-up comedy, and experimental new Canadian works.

places.name: What to See and Do
body: C'Mon In! An Island Kitchen Party: This is the flagship summer show for The Mack in 2026. Running from June 6 – August 29, it’s an immersive, foot-stomping tribute to East Coast music. Expect fiddles, storytelling, and a lot of audience interaction that makes you feel like you’ve been invited into a local’s living room.
The Studio Experience: Keep an eye out for workshops and community series.

Cabaret Atmosphere: Unlike traditional theaters, The Mack often features table seating. You can enjoy a local craft beer or a glass of wine during the performance, making it a popular choice for a more relaxed date night out.

Comedy and Culture: The venue continues its tradition of hosting Have Jokes, Will Travel, a showcase of Atlantic Canadian comedians that highlights the dry, self-deprecating humor the region is known for.
Tips and Key Information

Because there are only about 200 seats, there isn't a bad view in the house. However, the front-row tables for the Kitchen Party shows tend to sell out months in advance because performers often step off the stage to interact with those guests.

The building was originally the Capitol Theatre, a cinema built in the early 20th century. You can still see hints of its old-school movie palace proportions in the high ceilings, even though it has been modernized into a flexible performance space.
Directly at the corner of Great George and University Avenue. It is technically separate from the main Confederation Centre building, so make sure you head to the right entrance.
The Mack is fully accessible, with street-level entry and dedicated spaces for wheelchairs near the stage.

While the Sobey Family Theatre handles the big musicals (Anne and Come From Away), The Mack’s tickets are often more affordable (usually ranging from $30–$55), making it a great way to see world-class talent on a budget.

places.name: 6. St. Peter's Cathedral
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/round-flower-bed-at-rochford-square-in-charlottetown-prince-edward-island-canada-gm1619593243-531588475

St. Peter’s Cathedral is a grand Victorian-era church that serves as the second cathedral of the Anglican Diocese of Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. While many visitors are drawn specifically to the attached All Souls’ Chapel, the main cathedral is a magnificent destination in its own right, known for its rich Anglo-Catholic high church traditions, superb choral music, and historic role in the West Bog neighborhood.
What to See and Do

The Gothic Revival Nave: Explore the spacious interior of the main cathedral, built between 1867 and 1869. Unlike the sandstone chapel, the cathedral is constructed of red brick and features dark walnut-colored Douglas fir pews that were added in 1928.

Masterful Stained Glass: Admire the high-quality memorial windows, many of which were crafted in London, England, by Kemp & Son. The intricate designs fill the nave with a spectrum of colors, especially during the morning light.

The Rood Screen & Hanging Lamps: Look for the ornate Rood Screen (erected in 1872) and the seven hanging lamps in the sanctuary. These are hallmarks of the Oxford Movement, a 19th-century revival of Catholic traditions within the Anglican Church that defined the cathedral's identity.
Stations of the Cross: Follow the memorial Stations of the Cross along the walls, which further emphasize the parish’s high church heritage.
The Pulpit: Examine the beautifully carved pulpit, which was designed by William Critchlow Harris—the same architect who designed All Souls’ Chapel and the brother of painter Robert Harris.
Tips and Key Information

While the Cathedral and All Souls' Chapel are physically connected and share a history, the Cathedral is larger and more stately, whereas the Chapel is smaller and more artistic. Most visitors walk through both in a single visit.
The cathedral is located at 11 All Souls Lane, overlooking the quiet Rochford Square. It offers a peaceful retreat just blocks away from the busier government buildings and tourist docks.
You can enter through the main cathedral doors on All Souls Lane or via the chapel entrance. Both lead to the same shared complex.
Generally open daily from 9:00 AM – 5:00 PM for visitors, though access to certain areas may be limited during scheduled services or choir rehearsals.

Ask a guide about the cathedral's origins in the West Bog. In the 1860s, this area was considered disreputable, and the church was founded as a mission to serve the local community, eventually growing into the grand landmark it is today.

places.name: 7. Ardgowan National Historic Site of Canada
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/historic-home-ardgowan-in-charlottetown-pei-gm1329215016-413027839

Ardgowan National Historic Site is a quiet, picturesque retreat located just a few minutes from downtown Charlottetown. While many of the city’s historic sites focus on the formal debates of 1864, Ardgowan tells the story of the social side of Confederation. This cottage ornée was the home of William Henry Pope, a Father of Confederation who famously wooed reluctant delegates with Island hospitality, oysters, and champagne on these very grounds.
What to See and Do

Victorian Picturesque Grounds: The 5-acre estate is a beautifully restored example of 19th-century landscape design. You can stroll through the orchard, wander the perennial gardens, and enjoy the tranquil rural atmosphere that made this a favorite getaway for the Victorian elite.

The Cottage Ornée Architecture: Admire the exterior of the house, which was built in the early 1850s. Its Gothic Revival details—like the ornate fretwork on the veranda, the symmetrical H-shaped layout, and the pointed gables—make it one of the most charming buildings in the province.

Informative Heritage Plaques: Scattered across the grounds, these plaques tell the story of the Grand Luncheon of 1864. While the formal meetings happened at Province House, it was here at Ardgowan that the delegates truly bonded over seafood and local luxuries.

A Peaceful Picnic Spot: Unlike the busier waterfront parks, Ardgowan is a hidden gem for those seeking quiet. There are picnic tables and plenty of shade under the mature trees, making it a perfect spot to read a book or enjoy a quiet lunch.

Parks Canada Connection: The building now serves as the administrative headquarters for Parks Canada on Prince Edward Island. If you are visiting in March 2026, this is one of the few places in the city where you can purchase your Parks Canada Discovery Pass in person during the off-season.
Tips and Key Information

It is important to note that the interior of the house is not open to the public for tours, as it consists of modern office spaces for Parks Canada staff. The museum experience here is entirely focused on the architecture and the historic grounds.
The grounds are free to enter and are open year-round.
Administrative Office Hours: Monday to Friday (8:30 AM – 4:30 PM).
Grounds: Open daily until dusk.
Located at 2 Palmers Lane, Charlottetown. It is located in the Parkdale neighborhood, about a 5-minute drive or a 25-minute walk from the downtown core.
This is a popular spot for local photographers due to its secret garden vibe. The yellow board-and-batten siding of the house provides a stunning backdrop, especially in the late afternoon sun.
The grounds feature relatively flat, gravel and grass paths. While the terrain is mostly level, some areas may be soft or uneven depending on recent weather.
In early March, the gardens will still be in their winter slumber, but the site remains a peaceful spot for a walk. The snow-covered "cottage" looks like something off a Victorian Christmas card.

places.name: 1. Charlottetown Marina
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/marina-and-steeples-in-charlottetown-gm1223786288-359599054

Charlottetown Marina is a popular waterfront destination offering visitors the chance to enjoy the scenic beauty of Charlottetown Harbour. Located in the heart of the city, this marina is a hub for both boating enthusiasts and tourists who want to relax by the water. This place is a collection of three distinct locations—the Peake’s Quay Marina, SeaPort Marina, and the Charlottetown Yacht Club.
What to See and Do

The Floating Docks: Wander the boardwalks that connect the various marinas. In the summer, the docks are alive with activity, and it’s a popular spot for locals to congregate and watch the massive cruise ships dock just meters away at the SeaPort Marina.

On-Water Dining: Experience a uniquely Charlottetown meal at a floating restaurant tucked into the docks. There is nothing quite like enjoying fresh PEI oysters and local beef while literally floating on the historic waterfront.

Yacht Watching & Racing: Head to the Charlottetown Yacht Club (CYC) on West Street. On Monday and Wednesday evenings during the summer, you can watch the colorful spinnakers of the local racing fleet as they compete in the harbor. The CYC also houses Salt & Sol, which offers one of the best elevated views of the marina and harbor entrance.
Watersports & Adventures: For those wanting to get on the water, the marina is the departure point for:
Explore More Watersports: Offers high-energy options like Seadoo rentals, Flyboard flights, and eFoil surfing lessons.
Solar-Powered Cycling: Look for the Sol Paddle Tavern, a unique cycle-boat where you and your friends can pedal through the harbor.

Seals and Lobsters: Most of the city's popular harbor tours depart from these docks, including the famous Top Notch Lobster Tours, where you can experience the life of a fisherman on an authentic lobster boat.
Tips and Key Information

If you are a transient boater, the marinas offer full services, including electrical hookups, fresh water, laundry, and even wireless internet. The SeaPort Marina is particularly convenient for those wanting to be in the thick of it near the downtown shops.

The marina district spans the waterfront from the bottom of Great George Street (Peake's) to the bottom of West Street (Yacht Club). It is a central part of the city's 1.2km continuous waterfront boardwalk.
The Yacht Club has its own member parking, but general visitors should use the public lots at Peake's Wharf or the Harbourfront lot near the Delta Hotel.

The floating docks are generally accessible via ramps, though tides can affect the steepness of the gangways. The main boardwalk connecting the marinas is perfectly flat and easy for strollers and wheelchairs.

places.name: 2. Confederation Landing Parkhttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/confederation-landing-gm696978620-129047093
body: Confederation Landing Park is a beautifully landscaped 6-acre waterfront park that marks the literal landing site of the Fathers of Confederation. In September 1864, the delegates from the Province of Canada arrived here by rowboat (because the town's only circus was in town and all the wharf space was taken) to begin the talks that created Canada. Today, it serves as the city's premier outdoor event space and a tranquil spot for harbor watching.
What to See and Do

The Grand Promenade: Walk the wide, granite-paved path that leads from the water up toward Great George Street. The lighting fixtures and seating here were designed to mirror those in Ottawa’s Parliamentary precinct, reinforcing the connection between the birthplace and the capital.

Inline Skating & Recreation: The park features a unique dedicated area for inline skating and paved pathways that are a favorite for local joggers and cyclists. It’s is a key link in the city's Commuter Bike Lane system.

Heritage Interpretive Signs: Stop to read the series of panels that explain the Brownfield to Beauty transformation of this site. Before 1995, this was a contaminated industrial area; today, it is a model of urban ecological restoration.

The Gazebo & Gardens: Find a quiet moment in the circular flower gardens or under the large Victorian-style gazebo. It’s a popular spot for outdoor weddings and a shaded retreat for seniors and families.

Harbour Hopper Splashdown: If you’re at the park near the water's edge, you’ll likely see the Harbour Hopper—an amphibious military vehicle—make its dramatic entrance into the water for the sea portion of its city tour.
National Indigenous Peoples Day (June 21, 2026): The park will host a massive celebration from 11:00 AM – 4:00 PM featuring Mi’kmaq drumming, dancing, and traditional storytelling.
Island Tides Yoga & Wellness Festival (June 18–21, 2026): Look for large-scale outdoor yoga sessions and wellness workshops taking over the park’s elliptical lawn during the summer solstice.

PEI Marathon Finish Line: While the race starts at various points, the nearby Founders' Food Hall area serves as the festive after-party hub for runners who pass right through the park on their final kilometer.
Tips and Key Information

Clean, accessible public washrooms are located in the small building at the park entrance (near the parking lot). These are generally open seasonally from May to October, but year-round facilities are available just a 2-minute walk away in Founders' Food Hall.
Located at 2 Great George Street, right where the street meets the water.

The Confederation Landing parking lot is located right at the entrance. It is a pay-by-plate lot, though many visitors find it more convenient to use the nearby Pownal Parkade if they plan on staying downtown for several hours.
This is one of the most accessible parks in the city. The paths are flat, wide, and made of hard-packed stone or granite, making it perfect for wheelchairs and strollers.
The park is very popular with local dog owners. Ensure your pet is on a leash, and use the provided waste stations to keep the lawn pristine.

places.name: 3. Rochford Squarehttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/flower-arrangement-in-rochford-square-in-charlottetown-gm515246845-47874738
body: Rochford Square is often called the most beautiful of Charlottetown’s five historic squares. Laid out in the original 1771 town plan, this 4-hectare park was transformed in 2000 into a magnificent Victorian-style garden. It serves as a lush, quiet sanctuary on the western edge of downtown, famous for its intricate floral displays and dramatic mature trees.
What to See and Do

The Victorian Gardens: Unlike the more open play squares, Rochford is a formal ornamental park. Wander through perfectly manicured flower beds and shrubbery that change with the seasons. In the summer, the vibrant blooms make it the city's top choice for wedding and graduation photography.

The Drama Trees: Admire the massive, century-old trees that dominate the square. These include species planted as far back as the first Arbour Day in 1884. Their sprawling canopies provide deep shade and a secret forest feel in the middle of the urban grid.

Historic Stroll: Follow the paved asphalt paths that criss-cross the square. The layout is designed for passive recreation—meaning it’s built for strolling, sitting on heritage-style benches, and quiet contemplation rather than organized sports.

Architecture Watching: From the square, you have a perfect view of the Shaw Building (government offices) and the rear of St. Peter’s Cathedral. The contrast between the red sandstone of the church and the greenery of the park is quintessentially Charlottetown.

Mystic Nights (Seasonal): If you visit in October 2026, the square transforms for the Scarecrow Festival. Look for Mystic Nights, where the park is lit up and hosts open-air activities like oracle card readings in magical tents.
Tips and Key Information
Bordered by Pownal, Richmond, Rochford, and Kent Streets. It is directly across from the provincial government’s Shaw Building at 95 Rochford Street.
On the facade of the nearby Shaw Building, look for decorative lights that change colors to mark holidays or community events—on a clear night, the glow often spills into the square.
The square features flat, wide asphalt pathways that are fully accessible for wheelchairs and strollers.

Because it lacks the playground equipment found in Hillsborough or Connaught Squares, Rochford is significantly quieter and tends to attract artists, readers, and those looking for a peaceful lunch break.
For those playing the Birthplace of Confederation scavenger hunt in 2026, Rochford Square is a key landmark where you’ll often find clues hidden near the central garden beds.

places.name: 4. Hillsborough Bridge
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/hillsborough-river-bridge-at-sunset-gm1386531150-444755119

The Hillsborough Bridge (officially the Hillsborough River Bridge) is the vital gateway connecting Charlottetown to the fast-growing town of Stratford. Spanning the wide estuary of the Hillsborough River—a Canadian Heritage River—it is the busiest section of highway in Prince Edward Island. While most see it as a daily commuter route, the bridge is a fascinating piece of engineering with a history dating back to the early 1900s.

The first bridge (1905) was a narrow-gauge railway bridge that also allowed horse-drawn carriages—but only when a train wasn't coming. The current bridge was built in 1962 and significantly widened in 1995 to accommodate the massive increase in vehicle traffic from the growing suburbs across the water.
What to See and Do

The Active Transportation (AT) Lane: Completed in 2021, a wide, physically separated path runs along the side of the bridge. It’s a favorite for joggers and cyclists, offering one of the most panoramic views of the Charlottetown skyline, the historic waterfront, and the rolling hills of Stratford.

Birdwatching the Old Piers: Look south (downstream) from the bridge to see the crumbling stone piers of the original 1905 railway bridge. These ruins are now a bustling sanctuary for Double-crested Cormorants and Terns, who use the isolated rocks as nesting sites.

Photography at Golden Hour: The bridge is a prime spot for photographers. Looking toward the city at sunset, you can capture the spires of St. Dunstan’s Basilica reflecting in the water, often with a cruise ship or a local fishing boat framed in the foreground.
Tips and Key Information

The bridge is a busy corridor with roughly 40,000 vehicles per day. During peak rush hours (7:30–9:00 AM and 4:00–5:30 PM), traffic can be heavy. If you're visiting for the views, mid-day or early morning is best.

Keep an eye out for shoreline protection work near the Murchison Lane area (close to the Queen Elizabeth Hospital). This project is ongoing through Spring 2026 to stabilize the cliffs adjacent to the bridge's western approach.
For a great 10km workout, many locals start at Founders' Food Hall, cross the bridge's AT lane into Stratford, follow the trail to the Stratford Town Centre, and return.
Because it crosses an open estuary, the bridge can be significantly windier and colder than the downtown streets. If you plan to walk across, even in March, a windbreaker is a must.
The main bridge span is roughly 1.3 kilometers (about 0.8 miles). Walking across at a steady pace takes about 15–20 minutes.
The AT lane is fully paved, flat, and separated from traffic by a tall concrete barrier, making it safe and accessible for wheelchairs, strollers, and high-speed cyclists.

places.name: 5. Brighton Beach Range Lighthouseshttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/brighton-beach-range-lighthouse-in-the-sunset-gm1138427953-303927216
body: Brighton Beach Range Lighthouses are two iconic structures that guide ships safely into Charlottetown Harbor. If you’ve ever wondered how massive cruise ships navigate the narrow channel into Charlottetown Harbour without hitting a sandbar, these two lights are the answer. By aligning the front and rear towers vertically, mariners know they are safely in the center of the deep-water channel.
What to See and Do

The Front Range Light: This is the iconic postcard lighthouse sitting right on the shoreline at the end of York Lane. It’s a 40-foot square, tapered wooden tower with white shingles and a distinctive red vertical stripe. In 2026, it remains one of only two concrete-based lighthouses on the Island (following a major reconstruction of its foundation after a storm surge).

The Rear Range Light (The Apple Core): Located about 400 meters inland on Queen Elizabeth Drive, this lighthouse looks completely different. Built in 1968, it is a 60-foot octagonal concrete tower with a flared top, earning it the nickname The Apple Core. It is the only one of its design in Prince Edward Island.

The Alignment Walk: The best way to experience them is to walk the shoreline near the Front Light and then look back toward the neighborhood to find the taller Rear Light. When they line up perfectly, you are standing on the Range Line.
Photography: The Front Light is a favorite for photographers, especially during high tide when the water laps against its base.
Beachcombing: At low tide, the area around the Front Light reveals red sandstone flats and tidal pools. It’s a great spot for finding shells or sea glass, though the rocks can be slippery and muddy.
Tips and Key Information

Both lighthouses are active aids to navigation operated by the Canadian Coast Guard (and owned by the City). While you can walk right up to the base of the Front Light, the interiors are not open to the public.

These lights are located in a quiet, high-end residential area. There are private homes on both sides of the Front Light. Visitors are encouraged to stay on the public boardwalk and boat launch area to avoid trespassing.

If you look across the harbor from the Brighton shore, you can see the sister range lights at Warren Cove and the Blockhouse Point Lighthouse. On a clear day, you can see five different lighthouses just by turning your head.
Do not try to park on the narrow York Lane. Instead, park at the Victoria Park playground lot and enjoy the 5-minute walk along the waterfront boardwalk to reach the lights.
Location:
Front Light: Bottom of York Lane.
Rear Light: 63 Queen Elizabeth Drive.

places.name: 6. Prince Edward Battery
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/prince-edward-battery-in-charlottetown-prince-edward-island-canada-gm643698312-116819787

Prince Edward Battery is a historic coastal defense site located on the southern tip of Victoria Park. While it may look like a peaceful spot for a picnic today, this battery was a critical piece of Charlottetown’s military infrastructure for over a century. It stands as the sole survivor of the various fortifications that once guarded the Birthplace of Confederation from potential sea-bound threats.
What to See and Do
The Cannons: Explore the row of nine period guns that overlook the harbor. The collection includes:
Three 32-pounder smoothbore guns mounted on wooden ship-style carriages.
Three 9-pounder cannons on iron garrison carriages.
Three 64-pounder RML (Rifled Muzzle Loading) guns, which were the high-tech upgrades of the early 1900s.

The Powder Magazine: Admire the small, gabled stone building behind the guns. This was used to store gunpowder and was designed with thick masonry walls to contain an explosion if one were to occur. While the interior is generally closed to the public, its exterior is a perfectly preserved example of 19th-century military architecture.

The Sunken Earthworks: Notice the barbette style of the battery. Unlike a high stone fort, these guns are placed behind low earthworks and stone walls, designed to offer protection to the gunners while maintaining a low profile against enemy ships.

Harbour Vantages: This is arguably the best spot in the city to watch cruise ships enter and exit the harbor. Because the battery sits on a slight elevation, you can see clear across to Rocky Point and the Blockhouse Point Lighthouse.

Interpretive Panels: Take a moment to read the plaques that detail the site's history from its founding in 1805 through the War of 1812 and its reactivation during the Irish Fenian threat in the 1860s.
Tips and Key Information

The battery is fully accessible, year-round landmark. While the cannons are outdoors and can be visited anytime, the surrounding grounds are part of the municipal park system and are maintained daily.
Entry is completely free.
It is located on the harbor side of Victoria Park, right next to the waterfront boardwalk.
If you are visiting during a significant royal occasion or a state visit in 2026, the battery is still the site where honorary gun salutes are performed by the PEI Regiment.
Use the free parking lot at the entrance of Victoria Park. From there, it is a scenic 5-to-10-minute walk along the boardwalk to reach the battery.

The battery is located on a flat, grassy plateau adjacent to the paved boardwalk. While the immediate area around the cannons is grass, it is generally firm enough for strollers and wheelchairs in dry weather.

Look for the survey stones near the battery that mark the meridional line. These were placed in 1820 to help surveyors determine True North in Charlottetown and are some of the oldest scientific markers on the Island.

places.name: 7. Harbour Experience on Solar Boat
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/cruise-ship-dock-at-charlottetown-gm2189253577-607725254

The Harbour Experience on the Solar Boat is one of Charlottetown’s most unique and eco-friendly ways to see the city. Operated by Ride Solar, the vessel—named the Isola Solaretto—is actually a restored Canadian Heritage Vessel originally used as a "Vaporetto" at the 1967 Montreal Expo (the World's Fair). Today, it has been transformed into North America’s largest solar-powered tour boat, offering a whisper-quiet, emission-free cruise where you can literally see the batteries through a glass floor.
What to See and Do
Silent Navigation: Because the boat is 100% solar-electric, there is no diesel noise, vibration, or smell. You can glide silently past the shoreline and hear the calls of the harbor birds clearly.
The Glass Floor View: Look down into the hull to see the battery banks and the electric motors that power your journey, all fueled by the massive solar panels on the roof.

Live Music & Commentary: Most cruises feature live maritime music and historical commentary. The boat is equipped with four large video screens that show archival footage of the 1967 Expo and historical photos of the landmarks you pass.
Food & Drink: The boat is a fully licensed floating restaurant with a kitchen. You can order fresh PEI lobster, local mussels, and craft beer while you sail.

Historical Sightseeing Cruise (1.5 Hours): The standard daytime tour. It takes you past Victoria Park, Government House, and the Millionaire's Row in Stratford, offering a new perspective on the city's skyline.
Sunset Dinner Cruise (2 Hours): A premium experience featuring a five-course surf and turf meal served as the sun sets over the Northumberland Strait.
Kitchen Party Cruise: An adult-oriented evening cruise on Saturdays (starting at 9:00 PM) that includes fresh mussels, a roll, and a high-energy live band for a true East Coast party under the stars.
Tips and Key Information
Tours typically run daily from May 1st to October 31st.

The boat departs from a private dock at the Port of Charlottetown (1 Weymouth Street), located at the far end of the terminal building where the large cruise ships dock. Look for the green and white Ride Solar flags.
The boat holds up to 34 passengers, making it an intimate experience compared to larger harbor ferries.
The vessel has booth seating and a roof with opening hatches, making it a comfortable all-weather activity even if there’s a light drizzle.
Price for Daytime Cruises ranges from $49–$54 per adult.
Price for Dinner Cruises ranges from $120–$140 per person (includes the meal).
While the boat can accommodate strollers and walkers, it is generally not fully wheelchair accessible due to the boarding gangway and the nature of the heritage vessel.

places.name: 1. Queen Street
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/historic-facades-queen-street-downtown-charlottetown-prince-edward-island-canada-gm642276860-116593069

Queen Street is one of Charlottetown’s busiest and most walkable streets, lined with shops, cafés, theaters, and galleries. It stretches from the waterfront up to residential neighborhoods, offering a mix of local charm and urban energy.
What to See and Do

The Anne of Green Gables Store: Located at 72 Queen Street, this is the ultimate pilgrimage site for fans. Housed in the historic 1855 Duncan Building, it offers everything from straw hats with red braids to raspberry cordial. Even if you aren't a superfan, the building itself is an excellent example of pre-1860s commercial design.

Charlottetown City Hall: This National Historic Site at 100 Queen Street is a Romanesque Revival masterpiece. Built in 1888, it originally housed the police station and firehall (with stables). Look for the commanding corner tower and the deep-set rounded arch windows.

Confederation Court Mall: Stretching between Queen and Great George, this is the city's premier indoor shopping destination. It’s a mix of modern retail and historic charm, connecting several heritage buildings into one climate-controlled block—perfect for a chilly March day.
The Bookmark: An independent bookstore that has been a Queen Street staple for decades. It’s the best place to find works by Atlantic Canadian authors, local maps, and unique PEI stationery.

St. Dunstan’s Basilica (Rear View): While the main entrance is on Great George Street, the massive stone rear of the Basilica dominates the skyline as you walk up Queen. The sheer scale of the Victorian Gothic spires is most impressive from this street-level perspective.
Tips and Key Information
If you are driving, the Queen Parkade (222 Queen St) is the most convenient spot. In 2026, the rate is $1.25 per hour (including tax) with a daily max of $8.75. It is free on weekends and holidays.

Due to the ongoing $65 million rejuvenation project, the Queen Street entrance is currently the only open entrance for the Confederation Centre of the Arts. Look for the designated signage and accessible elevator access here.

Queen Street is well-paved with wide sidewalks. Many of the historic shops have street-level entries, though some older buildings may have one or two steps. The Confederation Court Mall and City Hall are fully accessible.
Most T3 Transit buses pass through or stop near the intersection of Queen and Grafton Street, making it the easiest point in the city to catch a bus to the suburbs or the University.

places.name: 2. Founders' Food Hall & Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/aerial-view-of-charlottetown-canada-gm2174673800-594340774#

Founders' Food Hall & Market is the modern culinary and social heart of the Charlottetown waterfront. Housed in a massive, light-filled 1906 brick building that once served as the CN Railway Car Shop, it was meticulously restored and opened in 2019. It combines industrial heritage with a European-style food hall experience, featuring high ceilings, original steel beams, and a mezzanine with some of the best people-watching views in the city.
What to See and Do
The Taste of the Island Crawl: With over 18 local vendors, this is the best place to sample PEI’s food scene under one roof.
Gourmet Comfort: Try the famous loaded fries at The Chip Shack or authentic Mexican street food from Taco Boyz.
Sweet Treats: Don't miss the Parisian-style cream puffs at Maid Marian’s or the locally beloved doughnuts at Doughy’s.
Artisanal Spirits: Visit the Founders' Bar for a flight of PEI craft beers or a cocktail made with local Upstreet spirits.

Artisanal Shopping: Beyond food, the market features a curated selection of retail boutiques. Look for Two Beggars (luxury pet accessories), Rustico Bay Pottery, and shops selling unique PEI sea glass jewelry and dirt shirts dyed with local soil.
The Mezzanine: Head upstairs to the quiet lounge area. It’s a great spot for remote work (free Wi-Fi) or to enjoy your food while looking out over the harbor and the bustling market floor below.
Visitor Information Centre: Attached to the market is the city’s primary visitor center. It features new interactive touch-screens that help you build a custom Island itinerary on the spot.
Tips and Key Information
Founders' is open 7 days a week, year-round.
Monday to Saturday: 10:00 AM – 8:00 PM
Sunday: 11:00 AM – 5:00 PM (though some food vendors may stay open later).
Located at 6 Prince Street, right at the intersection of Water and Prince. It is the southern anchor of the Great George Street Historic District.
There is a large public Pay-by-Plate lot directly in front of the building. In March, parking is usually easy to find, but it fills up fast during the Pride Night Market or weekend music sets.
The building is fully accessible with wide aisles and a modern elevator to reach the mezzanine level.
Look for the small brass house nearby—one of the few other surviving buildings from the rail era—and the historic rail cars parked along the Confederation Trail just outside the door.

places.name: 3. Anne of Green Gables Storehttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/anne-of-green-gables-store-gm1085763492-291330236
body: The Anne of Green Gables Store on Queen Street is the ultimate destination for fans of L.M. Montgomery’s world-famous redhead. While there are several Anne shops across the Island, this downtown location is the flagship, serving as a year-round hub for literary pilgrims and souvenir hunters alike. Housed in a charming historic brick building, it offers a sophisticated retail experience that balances nostalgic whimsy with high-quality Island craftsmanship.
What to See and Do
The AnnenEssentials: Find the most iconic souvenirs, including the classic straw hat with red braids, Kindred Spirits jewelry, and locally famous raspberry cordial.

Exclusive Literary Collections: The store carries the largest selection of L.M. Montgomery’s books in various editions, from beautiful leather-bound collector’s volumes to pocket-sized paperbacks. In 2026, look for the Kindred Spirits Publishing series, which features unique covers and photography by Island artists.
Hand-Painted Porcelain: Browse a wide array of licensed collectibles, including miniature porcelain dolls, ornaments, and teaware that reflect the Victorian aesthetic of the novels.

ANNE of Green Gables Chocolates: While there are standalone chocolate shops, this store features a dedicated section for these handmade treats. The Cow Chips (chocolate-covered potato chips) and fudgy truffles remain top-sellers in 2026.

Meet the Team: The store is often staffed by Anne experts who can help you plan your wider trip to Cavendish or point out subtle details in the merchandise that link back to specific chapters in the books.
Tips and Key Information
Unlike many seasonal tourist shops, the Queen Street store is open year-round.
Monday – Saturday: 10:00 AM – 5:00 PM
Sunday: 12:00 PM – 5:00 PM
Located at 72 Queen Street, right in the heart of the downtown shopping district. It is just a two-minute walk from the Confederation Centre of the Arts.
The store has expanded its ANNE of Greener Gables initiative, moving toward 100% plastic-free packaging and offering carbon-neutral shipping options for items bought in-store and sent home.
f you're looking for a specific item not in stock, ask the staff to check their A-Team headquarters at Milky Way, just a short drive away, which serves as their main distribution hub.
Even if you aren't shopping, the exterior of the building—with its gold-leaf Anne signage and beautiful window displays—is one of the most photographed storefronts in Charlottetown.
The store features a street-level entrance and wide aisles, making it fully accessible for wheelchairs and strollers.
If you’re visiting in the summer, this store is the best place to get Anne items signed by visiting Montgomery descendants, who occasionally stop by for meet-and-greet events.

places.name: 4. Anne of Green Gables Chocolates
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/downtown-charlottetown-gm1421427609-467062080

Anne of Green Gables Chocolates is a beloved Prince Edward Island tradition that has been delivering happiness since 1999. While they have several seasonal spots, their two Charlottetown locations are the heart of the operation, offering handmade treats crafted from time-tested Island recipes.
What to See and Do
You cannot visit without trying the COW Chips. These are arguably the most famous snack on the Island:
The Secret: Thick-cut, ridged potato chips (sourced from PEI’s famous spuds) are hand-dipped in premium milk chocolate.
The Taste: It is the ultimate sweet and salty combination. In 2026, they remain the #1 bestseller, often sold in iconic tins that make for perfect souvenirs.
Anne’s Chocolate Caramels: Slow-cooked and incredibly smooth, these are a close second to the COW Chips in popularity.
Raspberry Cordial: While not a chocolate, they sell the official version of Anne’s favorite drink in glass bottles—a must-have for the full Green Gables experience.
Truffles & Fudge: The glass display cases are packed with assorted truffles (the Dark Chocolate Sea Salt is a local favorite) and blocks of creamy fudge made on-site.
Gift Boxes: For 2026, they have expanded their Build Your Own Gift Box options, allowing you to mix and match treats in a custom souvenir box.
Tips and Key Information
Both Charlottetown locations are dog-friendly. If you’re walking your pup through downtown, feel free to bring them inside while you browse.
If you've never had a COW Chip, the staff are usually happy to provide a sample so you can understand the hype.
As part of their ANNE of Greener Gables program, the company is transitioning all packaging to environmentally friendly alternatives in 2026.
If your suitcase is already full, they offer reliable shipping across Canada (and free shipping on orders over $99).
Key Charlottetown Locations

Downtown (100 Queen Street): Located right next to the Anne of Green Gables Store, this shop is a colorful, whimsical space filled with the smell of cocoa. Open daily (Mon–Sat: 11 AM – 5 PM; Sun: 12 PM – 5 PM). It’s a great spot to grab a quick gift or a single truffle while exploring the historic district.

The Factory at Milky Way (15 Milky Way): This is the A-Team headquarters located just a 5-minute drive from downtown. This location features a large production viewing window where you can actually watch the chocolatiers hand-dipping chips and crafting fudge. It’s part of a larger complex that includes the COWS Creamery and Boom Burger, making it a one-stop shop for Island treats.

places.name: 5. Day Trip to Green Gables Heritage Place
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/green-gables-heritage-place-gm924288516-253667389

A day trip to Green Gables Heritage Place in Cavendish is the ultimate pilgrimage for any Anne fan. Located about 40 kilometers (25 miles) north of Charlottetown, this National Historic Site is where L.M. Montgomery found the inspiration for the farmstead that became Anne Shirley’s home.
What to See and Do (In Season)
The Green Gables House: Walk through the meticulously restored rooms, including Anne’s bedroom (complete with the brown dress with puffed sleeves) and Marilla’s austere pantry.
The Haunted Wood Trail: A short, atmospheric walk through the spruce grove that Anne and Diana were terrified to cross at night.
Balsam Hollow & Lover’s Lane: This was L.M. Montgomery’s favorite place to walk. The trail follows a bubbling brook and is especially beautiful in late spring and autumn.
The Visitor Centre: A modern, award-winning facility featuring interactive exhibits about Montgomery’s life, her struggles as a female author, and the global impact of her work.
Tips and Key Information
The site opens daily from May 1 to October 31, 2026 (9:00 AM – 5:00 PM).
The drive from Charlottetown takes approximately 40 minutes via Route 2 and Route 13.
There is no direct bus from Charlottetown to Cavendish in the winter/spring. In the summer, seasonal shuttles are sometimes available, but a rental car or taxi is usually required.
For 2026, admission fees are $10.00 for adults, $8.50 for seniors, and free for youth aged 17 and under.
you visit during the peak summer (July/August), aim to arrive before 10:30 AM or after 3:30 PM to avoid the large tour bus groups.
Between April 15–30 and November 1–30, you can book special appointments via email (greengables@pc.gc.ca).
If you're making the drive to Cavendish, don't miss these other sites:
L.M. Montgomery’s Cavendish Home: Just down the road, you can walk the foundations of the home where she actually lived and wrote the first Anne book.
Cavendish Cemetery: Visit the final resting place of L.M. Montgomery, which is beautifully maintained and marked with a simple, elegant headstone.
Cavendish Beach: Located within the PEI National Park, it features the stunning red sandstone cliffs and white sand dunes that Anne found so divine.

places.name: 6. The Great George Hotel
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/great-george-hotel-gm1421427485-467062079

The Great George is a sprawling 5-star hotel that defines the historic character of downtown Charlottetown. Consisting of 17 meticulously restored heritage buildings spread across nearly an entire city block, it offers a scattered hotel experience where your room might be in a former bishop’s palace, a 19th-century warehouse, or a doctor's private residence.
What to See and Do

The Pavilion (Main Lobby): Your journey starts at 58 Great George Street in the Pavilion building. Built in 1846, it originally served as a general store called London House before becoming a hotel that famously hosted delegates during the 1864 Charlottetown Conference.

A Landmark of Preservation: In the 1990s, local entrepreneurs Mike Cassidy and Kevin Murphy (of Murphy Hospitality Group) began buying and restoring the neglected buildings on this block. Today, it stands as the largest private heritage restoration project in Prince Edward Island’s history.

The Fathers of Confederation Connection: Because the hotel hosted the 1864 delegates, staying here feels like living inside a piece of Canadian history. You are literally steps away from Province House, where the country was conceived.
Complimentary Perks: The Great George is famous for its Island Hospitality. Every stay includes:
Freshly Baked Cookies: Available in the lobby throughout the day.
Evening Guest Reception: Weeknight socials (5:00 PM – 6:00 PM) with complimentary local craft beer or wine.
Deluxe Continental Breakfast: Served in the cozy, leather-clad lobby lounge.
Unique Rooms: No two rooms are exactly alike. You can choose from Romantic Hideaway suites with double Jacuzzis and fireplaces, or multi-bedroom townhouses that feel like private city apartments.
Heated Luxury: Many rooms feature heated bathroom floors, a small but high-value detail that guests rave about, especially during the cooler months.
Tips and Key Information
The hotel offers complimentary on-site parking (a rarity downtown), though the courtyard can be a bit of a puzzle to navigate. Valet service is also available.
You are at the epicenter of the Great George Street Historic District. You can walk to the waterfront, the Confederation Centre, and dozens of restaurants in under five minutes.
While many of the historic buildings have stairs, the main Pavilion and several designated suites are fully accessible.
Guests have 24-hour access to an on-site fitness center. The hotel also offers a City & Spa package that includes passes to the nearby Mysa Nordic Spa in St. Peter’s Bay.

places.name: 1. Walk the Chemainus Murals
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/street-in-chemainus-gm1369389215-439159693

Chemainus, once a struggling lumber town, transformed itself into a world-famous outdoor gallery through its extensive mural program. The Chemainus Murals tell the vivid history of the region’s indigenous roots, forestry heritage, and community life, turning the town's building exterior walls into a massive, walkable history book.
What to See and Do

The Mural Walk: Follow the yellow footprints painted on the sidewalks. This trail connects over 40 professional murals and several sculptures, ensuring you don't miss the major works like The Hermit or the massive Historical Series.

Heritage Square: This central area features some of the most intricate artworks and serves as a natural starting point. It is surrounded by tiered gardens and heritage-style architecture that complements the historical themes of the paintings.

Chemainus Theatre Festival: Located along the mural route, this award-winning theatre is a cultural anchor for the town. Even if you aren't catching a show, the building itself and its surrounding statues are essential stops.

Artisans and Antiques: The streets between murals are lined with independent art galleries, pottery studios, and antique shops, reflecting the town's transition from an industrial hub to an arts destination.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/a-sushi-house-at-chemainus-bc-canada-gm664727158-125261723
Tips and Key Information
While the footprints are helpful, a physical or digital map from the Chemainus Visitor Centre provides the backstory and artist information for each piece, adding significant depth to the experience.
Many of the murals are on south or west-facing walls. Visit during the mid-morning or late afternoon to avoid the harsh glare of the midday sun, which can wash out the colors in your photos.
While the town is compact, the full mural circuit covers several kilometers of walking on paved surfaces. Plan for at least two to three hours to see the majority of the works at a relaxed pace.

Chemainus is known for its quaint tea rooms and bakeries. Many visitors stop for a mural break at one of the cafes in Old Town to enjoy a locally baked treat while planning the second half of their walk.
The murals are a permanent, year-round attraction that can be enjoyed in any season.
The murals are spread throughout the downtown core of Chemainus, BC, primarily concentrated along Willow Street and Chemainus Road.
Viewing the murals is entirely free of charge and accessible to the public 24 hours a day.
The majority of the mural route follows level, well-maintained city sidewalks, making it highly accessible for wheelchairs, strollers, and those with limited mobility.
There is ample free street parking throughout the town, as well as a large public lot near the Waterwheel Park and the Visitor Centre.
The outdoor nature of the gallery makes it a very pet-friendly activity. Dogs are welcome on the sidewalks but should be kept on a leash, especially near the busier shop entrances.

places.name: 2. Visit the Chemainus Theatre Festival
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/chemainus-gm1369393732-439163652

The Chemainus Theatre Festival is a premier cultural destination on Vancouver Island, housed in a stunning neo-classical building that anchors the town’s arts district. Known for its high-production values and professional cast members recruited from across Canada, the theatre offers a sophisticated dinner and a show experience that complements the town's artistic atmosphere.
What to See and Do

Mainstage Performances: The theatre presents a year-round calendar of diverse productions, ranging from classic Broadway musicals and lighthearted comedies to powerful dramas and holiday-themed specials.

The Playbill Dining Room: Located within the theatre complex, this highly-rated restaurant offers a themed buffet that changes with each production. It is a popular tradition for guests to enjoy a relaxed, live-piano-accompanied meal before the curtain rises.

Gallery Gift Shop: The lobby houses a curated boutique featuring original works by British Columbia artisans, including hand-thrown pottery, jewelry, and fine art, often mirroring the themes seen in the town's famous murals.

Backstage Tours: On select dates, the theatre offers guided tours that take visitors behind the scenes to view the costume shop, set construction area, and dressing rooms, providing insight into the technical side of professional regional theatre.
Tips and Key Information
For the most seamless evening, it is recommended to book the combined package. This ensures your table in the Playbill Dining Room is timed perfectly with your show's intermission and conclusion.

If you prefer to avoid driving at night, the theatre offers several afternoon matinee performances each week. This allows you to explore the Chemainus Murals in the morning and catch a show after lunch.
While there is no formal dress code, most patrons opt for smart casual attire. The atmosphere is upscale yet welcoming, reflecting the relaxed coastal elegance of the region.

During popular runs, the immediate vicinity can get busy. Arriving 30–45 minutes early allows you to find parking and spend a few minutes admiring the statues and architecture of Heritage Square nearby.
Located at 9737 Chemainus Rd, Chemainus, BC.
Typically open Tuesday through Saturday, with extended hours on performance days. Tickets can be purchased online, by phone, or in person.

The theatre is fully accessible, featuring ramps, an elevator to the upper gallery seating, and dedicated spaces for those using wheelchairs. Infrared hearing assistance headsets are also available at the coat check.
There is a dedicated parking lot for theatre patrons located directly behind the building, along with ample street parking on the surrounding blocks.
Pre-ordering your intermission refreshments or dessert at the lobby bar before the show begins is a great way to skip the queues during the break.

places.name: 3. Browse the boutiques, galleries, and artisan shops
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/willow-street-gm1483640849-510183015

The shopping scene in Chemainus is an extension of its artistic identity, where the lack of big-box retailers allows independent boutiques, high-end galleries, and nostalgic specialty shops to thrive. Concentrated largely along Willow Street, these establishments offer curated goods that reflect the West Coast lifestyle and the town's creative spirit.
What to See and Do
The retail experience here is characterized by discovery and craftsmanship, with many shop owners also being the makers of the products they sell.

Artisanal Galleries: Several dedicated spaces, such as Rainforest Arts, focus specifically on local island artists. Visitors can find professional-grade pottery, fine jewelry, and paintings that range from abstract to traditional indigenous styles.

Specialty Fashion & Gifts: Boutiques like Bound To Be ~ Fashion & Gifts and Opposites Attract and friends offer a mix of ethical fashion, unique accessories, and home decor items that are difficult to find in larger urban centers.

The Antique Trail: For those who enjoy the hunt for vintage treasures, the Willow Antique Mall and Vintiquity provide multi-vendor spaces filled with heritage furniture, rare collectibles, and coastal memorabilia.
Nostalgic Confections: Hansel & Gretel's Candy Co. is a local landmark known for its whimsical decor and vast selection of traditional sweets, imported treats, and locally made fudges.
Tips and Key Information

Many independent shops in Chemainus operate on a Wednesday-to-Sunday schedule, particularly during the shoulder season. If you are planning a dedicated shopping trip, mid-week through the weekend ensures the most doors are open.

Several galleries, including The Gallery & Gift Shop at the theatre, are well-versed in shipping larger art pieces or fragile pottery internationally, so don't let travel logistics deter a significant find.
Look for shops that partner with local community groups. Some galleries are volunteer-run or operate as non-profits to support the regional arts council.
While Willow Street is the main artery, unique studios like Bramble and Brush Arts and Silvermine On Chemainus are located just a block away on Chemainus Road or near the waterfront.
The shopping district is compact and designed for pedestrian ease.
Primarily centered on Willow Street, extending to Chemainus Road and Maple Street.
Most shops are located at street level with accessible entrances, though some antique malls may have narrow aisles or heritage layouts that require more careful navigation.
Free street parking is plentiful on Willow Street, and there are designated public lots near Waterwheel Park and the theatre.
While almost all shops accept major credit and debit cards, having some cash on hand can be useful for smaller purchases at community artisan stalls.

places.name: 4. Enjoy the waterfront and harbour views
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/a-beautiful-photo-of-a-wooden-bench-that-looks-outward-to-the-ocean-full-of-boats-gm1169488747-323309535

The waterfront in Chemainus provides a serene counterpoint to the town’s busy mural-lined streets. While the community is famous for its inland art, the coastline offers expansive views of the Stuart Channel, the Gulf Islands, and the steady rhythm of the local working harbour.
What to See and Do
The shoreline is a mix of manicured parkland, sandy beaches, and industrial marine infrastructure.

Kinsmen Beach Park (Kin Beach): This is the town’s primary oceanfront park, featuring a mix of rocky and sandy shoreline. At low tide, the water recedes to reveal vast tidal pools and sandbars, making it possible to walk out toward Bird Rock.

Chemainus Municipal Wharf: A popular spot for sightseeing and birdwatching, the wharf allows you to see the local fishing fleet and moored sailboats up close. It is a prime location to spot eagles and seals frequenting the harbour.

Waterwheel Park Viewpoint: Located in the heart of the village, this park features a dedicated viewpoint overlooking the harbour. It serves as a scenic bridge between the new and old downtown districts.

Marine Activities: The calm waters around the harbour are a favorite for local kayakers and paddleboarders. From the shore, you can watch the Chemainus Ferry Terminal handle the regular sailings to Thetis and Penelakut Islands.
Tips and Key Information
For the best beachcombing and exploration at Kinsmen Beach Park, check a local tide table. The landscape changes dramatically when the tide is out, exposing shells and marine life.

The Chemainus Municipal Wharf is one of the best spots in town for evening photography. The sun sets behind the mountains of Vancouver Island, casting a golden glow over the water and the moored boats.

Even if you aren't catching a boat, walking down to the ferry terminal area offers a unique perspective of the coast. Just up the hill from the terminal, a scenic pathway leads directly back into Waterwheel Park.
The islands across the channel—Thetis and Tent Island—are often bustling with wildlife. Binoculars will help you spot marine birds and the occasional whale passing through the deeper channel waters.
The waterfront areas are well-maintained and integrated into the town’s walking routes.
Primary access is via Maple Street for the beach and Oak Street for the wharf.
Waterwheel Park and the Chemainus Municipal Wharf are highly accessible with paved surfaces. Kinsmen Beach Park has a paved boat launch and grassy lawns, though the beach itself is rocky in sections.
Public washrooms, playgrounds, and picnic tables are available at both Waterwheel Park and Kinsmen Beach Park.
A large paved parking lot is available at Waterwheel Park, with additional street-end parking at Kinsmen Beach Park on Pine Street.

places.name: 5. Stroll through Waterwheel Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/waterwheel-park-gm1483430845-510029357

Waterwheel Park is the civic and horticultural heart of Chemainus, acting as a central gathering point that bridges the town's industrial past with its artistic present. Named for the massive replica of the 19th-century wheel that once powered the local economy, the park offers a lush, shaded environment perfect for a mid-day break.
What to See and Do
The park is meticulously landscaped and serves as a transition zone between the main shopping district and the waterfront.
The Iconic Waterwheel: A towering wooden replica of the 1862 original stands near the entrance, providing a popular backdrop for photography and a reminder of the town's origins as a milling outpost.
Outdoor Performance Stage: The park features a large cedar bandshell that hosts the Music in the Park series during the summer, featuring local folk, jazz, and classical performers.
Heritage Statues: Interspersed among the flower beds are several life-sized wood carvings and bronze statues that complement the nearby murals, depicting various figures from the region's history.
The Labyrinth: Located in a quieter corner of the park, this stone-lined walking path offers a space for meditative reflection away from the main tourist thoroughfares.
Tips and Key Information
The park features several well-maintained grassy tiers and benches with views of the harbour. It is a common tradition to grab a sandwich or pastry from a nearby bakery on Willow Street and eat here.
During the holiday season or special summer events, the park is often illuminated with string lights, creating a festive atmosphere that is quite different from its daytime character.
The Chemainus Valley Museum is located directly adjacent to the park. It houses a collection of artifacts that provide the deeper stories behind the murals found throughout the town.
If traveling with children, the park includes a modern playground area that is safely tucked away from the main road, making it an easy spot for kids to burn off energy between mural viewings.
The park's central location makes it the most convenient starting point for any exploration of Chemainus.
Location: 3828 Croft St, Chemainus, BC.
The park is a public municipal space and is free to enter at all times.
The main paths through the park are paved and relatively flat, though there are some sloped sections leading toward the lower viewpoints and the museum.
A large, free public parking lot is located directly at the park entrance, providing easy access to the Chemainus Visitor Centre.
Dogs are welcome on the park grounds but must remain on a leash. Waste bags are often provided at dispensers near the park entrances.

places.name: 6. Explore the Chemainus Valley Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/vancouver-island-regional-library-gm1369392729-439162614

The Chemainus Valley Museum, located in the heart of Waterwheel Park, offers an intimate look at the regional history that shaped this coastal community. Operated by dedicated volunteers from the Chemainus Valley Historical Society, the museum provides the essential context behind the town's famous murals, detailing its transition from a 19th-century resource hub to an international arts destination.
What to See and Do
The museum’s collection is thoughtfully arranged to guide visitors through the distinct eras of the Chemainus Valley.

Logging and Industry Exhibits: Explore the town’s foundation as a mill town through displays of antique forestry equipment, including a steam whistle and items from the early days of the local lumber mill.

The Story Behind the Murals: A highlighted section is dedicated to the mural project, featuring original sketches, photographs of the artists at work, and the narratives that inspired the massive outdoor gallery.

Community Life and Archives: See how residents lived through artifacts like a player piano, vintage household items, and exhibits focusing on the Indigenous heritage of the Stz'uminus people and the early settler families.
Curated Gift Shop: The museum shop features unique handmade items donated by society members, local history books, and the official mural guide booklet, which is a must-have for the walking tour.
Tips and Key Information
The staff are often long-time locals with personal stories about the town’s evolution. Many visitors find that a quick conversation with a docent adds a meaningful layer to the historical displays.
The museum sells an informative booklet that provides the background and artist details for every mural in town. It is the perfect companion for the Footprint Trail walk.
Since the museum is adjacent to the park and the Chemainus Visitor Centre, it serves as an ideal starting point for a day in Chemainus.
While the museum is packed with treasures, its compact size means you can fully explore the main galleries in about 30 to 60 minutes, making it an easy addition to a busy itinerary.
Location: 9799 Waterwheel Crescent, Chemainus, BC.
Entry is typically by donation, supporting the historical society's efforts to preserve local records and artifacts.
The museum generally operates from 10:00 AM to 3:00 PM, Thursday through Sunday. It is advisable to check for seasonal changes in hours before your visit.
The building is ground-level and fully accessible, though some aisles within the displays may be narrow for larger mobility aids.
Public washrooms are located just outside in the surrounding park area, and there is ample free parking in the main lot nearby.

places.name: 7. Chemainus Public Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/chemainus-public-market-gm1483640895-510183014

The Chemainus Public Market is an indoor community hub that serves as a modern gathering space in the center of town. While the town’s famous murals provide an outdoor gallery experience, the public market offers a temperature-controlled environment where visitors can browse local wares, enjoy casual dining, and participate in community activities.
What to See and Do

Archie’s Ice Cream Parlour & Diner: A major anchor of the market, this nostalgic 1950s-style diner serves thick milkshakes, coffee, and hearty meals. It’s a popular spot for a casual lunch or a retro-themed treat.
Wizard’s Arcade: Tucked in the back of the market, this space features a variety of classic arcade games and pinball machines, making it a favorite for families and gaming enthusiasts.

Specialty Retailers: The market hosts unique shops like Brickitty Dooda, a LEGO specialty store with a massive inventory of mini-figures and sets, alongside booths featuring local lavender products, wellness items, and used books.

Artisan Studios: You can often find local artists at work within the market. Broken Wing Studio, for example, showcases clay items and paintings, and occasionally offers workshops for those looking to try their hand at a new craft.
Tips and Key Information
While the main market building and the diner are open daily, some of the smaller artisan stalls and the arcade operate on a reduced schedule (often Wednesday through Sunday).

If you are visiting on a Wednesday between May and September, look for the seasonal Make It, Bake It, Grow It market located directly across from Waterwheel Park. It’s a great way to combine the indoor market experience with a traditional farmers’ market.

Because it is primarily indoors, the Public Market is the ideal destination for a rainy Vancouver Island day. You can spend several hours browsing, eating, and playing in the arcade without worrying about the coastal weather.
The market is one of the most convenient spots in town for a quick and varied family meal.
The market is centrally located and easy to incorporate into a walking tour of the town.
Located at 9790 Willow St, Chemainus, BC Click to open side panel for more information .
There is ample street parking on Willow Street, and the market is within easy walking distance of the main public lot at Waterwheel Park.
The building is a single-level facility with wide aisles, making it fully accessible for those with mobility aids or strollers.
While service animals are permitted, pets are generally not allowed inside the market building due to the food service and retail regulations.

places.name: 8. Spend time on trails and outdoor areas nearby
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/trail-sign-in-stocking-creek-falls-gm2211662485-628636708

Chemainus is surrounded by a diverse network of trails and parks that cater to both casual walkers and dedicated hikers. These outdoor spaces transition from manicured community parks to rugged wilderness, showcasing the varied landscapes of the Cowichan Valley.
What to See and Do
