Lakefront Recreation: Fuller Lake Park is a premier destination for those looking to blend a walk with water activities. It features a sandy beach, a fishing pier stocked with trout, and quiet forested paths.
Wilderness Immersion: Askew Park offers a true forest experience right in town. Its trail system meanders through second and old-growth trees, providing a cool, shaded retreat along Askew Creek.

Waterfall Access: A short drive north leads to Stocking Creek Park, where well-maintained trails lead directly to Stocking Creek Falls. This area is particularly striking after a rainfall when the falls are at their most powerful.

The Trans Canada Connection: The Cowichan Valley Trail passes through the region, offering a wide, gravel-surfaced route that is perfect for long-distance cycling or a level afternoon stroll toward Saltair or Ladysmith.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/stocking-creek-falls-gm2211661776-628635885
Tips and Key Information
If you are visiting with a dog, Chemainus Lake Park features a popular 2.5km loop trail with designated off-leash zones. The path is smooth and relatively flat, making it ideal for older pets.
For the Cowichan Valley Trail, use the large gravel lot across from the Mount Brenton Golf Course. This provides the easiest access to the trailhead heading north.
Trails like those at Stocking Creek can become icy in late winter. Sturdy footwear with good grip is recommended during the shoulder seasons to navigate patches of mud or slick rocks near the water.

Many of these locations, especially Fuller Lake and Chemainus Lake, have excellent picnic facilities. Stopping at a local bakery in town before heading out allows for a full day of outdoor exploration.
Most parks are within a 5-to-10-minute drive of downtown Chemainus. Fuller Lake Park is located just off Highway 1 near the arena.
Fuller Lake Park and the Cowichan Valley Trail offer the most accessible surfaces for strollers and wheelchairs. Askew Park is more of a traditional wilderness trail with uneven terrain.
Washrooms and picnic tables are standard at the larger parks like Fuller Lake and Chemainus Lake. Smaller trails like Askew Park focus on a pack-in, pack-out philosophy.
Most municipal and regional parks are open from dawn until dusk, typically with posted hours such as 8:00 AM to 11:00 PM for gated areas.

places.name: 9. Chemainus Wednesday Market
body: The Chemainus Wednesday Market is a seasonal outdoor "Make It, Bake It, Grow It" market that transforms the heart of town into a lively community hub. Held in the parking lot area right across from Waterwheel Park, it showcases the best of the Cowichan Valley’s local artisans, farmers, and bakers.
What to See and Do
The market focuses on original, handmade, and locally produced goods, ensuring a high-quality selection of authentic Vancouver Island products.
Farm-Fresh Produce: Local growers bring seasonal fruits and vegetables directly from the valley’s fertile soil, alongside fresh-cut flowers and nursery plants.
Artisanal Crafts and Jewelry: You can find a diverse range of handmade items, including custom jewelry, West Coast-inspired textiles, pottery, and unique woodworking pieces.

Baked Goods and Treats: The air is often filled with the scent of fresh breads, pastries, and small-batch preserves. Many visitors stop here to pick up picnic supplies for a walk along the Chemainus Murals.
The Chamber Tent: Operated by the Chemainus & District Chamber of Commerce, this central hub often features specific regional information and a rotating selection of local produce.
Tips and Key Information
The market runs from 10:00 AM to 3:00 PM, but arriving closer to the opening hour is recommended if you are looking for the best selection of fresh produce and popular baked goods.
For those visiting in mid-July, keep an eye out for the Giant Street Market, a massive annual event that expands significantly with over 100 vendors stretching along Willow Street.

As an outdoor event, the market operates in most weather conditions. On a rainy Wednesday, you can easily duck into the nearby Chemainus Public Market to continue your shopping in a sheltered environment.
In keeping with the local commitment to sustainability, many vendors prefer that customers bring their own shopping bags for produce and larger finds.
Held in the Waterwheel Park/Square parking lot, directly adjacent to the Chemainus Visitor Centre.
Runs weekly on Wednesdays from mid-May through mid-September.
The market area is flat and paved, making it fully accessible for wheelchairs and strollers.
While the market takes up a portion of the main lot, ample free street parking and additional public lots are available within a short two-block radius.
Well-behaved dogs on leashes are generally welcome in the outdoor market area, though it can get quite crowded during the peak summer months.

places.name: 10. BC Forest Discovery Centre
places.section: Other Interesting Places In and Around Chemainus
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/train-trestle-surrounded-by-autumn-colors-viewed-by-drone-gm2181605951-600615712

The BC Forest Discovery Centre is a 100-acre open-air museum in Duncan, 17 kilometers away from Chemainus, that brings the coastal province's forestry heritage to life. It is widely considered a must-visit for families and history enthusiasts, offering an immersive look at the industry that built many Vancouver Island communities.
What to See and Do
The center is designed around a series of historical buildings and outdoor exhibits that illustrate the evolution of logging technology.
The Steam Train: One of the main highlights is a ride on the historic Samson narrow-gauge steam train. The track winds through the forest and crosses a scenic trestle over Somenos Lake.
Forestry Equipment: The grounds are home to a massive collection of big iron logging machinery, including steam donkeys, vintage trucks, and a fully restored sawmill.
Historical Buildings: Visitors can explore a series of relocated heritage structures, such as an authentic logging camp, a one-room schoolhouse, and a ranger’s station.
Educational Nature Trails: Beyond the machinery, the center features nature trails that educate visitors on sustainable forest management and the local ecosystem of the Cowichan Valley.
Tips and Key Information
The steam train is a major draw but typically operates on a specific seasonal schedule. Be sure to arrive at the station early to secure a spot for the next departure.
The center is famous for its holiday-themed events, such as the Halloween Train and the Christmas Express, which feature light displays and festive activities.
There are several picturesque picnic areas located throughout the 100-acre site. Enjoying a meal under the canopy of the forest is a great way to extend your visit.
Given the size of the property and the nature of the trails, sturdy walking shoes are highly recommended, especially if you plan to explore the more remote exhibits.
Location: 2892 Drinkwater Rd, North Cowichan, BC..
Ticket prices vary by age and season, with family passes often available for better value.
The main exhibition areas and the train station are accessible, though some of the natural forest trails feature uneven or unpaved terrain.
There is a large, free parking lot at the entrance capable of accommodating RVs and tour buses.
The site includes a gift shop, clean restrooms, and a seasonal concession stand for snacks and drinks.

places.name: 11. Thetis & Penelakut
places.section: Other Interesting Places In and Around Chemainus
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/scenic-waterfront-view-of-gulf-islands-in-british-columbia-canada-gm2221189242-637553049

Thetis Island and Penelakut Island are two distinct gems in the Southern Gulf Islands, accessible via a short ferry ride from the Chemainus Ferry Terminal. While they are close neighbors, each offers a unique atmosphere—Thetis is known for its quiet, rural charm and artisan community, while Penelakut Island is the home of the Penelakut Tribe and holds deep indigenous cultural significance.
What to See and Do

Kayaking and Paddling: The calm, sheltered waters of Telegraph Harbour on Thetis Island are perfect for beginners and experienced paddlers alike. The area is dotted with small islets and hidden coves that are best explored by water.
Artisans and Vineyards: Thetis is home to several boutique galleries and the Thetis Island Vineyard, where visitors can sample locally produced wines in a serene, pastoral setting.

Penelakut Cultural Respect: Penelakut Island is a private community. Visitors often enjoy the scenic beauty from the ferry or water, but it is important to remember that access to the island's interior is generally restricted to residents and invited guests.

Beachcombing at Pilkey Point: Located at the northern tip of Thetis, this park offers rugged shoreline and expansive views across the Stuart Channel. It is an ideal spot for sunset watching or spotting marine wildlife.
Tips and Key Information
The Thetis-Penelakut Ferry operates on a triangle route from Chemainus. Pay close attention to the schedule, as some sailings go to Thetis first, while others stop at Penelakut first.
The Thetis Island Marina & Post Office is the social heart of the island. It’s the best place to grab a casual meal, pick up supplies, or chat with locals about the best hidden trails.
Thetis is relatively small and very bike-friendly. Cycling the quiet island roads is an excellent way to see the different galleries and shoreline access points without needing a car.

When passing Penelakut Island, keep an eye out for traditional canoes and the beautiful longhouse architecture from the water, which provides a glimpse into the enduring heritage of the Penelakut people.
Accessible via a 25-minute BC Ferries crossing from Chemainus. The ferry carries both vehicles and foot passengers.
Thetis Island has limited commercial services. It is recommended to fuel up your vehicle and pick up any major groceries in Chemainus before heading over.

The ferry terminals are accessible, but many of the natural beach access points on Thetis involve steep paths or stairs. The Telegraph Harbour area is the most accessible for those with mobility concerns.
Public washrooms and basic amenities are located at the Thetis Island Marina. There are no public tourist facilities on Penelakut Island.

places.name: 12. Somenos Marsh Wildlife Refuge
places.section: Other Interesting Places In and Around Chemainus
body: Somenos Marsh Wildlife Refuge (now primarily known as the Somenos Conservation Area) is a 200-hectare sanctuary in Duncan, BC. It is a critical stop on the Pacific Flyway and is recognized as an Important Bird and Biodiversity Area (IBA).
What to See and Do

The Open Air Classroom: Located just off Highway 1, this is the primary access point. It features an elevated boardwalk that leads through the marsh, offering wide-open views of the wetlands without disturbing the habitat.
Drinkwater Dock: Accessible via a short spur off Drinkwater Road, this dock provides a panoramic viewing platform over Somenos Lake, ideal for spotting waterfowl in the deeper sections of the lake.

S’amunu (Dike) Trail: A flat gravel and boardwalk trail that follows the edge of the conservation area. It’s an easy, accessible walk that connects several interpretive stations explaining the ecological and Quw’utsun cultural history of the watershed.

Garry Oak Protected Area: This section protects one of the last remaining deep-soil Garry Oak ecosystems. It is home to the second-largest Garry Oak tree in British Columbia and comes alive with wildflowers like the Yellow Montane Violet in the spring.
Trumpeter Swans: The marsh is famous for hosting one of the largest over-wintering populations of Trumpeter Swans on Vancouver Island (often numbering between 600 and 1,000 birds).
Great Blue Herons: A specific sub-species of heron frequent the marsh year-round.
Mammals: Keep an eye on the water channels for river otters, beavers, and muskrats, which are frequently seen near the boardwalks at dawn and dusk.
Salmon Nursery: The creeks feeding the marsh (Bings, Averill, and Richards) serve as vital nurseries for coho and chum salmon.
Tips and Key Information

The golden hour here is particularly striking because the low sun reflects off the standing water and highlights the texture of the marsh grasses. Winter mornings often bring a low mist over the lake, providing a dramatic backdrop for photographing the swans.

While open year-round, late autumn through early spring is peak for birders due to the massive influx of migratory waterfowl. April and May are best for seeing the rare Garry Oak meadow wildflowers in bloom.
Take time to read the interpretive signs regarding Ye’yumnuts, an ancient Quw’utsun cultural site nearby, to understand the deep ancestral connection the Cowichan Tribes have with this land.
The main parking lot is located on the east side of Highway 1, just north of Beverly Street. It is a convenient nature pit stop if you are traveling between Victoria and Nanaimo.

places.name: 13. Mount Brenton Golf Club
places.section: Other Interesting Places In and Around Chemainus
body: Mount Brenton Golf Course is a scenic, par-71 course located in Chemainus, BC, known for its parkland setting and walkable layout. Established in 1948, it offers a blend of historical charm and a challenging variety of holes that wind through mature forests.
What to See and Do

Strategic Design: The course is relatively tight and heavily treed, demanding accuracy over distance. Many fairways are lined with towering firs and cedars, requiring careful club selection and shot placement.
Water Hazards: Several ponds and creeks come into play, particularly on the back nine, adding both visual appeal and technical difficulty.
Greens Quality: Reviewers frequently highlight the well-maintained, smooth-rolling greens and the consistent condition of the fairways throughout the season.
Walkability: Unlike many mountain courses, the terrain here is mostly flat or gently rolling, making it an excellent choice for golfers who prefer to walk rather than use a power cart.
Clubhouse: Features a fully stocked pro shop and a relaxed restaurant and lounge area, often praised for its welcoming atmosphere and views of the opening and closing holes.
Practice Area: There is a dedicated practice putting green and a chipping area to sharpen your short game before heading to the first tee.
Tips and Key Information

The golden hourh here creates long shadows through the old-growth trees, which is ideal for capturing the classic Pacific Northwest golf aesthetic. The 13th hole is often cited as one of the most picturesque spots on the course.
Thanks to the temperate climate of Vancouver Island, the course remains playable year-round. It is particularly vibrant in late spring when the surrounding vegetation is in full bloom.
Located just minutes from the famous Chemainus Murals, it is easy to combine a morning round with an afternoon exploring the town's art and local shops.

places.name: 14. Xihwu Reef
places.section: Other Interesting Places In and Around Chemainus
body: Xihwu Reef (pronounced "KEY-quot") is a unique artificial reef located just off the coast of Kinsmen Beach Park (Kin Beach) in Chemainus. It gained international attention in 2006 when a decommissioned Boeing 737-200 was submerged to create a complex marine habitat, making it the only aircraft of its kind used as an artificial reef in Canada.
What to See and Do

The Airframe: The 100-foot-long fuselage rests about 70 to 100 feet below the surface. It was prepared by the Artificial Reef Society of BC to ensure it was environmentally safe and accessible for divers, with several entry and exit points cut into the body.

Marine Colonization: Since its sinking, the Xihwu (the Hul’q’umi’num’ word for "Osprey") has become a thriving ecosystem. It is now home to a massive population of plumose anemones, rockfish, lingcod, and hundreds of red sea urchins.
The Experience: Divers can swim through the cabin and even visit the cockpit. Because it sits on 15-foot cradles off the ocean floor, marine life can circulate entirely around and under the aircraft.
Tips and Key Information

While the reef is just off Kin Beach, it is generally considered a boat-access dive. The distance and depth make it a difficult shore swim for most. Local charters out of Chemainus or Ladysmith are the most common way to reach the buoyed site.
Due to the depth (reaching 100 feet at the tail) and the potential for overhead environments inside the plane, this is typically categorized as an advanced dive.
For those looking for a slightly shallower experience, four wooden barges were sunk nearby in 2012. These lie in roughly 60 feet of water and are also teeming with local sea life.

The best diving conditions in the Salish Sea usually occur from late autumn through early spring. During these months, the water is colder, but the plankton blooms are minimal, leading to much clearer visibility for seeing the scale of the aircraft.

For postcard style underwater shots, wide-angle lenses are essential to capture the silhouette of the plane. The golden hour light from the surface can sometimes penetrate deep enough to create ethereal beams through the cabin windows on clear winter days.

If you are visiting Kin Beach but not diving, the park offers a paved boat launch, picnic tables, and views of Bird Rock and Tent Island. It’s a great spot to watch the dive boats head out to the reef site.

places.name: 15. Weyerhauser Mill
places.section: Other Interesting Places In and Around Chemainus
body: While the name Weyerhaeuser is synonymous with the history of the Chemainus Sawmill, the facility is currently owned and operated by Western Forest Products. It remains the industrial heartbeat of the town and a significant landmark for those interested in the evolution of the Pacific Northwest timber industry.
What to See and Do

The Big Mill: The site has hosted a sawmill since 1862, making it one of the oldest continuously operating industrial sites in British Columbia. Weyerhaeuser acquired the mill in 1999 as part of its purchase of MacMillan Bloedel, before it eventually transitioned to Western Forest Products in the mid-2000s.

Economic Anchor: For over a century, the mill has been the primary employer in Chemainus. Even as the town successfully diversified into tourism and the arts (following a major mill downsizing in the 1980s), the sawmill remains a critical contributor to the local economy.
Modern Operations: Today, the mill focuses on high-value wood products, particularly custom-cut Douglas fir and Western Red Cedar lumber destined for international markets.
Public Access: As an active industrial site, the mill is not open for public tours. However, its scale and the massive log booms in the water can be seen from various vantage points in town.
Waterfront Views: The best place to observe the mill's scale and the tugboat activity is from the Waterwheel Park area or while walking along the nearby shoreline trails.

Interpretive History: The Chemainus Valley Museum provides a deep dive into the mill’s history, featuring artifacts, old photographs, and stories about the Steam Donkey era of logging that built the community.
Tips and Key Information

Like many forestry operations in BC, the mill has faced temporary curtailments recently due to global market conditions. As of early 2026, operations have been intermittent, though the value-added division nearby typically continues to process specialized products.

To see the mill through an artistic lens, look for Mural #1 (Steam Train and Mill) and Mural #12 (The 1891 Mill) in the downtown core. These provide a then and now perspective that is hard to capture from the modern fence line.

For a dramatic industrial shot, visit the waterfront at golden hour. The silhouette of the mill machinery against the Stuart Channel, often with mist rising from the log booms, captures the gritty beauty of a working coastal town.

If you are looking for a mill experience you can actually walk through, the McLean Mill National Historic Site in Port Alberni (about 90 minutes away) is a restored steam-powered sawmill that offers full public access.

places.name: 1. West Edmonton Mall
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/west-edmonton-mall-ice-palace-gm2188899840-607395911

West Edmonton Mall is much more than a shopping center—it is a massive, self-contained entertainment city that spans the equivalent of 48 city blocks. Since opening in 1981, it has remained the largest shopping mall in North America and ranks among the top ten largest in the world.
What to See and Do
World Waterpark: Home to the world’s largest indoor wave pool and over 17 waterslides. It maintains a tropical temperature of 28°C year-round.

Galaxyland Powered by Hasbro: One of the world's largest indoor amusement parks, featuring over 27 rides, including the triple-loop Mindbender and family favorites themed after brands like Monopoly and My Little Pony.
Sea Life Caverns & Marine Life: An underground aquarium and certified zoo home to sharks, sea turtles, and penguins. You can even see live sea lion shows at Sea Lions' Rock.
Ice Palace: An NHL-sized skating rink located under a stunning glass dome where you can rent skates or watch local hockey practices.
DRIVE: A state-of-the-art, multi-level electric go-kart track—one of the only ones of its kind in North America.
BRBN St. (Bourbon Street): Modeled after New Orleans' French Quarter, this area features dim nighttime lighting and is the mall's primary hub for upscale dining and nightlife.
Europa Boulevard: Designed to look like a classic European streetscape with cobblestones and faux-balconies, housing boutique shops and the Simons department store.
Chinatown: An Asian-themed marketplace anchored by a T&T Supermarket, complete with traditional Far-Eastern décor.
Key Info & Tips
The Fantasyland Hotel is located right inside the mall and is famous for its immersive theme rooms, such as Space, Igloo, and Pirates.
It is a 25-minute drive from downtown Edmonton and has a major transit center for buses. It features the world's largest parking lot, with room for over 20,000 vehicles.
Wear your most comfortable walking shoes. Traversing the entire mall can easily result in several kilometers of walking.
In winter, use the lockers near the Waterpark or the coat check services to avoid carrying heavy parkas through the climate-controlled (23°C) interior.

places.name: 2. North Saskatchewan River Valley
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/edmonton-north-saskatchewan-river-valley-landscape-with-groat-bridge-gm2186859931-605485546

The North Saskatchewan River Valley is a massive, winding ribbon of green that is 22 times the size of New York's Central Park. As the largest urban parkland in North America, it offers a wilderness experience right in the middle of a major city, connecting over 20 major parks and 150 kilometers of trails.
What to See and Do
Traverse the Trail Network: Whether you are hiking, trail running, or mountain biking, the valley offers everything from paved, multi-use paths to single-track dirt trails that feel like deep forest.

High Level Bridge & Streetcar: For the best view in the city, ride the historic High Level Bridge Streetcar. It is the highest river crossing by streetcar in the world, providing a 360-degree panorama of the valley and the legislative grounds.
Paddle the River: During the summer, you can rent kayaks, canoes, or paddleboards. Floating from Terwillegar Park down to the downtown core is a quintessential Edmonton summer activity.

100th Street Funicular: This modern glass elevator/tramway connects the downtown core to the river valley floor. It features a viewing platform that extends out over the valley, offering a perfect spot for photography.

Winter Wonderland: The valley doesn't close in winter. It becomes a hub for cross-country skiing, fat biking on the snow, and outdoor skating at Victoria Park, which features a 400-meter scenic ice trail called the Freezeway.
Segway Tours: Several local operators offer off-road Segway tours through the valley, providing a fun way to cover a lot of ground while learning about the area’s history and ecology.
Tips & Key Info
It is very common to spot deer, coyotes, porcupines, and even the occasional moose. Keep your distance and keep dogs on a leash unless in designated off-leash areas like Buena Vista Park.
The river valley is home to major events like the Edmonton Folk Music Festival (held on the slopes of Gallagher Park) and the Silver Skate Festival in Hawrelak Park.
Because the valley is so large, it’s easy to get turned around. Always carry a phone with GPS or use the City of Edmonton Parks and River Valley digital map.
If you’re looking for a workout, locals flock to the Wolf Willow Stairs or the stairs near the Royal Alberta Museum for intense stair-climbing sessions with a view.

places.name: 3. Rogers Place
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/rogers-place-arena-edmonton-alberta-canada-gm1277958045-377025736

Rogers Place is a state-of-the-art sports and entertainment arena in downtown Edmonton and the home of the NHL’s Edmonton Oilers. Opened in 2016, it anchors the ICE District and brings high-energy crowds to concerts, games, and other large events throughout the year.

This place’s history is closely tied to the city’s revitalization plans, transforming a once-quiet zone into a vibrant commercial and cultural hub. The arena’s glass design, massive scoreboard, and sound quality make it a standout even by global standards. Whether you're a hockey fan or not, the energy around Rogers Place during events is hard to miss.
What to See and Do

Catch the Action: It is the home of the NHL's Edmonton Oilers and the WHL's Edmonton Oil Kings. With a capacity of over 18,500 for hockey and 20,000+ for concerts, it’s one of the most energetic venues in North America.

Great One Statue: No visit is complete without a photo with the bronze statue of Wayne Gretzky, located outside the arena. Inside, you can explore the Oilers Hall of Fame to see five replica Stanley Cups and historic jerseys.

Ford Hall: This 25,000-square-foot public atrium spans across 104th Avenue. Look up to see Tsa Tsa Ke K'e (Iron Foot Place), a massive 45-foot circular mosaic by world-renowned artist Alex Janvier, made of nearly one million glass tiles.
Scoreboard: Look up during a game to see the largest true high-definition center-hung scoreboard in the NHL—measuring a staggering 46 by 46 feet.
Guided Tours: For the ultimate fan experience, you can take a Classic Tour or an Alumni-Hosted Tour to see the press level, star rooms, and even the Oilers' bench (when available).
Tips & Key Info
Even if you don't have a ticket, the outdoor plaza often hosts massive watch parties on giant screens during the playoffs, as well as community markets and festivals.
Located in Ford Hall, Molson Hockey House is a popular pre-game spot for fans. It's open to the public (no ticket required) and features big-screen TVs and the home of the $7 beer.

Avoid the $30+ parking fees by using the LRT. The MacEwan Station is the closest, but the venue is also connected to the downtown pedway system, allowing you to walk from nearby hotels like the JW Marriott without going outside.
Like many modern arenas, Rogers Place is completely cashless. All concessions and retail stores accept debit, credit, and mobile payments (Apple Pay, etc.).
Use the Rogers Place app or website's Food Finder to locate specific snacks—from traditional pierogies to gourmet Korean brats—so you don't spend the whole intermission searching.

places.name: 4. Elk Island National Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/bison-at-elk-island-parc-edmonton-alberta-gm1448572787-486051875

Elk Island National Park is an ecological gem located 35 minutes east of Edmonton. It is Canada's only completely fenced national park and serves as a vital refuge for bison, elk, and over 250 species of birds. Unlike the mountain parks, Elk Island offers a serene, prairie safari experience through rolling aspen parkland and glassy lakes.
What to See and Do
Bison Watching: This is the primary draw. You can often spot herds of Plains Bison along the Bison Loop Road (near the south entrance) or Wood Bison along the trails in the park’s southern half.

Stargazing & Northern Lights: As part of the Beaver Hills Dark Sky Preserve, the park is one of the best places in Alberta to see the Milky Way or the Aurora Borealis. The dark skies here are protected from city light pollution.
Paddling Astotin Lake: Rent a canoe, kayak, or stand-up paddleboard to explore the many islands of Astotin Lake. It is particularly stunning at sunset.

Hiking the Trails: There are over 80 km of trails. The Amisk Wuche Trail (2.7 km) features floating boardwalks over beaver ponds, while the Hayburger Trail (11.6 km) is a favorite for spotting plains bison in open meadows.
Red Chairs: Seek out the iconic Parks Canada red Adirondack chairs placed at scenic viewpoints throughout the park—perfect for a quiet moment and a photo op.
Winter Adventures: In the winter, the lake becomes a giant skating rink, and the hiking trails are perfect for snowshoeing and cross-country skiing.
Tips & Key Information
Bison may look like cows, but they are fast and unpredictable. To stay safe, stay at least 100 meters away.
Don't be surprised if a herd decides to walk down the middle of the road. If this happens, stay in your car, keep your windows up, and wait patiently. Never honk.

There are very limited food options within the park. Pack a cooler with lunch and plenty of water, as the picnic areas at Astotin Lake are top-notch and have fire pits (bring your own wood or buy it on-site).
You will need a Parks Canada pass to enter. You can buy a day pass at the gate or use a Discovery Pass if you have one.
The park’s wetlands mean mosquitoes can be intense in the summer, and the open meadows offer little shade. Bring bug spray and sunscreen.

places.name: 5. Muttart Conservatory
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/muttart-conservatory-in-edmonton-canada-gm518522601-49636910

The Muttart Conservatory is one of Edmonton’s most recognizable landmarks, featuring four iconic glass pyramids, each housing a different climate and collection of plants, that dominate the river valley skyline. This place showcases global ecosystems, including arid deserts, lush rainforests, and temperate landscapes, all in one spot.
What to See and Do
Explore the Four Biomes: Each pyramid represents a different world climate, housing over 700 species of plants:
Tropical Pyramid: A lush, humid escape with towering palms, orchids, and a cascading waterfall. It’s the city's favorite refuge during the deep winter.
Arid Pyramid: Home to tough plants from five continents, including exotic cacti, succulents, and agave that thrive in dry, desert-like conditions.
Temperate Pyramid: This biome mimics the changing seasons. You’ll find plants from the southern Great Lakes, Australia, and Asia, including redwoods and eucalyptus.
Feature Pyramid: The surprise of the group. Its display changes 5–7 times a year to host themed floral exhibits (like the current Prehistoric Paradise featuring dinosaurs among the plants).
Dining at Café Bloom: This local favorite is located in the central foyer. They use fresh herbs and greens grown right on-site at the Muttart to create locally-sourced, seasonal dishes.

Adults-Only Evenings: On Wednesday and Thursday nights, the conservatory stays open until 10:00 PM. Wednesday evenings are strictly for adults (18+), often featuring Happy Hour drinks and a more tranquil atmosphere.

2026 Penguin/Prehistoric Exhibits: As of early 2026, the conservatory is running special family events like the Prehistoric Petals and Predators, where you can find hidden dinosaur statues lurking in the greenery.
Tips & Key Information
The conservatory is now incredibly easy to reach via the Valley Line Southeast LRT (Muttart Station), which drops you off right at the entrance.
If you are an Alberta resident, check for the seasonal promotion (running through March 2026) that offers 2-for-1 admission to both the Muttart and the Edmonton Valley Zoo.

The Tropical pyramid is a constant 24°C–28°C with high humidity, while the Arid and Temperate pyramids can be cooler. Use the on-site lockers to ditch your heavy winter parka before you start your tour.
The pyramids are a photographer's dream. For the best mirrored effect of the pyramids against the skyline, head to the grassy hills just outside the building at sunset.
While walk-ins are often welcome, it is highly recommended to book a timeslot online on weekends to ensure entry during busy hours.

places.name: 6. Alberta Legislature Building
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/view-of-the-alberta-legislature-building-across-the-water-gm115448367-7481248

The Alberta Legislature Building, affectionately known by locals as The Ledge, is the seat of democracy in Alberta. Built between 1907 and 1913, this Beaux-Arts masterpiece sits on 57 acres of lush parkland overlooking the North Saskatchewan River valley. It is an architectural gem and a key landmark in Edmonton, known for its grand Beaux-Arts design and beautifully landscaped grounds. Visitors flock here to explore its historic halls and learn about Alberta’s government and political heritage.
What to See and Do

Magic Spot: On the fifth floor, stand in a specific spot directly above the rotunda fountain. Due to the acoustic design of the dome, the sound of the falling water will seem to rain down on you from above rather than coming from below.

Rotunda: Marvel at the massive 16-ton Canadian marble pillars and the commemorative fountain built for Queen Elizabeth II’s 1959 visit. Look for the portraits of Alberta's Premiers and the hidden hamburger—a preserved 1969 burger kept in the Legislature Library.

Visitor Centre: Located nearby in the Queen Elizabeth II Building, the Visitor Centre features the Pehonan Theatre, which offers a 4D cinematic history of Alberta, and the Borealis Gallery for rotating exhibits.
Wading & Skating: The grounds are a community hub; you can wade in the massive reflecting pools during the summer or skate on the illuminated outdoor rink throughout the winter.

Purple City: A long-standing quirky tradition where visitors stare into the building's bright floodlights for a few seconds and then look away, causing their vision to be temporarily bathed in a surreal purple hue.
Tips & Key Information

Highly recommended 45-minute tours are free of charge. They cover the art, architecture, and parliamentary traditions of the building. It is best to register online in advance, especially during the summer.
When the Legislative Assembly is in session, the public can sit in the gallery to watch live debates. Check the Assembly calendar online to see if the MLAs are sitting during your visit.
The building is easily accessible via the LRT (Grandano/Government Centre Station), which is connected to the grounds via an underground walkway.
places.note: Note that the main public entrance for tours and visitors is located on the west side of the building.

places.name: 7. Fairmont Hotel Macdonald
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/fairmont-hotel-macdonald-gm1332897648-415607187

The Fairmont Hotel Macdonald, known affectionately by locals as The Mac, is Edmonton's most storied hotel. Opened in 1915, this “Castle on the River” is a classic example of Canada’s grand railway hotels, blending chateau-style architecture with over a century of royal and celebrity history.
What to See and Do

Confederation Lounge: Often cited as the best place for a drink in the city, this lounge feels like a private club from a bygone era, complete with library-style seating and a massive heritage painting of the Fathers of Confederation.

Famous Patio: During the summer, the hotel's terrace offers the most iconic panoramic view of the North Saskatchewan River Valley. It’s a premier spot for high tea or an evening cocktail while watching the sunset over the valley.

Empire Ballroom: A designated municipal heritage resource, this ballroom features breathtaking 21-foot ceilings and intricate crystal chandeliers. It has hosted countless gala events and remains one of the most elegant spaces in Western Canada.

Meet Smudge: One of the hotel’s most charming traditions is its Canine Ambassador. Visitors can often find a friendly yellow lab greeting guests in the lobby, carrying on the hotel's long-standing pet-friendly legacy.
Tips & Key Information

The hotel's weekend Afternoon Tea is a legendary Edmonton experience. It typically includes a guided tour of the hotel’s historic rooms, but you must book several weeks in advance as it frequently sells out.
You don't need to be a guest to enjoy the landmark. Many locals visit specifically to walk the grounds or dine at The Harvest Room, which is celebrated for its regional farm-to-fork Alberta cuisine.
Keep an eye out for heritage plaques throughout the lobby and hallways that detail the hotel's narrow escape from demolition in the 1980s and its subsequent multi-million dollar restoration.
The back gardens provide a stunning vantage point of the building's limestone facade against the modern downtown skyline—a favorite spot for wedding and graduation photos.

places.name: 8. Walterdale Bridge
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/walterdale-suspension-bridge-and-saskatchewan-river-with-skyline-in-edmonton-alberta-gm1468092463-499705738

The Walterdale Bridge is one of Edmonton’s most striking modern engineering feats, serving as a sleek gateway between the city’s south side and its downtown core. Replacing an older truss bridge, this signature cable-supported arch structure has quickly become a favorite subject for local photographers due to its graceful, minimalist design and bright white finish.
What to See and Do

Architectural Significance: The bridge features two towering 56-meter-high arches that lean slightly toward each other, creating a unique silhouette that stands out against the lush greenery of the River Valley.

Pedestrian Experience: A dedicated, wide pedestrian path on the east side of the bridge offers safe and scenic passage for walkers and cyclists, providing some of the best unobstructed views of the Edmonton skyline and the North Saskatchewan River Valley.

Photography Hub: The area surrounding the bridge—specifically the lookout points on the south bank—is arguably the most popular spot in the city for sunset photos, wedding shoots, and capturing the city lights at night.

Integration with Nature: The bridge design incorporates river-friendly engineering, with no piers in the water, which helps preserve the natural flow of the river and protects the local aquatic habitat.
Tips & Key Information
For the most iconic shot, head to the Walterdale Bridge Hillside Lookout on the south side of the river; it offers a perfect perspective of the arches framing the downtown skyscrapers.
The bridge is illuminated at night with soft white lights, making it a peaceful and beautiful destination for a late-evening walk.
It is easily accessible via the extensive river valley trail system, making it a natural stop if you are already exploring the nearby Kinsmen Park or the Alberta Legislature Building.

places.name: 1. Fort Edmonton Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/fort-edmonton-alberta-gm173757691-25828078

Fort Edmonton Park is Canada's largest living history museum, offering an immersive journey through four distinct eras of Edmonton's development. Spread across 158 acres in the river valley, it uses meticulously reconstructed streets and costumed interpreters to bring the past to life.
What to See and Do
Four Historical Eras: Visitors can explore the 1846 Hudson’s Bay Company Fort, followed by 1885 Street (Settlement Era), 1905 Street (Municipal Era), and 1920 Street (Metropolitan Era).

Vintage Transportation: The park features a functional steam train that transports guests from the entrance to the fort, as well as operational streetcars and horse-drawn carriages that travel the historic streets.

Indigenous Peoples Experience: This award-winning, world-class exhibit was created in partnership with local Indigenous communities. It uses stunning cinematography and oral histories to explore the deep connections between First Nations and Métis peoples and this land.
Midway: A recreation of a 1920s-style fairground, complete with a classic carousel, a Ferris wheel, and a vintage-style outdoor cinema showing silent films.
Tips & Key Information

The park primarily operates during the summer months (late May through Labor Day). However, it hosts popular ticketed events in the off-season, such as the spooky Dark during October and festive winter displays.
With over 150 acres to explore and uneven gravel or boardwalk paths, comfortable walking footwear is essential for a full day of touring.
Given the scale of the attractions and the live demonstrations (like blacksmithing or baking), most visitors spend at least 4 to 6 hours to see everything without rushing.

While many of the historic buildings have ramps, the vintage nature of some structures can pose challenges. The steam train is wheelchair accessible, and modern restrooms are available throughout the site.

places.name: 2. Royal Alberta Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/main-entrance-to-the-royal-alberta-museum-or-ram-a-museum-of-human-and-natural-gm1478264065-506574047

The Royal Alberta Museum is the largest museum in Western Canada and a premier cultural landmark located in the heart of Edmonton's Arts District. Housed in a massive, modern facility that opened in 2018, it offers a deep dive into the natural and human history of Alberta through expansive, world-class galleries.
What to See and Do

Human History Hall: This gallery explores the diverse stories of people who have called Alberta home for thousands of years. It features powerful displays on Indigenous cultures, including the sacred Manitou Stone, and stories of immigration and industry.

Natural History Hall: A favorite for all ages, this hall showcases the province’s diverse landscapes and prehistoric past. You can see life-sized Ice Age mammoths, ancient fossils, and an impressive collection of sparkling minerals and gems.

Bug Gallery: For those who aren't squeamish, this unique space features live invertebrates from around the world. It’s an immersive experience where you can see giant walking sticks, tarantulas, and colorful beetles up close.
Children’s Gallery: This is a dedicated, hands-on learning space designed specifically for kids to play, discover, and experiment with history and science in an interactive environment.
Tips & Key Information
To ensure a smooth visit, it is highly recommended to book your timed-entry tickets online in advance, especially during weekends and school holidays.
If you plan on visiting more than once, consider the Mammoth Pass, which provides unlimited admission for a full year for a very reasonable price.
The museum features a modern café with locally sourced snacks and a gift shop that is excellent for finding unique Alberta-made crafts and educational books.
The facility is fully accessible, with elevators serving all floors and manual wheelchairs available for loan at the admissions desk on a first-come, first-served basis.

places.name: 3. Art Gallery of Alberta
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/art-gallery-of-alberta-in-downtown-edmonton-canada-gm1277957204-377025421

The Art Gallery of Alberta is a focal point of Edmonton’s downtown Arts District. Known as much for its striking architecture as for its collection, the gallery is a premier destination for visual arts enthusiasts in Western Canada.
What to See and Do

Architectural Photography: Designed by Randall Stout, the building itself is a masterpiece. The exterior features a massive, winding stainless steel and glass borealis ribbon that mimics the movement of the Northern Lights and the North Saskatchewan River.
Diverse Collections: The gallery maintains over 6,000 works of art, ranging from historical and contemporary Canadian paintings and sculptures to significant international prints and photographs.
RBC New Works Gallery: This dedicated space features rotating exhibitions from contemporary Alberta artists, providing a platform for the province's emerging and established creative voices.
Art Rental and Sales: For a unique local experience, visit the Art Rental and Sales gallery on the lower level, where you can browse and even rent original works by regional artists.
Tips & Key Information
To make art more accessible, the AGA often offers free admission on the last Thursday of every month from 4:00 PM to 7:00 PM. They also provide free admission for all students and youths under 18.
Located on the main floor, May offers a sophisticated dining experience with a menu that changes seasonally, often drawing inspiration from current exhibitions.

Public tours are typically available on weekends and are included with the price of admission. These tours offer deeper insights into both the architecture of the building and the stories behind the art.
The gift shop is one of the best in the city for finding high-quality art supplies, unique jewelry, and beautifully curated coffee table books.

places.name: 4. Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Village
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/a-family-walking-around-the-ukranian-cultural-heritage-village-exploring-all-the-gm1665965507-535402416

The Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Village is an award-winning open-air museum located about 25 minutes east of Edmonton (just past Elk Island National Park). It offers a powerful, living history experience that recreates the life of early Ukrainian pioneers who settled in east-central Alberta between 1892 and 1930.
What to See and Do

Interact with History: The village features over 30 historic structures—including sod houses, grain elevators, and blacksmith shops—all relocated from nearby communities. Costumed role-players act as the original settlers; they stay strictly in character and will speak to you as if it is still the early 20th century.
Cultural Traditions: Visitors can observe traditional crafts and activities such as woodstove cooking, gardening with heirloom seeds, and vintage blacksmithing.
Authentic Cuisine: The food services on-site are highly rated, offering traditional Ukrainian staples such as handmade pierogies (pyrohy), cabbage rolls (holubtsi), and kielbasa.
Monument to the Pioneers: Don't miss the Centenary Pioneer Recognition Monument, which honors the families who first established the vibrant Ukrainian community in the region.
Tips & Key Information

Like Fort Edmonton, this is primarily a seasonal attraction, typically open from May (Victoria Day weekend) through September (Labor Day). It is best to check their website for specific Harvest Day or festival dates.
To get the most out of your visit, ask the role-players questions about their lives and families. They are highly trained in the history of the specific individuals they portray.
Since it is located right next to Elk Island National Park, many travelers visit the Village in the morning and head to the park for a sunset picnic or bison viewing in the afternoon.
While the site is large and outdoors, there is a shuttle service available to help transport visitors between the various neighborhoods within the village.

places.name: 5. Rutherford House Provincial Historic Site
body: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Rutherford_House_University_of_Alberta_Edmonton_Alberta_Canada_03.jpg

Rutherford House is a beautifully restored Edwardian mansion that served as the home of Alexander Cameron Rutherford, Alberta's first Premier. Located on the edge of the University of Alberta campus, it offers a glimpse into the lifestyle and politics of Edmonton's elite during the early 20th century.
What to See and Do

Guided Heritage Tours: Costumed interpreters guide visitors through the elegantly furnished rooms, sharing stories about the Rutherford family's daily life and the historical significance of the premier's work.
Period Architecture and Decor: The house is a stunning example of Edwardian design, featuring ornate woodwork, stained glass, and authentic artifacts from the 1911 era.
Arbour Tea Room: Visitors can enjoy a traditional light lunch or a formal afternoon tea within the historic setting of the house, though reservations are highly recommended.
Beautifully Landscaped Grounds: The exterior features manicured gardens and views overlooking the river valley, making it a popular spot for quiet walks and photography.
Tips & Key Information
The site is typically open from Wednesday to Sunday, between 10:00 AM and 5:00 PM. It is generally closed on Mondays and Tuesdays.
Since it is located on Saskatchewan Drive at the University of Alberta, it is easily accessible via the University LRT station and a short walk.
The house frequently hosts seasonal events, such as Christmas programs with traditional decorations and summer garden parties.
While the main floor is accessible, the historic nature of the building means that upper floors are reached via stairs, so it is best to inquire ahead if you have specific mobility needs.

places.name: 6. Citadel Theatre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/citadel-theatre-in-edmonton-gm518594371-49387170

The Citadel Theatre is one of North America’s largest and most respected non-profit regional theatres. Located in the heart of downtown Edmonton, this massive complex is a cornerstone of the city’s vibrant Arts District and is renowned for its architectural beauty and commitment to high-quality performance.
What to See and Do

Five Performance Spaces: The facility is unique in that it houses five distinct performance venues under one roof, ranging from the grand Shoctor Theatre for large-scale musicals to the more intimate Rice Theatre and Zeidler Hall.

Lee Pavilion: This stunning indoor glass garden features lush greenery, tropical plants, and a waterfall. It serves as a peaceful public space where visitors can relax before a show or during their lunch hour.

Diverse Programming: The Citadel is known for a balanced mix of classic plays, contemporary works, and world-class musical theatre. It also houses the Robbins Academy, a premier training ground for theatre professionals.

Architectural Marvel: The building’s design features a striking glass-enclosed atrium that allows natural light to flood the public spaces, creating a seamless connection between the theatre and the surrounding urban environment.
Tips & Key Information
The theatre is conveniently connected to the Edmonton pedway system, providing easy indoor access to various nearby restaurants and cafes in the downtown core.

All of the Citadel's performance spaces are wheelchair accessible. The theatre also offers assistive listening devices and select relaxed performances designed for guests who might benefit from a less formal theatre environment.
Keep an eye out for Beyond the Stage events, which often include post-show talkbacks with the actors and directors, giving you a behind-the-scenes look at the production.

places.name: 7. St. Joseph's Basilica
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/edmonton-alberta-canada-gm157564392-11895502

St. Joseph’s Basilica is a striking Roman Catholic church located just west of downtown Edmonton, known for its towering twin spires and stained-glass windows. The building blends Gothic Revival architecture with warm stone and wood interiors, offering a peaceful space for reflection and admiration. This place serves as the archdiocese’s central church and has hosted major religious and civic events, including a visit from Pope John Paul II in 1984.
What to See and Do

Architectural Splendor: The building features a classic cruciform design with stunning stained-glass windows that depict various biblical scenes and saints, casting vibrant colors throughout the sanctuary.

Historical Significance: Originally started in 1924 and completed in 1963, it was designated a minor basilica by Pope John Paul II during his visit to Edmonton in 1984, an honor reserved for churches of particular historical or architectural importance.
Casavant Pipe Organ: Music enthusiasts often visit to hear the powerful Casavant Frères pipe organ, which provides a majestic soundtrack to liturgies and special choral performances.

A Place of Serenity: Even for those not attending a service, the basilica offers a quiet, contemplative atmosphere with its high vaulted ceilings and intricate marble work, making it a peaceful retreat in the Oliver neighborhood.
Tips & Key Information

While the basilica is open to the public, visitors are reminded to be respectful of ongoing services and private prayer. Photography is generally permitted but should be done discreetly and never during a Mass.
While formal tours are less frequent than at the Legislature, you can often find informational pamphlets near the entrance that detail the history of the various altars and artistic elements.
Situated just west of the downtown core, it is easily reachable via several bus routes along Jasper Avenue or a pleasant walk from the Government Centre LRT station.

places.name: 1. William Hawrelak Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/edmonton-william-hawrelak-park-pavilion-gm1446348417-484470505

Hawrelak Park, originally known as William Hawrelak Park, is a 68-hectare centerpiece of Edmonton’s river valley. It is widely regarded as one of the city's premier locations for large-scale community gatherings and outdoor recreation, though it is currently undergoing significant rehabilitation to preserve it for future generations.
What to See and Do

A Festival Epicenter: Historically, the park is the primary home for major Edmonton events, including the Heritage Festival, which celebrates multiculturalism with food and performances, and the Silver Skate Festival, Edmonton’s longest-running winter festival.

Heritage Amphitheatre: This is Western Canada’s largest outdoor covered amphitheatre. It features excellent acoustics and is a favorite venue for the Symphony Under the Sky and various theatrical performances.

Recreational Lake: The park features a large man-made lake that is a hub for activity year-round, offering scenic paddle boating in the summer and transformed into a sprawling skating surface in the winter.
Expansive Trail System: It serves as a major node in the river valley trail network, providing paved and gravel paths that connect to nearby Buena Vista Park and the Edmonton Valley Zoo.
Tips & Key Information

As of 2026, the park is closed for a multi-year rehabilitation project to replace aging infrastructure, including water and sewer lines. It is expected to reopen in phases so always check the City of Edmonton website for the latest access updates.

When open, the park features several large parking lots, but they fill up quickly during major festivals. During these times, the city typically runs Park and Ride shuttle services from nearby transit centers.
The park is famous for its numerous picnic sites and sheltered pavilions, making it the top choice in the city for large family reunions and corporate outings.

places.name: 2. Mill Creek Ravine Parkhttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/mill-creek-ravine-bridge-edmonton-alberta-canada-gm651117150-118245605
body: Mill Creek Ravine is a beloved tributary of the North Saskatchewan River Valley, winding through some of Edmonton's most established neighborhoods. It is cherished by locals for its rustic charm, dense tree canopy, and peaceful atmosphere that makes you feel miles away from the city despite being just minutes from downtown.
What to See and Do
Historic Trestle Bridges: The ravine is famous for its collection of historic wooden trestle bridges that offer perfect vantage points for viewing the creek and the changing seasons.
Off-Leash Adventures: It features one of the most popular off-leash dog areas in the city, particularly the Mill Creek Ravine South, where pets can roam through varied terrain.
Mill Creek Outdoor Pool: Located on the northern edge of the ravine, this historic pool is a summer hotspot for families, offering a chance to swim surrounded by the forest.
Birdwatching and Wildlife: Visitors often report sightings of pileated woodpeckers, owls, and deer along the quieter stretches of the unpaved lower trails.
Tips & Key Information
The ravine offers both paved upper paths (ideal for cyclists and strollers) and more rugged, unpaved lower trails that run closer to the water for a true hiking experience.
A favorite local ritual is grabbing a coffee at a nearby cafe in Ritchie or Bonnie Doon before heading into the ravine for a walk.
The ravine is particularly stunning in the autumn when the leaves change color, and it remains a hub for fat biking and snowshoeing throughout the winter months.
There are numerous entrances, but the parking lot at 76 Avenue and 95A Street provides easy access to the central part of the trail system and the picnic areas.

places.name: 3. Rundle Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/rundle-park-in-edmonton-horizontal-view-of-lake-with-grasses-gm179361702-26817848

Rundle Park is an expansive recreational hub in Edmonton's northeast river valley, offering a massive array of sports facilities and family-friendly amenities that make it one of the city's most active green spaces.
What to See and Do

Year-Round Recreation: The park features a unique IceWay during winter, a scenic outdoor skating trail that winds through the trees, while summer brings visitors to its popular Disc Golf Course and Par 3 Golf Course.
Family Amenities: It is a top choice for gatherings due to its numerous picnic sites, creative playgrounds, and several small lakes that are often used for paddleboarding or RC boating.

Active Lifestyle Hub: Beyond traditional park space, it houses the ACT Aquatic and Recreation Centre, along with dedicated areas for tennis, beach volleyball, and a popular ACT Hill for tobogganing in the winter.

Scenic Trails: The park is a major link in the river valley trail system, providing beautifully paved paths for cyclists and runners that offer sweeping views of the river and the Strathcona Science Provincial Park across the water.
Tips & Key Information

If you are visiting in the winter to skate the IceWay, be aware that while the path is maintained, natural outdoor conditions can vary. It is often less crowded on weekday evenings when the trail is beautifully illuminated.

The Rundle Park Disc Golf Course is one of the most popular in the region. If you are a beginner, try to go during off-peak morning hours, and remember that players traditionally allow faster, smaller groups to play through.

For tobogganing at ACT Hill, ensure you follow the posted safety signs. The hill is designated by the city as a safe sliding site, meaning it is regularly inspected for hazards and has a safe run-out area at the bottom.
Because of the numerous ponds and proximity to the river, mosquitoes can be quite active in the summer evenings. It's a good idea to bring repellent if you're planning a sunset picnic.

The park is massive with multiple entry points. If you are heading to the recreation centre or the swimming pool, use the entrance off 113 Avenue. For the golf course or disc golf, the northern entrance near 118 Avenue is more convenient.

places.name: 4. Terwillegar Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/terwillegar-park-footbridge-gm1392594700-448788674

Terwillegar Park is a sprawling 186-hectare riverfront destination in southwest Edmonton. It is widely considered one of the city's best locations for those seeking a more rugged, nature-focused escape, and it is a major hub for both outdoor enthusiasts and pet owners.
What to See and Do

Elite Dog Haven: The park is most famous for its massive multi-use area, often referred to as Terwillegar Dog Park. It is one of the largest off-leash areas in North America, offering vast open fields and river access where dogs can run and swim freely.

Terwillegar Park Footbridge: A modern architectural highlight, this stressed-ribbon footbridge connects the park to the Oleskiw River Valley Park across the river. It is a favorite spot for walkers and cyclists, providing beautiful elevated views of the water and the valley.

Diverse Trail Network: The park features a mix of paved paths and extensive single-track dirt trails. These hidden forested paths are highly popular among local mountain bikers and trail runners for their varied terrain and natural obstacles.
Water Access: With its long stretch of riverbank, the park is a primary launch and recovery point for canoeists and kayakers traveling along the North Saskatchewan River.
Tips & Key Information

Because of its popularity with dog owners, the main parking lot can fill up very quickly on sunny weekend mornings. If you prefer a quieter experience, try visiting on a weekday or earlier in the morning.

While the paved upper trails are great year-round, the lower unpaved trails can become extremely muddy and slippery after rain or during the spring melt. Sturdy, waterproof footwear is highly recommended.
Because the single-track trails are shared between hikers and mountain bikers, it's important to stay alert. Cyclists are encouraged to use bells and yield to pedestrians.
The river current at Terwillegar can be deceptively strong, especially during high-water periods in the spring. Keep a close eye on children and pets if they are near the riverbank.

places.name: 5. Sir Winston Churchill Square
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/a-grand-view-of-edmonton-city-halls-unique-pyramid-architecture-and-tower-with-gm2216284436-632968806

Sir Winston Churchill Square is a vibrant public space located in the heart of Edmonton, known for hosting events, festivals, and cultural celebrations. Surrounded by the city’s major attractions, including the Art Gallery of Alberta and City Hall, the square offers visitors a lively atmosphere and a chance to engage with Edmonton’s rich arts and culture scene.
What to See and Do

Year-Round Festival Hub: From the Edmonton International Fringe Festival’s outdoor events in the summer to the festive holiday light displays in the winter, there is almost always a community event or market happening here.

Architectural Gateway: The square offers some of the best unobstructed views of the city's modern architecture, including the striking glass pyramids of the nearby Muttart Conservatory in the distance and the borealis ribbon of the Art Gallery of Alberta.
Public Amenities: Visitors can enjoy several interactive water features, plenty of outdoor seating, and a large lawn area perfect for relaxing between museum visits or catching a live performance.
Tips & Key Information
The square is directly served by the Churchill LRT Station, making it one of the easiest landmarks to reach from anywhere in the city via the Capital, Metro, or Valley lines.
During colder months, you can access the square through the city's climate-controlled underground pedway system, which connects it to the Citadel Theatre and various shopping centers.
It is highly recommended to check the City of Edmonton’s events calendar before visiting, as the square often hosts ticketed festivals that might affect general public access.

places.name: 1. High Level Bridge Streetcar
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/streetcar-crossing-overhead-gm1068614714-285846136

The High Level Bridge Streetcar offers one of the most unique and scenic ways to experience Edmonton's river valley. Operated by the Edmonton Radial Railway Society, this historic transit experience takes passengers across the top of the High Level Bridge, providing breathtaking 360-degree views from over 150 feet above the North Saskatchewan River.
What to See and Do

Historic Fleet: The society operates a rotating fleet of beautifully restored streetcars from all over the world, including cars from Osaka, Japan, and Melbourne, Australia, as well as local Edmonton heritage cars.

Bridge Crossing: The highlight of the trip is the slow-paced crossing of the High Level Bridge. It is currently the highest streetcar river crossing in the world, offering a perspective of the city skyline and the lush river valley that you can't get any other way.

Connecting Districts: The line serves as a functional and charming link between the Old Strathcona heritage district and the downtown core, with stops at the Alberta Legislature Building and several others along the route.
Tips & Key Information
The streetcar typically runs from the May long weekend through to Canadian Thanksgiving in October. It is a seasonal attraction and does not operate during the winter months.
Payment is usually cash-only at the streetcar, though you can often purchase tickets at their station museums. It’s a good idea to have small bills or exact change ready.
The route includes stops at the Strathcona Terminus, which features a small museum dedicated to the history of streetcars in Edmonton, and the Grandin (Government Centre) stop near the Legislature.
If you can time your trip for the late afternoon or early evening, the views of the sun setting over the river valley are particularly spectacular and highly popular for photography.

places.name: 2. Old Strathcona Farmers' Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/old-stathcona-farmers-market-edmonton-gm2147643070-569006997

The Old Strathcona Farmers' Market is Edmonton’s original indoor farmers' market, housed in a sprawling historic bus barn. Since 1983, it has been a Saturday morning tradition for locals, offering a vibrant, community-focused atmosphere where everything sold is made, baked, or grown by the vendors themselves.
What to See and Do
Diverse Vendor Mix: With over 130 stalls, you’ll find everything from seasonal Alberta produce and locally raised meats to artisanal breads, handmade jewelry, and unique pottery.
Authentic Local Flavors: It is a prime spot to pick up classic regional treats like Ukrainian pierogies, locally fermented kombucha, and Saskatoon berry preserves.
Historic Setting: The high ceilings and brick walls of the renovated warehouse provide a rustic backdrop that stays warm and bustling even during the coldest winter months.
Community Hub: Beyond shopping, the market often features local musicians and serves as a social gathering point for the residents of the surrounding Old Strathcona neighborhood.
Tips & Key Information
Historically, this market was only open on Saturdays, but it has recently expanded its schedule. It is currently open Saturdays from 8:00 AM to 3:00 PM and Sundays from 11:00 AM to 3:00 PM.
The market offers free parking for customers in the lot directly across the street while you shop, which is a significant bonus in the busy Strathcona area.
While many vendors provide packaging, the market strongly encourages a green experience, so bringing your own sturdy bags or a small cart is highly recommended.
For the freshest produce and the most popular baked goods (which often sell out by noon), aim to arrive within the first two hours of opening.

places.name: 3. Edmonton City Hall
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/city-hall-gm139861142-1352938

Edmonton City Hall is a striking civic landmark that combines modern architecture with a rich sense of community. The building is home to the city's municipal offices, but it also serves as a public gathering place, featuring an impressive open atrium and various art displays.

What makes this place special is its stunning glass-and-steel design, which allows natural light to fill the space, creating a welcoming and open atmosphere. City Hall is also known for its seasonal events and live performances, making it a lively part of the city throughout the year.
What to See and Do

City Hall Plaza and Wading Pool: In the summer, the large outdoor plaza features a shallow wading pool that is a favorite for families looking to cool off. In the winter, this same area is transformed into a scenic public skating rink, often accompanied by festive music and colorful lights.

Public Art and Architecture: The building's interior is just as impressive as its exterior, featuring a massive open-concept atrium and various pieces of public art that tell the story of Edmonton’s growth and its Indigenous heritage.
Friendship Tower: Standing tall as part of the complex, the tower houses a 23-bell carillon that rings out over the downtown core, adding a melodic backdrop to the busy Arts District.
Tips & Key Information
Visitors can often take advantage of free guided tours of the facility, which provide insights into municipal government and the building’s unique green design features.
Because it is connected to the city's extensive pedway system, City Hall is a popular pass-through and warming station during Edmonton's colder months.

Take a moment to view the Treaty 6 and Métis Nation of Alberta flags permanently displayed in the City Room, reflecting the city's commitment to reconciliation and its history as a traditional gathering place.

places.name: 4. Edmonton Convention Centre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/edmonton-skyline-and-convention-center-gm116062785-4564046

The Edmonton Convention Centre is an architectural landmark built into the side of the North Saskatchewan River Valley. It is recognized globally for its innovative stepped design, which allows for stunning panoramic views of the river valley from multiple levels.
What to See and Do

Sustainability Focus: The facility is a leader in environmental stewardship, featuring one of Canada’s largest building-integrated photovoltaic (solar cell) glass installations. This initiative helps power the building while showcasing its commitment to a green future.

A Living Atrium: The interior features a massive greenhouse-like atrium filled with lush plants and natural light. This serves as a serene public space where visitors can enjoy the greenery regardless of the weather outside.

Culinary Excellence: Unlike many standard conference venues, this centre is renowned for its high-end culinary program. The award-winning kitchen team prioritizes locally sourced Alberta ingredients and is famous for its in-house honey produced by its own rooftop beehives.

Versatile Event Space: The complex houses over 150,000 square feet of flexible space, including a massive exhibit hall, a grand ballroom, and a dedicated theatre, making it the city's go-to venue for everything from international conventions to major concerts.
Tips & Key Information
The centre provides a unique pedestrian link to the river valley trail system. You can walk directly from the lower levels onto the paved paths that wind through the forest.
It is fully integrated into Edmonton’s downtown pedway system, allowing you to walk indoors to nearby hotels, the LRT station, and other major downtown attractions during the winter.
Keep an eye out for various public art installations throughout the halls, including works that highlight the history and diverse cultures of the region.

places.name: 5. 100 Street Funicular
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/funicular-edmonton-gm1332897539-415607172

The 100 Street Funicular, formally known as the Mechanized River Valley Access, is a modern engineering marvel that provides a seamless and accessible link between Edmonton's downtown core and the vast North Saskatchewan River Valley. It is much more than just a transit vehicle; it's a scenic destination that offers some of the best views of the city's natural landscape.
What to See and Do

Scenic River Valley Access: The funicular features a glass-walled cabin that descends from the top of the bank near the Hotel Macdonald down to a beautiful promenade, offering an effortless way to navigate the steep terrain.

Frederick G. Todd Lookout: At the midway point, visitors can step onto a stunning cantilevered lookout that extends over the river valley. It provides an unobstructed panoramic view of the North Saskatchewan River and the Walterdale Bridge.

A Multi-Stage Experience: The journey includes the funicular ride itself, followed by a spacious promenade, an elevator for further descent, and a bridge that connects directly to the extensive trail system in the valley.

Urban Integration: The site is a popular spot for both commuters and tourists, featuring public art, comfortable seating areas, and a design that blends sleek modern materials with the surrounding greenery.
Tips & Key Information
The funicular is part of the city's public transit infrastructure and is free for everyone to use. It operates daily from 7:00 AM to 9:00 PM.
The cabin is designed to be fully accessible, with enough room to easily accommodate wheelchairs, strollers, and bicycles, making it a favorite for river valley adventurers.
The cantilevered lookout is widely considered one of the best selfie spots in Edmonton, particularly during the golden hour or when the river valley is in full autumn color.

While the funicular operates year-round, it may occasionally close for maintenance or during extreme weather events. The cabin itself is climate-controlled, ensuring a comfortable ride even in the winter.

places.name: 6. Whyte Avenue
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/restored-old-strathcona-post-office-gm1499195219-521003742

Whyte Avenue, the heart of the Old Strathcona neighborhood, is Edmonton’s most iconic and vibrant shopping and entertainment district. Blending historic charm with a bohemian spirit, it is a bustling corridor known for its walkable streets, independent boutiques, and energetic nightlife.
What to See and Do

Shopping and Boutiques: The avenue is a haven for unique finds, featuring everything from curated vintage clothing at the Old Strathcona Antique Mall nearby to local designer wares and specialized bookstores.

Dining and Nightlife: As a culinary hotspot, it offers an incredible density of pubs, high-end cocktail bars, and diverse eateries. It is particularly famous for its lively patio scene in the summer months.
Historic Architecture: Many of the buildings date back to the early 20th century, providing a picturesque backdrop of red brick and ornate facades that house modern, trendy businesses.

Festival Hub: The area serves as the primary grounds for the Edmonton International Fringe Theatre Festival and is frequently filled with buskers and street performers, adding to its artistic atmosphere.
Tips & Key Information
While there is street parking, it can be difficult to find. The best way to experience Whyte Avenue is on foot, allowing you to duck into the many narrow side streets and hidden alleys.
The area is well-connected by bus, and during the summer, the High Level Bridge Streetcar provides a scenic link from downtown directly to the heart of Strathcona.
Saturday mornings are especially busy as locals flock to the Old Strathcona Farmers' Market just a block off the main avenue.
On Friday and Saturday nights, the avenue becomes the city's nightlife center and can get very crowded. Plan ahead if you are looking for a quiet dinner, as popular spots often require reservations.

places.name: 7. Winspear Centre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/edmonton-symphony-orchestra-gm518309263-49521224

The Winspear Centre is widely considered one of the finest concert halls in North America, renowned specifically for its near-perfect acoustics. Located in Edmonton's downtown Arts District, it serves as the home of the Edmonton Symphony Orchestra and hosts a diverse range of international performers.

The hall was designed specifically to provide a superior listening experience, with every architectural detail—from the adjustable acoustic canopies to the curvature of the walls—engineered to enhance sound quality.
What to See and Do
Davis Concert Organ: A centerpiece of the hall, this massive pipe organ features 6,538 pipes and is often showcased in dedicated organ recitals and symphonic works.

Intimate Seating: Despite its large capacity, the shoebox design of the main performance space ensures that every seat feels relatively close to the stage, providing an intimate connection between the audience and the musicians.
Enmax Hall: This primary performance space is named for its clean, modern aesthetic and its ability to host everything from delicate soloists to thunderous choral works.

Expansion Project: The centre is currently undergoing a significant expansion called The Winspear Project, which will add a second performance space, community programming areas, and more public-facing amenities.
Tips & Key Information
The lobby often hosts pre-concert talks or live music, providing a great opportunity to learn about the evening's program or simply enjoy the atmosphere before the main show.
While some gala events are formal, most concerts at the Winspear have a smart casual vibe; you will see people in everything from suits to nice jeans.
Because the hall is so quiet, even small sounds carry. It is tradition to wait for a break in the music or an intermission before unwrapping candies or entering/exiting the hall.
Several heated underground parkades are located nearby, and the building is directly accessible via the Edmonton pedway system and the Churchill LRT station.

places.name: Vancouver Downtown Farmers Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/an-assortment-of-green-and-red-apples-in-baskets-gm2165609005-585792941

Situated on the scenic plaza of the Vancouver Art Gallery, this market transforms the bustling city center into a vibrant hub of local agriculture and artisan craft. It is the perfect stop for office workers, tourists, and downtown residents looking to stock up on fresh goods without leaving the metropolitan core.
What to Expect
Urban Convenience: This market is uniquely positioned amidst skyscrapers and historical architecture, offering a curated selection of the best the region has to offer.
Fresh Seasonal Produce: Expect a rotating variety of BC-grown fruits and vegetables, from crisp Okanagan apples in the fall to vibrant berries and leafy greens in the summer.
Artisanal Goods: Beyond the produce, the market features local honey, small-batch preserves, handmade soaps, and unique crafts that make for excellent gifts or souvenirs.

Ready-to-Eat Treats: There is usually a strong presence of local bakers and food trucks, offering everything from fresh sourdough and flaky pastries to gourmet street food for a quick lunch on the plaza.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/close-up-and-textures-of-freshly-harvested-organic-okanagan-cherries-at-trout-lake-gm2166548909-586648366
Key Information
Location: Vancouver Art Gallery North Plaza (West Georgia Street between Hornby and Howe).
Season: Typically runs from early June through late September.
Hours: Wednesdays, 2:00 PM – 6:00 PM.
Access: Easily accessible via public transit. It is a short walk from the Vancouver City Centre and Granville SkyTrain stations.
Payment: Most vendors accept credit and debit cards via mobile tap, but carrying some cash is always helpful for smaller transactions.
Tips
Arriving right at 2:00 PM ensures the best selection of highly sought-after items like fresh eggs or limited-run pastries, which often sell out quickly.
In line with Vancouver’s sustainability goals, vendors do not provide plastic bags. Bring a sturdy tote or a backpack to carry your haul comfortably through the city.
Since the market opens in the early afternoon, it’s a great spot to grab a fresh lunch from a food truck and enjoy it on the Art Gallery steps while people-watching.
