For one of the best hidden views in the city, reviewers recommend The Galley Patio & Grill, located on the upper deck of the Sailing Centre. It offers casual fare like burgers and local beer with an unobstructed panoramic vista.

There are two main pay-parking lots available. If you prefer public transit, the #4 or #44 buses stop nearby on 4th Avenue, leaving you with a pleasant short walk through the residential neighborhood to reach the sand.
The park is home to a large population of wild rabbits. While they are a favorite for children to spot, visitors are reminded not to feed them to help preserve the local ecosystem.

places.name: 1. Granville Island Public Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/granville-island-public-market-vancouver-canada-gm1306359810-396965026

Granville Island Public Market is one of Vancouver’s most vibrant spots, brimming with fresh local produce, artisan goods, and unique eats. Located just under the Granville Street Bridge, the market buzzes with life, offering visitors a true taste of the city’s culture and creativity. The atmosphere is vibrant and energetic, particularly on weekends when the narrow aisles are filled with the scents of fresh-baked bread, exotic spices, and ocean-fresh seafood.
What to See and Do

Gourmet Food Stalls: The market is famous for its high-quality ready-to-eat options and specialty ingredients. Highlights include artisanal cheeses, handcrafted chocolates, and local smoked salmon that are perfect for a picnic or a souvenir.
Artisan Boutiques: Beyond the food, the market features rotating stalls of local artists selling everything from handmade jewelry and pottery to intricate wood carvings and textiles.
Courtyard Performances: The outdoor seating area overlooking False Creek is a premier spot for world-class street performers and musicians, providing a lively backdrop to your meal.

Net Loft and Railspur Alley: While the main market is the focus, the adjacent Net Loft building and nearby Railspur Alley house even more permanent artisan studios, high-end stationary shops, and fashion boutiques.
Tips & Key Information
Arrive right when the doors open at 9:00 AM to enjoy a quieter experience. By lunchtime, especially on sunny days, the market can become extremely crowded.

Finding a table inside the food court can be difficult. Many locals prefer to take their food outside to the boardwalk or the hilly grassy area near the ferry dock for better views of the marina and city skyline.
Parking on Granville Island is limited and expensive. The most scenic and stress-free way to arrive is via the The Aquabus or False Creek Ferries from various points around False Creek.
Many vendors offer small samples of their products. Don't be afraid to try a new fruit or a slice of artisanal fudge before you commit to a purchase.

places.name: 2. Commercial Drive
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/corner-of-commercial-drive-and-charles-street-people-relax-over-beverages-under-gm912497606-251208537

Commercial Drive, known to locals simply as The Drive, is one of Vancouver’s most diverse and culturally rich neighborhoods. Spanning 21 blocks, this historic district was originally the heart of the city's Italian community and has evolved into a vibrant hub for artists, activists, and food lovers, maintaining an authentically un-gentrified feel.
What to See and Do

Little Italy Roots: While the neighborhood is now multicultural, its Italian heritage remains strong. You’ll find traditional espresso bars, old-school delis, and pasta shops that have been family-run for generations.

Alternative Spirit: The area is a center for counter-culture and social activism. It is home to a high concentration of vegetarian and vegan eateries, independent bookstores, and community-run co-ops.

Live Performance & Arts: The Drive features several historic venues, including The Cultch, a former church turned premier arts center, and various small stages for live jazz, slam poetry, and fringe theater.
Grandview Park: Serving as the neighborhood's living room, this park is a popular spot for people-watching, drum circles, and community festivals.
Tips & Key Information
This is arguably the best place in the city for coffee. Skip the chains and visit long-standing spots like Continental Coffee or Joe's Cafe Bar for a true local experience.

If you visit in the summer, check the schedule for Car-Free Day, when the entire street is closed to traffic and transformed into a massive block party with multiple stages and hundreds of street vendors.

During the World Cup or Euro Cup, the Drive is the place to be. The local cafes spill out onto the sidewalks, and the air is filled with the sounds of cheering fans and honking cars draped in various international flags.

The neighborhood is easily accessible via the SkyTrain; get off at the Commercial-Broadway Station, which serves both the Expo and Millennium lines. From there, it's just a short walk north into the heart of the district.

places.name: 3. Bloedel Conservatory
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/vancouver-canada-the-sun-hangs-ominously-over-the-bloedel-conservatory-gm1023919048-274775712

The Bloedel Conservatory is a lush, glass-domed paradise perched at the highest point of Vancouver in Queen Elizabeth Park. This tri-level temperature-controlled environment offers a year-round tropical escape, housing a vibrant collection of exotic birds and plants that thrive under its iconic geodesic dome. It is a peaceful and magical oasis, particularly during Vancouver's rainy months, where the warmth and colors provide a perfect contrast to the city's gray skies.
What to See and Do

Aviary Adventures: The dome is home to over 100 free-flying exotic birds, including colorful macaws, parrots, and finches. Visitors often enjoy spotting the different species as they interact within the canopy.

Three Tropical Zones: The plant life is organized into three distinct climatic zones—Tropical Rainforest, Subtropical Rainforest, and Desert—featuring more than 500 species, from towering palms to rare cacti and orchids.

Architectural Landmark: The conservatory is a designated heritage building, famous for its unique modernist design consisting of 1,490 acrylic bubbles, which creates a bright, airy atmosphere even on overcast days.
Healing Garden: A dedicated area within the conservatory is designed to be a sensory experience, encouraging visitors to slow down and enjoy the calming scents and textures of the flora.
Tips & Key Information
Mid-day provides the brightest light for capturing the vibrant colors of the birds and flowers. However, it’s recommended going right at opening for the quietest, most tranquil experience.
While it is a very affordable attraction, tickets are timed and should be booked online in advance to ensure your preferred entry time, especially on weekends.
Since it’s located within Queen Elizabeth Park, it's easy to pair a visit here with a stroll through the outdoor quarry gardens or a meal at the nearby Seasons in the Park.

Like the rest of the park, parking is metered. If you're visiting on a budget, consider taking the Canada Line SkyTrain to King Edward Station and enjoying the uphill walk through the park's beautiful grounds.

places.name: 4. The Aquabus
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/aquabus-ferry-in-false-creek-bay-granville-island-vancouver-canada-gm608009912-104313907

The Aquabus is one of Vancouver's most charming and practical modes of transport. These iconic, rainbow-colored mini-ferries have been a staple of False Creek since 1985, providing a scenic shortcut between major downtown hubs and the South Shore.
What to See and Do
Rainbow Fleet: The fleet consists of several distinct vessel types. The most famous are the traditional 12-passenger ferries designed by Jay Benford, which look like something out of a storybook.
Cyquabus: For those with wheels, the larger Cyquabus vessels are designed to accommodate bicycles, strollers, and wheelchairs, making the entire False Creek water transit system highly accessible.

Eco-Friendly Innovation: In recent years, the company has begun transitioning to electric power. You might find yourself on one of their whisper-quiet electric ferries, which enhance the peaceful experience of gliding across the water.
Expo 86 Legacy: The Aquabus rose to fame during Vancouver's 1986 World Exposition, serving as a primary way for millions of visitors to navigate the various fair sites along the water.
Tips & Key Information

The Aquabus serves 8 main stops: Hornby Street (West End), Granville Island, David Lam Park, Stamps Landing, Spyglass Place (near Cambie Bridge), Yaletown, Plaza of Nations, and The Village (Science World).

While they do not accept the TransLink Compass Card, you can pay on board using cash or any tap-enabled credit/debit card. For tourists, the Day Pass (approx. $20) is the best value, allowing unlimited hopping on and off.
If you are staying for a few days but don't need a full day pass, you can buy a strip of Aquabucks—prepaid tickets that never expire and can be shared among a group.
Unlike many public transit options, well-behaved dogs on leashes are generally welcome on board, making it a favorite for locals heading to the dog parks in Yaletown or Olympic Village.
During peak hours, ferries arrive at most docks every 5 to 15 minutes, meaning you rarely have to wait long.

places.name: 5. CF Pacific Centre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pacific-centre-shopping-mall-in-downtown-vancouver-british-columbia-canada-gm1068076428-285677641

CF Pacific Centre is a bustling shopping destination in downtown Vancouver, known for its sleek underground design and collection of high-end retailers. Spanning several city blocks beneath the intersection of Georgia and Granville Streets, it offers a sophisticated climate-controlled environment that serves as a major hub for both fashion-conscious locals and international visitors.
What to See and Do
Flagship Retailers: The mall is anchored by prestigious department stores, including a massive Holt Renfrew for luxury designer goods and a large Nordstrom.
Designer Brands: It features a high concentration of premium international brands such as Apple, Harry Rosen, Lululemon, and Sephora, making it the city's go-to for top-tier retail.

Underground Connectivity: The centre is uniquely integrated into the city's infrastructure, providing direct indoor access to the Vancouver City Centre and Granville SkyTrain stations, as well as several major office towers and the Fairmont Hotel Vancouver.

Dining and Refreshments: In addition to a large, modern food court, the mall is surrounded by upscale dining options and specialty cafes, providing plenty of places to recharge during a shopping spree.
Tips & Key Information
While there are many street-level entrances, the most dramatic entry is the glass rotunda at the corner of West Georgia and Howe Street, which floods the underground corridors with natural light.
Visit on Thursday or Friday evenings when the mall stays open until 9:00 PM. Weekends can become exceptionally busy, especially in the afternoon.

The mall has a large underground parkade, but it is one of the more expensive options in the city. If you're on a budget, taking the SkyTrain is highly recommended as it drops you directly inside the mall.
Located on the lower level, Guest Services offers mall maps, gift cards, and can even help with stroller rentals or coat checks during the winter months.

places.name: 6. A-maze-ing Laughter Sculpture
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/a-maze-ing-laughter-statues-in-downtown-vancouver-bc-canada-gm1325315385-410381550

A-maze-ing Laughter is a collection of 14 oversized bronze statues located in Morton Park, right across from English Bay Beach. Created by Beijing-based artist Yue Minjun, these three-meter-tall figures have become a symbol of Vancouver’s playful spirit and are easily the most photographed public art installation in the city.
What to See and Do

Cynical Realism: The figures are part of an art movement called Cynical Realism, which emerged in China in the 1990s. While the statues appear joyful, the exaggerated, hysterical laughter is often interpreted as an ironic response to the social and political environment of the time.

Self-Portraiture: Every one of the 14 statues is a stylized self-portrait of the artist himself. Despite the repetition, each figure is posed in a different gesture, creating a maze of movement that invites you to walk between them.

A Gift to the City: Originally a temporary exhibit for the 2009–2011 Vancouver Biennale, the statues were so beloved that they were purchased for $1.5 million by Chip and Shannon Wilson (founders of Lululemon) and donated permanently to the city.
Inscription: At the base of the sculptures, a simple message reminds visitors of the work's intent: "May this sculpture inspire laughter playfulness and joy in all who experience it."
Tips & Key Information
Unlike many statues, you are encouraged to touch, lean on, and mimic the poses of the Laughing Men. It is a favorite for families and groups looking for creative mirror photos.
For the best lighting, visit during the hour before sunset. The bronze captures the warm light of English Bay beautifully, and the beach sunset provides a stunning backdrop.
Keep an eye out during special events or holidays; locals occasionally dress the statues in Santa hats, scarves, or jerseys to celebrate the season.

This is a major tourist stop. If you want the sculptures to yourself for a clean shot, aim to arrive before 9:00 AM. After 11:00 AM, there is almost always a crowd of people interacting with the figures.
Morton Park is surrounded by the cafes and ice cream shops of Denman Street. Grab a cone and enjoy the show of people reacting to the art from one of the nearby park benches.

places.name: 7. Marine Building
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/marine-building-in-vancouver-gm1141102550-305579420

The Marine Building is an Art Deco masterpiece in downtown Vancouver, once the tallest building in the British Empire when it opened in 1930. Designed to resemble a great crag rising from the ocean, it is one of the world's most beautiful examples of marine-themed architecture, capturing the spirit of the city's maritime history.
What to See and Do

Entrance & Lobby: The massive brass doors are famously ornate, featuring reliefs of sea creatures and ships. Once inside, the lobby is designed to feel like you are underwater, with intricate floor mosaics of sea life and stained-glass windows depicting marine scenes.

Art Deco Details: Every corner of the building is covered in period-appropriate symbolism, from the terra-cotta figures on the exterior to the customized elevators that were once the fastest in the world.

Pop Culture Fame: Because of its timeless and majestic aesthetic, the building has served as a filming location for numerous movies and TV shows, most notably as the Daily Planet headquarters in the TV series Smallville.
Tips & Key Information

While it is an active office building, the lobby is generally open to the public during business hours. Visitors are welcome to walk in and admire the architecture for free, though you should be respectful of the professionals working there.
For those who want to see beyond the lobby, the Vancouver Heritage Foundation occasionally offers guided tours that provide access to the upper floors and more in-depth history of the construction.

You are permitted to take photos of the lobby for personal use, but flash photography and tripods are usually discouraged. The best light for capturing the golden brass and rich wood of the interior is often mid-morning.
The lobby is typically accessible Monday through Friday, 7:00 AM to 6:00 PM. It is closed to the public on weekends and holidays.

places.name: 1. Halifax Citadel National Historic Site
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/halifax-citadel-hill-national-historic-site-gm487604796-73450045

The Halifax Citadel National Historic Site (officially Fort George) stands proudly on a hilltop, overlooking the vibrant city of Halifax and its picturesque harbor. This star-shaped fortress is a living history museum that transports you back to 1869 and played a key role in the defense of the city.
What to See and Do

Noon Gun: A Halifax tradition since 1857. Every day (except Christmas) at exactly 12:00 PM, the 3rd Brigade Royal Artillery fires a 12-pounder cannon. You can watch the gunners prepare and fire from the ramparts.
78th Highlanders re-enactors: Dressed in authentic kilts and feather bonnets, these soldiers perform rifle drills, pipe and drum concerts, and formal Sentry Changes every hour at the front gate.
Army Museum: Located in the Cavalier Building, this museum houses an extensive collection of rare medals, weapons, and uniforms, including a poignant exhibit on Nova Scotia's role in the World Wars.
Fortress Halifax Exhibit: A newer, immersive indoor exhibit that tells the story of the four different citadels built on this hill and how they shaped the city.
Ghost Tours: On select nights from July to October, you can walk the tunnels, dungeons, and ramparts by candlelight to hear the darker, haunted history of the fort.
Tips and Key Information
If you want to see the Noon Gun, arrive at the fort by 11:40 AM to get a good spot on the ramparts overlooking the gun deck.
Walk the entire perimeter of the upper ramparts. It offers the best 360-degree view of the Halifax Harbour, the Old Town Clock, and the downtown core.

For an extra fee, you can do the Soldier for a Day program, where you're enlisted, fitted for a uniform, and taught to drill. Or, try the Distilled Experience to taste spirits aged in the fort’s barrels.
The Citadel is high and exposed. Even on a warm day, it can be quite windy and chilly up top. Bring a light jacket or windbreaker.
Open daily year-round from 9:00 AM – 5:00 PM. (Note: Full living history programming and period rooms are open from May 7 to October 31.)
Admission is free during the Canada Strong Pass period from June 19 to September 7. On regular season, fees apply (approx. $13.25 for adults).
The site is accessible, with elevators in the main buildings and accessible washrooms. However, the gravel parade square and some ramparts can be uneven.
On-site parking is available for a small fee, but many people walk up the hill from the Public Gardens or the Waterfront.

places.name: 2. Halifax Public Gardenshttps://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/halifax-public-gardens-gm1392214602-448532252
body: The Halifax Public Gardens is one of the oldest Victorian gardens in North America, offering a tranquil escape in the heart of the city. Spanning 16 acres, this enclosed oasis features stunning flower beds, fountains, and historic statues, making it a picturesque spot for both locals and visitors.
What to See and Do
The Bandstand: This ornate, cream-and-blue structure is the heart of the gardens. It was built in 1887 to celebrate Queen Victoria’s Golden Jubilee and still hosts free concerts on Sunday afternoons.

The Gates: The main entrance at the corner of Spring Garden Road and South Park Street features massive, wrought-iron gates cast in Scotland. They are adorned with the city’s coat of arms and the crest of the Horticultural Society.
Duck Pond & Models: Look for the resident ducks swimming around a miniature replica of the Titanic (a nod to the city's history) and the floating HMS Shannon.
Victorian Flower Beds: The gardens are famous for their carpet bedding—intricate, three-dimensional floral displays that are replanted annually to create living works of art.
Statuary and Fountains: Wander the winding paths to find the Jubilee Fountain and statues of Roman deities like Flora and Ceres, which have stood in the gardens for over a century.
Tips and Key Information
Keep an eye out for the weeping beech trees. Their twisted, drooping branches create natural caves that are a favorite for photographers.
There is a small café located in the Horticultural Hall (the oldest building on site) that serves good coffee and ice cream. It’s the perfect spot to sit on the porch and people-watch.

To maintain the Victorian atmosphere, certain activities are prohibited. You cannot ride bikes, jog, or bring pets (other than service animals) inside the gates. It is strictly for strolling and sitting.
If you visit in late June, the rhododendrons and azaleas are in peak explosion; August is best for the vibrant tropical displays and dahlias.
The gardens open at 8:00 AM daily. The gates close precisely 30 minutes before sunset every day. In the summer, this is around 8:30–9:00 PM; in the winter, it can be as early as 4:00 PM.
It remains one of the best high-quality, zero-cost experiences in the city.
Bordered by South Park St, Sackville St, and Spring Garden Rd. It is an easy 10-minute walk from the Halifax Citadel.
Free horticultural tours are typically offered at 10:30 AM and 2:30 PM daily during the summer months, starting at the Horticultural Hall.

places.name: 3. Halifax Waterfront Boardwalk
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/skyline-der-stadt-und-lebhafter-halifax-waterfront-boardwalk-nova-scotia-kanada-gm1778433568-546558179

The Halifax Waterfront Boardwalk is the city’s social and cultural heart. Spanning roughly 4 kilometers (about 2.5 miles), it is one of the longest urban boardwalks in the world and serves as a front-row seat to the world’s second-largest natural harbor.
What to See and Do

Wave & Interactive Art: The Wave is a massive, blue sculpture that is the boardwalk's most famous photo op. Nearby, you’ll find the Drunken Lamp Posts—three modern art installations that look like they’ve had one too many at the local pub.

Queen’s Marque District: This new, ultra-modern area features stunning architecture, luxury shops, and Rise Again—a series of granite steps that disappear directly into the harbor, perfect for sitting and watching the tide.
Salt Yard: A cluster of colorful kiosks serving up local favorites like poutine, lobster rolls, and local crafts. It’s also home to a popular public beer garden.
Harbour Hopper: You’ll see these bright green amphibious vehicles everywhere. They tour the city streets before making a literal big splash into the harbor for a water tour.

Historic Properties: A collection of stone warehouses dating back to the late 1700s. Once the haunt of privateers and smugglers, they now house high-end boutiques and pubs like The Lower Deck, famous for live Atlantic fiddle music.
Tips and Key Information

Instead of a pricey harbor cruise, hop on the Halifax-Dartmouth Ferry. It’s the oldest saltwater ferry in North America. For the price of a bus ticket, you get a 12-minute crossing with the best panoramic views of the Halifax skyline.
Along the Salter Sands section, the city has installed bright orange hammocks. They are free to use and are the ultimate spot for a mid-walk nap with a sea breeze.

If you prefer a quiet walk, head to the boardwalk at sunrise. The harbor is glass-calm, the fog often rolls in for great photos, and you'll beat the thousands of cruise ship passengers that arrive later in the morning.
There are several free public water-bottle filling stations along the route, so bring a reusable bottle.
The length is 3.8 km to 4.4 km depending on which piers you detour onto.
The entire boardwalk is flat and wheelchair/stroller accessible.
Major 2026 Events:
SailGP (June 21–26): High-speed racing boats will take over the harbor.
Halifax Jazz Festival (July 7–12): The main stage is located right on the waterfront.
International Busker Festival (July 29 – Aug 3): The boardwalk turns into a massive outdoor circus with world-class performers.

places.name: 4. Maritime Museum of the Atlantic
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/das-maritime-museum-of-the-atlantic-in-halifax-nova-scotia-gm1085576504-291282445

The Maritime Museum of the Atlantic is Canada’s oldest and largest maritime museum. Located right on the waterfront, it serves as the definitive storyteller of the city’s relationship with the sea—from the golden age of sail to the tragedies that shook the world.
What to See and Do

Titanic Exhibit: This is the museum’s most famous draw. Because Halifax was the base for the recovery mission in 1912, the museum holds a hauntingly beautiful collection of artifacts. Don't miss the one of only a few remaining Titanic deck chairs in existence and a pair of tiny leather shoes belonging to the Unknown Child (later identified through DNA).

Halifax Explosion (1917): A massive gallery dedicated to the largest man-made explosion prior to the atomic bomb. It features shrapnel objects—like a window frame with glass still embedded—and tells the story of how the city rebuilt from the ashes.
CSS Acadia: Moored right outside in the harbor, this 100-plus-year-old steamship survived both World Wars and the Halifax Explosion. You can walk its decks during the summer months.
Shipwright’s Workshop: Watch master craftsmen at work as they maintain traditional wooden boats. It’s a living part of the museum where the smell of cedar and sawdust fills the air.
Merlin the Parrot: A local celebrity. Merlin is a rainbow macaw who lives at the museum and often greets visitors with a squawk near the gift shop.
Tips and Key Information
While you can't sit in the original Titanic deck chair, the museum has high-quality replicas you can actually sit in to get a feel for what life was like on the Ship of Dreams.
Traditionally, the museum offers free admission on Tuesday evenings from 5:00 PM to 8:00 PM. It’s a great way to save a few dollars if you’re on a budget.
The museum is located at the halfway point of the Halifax Waterfront. It makes for a perfect indoor break if the Atlantic weather turns rainy or foggy.
Check the Gift Shop. It is one of the best spots in the city for unique, high-quality nautical gifts, local books, and authentic Titanic memorabilia that isn't just tourist kitsch.
The museum is open daily 9:30 AM – 5:30 PM (Extended to 8:00 PM on Tuesdays).
Admission (2026) is approximately $9.55 for adults in summer and $5.15 in winter, with discounted rates available for seniors and students
It is located at 1675 Lower Water Street (right on the boardwalk).
A new temporary exhibit, The Age of Sail 2.0, is debuting in 2026, focusing on the modern environmental technology being used to bring wind-powered cargo ships back to the Atlantic.

places.name: 5. Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/pier-21-in-halifax-nova-scotia-gm458675987-18778071
body: Often referred to as the Ellis Island of Canada, the Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21 is a powerful National Historic Site. From 1928 to 1971, this very building served as the gateway for nearly one million immigrants beginning their lives in Canada, as well as the departure point for nearly 500,000 Canadian military personnel during World War II.
What to See and Do
The Pier 21 Story: Walk through the restored assembly hall and immersive exhibits that recreate the immigrant experience, from the ocean crossing to the medical exams and customs processing.
The Empress of Ireland Exhibit: Learn about Canada’s deadliest maritime disaster through a permanent collection that honors the 1,012 people who lost their lives in 1914.
BMO Family History Centre: This is a highlight for many visitors; you can work with on-site researchers to explore ship manifests and immigration records to trace your own family’s arrival in Canada.

Interactive Art & Films: Watch In Canada, a film shown in the museum’s theater that features personal stories of immigrants from different eras, providing a modern perspective on the Canadian identity.
Tips and Key Information
If you plan to research your ancestry, head to the Scotiabank Family History Centre first to get your search started, as it can take some time to sift through the digitized records.
Take advantage of the 30-minute guided tours included with your admission. The museum's interpreters are excellent storytellers who bring the personal letters and artifacts to life.
Plan for 2-3 hours. The museum is quite large and emotionally impactful.
Typically open Wednesday through Sunday from 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM. It is currently closed on Mondays and Tuesdays.
Situated at the southernmost end of the Halifax Waterfront (1055 Marginal Road), near the Halifax Seaport Farmers' Market.
The museum is fully accessible with elevators and ramps, making it easy to navigate for all visitors.

places.name: 6. St. Paul's Church
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/st-pauls-church-at-grand-parade-in-halifax-nova-scotia-gm641912978-116449753

Located at the south end of the Grand Parade in downtown Halifax, St Paul’s Anglican Church is the oldest building in the city and the oldest Protestant place of worship in Canada. Founded in 1749, it stands as a testament to the early British settlement of Halifax and is a significant piece of North American architectural history.
What to See and Do

The Silhouette in the Window: One of the church's most famous legends involves a window on the second floor. Following the 1917 Halifax Explosion, a shadow appeared in the glass that resembles the profile of a man; locals often say it is the silhouette of a curate from that era.

Architectural Heritage: Modelled after Marybone Chapel in London, it features a classic Georgian design. You can still see a piece of a wooden window frame from the Halifax Explosion embedded in the interior walls of the vestibule.
The Crypt: Beneath the church lies a historic crypt containing the remains of several notable figures from Nova Scotia's history, including early governors and military leaders.

Living History: Beyond its role as a landmark, it remains an active parish with a vibrant music program, often hosting choral performances and organ recitals that take advantage of its historic acoustics.
Tips and Key Information
When you enter, ask a guide to point out the wooden debris lodged above the interior door—a sobering physical reminder of the 1917 disaster.
The church faces the Halifax City Hall across the Grand Parade. This plaza is a central meeting point and often hosts civic ceremonies or seasonal displays.
While photography is generally permitted, be mindful of any ongoing services or private prayer, as it is a quiet sanctuary in the middle of a busy city.
Generally open for visitors Monday through Friday from roughly 9:30 AM to 3:00 PM (hours can vary on Wednesdays and during special services).
isiting the church is free, though donations are welcome to help maintain the historic structure.
Located at 1749 Argyle Street, directly across from the busy entertainment district of downtown Halifax.

places.name: 7. Alexander Keith's Brewery
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/brewery-gm1701188823-538721467

Alexander Keith’s Brewery is a Halifax landmark where visitors can experience one of Canada’s oldest breweries in a beautifully preserved 1820 building. Founded by the three-time mayor of Halifax, Alexander Keith, whose brewing legacy has become an integral part of Nova Scotia’s history. Located in a historic ironstone building on Lower Water Street, it offers a theatrical glimpse into the city's brewing heritage.
What to See and Do

Theatrical Brewery Tour: This is not your average technical tour. Actors in full Victorian period costume lead you through the brewery, sharing stories of 1863 Halifax, singing traditional songs, and teaching you about the brewing process of the time.

Stag's Head Tavern: The tour concludes in this authentic underground tavern located within the brewery's cavernous basement. Here, you can sample various Keith's brews while enjoying live maritime music and traditional games.

Historic Architecture: Even if you don't take the tour, the building itself is a landmark. Known as Keith's Hall, it features beautiful mid-19th-century masonry and connected the brewery to Mr. Keith's personal residence.
Tips and Key Information
Tours are popular, especially when cruise ships are in port or during summer weekends. It's highly recommended to reserve your spot online ahead of time.

While the focus is on beer, the tour is surprisingly family-friendly due to the costume performances and music. Non-alcoholic beverages (like local ginger ale) are provided for children and non-drinkers.
The brewery is a short walk from the Historic Properties area, making it easy to pair a tour with a meal at a nearby waterfront pub.
Typically open Monday through Thursday from 11:30 AM to 7:00 PM, and Friday/Saturday with slightly earlier or later starts. It is currently closed on Sundays.
It is located at 1496 Lower Water Street, situated within the Brewery Market complex.
Tour tickets are required for the full experience and usually include beer samples for those of legal drinking age.

places.name: 8. St. Mary's Basilica
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/st-marys-basilica-in-halifax-gm1019949114-274061517

Saint Mary's Cathedral Basilica is a striking cornerstone of Halifax’s religious and architectural history, located at the busy intersection of Spring Garden Road and Barrington Street. Built in the Gothic Revival style, it is the cathedral church of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Halifax-Yarmouth and is designated as a National Historic Site of Canada.
What to See and Do

The Granite Spire: The cathedral boasts the tallest granite spire in North America, a magnificent architectural feat that dominates the local skyline and serves as a landmark for those navigating the downtown core.

Stained Glass Masterpieces: The interior is illuminated by breathtaking stained glass windows that depict various biblical scenes and saints, creating a tranquil and colorful atmosphere even on foggy Atlantic days.
Gothic Revival Details: Observe the intricate stone carvings and the sweeping arches of the nave, which reflect the mid-19th-century European architectural influences brought to the New World.

Spiritual Sanctuary: Visitors often step inside to find a peaceful respite from the bustling shopping district outside, whether to attend a mass or simply to admire the quiet dignity of the sanctuary.
Tips and Key Information

As an active place of worship, it is best to plan your visit around scheduled masses if you wish to tour the interior; if a service is in progress, visitors are asked to remain in the back or join the congregation.
The best time for exterior photography is in the late afternoon when the sun hits the light-colored granite, highlighting the texture of the stonework against the sky.
Since it is located right on Spring Garden Road, it is perfectly situated for a quick visit between exploring the Halifax Public Gardens and the downtown waterfront.
Typically open for visitors Monday through Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM. It is closed to the public on Saturdays and open Sunday mornings for services.
Entry is free, though as with most historic churches, donations for the upkeep of the building are appreciated.
Located at 5221 Spring Garden Road, Halifax.

places.name: 9. Old Town Clock
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/altstadt-uhr-gm1425400272-469878639

The Old Town Clock is one of Halifax's most enduring and recognizable symbols. Perched on the eastern slope of Citadel Hill, it has kept time for the city since 1803. The clock was a gift from Prince Edward, Duke of Kent, who served as the commander-in-chief of British forces in North America and was famously obsessed with punctuality.
What to See and Do

Palladian Architecture: The structure features a classic white circular tower set atop a copper-roofed rectangular building. Its design is a prime example of the Palladian style that was popular in the British Empire during the early 19th century.

The Original Mechanism: Remarkably, the clock still uses much of its original wind-up mechanism, which was crafted by the House of Vuillamy, the royal clockmakers in London. It is still meticulously maintained by Parks Canada staff today.

Four-Sided Visibility: The clock has four faces, each facing one of the cardinal directions, ensuring that soldiers at the Halifax Citadel National Historic Site and sailors in the harbour alike could always stay on schedule.
Tips and Key Information

For the most iconic Halifax shot, stand on the sidewalk of Brunswick Street looking up toward the clock with the grassy hill as your backdrop. Alternatively, capture it from the top of the hill to get the clock in the foreground with the modern downtown and harbour behind it.
Most visitors encounter the clock while walking from the downtown core up to the Citadel. It is a steep climb, so the benches near the clock offer a perfect spot to catch your breath.
The clock is beautifully illuminated at night, making it a striking landmark for those enjoying the nearby entertainment district on Argyle Street.
While you cannot go inside the clock tower itself, the exterior is accessible 24/7 as it is located on public land managed by Parks Canada.
Free to view and photograph.
Located in Brunswick Street at the foot of Citadel Hill, Halifax.

places.name: 10. Government House
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/government-house-gm176979573-19883590

Government House is the official residence of the Lieutenant Governor of Nova Scotia and stands as one of the oldest viceregal residences in North America. Completed in 1805, this elegant stone mansion has hosted members of the Royal Family for over two centuries and remains a premier example of Adam-style Georgian architecture in Canada.
What to See and Do

State Rooms and Art: The interior is filled with period antiques, portraits of British monarchs, and a significant collection of silver. Visitors often admire the grand staircase and the drawing room where formal receptions are held.

Royal Connection: As a functioning royal residence, it features a dedicated suite for the reigning monarch. You can see the Royal Standard flying from the roof whenever the Lieutenant Governor or a member of the Royal Family is in residence.

Architectural Detail: Built using native Nova Scotian sandstone, the exterior features classic symmetry and delicate decorative flourishes that reflect the status of the British Crown in the early 19th century.
Tips and Key Information

While it is a private residence, free guided tours are typically offered to the public during the summer months (July and August). It is best to check the official website of the Lieutenant Governor for specific dates and to book a time slot.
Even if you aren't visiting for a tour, the exterior and the well-manicured grounds are visible from the street and offer a stately backdrop for photos in the downtown South End.
Because this is an active government office and home, security is present. Visitors for tours should be prepared for a standard security screening upon entry.
Open for pre-booked public tours during the summer season; otherwise, the building is closed to the public for official state business.
Tours are free of charge.
Located at 1451 Barrington Street, Halifax—just a short walk from Saint Mary's Cathedral Basilica.

places.name: 1. Art Gallery of Nova Scotia
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/old-stone-government-customs-building-has-been-repurposed-as-the-art-gallery-of-nova-gm1336989932-418034621

The Art Gallery of Nova Scotia is the largest art museum in Atlantic Canada, housing a premier collection of over 18,000 works. It serves as a vital cultural hub, celebrating both the traditional heritage and contemporary spirit of the region.
What to See and Do

Maud Lewis House: The gallery’s most beloved exhibit is the actual tiny, brightly painted house of folk artist Maud Lewis. Visitors can step inside the fully restored structure, which she covered in cheerful birds, flowers, and animals despite her physical struggles.
Permanent Collection: Explore a vast array of Atlantic Canadian art, ranging from historical portraiture and landscapes to Inuit stone carvings and modern sculptures.
Rotating Exhibitions: The gallery frequently hosts high-caliber traveling exhibitions, showcasing international masters alongside emerging local talent in its expansive contemporary wings.
Tips and Key Information
If you are visiting on a budget, the gallery typically offers free admission on Thursday evenings from 5:00 PM to 9:00 PM, though it can get quite busy during these hours.
The gallery shop is widely considered one of the best places in Halifax to buy authentic local crafts, high-quality prints of Maud Lewis's work, and unique jewelry made by Nova Scotian artisans.
The gallery is located directly across from Province House and very close to the Halifax Waterfront Boardwalk, making it an easy addition to a day spent exploring the city's historic core.
Open Tuesday through Sunday from 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM (extended until 9:00 PM on Thursdays). It is closed on Mondays.
Located at 1723 Hollis Street, Halifax.
Admission fees apply for adults, with discounts for seniors and students. Children under 5 are usually free.

places.name: 2. HMCS Sackville (Historic Warship)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/halifax-am-wasser-gm1425747894-470127288

The HMCS Sackville is a crown jewel of Canada’s naval history, serving as the country's oldest warship and the last surviving Flower-class corvette from the Second World War. Moored prominently along the waterfront, it serves as a moving memorial to the Royal Canadian Navy and the Battle of the Atlantic.
What to See and Do

Battle of the Atlantic Experience: Visitors can step back into 1941 to see how sailors lived and worked during the longest continuous military campaign of WWII. The ship is meticulously restored to its wartime configuration, from the cramped mess decks to the bridge.
The Convoy Story: The museum highlights the critical role these small ships played in escorting merchant convoys across the treacherous Atlantic, providing a visceral look at the North Atlantic Run.
Summer Mooring: During the summer months, the ship is typically docked at Sackville Landing, right next to the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic, allowing for an easy double feature of naval history.
Winter Berth: Note that in late autumn, the ship is often moved to the nearby HMC Dockyard for maintenance and protection against the harsh Atlantic winter, so it is primarily a seasonal attraction.
Tips and Key Information
Being a genuine warship, the stairs are actually steep naval ladders. Wear sturdy, comfortable footwear and be prepared for some tight spaces as you explore below deck.
The ship is often staffed by veterans and dedicated volunteers who have a deep passion for naval lore; don't hesitate to ask them questions, as their personal stories add immense value to the tour.
Because it sits right on the boardwalk, it’s a perfect stop between the Maritime Museum and the ferry terminal.
Generally open daily from June to October, roughly 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM.
Small admission fees apply, which go directly toward the preservation and maintenance of this historic vessel.
Located at Sackville Landing, 1675 Lower Water Street (summer location).

places.name: 3. Fairview Lawn Cemetery (Titanic Gravesite)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/titanic-grave-site-gm535313093-57377962

The Fairview Lawn Cemetery is a site of international pilgrimage, known primarily as the final resting place for 121 victims of the RMS Titanic disaster. While a somber location, it is a beautifully maintained and peaceful landscape that offers a profound connection to one of the 20th century's greatest maritime tragedies.
What to See and Do
Titanic Graves: The most visited section features three long lines of granite headstones. Most of these markers were paid for by the White Star Line and are dated April 15, 1912.

Unknown Child Monument: For decades, this grave stood as a symbol of all the lost children of the Titanic. Although DNA testing in 2007 identified the child as Sidney Leslie Goodwin, the monument remains a deeply emotional focal point for visitors.

Grave of J. Dawson: This headstone (belonging to Joseph Dawson) gained worldwide fame after the 1997 James Cameron film Titanic. Despite the character Jack Dawson being fictional, many fans leave flowers and tokens at this real grave.

Halifax Explosion Victims: Beyond the Titanic, the cemetery also contains a section dedicated to those who perished in the 1917 Halifax Explosion, providing another layer of the city's resilient history.
Tips and Key Information
As this is an active municipal cemetery, visitors are asked to maintain a quiet and respectful demeanor.
The Titanic section is located in the northern part of the cemetery. There are often small signs or maps at the main entrances to guide you toward the Titanic Gravesite.
To fully appreciate the site, visit the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic first to understand the context of the recovery effort before heading to the cemetery.
Generally open from dawn until dusk.
Free to the public.
Located at 3720 Windsor Street, Halifax. It is about a 10-15 minute drive from the downtown core.

places.name: 4. C.S.S. Acadia
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/css-acadia-gm2211828002-628793069

The C.S.S. Acadia is a Grand Old Lady of the sea and one of Canada’s most significant historic vessels. Permanently moored at the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic, this retired hydrographic research ship has a resume unlike any other: she is the only vessel still afloat that survived the 1917 Halifax Explosion and served in the Royal Canadian Navy during both World Wars.
What to See and Do

Step Back to 1913: Walk the teak decks of a ship that looks much as she did when she was launched over 110 years ago. You can explore the beautifully preserved Captain’s Quarters, complete with period furniture and brass fittings that reflect the Edwardian era.

The Engine Room: Descend into the heart of the ship to see the massive, immaculately maintained triple-expansion steam engine. It is a masterclass in industrial-age engineering and remains a favorite for gearheads and history buffs alike.
Explore Scientific Labs: See the original chart rooms and labs where hydrographers lived for months at a time while mapping the uncharted, ice-infested waters of the Arctic and Hudson Bay.
Wartime History: Learn about her time as H.M.C.S. Acadia, when she was outfitted with guns and depth charges to patrol for German U-boats along the Nova Scotian coast during the Atlantic campaigns.

The Ship's Cat: Look for the current Rodent Control Officer. Since 1982, the Acadia has maintained a tradition of having a resident ship's cat to keep the vessel company and carry on a centuries-old maritime custom.
Tips and Key Information

As of March 2026, the interior of the ship is generally open for tours from May to October. During the winter months, you can still view the ship from the wharf, but the decks and interior are closed for maintenance.
Access to the C.S.S. Acadia is included in your ticket to the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic (approx. $9.55 for adults in peak season). You do not need a separate ticket to board.

Because this is an authentic historic vessel, the stairs between decks are steep, ladder-like maritime steps. Wear sensible, flat-soled shoes—heels or flip-flops can be tricky on the metal gratings and teak decks.

While the main deck is accessible to many, the lower decks and engine room require navigating narrow passages and steep ladders. If you have limited mobility, the museum offers a virtual tour and detailed exhibits about the ship inside the main building.

When you are on the deck, look toward the Narrows (under the Macdonald Bridge). This is where the Mont-Blanc exploded in 1917. The Acadia was anchored nearby and survived with only minor damage, making your spot on the deck a literal piece of living history.
She is hard to miss—look for the gleaming white hull and buff-colored funnel at 1675 Lower Water Street, right on the Halifax Waterfront Boardwalk.

places.name: 5. Old Burying Ground
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/old-burying-ground-gm1958264321-557661282

The Old Burying Ground is a significant historic site in downtown Halifax that served as the city's primary cemetery from its founding in 1749 until 1844. This designated National Historic Site of Canada offers a quiet, reflective space that chronicles the early history and genealogy of the city's settlers.
What to See and Do
Historical Significance: It is the final resting place of approximately 12,000 people, including many of Halifax's earliest residents, British soldiers, and sailors.

Artistic Gravestones: The site is renowned for its collection of 18th and early 19th-century headstones, which feature intricate carvings of cherubs, death's heads, and other traditional motifs that reflect the era's views on mortality.
Welsford-Parker Monument: At the entrance stands an impressive stone arch topped by a lion, which is the only monument in North America dedicated to the Crimean War.
Guided Insight: During the summer months, student interpreters are often on-site to provide historical context and help visitors decipher the weathered inscriptions.
Tips and Key Information
To protect the fragile, centuries-old headstones and the surrounding landscape, visitors are requested to remain on the gravel walkways.
While the carvings are beautiful, taking gravestone rubbings is strictly forbidden to prevent further erosion of the delicate sandstone.
It is conveniently located at the corner of Barrington Street and Spring Garden Road, right across from Saint Mary's Cathedral Basilica, making it an easy addition to a downtown walking tour.
Typically open to the public daily from May through October, from dawn until dusk.
Entry is free, and the site is maintained by a dedicated volunteer foundation.

places.name: 6. McNabs Island Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/mcnabs-insel-leuchtturm-gm638848164-114807077

McNabs and Lawlor Islands Provincial Park is a hidden gem located at the entrance of the Halifax Harbour. As the largest island in the harbour, it offers a rugged escape into nature combined with fascinating military and social history, making it a favorite for hikers and history buffs alike.
What to See and Do

Fort Ives and Military Ruins: Explore the remains of several coastal defense batteries, including Fort Ives, which served as a crucial part of the city's defense system from the mid-19th century through World War II.

Hiking and Beachcombing: The island features over 22 kilometers of hiking trails that wind through forests and along the shoreline. Visitors often head to Maugers Beach for spectacular views of the harbour and the lighthouse.

Victorian Gardens and Teahouse Ruins: Discover the overgrown remnants of Victorian-era gardens and the foundations of the island's former teahouse, which hint at its past life as a popular Victorian recreation destination.
Birdwatching: The park is a significant habitat for various bird species, making it an excellent spot for quiet observation away from the city's noise.
Tips and Key Information
Since there is no bridge, you must arrange a trip via a private boat charter or water taxi from Halifax, Dartmouth, or Eastern Passage. It is essential to book your return trip in advance.
There are no stores or restaurants on the island. You must bring all your own water, food, and supplies, and ensure you take all your trash back with you (Leave No Trace).
The trails can be rugged and overgrown in sections. Wear comfortable, closed-toe hiking shoes to navigate the gravel paths and forested terrain safely.
Like many outdoor areas in Nova Scotia, ticks are present on the island. It is highly recommended to wear long pants and use insect repellent.
Open daily from 8:00 AM to 11:00 PM year-round.
There is no fee to enter the provincial park itself, though you will need to pay for your boat transportation to and from the island.
Accessible only by water; charters typically depart from various points around the Halifax Harbour.

places.name: 7. Province House
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/province-house-halifax-canada-gm669131082-122252939

Province House is the oldest legislative building in Canada and a stunning example of Palladian architecture. Completed in 1819, it was famously described by Charles Dickens as looking like a short-lived palace of ivory, and it continues to serve as the seat of the Nova Scotia House of Assembly.
What to See and Do

Legislative Assembly Chamber: Step into the room where Canadian democracy was shaped. This ornate chamber is where responsible government was first established in the British Empire outside of the UK in 1848.

Red Chamber: Formerly the home of the Legislative Council (the upper house), this room is renowned for its portraits of King George III and Queen Charlotte, as well as its intricate plasterwork and historical artifacts.
Legislative Library: This beautiful room was once the Supreme Court of Nova Scotia and was the site of Joseph Howe’s famous 1835 libel trial, a landmark case for freedom of the press in Canada.
Tips and Key Information
When the House of Assembly is in session, you can actually sit in the public gallery and watch the democratic process in action.
Guided tours are available year-round and are the best way to hear the colorful stories of the politicians and events that shaped the province.
Because it is an active government building, access to certain rooms may be restricted during official functions or when the House is sitting.
Open Monday through Friday from 8:30 AM to 4:00 PM. It is closed on weekends.
Free of charge for both self-guided and guided tours.
Conveniently located across from the Art Gallery of Nova Scotia.

places.name: 8. Georges Island National Historic Site
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/boot-vorbei-an-georges-island-gm2155085303-575914396

Georges Island National Historic Site is a teardrop-shaped island in the heart of Halifax Harbour that only recently opened to the general public. Historically used as a defensive fortification, a prison, and a tragic internment camp for Acadians, it now offers some of the most unique underground perspectives of the city's military past.
What to See and Do

Fort Charlotte & Tunnel Tours: The main attraction is the network of dark, stone tunnels beneath Fort Charlotte. Guided tours (included with admission) lead you through the magazine complex where gunpowder was once stored in bomb-proof safety.

The Acadian & Mi'kmaq History: Visit the interpretive panels that share the island's difficult history as an internment camp for Acadians during the Great Upheaval (1755–1764) and its significance to the Mi'kmaq, who call it Elpaqkwitk.
Lighthouse Views: While the lighthouse itself is automated and closed to the public, the area around it offers stunning, sea-level views of the Halifax and Dartmouth skylines.
Parks Canada Perfect Picnic: Many visitors pre-order a Perfect Picnic from local vendors on the mainland to enjoy at the red chairs or picnic tables overlooking the harbour.
Tips and Key Information
The island is only accessible by water. Most visitors take the ferry from the Halifax Waterfront (near the Cable Wharf), but you can also arrive via private boat or kayak.
Even on a hot summer day, the tunnels are damp and cool, and the winds off the Atlantic can be quite biting. Sturdy, closed-toe shoes are essential for the slippery stone floors.
There are no trash cans, shops, or cafes on the island. You must bring your own water and supplies and take all your waste back to the mainland.
Expect to spend about 2 hours on the island, plus travel time. It’s a perfect half-day excursion.
The island is typically open from mid-June to mid-October. It is often only open on specific days (like weekends and select weekdays), so check the schedule before booking.
Admission is free from June 19 to September 7 as part of the Canada Strong Pass promotion, though ferry fees still apply.
While the ferry and main paths are accessible, the interior of the fort has steep ditches and steps that may be difficult for those with mobility issues.

places.name: 9. York Redoubt National Historic Site
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/herbst-an-einer-felsigen-k%C3%BCste-in-ferguson-es-cove-york-redoubt-national-historic-gm1182346388-331970144

Perched on a high bluff overlooking the entrance to the Halifax Harbour, the York Redoubt National Historic Site is a formidable 200-year-old fortification that served as a key element of the city's defense system until the end of World War II. It offers a more rugged and sprawling experience than the Citadel, with a focus on coastal defense and panoramic Atlantic vistas.
What to See and Do
Coastal Defense Batteries: Explore the remnants of massive rifled muzzle-loading guns and concrete searchlight emplacements that were designed to protect the harbour from enemy ships.
Command Post View: The site offers some of the most spectacular, unobstructed views of the Halifax Harbour, McNabs Island, and the open ocean, making it a premier spot for ship-watching.
Tunnels and Bunkers: Wander through the gatehouse and explore various stone and concrete structures that housed soldiers and ammunition for over two centuries.
Hiking Trails: The site features several kilometers of trails that wind through the old fortifications and natural wooded areas, providing a blend of history and outdoor recreation.
Tips and Key Information
Because of its exposed position on the bluff, it is almost always windier and cooler here than in downtown Halifax. A windbreaker or layers are highly recommended.
York Redoubt is typically much less crowded than the Halifax Citadel, making it an excellent choice for those looking for a quiet, self-guided historical walk.
While many areas are open to the sky, a small flashlight can be helpful for peering into some of the darker corners of the bunkers and gun emplacements.
The grounds are generally open daily from dawn until dusk.
Entry to the site is free of charge.
Located at 300 Fergusons Cove Road, about a 15-20 minute drive south of downtown Halifax.

places.name: 10. Halifax Explosion Memorial Bell Tower
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/halifax-explosion-memorial-glockenturm-gm1127397687-297126187

The Halifax Explosion Memorial Bell Tower stands as a solemn reminder of the tragic 1917 Halifax Explosion that devastated the city. Located at Fort Needham Memorial Park, near the former Richmond District and close to the blast’s epicentre, the tower commemorates the lives lost and the resilience Halifax showed in the aftermath.

Its significance comes from its connection to one of the deadliest explosions in history, which killed nearly 2,000 people and injured thousands more. Today, visitors come here to reflect, pay tribute to those affected, and better understand this defining chapter in Halifax’s history.
What to See and Do
The Memorial Bells: The tower houses a carillon of ten bells, which are rung annually during the memorial ceremony at 9:04 AM on December 6th, marking the exact moment of the explosion.

Commemorative Plaques: Surrounding the tower are plaques that provide historical context, detailing the collision of the Mont-Blanc and the Imo and the subsequent devastation of the Richmond neighborhood.

Fort Needham Memorial Park: The park itself was created on the hill that shielded part of the city from the blast. It offers walking trails and interpretive displays that explain how the area was rebuilt.
Panoramic Views: Due to its elevated position, the site provides a clear view of the Narrows in the Halifax Harbour, allowing visitors to visualize exactly where the disaster occurred.
Tips and Key Information
To fully grasp the magnitude of the event, see the Halifax Explosion exhibit at the Maritime Museum of the Atlantic before visiting the tower.
If you are in Halifax in early December, attending the annual memorial service is a deeply moving experience that brings the entire community together.
The park is generally very peaceful and offers a quieter alternative to the busy downtown landmarks, making it ideal for those who want a somber, historically significant walk.
The monument is located in a public park and is accessible 24 hours a day.
Free to the public.
Located at 3340 Union Street, Halifax. It is situated in the North End, approximately a 10-minute drive from the city center.

places.name: 1. Peggy’s Cove Lighthouse
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/peggy-es-cove-lighthouse-gm1401589722-454789966

The Peggy’s Point Lighthouse (widely known as Peggy’s Cove Lighthouse) stands as a stark, white sentinel against the rugged Atlantic coastline. Perched atop massive, wave-worn granite rocks, this iconic red-and-white tower has become the most famous symbol of Nova Scotia and one of the most photographed landmarks in all of Canada.
What to See and Do

The Lighthouse and Granite Barrens: Walk across the vast, undulating granite rocks that surround the tower. These unique geological formations were carved by retreating glaciers thousands of years ago and offer a dramatic, lunar-like landscape for exploration.

Fishing Village: Wander through the actual village of Peggy’s Cove. It is a tiny, active community where you can see colorful fish stores, weathered wharves, and lobster traps stacked high against the backdrop of the crashing surf.

William deGarthe Memorial Monument: Visit this 100-foot-long sculpture carved directly into a granite rock face by a local artist. it depicts 32 fishermen, their families, and the legendary Peggy of the Cove amidst maritime wings and waves.

Village Post Office: Located inside the lower level of the lighthouse during the summer months, this is one of the only post offices in the world located inside an active lighthouse. You can send a postcard with a special lighthouse cancellation stamp.
Degarthe Gallery: Explore the former home and studio of sculptor William deGarthe to see his paintings and smaller sculptures that capture the rugged beauty of the Atlantic coast.
Tips and Key Information

Stay off the black rocks. This is a vital safety warning. The black rocks"are dark because they are frequently hit by rogue waves and are extremely slippery. People are swept into the Atlantic every year; always stay on the dry, white rocks.
Peggy’s Cove is an incredibly popular destination. To experience the site without the crowds of tour buses, try to arrive before 9:00 AM or stay for a spectacular sunset after 6:00 PM.
The cove is highly exposed to the Atlantic Ocean. Even if it is a warm day in Halifax, the wind at the lighthouse is often biting and much cooler. A windbreaker or light jacket is highly recommended.
For those with mobility concerns, a large wooden viewing platform provides a safe, level surface to view the lighthouse and the ocean without having to navigate the uneven granite rocks.
Located approximately 45 minutes (43 km) from downtown Halifax via Route 333 (the Lighthouse Route). Parking is free in the large lot at the entrance to the village.
There is no fee to visit the lighthouse, the rocks, or the village. It is a public site accessible year-round.

The Sou'Wester Gift & Restaurant is located right next to the lighthouse for a classic lobster roll, but several smaller shacks in the village offer local seafood and ice cream during the peak season.

places.name: 2. Halifax Harbour Ferry
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/halifax-nova-scotia-gm2197859584-615781244

The Halifax Harbour Ferry is the oldest continuously operating saltwater ferry service in North America, having begun in 1752. For the price of a bus fare, it provides a scenic 15-minute mini-cruise across one of the world’s deepest natural harbors, connecting the bustling Halifax Waterfront with the trendy Alderney Landing in downtown Dartmouth.
What to See and Do
Skyline Views: Enjoy the best panoramic view of the Halifax skyline, including the Citadel, the Old Town Clock, and the rising glass towers of the Queen’s Marque, all from the open-top deck.

The Fleet of Heroes: Look for the names on the vessels. Each ferry is named after a local legend, such as Vincent Coleman (the heroic dispatcher who warned trains during the 1917 Halifax Explosion) or Viola Desmond (the civil rights icon featured on the Canadian $10 bill).
Alderney Landing: Once you dock in Dartmouth, explore this multi-purpose complex. It houses an art gallery, a theater, and a popular weekend Farmers' Market featuring local produce and crafts.

Dartmouth Food Scene: Just a few steps from the terminal, you can visit local favorites like The Canteen, Battery Park Beer Bar, or Lake City Cider. It’s the perfect spot for a lunch break before heading back to Halifax.
Harbour Traffic: Keep your eyes peeled for massive container ships, naval frigates, and occasionally a visiting cruise ship or a traditional tall ship like the Silva gliding through the water.
Tips and Key Information
The ferry terminals do not give change. As of 2026, the fare is $3.00 for adults. You can also use a Halifax Transit bus pass or the HfxGO mobile app.
If you pay with cash, be sure to ask the attendant for a paper transfer. This allows you to ride the ferry back for free (or catch a bus) within a 90-minute window.
The Alderney Ferry runs every 15 minutes during weekday peak hours and every 30 minutes during evenings and weekends. The Woodside Ferry (targeting commuters) only runs Monday through Friday.
If you want the best photos, head straight for the upper deck. However, it is often much windier and colder on the water than on land, so hold onto your hat!
The ferries and terminals are fully accessible with ramps and elevators, making this one of the easiest ways for travelers with limited mobility to see the harbor.
Children ages 12 and under ride all Halifax Transit services, including the ferry, for free.

places.name: 3. Sir Sandford Fleming Park (The Dingle)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/dingle-turm-an-sir-sandford-fleming-park-halifax-nova-scotia-kanada-gm846819220-138761803

Sir Sandford Fleming Park, affectionately known by locals as The Dingle, is a 95-acre urban oasis donated to the city in 1908 by the man who gave the world Standard Time. Nestled along the Northwest Arm, this park combines lush woodlands, saltwater beaches, and a towering monument that commemorates Nova Scotia’s role in democratic history.
What to See and Do

The Dingle Tower: The park’s centerpiece is a massive Italianate-style stone tower built between 1908 and 1912. It was erected to mark the 150th anniversary of the establishment of representative government in Nova Scotia—the first of its kind in the British Commonwealth.

The Bronze Lions: Guarding the entrance to the tower are two magnificent bronze lions, donated by the Royal Colonial Institute of London. They are replicas of the famous lions in Trafalgar Square and are a favorite spot for children to climb and take photos.

Coastal Trails: Walk the extensive network of wooded trails that wind along the shoreline of the Northwest Arm. These paths offer peaceful views of the private yacht clubs and historic estates on the opposite side of the water.

The Frog Pond: Just across the road from the main park entrance, this trail loops around a picturesque pond. In the summer, it’s a haven for birdwatchers; in the winter, it’s a classic local spot for outdoor skating.
Sandy Beach and Boat Launch: While the water is chilly, the small sandy beach is a popular spot for a picnic or for launching a kayak to explore the calm waters of the Arm.
Tips and Key Information

During the summer months (typically June to Labour Day), you can climb the interior staircase to the top of the Dingle Tower. The observation deck provides a stunning, bird’s-eye view of the entire Northwest Arm and the surrounding forest.

Look for the plaques inside the tower. They represent various parts of the British Empire at the time of construction. Fleming himself was the engineer who oversaw the Canadian Pacific Railway and championed the adoption of 24 standard time zones.
There are two main parking lots. The lower lot near the tower fills up quickly on sunny weekends, so try the upper lot near the Frog Pond if you’re looking for a longer hike.
This is one of the most popular spots in Halifax for dog walkers. Dogs are welcome but must remain on a leash in most areas of the park.
Unlike the downtown waterfront, there are fewer food vendors here. Bring your own snacks to enjoy at one of the many picnic tables overlooking the water.
Located on the western side of the Northwest Arm (Dingle Road, off Purcells Cove Road). It’s about a 10-minute drive from downtown Halifax or a 20-minute bike ride.

places.name: 4. Long Lake Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/herbst-long-lake-provincial-public-park-halifax-nova-scotia-kanada-gm1055919942-282180870

Long Lake Provincial Park is a massive 2,000-hectare wilderness escape located just minutes from the urban core of Halifax. It offers a perfect balance between rugged Nova Scotian backcountry and accessible, well-groomed trails. Whether you are looking for a high-intensity trail run or a quiet afternoon by the water, this park is the city’s favorite backyard for outdoor enthusiasts.
What to See and Do

The Lake Loop: Explore the 5-kilometer groomed crusher-dust trail that circles a portion of the park. It is wide, flat, and perfect for strollers, bicycles, and joggers who want a scenic view of the water without the technical terrain of a mountain hike.

Swimming and Sunbathing: During the summer months, the lake’s clean, clear water makes it one of the most popular swimming holes in the region. There are several rocky outcrops and a small sandy area near the main entrance that serve as makeshift beaches.

Paddling: Bring your own kayak, canoe, or paddleboard (or rent one seasonally at the Northwest Arm Drive entrance). With its many hidden coves and small islands, Long Lake is a paddler’s paradise that feels miles away from the city noise.

The Old Trails: For those seeking a more rugged experience, the western side of the park features narrow, root-filled goat paths that wind through dense pine forests and over granite barrens, offering a true taste of the Acadian forest.

Winter Activities: When the snow falls, the groomed trails become a hub for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing. On particularly cold winters, the lake freezes over for wide-open skating (though ice thickness should always be checked first).
Tips and Key Information

There are two distinct sides to the park. The Northwest Arm Drive entrance features the groomed Lake Loop and the kayak rentals, while the St. Margarets Bay Road entrance offers more rugged, traditional hiking trails.
Because of its proximity to the Bayers Lake shopping district and residential areas, the main parking lots fill up very quickly on sunny weekends. Arrive before 10:00 AM to secure a spot.
Long Lake is incredibly popular with dog owners. Dogs must be kept on a leash at all times to protect the local wildlife and ensure the safety of other trail users.
As a Provincial Park, there are limited trash cans along the interior trails. Be prepared to carry your waste back to the main trailheads to help keep the water and forest pristine.
The lake is very deep in some areas and there are no lifeguards on duty. If you are swimming or paddling, use caution and consider wearing a life jacket.
Access points are located off Northwest Arm Drive and St. Margarets Bay Road. It is roughly a 10-15 minute drive from downtown Halifax and is accessible via several Halifax Transit bus routes.

places.name: 5. Hemlock Ravine Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/herbstliebe-gm1180881470-330975639

Hemlock Ravine Park is a hidden natural gem located in the Bedford Basin area of Halifax. Once part of the sprawling country estate of Prince Edward, Duke of Kent (the father of Queen Victoria), this 200-acre park is famous for its towering old-growth trees and a heart-shaped pond that serves as a romantic tribute from the city’s past.
What to See and Do

The Heart-Shaped Pond: This is the park's most famous feature. Originally built by Prince Edward in the 1790s as a gift for his mistress, Julie St. Laurent, the pond remains a perfectly shaped heart. It is a quiet, reflective spot surrounded by benches and a favorite for wedding photography.

Old-Growth Hemlocks: Hike through the Ravine to see massive Eastern Hemlock trees, some of which are over 300 years old. These giants escaped the massive 1917 Halifax Explosion and provide a thick, cooling canopy even on the hottest summer days.

Julie’s Walk Trail: This 4-kilometer loop is a well-maintained, gravel-surfaced trail that takes you through the heart of the ravine. It’s an easy-to-moderate walk that feels like stepping into a deep, ancient forest.

Birdwatching: Because of the dense, multi-layered forest, the park is a sanctuary for local birdlife. Keep an ear out for woodpeckers and owls, especially in the quieter sections of the ravine furthest from the road.

Historic Ruins: Keep an eye out for stone foundations and remnants of the original estate. While the grand Prince's Lodge rotunda sits across the highway, the park itself contains traces of the elaborate gardens and pathways of the 18th-century royal retreat.
Tips and Key Information

The park features some significant elevation changes. While the area around the Heart-Shaped Pond is relatively flat, the trails leading into the ravine involve steep inclines that can be a great workout but may be challenging for those with limited mobility.

A portion of the park is a designated off-leash area for dogs. If you are walking with a pet or have children who are nervous around dogs, check the trail signs to know which loops allow for off-leash play.

Unlike the busy Halifax Public Gardens, Hemlock Ravine is often very quiet. It is the perfect spot for meditation, reading, or escaping the city's hustle and bustle without leaving the municipal limits.
The main entrance and parking lot are located at the end of Kent Avenue (off the Bedford Highway). There is also an entrance via the residential neighborhood on Starboard Drive.

Because the ravine is deep and shaded by evergreen trees, snow and ice tend to linger on the trails much longer than in the rest of the city. Micro-spikes or sturdy boots are recommended for winter hiking.
Located in 40 Kent Avenue, Halifax. It is roughly a 15-minute drive from downtown and is easily accessible via the Bedford Highway bus routes.

places.name: 6. Emera Oval
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/eislaufen-im-emera-oval-gm459019911-22849922

The Emera Oval is a massive outdoor refrigerated ice surface located on the Halifax Common. Originally built as a temporary venue for the 2011 Canada Winter Games, it was so beloved by locals that it was made a permanent fixture. Equivalent in size to three NHL hockey rinks, it is the largest outdoor artificially frozen ice surface east of Quebec City, offering free year-round recreation in the heart of the city.
What to See and Do

Ice Skating (Winter): From December to March, the Oval is a winter wonderland. Thousands of skaters of all skill levels glide around the 400-meter track. There are designated lanes for fast speed skaters and inner areas for those just learning.

Rollerblading and Biking (Summer): Once the ice melts, the concrete surface is perfect for inline skating, roller skating, and cycling. It is a smooth, safe environment away from car traffic, making it ideal for kids and beginners.

Night Skating: The Oval is beautifully illuminated at night with large floodlights, often accompanied by music playing over the loudspeaker system. It creates a magical, high-energy atmosphere during cold winter evenings.
Community Events: Throughout the year, the Oval hosts various festivals, including New Year’s Eve fireworks, Learn to Skate clinics, and charity races.
The Common Surroundings: After your skate, take a walk through the rest of the Halifax Common, Canada’s oldest urban park, which features playgrounds, a skatepark, and sprawling green space.
Tips and Key Information

One of the best things about the Oval is that it’s completely free. You can borrow skates, helmets, and even snowshoes (for the nearby fields) or rollerblades in the summer at no cost. You just need a valid government-issued ID.
Before heading out, always check the Halifax.ca website or the @hfxgov social media accounts. The Oval can close temporarily for flooding (resurfacing) or if the weather becomes too warm or rainy.
CSA-approved hockey helmets are mandatory for all children 12 and under, and highly recommended for everyone else. If you don't have one, you can borrow one for free on-site.
Skating always flows in one direction (usually counter-clockwise). Watch the staff and signs to see when the direction changes to ensure everyone stays safe.

There is a small pavilion on-site with washrooms and a place to lace up, but it can get crowded. Several local cafes on Quinpool Road or North Street are just a 5-minute walk away for a post-skate hot chocolate.
Located in 5775 Cogswell Street, Halifax (The North Common). It is centrally located and easily reachable by foot from downtown or via numerous bus routes.

places.name: 7. Point Pleasant Parkhttps://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/point-pleasant-park-gm2182719704-601652363
body: Point Pleasant Park is a sprawling 75-hectare wooded oasis situated at the southern tip of the Halifax peninsula. It is a unique blend of natural forest, coastal scenery, and deep military history. Once a key component of the city’s defense system, the park is now a beloved retreat for runners, dog walkers, and anyone looking to breathe in the fresh salt air of the Atlantic.
What to See and Do

The Prince of Wales Tower: This National Historic Site is the oldest Martello tower in North America (built in 1796). Its thick stone walls were designed to defend British batteries from a sea-based French attack. While you can't always go inside, its exterior is a focal point for history buffs.

Fortification Ruins: As you explore the 39 kilometers of trails, you’ll stumble upon the haunting stone remains of several coastal forts, including Fort Ogilvie and the Cambridge Battery. Many of these ruins are open for exploration and offer elevated views of the harbor entrance.

The Sailors' Memorial: Located near the shoreline, this large monument commemorates the members of the Royal Canadian Navy, Merchant Navy, and Army who lost their lives at sea during the World Wars and have no known grave.

Shakespeare by the Sea: During the summer months, the park’s Cambridge Battery transforms into an outdoor theater. This professional theater company performs classic plays under the stars, often using the historic ruins as a natural backdrop.

Black Rock Beach: A popular spot for sunbathing and watching the massive container ships enter the harbor. While the water is quite cold, it’s a favorite place for locals to sit on the rocks and enjoy the maritime breeze.
Tips and Key Information

Point Pleasant is arguably the most popular dog park in the city. Many of the interior trails are designated off-leash, so expect to meet plenty of friendly four-legged residents. If you prefer to avoid dogs, stick to the main perimeter road (Sailors' Memorial Way), which is strictly on-leash.

You may notice the forest looks relatively young in some areas. In 2003, Hurricane Juan leveled nearly 75% of the park's trees. The city has since replanted thousands of trees, and the park has become a living laboratory for forest regeneration.
