Vehicles are not permitted inside the park, making it a safe haven for pedestrians and cyclists. The wide, gravel-packed trails are mostly level and easy to navigate, though some interior paths have steep inclines.
Due to the dense forest and the history of wind damage, the park has a strict no-smoking policy to prevent forest fires.

The park is located at the very south end of Young Avenue and Tower Road. There are large parking lots at both the Tower Road and Point Pleasant Drive entrances. It is a 30-minute walk from downtown or a short ride on the #29 bus.
Entry is free, and the park is open daily from 6:00 AM to midnight.

places.name: 8. Angus L. Macdonald Bridge
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/angus-l-macdonald-bridge-gm2150467483-571632110

The Angus L. Macdonald Bridge stands as a majestic suspension span, arching over the deep blue waters of the Halifax Harbour. Connecting the downtown cores of Halifax and Dartmouth, this iconic Old Bridge is a vital transportation link and a premier vantage point for capturing the maritime essence of Nova Scotia.
What to See and Do

The Pedestrian Walkway: Located on the south side of the bridge, this high-altitude path offers the most famous panoramic view in the city. From 154 feet above the water, you can see the Halifax waterfront, George’s Island, and the sprawling Atlantic Ocean beyond.

Navy Ship Spotting: The bridge passes directly over HMCS Dockyard, the headquarters of the Royal Canadian Navy’s Atlantic Fleet. It is one of the few places in the world where you can walk directly over active frigates, coastal defense vessels, and visiting NATO warships.

Bicycle Lane: On the north side, a dedicated, separated lane allows cyclists to cross the harbor safely. It is a key segment of the Great Trail (Trans Canada Trail), providing a thrill for riders as they feel the slight sway of the suspension cables.

Big Lift Engineering: Look closely at the deck segments while walking; you are standing on a modern engineering marvel. Between 2015 and 2017, the entire suspended structure was replaced segment by segment while the bridge remained open to daytime traffic—a feat rarely attempted globally.

Evening Illuminations: After sunset, the bridge’s two massive steel towers are lit with decorative LED lighting. The reflection on the harbor water makes it a favorite subject for night photography from either the Dartmouth or Halifax shorelines.
Tips and Key Information
As of early 2025, the Macdonald Bridge is completely free for all users. The old toll plazas have been decommissioned, meaning you no longer need coins or a MACPASS to cross.

The bridge is highly exposed. Even on a mild day, the harbour blow can make the walkway feel 5–10 degrees colder than the street. Secure your hats and bring a windbreaker if you plan to walk the full 1.3 km span.
In Halifax, enter the walkway at the corner of North and Gottingen Streets. In Dartmouth, the entrance is located near the intersection of Wyse Road and Nantucket Avenue.
For the best golden hour shots of the Halifax skyline, walk from the Dartmouth side toward Halifax about an hour before sunset. The sun will illuminate the glass towers of downtown perfectly.

While the bridge is open to cars and transit buses, it has a strict weight limit. Heavy trucks and large tractor-trailers are prohibited and must use the A. Murray MacKay Bridge located further up the harbor.

While open 24/7, the bridge occasionally undergoes LifeSpan maintenance on weekends. Check the Halifax Harbour Bridges (HHB) website or social media for real-time updates on any scheduled sidewalk or lane closures.

If visiting in early August, check for the annual Bridgewalk day. The bridge closes to all motorized traffic, allowing thousands of people to walk the vehicle lanes for a massive mid-air community festival.

places.name: 1. Halifax Central Library
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/halifax-central-library-gm483425360-70999943

The Halifax Central Library is a striking architectural landmark that serves as the community living room for the city. Opened in 2014 and designed as a stack of four glass boxes, it has won numerous international awards, including the Governor General’s Medal in Architecture. More than just a place for books, it is a vibrant cultural hub in the heart of the Spring Garden Road shopping district.
What to See and Do

The Fifth Floor Living Room: Visit the top floor, which is a massive glass cantilever that hangs dramatically over the street. This quiet lounge offers floor-to-ceiling windows with the best free indoor views of Citadel Hill and the downtown core.
The Escher-esque Atrium: Walk through the center of the building to see the sculptural, criss-crossing staircases and walkways. The five-story skylit atrium is a masterpiece of light and geometry.
Rooftop Terrace: Step outside on the fifth floor to the seasonal rooftop garden. It’s a peaceful spot to enjoy the fresh air, surrounded by greenery and panoramic city views.

Paul O’Regan Hall: Check the schedule for this 300-seat performance space on the ground floor. It frequently hosts free concerts, film screenings, and author readings. In early 2026, it serves as a hub for African Heritage Month showcases.

Creative Studios: Explore the media labs where you can use 3D printers, recording studios, and high-end video editing software. The library even offers instruments like guitars and keyboards for public use in sound-resistant pods.
Tips and Key Information

As of early 2026, the library has welcomed East Cup Café and Roastery. There are two locations: one on the ground floor for a quick grab-and-go and another on the fifth floor where you can enjoy a latte while looking out over the city.
It is a traveler’s haven. The building offers free Wi-Fi and over 120 public-use computers. If you need a charge, there are power outlets integrated into almost every seating area.
Because the library is designed with high-efficiency glass and passive solar heating, it is the perfect warm-up spot during a chilly Halifax winter or a cool-down zone during a humid summer day.
Situated at 5440 Spring Garden Road, the library is fully accessible with elevators serving all floors. It is a 5-minute walk from the Public Gardens and a 10-minute walk up from the Waterfront.
Generally open Monday–Thursday (9:00 AM – 9:00 PM), Friday–Saturday (9:00 AM – 6:00 PM), and Sunday (12:00 PM – 6:00 PM). Always check the official website for holiday-specific hours.
If you're interested in your roots or the city's past, visit the 4th floor to access extensive archives on Nova Scotian and Atlantic Canadian history.

places.name: 2. Historic Properties
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/die-lagerh%C3%A4user-von-historic-properties-auf-dem-halifax-boardwalk-in-halifax-gm1335884948-417364314

The Historic Properties (also known as Privateers' Wharf) is a collection of stone and timber warehouses that date back to the late 1700s and early 1800s. Originally the base of operations for swashbuckling privateers and merchants during the Napoleonic Wars and the War of 1812, these three city blocks were saved from demolition in the 1960s. Today, they form a charming National Historic Site filled with boutiques, pubs, and restaurants along the Halifax waterfront.
What to See and Do

Walk the Cobblestone Streets: Wander through the narrow alleys between buildings like the Privateer Warehouse (c. 1790) and the Red Store (1812). The architecture features original ironstone walls and heavy timber beams that make you feel like you’ve stepped into the Age of Sail.

Spot the Privateer History: Look for the old stocks and pillory—reproductions of the 18th-century punishment devices—located near the wharf. It’s a popular (if slightly grim) spot for a classic Halifax photo.

The Lower Deck Experience: Visit the world-famous Lower Deck Pub. On most nights, you can catch live Atlantic Canadian folk music. In 2026, it remains the ultimate spot to hear Barrett’s Privateers sung at full volume by a crowded room of locals and travelers.

Unique Boutique Shopping: Avoid the typical malls and explore local shops like Sitamuk Kjipuktuk Cultural Trading Post for Indigenous art, or Frabjous Delights for specialty local chocolates and treats.

Outdoor Patios: During the summer months, the Historic Properties host some of the city's best boardwalk patios. It’s the perfect place to grab a local craft beer and watch the Bluenose II or the Theodore Tugboat replica sail past.
Tips and Key Information
The TD Halifax Jazz Festival is celebrating its 40th Anniversary from July 7–12, 2026. The Historic Properties area serves as a major gateway to the waterfront stages during this massive celebration.

Many of these buildings were owned by Enos Collins, a legendary privateer and smuggler who became one of the richest men in North America. His original bank building, the Collins Bank, still stands and is part of the complex.

Found at 1869 Upper Water Street, the site is directly on the waterfront boardwalk. While the cobblestones are beautiful, they can be uneven; travelers with mobility issues may prefer the paved sections of the boardwalk immediately adjacent to the buildings.
Parking downtown can be difficult. The Marriott Harbourfront and Scotia Square parking garages are the closest options, located just a two-minute walk from the Historic Properties.
The best time for photos is early morning when the sun hits the stone facades, or at night when the wharf is illuminated by warm, vintage-style street lamps.
The Historic Properties are a major stop for the Harbour Hopper (amphibious tour) and are just a short walk from the Halifax-Dartmouth Ferry terminal.

places.name: 3. Royal Nova Scotia International Tattoo
body: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_United_States_Air_Force_Honor_Guard_Drill_Team_performs_at_the_2023_Royal_Nova_Scotia_International_Tattoo_July_2,_2023_in_Halifax,_Nova_Scotia.jpg

The Royal Nova Scotia International Tattoo is a world-class spectacular that blends military tradition with high-energy entertainment. Held annually at the Scotiabank Centre, it is the largest indoor show of its kind in the world, featuring over 2,000 performers from across the globe. Part Broadway show, part military display, it is a fast-paced journey through history, music, and jaw-dropping acrobatics.
What to See and Do
The Massed Pipes and Drums: Experience the spine-tingling moment when hundreds of bagpipers and drummers march onto the arena floor in a powerful display of Celtic heritage.

Military Skill Displays: Watch elite units perform high-speed drills and dangerous stunts. A fan favorite is the Naval Gun Run, where teams race to dismantle and reassemble massive field guns over obstacles.

International Acrobatics and Dance: The show isn't strictly military; it features world-renowned trampoline acts, bicycle stunt teams, and traditional dancers from countries like Germany, Kenya, and the UK.

The Grand Finale: Stay for the emotional conclusion where the entire cast fills the floor for O Canada. It is widely considered the most patriotic rendition of the national anthem in the country, often moving the audience to tears.

Backstage Tours: For a behind-the-scenes look, you can book an hour-long guided tour to see the inner workings of the show, from the massive wardrobe department to the gun deck where equipment is prepped.
Tips and Key Information
The Tattoo runs from July 1 to July 5, 2026. Matinee performances (2:00 PM) are held on July 1, 4, and 5, while evening shows (7:00 PM) take place on July 2 and 3.
A long-standing Tattoo tradition—you can get one free ticket for a child (18 & under) with the purchase of every adult or senior ticket in certain seating categories.
Military members, veterans, and first responders can save 10% on tickets by using the promo code THANKYOU2026 at checkout.
For ultimate fans, this VIP ticket includes premium seating, a backstage tour, and being piped to your seats by a member of the cast.
Doors open 60–90 minutes before showtime. Arriving early allows you to visit the Nova Scotia Sports Hall of Fame, which is located inside the Scotiabank Centre and accessible from the concourse.
The Scotiabank Centre is located at 1800 Argyle Street. It is fully accessible, with designated seating for wheelchairs and companion seats available at the top of several sections.
During the show's run, keep an eye out for Tattoo Festival events—free noon-hour concerts and mini-performances held at various outdoor locations around downtown Halifax.

places.name: 4. Halifax Seaport Farmer's Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/halifax-hafen-bauernmarkt-in-kanada-gm1129652758-298492500

The Halifax Seaport Farmers' Market is the oldest continuously operating farmers' market in North America, having been founded in 1750. Now located in the historic Seaport District at Pavilion 23, this bustling waterfront market is a vibrant celebration of Nova Scotian agriculture, craftsmanship, and global flavors, all housed under one roof next to the Atlantic Ocean.
What to See and Do

The Global Food Court: Arrive hungry to sample an incredible array of international cuisines. From Masita’s Korean BBQ Hot Dogs to Pinoy’s Best steamed buns and fresh Acadian seafood chowder, the market is a culinary map of Halifax’s diverse community.

Artisan Alley: Browse the stalls of local makers for unique Atlantic Canadian souvenirs. You’ll find everything from hand-poured sea salt sourced from St. Margaret’s Bay to rugged woolens, maritime-inspired jewelry, and original folk art.

The Rooftop Terrace: Take your coffee or snacks up to the rooftop garden. It offers a peaceful retreat with stunning, unobstructed views of the Halifax Harbour, the cruise ship terminals, and Georges Island.
Live Local Music: Most weekends feature local buskers and musicians performing near the main entrance or common areas, adding a lively, rhythmic backdrop to your shopping.

Pier 21 Connection: Because the market is located right next to the Canadian Museum of Immigration at Pier 21, it’s easy to combine a morning of local shopping with a deep dive into Canada’s moving immigration history.
Tips and Key Information
The market is a weekend-only event at Pavilion 23. It is open Saturdays from 8:00 AM – 2:00 PM and Sundays from 10:00 AM – 2:00 PM.
For the best selection of fresh-baked breads and seasonal produce (like Annapolis Valley strawberries in July or peaches in August), aim to arrive by 8:30 AM on Saturdays.
Free parking is typically available at the Halifax Seaport lots (like Lot D) on Saturdays and Sundays for market-goers, though these spots fill up quickly during the peak summer cruise season.
Many vendors have moved toward digital payments, but some smaller farm stalls are still cash-only. Bring a reusable tote bag to help reduce plastic waste—it’s the local way.

Don't confuse this with the Halifax Brewery Farmers' Market located nearby in the historic Keith's Brewery. Both are excellent, but the Seaport Market is the larger, primary hub at the end of the boardwalk.
The market is located on a single, flat level in Pavilion 23, making it fully wheelchair and stroller accessible. Accessible washrooms are located near the rear of the hall.

places.name: 5. Halifax City Hall
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/rathausgeb%C3%A4ude-von-halifax-gm1174910308-326951884

Halifax City Hall stands as a magnificent example of late Victorian architecture and remains the heart of municipal government for the Halifax Regional Municipality. Completed in 1890 on the site of the old Dalhousie College, this National Historic Site is famous for its striking cream-and-red sandstone exterior and its iconic clock tower that defines the northern end of the Grand Parade.
What to See and Do

The Six O’Clock Clock: Look up at the north face of the silver-domed clock tower. You will notice the clock is permanently fixed at 9:04. This is a solemn memorial to the exact moment of the 1917 Halifax Explosion, a tribute that has remained unchanged for over a century.

Grand Parade Square: Explore the historic military parade ground directly in front of City Hall. It serves as a civic living room, hosting everything from the cenotaph Remembrance Day ceremonies to the Grand Parade Concert Series during the summer months.

Council Chamber: When the municipality is not in session, visitors can often peek into the ornate Council Chamber. It features heavy oak carvings, stained glass, and portraits of past mayors that reflect the city’s long political lineage.

Art and Artifacts: The interior halls are lined with historical photographs and significant gifts from Halifax’s Sister Cities, including Hakodate, Japan. It is a quiet, dignified space to escape the bustle of Barrington Street.

The 1890 Architecture: Admire the eclectic second empire style, characterized by the mansard roof, arched windows, and the intricate stone carvings of the province’s floral emblem, the Mayflower, tucked into the facade.
Tips and Key Information

City Hall is generally open to the public Monday–Friday (8:30 AM – 4:30 PM). While it is a working government building, respectful visitors are welcome to walk through the main floor and view the public displays.

For the classic Halifax Postcard shot, stand at the southern end of the Grand Parade near St. Paul’s Anglican Church. From here, you can frame City Hall perfectly with the modern glass skyscrapers of downtown rising behind it.
Check the Grand Parade schedule for July and August 2026. The square often hosts free Noon-Hour concerts and outdoor movie nights that are perfect for a budget-friendly break.
The main entrance on the Grand Parade side is accessible via a ramp. Inside, an elevator provides access to the upper floors and the Council Chamber.
As this is an active government office, you may be asked to sign in at the front desk, and certain areas may be restricted during private meetings or sensitive council sessions.
City Hall is a major landmark for navigation. It is located at 1841 Argyle Street, placing it directly between the World Trade and Convention Centre and the popular restaurants of Argyle Street.

places.name: 6. Garrison Brewing Co.
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/garrison-brewing-company-gm1129652778-298492503

Garrison Brewing Co. is a cornerstone of the East Coast craft beer scene and a pioneer in the Halifax Seaport District. Since 1997, they have been brewing fiercely independent beers in historic buildings near the harbor. Their main Seaport taproom—housed in a former 1929 immigration annex—is a vibrant, industrial-chic space where the aroma of hops meets the salty Atlantic air.
What to See and Do

The Seaport Taproom Experience: Grab a seat in the high-ceilinged taproom and watch the active brewhouse in action. You can sample a flight of five distinct beers while looking out at the cruise ship terminals just steps away.

Sample the Flagships: Try the Tall Ship East Coast Ale, a crisp local classic, or the Irish Red Ale. For those who prefer bold flavors, the award-winning Juicy! New England IPA is a fan favorite for its tropical, hazy notes.

The Oxford Taproom: If you’re in the West End, visit their second location in the historic Oxford Theatre on Quinpool Road. It’s a cozy, dog-friendly neighborhood spot that serves as a café by day and a lively taproom by night.

Seasonal Releases: Garrison is famous for its creative seasonal brews. Depending on when you visit, you might find the Spruce Beer (made with local spruce tips), Georgia Peach wheat ale, or their legendary Pussywillow spring seasonal.
Brewery Merchandise: The Garrison Town shop at the Seaport has an extensive collection of local gear, from tall ship hoodies to specialty glassware and locally made hot sauces.
Tips and Key Information
Like much of the Seaport, Garrison is famously pet-friendly. You’ll often find local dogs schmoozing with patrons on the patio or even inside the taproom.
Garrison doesn't serve full meals, but they encourage a bring your own food policy. You can grab a world-class snack from the Halifax Seaport Farmers' Market next door and enjoy it with your pint.
In 2026, the Seaport Taproom moves to expanded summer hours: Sunday–Thursday (10:00 AM – 8:00 PM) and Friday–Saturday (10:00 AM – 9:00 PM).
Garrison is a premier stop on the Nova Scotia Good Cheer Trail. Be sure to get your digital or paper passport stamped here to earn rewards as you explore the province's breweries and distilleries.

The main brewery is at 1149 Marginal Road, tucked behind the Westin Nova Scotian hotel. It is fully wheelchair accessible and conveniently located at the southern end of the Halifax Waterfront Boardwalk.
They brew their own line of craft sodas, including a spicy ginger beer and a classic root beer, making it a great stop even for non-drinkers or families with kids.

places.name: 7. Neptune Theatre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-neptune-theatre-in-halifax-nova-scotia-gm1597187410-529894244

Neptune Theatre stands as Atlantic Canada’s largest professional regional theatre, a cultural cornerstone located in the heart of downtown Halifax. Since opening its doors in 1963 with a mission to bring world-class performance to the East Coast, it has become a vibrant hub for Broadway-style musicals, provocative dramas, and local premieres, all housed within its sleek, modern facility on Argyle Street.
What to See and Do

The Fountain Hall Experience: Attend a production on the main stage, known as Fountain Hall. With 521 seats, it offers the big theatre feel with incredible acoustics. In Spring 2026, don't miss the blockbuster production of Come From Away (running April 1 – June 7), the hit musical about the generosity of Newfoundlanders during 9/11.

The Scotiabank Stage: For a more intimate experience, head to the 200-seat studio stage. This space is dedicated to contemporary works and edgy, experimental plays. In 2026, look for solo performances like Vanya starring Canadian theatre legend Daniel MacIvor.

Dinner & Show Packages: Neptune partners with several nearby Argyle Street restaurants (like Gahan House and The Stubborn Goat) to offer prix-fixe Dinner & Show vouchers, making it easy to plan a complete night out in the city's entertainment district.

Theatre School & Camps: If traveling with family in the summer, the Neptune Theatre School offers world-class youth camps (ages 4–18) that focus on everything from musical theatre to Spells & Sorcery drama workshops.

2026-2027 Season Launch: If you are visiting in late 2026, be among the first to see the new season themed No Day But Today, featuring massive titles like RENT, Les Misérables, and the Neptune debut of Dr. Seuss’s How the Grinch Stole Christmas!
Tips and Key Information

To keep theatre accessible, Neptune offers Pay-What-You-Choose nights for most productions (typically the first Tuesday of a run). Tickets start as low as $15 and can be purchased in person starting at 9:00 AM on the day of the show.
If you are 25 or under, take advantage of the Telus Rush program. You can snag any available seat on the day of a performance for just $20 (non-musicals) or $25 (musicals).

Located at 1593 Argyle Street. While there is no on-site parking, the Nova Centre and Scotiabank Centre garages are just a block away. It is also an easy walk from the Halifax Waterfront or any downtown hotel.

The theatre is fully wheelchair accessible, with designated seating and accessible washrooms. Neptune also offers ASL-interpreted, Relaxed, and Sensory-Friendly performances for select dates—check the Accessibility tab on their website for the 2026 schedule.
There is no formal dress code. You’ll see people in everything from evening wear to casual jeans and sneakers. Most locals opt for smart casual.
The theatre bar almost always creates a themed cocktail or mocktail for each production. Be sure to ask the bar staff what’s on the menu for a drink that matches the show’s vibe.

places.name: 8. Dalhousie University
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/geb%C3%A4ude-der-dalhousie-university-gm1425661176-470075423

Dalhousie University is one of Canada's oldest and most prestigious universities, founded in 1818 by the 9th Earl of Dalhousie. The Studley Campus, in particular, is a landmark of academic history, featuring grand stone buildings and mature tree-lined pathways that create a classic Ivy League atmosphere in the heart of Halifax.
What to See and Do

The Henry Hicks Building: This is the iconic centerpiece of the campus. Completed in 1915, its striking limestone facade and clock tower are a prime example of the university's enduring architectural legacy.
The Quad: The central green space is the heart of student life. It is surrounded by historic structures and provides a peaceful, park-like setting that is open for the public to stroll through.

Dalhousie Art Gallery: Located within the Dalhousie Arts Centre, this is the oldest public art gallery in Halifax. It features a diverse range of contemporary and historical exhibitions that are free for the public to enjoy.
Shirreff Hall: Known for its beautiful Victorian-style architecture, this historic residence building features an impressive library and a traditional dining hall that feels like a step back in time.
Tips and Key Information
The university often provides self-guided walking tour maps online that highlight the historical and architectural significance of the various campus buildings.
Look for the small, quiet courtyards tucked between the older stone buildings; they offer some of the most tranquil spots in the city for reading or a quick break.
Check the schedule for the Rebecca Cohn Auditorium, which is located on campus and serves as the city's premier venue for symphony performances and major concerts.
The campus grounds are open 24/7 for walking tours. Individual building and gallery hours vary, typically following standard business hours (9:00 AM – 5:00 PM).
Walking the campus and visiting the Dalhousie Art Gallery is free of charge.
Located at 6299 South Street, Halifax. It is a roughly 15-minute walk from the Halifax Public Gardens.

places.name: 9. Halifax Brewery Farmers Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/halifax-farmers-market-gm178774491-25121214

The Halifax Brewery Farmers' Market is a charming, community-run cooperative tucked inside the 200-year-old Alexander Keith’s Brewery building. While the larger Seaport Market is known for its modern, airy feel, the Brewery Market is celebrated for its old-world atmosphere, featuring granite walls, ironstone courtyards, and hidden rooms that create one of the most intimate shopping experiences in Canada.
What to See and Do

The Historic Courtyard: Wander through the sunlit atrium and winding corridors of a building constructed in 1837. The mix of heritage stone and glass makes it feel more like a hidden European village than a typical market.

Breakfast in the Brewery: This market is a local favorite for a slow Saturday morning. Grab a fresh coffee from the on-site café and a hot, made-from-scratch meal—options range from authentic Indian curries and Ethiopian platters to classic egg sandwiches and gluten-free pastries.

Artisanal Finds: The vendors here are primarily small-scale and high-quality. You’ll find hand-crafted jewelry, natural skin care, solid wood furniture, and cozy woolens, alongside year-round local produce, grass-fed meats, and fresh Atlantic fish.

The Stag’s Head Connection: The market is located in the same complex as the Alexander Keith's Brewery tour. After the market closes, you can transition directly into a tour of the aging caverns or grab a pint at the historic Stag’s Head Tavern tucked into the basement.

Live Acoustic Music: Local musicians perform throughout the market’s various hidden rooms every Saturday. The acoustics of the stone walls make the music travel beautifully through the space, adding to the relaxed, community vibe.
Tips and Key Information
The main market is open Saturdays from 8:00 AM – 1:00 PM, year-round.

Unlike most downtown locations, free parking is graciously provided to market-goers on Saturday mornings. Look for the designated lot just across the street on Lower Water Street (provided by Build Nova Scotia).
Found at 1496 Lower Water Street, with entrances on both the street side and via the interior courtyards of the Brewery Square.

Locals distinguish between the Seaport Market (the large, modern one near the cruise ships) and the Brewery Market (this historic one). If you prefer a quieter, more relaxed pace with fewer crowds, the Brewery Market is your best bet.
While the interior market floor is for service animals only, the outdoor courtyard areas are very dog-friendly and a popular spot for locals to congregate with their pets.
Despite its 19th-century origins, the market is largely accessible via the Lower Water Street entrance, though some of the smaller hidden rooms may have narrow passages or a single step.

places.name: 10. Casino Nova Scotia
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/de/foto/casino-nova-scotia-in-halifax-kanada-gm1594460546-529709757

Casino Nova Scotia is Atlantic Canada’s premier gaming and entertainment destination, famously built on a caisson-based structure that extends over the harbor waters like a modern-day wharf. Located at the northern end of the Halifax Waterfront Boardwalk, it offers a Vegas-style experience with a distinct maritime flair, serving as a hub for nightlife, live music, and waterfront dining.
What to See and Do
The Gaming Floor: Explore over 40,000 square feet of excitement featuring more than 600 slot machines and over 30 live table games, including Blackjack, Roulette, and Baccarat.

The Bruce Guthro Theatre: Catch a show in this premiere 650-seat venue (formerly the Schooner Showroom). In March 2026, the theater is hosting a legendary lineup including The Irish Descendants (March 14), Bruce Guthro’s Songwriters’ Circle (March 28), and the musical spectacular Music of the Night (March 31).

3Sixty Lounge: Located at the heart of the casino floor, this circular bar and lounge features live local bands every Friday and Saturday night. It’s the perfect spot to grab a drink and soak in the high-energy atmosphere without a cover charge.

The Compass Room: Visit this elegant, dome-topped circular room for one of the most unique architectural views in the city. Its outdoor terrace offers a panoramic 270-degree view of the Halifax Harbour and the Dartmouth shoreline.
Harbourfront Dining: Enjoy a meal at Trapeze Restaurant, which specializes in Atlantic seafood and prime cuts of steak, all paired with floor-to-ceiling views of the moving ships in the harbor.
Tips and Key Information
You must be 19+ to enter any part of the casino, including the restaurants and theater. Always carry a valid government-issued photo ID; security checks are mandatory at all entrances.
If you're planning a spring visit, tickets for the Alan Jackson Experience (May 29) and Steve Earle (June 27-28) are already on sale and expected to sell out quickly.

The casino features a large multi-level parking garage. Members of the Great Canadian Rewards program can often earn free or discounted parking based on play, but the garage is also available to the public for a fee.
You can reach the casino without stepping outside! It is connected via the Pedway system (elevated indoor walkways) to the Halifax Marriott Harbourfront, Purdy's Wharf, and Scotia Square.
The casino is open 24/7 on weekends (from 12:00 PM Friday through 4:00 AM Monday) and typically from 12:00 PM to 4:00 AM during the week.
If you need a break, the on-site PlayWise Centre provides information and resources on how to keep gambling fun and within your limits.
The vibe is casual-nice. While you’ll see people in jeans and tees, many guests dress up for dinner and a show, especially on Saturday nights.

places.name: 25. Wilcox Pass
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/herd-of-bighorn-sheeps-in-canadian-rockies-banff-canada-gm181886724-23998743

Wilcox Pass is the ultimate alpine shortcut. Located right on the boundary between Jasper and Banff National Parks, this trail was used by early travelers to bypass the difficult, icy terrain of the Athabasca Glacier. Today, it is famous for providing the most spectacular front-row seat to the Columbia Icefield without actually having to step on the ice.
What to Do and See

The Red Chair Viewpoint: About 1.5 km (0.9 miles) into the hike, you’ll find two Parks Canada Red Chairs. This is the most famous photo spot on the Icefields Parkway. Sitting here, you are looking directly across the valley at the massive Athabasca Glacier and the towering peaks of Mount Athabasca and Snow Dome.

Bighorn Sheep Haven: The wide-open alpine meadows of the pass are a favorite summer grazing spot for large rams. Because they are protected here, they are often quite calm, allowing for incredible wildlife photography (from a safe distance).

The Icefield Panorama: If you continue past the red chairs to the top of the pass (2,375 meters / 7,792 feet), the view opens up to show the Dome Glacier and the vast white expanse of the Columbia Icefield—the largest body of ice in the Rocky Mountains.

Tundra Trekking: Once you reach the pass, the terrain becomes a flat, rocky moonscape. It is a rare chance to walk on fragile alpine tundra where the plants are hundreds of years old but only a few inches tall.

Mount Wilcox Scramble: For very experienced hikers/scramblers, a faint trail leads from the pass to the summit of Mount Wilcox. It involves some hands-on-rock climbing and offers a terrifyingly beautiful look straight down onto the glacier.
Tips & Key Information

The trail is not marked in winter, and there is a significant avalanche risk from the slopes of Mount Wilcox. Most visitors this week stick to the parking lot area to photograph the glacier from across the road.
Difficulty & Distance:
To the Red Chairs: 3 km (1.8 miles) round trip.
To the Pass Summit: 8 km (5 miles) round trip.
Elevation Gain: 335 meters (1,100 feet).

Because it is right next to a giant field of ice, Wilcox Pass is always colder and windier than the town of Jasper. Even in the middle of summer, it can snow here. Always pack a winter hat and gloves in your daypack.

When the snow finally melts in July, please stay on the established trail or on durable rock surfaces. The alpine flowers (like moss campion) take decades to grow and can be killed by a single footprint.
The trailhead is located at the Wilcox Creek Campground entrance, just south of the Columbia Icefield Discovery Centre. In the summer, this lot fills up by 10:00 AM, so arrive early.

places.name: 24. Overlander Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/canadian-rockies-jasper-national-park-landscape-background-beautiful-scenery-gm2246993942-660920879

The Overlander Trail is a historic trek that follows the footsteps of the Overlanders—gold seekers who traveled across the Canadian Rockies in 1862. It is a unique, long-distance trail that stays relatively low in the Athabasca Valley, offering a mix of open meadows, pine forests, and dramatic riverside views.
What to Do and See

The Moberly Homestead: About 5 km (3 miles) from the 6th Bridge trailhead, you will find the ruins of the Moberly family home. Built in the late 1800s, these log cabin remains offer a hauntingly beautiful look at early pioneer life in the Rockies.

Cinquefoil Mountain Views: As you hike through the open meadows, the massive, slanted rock face of Cinquefoil Mountain looms over you. In March, the contrast between the dark rock and the white snow in the crevices is a photographer's dream.

Wildflowers and Meadows: Because this trail gets so much sun, it is the first place in Jasper to see crocuses in late March and yellow buttercups in April. It feels like spring here weeks before it does in the rest of the park.
Wildlife Corridor: It is very common to see large herds of elk, mule deer, and even the occasional coyote or wolf trotting through the grasslands.

The Sixth Bridge Connection: Most people start at the Maligne Canyon 6th Bridge and hike toward the East Gate. Crossing the suspension bridge over the rushing Athabasca River is a great way to start the journey.
Tips & Key Information
Distance Options:
Full Point-to-Point: 15.5 km (9.6 miles). This requires leaving a second car at the other end.
Homestead Return: 10 km (6 miles) round trip. This is the most popular way to do the hike, turning back once you reach the Moberly ruins.

While the snow is melting fast here, the trail can be extremely muddy in the meadows. Wear waterproof hiking boots. There may still be some hidden ice in the shaded forest sections, so take care on the slopes.

Because this trail has lots of tall grass and is frequented by deer, it is a hotspot for ticks in the spring. Wear long pants, tuck your socks in, and do a tick check on yourself and your pets when you get back to the car.

Since this is a low-valley trail with lots of new green grass, grizzly and black bears love to forage here in March and April. Always carry your bear spray in a holster on your belt or chest—never inside your pack.
The Athabasca Valley is a natural wind tunnel. On a sunny day, the wind can still feel quite chilly, so a light windbreaker is a must-have.

places.name: 23. Sulphur Skyline Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sulphur-skyline-trailhead-jasper-national-park-gm1226059249-361109999

The Sulphur Skyline is often called the ultimate Jasper hike because it offers a 360-degree mountain panorama that feels like it belongs in a movie. Starting from the Miette Hot Springs parking lot, the trail climbs steadily through the forest before breaking out onto a dramatic, rocky ridge that looks deep into the Fiddle Valley and the wild peaks of the Ashlar Ridge.
In winter, the Miette Road is seasonally closed. Even once the road opens, the upper sections of this trail usually remain covered in deep snow and ice until late June.
What to Do and See

The Top of the World View: From the summit (2,050 meters / 6,725 feet), you can see the Fiddle River winding like a silver thread far below. On a clear day, the layers of mountain ranges look like blue waves stretching toward the horizon.
The Famous Thumb: Look for a massive, thumb-shaped rock formation near the summit. It’s a favorite spot for hikers to take a victory photo after the steep climb.

The Ultimate Reward: The trailhead is located right at the Miette Hot Springs. There is no better feeling in Jasper than hiking for 3–4 hours and then immediately jumping into 40°C (104°F) mineral water to soak your tired muscles.
Bighorn Sheep: This ridge is a major highway for bighorn sheep. They are very common near the summit, often lounging on the rocks and watching the hikers go by.
Wildflowers and Whistlers: In the summer, the alpine meadows are filled with vibrant flowers and the high-pitched whistle of the hoary marmots living in the rock piles.
Tips & Key Information

This trail is not technical, but it is steep. It climbs nearly 700 meters (2,300 feet) in just 4 kilometers. Most hikers find the first half through the trees to be the hardest part; once you see the views, the adrenaline kicks in.
Difficulty & Distance:
Round Trip: 8.8 km (5.5 miles)
Elevation Gain: 700 meters (2,300 feet)
Time: Allow 3 to 5 hours depending on your fitness.
The summit is completely exposed. Even if it is 25°C at the Hot Springs, it can be 10°C with 60 km/h winds at the top. Always bring a windbreaker and a warm hat.
Because the trail is steep and south-facing, it can get very hot in the afternoon sun. If you visit in July or August, try to start your hike by 9:00 AM to beat the heat and the crowds.
The Skyline part of the trail is a narrow ridge. To protect the fragile alpine plants and for your own safety, stay on the marked path. The limestone rocks can be very slippery when wet.

places.name: 22. Horseshoe Lake
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/horseshoe-lake-in-jasper-national-park-alberta-canada-gm2192018283-610319814

Horseshoe Lake is a hidden gem located along the Icefields Parkway, about 25 km south of the Jasper townsite. Named for its distinct U shape, it is famous for its deep, crystal-clear water and the dramatic limestone cliffs that surround it.
Horseshoe Lake is open to the public. While the 2024 wildfires affected the forest immediately surrounding the lake, the water itself remains as stunningly clear as ever.
What to Do and See

Cliff Jumping (Summer Only): This is the most famous activity at the lake. There are ledges ranging from 1 meter to over 20 meters (80 feet) high. Warning: This is extremely dangerous and Parks Canada does not recommend it due to the high number of injuries and rescues each year.

Paddling & Swimming: Because the lake is sheltered by high cliffs, the water is often perfectly still, making it a favorite for paddleboarding and kayaking. In the summer, it's a popular (but very cold) swimming hole.

The Shoreline Trail: A short, 1.5-km (0.9-mile) lollipop loop winds along the top of the cliffs. It offers several high-angle viewpoints where you can look straight down into the deep blue-green water.

Scuba Diving: Horseshoe is one of the deepest lakes in the park (over 30 meters in spots). Divers often come here to explore the underwater rock formations and fallen trees that are preserved in the cold water.

Wildfire Observations: As you walk the trail in 2026, you can see the mosaic effect of the recent fire. While many trees were burnt, the low-lying shrubs and wildflowers are returning rapidly, providing a unique look at forest regeneration.
Tips & Key Information

There is no large sign for Horseshoe Lake on the highway (Parks Canada removed it to reduce overcrowding). Look for a small, paved parking lot on the west side of Highway 93, about 4 km south of Athabasca Falls.

Under the new 2026 regulations, you must clean, drain, and dry all paddleboards and gear. If you used your gear outside of BC, Alberta, or the Territories in the last 30 days, it must be professionally decontaminated to protect the lake from invasive mussels.
There are no washrooms or garbage bins at Horseshoe Lake. Please use the facilities at nearby Athabasca Falls before you arrive, and be sure to pack it in, pack it out.
In winter,, be extremely careful near the cliff edges. The spray from the lake and melting snow can create black ice on the rocks, making them incredibly slippery.
In the summer, this small parking lot fills up by 11:00 AM. It's still a good idea to visit in the morning for the best reflections on the water.

places.name: 21. Bald Hills Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/clouds-gathering-above-mighty-rock-massive-of-evelyn-peak-and-green-valley-bellow-gm1314706378-402862449

The Bald Hills Trail is widely considered the crown jewel of day hikes in the Maligne Lake area. It follows an old fire lookout road that climbs steeply through the forest before breaking out into wide-open, treeless alpine meadows (the Bald Hills). From the top, you get what many call the best view in the entire park: a literal bird's-eye look at the entire 22-kilometer length of Maligne Lake.
What to Do and See

The Panoramic Reward: Once you reach the ridge (about 2,300 meters high), you are treated to a 360-degree view. To the south, Maligne Lake stretches out like a turquoise ribbon surrounded by jagged, snow-capped peaks like Mount Charlton and Mount Unwin.

The Old Lookout Site: At the top of the first major climb, you’ll find the site where a fire lookout tower once stood. It’s a perfect spot for a high-altitude lunch while looking down at the tiny tour boats on the lake below.

Alpine Wildlife: These high ridges are prime habitat for woodland caribou (though they are very rare) and hoary marmots. In March, you are more likely to see the tracks of white-tailed ptarmigan, birds that turn completely white to blend in with the snow.
Wildflower Explosion (Summer): If you return in July or August, the Bald Hills aren't bald at all—they are covered in a carpet of purple, yellow, and red wildflowers.

The Extra Summit: For those with extra energy, you can continue past the old lookout site along the ridge to the true summit. The trail becomes a bit rockier, but the views of the Queen Elizabeth Range are even more dramatic.
Tips & Key Information
In winter, snowshoes or heavy-duty ice cleats are mandatory. The trail is steep, and the upper sections are prone to deep post-holing (where your leg sinks up to the hip in soft snow).

Because this trail climbs into high alpine terrain, avalanche risk is a serious factor in winter. Always check the Parks Canada Avalanche bulletin before heading up. If you don't have avalanche training, it is safer to stick to the lower forest sections until the snow melts in late June.
Difficulty & Distance:
Loop Distance: Approx. 10.4 km (6.5 miles)
Elevation Gain: Approx. 500 meters (1,640 feet)
Time: Allow 4–6 hours round trip.

The trail splits early on. The left fork is a steep, direct climb (the shortcut). The right fork follows the old fire road and is much more gradual. In winter, the fire road (right fork) is usually the safer and easier path to follow.
Once you leave the trees, you are completely exposed to the elements. The wind at the summit can be incredibly strong and cold, even on a sunny day. Bring an extra warm layer and a windproof jacket.

places.name: 20. Lake Annette & Lake Edith
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/lake-annette-lake-shore-beach-jasper-national-park-canadian-rockies-alberta-canada-gm2257051217-670166798

Lake Annette and Lake Edith are the twin lakes of Jasper. Sitting side-by-side on a large glacial terrace just across the river from town, they are the go-to spots for locals to hang out. While most alpine lakes are freezing cold, these two are relatively shallow, meaning they warm up (to about 18°C or 65°F) enough for a brave summer swim.
What to Do and See

The Lake Annette Loop: This is a 2.4-kilometer (1.5-mile) trail that is completely paved and flat. It is one of the most accessible trails in the park, perfect for wheelchairs, strollers, or an easy jog.

Ochre-Colored Sand: Lake Annette is famous for its wood-chip colored sandy beaches. In the summer, this is Jasper’s Tropical Beach. In March, you can walk along the shoreline and see the crystal-clear water lapping against the snowy sand.

The Lakeside Red Chairs: There is a set of Parks Canada Red Chairs on the north shore of Lake Annette. They face directly toward Mount Edith Cavell, providing one of the most symmetrical and stunning views in the valley.
Stand-Up Paddleboarding (SUP): Lake Edith is a favorite for paddlers. Because it’s sheltered from the heavy winds of the main valley, the water is often calm and glassy.
Spot the Loons: Both lakes are protected nesting grounds for common loons. In late March and April, you can start to hear their famous, haunting yodel echoing across the water.
Tips & Key Information

Lake Annette is more developed with picnic tables, fire pits, a playground, and changing rooms. Great for families. Lake Edith is a bit more wild and quiet, surrounded by a few private historic cabins. Perfect for a peaceful walk.
Because these trails are paved, they are much less muddy than the dirt trails in the woods. However, watch out for black ice in the early mornings where snow has melted and refrozen on the pavement.

You’ll notice some burnt trees in the distance from the 2024 fires. Parks Canada has cleared the immediate shoreline and picnic areas to make them safe, but stay on the main paths to avoid any hazard trees in the thicker forest.
Like most lakes in Jasper, gas-powered motors are banned. This keeps the water incredibly clear and the atmosphere quiet.
You can drive there in 5 minutes from town, or take the Bighorn Alley bike path from the Jasper townsite for a beautiful 20-minute ride.

places.name: 19. Jasper Lake
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/jasper-national-park-in-alberta-canada-gm1126200405-296380296

Jasper Lake is a unique geographical feature located about 20 minutes east of the Jasper townsite. It isn't a typical deep lake; instead, it is a massive, shallow widening of the Athabasca River. It is famous for its wind-swept sand dunes and a phenomenon that makes it look like you are walking on water.

Jasper Lake is a beautiful, windswept landscape. Because it is so shallow, large sections of the lakebed in winter are exposed or covered in a thin layer of ice and snow. This is a great time to see the bones of the lake before the spring melt fills it up in May.
What to Do and See

Walk on Water: In the summer, you can wade out hundreds of meters into the lake and the water will only reach your ankles. In winter, the water is mostly frozen or receded, allowing you to walk far out onto the sandy, silty flats to get incredible photos of the surrounding peaks like Roche Miette.

Jasper Lake Sand Dunes: On the north shore of the lake, you'll find the only sand dunes in the Canadian Rockies. These dunes were formed by thousands of years of wind blowing silt off the lakebed. They are a blast to climb, though they can be quite windy.

Bald Eagle Nesting: March 15 marked the start of the seasonal closure for certain eagle nesting areas around the lake. Keep your eyes on the tall trees—this is one of the best spots in the park to see bald eagles and ospreys as they prepare for the spring.

The Bottomless Illusion: From the highway, the lake looks deep and blue, but it rarely gets deeper than one meter (three feet). It is a popular spot for SUP (Stand-Up Paddleboarding) in the summer because you never have to worry about falling into deep water.
Stargazing: Because Jasper Lake is wide open and away from the mountain shadows, it offers a massive view of the sky. In late March, it’s a premier spot to park and wait for the Northern Lights.
Tips & Key Information
Jasper Lake is one of the windiest spots in the park. The wind funnels through the valley and can be very strong. In wind, this wind feels biting cold, so make sure you have a windproof outer layer.
There is a large roadside pull-off on Highway 16 with plenty of parking. You can walk from your car directly onto the sand and silt flats in less than two minutes.

Be careful when walking on the exposed lakebed in the spring. As the ice melts, some patches of silt can become like quick-sand. If the ground looks wet and shiny, stick to the drier, light-colored sand.
There are no marked hiking trails at Jasper Lake; it’s more of an explore-at-your-own-pace destination. It's a great spot to stretch your legs if you are driving in from Edmonton.
This area is a major corridor for bighorn sheep and elk. They often stand right on the edge of the highway near the lake, so please keep your speed down and stay alert.

places.name: 18. Old Fort Point Loop
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/scenic-overlook-at-old-fort-point-jasper-national-park-alberta-canada-gm2206610257-623913879

Old Fort Point is widely considered the best bang for your buck hike in Jasper. It is a prominent bedrock hill that stands 130 meters (426 feet) above the Athabasca River, offering a 360-degree view of the townsite, the winding river, and the surrounding mountain ranges.

As of March 2026, the trail is partially open. While it is a local favorite, you will notice a significant change: the 2024 wildfires moved through this area, leaving many of the trees as blackened skeletons. However, the lack of needles and leaves actually makes the panoramic views from the top even more wide-open and dramatic than before.
What to Do and See

The Steep Stairs Challenge: If you go counter-clockwise, you start with a long flight of wooden stairs. It’s a workout for your lungs, but it gets you to the first great viewpoint in just a few minutes.

The Red Chairs: Like many iconic spots in Canada’s National Parks, there are two red Adirondack chairs near the summit. Sitting here gives you a perfect view of Pyramid Mountain and the town of Jaspe.

Bighorn Sheep: This hill is a favorite hangout for bighorn sheep. Even in March, they can often be seen grazing on the grassy slopes or licking minerals off the rocks. They are very used to people, but remember to keep at least 30 meters (three bus lengths) of distance.

Witness the Regrowth: Look closely at the ground among the burnt trees. In the spring of 2026, you’ll see vibrant green shoots of aspen and fireweed popping up from the black soil—a powerful sign of how the forest heals itself.
The Summit Panorama: From the highest point, you can see the Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge and Lac Beauvert to the east, and the massive face of Mount Edith Cavell to the south.
Tips & Key Information

As of March 2026, the trail is currently a mix of slush, ice, and mud. There is a partial closure on the back side of the loop near the junction with Trail 7 due to seasonal flooding. Most hikers are doing an out and back to the summit from the main parking lot to avoid the wet sections.
Because the trail is steep, the icy patches can be very slippery during winter. Small ice spikes for your boots are highly recommended.
Choose your direction.
Clockwise: A steadier, gradual climb through the forest (best for knees).
Counter-Clockwise: Up the stairs for a fast, heart-pumping climb to the views.
Because the hill is so exposed (especially now with fewer trees), it can be incredibly windy at the top. Even if it feels warm in the parking lot, bring a windbreaker or a hat.
Despite the name, there was never actually a fort on this hill. It was named by early explorers who thought the location would have been a perfect spot for one.

places.name: 17. Valley of the Five Lakes
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/scenic-view-of-valley-of-the-five-lakes-in-jasper-national-park-in-alberta-canada-gm1464317718-497041990

The Valley of the Five Lakes is one of the most beloved hiking spots in Jasper. It is famous because each of the five lakes has a slightly different shade of blue or green, ranging from clear jade to deep sapphire. The colors come from unique glacial minerals and different depths in each lake.

As of March 2026, this trail system is partially open. Parts of the valley were affected by the 2024 wildfires, and Parks Canada has been busy clearing hazard trees (burnt trees that might fall). The main loop to Lakes 1 through 4 is open, but the longer trail to the Fifth Lake is still being repaired.
What to Do and See
The Red Chair: At the shore of the Third Lake, you will find the famous Parks Canada Red Chairs. Sitting here is the best way to soak in the view of the bright green water and the surrounding peaks.

The Color Challenge: Bring your camera and see if you can capture the difference between the lakes. The Third Lake is usually the brightest teal, while the Second Lake is often a darker, mysterious green.

Bridge Crossings: The trail takes you over several wooden bridges and through boardwalks over marshy areas. In the spring (March/April), these are great spots to look for frogs and salamanders waking up from winter.

Spring Wildflowers: By late April and May, the sunny, burnt areas of the forest will be the first places to show new life. Look for purple crocuses poking through the soil—they are the first sign of spring in Jasper.

Nature’s Recovery: Walking through the burnt sections of the trail is actually very cool. You can see how the fire cleared out old brush to make room for new berries and grasses that grizzly bears love to eat.
Tips & Key Information
The main circuit is about 4.5 kilometers (2.8 miles) and takes about 2 hours at a relaxed pace. It is mostly flat but has a few short, steep hills.
In winter, trails are a mix of slush, mud, and ice. Wearing crampons or icers on your boots is highly recommended so you don't slip on the shaded parts of the path.

This valley is prime habitat for bears. Since they are just starting to wake up in March and April, they are very hungry. Always carry bear spray in an easy-to-reach spot (not inside your backpack) and make noise as you hike.
Even with the partial closures, this is a very popular spot. If the parking lot is full, do not park on the side of the highway (you will get a ticket). Try coming before 10:00 AM or after 4:00 PM.
There are no facilities or water taps at the trailhead or on the hike. Make sure you have a full water bottle before you leave your car.

places.name: 16. Marmot Basin
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/view-of-jasper-from-the-ski-area-gm1226959990-361689423

Marmot Basin is the only ski resort in Jasper National Park. It is famous for having the highest base elevation of any ski area in Canada, which means the snow stays soft and powdery for a very long time. It is a hidden gem because it is rarely crowded, so you don't have to wait in long lines to get on the chairlifts.
What to Do and See

Ski or Snowboard: With 91 runs, there is something for everyone. Beginners can stay on the lower easy slopes like School House, while experts can take the knob chair to the very top for steep, powdery bowls.

Jasper View: Even if you aren't a pro skier, take the Canadian Rockies Express (one of the fastest lifts in the world). From the top, you get a breathtaking view of the town of Jasper and the Athabasca Valley far below.
The Tres Hombres: If you are a very brave and expert skier, this is a massive area of steep, open terrain that was opened a few years ago. It is legendary among locals for its deep snow.
Mid-Mountain Dining: Stop at the Eagle’s Nest or the Mid-Chalet for a mountaintop poutine or a hot chocolate. Sitting on the outdoor deck in the March sun is a classic Jasper experience.
Spring Events: In late March and April, Marmot often hosts fun events like Aloha Day or outdoor concerts. Keep an eye out for people skiing in Hawaiian shirts.
Tips & Key Information

In 2026, ticket prices are approximately CAD $125 to $135 for adults aged 13 to 64 and around CAD $45 for children aged 6 to 12. If you buy your tickets online at least three days in advance, you can usually save 10% to 20%.

You don’t need to drive up the mountain. A shuttle bus picks up skiers at most hotels in the town of Jasper and brings them right to the lodge. It’s safer and easier than driving on snowy mountain roads.
If you don't have your own gear, the rental shop at the mountain has everything you need—skis, boots, poles, and helmets. You can even rent high-quality performance skis to try something new.
Wear layers so you can take a sweater off when the sun gets hot.
Because you are so high up and the snow reflects the sun, you can get a goggle tan (or a sunburn). Don't forget to put sunscreen on your face.

places.name: 15. Lac Beauvert
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/docked-boats-with-three-people-canoeing-in-lac-beauvert-at-fairmont-jasper-park-gm1050915992-280998486

Lac Beauvert (French for Beautiful Green Lake) is famous for its surreal, neon-green water and incredible clarity. On a calm day, you can see all the way to the bottom, where ancient logs and white rocks make the lake look like a giant aquarium. It is located right next to the historic Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge.
What to Do and See

Walk the Lake Loop: This is an easy, flat 3.5-kilometer (2.2-mile) trail that circles the entire lake. It takes about an hour to walk and offers constant views of Pyramid Mountain and Mount Edith Cavell.

Paddle in Paradise: Once the ice melts in May, the Boathouse opens for rentals. Renting a bright green canoe or a stand-up paddleboard is the best way to see the underwater forest of logs at the bottom of the lake.

The Fairmont Boardwalk: Even if you aren't staying at the hotel, you can walk along the beautiful wooden boardwalks. There are plenty of benches and Adirondack chairs where you can sit and soak up the sun.

Wildlife Watching: Because it is tucked away from the main highway, Lac Beauvert is a secret spot for wildlife. It is very common to see elk grazing on the grass near the cabins or loons diving for fish in the center of the lake.

Stargazing: Since the Fairmont is a bit further from the town lights, the docks at Lac Beauvert are a premier spot for the Dark Sky Preserve. In March, this is a top location to try and spot the Northern Lights.
Tips & Key Information
Many people think the lake is private because of the hotel, but it is public property. You can park in the main Fairmont parking lot and walk down to the water for free.
The water is so clear that it looks shallow, but it can be very deep in spots. If you are paddling, always wear your life jacket, as the glacial water is cold enough to take your breath away.
After your walk, head into the Fairmont lodge for a hot chocolate or a snack by the massive stone fireplace. It’s a great way to feel fancy without spending a fortune.
To keep the water clear and the loons happy, gas-powered boats are strictly banned on Lac Beauvert. This makes it one of the quietest lakes in the park.

places.name: 14. Jasper Planetarium & Dark Sky Preserve
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/milky-way-galaxy-jasper-dark-sky-preserve-gm1497296718-519711535

Jasper National Park is the second-largest Dark Sky Preserve in the world. This means the town and park have special rules to keep artificial lights low, making the stars look brighter than almost anywhere else on Earth. Even right from the middle of town, you can see thousands of stars and the glowing stripe of the Milky Way.

The Jasper Planetarium is fully open and operating from its base at the Fairmont Jasper Park Lodge. March is actually one of the best times of year to visit, as the long, dark nights and clear mountain air make for perfect stargazing and frequent sightings of the Northern Lights (Aurora Borealis).
What to Do and See

Planetarium Dome Experience: Step inside a 34-seat domed theatre for a live tour led by astronomy experts. You’ll see local Indigenous constellations, fly through the solar system, and see 4K instant replays of the Northern Lights caught in Jasper just days before.

Telescope Tour: After the dome show, head outside to use the largest and most powerful telescopes in the Canadian Rockies. On a clear night, you can see the rings of Saturn, distant galaxies, and sparkling star clusters.
Touch a Meteorite: During the tour, you actually get to hold real pieces of space. The planetarium has meteorites and rocks from the Moon and Mars that you can touch and photograph.
Photograph the Stars: The guides are experts at night photography. They can help you set up your smartphone or camera to take amazing pictures of the stars or the Aurora if it’s dancing that night.
Dark Sky Festival: If you visit in October 2026, the town hosts a huge two-week festival with famous astronauts, drone shows, and giant outdoor star parties.
Tips & Key Information

The weather in the mountains can change fast. If it’s too cloudy to see through the telescopes, don’t worry. The Planetarium gives you a free two-year rain check so you can come back for the telescope portion on a clearer night.
Even in the summer, standing outside at night in the Rockies is cold. In winter, wear your warmest winter coat, boots, gloves, and a hat. If you aren't warm, you won't enjoy the stars.
For the best experience, book the Planetarium + Telescope combo. It takes about 1.5 to 2 hours total and costs approximately $65–$75 CAD for adults.
The indoor Dome Theatre is great for kids, but children under 4 years old are usually not permitted inside the dome to keep the environment quiet for other guests.
Before your tour, check the Jasper Planetarium Astronomy forecast online. It will tell you the KP-index, which helps predict how likely you are to see the Northern Lights that night.

places.name: 13. Miette Hot Springs
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/miette-hotsprings-jasper-in-the-spring-canadian-rockies-alberta-canada-gm665518510-121246287

Miette Hot Springs is home to the hottest mineral water in the Canadian Rockies. While the water flows out of the mountain at a scorching 54°C (129°F), it is cooled down to a perfect 40°C (104°F) before it enters the pools. It is located at the end of a beautiful, winding 17-kilometer road in the Fiddle Valley.

The hot springs are closed during winter. In 2026 season, it is scheduled to reopen on May 15. Also, please note that a small section of Miette Road is still being repaired from a previous washout, so you may encounter a short delay with a one-lane traffic light on your way up.
What to Do and See

Soak in the Pools: There are four outdoor pools to choose from: two hot pools for relaxing and two cool plunge pools for waking up your senses. Alternating between hot and cold is a local secret for feeling totally refreshed.

Source of the Springs Trail: Take a short, easy 20-minute walk from the pool building. The trail leads you to the ruins of the old Aquacourt and the actual spot where the hot water bubbles out of the rocks. You can even feel the steam rising from the ground.

Wildlife on the Road: The drive to the springs is famous for animal sightings. Bighorn sheep often hang out right in the parking lot or lick salt off the road, and it is a very common spot to see black bears in the spring.

Sulphur Skyline Hike: The trailhead for this famous hike is in the same parking lot. It is a steep climb, but it offers one of the best 360-degree views in the park. Most people do the hike first and then reward their tired legs with a soak in the hot springs.
Fiddle Valley Café: Located inside the main building, this is a great spot to grab a healthy wrap, a hot soup, or a coffee after your swim.
Tips & Key Information
You can rent swimsuits and towels at the front desk for a small fee, but bringing your own will save you money and time.
You cannot book tickets online for the hot springs. During busy summer weekends, there might be a short wait to get in if the pools are at their lifeguard limit.
While many park areas are free this summer, fees still apply at the hot springs. An adult entry is approximately $16–$18 CAD.
The road to Miette is very twisty and narrow. If you get car sick easily, you might want to sit in the front seat or drive a little slower.
Because the road has very sharp turns, vehicles longer than 7.5 meters (25 feet) are not allowed to drive all the way to the hot springs.

places.name: 12. Patricia Lake
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pyramid-mountain-gm1497296829-519711666

Patricia Lake is a calm, crystal-clear lake located just a few minutes from the town of Jasper. It is often quieter than its neighbor, Pyramid Lake, making it the perfect spot for travelers who want to escape the crowds. While it looks like a typical mountain paradise, it holds a top-secret history beneath its surface.

Patricia Lake is fully open. While some wildfire risk reduction (thinning out trees) is happening in the surrounding forest to keep the town safe, the lake itself remains a peaceful haven for visitors.
What to Do and See

Find the Iceberg Ship Secret: During World War II, this lake was the site of a top-secret mission called Project Habbakuk. Scientists tried to build a giant aircraft carrier out of Pykrete (a mix of ice and wood pulp). Today, the remains of the prototype are at the bottom of the lake. You can read all about it on the commemorative plaque along the shore.

Scuba Diving: Believe it or not, Patricia Lake is a famous diving spot. Divers with a Cold Water certification can go down to see the wreckage of the Habbakuk ship. Because the water is so cold, the wood and pipes have stayed in great shape for over 80 years.

Patricia Lake Circle Loop: This is a 4.8-kilometer (3-mile) easy hiking trail. It winds through the forest and offers beautiful peeks of the lake. It is a fantastic spot to look for Beaver ponds and Loons.

Wildlife Watching: Because it’s so quiet, Patricia Lake is a favorite hangout for elk and deer, especially in the early morning. It’s also one of the best places to hear the haunting call of a Loon echoing across the water.

Boating & Paddling: You can rent canoes, kayaks, and rowboats from the Patricia Lake Bungalows. Since gas motors are banned on the lake, the only sound you’ll hear is your own paddle hitting the water.
Tips & Key Information
For the perfect photo, visit at sunrise. The lake is usually as flat as a mirror, creating a double image of Pyramid Mountain in the water.

The southern end of the lake is home to the Patricia Lake Bungalows (a private resort). If you aren't staying there, use the public parking lot on the other end of the lake to access the beach and trails.
The lake is full of trout. If you want to fish, you need a National Park Fishing Permit (which you can buy at the Information Centre in town). Remember, you cannot use live bait here.
In winter, the lake is frozen. It is a beautiful spot for a quiet snowshoe walk, but most winter rinks and activities are found at nearby Pyramid Lake.
The forest around Patricia Lake is a wildlife corridor. Even if you are close to town, always carry bear spray and make noise while you are hiking the loop.

places.name: 11. Pyramid Island
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/banff-national-park-gm1068416894-285790670

Pyramid Island is a tiny, peaceful gem located on Pyramid Lake, sitting right at the base of the massive, reddish-colored Pyramid Mountain. It is one of the most photographed spots in Jasper because of its iconic wooden bridge and the perfect mountain reflections in the water.
The Pyramid Lake area is fully open and was completely untouched by the 2024 wildfires. It remains a favorite quick escape because it is only a 10-minute drive from the Jasper townsite.
What to Do and See

Cross the Wooden Bridge: The highlight of any visit is walking across the rustic wooden bridge that connects the shore to the island. It’s the perfect place for a family photo with the mountain in the background.

Island Loop Trail: Once you’re on the island, there is a very short, flat trail that circles the entire thing. It only takes about 10 minutes to walk, but there are plenty of benches where you can sit and listen to the birds.

Sunrise & Sunset: This is the best spot in Jasper to watch the sun. In the morning, the light hits Pyramid Mountain and turns it a glowing orange. At night, it is a dark sky favorite for seeing the stars or Northern Lights.
Paddle the Lake: In the summer, you can rent canoes, kayaks, or even pedal boats from the nearby Pyramid Lake resort. Paddling around the island gives you a totally different view of the cliffs.
Winter Fun: In March and April, the lake is often still frozen. You can go ice skating on the cleared rinks, try fat biking on the snow, or even take a horse-drawn sleigh ride along the shore.
Tips & Key Information

There are only about 8 parking spots right at the island trailhead. Because it is so popular, the lot is usually full between 10:00 AM and 5:00 PM. If it's full, try the larger Pyramid Beach parking lot nearby and walk over.
Since it’s so close to town, many people bike to the island instead of driving. This saves you the stress of finding a parking spot.
The road to the island is narrow. If you are driving an RV or a large trailer, you are not allowed to drive past the resort. Vehicles must be shorter than 7.5 meters (25 feet).
Pyramid Bench is a major travel path for animals. It is very common to see elk or deer standing right on the road or near the bridge. Always give them plenty of space.
There is no extra cost to visit the island, but you must have your Parks Canada Pass displayed on your car windshield.

places.name: 10. Sunwapta Falls
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sunwapta-falls-with-traveler-sitting-on-rock-in-autumn-forest-at-sunset-gm1207319205-348546476

Sunwapta Falls is a dramatic pair of waterfalls fed by the Athabasca Glacier. The name Sunwapta comes from the Stoney Indigenous language and means turbulent water—a perfect name for the roaring river that crashes through this deep limestone canyon.

Sunwapta Falls is fully open and was not affected by the 2024 wildfires. It remains one of the most popular and scenic stops along the Icefields Parkway, located about 55 km south of the Jasper townsite.
What to Do and See

The Upper Falls & Bridge: Just a short, 1-minute stroll from the parking lot, the Upper Falls is the main attraction. A footbridge takes you directly over the 18-meter (60-foot) drop. It’s famous for the tiny, forested island that splits the river just before it plunges into the canyon.

Hike to the Lower Falls: Follow the 1.3 km (0.8 mile) trail downstream. Most tourists skip this, so it’s much quieter. You’ll see three more waterfalls stacked on top of each other. It’s an easy downhill walk on the way there and a gentle climb back up.
Whitewater Rafting: In the summer months, you can join a Class III rafting trip that starts near the falls. This is a white-knuckle adventure with bigger waves than the rafting trips closer to town.

Winter Ice Formations: In March, the falls are often partially frozen. You’ll see massive blue ice pillars and snow pillows decorating the canyon walls, while the water still thunders through the center.

Sunwapta Lodge: Right next to the falls is a historic mountain lodge. You can stop here for a warm meal or a souvenir. It’s a great halfway point if you are driving between Jasper and the Columbia Icefield.
Tips & Key Information
If you want to see the water at its most powerful, visit in late May or June. This is when the spring melt from the glaciers is at its highest.
The best light for photos on the bridge is usually in the late afternoon or evening when the sun begins to dip behind the mountains, casting a golden glow on the spray.
If you are visiting in March or April, the trail to the Lower Falls can be very icy and packed with snow. Wearing ice cleats or spikes over your boots is a very good idea to prevent slipping.
The rocks near the edge of the canyon can be very crumbly and wet. Always stay behind the sturdy wooden railings, especially if you have children with you.
Plan for about 15 minutes if you only want to see the main falls, or about 1 hour if you want to hike down to the Lower Falls and back.

places.name: 9. Medicine Lake (The Disappearing Lake)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/medicine-lake-in-jasper-national-park-canada-gm115903801-1875000

Medicine Lake is one of the most mysterious places in the world. For half the year, it looks like a beautiful, deep blue mountain lake. But for the other half, the water completely vanishes, leaving behind a giant mudflat with a small stream running through it.
In early spring, the lake is in its disappeared state. You will see a snowy basin rather than a full lake, which is a great time to see the drain in action.
What to Do and See

Watch the Bathtub Drain: The lake doesn't have a normal river leading out of it. Instead, the bottom is full of sinkholes—like a bathtub without a plug. The water drains into a secret underground cave system and travels 16 kilometers (10 miles) before popping back up at Maligne Canyon.

Wildlife Spotting: This is one of the best places in Jasper to see animals. Because the water level is low in the spring (March/April), moose often come down to the muddy flats to eat salty minerals. You can also spot bald eagles and ospreys nesting in the tall trees nearby.
Photography: The Disappearing Lake offers a very different view than other spots. In March, the cracked mud and ice create cool patterns that look like another planet.
The Magic History: Indigenous people called this lake Medicine because its vanishing act seemed like powerful magic. There are signs at the viewpoint that tell the stories and legends of the area.

Wildfire Regrowth: The area around Medicine Lake was touched by the 2024 fires. From the lookout, you can see how the fire moved in a mosaic pattern, leaving some trees green while others were burnt, which actually helps create new homes for birds.
Tips & Key Information
If you want to see Medicine Lake looking like a real lake, you have to visit in July or August. This is when the melting snow from the glaciers fills the bathtub faster than it can drain out.
From October to May, the lake is mostly empty.
Because the lakebed is so wide, the animals are often far away. Binoculars will help you spot a moose or a bear on the far shore.
The road near Medicine Lake is a high-crash zone for wildlife. Please drive slowly, especially at dawn and dusk, to keep the animals safe.
It might look fun to walk on the empty lake bottom, but the mud can be very deep and sticky, like quicksand. Stay on the paved viewing platforms for safety.

places.name: 8. Jasper SkyTram
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sky-tram-gm90392872-1591422

The Jasper SkyTram is the highest and longest aerial tramway in Canada. In just 7 minutes, it whisks you up to an elevation of 2,263 meters (7,425 feet) on the side of Whistlers Mountain. It is the absolute best way to see the big picture of the Canadian Rockies without having to hike for hours.
The SkyTram is closed during the winter season. It is officially scheduled to open for the 2026 season on April 15, 2026.
What to Do and See

The Flight: Each tram car carries about 26 people and a flight attendant who tells you cool facts about the mountain. Keep your eyes peeled as you go up—you can often see grizzly bears or mountain goats on the slopes below.

Summit Hike: Once you get off at the Upper Station, the adventure isn't over. You can hike another 1.4 kilometers (0.8 miles) to the very top of Whistlers Mountain. From there, you get a 360-degree view. On a clear day, you can even see Mount Robson, which is the tallest mountain in the Rockies and over 100 kilometers away.

Boardwalk Views: If you don't want to hike to the summit, there are easy wooden boardwalks right outside the Upper Station. They have great viewpoints where you can look down at the town of Jasper and the turquoise Athabasca River.
Summit Café: You can eat lunch at the Treeline Restaurant inside the Upper Station. It is the highest restaurant in the area, and the views from your table are unbeatable.
Meet a Marmot: Whistlers Mountain is named after the Hoary Marmot. These cute, chubby animals live in the rocks near the top and make a loud whistling sound to warn their friends if they see a hawk.
Tips & Key Information

In 2026, ticket prices are approximately CAD $77 for adults aged 16 and over, CAD $48 for youth aged 6 to 15, and free for children under 6. If you are visiting in summer, look out for Early Bird or Sunset deals, which can help you save around 20%.
The SkyTram uses a reservation system. It is much better to book your tickets online before you go so you don't have to wait in a long line at the bottom.
It is usually 10°C colder at the top than it is in the town of Jasper. Even in the summer, there can be snow at the summit. Bring a warm jacket, even if you are wearing shorts at the bottom.
Before you buy your ticket, look at the webcam at the Lower Station or the Jasper SkyTram website. If the mountain is covered in clouds, you won't be able to see anything from the top.
Unlike many attractions, the Jasper SkyTram allows dogs. You can buy a special Dog Ticket (about $10) so your furry friend can join you on the mountain.

places.name: 7. Mount Edith Cavell & Angel Glacier
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/edith-cavell-landscape-gm642910818-117741939
