Mount Edith Cavell is one of the most striking peaks in the park, standing at 3,363 meters (over 11,000 feet). It is famous for its massive, vertical north face and the stunning Angel Glacier, which clings to the cliffside in a shape that looks just like an angel with outspread wings.

As of March 2026, the Cavell Road is closed to all vehicles and hikers. This road was heavily impacted by the 2024 wildfires in the first few kilometers. Because the trees are gone, the slopes are now unstable, and there is a high risk of falling rocks and landslides. Parks Canada is working on a plan to fix the road, but it will remain closed until further notice to keep everyone safe.
What to Do and See (When it Reopens)
Path of the Glacier Trail: This is a short, 1.6-kilometer (1-mile) paved walk. It takes you to a viewpoint where you can look across a small, iceberg-filled pond directly at the Angel Glacier.

Listen for Mountain Thunder: While standing at the viewpoint, you might hear a loud crack followed by a roar. This is the sound of huge chunks of ice breaking off the glacier and falling into the pond below.

Cavell Meadows Trail: For a bigger challenge, this 8-kilometer (5-mile) hike climbs up into alpine meadows. In July and August, the ground is covered in colorful wildflowers like Indian Paintbrush and Western Anemone.

The Ghost of the Glacier: In 2012, a different glacier on this mountain (the Ghost Glacier) fell off the cliff, causing a massive flood. You can still see the path of the debris and rocks that were pushed across the valley.

Icebergs in the Pond: The small lake at the base of the mountain often has mini-icebergs floating in it. Even in the middle of summer, the water stays freezing cold because it is fed directly by the melting ice.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/glacier-ice-water-gm1220902297-357674840
Tips & Key Information

Since the road is closed to private cars in 2026, keep an eye on the Parks Canada website. Sometimes they offer special guided bus tours or shuttles if parts of the road are cleared for professional drivers.

It might be tempting to walk down to the water to touch the ice, but it is extremely dangerous. Large blocks of ice the size of houses can fall off the glacier at any second without warning. Stay behind the rope at the viewpoint.
The Cavell Meadows are famous for two things: beautiful flowers and very hungry mosquitoes. If you plan to hike the meadows, make sure to bring spray.
Even when the road is open, it is very narrow with sharp switchback turns. Vehicles longer than 7 meters (25 feet) are never allowed on Cavell Road.
This area is a special home for the Tonquin Caribou herd. Because of this, the road always has a seasonal closure from November 1 to May 15 every year to give the caribou peace during the winter.

places.name: 6. Columbia Icefield Skywalk
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/columbia-icefield-skywalk-tourists-jasper-canada-gm2148606879-569773236

The Columbia Icefield Skywalk is a world-class feat of engineering that lets you walk on air. It is a glass-bottomed observation platform that curves out from a sheer cliff, hanging 280 meters (918 feet) above the Sunwapta Valley. If you want a massive adrenaline rush and the best views of the high peaks, this is the place to be.
The Skywalk is closed during winter season. Because it is located in a high-altitude mountain pass, it only operates during the warmer months when the ice on the glass can be safely managed.
What to Do and See
Glass Floor: You walk out onto a transparent horseshoe-shaped bridge. Looking straight down between your feet, you’ll see the Sunwapta River winding like a silver thread nearly 1,000 feet below.

Discovery Trail: Before you reach the glass, you walk along a 1-kilometer cliff-edge path. This walkway is lined with interactive storytelling stations where you can learn about the fossils, birds, and waterfalls of the valley.

Wildlife Spotting: Look down at the rocky slopes beneath the bridge. This area is a favorite home for mountain goats. They are amazing climbers and can often be seen standing on tiny ledges right under your feet.

The Hydrological Apex: From the Skywalk, you can see Snow Dome mountain. It is one of only two places in North America where water drains into three different oceans: the Pacific, the Atlantic, and the Arctic.

Audio Guide: Pick up a free handheld audio player (available in many languages). It tells cool stories about how the canyon was formed and how the Skywalk was built to withstand massive winds and heavy snow.
Tips & Key Information
You cannot drive your own car directly to the Skywalk. You must park at the Columbia Icefield Discovery Centre and take a free shuttle bus to the platform. The shuttles leave every 15 to 30 minutes.
Most people buy a ticket that includes both the Athabasca Glacier Ice Explorer and the Skywalk. Buying them together saves you money compared to buying them separately.
An adult ticket for just the Skywalk is approximately $40–$48 CAD. Children under 5 are free but still need a reserved ticket to board the shuttle.

The entire Skywalk—including the shuttle buses and the 1-km trail—is fully wheelchair and stroller accessible. It is one of the best ways for people of all mobility levels to experience a high-mountain view.
The Skywalk is very busy in the middle of the day. If you visit after 5:00 PM, the crowds are much smaller, and the golden hour light makes the mountains look incredible for photos.

places.name: 5. Maligne Canyon
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/malignant-canyon-in-alberta-gm1330596452-413969036

Maligne Canyon is the deepest canyon in Jasper National Park, with some sections dropping more than 50 meters (160 feet) down. It was carved out of limestone over thousands of years by the rushing Maligne River. It is famous for its narrow walls, hidden waterfalls, and unique rock formations.

Due to damage from the 2024 wildfires and the risk of landslides on the steep slopes, Maligne Canyon remains closed for the 2026 season. Parks Canada is working hard to fix the bridges and trails so they are safe again. While you cannot hike the main canyon trail right now, you can still see parts of the river from the nearby Fifth and Sixth Bridge areas, which were deemed safe to reopen.
What to Do and See (When Open)
The Six Bridges: The canyon trail features six different bridges. Bridges 1 and 2 are the most dramatic, looking straight down into the deepest, skinniest parts of the gorge.
Frozen Waterfalls: In the winter, the water turns into giant ice curtains. Professional guides lead Icewalk tours where you wear special spikes on your boots to walk right on the frozen river bed.
Fossil Hunting: If you look closely at the rocks near the first and second bridges, you can see tiny fossils of ancient sea creatures from millions of years ago.
Black Swifts: These rare birds build their nests on the mossy cliffs inside the canyon. They are one of the few birds that can fly through the heavy mist of a waterfall.
Wildfire Recovery: From the open viewpoints at the Fifth Bridge, you can see how the new green plants are starting to grow back among the burnt trees.
Tips & Key Information
Even if a trail looks okay, do not go past the closure signs. Falling trees and loose rocks are very dangerous in fire-affected areas.
Since the upper canyon is closed, head to the Fifth Bridge trailhead. It offers a beautiful, flatter walk along the Maligne River where it begins to widen out.
Safety conditions change quickly in the mountains. Check the Jasper National Park trail report online before you drive out.
There is no drinking water available at the trailheads, so make sure to fill up your bottle in town.
The Maligne Valley is a favorite spot for Moose and Elk. Drive slowly and keep your camera ready.

places.name: 4. The Icefields Parkway (Hwy 93N)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/canadian-rockies-icefields-parkway-jasper-national-park-gm1342153532-421672787

The Icefields Parkway is widely considered one of the most beautiful drives in the world. This 232-kilometer (144-mile) highway connects the town of Jasper to Lake Louise, winding through the heart of the Canadian Rockies.
While the drive takes about 3 hours without stopping, most travelers spend a whole day (8–10 hours) exploring the incredible lakes and viewpoints along the way.
What to Do and See
Peyto Lake: This is the famous wolf-shaped lake. After a short 10-minute walk from the parking lot to the wooden platform, you’ll see water so bright blue it looks like it was painted.
Bow Lake: One of the largest lakes on the drive, sitting right at the foot of massive cliffs. In the morning, the water is often like a mirror, reflecting the mountains perfectly.
Mistaya Canyon: A hidden gem where the river has carved deep, curvy swirls into the rock. A short 10-minute walk downhill from the highway leads you to a bridge directly over the roaring water.

The Big Bend & Big Hill: This is the most exciting part of the drive. The road makes a giant U-turn as it climbs high up the mountainside. There is a large pull-off at the top where you can look back down at the valley you just drove through.

Weeping Wall: Look for a massive limestone cliff on the side of the road. In the spring and summer, dozens of small waterfalls trickle down the face like tears. In the winter, it turns into a giant wall of blue ice.
Wildlife Spotting: This highway is the best place to see animals from your car. Keep an eye out for grizzly bears, black bears, and mountain goats on the rocky slopes.
Tips & Key Information

There is only one gas station on the entire 232-kilometer road (at Saskatchewan River Crossing). The gas there is very expensive, so it is much smarter to fill your tank completely in the town of Jasper before you start.
There are very few places to buy food, and they can be busy. Bringing your own lunch means you can eat at one of the many beautiful picnic spots along the river.
You will lose your phone signal almost as soon as you leave Jasper. Download your maps or bring a paper map so you don’t get lost if you decide to take a side road.
In March and April, the Parkway can still have snow or ice. Check the Alberta 511 website before you go to make sure the road is safe and clear.
To see the best wildlife and avoid the big tour buses, try to hit the road by 7:00 AM. The morning light also makes the lakes look much prettier for your photos

places.name: 3. Athabasca Glacier
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/athabasca-glacier-melting-into-turquoise-water-in-jasper-national-park-gm2253463050-666847204

The Athabasca Glacier is the most visited glacier in North America and a true wonder of the natural world. It is a massive toe of ice that flows down from the Columbia Icefield, which is the largest icefield in the Rocky Mountains.
While it is melting (receding) every year due to climate change, it is still over 300 meters (1,000 feet) thick in some spots—that's as deep as the Eiffel Tower is tall.
What to Do and See

Ice Explorer Adventure: This is the most famous tour. You board a giant, six-wheeled bus called an Ice Explorer (one of only 23 in the world) that drives you directly onto the glacier. You get to step out onto the ancient ice for about 20 minutes.

Toe of the Glacier Trail: If you don't want to take a tour, you can hike this 1.8-kilometer (1.1-mile) trail for free. It takes you right up to the edge of the ice. Along the way, look for the year markers that show where the glacier used to reach in the past.

Columbia Icefield Discovery Centre: Located across the highway, this building has a museum about glaciers, a Starbucks, and a gift shop. It’s a great place to warm up and learn how glaciers are formed.

Glacier IceWalks: For a bigger adventure, you can join a guided hiking tour. Professional guides provide you with crampons (spikes for your shoes) and lead you safely deep onto the glacier for a 3-hour or 6-hour trek.
Fill Your Water Bottle: On the glacier tours, you can find small streams of crystal-clear meltwater. It is perfectly safe to drink and is likely the freshest, coldest water you will ever taste.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/athabasca-glacier-canada-with-people-gm2200469876-618174615
Tips & Key Information

Stay behind the ropes and never walk onto the glacier alone. There are hidden cracks called crevasses that can be covered by thin snow. They are hundreds of feet deep and very dangerous. Only go on the ice with a guided tour or stay in the roped-off safe zones.
Tours typically run from early May to mid-October. In March and April, the Ice Explorer buses are not running yet, but you can still view the glacier from the Discovery Centre or the trail.
Even if it is a hot 25°C in the town of Jasper, it can be 0°C and very windy on the glacier. Bring a warm jacket, pants, and a hat even in July.
Sunglasses are must-haves. The sun reflecting off the white ice is extremely bright. Without sunglasses, you will be squinting the whole time and might even get snow blindness.
The glacier is at a high altitude (over 2,000 meters). You might find that you get out of breath more easily than usual while walking up the trails.

places.name: 2. Athabasca Falls
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/athabasca-falls-in-jasper-national-park-during-summer-alberta-canada-gm1464317871-497042154

Athabasca Falls is known as the most powerful waterfall in the Canadian Rockies. While it isn't the tallest, the sheer amount of water from the Athabasca River slamming into a narrow canyon creates a thunderous roar you can feel in your chest.
This site is fully open and remains a must-see stop along the Icefields Parkway. The area around the falls is also a great place to see how the forest is naturally regrowing after the 2024 wildfires.
What to Do and See
Main Overlook: Just a few steps from the parking lot, you’ll find the primary viewing platform. This is the best spot to see the river take its 23-meter (75-foot) drop into the gorge.
Potholes: As you walk the paved paths, look at the rock walls. You will see smooth, circular holes worn into the stone. These were carved over thousands of years by swirling water and spinning rocks.

Canyon Walk: Don't just look at the falls and leave. Follow the paved trail downstream. It takes you across several bridges and down into the lower canyon where the water calms down and the cliffs tower above you.
Whitewater Rafting: For an extra thrill, you can join a guided rafting tour that starts right at the base of the falls. It’s a Class II trip, which means it’s splashy and fun but safe for families.
Winter Ice Formations: If you visit in early spring (March or April), the falls are often surrounded by giant ice curtains and frozen mist, making it look like a winter palace.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/spectacular-view-of-athabasca-falls-in-jasper-national-park-gm887209118-246254069
Tips & Key Information

Stay behind the railings. This is the most important rule. The rocks near the falls are always wet and extremely slippery. Every year, people get into trouble by climbing over the fence for a better photo. The view from the safe side is just as good.
Athabasca Falls is one of the busiest spots in the park. To avoid the big tour buses, try to get there before 9:00 AM or after 5:00 PM.
Even though the main paths are paved, they can be slippery from the waterfall’s mist. Wear shoes with a good grip (no flip-flops).
Depending on which way the wind is blowing, the mist from the falls can soak you in seconds. A light waterproof layer will keep you dry while you take pictures.
The upper viewing area and the bridge are wheelchair and stroller friendly. However, the lower canyon trail has some stairs and uneven ground.

places.name: 1. Maligne Lake & Spirit Island
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/spirit-island-on-maligne-lake-in-jasper-canada-gm2257882789-670922274

Maligne Lake is the largest natural lake in the Canadian Rockies and is world-famous for its bright, glacial-blue water. Tucked away in the middle of this 22-kilometer (14-mile) lake is Spirit Island, a tiny, sacred grove of trees surrounded by massive mountain peaks.
While the 2024 wildfires affected parts of the surrounding valley, the lake area is open and provides a beautiful look at how the forest begins to grow back.
What to Do and See

Boat Cruise: This is the most popular way to see the lake. The 90-minute Classic Cruise takes you deep into the mountains to Spirit Island. The boats are heated and have big glass windows so you can see the views even if it’s chilly outside.

Spirit Island Viewpoint: Once the boat docks, you take a very short walk (about 4 minutes) to a platform. This is where you get the famous postcard view of the island. Note that you cannot walk onto the island itself because it is a holy place for Indigenous people.

Paddling: If you want an adventure, you can rent a canoe or kayak at the Boathouse. It takes about 4 to 5 hours of rowing each way to reach Spirit Island, so only try this if you are a strong paddler and have the whole day.
Mary Schaffer Loop: For an easy walk on land, try this 3-kilometer trail. It follows the lakeshore and has great spots to sit in the famous Parks Canada Red Chairs.
Waffle Hut: After your boat ride, stop by this small cabin near the docks for a fresh, warm waffle. It is a local favorite.
Tips & Key Information
The boat cruises are very popular and often sell out weeks in advance. In 2026, cruises are scheduled to run from May 29 to October 12.
Even in the middle of summer, it can be very cold on the water. Bring a jacket, a hat, and gloves just in case.
If you are paddling, try to get to the lake by 8:00 AM. The water is usually calm like a mirror in the morning, which makes for the best reflections.
Keep your eyes on the shoreline during the boat ride. It is common to see moose, bears, and eagles near the water's edge.
Maligne Lake is high in the mountains. If the wind gets too strong, the boat cruises or canoe rentals might close for a few hours for safety.

places.name: 1. Notre-Dame Basilica
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/notre-dame-basilica-montreal-gm462576645-30688948

The Notre-Dame Basilica is a masterpiece of Gothic Revival architecture and arguably the most visually stunning interior in North America. Located in the heart of Old Montreal, its history is intertwined with the city's identity, having hosted the wedding of Céline Dion and the funeral of Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau.
What to See and Do
Blue Vaults: Look up to see the breathtaking ceiling, a deep azure sky decorated with thousands of 24-karat gold stars.

AURA Experience: This world-renowned light and sound show by Moment Factory uses the Basilica’s architecture as a canvas. It starts with an exploration of illuminated art stations and culminates in a 25-minute orchestral light performance.
Storytelling Stained Glass: Unlike most cathedrals that depict biblical stories, the windows here illustrate the founding history of Montreal (the Ville-Marie colony).
Casavant Pipe Organ: Dating back to 1891, this massive instrument features four keyboards and 7,000 individual pipes. You can often hear it during mass or special recitals.
Chapel of Notre-Dame du Sacré-Cœur: Located behind the main altar, this chapel was rebuilt after a fire in 1978 and features a striking modern bronze altar and contemporary woodwork.
Tips and Key Information

General sightseeing tickets are approximately $16 CAD. If you want to see the AURA show, tickets are separate and cost about $35 CAD. Because this is Montreal’s top attraction, booking online in advance is highly recommended to secure your time slot.

The Basilica is typically open for visitors Monday through Friday from 9:00 AM to 4:30 PM, Saturday from 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM, and Sunday from 12:30 PM to 4:00 PM. Be aware that these hours can change suddenly for weddings, funerals, or special liturgical events.

As an active place of worship, modest dress is required. Ensure your shoulders are covered, and hats should be removed upon entry. While photography is allowed during sightseeing (no flash), it is strictly prohibited during the AURA show and during religious services.
The Basilica is located at Place d'Armes in Old Montreal. The easiest way to arrive is by taking the Metro (Orange Line) to Place-d'Armes Station, which is just a two-minute walk away.

If you want to experience the Basilica's world-class acoustics for free, attend a Sunday mass. However, please note that sightseeing (walking around to take photos) is not allowed during service times.

places.name: 2. Old Montreal (Vieux-Montreal)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/old-montreal-during-fall-season-quebec-canada-gm1266475864-371281286

Old Montreal (Vieux-Montreal) is the heart of Montreal’s rich history, showcasing stunning colonial architecture and cobblestone streets. The district transports visitors back in time with its preserved 17th and 18th-century buildings, including charming boutiques and cafes. Old Montreal is best experienced on foot, where every corner reveals a piece of the city's 375-plus-year history.
What to See and Do

Place Jacques-Cartier: The district's main social hub. This sloping pedestrian square is lined with flower stalls, street performers, and sun-drenched terrasses. In the winter, it often hosts holiday markets and ice sculptures.

Old Port (Vieux-Port): A massive recreational space along the St. Lawrence River. You can ride the Grande Roue de Montréal (Canada's tallest Ferris wheel), rent pedal boats, or visit the Montreal Science Centre.

Place d'Armes: A historic square surrounded by buildings representing different eras of Montreal’s history, including the Notre-Dame Basilica, the Art Deco Aldred Building, and the Saint-Sulpice Seminary (the oldest building in the city).
Saint-Paul Street: The oldest street in Montreal. It is famously photogenic, filled with high-end art galleries, souvenir shops, and some of the city's most celebrated restaurants and jazz clubs.
Pointe-à-Callière Museum: Built over the actual birthplace of Montreal, this archaeology museum allows you to walk through underground excavations of the original 17th-century settlement.
Tips and Key Information

To avoid the heaviest crowds, aim to explore before 10:00 AM. However, the area truly glows at night; the Cité Mémoire project projects giant historical films onto the stone walls of the neighborhood after dusk—it’s a free, open-air museum experience.

Wear comfortable, flat shoes. The cobblestones are charming but notoriously difficult for high heels or small-wheeled strollers. While the main thoroughfares are accessible, some smaller boutiques and older restaurants have narrow entrances or steep stairs.

Old Montreal has everything from tourist traps to Michelin-worthy dining. If you want to eat at popular spots like Joe Beef, Olive et Gourmando, or Garde Manger, you often need to book weeks in advance. For a more casual experience, the Marché Bonsecours offers local crafts and quick bites.

Parking is extremely difficult and expensive in this area. It is highly recommended to take the Metro (Orange Line) and exit at either Place-d'Armes or Champ-de-Mars. Both stations are within a 5-minute walk of the historic center.

Don't be deterred by the cold. The city clears the cobblestones quickly, and the district is magical under snow. Many restaurants have heated patios, and the Natrel Skating Rink in the Old Port offers one of the best skating views in the country.

places.name: 3. Mount Royal Park (Parc du Mont-Royal)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/beaver-lake-mount-royal-park-in-autumn-montreal-quebec-canada-gm2161438387-581883564

Mount Royal Park (Parc du Mont-Royal) is one of Montreal's most iconic natural landmarks, offering stunning views of the city skyline. This large urban park, designed by landscape architect Frederick Law Olmsted (landscape architect behind New York's Central Park), covers 200 hectares of green space, with plenty of paths, forests, and lakes. This location's significance stems from its central role in Montreal’s landscape and as a recreational haven for both locals and visitors.
What to See and Do
Kondiaronk Belvedere: This semicircular lookout in front of the Mount Royal Chalet offers the most famous panoramic view of Montreal's downtown skyline and the St. Lawrence River.

Beaver Lake (Lac aux Castors): A picturesque man-made lake that serves as a focal point for the park. In the summer, you can enjoy boat rentals and picnics on the surrounding grass; in the winter, it transforms into a popular skating rink.

Tam-Tams: If you visit on a Sunday between May and September, you'll encounter a massive, informal drum circle near the Sir George-Étienne Cartier Monument that draws thousands of dancers and picnickers.
Mount Royal Cross: Standing 31 meters high, this illuminated steel cross commemorates the founding of the city and is a constant landmark visible from across the island.
Outdoor Activities: The park features an extensive network of trails for walking, jogging, and cycling. During winter, it becomes a destination for cross-country skiing, snowshoeing, and tubing.
Tips and Key Information
While you can hike up from various points downtown (like the Peel Street steps), you can also take the #11 bus from Mont-Royal Metro station, which drops you off directly at the summit lookouts.
There are paid parking lots near Beaver Lake and the Smith House, but they fill up very quickly on weekends. It is highly recommended to use public transit or walk if possible.
The park is open daily from 6:00 AM to 12:00 AM, making it a great spot for both sunrise photography and evening views of the city lights.
Head to the Smith House (Maison Smith) for visitor information, educational exhibits about the park's history and biodiversity, and a small cafe for snacks.
If you're visiting in the colder months, the Les Amis de la Montagne kiosk at Beaver Lake offers rentals for skates, cross-country skis, and snowshoes.

places.name: 4. Montreal Botanical Gardenhttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/montreal-canada-gm171278797-20869400
body: The Montreal Botanical Garden is recognized as one of the world’s greatest botanical institutions. Spanning 75 hectares, it offers a global tour of flora through its intricate thematic gardens and massive greenhouse complex. It is a place where art, culture, and nature intersect, providing a tranquil escape right next to the Olympic Stadium.
What to See and Do

Thematic Cultural Gardens: Explore the Chinese Garden, which is the largest of its kind outside Asia, the serene Japanese Garden with its Zen aesthetic and tea room, and the First Nations Garden highlighting the relationship between Indigenous peoples and the plant world.
Greenhouse Complex: Wander through 10 exhibition greenhouses that house everything from arid desert cacti to lush tropical rainforest plants and a world-class bonsai collection.
Arboretum: This massive wooded area features around 7,000 specimens of trees and shrubs, perfect for long walks and birdwatching away from the more manicured sections.

Gardens of Light: If visiting in the autumn (September to October), don't miss this evening event where the cultural gardens are transformed by thousands of hand-painted silk lanterns and immersive light projections.
Insectarium: Located on the same grounds, this recently renovated living museum offers a fascinating, up-close look at the world of insects through innovative, immersive galleries.
Tips and Key Information

Entry requires a paid ticket (approx. $23 CAD for adults). Since it is part of the Espace pour la vie complex, you can buy multi-site bundles that include the Planetarium, Biosphere, or Insectarium for a discounted rate.
The garden is easily accessible via the Pie-IX Metro station (Green Line). From the station, follow the signs for a short 5-minute walk to the main entrance.
While the outdoor gardens are most vibrant from May to October, the greenhouses remain open year-round. The Butterflies Go Free event in early spring is a major draw for families.
Given the 75-hectare size, wear very comfortable walking shoes. A small shuttle often operates seasonally to help visitors move between the main entrance and the more distant parts of the gardens.
The Garden Restaurant offers seasonal menus often featuring ingredients grown on-site, and there are several designated picnic areas if you prefer to bring your own food.

places.name: 5. Saint Joseph’s Oratory of Mount Royalhttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/saint-josephs-oratory-of-mount-royal-with-steps-and-people-gm622052150-108850753
body: Standing majestically on the northern slope of Mount Royal, this National Historic Site is Canada's largest church and a world-renowned pilgrimage site. Its massive copper dome reaches a height of 97 meters, making it the highest point in Montreal and a permanent fixture of the city's skyline. This impressive basilica is dedicated to Saint Joseph, the patron saint of Canada.
What to See and Do

Dome and Basilica: Enter the Great Basilica to appreciate its sheer scale and the modern, minimalist interior. The outer dome is the third largest of its kind in the world, surpassed only by St. Peter’s in Rome and Yamoussoukro in Ivory Coast.
Crypt Church: A more intimate, 1,000-seat church located at the base of the Oratory. It features a beautiful mosaic and is where most daily masses are held.

Votive Chapel: One of the most striking areas of the Oratory, this chapel contains 10,000 candles and hundreds of crutches hung on the walls, left behind by people claiming to have been healed through the intercession of Brother André.
Heart of Brother André: In a small museum area, you can view the preserved heart of the Saint, a traditional Catholic relic.
Garden of the Way of the Cross: A peaceful, wooded outdoor space featuring monumental sculptures. It is a perfect spot for quiet reflection or a nature walk away from the crowds.
View from the Terrace: The front steps and terrace offer an unparalleled sunset view looking northwest over the city toward the Laurentian Mountains.
Tips and Key Information

There are 283 steps leading from the street to the Basilica. While there is a central set of wooden steps reserved specifically for pilgrims who climb them on their knees, there are concrete stairs for regular foot traffic.

For those who cannot or prefer not to climb the stairs, a free shuttle bus operates between the main gate and the entrance of the Oratory. Elevators also provide access between the various levels inside.
The easiest way is via the Metro (Blue Line) to Côte-des-Neiges Station, followed by a 10-minute walk or a short bus ride.

Access to the Oratory is generally free, though donations are encouraged. There is a small fee (approx. $5) to visit the Oratory Museum, which houses a world-class collection of nativity scenes from around the globe.
This is a very active site for prayer and pilgrimage. Visitors are asked to maintain a quiet demeanor, and photography is generally permitted except during mass.

places.name: 6. Biodôme de Montreal
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/biodome-of-montreal-gm1483372040-509986017

The Montreal Biodôme is a world-class house of life where you can walk through four distinct ecosystems of the Americas under one roof. Located within the Space for Life complex in a building originally designed as a velodrome for the 1976 Olympics, it offers an immersive experience that blurs the lines between a zoo, an aquarium, and a botanical garden.
What to See and Do
Tropical Rainforest: This is the largest and most popular ecosystem, featuring lush vegetation, a humid climate, and free-roaming wildlife like parrots, sloths, and golden lion tamarins.

Laurentian Maple Forest: This section replicates the Quebec wilderness. Depending on when you visit, you will see the foliage change with the seasons, and you might spot North American beavers, river otters, and lynx.

Gulf of Saint Lawrence: This ecosystem features a massive 2.5-million-litre basin of seawater. Visitors can observe hundreds of Atlantic fish and various seabirds from both above and below the waterline.
Sub-Antarctic Islands: A favorite for many, this climate-controlled environment is home to several species of penguins, including Gentoo and Macaroni penguins, diving into icy waters.
Bio-Machine: This interactive gallery allows you to go behind the scenes to see the massive mechanical systems required to maintain five different climates simultaneously.
Tips and Key Information
Entry is by timed reservation only. It is strongly recommended to book online in advance, as popular time slots—especially on weekends and holidays—sell out quickly.
You will be walking through everything from a humid 28°C (82°F) rainforest to a chilly sub-polar zone. It is best to dress in layers and use the on-site lockers for heavy coats.
The easiest way to arrive is via the Viau Metro station (Green Line). Follow the signs through the Olympic Park toward the entrance of the Biodôme.
Photography is permitted, but the use of flash is strictly prohibited throughout the ecosystems to avoid distressing the animals.
The entire path is fully accessible for strollers and wheelchairs. Elevators connect the various levels, and there are designated rest areas throughout the circuit.

places.name: 7. Montreal Museum of Fine Arts
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/montreal-museum-of-fine-arts-gm1209677511-350134827

The Montreal Museum of Fine Arts (Musée des beaux-arts de Montréal) is the city's largest museum and one of the most prominent artistic institutions in North America. Spread across five interconnected pavilions on the historic Golden Square Mile, the museum is celebrated for its encyclopedic collection that spans from ancient archaeology to cutting-edge contemporary design.
What to See and Do
Jean-Noël Desmarais Pavilion: The museum's main entrance, which houses modern and contemporary art galleries, as well as major temporary international exhibitions.

Michal and Renata Hornstein Pavilion: Known for its classical architecture, this section is dedicated to archaeology and ancient art, featuring impressive collections from the Mediterranean and beyond.

Claire and Marc Bourgie Pavilion: A converted 19th-century church that now houses the Quebec and Canadian art collections. It features 20 magnificent Tiffany stained-glass windows and an exquisite concert hall.
Sculpture Garden: An outdoor museum without walls along Sherbrooke Street and Du Musée Avenue, featuring over 30 monumental works by international and Canadian artists.
World Cultures and Decorative Arts: Extensive galleries dedicated to art from Africa, Asia, and Oceania, as well as a significant collection of decorative arts and industrial design.
Tips and Key Information

General admission is approximately $24 CAD for adults, but the museum offers a significant discount (around $16 CAD) for those aged 21–30. Admission is free for everyone under 20. On the first Sunday of every month, admission to the Discovery Exhibitions and the permanent collection is free for Quebec residents.
The museum is located in the downtown core and is easily accessible via the Peel or Guy-Concordia Metro stations (Green Line).

The museum offers free 60-minute guided tours of the permanent collections, which are included with the price of admission. These are available in both English and French at scheduled times throughout the day.
The museum is typically open Tuesday to Sunday from 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM, with extended hours until 9:00 PM on Wednesdays for major exhibitions. The museum is generally closed on Mondays.
The museum boutique is widely considered one of the best in the city for unique gifts and art books.

places.name: 8. Old Port of Montreal
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/aerial-view-of-montreal-old-port-gm2182735276-601667394

The Old Port of Montreal (Vieux-Port) is a sprawling historic riverfront complex that stretches over two kilometers along the St. Lawrence River. Formerly the commercial heart of the city, it has been reimagined as one of Canada's most popular recreational and cultural destinations, offering a mix of year-round adventures and maritime charm.
What to See and Do
La Grande Roue de Montréal: Ride Canada's tallest Ferris wheel for spectacular panoramic views of the city and the river from climate-controlled gondolas.
Montreal Science Centre: A family-favorite destination featuring interactive exhibitions, an IMAX TELUS theatre, and hands-on workshops focused on technology and innovation.
Active Recreation: Visitors can rent pedal boats, quadricycles, or take a zip-line flight over the crowds for an adrenaline rush.
Clock Tower (Tour de l'Horloge): Climb the 192 steps of this historic memorial for a great vantage point, or relax on the seasonal Clock Tower Beach at its base.
Tips and Key Information
The general outdoor site is typically accessible daily from 6:00 AM to 12:00 AM, though specific attractions like the Science Centre or the Ferris wheel have their own distinct schedules.
In the summer, the area is a hub for street performers and food trucks; in the winter, it hosts one of the city's most beautiful outdoor skating rinks (Natrel Rink) with themed music nights.
The easiest access is via the Champ-de-Mars or Place-d'Armes Metro stations (Orange Line). Walking from Old Montreal toward the river will lead you directly into the port area.
The riverfront can be significantly windier and cooler than the interior streets of the city, so carrying an extra layer is often recommended even in the summer.

places.name: 9. Jean-Talon Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/jean-talon-market-montreal-quebec-gm1408479114-459326100

Jean Talon Market is one of North America's largest and most famous open-air public markets, serving as a vibrant focal point for Montreal's Little Italy neighborhood since 1933. It offers an incredible sensory experience where the city's diverse culinary culture comes to life through local farmers, artisans, and specialty food producers.
What to See and Do
Fresh Local Produce: The central aisles are filled with seasonal fruits and vegetables from Quebec farms, known for their high quality and vibrant displays.
Specialty Food Boutiques: Explore the permanent shops surrounding the main stalls, which include world-class cheesemongers (fromageries), butchers, spice shops, and bakeries.
Prepared Foods and Tastings: Visitors can enjoy fresh oysters, handmade tacos, artisanal ice cream, or traditional Quebecois maple products as they wander.
Flower Stalls: The market is particularly famous for its extensive selection of plants, flowers, and garden supplies that line the perimeter in the spring and summer.
Tips and Key Information
During the summer, the market is largely open-air and pedestrian-only; in the winter, walls are erected around the central area to create a cozy, heated indoor shopping environment.
Arrive early on weekday mornings for the quietest experience, or join the bustling crowds on Saturday for the full local atmosphere.
While many larger stalls and boutiques now accept cards, it is still helpful to carry some cash for smaller transactions with independent farmers.
The market is easily accessible via the Jean-Talon Metro station (Blue and Orange Lines), followed by a 5-minute walk.
Like many Montreal public spaces, the market encourages visitors to bring their own reusable bags or baskets to transport their finds.

places.name: 10. Biospherehttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/aerial-view-of-montreal-biosphere-in-autumn-sunset-time-jean-drapeau-park-saint-gm2171492627-591349227
body: The Biosphere, Environment Museum is a striking architectural icon located on Saint Helen's Island. Originally designed as the United States pavilion for Expo 67, this massive geodesic dome now serves as a museum dedicated to environmental awareness and sustainability.
What to See and Do
Geodesic Dome: Observe the intricate steel structure designed by Buckminster Fuller, which stands as the largest of its kind in the world and provides an incredible backdrop for photography.
Environmental Exhibits: Explore interactive displays that focus on climate change, water conservation, and biodiversity, designed to educate visitors of all ages on ecological challenges.
Panoramic Views: Visit the viewing platforms for a unique vantage point of the St. Lawrence River and the Montreal skyline through the geometric patterns of the dome's structure.
Outdoor Gardens: Walk through the surrounding parkland of Parc Jean-Drapeau, which features public art, seasonal floral displays, and easy access to riverside paths.
Tips and Key Information
The easiest way to reach the island is by taking the Metro (Yellow Line) to Jean-Drapeau station. From there, it is a short, scenic walk to the dome.
As part of the Space for Life (Espace pour la vie) complex, you can purchase individual tickets or multi-site passes that include the Botanical Garden, Biodôme, and Planetarium.
While many exhibits are indoors, the structure is open to the elements in some areas, and getting between attractions involves walking outdoors.
The museum is typically open from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM, though it is closed on Mondays. It is always best to check the official website for seasonal changes or holiday closures.

places.name: 1. Pointe-à-Callière, Montreal Archaeology and History Complex
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pointe-%C3%A0-calli%C3%A8re-museum-gm1209677586-350134969

Built upon the actual birthplace of the city, the Montreal Museum of Archaeology and History (Pointe-à-Callière) offers a unique underground journey through centuries of North American history. It is the only major archaeology museum in Canada and is situated on a site that has seen over 1,000 years of human activity.
What to See and Do

Archaeological Crypt: Walk through a unique underground circuit that takes you through the remains of the city's first cemetery, the first Catholic cemetery in Montreal, and the original stone foundations of the 17th-century settlement.
Collector’s Sewer: Experience a world-first by walking through a 110-meter section of North America's first stone-built vaulted collector sewer, dating back to 1832.
Generations MTL: Watch a high-tech immersive show that uses state-of-the-art projections to tell the story of Montreal's evolution from indigenous lands to a modern metropolis.
Memory Collector: Explore the First Collector Sewer, a multisensory experience that combines light and sound in a beautifully preserved 19th-century engineering marvel.
Fort Ville-Marie: Visit the site of the city's original fort, where you can see the remains of the very first European settlement in Montreal.
Tips and Key Information
The main entrance is located at the Éperon building, a modern structure shaped like the prow of a ship, situated at the corner of Place Royale and de la Commune Street.
Free 45-minute guided tours are often included with admission and provide essential context for the complex archaeological remains; they are available in both English and French.
The museum is located in Old Montreal and is a short 5-minute walk from the Place-d'Armes Metro station (Orange Line).
The majority of the museum, including the underground tunnels, is fully accessible via elevators and ramps. However, the cobblestone paths surrounding the entrance can be uneven.
The museum's restaurant, L'Arrivage, is located on the second floor and offers one of the best views of the Old Port and the St. Lawrence River.

places.name: 2. Château Ramezay Historic Site and Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/ch%C3%A2teau-ramezay-in-montreal-quebec-gm175209184-21860873

The Château Ramezay is a remarkable portal into the daily life of Montreal's 18th-century elite. Built in 1705 as the residence for the Governor of Montreal, it was the first building in Quebec to be classified as a historic monument and famously served as the Canadian headquarters for the American Revolutionary Army in 1775.
What to See and Do
Governor's Garden: Wander through this meticulously recreated 18th-century urban garden, divided into sections for kitchen produce, medicinal herbs, and ornamental flowers.
Nantes Panels: Marvel at the intricate mahogany carvings in the Salle de Nantes, which were originally designed for the French India Company in the 1700s.
Multimedia Circuit: Follow an immersive "World-Bound" circuit that uses high-tech projections and audio to bring historical figures to life within the castle walls.
Daily Life Exhibits: Explore a vast collection of artifacts ranging from indigenous tools and colonial furniture to early Canadian artwork that illustrates the evolution of Montreal.
Tips and Key Information
You will find it directly across from City Hall in Old Montreal, making it an easy addition to a walking tour of the historic district.
Visitors often recommend taking the costumed guided tours when available, as they provide colorful anecdotes about the famous guests who stayed here, including Benjamin Franklin.
While the main floor and garden are accessible, the building’s historic nature means some areas, such as the vaulted cellars, may have limited access for those with mobility issues.
The museum offers a historical scavenger hunt specifically designed to keep younger visitors engaged with the exhibits.

places.name: 3. McCord Stewart Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/mccord-museum-sherbrooke-street-west-with-people-enjoying-their-time-after-the-ease-gm1329208348-413022416

The McCord Stewart Museum is a social history museum dedicated to the preservation and appreciation of Montreal's history, its people, and its communities. Located directly across from McGill University, it houses one of the most significant historical collections in North America, offering a deeply human perspective on the city's evolution.
What to See and Do

Indigenous Cultures Collection: This is one of the museum's core strengths, featuring over 16,000 artifacts that document the history and artistry of Indigenous peoples from across Canada, with a focus on the nations of the Northeast.

Dress, Fashion, and Textiles: Explore an extensive collection of over 20,000 garments and accessories that trace the history of fashion in Montreal and Canada from the 18th century to the present day.

Notman Photographic Archives: This world-famous collection contains over a million photographs, including the iconic work of William Notman, providing an unparalleled visual record of 19th and 20th-century Canada.
Outdoor Exhibitions: The museum often utilizes the adjacent pedestrianized McGill College Avenue for large-scale outdoor photography exhibitions that are free to the public.
Tips and Key Info
If you are visiting during the week, take advantage of the Wednesday evening hours when the museum stays open until 9:00 PM.

General admission is approximately $20 CAD for adults. However, the museum often offers free admission to its permanent collections on Wednesday evenings starting at 5:00 PM (though a fee may still apply for major temporary exhibitions).
Situated on Sherbrooke Street West, the museum is easily reached via the McGill Metro station (Green Line).
Personal photography without flash is generally permitted in the permanent collection galleries, but it is often restricted in temporary or visiting exhibitions.

places.name: 4. Musée d'art contemporain de Montréal
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/building-exterior-of-the-modern-museum-of-contemporary-art-in-downtown-montreal-gm1468665591-500126393

The Musée d'art contemporain de Montréal (MAC) is Canada's premier institution dedicated exclusively to contemporary art. It is currently in a fascinating stage of its history; while its main building in the Quartier des Spectacles undergoes a massive architectural transformation (scheduled to finish around 2028), the museum has set up a sleek, temporary home in the heart of downtown.
What to See and Do

Temporary Gallery: Visit the current museum space at Place Ville Marie. While smaller than the original building, it hosts cutting-edge temporary exhibitions that often challenge traditional perceptions of art.

Permanent Collection Highlights: The museum owns over 8,000 works. Since space is limited at the temporary site, the MAC frequently collaborates with the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts to display recent acquisitions and key pieces of Quebec and Canadian art.
Creative Workshops: The MAC is famous for its hands-on approach. You can often find workshops where you can create your own art inspired by the current exhibitions, led by professional artists.

Transformation Mural: While the original site is closed, check out the large-scale outdoor murals on the construction fences at Place des Arts. These Graphic Worlds installations change periodically and turn the construction site into an open-air gallery.

Habiter le MAC (New for 2026): Starting in spring 2026, the museum is shifting its temporary space into a vibrant hub for artist residencies. Visitors can witness the creative process firsthand as emerging artists inhabit the museum to develop new work.
Tips and Key Information
The museum is located on the Gallery Level of Place Ville Marie (PVM), at the corner of Mansfield and Cathcart. Use the Mansfield Street entrance for the easiest access.
Admission to the temporary space is generally more affordable than typical museums (often around $10 CAD). It is free for those 18 and under. You can save $2 by booking online in advance.
Closed on Mondays. Open Tuesday to Friday from 11:30 AM to 7:00 PM, and weekends from 11:00 AM to 5:30/6:00 PM.
Because the current space is a temporary retail-style conversion, there is no cloakroom. Avoid bringing large bags or heavy luggage, as you will have to carry them through the galleries.
The PVM location is incredibly central. Take the Green Line Metro to McGill or the Orange Line to Bonaventure; both are connected via the Underground City.

places.name: 5. Mary, Queen of the World Cathedral
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/interior-of-mary-queen-of-the-world-cathedral-montreal-quebec-canada-gm2160865817-581361008

Mary, Queen of the World Cathedral is a striking piece of Renaissance-inspired architecture right in downtown Montreal, modeled after St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome. Though smaller in scale, the cathedral impresses with its ornate interior, massive dome, and finely detailed chapels.
What to See and Do

Façade and Statues: Unlike St. Peter's, which features statues of the twelve apostles, the roofline of this cathedral is adorned with statues representing the patron saints of the thirteen parishes of Montreal that contributed to its construction.
Baldachin: Inside, you can see a magnificent copper baldachin (canopy) over the high altar, which is a hand-sculpted reproduction of the famous Bernini masterpiece found in Rome.

Historical Paintings: The interior walls feature nine large-scale paintings that depict significant events in the early history of Montreal, providing a visual narrative of the city's religious roots.

Bishop's Mortuary Chapel: Located within the cathedral, this chapel serves as the final resting place for many of Montreal's bishops and archbishops, featuring impressive marble work and quiet areas for reflection.
Tips and Key Information
There is no fee to enter the cathedral for sightseeing, though donations for the maintenance of the historic building are welcomed.
It is situated at the corner of René-Lévesque Boulevard and Mansfield Street, directly across from Dorchester Square. The closest Metro station is Bonaventure (Orange Line).
The cathedral is open daily from 7:00 AM to 7:00 PM. If you wish to take photos, it is best to visit between mass times, as photography is not permitted during services.
Visitors often note that while it is in the heart of the busy business district, the interior offers a profound sense of peace and silence.

places.name: 6. Redpath Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/exterior-view-of-redpath-museum-at-mcgill-university-under-a-winter-sky-gm1460469625-494643642

The Redpath Museum in Montreal is a must-see for those interested in history and natural sciences. Located at McGill University, it houses an impressive collection of artifacts and exhibits that span geology, paleontology, and ancient cultures.
What to See and Do
Dinosaur Skeletons and Fossils: The second-floor gallery is a major draw, featuring an Albertosaurus skeleton, prehistoric fish, and a vast collection of local Quebec fossils.
World Cultures and Mummies: The museum houses a significant collection of Egyptian antiquities, including three mummies, alongside artifacts from various indigenous cultures around the world.
Mineralogy and Biodiversity: Explore extensive displays of minerals, many of which are from the local region, as well as taxidermy specimens of animals ranging from local birds to exotic mammals.
Historic Architecture: The building itself is a highlight, with its grand wooden staircases and high-ceilinged galleries that evoke a classic 1800s scientific institution.
Tips and Key Information
Entry to the museum is generally by voluntary donation for individuals (suggested around $10 CAD), making it one of the most accessible cultural stops in the city.
The museum is typically open Tuesday to Friday from 9:00 AM to 4:30 PM and Saturdays from 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM. It is closed on Sundays and Mondays.
The easiest way to reach the museum is by taking the Metro (Green Line) to McGill Station. It is a short walk from there onto the university campus.
As it is on a university campus, visitors are asked to maintain a relatively quiet demeanor, especially during exam periods when students may be studying in nearby areas.

Due to the historic nature of the building, accessibility can be limited. There is a wheelchair-accessible entrance and an elevator, but it is recommended to contact the museum in advance to ensure a smooth visit.

places.name: 7. Place d'Armes
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/notre-dame-basilica-in-montreal-quebec-gm458971511-22109793

Place d’Armes is one of the oldest public squares in Montreal, surrounded by striking architecture that reflects the city’s evolving history. Anchored by the Notre-Dame Basilica, the square offers a clear view of Montreal’s past through its surrounding buildings, ranging from 18th-century banks to modern office towers.
What to See and Do

Architectural Diversity: The square is framed by iconic landmarks, including the Gothic Revival Notre-Dame Basilica, the neoclassical Bank of Montreal Museum, and the Art Deco Aldred Building, which was modeled after the Empire State Building.

Maisonneuve Monument: At the center of the square stands a majestic bronze monument dedicated to Paul de Chomedey, Sieur de Maisonneuve, the founder of Montreal, commemorating the city's 250th anniversary.

Historic Significance: The square was originally used for military drills and parades in the 1600s and later became the city's main financial hub, often referred to as the Wall Street of Canada in the early 20th century.

Social Hub: Today, it is a bustling pedestrian space where visitors can enjoy street performances, rest on stone benches, or take in the impressive Cité Mémoire projections that appear on the surrounding walls after dark.
Tips and Key Information

To experience the square at its most peaceful, aim for early morning (before 10:00 AM) or late evening. During peak hours (11:00 AM to 3:00 PM), the area can become very congested with tour groups and cruise ship visitors.

Parking in Old Montreal is notoriously difficult and expensive. It is highly recommended to take the Metro (Orange Line) and exit at the Place-d'Armes station. From there, it is a short, 4-minute walk up the hill to the square.

Stay until after dusk to witness the Cité Mémoire projections. Historical scenes are projected onto the stone walls of the buildings surrounding the square. Download the free Montréal en Histoires app to hear the accompanying soundtrack and stories via your smartphone.

For the best shot of the Notre-Dame Basilica, stand near the Maisonneuve monument in the center of the square. For a bird's-eye view, head to the Terrasse Place d’Armes, a rooftop bar on top of the Hôtel Place d’Armes, which offers a stunning vantage point over the square.

The square itself is a flat, open pedestrian area, but the surrounding streets are paved with historic cobblestones, which can be uneven for strollers or wheelchairs. Comfortable, flat walking shoes are essential.

If you need a break, the Bank of Montreal Museum (located on the north side) is free to enter and offers a quiet, climate-controlled environment. Public restrooms are available inside the nearby Palais des congrès (Convention Centre) or for a small fee inside the Notre-Dame Basilica.

places.name: 8. Habitat 67
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/habitat-67-in-montreal-gm1074658170-287680180

Habitat 67 is one of the most recognizable and significant architectural landmarks in the world. Originally created as a pavilion for Expo 67, this housing complex designed by Moshe Safdie was intended to reinvent the apartment building by combining the benefits of suburban homes—namely gardens, fresh air, and privacy—with the density of a modern city.
What to See and Do
Architectural Marvel: The complex is made up of 354 identical, prefabricated concrete forms (cubes) arranged in various combinations to create 148 residences, each with its own private roof terrace.
Brutalist Icon: It is a prime example of Brutalist architecture and remains a pilgrimage site for architects and students from around the globe.

Guided Tours: While it is a private residential building, you can book official 90-minute guided tours that allow you to walk through the complex, visit a restored unit, and learn about its complex engineering history.
Tips and Key Information

Visitors are welcome to view the exterior from the public road or the nearby riverside path, but wandering into the residential corridors or onto the private terraces is strictly prohibited unless you are part of an official tour.
The best vantage points for photography are from the Cité du Havre park area or from across the water in the Old Port, which allows you to capture the full stacked silhouette of the building.

It is somewhat isolated compared to other downtown sites. The easiest way to get there is by car or ride-share, though you can also take the #168 bus from McGill Metro or bike along the scenic multi-use paths from the Old Port.
Tours are seasonal (typically May to October) and must be booked well in advance through the official Habitat 67 website, as they are kept to small groups and sell out quickly.

places.name: 9. Montreal Science Centre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/people-walking-and-riding-their-bikes-in-montreal-gm508817007-46267156

The Montreal Science Centre is a must-visit destination for anyone interested in science, technology, and interactive exhibits. Located in the heart of Old Montreal, this modern museum offers a variety of hands-on displays that engage visitors of all ages.
What to See and Do

Interactive Exhibitions: The centre features several permanent galleries where you can explore themes like human biology, physical forces, and environmental sustainability through tactile experiments and creative challenges.

IMAX TELUS Theatre: Home to a massive screen and state-of-the-art sound system, this theatre regularly screens breathtaking 3D documentaries that transport viewers into the deep ocean, outer space, or remote wilderness.
Fabrik Workshop: A popular space for tinkering where visitors are given specific challenges to solve using a variety of odds and ends, encouraging inventive thinking and engineering skills.
Mini Mondo: A specially designed discovery zone for children under seven, allowing younger explorers to learn about their environment in a playful, sensory-driven setting.
Tips and Key Information

You can purchase separate tickets for the exhibitions or the IMAX films, but many visitors find the Combo tickets to be the best value if they plan to spend the whole afternoon. It is highly recommended to book IMAX showtimes in advance, especially on weekends.
Situated at the end of the King Edward Pier in the Old Port, it is easily reached by walking from the Place-d'Armes Metro station (Orange Line).

While there is a snack bar inside, you are also steps away from the many food trucks and restaurants along the Old Port promenade. There are also designated indoor areas if you prefer to bring your own lunch.
Weekday afternoons after 2:00 PM are generally much quieter once the morning school groups have departed, offering a more relaxed environment for the interactive stations.

places.name: 10. The Marguerite Bourgeoys Site
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/notre-dame-de-bon-secours-chapel-marguerite-bourgeoys-historic-site-montreal-quebec-gm2161438235-581883432

The Marguerite Bourgeoys Site (formerly known as the Marguerite Bourgeoys Museum) is an exceptional historical complex located in Old Montreal. It is uniquely situated within and beneath the Notre-Dame-de-Bon-Secours, one of the oldest churches in the city, and serves as a tribute to Montreal's first teacher and the founder of the Congrégation de Notre-Dame. The museum offers a rare opportunity to explore the layering of Montreal's history, moving from an 18th-century chapel down into archaeological excavations.
What to See and Do
Archaeological Site: Descend into the stone foundations of the original 1675 chapel, where you can see 2,000-year-old Indigenous artifacts and traces of the earliest French colonial life.
Sailors' Church: Explore the stunning 1771 chapel, famous for its maritime theme and small wooden ships hanging from the ceiling, left by sailors as votive offerings for safe passage.
Tower Views: Climb the chapel’s tower for an incredible vantage point over the St. Lawrence River, the Old Port, and the historic streets of Old Montreal.
St. Marguerite’s Tomb: Visit the final resting place of Marguerite Bourgeoys herself, which has become a significant site of pilgrimage for many visitors.
Tips and Key Information
Access to the chapel itself is typically free (though donations are encouraged), while a ticket is required to enter the museum and archaeological site (approximately $12-$15 CAD for adults).
You will find it at the eastern end of Old Montreal, right next to the Bonsecours Market. The closest Metro station is Champ-de-Mars (Orange Line).
The site is generally open Tuesday to Sunday from 11:00 AM to 5:00 PM, though it opens slightly earlier on Sundays (10:00 AM). It is closed on Mondays.
Because of its location, it is very easy to combine this visit with a trip to the Sir George-Étienne Cartier National Historic Site, which is just a few blocks away.

places.name: 1. Parc Jean-Drapeau
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/autumn-trees-in-montreal-parc-jean-drapeau-in-quebec-canada-gm1216629042-354840615

Parc Jean-Drapeau is a large urban park in Montreal, comprising two islands in the St. Lawrence River: Saint Helen's Island (Sainte-Hélène) and the man-made Notre Dame Island. Originally the site of the legendary Expo 67 world’s fair, it is now a 268-hectare recreational hub that hosts a variety of attractions, including art installations, festivals, and natural spaces for outdoor activities.
What to See and Do
Circuit Gilles-Villeneuve: This is the world-famous Formula 1 track that hosts the Canadian Grand Prix. When the race isn't on, it is open to the public for cycling, rollerblading, and walking.
La Ronde: Operated by Six Flags, this is the largest amusement park in Quebec, featuring world-class roller coasters and the site of the International Fireworks Competition.
Jean-Doré Beach: A surprising sandy oasis in the middle of the river, perfect for swimming and paddleboarding during the summer months.
Biosphere: This massive geodesic dome stands as a landmark for environmental education on Saint Helen's Island.

Public Art & Gardens: The park is dotted with massive sculptures (like Alexander Calder’s Trois disques) and features the beautiful Floralies Gardens, created for the 1980 international floral exhibition.
Tips and Key Information

The Jean-Drapeau Metro station (Yellow Line) is the most efficient way to arrive. It drops you right in the heart of Saint Helen's Island. During summer, a river shuttle (Navette fluviale) also connects the Old Port to the park.
The park is massive. Renting a BIXI bike at the Metro station is highly recommended to get from the Biosphere to the far ends of the F1 track on the adjacent island.
The park hosts major festivals like Osheaga, ÎleSoniq, and Piknic Électronik. On festival weekends, the park becomes extremely crowded, and some areas may be restricted to ticket holders.
During the colder months, the park transforms into a winter wonderland with a massive skating path, snowshoeing trails, and the popular Fête des neiges family festival.
While there are concession stands near the Metro and La Ronde, they can be pricey. Many locals bring a picnic to enjoy at the many tables overlooking the Montreal skyline.

places.name: 2. La Fontaine Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pond-at-la-fontaine-park-in-montreal-quebec-gm175212097-21965632

La Fontaine Park is a beloved 34-hectare urban oasis in the Plateau-Mont-Royal borough, cherished by locals for its dual-style landscaping. The western section of the park is designed in the formal French style with symmetrical paths, while the eastern portion offers a more natural, English-style garden feel with winding trails and mature trees.
What to See and Do
Scenic Lakes and Fountains: The park features two interconnected lakes, with the iconic high-shooting fountain serving as a central landmark and a favorite backdrop for picnics.
Théâtre de Verdure: This recently renovated open-air theater hosts free cultural performances, including dance, music, and film screenings, during the summer months.
Active Recreation: Visitors can enjoy a wide range of facilities, including tennis courts, baseball diamonds, and dedicated paths for cycling and jogging that connect to the city's broader network.
Seasonal Transformation: In the winter, the larger pond is converted into one of the city's most atmospheric outdoor skating rinks, complete with music and holiday lighting.
Tips and Key Information
The park is easily accessible via the Sherbrooke or Mont-Royal Metro stations (Orange Line), followed by a short walk through the picturesque streets of the Plateau.
Located within the park, this chalet houses a bistro and terrace where you can grab a meal or coffee while enjoying views of the lake.

During the summer, the park becomes the city's living room. It is one of the designated parks where you are legally allowed to enjoy wine or beer with a meal, making it a prime spot for an afternoon gathering.
The park is home to a very active population of squirrels and various bird species; locals often spend hours by the water watching the ducks and heron that frequent the ponds.

places.name: 3. Circuit Gilles Villeneuve
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/gilles-villeneuve-circuit-gm1400412615-453995216

Located on Notre Dame Island within Parc Jean-Drapeau, the Circuit Gilles Villeneuve is a world-renowned motor racing venue. While it is most famous for hosting the Formula 1 Canadian Grand Prix, its unique setting and public access make it a versatile destination for both high-speed sports fans and local recreation enthusiasts.
What to See and Do

Public Access: Outside of race events, the track is open to the public as a paved multi-use path. It is a legendary spot for cyclists, in-line skaters, and runners who want to test their speed on the same asphalt as professional racers.
Iconic Landmarks: As you navigate the 4.36 km loop, you'll pass through scenic sections like the Wall of Champions and enjoy views of the Saint Lawrence River and the Montreal skyline.

Historical Significance: Named in honor of the legendary Canadian driver Gilles Villeneuve, the circuit is steeped in racing history and remains one of the fastest and most challenging tracks on the F1 calendar.
Tips and Key Information

The track is typically open for public use from spring through autumn. However, it closes to the public for several weeks before and after the Grand Prix (usually held in June) for setup and teardown.
The best way to reach the track is via the Jean-Drapeau Metro station (Yellow Line). From the station, you can walk or bike across the bridge to Notre Dame Island.
The track is very popular with serious cyclists. If you are there for a leisurely stroll or slow skate, it is best to stay to the sides to allow faster riders to pass safely in the center lanes.
There are water fountains and restrooms located at various points around the circuit, particularly near the paddock area and the entrance to the Floralies Gardens.

places.name: 4. Lachine Canal National Historic Site
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/lachine-canal-gm1601636911-530237851

The Lachine Canal National Historic Site is a 14.5-kilometer waterway that served as the industrial heart of Canada during the 19th century. Today, it is one of Montreal's most popular linear parks, stretching from the Old Port to Lake Saint-Louis and offering a unique blend of heritage architecture, green spaces, and recreational activities.
What to See and Do

Industrial Heritage: As you travel along the canal, you can see significant landmarks like the Old Port Locks and historical industrial structures that have been converted into modern residential and commercial lofts.

Multi-use Path: The canal features one of the city's most scenic paths for cycling, running, and in-line skating. It is a key link in Montreal's bike network, providing a flat and paved route away from car traffic.

Water Activities: During the summer navigation season (mid-May to mid-October), visitors can rent kayaks, canoes, or swan-shaped pedal boats. You can also take guided boat tours with operators like Le Petit Navire to learn about the canal's five locks.

Atwater Market Access: The canal path passes directly by the iconic Atwater Market, making it a perfect spot to stop for fresh local food, a picnic on the canal banks, or a visit to the floating Canal Lounge cafe.
Tips and Key Information

While the canal ice itself is strictly off-limits for safety reasons, a groomed winter trail is maintained along the banks for walking and snowshoeing, offering a quiet perspective of the snow-covered industrial landscape.
Multiple Metro stations provide easy access to different points along the canal, including Place-d'Armes (East end), Lionel-Groulx/Charlevoix (Atwater area), and Angrignon (West end).

Unlike many city parks, alcohol consumption is permitted only with a meal in designated areas. Barbecues are generally prohibited on the grounds of the historic site to protect the heritage environment.
places.note: Note that swimming and magnet fishing are strictly prohibited. If you are cycling, be mindful that the path can become very crowded on sunny weekends, so keep a moderate speed.

places.name: 5. Mont Royal Chalet
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/mount-royal-chalet-gm835881854-135937003

The Mount Royal Chalet is a landmark 1932 heritage building perched atop Mount Royal. It is most famous for its location adjacent to the Kondiaronk Belvedere, offering what is arguably the most iconic and sweeping panoramic view of Montreal's downtown skyscrapers, the St. Lawrence River, and the hills of the South Shore.
What to See and Do

Historic Architecture: The stone chalet features a grand interior with high ceilings and impressive paintings that depict various stages of Montreal's history, providing a regal resting spot for hikers.
Belvedere: Just outside the chalet’s front doors, this massive semicircular terrace is a favorite for photographers, sunrise seekers, and anyone looking to capture the classic shot of the city.
A Scenic Reward: Since no cars are allowed on the road immediately leading to the chalet, reaching it feels like a rewarding journey, whether you take the woodland stairs or the winding Olmsted path.
Tips and Key Information

You can take the 11 Bus to the Camillien-Houde lookout and walk about 10 minutes, or for a more active route, climb the famous Staircase to Heaven (over 250 steps) starting near the corner of Peel and Pine Avenue.
The chalet interior is typically open daily from 10:00 AM to 5:00 or 6:00 PM, though the Belvedere and the surrounding park trails remain accessible from 6:00 AM to midnight.
Inside the chalet, you'll find public restrooms and a small snack bar/vending area, making it an essential pitstop during a day of exploring the park.
For the best lighting on the skyline, visit in the late afternoon or at sunset when the sun is behind you, illuminating the downtown glass towers in a golden hue.

places.name: 6. Olympic Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/olympic-stadium-in-montreal-gm458565687-16232884

The Montreal Olympic Park is a colossal architectural and cultural hub built for the 1976 Summer Games. Today, it stands as one of the city's most recognizable symbols, blending high-performance sports facilities with a vast array of tourist attractions and public event spaces.
What to See and Do

Olympic Stadium: Known for its striking Big O shape, this is the largest stadium in Canada by seating capacity. While it no longer hosts a permanent sports team, it is a major venue for massive concerts, monster truck shows, and trade fairs.

Montreal Tower: Leaning at a 45-degree angle, this is the tallest inclined tower in the world. Visitors can typically ride a glass-encased funicular up the spine of the tower to an observation deck that offers breathtaking, 80-kilometer views of the city and the Laurentian mountains.

Esplanade: This massive outdoor space has been transformed into a vibrant community hub. During the summer, it hosts Les Premiers Vendredis (Canada's largest food truck gathering), while the winter months feature an outdoor skating rink and village.
Skateboarding Mecca: The park is home to a world-famous skatepark area integrated into the concrete architecture, which has become a legendary spot for local and international skaters.
Tips and Key Information
The park is serviced by two Metro stations on the Green Line: Viau (closest to the Biodome and Planetarium) and Pie-IX (closest to the Stadium and Tower).

The Olympic Stadium and Tower are currently undergoing significant long-term renovations. It is essential to check the official website before visiting to see if the Tower observatory is open or if tours of the stadium interior are being offered.

The Olympic Park is part of the Space for Life (Espace pour la vie) district. You are within walking distance of the Montreal Biodome, the Botanical Garden, and the Planetarium, making it easy to spend an entire day in the area.
There are several large underground parking lots (P1 through P5), but they can be expensive. If there is a major event at the stadium, these lots fill up hours in advance.

places.name: 7. Mount Royal Summit
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/skyline-of-montreal-in-canada-gm1497434257-519801190

The Mount Royal Summit offers stunning panoramic views of Montreal, making it one of the city's most beloved outdoor spots. As the highest point in the city, it provides a breathtaking perspective of the skyline, the St. Lawrence River, and the surrounding areas.
What to See and Do

Summit Cross: A short walk from the chalet leads you to the Mount Royal Cross, an illuminated 31-meter steel structure that has stood as a symbol of the city since 1924, commemorating a vow made by the city's founder.

Kondiaronk Belvedere: This massive semicircular plaza directly in front of the summit chalet offers the most famous postcard view of the Montreal skyline, looking out over the downtown core toward the St. Lawrence River.

Olmsted Path: The summit is the focal point of a wide, gravel trail designed by Frederick Law Olmsted (who also designed New York's Central Park); it winds gently up the mountain, making the peak accessible to strollers, cyclists, and runners.
Tips and Key Information
To avoid the steep climb, take Bus 11 from the Mont-Royal Metro station; it will drop you off at the Remembrance Road parking lot, leaving just a short, flat walk to the summit.

For those seeking a workout, the most direct pedestrian route is the series of wooden stairs starting at the end of Peel Street; there are over 250 steps, but they lead you directly to the spectacular lookout.

The summit chalet provides a climate-controlled space with public restrooms, water fountains, and a small counter for snacks, which is particularly helpful during the humid summer or freezing winter months.
In the winter, the area near the summit transforms into a hub for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, with rentals available at the nearby Beaver Lake pavilion.

places.name: 8. Parc des Rapides
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-wild-river-gm1501846685-522567127

Rapids Park (Parc des Rapides) is a hidden gem located in the LaSalle borough, offering a front-row seat to the powerful Lachine Rapids. This 30-hectare waterfront park is a sanctuary for nature lovers and birdwatchers, providing a peaceful contrast to the city's more urban green spaces.
What to See and Do
Lachine Rapids: The park offers several lookout points where you can witness the raw power of the St. Lawrence River's rapids, which are a designated migratory bird sanctuary.
Birdwatching: It is one of the best spots in Montreal to see various species of herons, ducks, and even the occasional bald eagle, especially during migration seasons.
Outdoor Activities: The park features well-maintained paths for walking and cycling in the summer, which transform into scenic trails for cross-country skiing during the winter months.
Vague de bise: From the shore, you can often spot daring river surfers taking on the eternal wave created by the rushing water, a unique local spectacle.
Tips and Key Information

The easiest way to reach the park by public transit is to take the Green Line Metro to Angrignon station and then transfer to the 110 or 112 bus, which drops you off near the park entrance on LaSalle Boulevard.
The park is generally open daily from 7:00 AM to 9:00 PM.

Bring a zoom lens if you are interested in bird photography, as many of the herons nest on the small islands just offshore. The golden hour before sunset is particularly beautiful here as the light hits the rushing water.
This park is much quieter than Mount Royal or Parc Jean-Drapeau, making it ideal for a peaceful retreat or a contemplative walk along the river.

places.name: 9. Atwater Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/exterior-view-of-atwater-market-building-and-its-clock-tower-gm1165690004-320833581

Established in 1933, Marché Atwater is one of Montreal’s most iconic public markets, housed in a striking Art Deco building featuring a prominent clock tower. Located right along the Lachine Canal, it is a favorite for both locals and tourists looking for high-quality gourmet products and a lively community atmosphere.
What to See and Do

Gourmet Specialities: The market is renowned for its high-end butchers, specialty cheese shops (fromageries), and artisanal bakeries. Reviewers often highlight the selection of unique olive oils, spices, and locally produced maple products.
