Seasonal Highlights: During the summer, the outdoor stalls overflow with fresh Quebec produce and vibrant flowers. In the winter, the market transforms into a festive destination, often hosting a popular Christmas market with artisanal crafts and holiday treats.

Dining and Atmosphere: Beyond grocery shopping, there are several ready-to-eat stalls offering everything from Satay Brothers’ famous Singaporean street food to classic French pastries. Many visitors enjoy grabbing a meal and heading to the nearby canal banks for a picnic.

Architectural Charm: The building itself is an architectural landmark in the Saint-Henri neighborhood. Even if you aren't shopping, the interior's historic layout and the bustling energy of the vendors make it a great place to soak in the local culture.
Tips and Key Information
The market is just a short walk from the Lionel-Groulx Metro station (Green and Orange lines). If you are cycling, the Lachine Canal bike path leads you directly to its doorstep.
To avoid the heaviest crowds, try visiting on a weekday morning. Saturday mornings are the busiest, but they also offer the most vibrant atmosphere with the full range of outdoor vendors.
There is a dedicated parking lot, but it fills up very quickly on weekends. Street parking in the surrounding neighborhood is also an option but can be competitive.
Its location makes it a perfect starting or ending point for a walk along the Lachine Canal National Historic Site.

places.name: 1. Bonsecours Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/old-montreal-restaurant-patios-canada-gm2244042185-658144884

Inaugurated in 1847, the Bonsecours Market is an architectural masterpiece of the neoclassical style, easily recognized by its grand silver dome. Once serving as Montreal's main public market and even as the temporary Parliament of United Canada, it is now a prestigious multi-purpose center housing high-end boutiques and exhibition spaces.
What to See and Do

Quebec Craftsmanship: The market is a premier destination for discovering Made in Quebec products. Visitors often highlight the unique selection of designer clothing, jewelry, and artisanal home decor found in its various boutiques.
Art Galleries: Several galleries within the building showcase local art, providing a sophisticated cultural experience alongside your shopping.
Dining with a View: The market features terraces and restaurants where you can enjoy a meal while overlooking the historic cobblestone streets of Old Montreal.
Grand Architecture: Even if you aren't shopping, the interior's vaulted ceilings and historic stonework make it a worthwhile stop for architecture enthusiasts.
Tips and Key Information

The market is located on Saint-Paul Street East, just a short walk from the Champ-de-Mars Metro station (Orange Line). Its location near the Old Port makes it an easy addition to a day of historic sightseeing.
The boutiques generally operate daily from 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM, with extended hours until 7:00 PM on Thursdays, Fridays, and Saturdays.
The large hall on the upper floor frequently hosts major events, such as the World Press Photo exhibition or artisanal craft fairs, so it is worth checking the event calendar before your visit.
Since it is located right next to the Notre-Dame-de-Bon-Secours Chapel, it is convenient to visit both sites in one go.

places.name: 2. Underground City (Réso)https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/underground-city-shopping-mall-in-downtown-area-at-niveau-metro-in-quebec-region-gm812782288-131475705
body: The Montréal Underground City, locally known as RÉSO, is one of the largest subterranean pedestrian networks in the world. Spanning over 32 kilometers, this climate-controlled labyrinth connects shopping malls, office towers, hotels, and transit hubs, making it a vital part of Montreal life—especially during the cold winter months.
What to See and Do

Shopping and Dining Hub: The network links several major shopping complexes, including Eaton Centre, Place Montréal Trust, and Complexe Desjardins, offering hundreds of stores and a vast array of food courts ranging from quick bites to upscale dining.

Cultural and Transit Connectivity: Beyond retail, it provides indoor access to major cultural venues like Place des Arts, several universities, and over 10 Metro stations, allowing you to traverse much of the downtown core without ever stepping outside.

Public Art and Architecture: As you walk through the various segments, you'll encounter segments of the Berlin Wall, impressive stained glass murals, and modern architectural features that change as you move between different building segments.
Tips and Key Information

Look for the RÉSO logo (a distinctive white R on a blue background) at building entrances and Metro stations. Using a digital map or the Montréal souterrain app is highly recommended, as the tunnels can be confusing for first-time visitors.

While the tunnels generally follow the operating hours of the Metro (roughly 5:30 AM to 1:00 AM), many of the shops and food courts within the network close earlier, typically around 6:00 PM or 9:00 PM depending on the day.

Great entry points include the McGill Metro station for shopping or Place-des-Arts for culture. Entering through the Central Station (Gare Centrale) is also a popular choice for those arriving by train.

Most of the modern segments are fully accessible with elevators and ramps, but some older sections may have narrow corridors or stairs. It is best to plan your route through major malls for the most reliable accessibility.

places.name: 3. Rue Ste.-Catherine
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/people-walking-on-sainte-catherine-street-in-montreals-gay-village-in-quebec-region-gm817672962-132273829

Spanning over 11 kilometers, Rue Sainte Catherine is the primary commercial artery of Montreal and one of the longest shopping streets in North America. It serves as the backbone of the downtown core, connecting major department stores, entertainment venues, and diverse neighborhoods.
What to See and Do

Shopping Destination: The street is home to flagship locations of major retailers like La Maison Simons, Hudson's Bay, and various international brands, alongside several interconnected shopping malls like the Eaton Centre.

Entertainment and Festivals: A significant portion of the street passes through the Quartier des Spectacles, where it often becomes pedestrian-only during the summer to host massive festivals like the Montreal International Jazz Festival and Just for Laughs.
Village: Toward the eastern end, the street enters the Gay Village, marked by vibrant public art installations and a lively atmosphere of terraces and nightlife.

Underground Connectivity: Many points along the street provide direct access to the Underground City (RÉSO), allowing shoppers to move between stores and Metro stations without facing the outdoor elements.
Tips and Key Information
During the summer months, large sections of the street (particularly in the Village and the Quartier des Spectacles) are closed to car traffic, creating a festive, walkable environment.
Because the street is so long, it is serviced by numerous Metro stations on the Green Line, including Atwater, Guy-Concordia, Peel, McGill, Place-des-Arts, Saint-Laurent, and Beaudry.
If you need a break from shopping, the steps of Saint James United Church or the many terraces in the Village offer excellent vantage points to soak in the city's diverse energy.

As a major artery, there are often ongoing revitalization projects along different segments of the street; it’s helpful to check for local signage regarding detours if you are driving or taking the bus.

places.name: 4. Plateau Mont-Royal
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/plateau-mont-royal-montreal-canada-gm1225094189-360479643

The Plateau-Mont-Royal is arguably Montreal’s most colorful and creative borough. This densely populated neighborhood is famous for its distinct architectural identity—specifically its iconic exterior spiral staircases—and its vibrant, bohemian atmosphere that has long attracted artists, students, and young professionals.
What to See and Do
Architectural Charm: The neighborhood is a photographer's dream, known for rows of Victorian-style houses with brightly painted doors and winding outdoor staircases designed to save interior space.
Artistic Soul: You’ll find some of the city's most impressive murals and street art here, particularly in the alleys and along Saint Laurent Boulevard, which hosts the annual MURAL Festival.
Culinary Institutions: The Plateau is home to legendary food spots, including Schwartz's Deli for world-famous smoked meat and St-Viateur Bagel for traditional Montreal-style bagels.
Green Corridors: While it is an urban district, it contains major green spaces like La Fontaine Park, providing a natural balance to the dense residential streets.
Tips and Key Information

The area is primarily served by the Orange Line Metro. Mont-Royal Station puts you right in the center of the action, while Sherbrooke and Laurier stations offer access to the southern and northern edges.
During the summer, major arteries like Avenue du Mont-Royal often become pedestrian-only zones, filled with public seating, outdoor art, and expanded terraces for dining.
Avoid the big-box stores and head to Saint-Denis Street for local boutiques, bookstores, and specialty craft shops that define the neighborhood's independent spirit.
If you are driving, be extremely cautious. The Plateau has some of the city's most complex parking permit regulations; it is generally much easier to use public transit or a BIXI bike.

places.name: 5. Place Jacques-Cartier
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/place-jacque-cartier-square-montreal-canada-gm1273493289-375349253

Place Jacques-Cartier is a historic square that serves as the heart and soul of Old Montreal. Sloping gently from City Hall down to the Old Port, this lively pedestrian plaza is the primary gathering spot for visitors, known for its vibrant atmosphere, street performers, and European-inspired charm.
What to See and Do

Street Performance and Art: During the summer, the square becomes a stage for caricaturists, musicians, and buskers, creating a festive environment that reviewers frequently describe as the quintessential Old Montreal experience.

Dining and Terraces: Both sides of the square are lined with historic buildings housing restaurants and cafes that spill out onto large outdoor terraces, offering some of the best people-watching spots in the city.
Historic Monuments: At the top of the square stands the Nelson Column, erected in 1809, which is the oldest public monument in Montreal and a significant landmark of the city's British history.
Flower Stalls: Keeping with its 19th-century traditions as a public market, the square is often decorated with seasonal flower displays and traditional stalls that add to its romantic aesthetic.
Tips and Key Information
In the peak summer months, the square and many surrounding streets are closed to vehicles, making it exceptionally walkable and safe for families.
It is conveniently located between the Champ-de-Mars and Place-d'Armes Metro stations (Orange Line).
While summer is peak season, the square is beautifully illuminated during the winter holidays and serves as a central hub for New Year's Eve celebrations.

Because it is a major tourist destination, the restaurants directly on the square can be more expensive than those tucked away on side streets; it’s a great place for a drink, but you might find more local dining gems a few blocks away.

places.name: 6. Little Italy
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/montreals-little-italy-saint-laurent-street-springtime-scene-gm1039202640-278196773

Little Italy (Petite Italie) is a charming and historic neighborhood in Montreal, centered around Saint Laurent Boulevard and Saint Zotique Street. It is the heart of the city's Italian community, offering a warm, village-like atmosphere filled with traditional cafes, trattorias, and specialty grocery stores. While the neighborhood has modernized over the years, it retains a deep sense of heritage and is home to some of the most authentic culinary experiences in Montreal.
What to See and Do

Jean-Talon Market: Located at the edge of the neighborhood, this is one of North America's largest open-air markets, offering an incredible selection of fresh produce, local cheeses, and artisanal products.
Traditional Coffee Culture: The area is famous for its long-standing coffee shops, like Caffè Italia, where locals have gathered for decades to enjoy traditional espresso and talk soccer.

Church of the Madonna della Difesa: This stunning 1918 church is a National Historic Site of Canada, famous for its beautiful brick architecture and a unique fresco that includes a depiction of Benito Mussolini.

Italian Gastronomy: From high-end dining to casual pizzerias, the neighborhood is packed with authentic eateries. Reviewers often recommend visiting for the homemade pasta and traditional pastries like cannoli.
Tips and Key Information
The neighborhood is easily accessible via the Jean-Talon or Beaubien Metro stations (Orange and Blue lines).
Little Italy is best explored on foot. Start at the Jean-Talon Market and wander south along Saint Laurent Boulevard to soak in the local sights and smells.
During the warmer months, sections of the neighborhood often host street festivals and pedestrian-only zones, perfect for enjoying a gelato while you walk.
Beyond food, the area features specialized Italian boutiques and import shops where you can find high-quality kitchenware and fashion.

places.name: 7. Chinatown
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/people-beaides-montreal-chinatown-gate-gm1384344767-443717204

Montreal’s Chinatown offers visitors a vibrant blend of rich cultural heritage and modern urban charm. Located in the heart of the city, this bustling neighborhood is home to a variety of restaurants, shops, and temples that reflect the deep influence of Chinese culture in Montreal.
What to See and Do
Pedestrian Paifang Entrances: The neighborhood is marked by four impressive traditional gates that define its boundaries, making it a highly photogenic and walkable area.

A Culinary Destination: The district is world-renowned for its diverse food scene, ranging from legendary hand-pulled noodle shops and dim sum halls to modern bubble tea spots and Dragon’s Beard candy stalls.
Cultural Hub: Beyond dining, you’ll find specialized Asian grocery stores, herbal medicine shops, and gift boutiques selling traditional crafts and unique souvenirs.
Place de la Paix: This nearby open space often hosts community events and is a favorite spot for skateboarders and people-watching on the edge of the district.
Tips and Key Information
The area is perfectly situated between the Place-d'Armes and Saint-Laurent Metro stations (Orange and Green lines), making it extremely easy to access from almost anywhere in the city.
If you plan on having dim sum, many popular spots get very crowded on weekend mornings, so arriving before 11:00 AM is highly recommended to avoid long waits.
For a casual experience, try a walking meal by grabbing a steamed bun from a bakery and watching the Dragon's Beard candy being made by hand at a street-side stall.
Take the time to explore the smaller side streets and hidden courtyard plazas where you’ll often find quieter tea shops and local community centers.

places.name: 8. Crescent Street
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/crescent-street-in-montreal-gm477707718-67322343

Located in the heart of downtown, Rue Crescent is one of Montreal's most famous nightlife and dining strips. While only three blocks long between Sherbrooke and René-Lévesque, it is packed with Victorian architecture housing upscale boutiques, lively pubs, and fine-dining restaurants, making it a major hub for the city's festive energy.
What to See and Do
Formula 1 Festival: During the Grand Prix weekend in June, the street is closed to traffic for a massive festival featuring luxury car displays, live music, and outdoor bars.
Mural Landmark: The street features the iconic Leonard Cohen Mural (technically overlooking Crescent from a nearby building), a massive tribute to the legendary Montreal poet and singer.
Pub Culture: It is home to long-standing Montreal institutions where people go for live music, happy hours, and classic pub fare.
Architectural Beauty: The northern block near Sherbrooke Street retains its elegant 19th-century charm, housing high-end art galleries and fashion boutiques.
Recommended Spots on Crescent Street

Hurley's Irish Pub is a legendary establishment known for its cozy, wood-paneled interior and its status as a cornerstone of the city's Irish community. It is widely considered the gold standard for an Irish pub experience in the city. It holds the title for selling the most Guinness in Montreal, ensuring fresh kegs are tapped daily.
Offers an extensive selection of single malts and beers on tap.
Regularly hosts live traditional Irish and folk music.
Features a popular outdoor patio for people-watching during the summer.
Sir Winston Churchill Pub is a landmark three-level venue that has been at the center of Crescent Street’s social scene since 1967.
Functions as a pub, lounge, and terrace, catering to different moods throughout the day.
Known for a bustling happy hour and late-night DJs on the upper floors.
The large streetside terrace is a prime spot for soaking in the neighborhood's energy.
Burger Bar Crescent is a collegial hangout that offers a more modern dining experience with creative, over-the-top comfort food.
Specializes in adventurous, stacked burgers and poutine-inspired sides.
Offers a curated list of cocktails and pitchers, making it popular for groups.
Provides a relaxed alternative to the more traditional pubs nearby.

places.name: 9. Quartier des Spectacles
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/montreal-by-night-the-quartier-des-spectacles-of-montreal-qu%C3%A9bec-canada-gm1359563786-432873054

The Quartier des Spectacles is the cultural heart of Montreal, a square-kilometer district dedicated to the arts, performance, and year-round festivities. It is world-renowned for hosting some of the globe's largest festivals, including the Montreal International Jazz Festival and Just for Laughs, transforming its streets into massive open-air stages.
What to See and Do

Place des Festivals: This massive public plaza serves as the district's focal point, featuring the country's largest interactive fountain with 235 jets and sophisticated lighting systems that animate the space during major events.

Luminous Pathway: At night, the district is unified by a unique lighting design—a red Luminous Pathway of dots on the sidewalk—that guides visitors to the more than 80 cultural venues and performance spaces in the area.

Venue Density: The neighborhood boasts the highest concentration and diversity of cultural venues in North America, including the ultra-modern Maison Symphonique and the historic Théâtre du Nouveau Monde.

Winter Programming: Far from being a summer-only destination, the area hosts Luminothérapie in the winter, featuring interactive art installations like giant illuminated seesaws and immersive light projections on building facades.
Tips and Key Information
Most of the district's core streets are closed to vehicles during the summer festival season, making it one of the most walkable and family-friendly areas in the city.
The district is perfectly served by the Place-des-Arts and Saint-Laurent Metro stations (Green Line), which drop you directly into the heart of the festival action.

Most of the outdoor plaza spaces and modern venues are fully accessible, though some older, independent theaters may have limited elevator access; it’s best to check with specific venues ahead of time.
While there are upscale options, the area is also famous for its vibrant food truck culture that takes over the Esplanade during the warmer months.

places.name: 10. Montreal Insectarium
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/montreal-insectarium-in-winter-gm1138018344-303666618

The Montreal Insectarium has recently completed a massive $38 million renovation known as Metamorphosis, transforming it into one of the most innovative and immersive natural science museums in the world. Rather than just looking at bugs in boxes, the experience is designed to make you feel like an insect, utilizing cutting-edge architecture and sensory storytelling to dissolve the boundaries between humans and the natural world.
What to See and Do
The museum is organized as a "choreographed route" that moves visitors through different emotional and sensory states.

The Alcoves: This underground, labyrinthine space is designed to disorient your human senses. You’ll walk through tunnels with vibrating floors, squeeze through tight passages, and see flickering screens that mimic a fly's compound vision.

The Dome: A dramatic, 10-meter-high hall that erupts from the earth like a planted mound. Inside, over 3,000 preserved specimens are displayed in a massive chromatic frieze that highlights the incredible beauty and diversity of insect life.

The Grand Vivarium: The highlight for many, this is a massive, light-filled greenhouse where thousands of butterflies and other insects roam free among lush vegetation. It is the first space of its kind in North America where so many species live in semi-containment with visitors.
Tête-à-Tête Gallery: This area features six bespoke viewing boxes that allow for extreme close-up encounters with live insects, providing a literal face-to-face perspective.
Tips and Key Information
The renovation has not only updated the exhibits but also modernized the entire facility with a focus on sustainability and accessibility.

The building itself is a feat of bioclimatic design, utilizing geothermal energy, natural ventilation through its sawtooth roof, and extensive glass walls to blend seamlessly with the surrounding botanical gardens.
Visitors are strongly encouraged to download the free mobile app, which acts as a real-time identification tool and provides exclusive digital content as you move through the galleries.
The entire circuit is wheelchair accessible, though some of the alcove experiences involve narrower paths; staff can provide guidance for those with claustrophobia or mobility concerns.
Because the museum is highly immersive and popular, it is strongly recommended to reserve timed tickets online in advance to ensure entry.

places.name: 11. Casino de Montreal
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-casino-de-montreal-owned-by-the-provincial-government-helps-attract-tourists-to-gm1475579842-505038519

The Casino de Montréal is Canada's largest casino, uniquely housed within two iconic pavilions from the 1967 World Exposition (Expo 67). Located on Notre Dame Island in Jean-Drapeau Park, it offers a distinct architectural experience with its unconventional numerous windows and low ceilings, set against a backdrop of river views. The casino is a major entertainment hub, featuring over 500,000 square feet of floor space dedicated to a wide variety of games and live performances.
What to See and Do
Gaming Variety: It boasts more than 3,000 slot machines and over 80 gaming tables, including classics like Blackjack, Roulette, and Baccarat.
The Zone: An interactive and immersive area that features electronic gaming tables with lower minimum bets and a festive atmosphere hosted by live presenters.
ARcade by Moment Factory: A unique, non-gambling space that blends multimedia and video game technology into life-size augmented reality games for teams.
Cabaret du Casino: A state-of-the-art multi-purpose venue with 3D surround sound that hosts comedy shows, live concerts, and tribute acts.
Le Montréal: A seafood and grill restaurant on the fifth floor known for its market-fresh products and stunning views of the city skyline.
Pavillon 67: Named in honor of Expo 67, this gourmet buffet is celebrated for its wide selection of international dishes and extensive dessert table.
L’Instant: A deli-style option perfect for those looking for a quick meal, offering classic sandwiches and pasta.

Trio of Bars: The Dame de Cœur and Roi de Pique are ideal for relaxed drinks, while the Valet bar serves as the entertainment nerve center with a three-story multimedia wall and a central dance floor.
Tips and Key Information
All visitors must be 18 years of age or older. A government-issued photo ID is strictly required for admission to the gaming floors, restaurants, and the Cabaret.
The dress code is generally described as casual or appropriate. While not overly formal, clothing depicting violence or associated with violent groups is prohibited.
Backpacks, motorcycle helmets, and umbrellas are not permitted inside the casino. A coat check service is available at the Annex for these items.
The entire complex is a smoke-free environment, which includes the prohibition of vaping and cannabis use both inside and outside the establishment.

places.name: Saysutshun (Newcastle Island Marine Provincial Park)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/tree-lined-pier-at-harbor-on-saysutshun-with-views-of-nanaimo-bc-canada-gm1748543426-543556109

Saysutshun (Newcastle Island Marine) Park is a unique island park located just a few hundred meters off the Nanaimo harbor. Accessible only by water, this marine provincial park is rich in Snuneymuxw First Nation history and offers a tranquil escape from the city with its varied landscapes of sandstone cliffs and forested trails.
What to See and Do

Snuneymuxw Cultural Experience: Visitors can explore the island's deep Indigenous roots through interpretive signage or by booking cultural tours. The island remains a place of spiritual and historical significance to the Snuneymuxw people.

Trail Network: The island features an extensive 22-kilometer trail system. The 6-kilometer perimeter trail is particularly popular, offering consistent views of the Salish Sea, the Coastal Mountains, and Nanaimo's waterfront.

Beaches and Tide Pools: Kanaka Bay and Maffeo Sutton Park (across the water) flank the island's access, but once on-site, small sandstone bays provide excellent opportunities for beachcombing and examining intertidal life.

Historic Landmarks: Look for remnants of the island's colonial history, including sites of former coal mines and the sandstone quarries that provided stone for landmark buildings in Victoria and San Francisco.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/trail-running-through-a-coastal-forest-on-saysutshun-near-nanaimo-bc-canada-gm1748540046-54355
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/view-of-sandstone-beach-at-saysutshun-near-nanaimo-bc-canada-gm1748537181-543556071
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/newcastle-island-saysutshun-marine-park-nanaimo-bc-gm2227461798-643331467
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/scenic-view-of-sea-against-sky-gm2182430253-601377218
Tips and Key Information

The primary access is via a small orange foot ferry that departs from Maffeo Sutton Park. During the summer, it runs roughly every 30 minutes, but it is always best to check the seasonal schedule at the Saysutshun Newcastle Island Ferry Terminal.

The island is a sanctuary for local wildlife, including a rare population of golden raccoons. Dogs are welcome but must remain on a leash at all times to protect these species and the natural habitat.

You can bring your own bicycle on the ferry for an additional fee or rent one on the island during the peak season. It is also a favorite destination for kayakers paddling from the downtown boat basin.
Accessible via ferry from the Harbourfront Walkway in downtown Nanaimo.
The island is well-equipped with a seasonal restaurant (the Dinghy Dock Pub is nearby but on its own dock), public washrooms, a large playground, and a designated campground.
While entry to the provincial park is free, there is a round-trip fee for the foot ferry. If you arrive by private boat, mooring and docking fees apply.

places.name: Harbourfront Walkway
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/harbourfront-walkway-in-nanaimo-vancouver-island-canada-gm1394037822-449668418

The Harbourfront Walkway is a scenic, multi-use pathway that stretches along Nanaimo's shoreline, offering a seamless connection between the city’s downtown core and its vibrant marine environment. This paved promenade is a favorite for both residents and visitors, providing constant views of the Nanaimo Harbour, Saysutshun (Newcastle Island Marine) Park, and the constant activity of seaplanes and ferries.
What to See and Do
The walkway serves as a central artery for exploring the waterfront, passing through several key landmarks and offering numerous spots to stop and enjoy the maritime atmosphere.
Scenic Strolling: The path is well-maintained and relatively flat, making it ideal for a leisurely walk, morning run, or sunset stroll while watching the boats navigate the harbor basin.

Park Connections: It directly connects to Maffeo Sutton Park, the city’s signature waterfront park, which features a large playground, public art, and the ferry terminal for Saysutshun (Newcastle Island).

Public Art and History: Along the route, you will find various interpretive signs detailing the area's coal mining and maritime heritage, along with statues and installations that celebrate local culture.

Dining and Shopping: The promenade is lined with several waterfront eateries and boutique shops, particularly near the Harbourfront Walkway's southern end, where you can grab a coffee or a famous Nanaimo Bar.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/downtown-nanaimo-park-waterfront-british-columbia-canada-gm2259884122-672796635
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/nanaimos-harbour-gm1161658574-318381594
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/nanaimo-harbour-gm1063964134-284462923
Tips and Key Information
Find a bench near the seaplane terminals to watch the frequent take-offs and landings; it is one of the most iconic sights of the Nanaimo waterfront.
The walkway faces east, but the evening light hitting the mountains across the Salish Sea and the glow over the harbor make it a premier location for late-day photography.
Parking is available at Maffeo Sutton Park or in various downtown parkades. Using the park as a starting point allows for a convenient loop through the downtown shops and back along the water.
Access points are available all along the downtown Nanaimo waterfront, from the cruise ship terminal to Maffeo Sutton Park.
The entire length of the main walkway is paved and wide enough to comfortably accommodate wheelchairs, strollers, and bicycles.
The walkway is a public space and is open 24 hours a day, though individual businesses along the path have their own operating hours.

places.name: Whale watching and marine tours
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/humpback-whale-fin-vancouver-island-gm2148532206-569678908

Nanaimo is a premier departure point for exploring the nutrient-rich waters of the Salish Sea, where sightings of humpback whales, orcas, and sea lions are highly frequent. Most tours operate out of the downtown boat basin, providing immediate access to the diverse marine ecosystems surrounding the local islands.
What to See and Do

Whale Sightings: Tours primarily focus on spotting Humpback whales and Bigg’s (Transient) Orcas. Many operators offer a sightings guarantee, providing a complimentary return trip if whales are not spotted during your excursion.
Diverse Marine Wildlife: Beyond whales, you are likely to see Steller and California sea lions, harbor seals, porpoises, and a variety of seabirds like bald eagles and cormorants.
Geological Formations: Several tours include scenic detours to view the striking sandstone galleries on Gabriola Island or the rugged coastline of Five Finger Island.
Educational Naturalism: Most excursions feature certified marine naturalists who provide live commentary on animal behavior, conservation efforts, and the complex history of the local ecosystem.
Recommended Operators

Vancouver Island Whale Watch is centrally located on the Harbourfront Walkway and is highly rated for its professional naturalists and variety of vessel types. They offer both open-air zodiacs for a high-speed, immersive experience and semi-covered boats for those seeking more protection from the elements.

Island Marine Adventures operates from Stewart Avenue and offers a more intimate, personalized experience with a focus on small-group tours. As a smaller operator, they focus on flexible itineraries that can be adjusted based on real-time wildlife reports and passenger interests. Their trips often combine whale watching with close-up views of sea lion colonies and local landmarks like the Saysutshun (Newcastle Island Marine) Park shoreline.

Reel Time Fishing Charters & Marine Tours provides a broader range of marine experiences, including specialized wildlife photography tours and combined fishing/sightseeing excursions. They are a top choice for those looking for private rentals or tours tailored to specific interests like birdwatching or sunset photography. The captains are known for their deep knowledge of the local currents and secret spots where wildlife frequently gathers away from the larger tour groups.
Tips and Key Information

Even on warm summer days, the temperature on the water is significantly cooler due to the wind and spray. Most companies provide thermal cruisers or survival suits, but bringing your own gloves and a toque is recommended.
Summer is peak season for both whales and tourists; it is advisable to book at least a week in advance to secure your preferred time and vessel type.
Bring a camera with a decent zoom lens, but remember to protect it from potential salt spray with a dry bag or a simple plastic cover.
Most tours depart from the Downtown Boat Basin or along Stewart Avenue in North Nanaimo.
Excursions typically last between 3 and 5 hours, depending on how far the whales have traveled from the harbor.
While many semi-covered boats can accommodate passengers with limited mobility, high-speed zodiacs are generally not recommended for those with back or neck issues or for pregnant women.

places.name: Fishing
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/vancouver-island-british-columbia-gm1245628468-363092312

Nanaimo is a premier destination for anglers, offering a diverse range of opportunities that span from calm freshwater lakes to the productive saltwaters of the Salish Sea. Whether you are looking for a casual afternoon at a local dock or a deep-sea excursion, the region provides year-round action.
What to See and Do

Saltwater Fishing: The waters around Departure Bay and the Five Finger Island area are renowned for Chinook (King) and Coho (Silver) salmon. In the winter months, anglers often target winter springs (resident Chinook) which provide consistent activity when migratory runs are lower.

Freshwater Lakes: Nanaimo features several urban lakes that are regularly stocked by the Freshwater Fisheries Society of BC. Westwood Lake and Colliery Dam Park are top choices for catching Rainbow and Cutthroat trout, offering easy shore access and dedicated fishing piers.

Crabbing and Prawning: The Maffeo Sutton Park fishing pier is a popular community spot for dropping crab traps to catch Dungeness and Red Rock crabs. For those with boats, the deeper waters outside the harbor are productive for spot prawns.
River Fishing: During the autumn months, the Nanaimo River becomes a hub for the annual salmon return. Anglers gather to target Pink and Chum salmon as they move upstream to spawn.
Tips for the Best Experience

Ensure you have the correct license before heading out. A Non-Tidal (Freshwater) License is required for lakes and rivers, while a Tidal (Saltwater) License with a Salmon Conservation Stamp is necessary for the ocean. Both can be purchased online via the provincial and federal government portals.

Visit shops like Gone Fishin' or Cabela's in Nanaimo to get up-to-date reports on which lures are working and where the fish are biting. Local expertise is invaluable for understanding current depths and water conditions.

If you are new to the area or looking for a high-success outing, several professional charters operate out of the downtown boat basin. They provide all necessary gear, bait, and knowledge of the hot spots along the coast.

Fishing regulations in BC are strictly enforced. Always check the current Fisheries and Oceans Canada (DFO) website for saltwater openings and size limits, or the BC Freshwater Fishing Regulations for lake and river rules.
Practice catch-and-release when required and be mindful of Rockfish Conservation Areas (RCAs) in the Salish Sea where fishing is prohibited to protect vulnerable species.
Seasons:
Salmon (Ocean): Year-round, peaking May to September.
Trout (Lakes): Best in Spring (April–June) and Fall (September–November).
Salmon (River): September to November.

places.name: Kayaking, Boating, and Harbour Activities
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pier-at-departure-bay-in-nanaimo-on-vancouver-island-gm1794151220-547975344

The waters surrounding Nanaimo are a primary draw for outdoor enthusiasts, offering a mix of sheltered harbor paddling, expansive island exploration, and deep-sea adventures. The unique geography of the Nanaimo Harbour and nearby islands creates a diverse marine playground for both motorized and human-powered vessels.
Paddling and Kayaking
The Nanaimo coastline is ideal for kayaking, with the sheltered passage between the downtown core and Saysutshun (Newcastle Island Marine) Park serving as a popular route.

Island Hopping: Kayakers can easily cross the harbor to explore the shoreline of Saysutshun (Newcastle Island) and Protection Island. The waters are generally calm, but paddlers should remain alert for the frequent seaplane and ferry traffic.

Rentals and Tours: Coastal Expressions Drinks & Gear, located near the waterfront, is a key spot for renting kayaks and paddleboards. They often provide introductory tips for navigating the local currents and busy harbor lanes.
Scenic Routes: For a quieter experience, the northern reaches near Pipers Lagoon Park offer rocky outcrops and tidal areas that are perfect for low-impact exploration.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/a-woman-kayaking-around-protection-island-visiting-a-dinghy-dock-restaurant-for-a-gm1271757417-374239473
Boating and Marine Access
As a major island hub, Nanaimo features extensive infrastructure for powerboats, sailboats, and visiting cruisers.

The Boat Basin: The Nanaimo Port Authority manages the central boat basin, providing transient moorage for vessels of various sizes. It is located steps away from downtown restaurants and shops, making it a convenient base for sailors.
Public Boat Launches: For those bringing their own trailers, the Brechin Boat Launch is the primary multi-lane facility. It offers easy access to the Departure Bay area and the northern islands.
Island Moorage: Marine parks like Saysutshun offer mooring buoys and dock space, allowing boaters to stay overnight and enjoy the island's trail networks.
Harbour Excursions and Unique Stops
The harbor is home to several distinctive attractions that are best experienced by water.

Dinghy Dock Pub: Located on Protection Island, the Dinghy Dock Pub & Restaurant is Canada’s only registered floating pub. It is accessible via its own ferry from the downtown boat basin or by private boat.

Seaplane Tours: Witnessing the harbor from above is possible through Harbour Air Seaplanes, which offers scenic flights over the Salish Sea and the Gulf Islands, departing directly from the waterfront terminals.
Whale Watching: Several operators, such as Vancouver Island Whale Watch, depart from the harbor to track orcas, humpbacks, and sea lions in the open waters of the Georgia Strait.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/victoria-vancouver-island-gm1389061165-446489906
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/waterfront-in-nanaimo-vancouver-island-bc-canada-gm1286738442-383157490
Tips and Key Information
The harbor is extremely active. Paddlers must stay within the designated non-motorized lanes and avoid the flight paths of arriving seaplanes.
Conditions in the Salish Sea can change rapidly. Always check the marine forecast for wind and swell before heading outside the sheltered harbor.
When encountering marine mammals, maintain the legally required distance to avoid disturbing the animals in their natural habitat.

places.name: Protection Island
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sailboat-past-protection-island-gm901898872-248809764

Protection Island is a small, primarily residential island located just a few hundred meters across the harbor from downtown Nanaimo. Known for its quirky atmosphere, golf-cart-filled streets, and the fact that it is home to Canada’s only floating pub, it offers a distinct pace of life that feels far removed from the city.
What to See and Do

The Dinghy Dock Pub: This is the island's most famous landmark. The Dinghy Dock Pub & Restaurant is a registered floating vessel permanently moored to the island. It features a family-friendly section, an outdoor patio with harbor views, and even a fishing hole in the floor of the dock.

Island Exploration: With no public cars allowed, the island is best explored on foot or by bicycle. The narrow, tree-lined roads lead past unique island homes and quiet community gardens, offering a peaceful glimpse into island living.

Parks and Beaches: Gallows Point Light Park at the southern tip provides a scenic spot to watch the large BC Ferries navigate the narrow gap into Departure Bay. Nearby, several small community beaches offer quiet spots for beachcombing and watching the sunset over the Nanaimo skyline.

Wildlife Viewing: The island and its surrounding waters are home to a variety of marine life. It is common to see seals hauled out on nearby rocks and a wide array of shorebirds along the intertidal zones.
Tips and Key Information

Access is via a small, privately operated foot ferry that departs regularly from the Nanaimo Boat Basin. The crossing takes about 10 minutes. Be sure to check the current schedule at the dock, as sailings can vary by season.
Since the island is largely a residential community, visitors are encouraged to stay on public roads and paths and to keep noise levels down while exploring the neighborhoods.
For experienced kayakers, the paddle from downtown Nanaimo to Protection Island is a short and rewarding trip, though you must stay vigilant regarding seaplane and ferry traffic in the harbor.
Directly across from downtown Nanaimo; ferry terminal located at 150 Front Street.
The primary facilities are at the Dinghy Dock Pub, which includes a restaurant and washrooms. The island itself has a small library and several public park benches.
Dogs are allowed on the ferry and the island but must be kept on a leash to respect the local residents and wildlife.

places.name: Gabriola Island
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/vancouver-island-british-columbia-gm1245544630-363087861

Gabriola Island, known as the Isle of the Arts, is located just a 20-minute ferry ride from downtown Nanaimo. It is the northernmost of the Gulf Islands and is celebrated for its high density of world-class artists, unique sandstone formations, and rugged coastal scenery.
What to See and Do

The Malaspina Galleries: These spectacular sandstone formations are the island's most iconic natural feature. The ocean has carved a massive, curved overhang into the shoreline cliffs, creating a natural gallery that looks like a frozen stone wave.

Artisan Galleries and Studios: The island is home to over 70 artist studios. Visitors can follow the Yellow Flag studio tour to visit local painters, potters, and weavers in their creative spaces, especially during the annual Thanksgiving Studio Tour.

Beachcombing and Parks: Gabriola Sands Provincial Park (locally known as Twin Beaches) offers two sandy shores facing opposite directions, providing views of both the Salish Sea and the Coastal Mountains.
Petroglyph Exploration: Near the Gabriola Museum, a short trail leads to ancient Snuneymuxw petroglyphs carved into the sandstone, offering a glimpse into the island's deep Indigenous history.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/gabriola-island-sunset-gm1144937093-308000897
Tips and Key Information
The ferry departs from the Nanaimo Harbour Ferry Terminal on Front Street. While frequent, the ferry can be busy on weekends; arriving early is recommended if you are bringing a vehicle.
The island is popular for cycling due to its rolling hills and scenic roads. There is also a community bus service (GERTIE) that connects the ferry terminal with various island hubs.
The Village Core near the ferry terminal has a grocery store, a pharmacy, and several cafes. It is the best place to stock up before heading to the quieter northern or southern ends of the island.
Accessible via BC Ferries from downtown Nanaimo.
The island has multiple public parks with washrooms, a library, and a medical clinic. Most commercial services are concentrated at the north end near the ferry.
While a vehicle is helpful for exploring the full island, many visitors walk onto the ferry and use the community bus or bicycles to get around.

places.name: Pipers Lagoon Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pipers-lagoon-park-in-nanaimo-british-columbia-gm1390921614-447718498

Pipers Lagoon Park is one of Nanaimo’s most scenic waterfront destinations, known for its unique geography that includes a large tidal lagoon, rugged rock formations, and views of the Georgia Strait. It is a favorite spot for beachcombing, photography, and witnessing dramatic coastal sunrises and sunsets.
What to See and Do

Beach and Lagoon Exploration: At low tide, the large lagoon becomes a haven for exploration. Visitors can walk along the sandbar that separates the quiet lagoon from the more active waves of the open ocean.

Scenic Lookouts: A network of well-worn trails leads up onto the rocky headlands. These elevated paths offer panoramic vistas of Shack Island—famous for its historic colorful fishing shacks—and the distant Coast Mountains on the mainland.

Birdwatching: The mix of saltwater marsh and rocky shore attracts a high volume of birdlife. Keep an eye out for bald eagles, blue herons, and various migratory waterfowl that frequent the sheltered waters.
Beachcombing: The shoreline is scattered with driftwood and unique pebbles. It is a popular spot for families to search for sea glass and shells along the tide line.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pipers-lagoon-trail-in-nanaimo-gm1193981664-339812482
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pipers-lagoon-park-in-nanaimo-on-vancouver-island-gm1665834477-535387167
Tips and Key Information
To walk out toward the headlands or around the lagoon, it is helpful to check the local tide tables. High tide can sometimes cover sections of the lower beach paths.
While the main paths near the entrance are relatively flat, the trails leading up onto the bluffs are rocky and uneven. Wearing shoes with good grip will make the climb much easier.
Because the park faces east and north, it catches incredible colors during the golden hour, and the silhouettes of the historic shacks on Shack Island make for iconic photos.
Located at 3600 Place Road, located in North Nanaimo.
The park is equipped with public washrooms near the parking area and several benches along the viewpoints.
The park is open daily from 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
Dogs are allowed but must remain on a leash at all times to protect the nesting birds and natural vegetation.

places.name: Neck Point Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/neck-point-park-gm1345369088-423465398

Neck Point Park is a 36-acre waterfront park in North Nanaimo, recognized for its diverse coastal scenery that includes rugged cliffs, pebble beaches, and winding oak-strewn paths. It is widely considered one of the city's best locations for photography and marine wildlife viewing due to its position jutting out into the Salish Sea.
What to See and Do

Scenic Viewpoints: A network of boardwalks and gravel trails leads to several neck points, such as Sunset Bluff and Last Beach. These elevated lookouts provide unobstructed views of the Winchelsea Islands and the mainland mountains.

Whale and Wildlife Watching: Because the park extends into the deep water of the Georgia Strait, it is a prime land-based spot for spotting orcas, humpback whales, and sea lions, especially during migratory seasons.

Unique Geology: The park is named for a gravel bar neck that connects to a rocky island at low tide. Visitors can explore a mix of sandy coves like Finn Beach and Indian Beach, which are popular for beachcombing and cold-water swimming.
Scuba Diving: The area off the park's northern points is a popular entry spot for local divers who come to explore the underwater rock walls and vibrant marine life.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/neck-point-park-gm1345368989-423465393
Tips and Key Information
As the name of one of its primary lookouts suggests, this is a premier location for watching the sunset. The westward-facing bluffs catch the full spectrum of evening light over the water.

Keep a close eye on the base of the Garry oak and Douglas fir trees along the woodland trails. Local artists have hidden small, intricate fairy doors throughout the park, making it a popular scavenger hunt for children.
While many paths are accessible boardwalks, some sections of the trail involve steep wooden stairs or uneven forest floor, so comfortable walking shoes are recommended.
Located at 1050 Morningside Drive, Nanaimo.
The park features a large paved parking lot, public washrooms near the entrance, and numerous benches and picnic tables at the most scenic viewpoints.
Open daily from 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a leash at all times to protect the sensitive coastal environment and nesting birds.

places.name: Maffeo Sutton Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/view-of-a-footbridge-in-maffeo-sutton-park-nanaimo-gm1303057448-394628360

Maffeo Sutton Park serves as Nanaimo's signature waterfront gathering place, acting as the anchor for the downtown shoreline. It is a multi-use space that hosts the city's major festivals and serves as the primary gateway for those heading to the nearby islands.
What to See and Do
Island Access: The park is the departure point for the Saysutshun Newcastle Island Ferry. Visitors often use the park as a staging area before heading across the passage for hiking or camping.
Recreation and Play: It features an expansive, modern playground and an outdoor covered stage that frequently hosts live music and community events during the summer months.
Swimming and Fishing: A designated swimming beach and a public fishing pier allow for direct interaction with the harbor. The pier is a popular spot for crabbing and watching the seaplanes take off.
The NANAIMO Sign: A large, colorful 3D sign spelling out the city's name is located near the waterfront, providing a popular backdrop for photography and social media.
Tips and Key Information
Check the local community listings before visiting; the park is the central venue for events like the Silly Boat Regatta, Dragon Boat Festival, and Canada Day celebrations.
The park is the northern terminus of the Harbourfront Walkway. It is easy to park here and walk the entire waterfront promenade to the shops at the southern end.
With large grassy lawns and numerous benches, it is one of the best spots in the city to enjoy takeout from the nearby Old City Quarter or downtown cafes.
Location: 100 Comox Road, Nanaimo.
The park is well-equipped with large public washroom facilities, seasonal concession stands, and paved paths that are fully accessible.
A large on-site parking lot is available, though it can fill up quickly during major festivals or sunny weekend afternoons.
The park is open daily from 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM.

places.name: Westwood Lake Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/westwood-lake-water-reflection-gm1195650148-340864083

Westwood Lake Park is one of Nanaimo’s most popular year-round recreation destinations, nestled at the base of Mount Benson. Centered around a sprawling freshwater lake, the park offers a scenic mix of sandy beaches, dense forest, and a well-maintained trail system that appeals to swimmers, runners, and nature lovers alike.
What to See and Do

The Perimeter Trail: A roughly 6-kilometer loop circles the lake, providing a relatively flat and well-groomed path. It is widely considered one of the best running and walking trails in the city, offering constant views of the water and the surrounding foothills.

Swimming and Sunbathing: The park features two main beaches. The primary beach near the entrance is wide and sandy, equipped with a designated swimming area that is frequently monitored by lifeguards during the summer months.

Fishing and Paddling: The lake is regularly stocked with rainbow trout, making it a favorite spot for local anglers. The calm waters are also ideal for kayaking, canoeing, and stand-up paddleboarding, with a non-motorized vessel policy ensuring a quiet environment.

Bluff Trails: For those seeking more of a challenge, several offshoot trails lead away from the main loop and up onto the rocky bluffs, providing elevated perspectives of the lake and the city of Nanaimo beyond.
Tips and Key Information
As one of the city's busiest parks, the main parking lot can fill up quickly on sunny weekends and holidays. Arriving before 10:00 AM is recommended during the peak summer season.
If you are visiting with children, the main beach typically has lifeguards on duty from late June through August. Always check the posted signs for current patrol hours.

The park is a sensitive natural area; dogs must be kept on a leash on the main lakeside trail. However, there is a designated off-leash area located at the far end of the lake for those wanting to let their pets run.
Location: 2110 Westwood Road, located just a short drive west of the downtown core.
The park is well-equipped with public washrooms, change houses, and a playground near the main beach. There are also several accessible picnic tables and benches positioned along the shoreline.
The park is open daily from 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
The main perimeter trail is largely accessible, featuring a hard-packed gravel surface, though some sections on the far side of the lake have slight inclines and roots.

places.name: Bowen Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/millstone-river-at-bowen-park-gm1214351304-353276142

Bowen Park is a sprawling 36-hectare natural oasis located just minutes from downtown Nanaimo. It serves as a central hub for both active recreation and peaceful nature walks, following the scenic curves of the Millstone River.
What to See and Do

The Waterfall and Duck Pond: A highlight of the park is the scenic waterfall on the Millstone River, easily accessible via paved and gravel trails. Nearby, a large duck pond provides a tranquil spot for families and photographers.
Rhododendron Garden: The park features a stunning garden with over 350 species of rhododendrons, which create a vibrant display of color during the peak blooming season in late spring.
Active Recreation: For those seeking activity, the park is exceptionally well-equipped with tennis courts, a disc golf course, an outdoor pool, and multiple playgrounds.
Interpretive Trails: A network of trails winds through the forest, offering interpretive signs that detail the local flora, fauna, and the history of the area’s coal mining past.
Tips and Key Information
If you visit during the autumn months, particularly October and November, you can often witness salmon returning to the Millstone River to spawn from various vantage points along the river trails.
The park offers several covered picnic shelters and open grassy areas, making it a premier choice for group gatherings or a simple outdoor lunch.
While the park is very dog-friendly, pets must remain on a leash at all times to protect the resident wildlife and the integrity of the gardens.
Location: 500 Bowen Road, Nanaimo.
The park features public washrooms, change rooms for the pool, and ample benches throughout the trail network.
The park is generally open daily from dawn until dusk, though specific facilities like the pool and tennis courts have their own operating schedules.

places.name: Jack Point and Biggs Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/scenic-view-of-the-ocean-overlooking-the-bay-of-nanaimo-in-vancouver-island-british-gm925431960-253958690

Jack Point and Biggs Park is a stunning 13-hectare coastal park located on the southern tip of the Nanaimo estuary. It is celebrated for its dramatic sandstone formations and panoramic views of the Northumberland Channel, the downtown skyline, and the mountains of the mainland.
What to See and Do
The park features a relatively easy 2.5-kilometer loop trail that winds through a mix of coastal forest and exposed rocky bluffs.

Sandstone Galleries: Much like Gabriola Island, the shoreline here has been sculpted by the wind and sea into intricate, honeycomb-like formations and smooth sandstone shelves that are perfect for exploring at low tide.

Wildlife and Marine Activity: This is an exceptional location for observing marine traffic, including the massive BC Ferries as they pass through the channel. It is also a prime spot for viewing bald eagles, sea lions, and harbor seals.
Panoramic Sunsets: The point offers unobstructed views to the west, making it one of the premier locations in the city to watch the sunset over the water and the Coast Mountains.
Tips and Key Information
While the main loop is accessible at any time, the best sandstone exploration happens at low tide. Check the local tide charts to ensure you can safely access the lower rock shelves.

The trail is generally flat but can be root-filled in the forest sections and uneven on the rocky points. Sturdy walking shoes or hiking boots are recommended, especially if you plan to scramble on the sandstone.
Keep your eyes on the channel; orcas and humpback whales are frequently spotted moving through these waters, particularly in the late spring and summer.
Access is via Jackson Road, located just past the Duke Point Ferry Terminal in South Nanaimo.
There is a dedicated parking area Click to open side panel for more information and basic trail signage, but no washrooms are available within the park itself.
Open daily from 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
Dogs are welcome but must remain on a leash to protect the sensitive ecosystem and nesting birds.

places.name: Colliery Dam Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/autumn-fall-colors-in-nanaimo-british-columbia-vancouver-island-canada-gm492884118-76571889

Colliery Dam Park is a historic and scenic 18-hectare park in South Nanaimo that features two distinct lakes—Upper and Lower Colliery Dams—connected by a network of forested trails and rushing waterfalls. Built in the 1910s by the Western Fuel Company to supply water for coal washing, the dams now form the centerpiece of one of the city's most beloved multi-use natural areas.
What to See and Do

Lakeside Trails: A well-maintained loop trail circles both the upper and lower dams, offering a mix of flat gravel sections and more rugged forest paths. The trail features several wooden bridges and viewpoints overlooking the water and the spillways.

Freshwater Fishing: The lower dam is a popular spot for freshwater angling and is frequently stocked with Rainbow Trout. A dedicated fishing pier provides easy access for families and shore-based fishers.

Waterfalls and Creeks: Between the two dams, the water navigates a series of rocky drops and small waterfalls that are particularly dramatic during the spring runoff. These spots are favorites for local photographers and nature watchers.
Off-Leash Dog Area: The upper dam area includes a popular off-leash dog park and a designated swimming spot where pets can cool off in the water.
Tips and Key Information
The lower dam loop is generally flatter and easier to navigate, while the trails connecting to the upper dam involve more significant elevation changes and stairs, providing a more vigorous workout.
In the autumn, the park's deciduous trees provide a vibrant display of fall colors, and the increased water flow makes the waterfalls significantly more impressive.
While swimming is popular in the summer, be aware that there are no lifeguards on duty. Stick to designated access points to protect the shoreline vegetation.
Location: 635 Wakesiah Avenue, Nanaimo. There are multiple entry points, including Nanaimo Lakes Road and Sixth Street.
The park is equipped with public washrooms near the lower dam parking lot, several picnic tables, and benches situated at scenic viewpoints.
Open daily from 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
The lower dam trail is partially accessible, though the full loop around both dams includes steep sections and uneven terrain that may be challenging for strollers or wheelchairs.

places.name: Ammonite Falls
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/ammonite-falls-long-exposure-nanaimo-bc-canada-gm2008997423-560684179

Ammonite Falls is a signature natural attraction within Benson Creek Falls Regional Park on the western edge of Nanaimo. This picturesque waterfall cascades over a series of layered sandstone ledges into a deep ravine, offering a classic Vancouver Island rainforest experience.
What to See and Do

The Waterfall: The main draw is the 10-meter falls, which are particularly powerful in the spring or after heavy rainfall. The rock formations surrounding the water are embedded with marine fossils, giving the falls their name.

Forest Hiking: The trail to the falls winds through a second-growth forest of Douglas fir and Western Red Cedar. Recent infrastructure improvements, including a staircase and a viewing platform, have made reaching the falls significantly safer than the old rope assist scramble.

Creek Exploration: Hikers can explore the base of the falls where Benson Creek carves through the sandstone. The lower viewpoint provides excellent angles for photography, capturing the curtain of water against the mossy ravine walls.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/a-forest-path-on-the-hike-to-ammonite-falls-nanaimo-british-columbia-canada-gm2252050120-665545415
Tips and Key Information

You can access the falls via the Ammonite Falls South Trailhead on Jameson Road or the Weigles Road entrance. The Jameson Road route is generally flatter for the majority of the hike, though both require a final descent to the water.
Even with the new stairs, the trails can be muddy and slippery, especially during the wetter months. Waterproof boots with good traction are recommended.
If you visit in late summer, the falls may slow to a trickle. For the most dramatic views, plan your trip between November and May.
Located within Benson Creek Falls Regional Park at the end of Jameson Road or Weigles Road.
Rated as moderate in terms of difficulty. The round-trip hike is roughly 5 to 6 kilometers depending on the starting point, taking about 1.5 to 2 hours.
There is a portable toilet at the Jameson Road trailhead. However, there is no potable water on-site, so carry enough for the duration of your hike.
Dogs are allowed but must be kept on a leash to protect the sensitive riparian environment.

places.name: Sugarloaf Mountain Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/departure-bay-gm1153147670-313087677

Sugarloaf Mountain Park is a popular local hiking destination in South Nanaimo, centered around a rocky hilltop that offers one of the most accessible viewpoints in the city. While smaller than the major provincial parks, it provides a high-impact panoramic reward for a relatively short ascent.
What to See and Do

The Summit View: The primary attraction is the rocky summit, which offers clear, sweeping views of Departure Bay, the downtown Nanaimo skyline, and the mountains of the mainland across the Salish Sea.

The Stairs: A well-maintained wooden staircase leads visitors through a mix of Garry oak and arbutus trees to the peak. This infrastructure makes the steep climb manageable for most fitness levels and provides a stable path during wetter weather.
Birdwatching: The elevated position and surrounding tree canopy make it a great spot for observing eagles and hawks as they catch thermals rising from the hillside.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/looking-at-the-view-on-sugarloaf-mountain-gm1153147651-313087674
Tips and Key Information
This is an ideal stop if you are short on time but want to see the city's coastal geography. The round-trip hike typically takes less than 30 minutes.
Visit during the golden hour just before sunset to capture the best light on the bay and the ferry traffic moving in and out of the terminal.
While there are stairs, some of the upper sections near the summit involve walking on exposed rock that can be slippery when wet, so shoes with decent grip are recommended.
Access is via a small trailhead on Sugarloaf Place, located in a residential neighborhood in South Nanaimo.
As a small community park, there are no washrooms or water stations on-site; it is designed for short, passive recreation.
Street parking is very limited as it is situated in a cul-de-sac. Visitors are encouraged to be mindful of local residents when parking.

places.name: Mount Benson
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/nanaimo-harbour-waterfront-and-mount-benson-canada-in-spring-gm484763345-38548618

Mount Benson (Te’tuxw’tun) is the most prominent natural landmark in Nanaimo, rising over 1,000 meters to form the city's dramatic mountain backdrop. Primarily contained within Mt. Benson Regional Park, this massive undeveloped area is the go-to destination for hikers seeking a challenging ascent and some of the most expansive views on Vancouver Island.
What to See and Do

Summit Panorama: Reaching the top rewards you with 360-degree views that include the Salish Sea, the Sunshine Coast, the North Shore mountains near Vancouver, and even Mt. Baker on exceptionally clear days. Looking inland, you can see the rugged wilderness toward Port Alberni.

Witchcraft Lake Access: The most popular route to the summit begins at the edge of Witchcraft Lake. The trail crosses a scenic floating boardwalk and wooden bridge before beginning a steady, steep climb through diverse forest zones.

Historical Markers: The mountain holds local historical significance, including the site of a 1951 plane crash on its lower slopes. While little remains, some markers and debris can still be found near specific trails by those familiar with the mountain’s history.

Whiskey Jacks: Near the rocky summit area, you are likely to encounter Whiskey Jacks (Grey Jays). These curious and bold birds are known to land on hikers in hopes of a snack, providing a unique wildlife interaction.
Tips and Key Information

This is considered a difficult hike with an elevation gain of approximately 730 meters over a roughly 8km return trip. Expect a steady, steep incline for most of the way up; trekking poles are highly recommended to save your knees on the descent.

he trail network is extensive and can be confusing, as many mountain bike paths criss-cross the hiking trails. Follow the official regional park signage carefully to stay on the main Te’tuxwtun or Gordie's Trail routes.
If you aren't up for the full summit, there is a respectable viewpoint about halfway up that offers great views of the city and harbor, making for a shorter but still rewarding outing.
The mountain actually has two main peak areas. The Northwest summit typically holds the official sign and flag, while the Southeast summit features the prominent radio towers seen from the city.
The primary trailhead and parking lot are located at 2761 Benson View Road, Nanaimo.
The Mt. Benson Regional Park parking area offers over 100 stalls, a bus drop-off zone, kiosk maps, and an accessible vault toilet.
Parking gates are generally open from 5:00 AM to 11:00 PM in the summer and 5:00 AM to 8:00 PM in the winter.
There is no potable water on the mountain. Given the physical nature of the climb, ensure you carry at least 2 liters of water and high-energy snacks.

places.name: WildPlay Nanaimo
body: WildPlay Nanaimo is an outdoor adventure park situated along the banks of the Nanaimo River. It is a destination for those seeking high-adrenaline activities in a forested setting, featuring a variety of aerial obstacles and gravity-based challenges.
What to See and Do
Bungy Jumping: This location is home to one of the most famous bungy jumps in North America, where participants leap from a 46-meter (150-foot) trestle bridge above the Nanaimo River.
Primal Swing: A massive pendulum-style swing that launches guests from the bridge, reaching speeds of up to 140 km/h as they arc through the river canyon.

Adventure Courses: The park offers multiple levels of aerial trekking courses, including ziplines, suspended bridges, and rope swings. These range from Kids and Classic courses to the Extreme level for more experienced climbers.
What's New: The WTF Jump (What-The-Freefall) is a newer addition that provides a tethered vertical drop from a high platform, simulating a free-fall experience.
Tips and Key Information
Because many activities are timed and have limited capacity, it is highly recommended to reserve your spots online before arriving, especially during summer weekends.
Wear comfortable athletic clothing and closed-toe shoes with good grip. For those with long hair, it is safer to keep it tied back during the courses.
If you aren't a fan of heights, there are several viewing areas where you can watch the bungy jumpers and swingers without participating in the activities yourself.
Location: 35 Nanaimo River Road, located about 15 minutes south of downtown Nanaimo.
The park features a main guest services building for check-in, public washrooms, and a small area for snacks and drinks.
WildPlay is seasonal, typically opening in early spring and closing in late autumn. Hours vary significantly depending on the month and daylight.
All participants are given a full safety briefing and are equipped with professional harnesses and helmets. Height and weight restrictions apply to most activities.

places.name: Diving
body: Nanaimo is widely recognized as one of the premier cold-water diving destinations in the world. The combination of nutrient-rich currents, massive artificial reefs, and diverse marine life—from giant Pacific octopuses to inquisitive sea lions—makes it a bucket-list location for scuba enthusiasts.
The Artificial Reefs (Wreck Diving)
Nanaimo is home to three significant shipwrecks, all scuttled by the Artificial Reef Society of BC to create thriving marine habitats.

HMCS Saskatchewan: A 366-foot former naval destroyer that sits upright at depths between 80 and 130 feet. It is famously covered in white plumose anemones and serves as a home for large lingcod and rockfish.
HMCS Cape Breton: One of the largest artificial reefs in the world, this 442-foot Victory-class ship rests at 140 feet. It offers impressive swim-throughs for advanced divers.
Rivtow Lion: A smaller 150-foot tugboat sitting at a more accessible depth of 50 to 80 feet, making it an excellent site for intermediate divers or those completing their second dive of the day.
Natural Reefs and Wall Dives

Snake Island Wall: Located just a short boat ride from Departure Bay, this dramatic vertical wall drops to over 500 feet. It is renowned for its fields of white anemones and frequent sightings of seals and sea lions.
Snake Island Pinnacle: A plumose-covered rock spire that rises from the depths. It is a favorite for spotting wolf eels and octopuses tucked into rocky crevices.
Shore Diving Sites
For those who prefer to dive from land, the Nanaimo area offers several world-class shore entries within a 20-minute drive of the city.
Madrona Point: A site in Nanoose Bay known for its series of rocky ledges and consistent sightings of giant Pacific octopuses and wolf eels.
Tyee Cove: A sheltered, beginner-friendly bay that is popular for training and night diving due to its easy entry and diverse macro life.
Neck Point Park: Offers several entry points (like Finn Beach) that lead to kelp forests and rocky reefs teeming with nudibranchs and small fish.
Tips for the Best Experience

The prime season for clear water is from September through March. During these months, horizontal visibility can often reach 50–60 feet. Spring and summer can bring algae blooms, though you can often drop below the murk at around 30 feet.
Cold-water gear is essential. While thick 7mm wetsuits are used in the summer, most local divers prefer drysuits year-round for comfort and longer bottom times.
Nanaimo Dive Outfitters and Sundown Diving provide full services, including equipment rentals, air fills, and guided boat charters to the wrecks.

places.name: Golfing
body: Nanaimo is a prominent hub for golfers on Vancouver Island, offering a variety of courses that cater to different skill levels while taking advantage of the region's mild climate and coastal scenery. Whether you are looking for a championship-level challenge or a casual nine-hole round, the city provides several high-quality options that remain playable year-round.
Premier Golf Courses
Nanaimo Golf Club is a semi-private, 18-hole par 72 course recognized for its exceptional conditioning and panoramic views of Departure Bay.
Course Design: Stretching 6,700 yards from the championship tees, the layout features strategic bunkers, majestic evergreen trees, and fast greens that provide a solid test for low-handicap players.
Practice Facilities: The club includes a covered and heated driving range open daily, as well as full chipping and putting greens.
Clubhouse Amenities: Rebuilt in 2013, the clubhouse features two dining lounges with patios that overlook the 18th green and the coastal mountains.
Fairwinds Golf Club, located just 15 minutes north in Nanoose Bay, offers a challenging 18-hole experience designed by architect Les Furber.
Signature Terrain: The course is carved into a scenic peninsula, demanding strategic play through tree-lined fairways and contoured greens set within a lush rainforest environment.
Year-Round Access: Like most in the area, it is open throughout the winter and features 18 hitting stalls at the driving range, six of which are covered and heated.
Dining: The Greenview Taphouse on-site serves a wide selection of BC craft beers and handcrafted pizzas, making it a popular social spot after a round.
Casual and Accessible Options
Pryde Vista Golf Course is a family-run 9-hole course located near the center of the city, offering a more relaxed and affordable environment.
Playability: It is often praised for its welcoming staff and is an excellent choice for families or those looking for a quick round without the time commitment of a full 18 holes.
Disc Golf: The facility also hosts an 18-hole disc golf course that integrates with the traditional golf layout, providing a technical challenge for the local disc golf community.
Cottonwood Golf Course is a public par 72 course located near the south edge of the city, providing a forgiving yet engaging layout.
Walkable Layout: With few elevation changes and wide-open fairways, it is a highly walkable course that appeals to players of all fitness levels.
Unique Features: Its proximity to the airport allows for scenic views of planes taking off, and the on-site restaurant is known for its high-quality food and signature "Saltwater Cowboy" cocktail.
Tips and Key Information
Due to the temperate coastal climate, many Nanaimo courses do not close for the winter. However, it is always wise to check for seasonal maintenance like aeration before booking.
While Nanaimo Golf Club maintains a more traditional golf attire policy, public courses like Cottonwood and Pryde Vista are generally more relaxed.
During the peak summer months, weekend morning slots fill up quickly. Using online booking portals for the larger clubs is recommended.

places.name: Nanaimo Museum
body: The Nanaimo Museum serves as the city's premier cultural anchor, located in the heart of downtown within the Vancouver Island Conference Centre. It offers an immersive look into the regional history, transitioning from the traditions of the Snuneymuxw First Nation to the gritty industrial era of coal mining.
What to See and Do

The Coal Mine Exhibit: This is the museum’s centerpiece—a realistic walk-through replica of a 1920s coal mine. It features tight passages and low ceilings that effectively convey the challenging conditions faced by Nanaimo’s early miners.

Nanaimo Bar History: As a pillar of local culture, the museum hosts a dedicated display about the world-famous dessert. You can view the original recipe and learn about the local contest that helped cement its status as a Canadian icon.

Indigenous Gallery: Developed in collaboration with the Snuneymuxw First Nation, this gallery showcases traditional artifacts, cedar weaving, and oral histories that highlight the deep connection between the people and the land.
Pioneer and Sports Exhibits: Other sections detail the lives of early settlers and celebrate local sporting achievements, providing a well-rounded view of the community's evolution.
Tips and Key Information
The museum is highly interactive, making it a great choice for families. Children often enjoy the blast lever in the coal mine and the hands-on displays in the pioneer section.
The on-site gift shop is one of the best locations in the city for unique Vancouver Island souvenirs, local jewelry, and books authored by regional historians.
Don't miss the chance to sit on the oversized Nanaimo Bar-shaped benches located just outside the museum entrance for a signature vacation photo.
Location: 100 Museum Way, centrally located near the Harbourfront Walkway.
Typically open Tuesday through Saturday, from 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM. It is usually closed on Sundays and Mondays.
The facility is fully modern and accessible to wheelchairs and strollers, with elevators connecting the different levels.
There are public washrooms and lockers available on-site, and it is within immediate walking distance of numerous downtown cafes.

places.name: Nanaimo Art Gallery
body: The Nanaimo Art Gallery is a contemporary public art museum located in the heart of downtown Nanaimo. It serves as a creative hub for the region, focusing on thought-provoking exhibitions and community-driven art education.
What to See and Do

Rotating Exhibitions: The gallery features a dynamic schedule of exhibitions that highlight local, national, and international artists. These installations often explore themes relevant to Vancouver Island’s history, environment, and social landscape.

The Art Store: A dedicated space within the gallery offers unique, handcrafted pieces from local artisans, including ceramics, jewelry, and prints, making it an excellent stop for high-quality regional gifts.

Public Programs: The gallery hosts frequent workshops, artist talks, and family-friendly art activities. Their Saturdays at the Gallery program is particularly popular for those looking to engage in hands-on creative projects.

Indigenous Art: Many exhibitions are developed in collaboration with Indigenous artists, reflecting the deep cultural heritage of the Snuneymuxw First Nation and providing space for important traditional and contemporary voices.
Tips and Key Information
The gallery operates with a suggested donation model, making it an accessible cultural experience for all visitors.
