If you didn't book online, you can try to get same-day tickets at the Visitor Welcome Centre (on the Hill) or the Info-Tent (in summer), but these are limited and often run out by 10:00 AM.
When Parliament is sitting, you can actually sit in the public galleries to watch the House or Senate in session for free. This is separate from the guided tours.
While the Senate building is a 5-minute walk from the Hill, give yourself at least 45 minutes between different building tours to account for walking and rescreening at security.

places.name: 2. Rideau Canal National Historic Site
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/parliament-hill-on-the-rideau-canal-gm182789593-13127508

A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the Rideau Canal is an engineering marvel stretching 202 km from Ottawa to Kingston. It is the only 19th-century canal in North America still operating on its original route with most of its original structures intact.
What to Do and See
Ottawa Locks (Downtown): Located right beside Parliament Hill, this flight of eight massive stone locks connects the canal to the Ottawa River.
Watch the Step-Up: In the summer, you can watch Parks Canada staff hand-crank the iron winches to raise and lower boats—a process that hasn't changed since 1832.
Bytown Museum: Housed in the canal’s oldest stone building (the former treasury and storehouse), this museum tells the story of the canal’s grueling construction.

Rideau Canal Skateway (Winter): When the canal freezes (typically January to early March), it transforms into the world’s largest naturally frozen skating rink, stretching 7.8 km through the heart of the city.
BeaverTails and Hot Chocolate: Numerous kiosks on the ice sell these iconic flat pastries and warm drinks.
Non-Skaters: There is a packed-snow walking lane alongside the ice, allowing you to experience the atmosphere without putting on skates.
Boating and Paddling (May to October): Several companies offer electric boat cruises departing from downtown, providing a relaxed way to see the city's landmarks.
Kayaking & Canoeing: Rent a paddleboat, canoe, or kayak at Dow’s Lake Pavilion to explore the wider, more scenic parts of the canal.

Canal Pathways: The pathways lining both sides of the canal are a haven for cyclists, runners, and walkers. They offer some of the most scenic views of the city, especially during the Tulip Festival in May, when over a million tulips bloom along the route.
Tips and Key Information
The canal officially opens for boats on May 15, 2026, and runs until October 12, 2026. During this time, you can see the locks in full operation.
The Skateway features universal access ramps at several points, including the National Arts Centre and Dow's Lake.
In winter, never walk on the ice unless the Green Flag is flying. Parks Canada monitors ice thickness daily; if the Red Flag is up, the ice is unsafe.
For the best photo of the locks with Parliament Hill in the background, head to the Plaza Bridge or the terrace of the Fairmont Château Laurier.

places.name: 3. Canadian War Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/canadian-war-museum-in-ottawa-ontario-canada-gm960641148-262320167

The Canadian War Museum, located on the banks of the Ottawa River, stands as a significant landmark in Ottawa. It is one of the world’s most respected museums of military history known not only for its extensive collection of tanks, artillery, and aircraft but also for its powerful, brutally honest depiction of the human experience of conflict.
What to See and Do

Canadian Experience Galleries: These four main galleries take you on a chronological journey from early Indigenous warfare and the War of 1812 through the World Wars and into the Cold War and modern peacekeeping.

LeBreton Gallery: A massive, sun-filled hall of heavy metal featuring scores of tanks, military vehicles, and artillery. You’ll find everything from a First World War ambulance to a T-34 tank and a CF-5 fighter jet suspended from the ceiling.
Memorial Hall: A serene, contemplative space featuring the original headstone of Canada’s Unknown Soldier.

Regeneration Hall: An architectural highlight with soaring, angled walls of recycled copper. It is designed to offer a direct sightline to the Peace Tower on Parliament Hill, symbolizing hope for the future.
Architectural Symbolism: The building itself, designed by Raymond Moriyama, is an artifact.
Morse Code Windows: The small windows on the roof peak are arranged in Morse code to spell out Lest We Forget and N'oublions jamais in English and French.
Regeneration: The green roof is covered in self-seeding grasses from the Ottawa River. It represents nature's ability to heal and regenerate even after the devastation of war.
Tips and Key Information

The museum is typically open Wednesday to Sunday, 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM (open late until 8:00 PM on Thursdays). Admission is approximately $21 for adults, but it is Free on Thursdays from 5:00 PM to 8:00 PM (though you still need to book a timed ticket).
It is highly recommended to reserve timed entry tickets online in advance, as the museum often reaches capacity, especially on weekends and holidays.
While the famous light-alignment event happens on November 11 at 11:00 AM, the Memorial Hall is a powerful visit any time of year.
The museum is fully accessible. Courtesy wheelchairs and strollers are available at the information desk.
It is located on LeBreton Flats. You can reach it via the O-Train Line 1 (Pimisi Station) or by cycling along the scenic Ottawa River Pathway.

places.name: 4. National Gallery of Canada
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/national-gallery-of-canada-in-downtown-ottawa-ontario-canada-gm2181429962-600456574

The National Gallery of Canada, designed by renowned architect Moshe Safdie, is one of the most significant art institutions in North America. Located in a stunning structure of glass and pink granite, it houses a vast collection that spans from indigenous artifacts and traditional Canadian art to European masterpieces and cutting-edge contemporary works.
What to See and Do

Iconic Architecture: The building itself is a masterpiece, featuring the Scotiabank Great Hall, a soaring glass pavilion that offers what many consider the best panoramic view of Parliament Hill and the Ottawa River.
Maman Sculpture: Visitors are greeted outside by Louise Bourgeois’s famous 30-foot bronze spider sculpture, a world-known landmark that has become a favorite photo spot for tourists.
Indigenous and Canadian Art: The museum features dedicated galleries for Indigenous art and the Group of Seven, providing a deep dive into the nation's visual identity and natural landscapes.
Quiet Courtyards: Inside, the Garden Court provides a peaceful, light-filled interior space with real trees and water features, perfect for a contemplative break during your visit.
Tips and Key Information

The gallery is typically open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM, with extended hours until 8:00 PM on Thursdays. While adult admission is approximately $20, you can visit for free on Thursday evenings starting at 5:00 PM (though advanced booking is still recommended).
For the most dramatic interior shot, head to the colonnade—the long glass ramp leading up to the Great Hall—which creates incredible light patterns on sunny days.
The 7 Tapas Bar within the gallery offers a sophisticated setting for a light meal or drink, often featuring locally sourced ingredients and views of the surrounding sculptures.
It is located at 380 Sussex Drive, within walking distance of both the ByWard Market and Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica.

places.name: 5. Notre Dame Cathedral Basilica
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/notre-dame-cathedral-ottawa-gm579737278-99694067

Located across from the National Gallery, the Notre Dame Cathedral Basilica is the oldest and largest church in Ottawa. This National Historic Site is a stunning example of Neo-Gothic architecture, famous for its twin silver spires that have defined the city's skyline since the mid-19th century.
What to See and Do

Breathtaking Interior: While the exterior is impressive, the interior is truly spectacular. It features a deep blue vaulted ceiling studded with thousands of gold stars, intricately carved wooden altars, and over 200 statues of religious figures.
Artistic Heritage: Visitors often marvel at the brilliant stained-glass windows that depict various biblical scenes and the massive pipe organ, which is one of the most significant in the country.
Architectural Transition: The building's design reflects a transition from Neoclassical to Gothic Revival styles, making it a key site for those interested in Canadian architectural history.
Tips and Key Information
If you can, visit during a mass or a scheduled concert to hear the organ in action; the acoustics within the cathedral are exceptional.
As this is an active place of worship, visitors are asked to remain quiet and respectful. Avoid wandering through the aisles during mass services.
While you can walk through on your own, the cathedral occasionally offers guided tours that provide deeper insight into the history of the carvings and the symbolism of the art.
Its location on Sussex Drive makes it very easy to combine a visit here with a trip to the National Gallery of Canada or a stroll through the ByWard Market.

places.name: 6. Rideau Hall
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/rideau-hall-in-ottawa-ontario-canada-gm960641156-262320170

Rideau Hall is the official residence and workplace of the Governor General of Canada. Located on a vast 79-acre estate just minutes from downtown Ottawa, it serves as a site for state ceremonies, international welcomes, and honors for deserving Canadians. Unlike many other world leader residences, the grounds and much of the building are open to the public, fostering a sense of a home for all Canadians.
What to See and Do

Guided Tours of the Residence: Explore the elegant State rooms where the Governor General fulfills official duties and welcomes dignitaries. You'll see incredible collections of Canadian art and furniture.
Grounds and Gardens: Wander through the meticulously landscaped heritage gardens. The estate features over 10,000 trees, including many planted by world leaders and royalty during state visits.
Changing of the Guard: During the summer months, the Ceremonial Guard performs a relief of the sentries at the main gate, adding a touch of military pageantry to your visit.

Outdoor Activities: In the winter, a public skating rink is often maintained on the grounds, continuing a tradition that dates back to the 19th century. In the summer, the cricket pitch is frequently in use.
Tips and Key Information
All tours and access to the grounds are free of charge. However, guided tours of the residence must be booked in advance, especially for groups.

The grounds are generally open daily from 8:00 AM until sunset. Tour schedules for the interior change based on the season and official events, so it is essential to check the official website before visiting.
As it is a secure government site, visitors must undergo security screening before entering the residence for a tour.
Situated at 1 Sussex Drive, it is easily accessible by public transit or via a scenic walk or bike ride along the Sussex Drive corridor.

places.name: 7. Canadian Museum of Nature
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/canadian-museum-of-nature-in-ottawa-gm1248279478-363547746

Housed in a magnificent building that looks like a castle, the Canadian Museum of Nature is Canada's national natural history and sciences museum. Often referred to as a castle of nature, it combines historic Scottish baronial-style architecture with modern glass additions to create one of the most visually striking landmarks in the city.
What to See and Do
Fossil Gallery: This world-class exhibit features more than 30 complete dinosaur skeletons and hundreds of fossils, including the iconic horned dinosaurs and a dramatic Death of a Dinosaur scene.
Water Gallery: Centered around a massive, 19-meter blue whale skeleton suspended from the ceiling, this gallery explores the diverse life found in Canada's oceans and freshwater systems.
Mammal Gallery: Features lifelike dioramas that showcase Canada's iconic wildlife—including polar bears, grizzly bears, and caribou—in their natural habitats.
Queens' Lantern: This stunning glass tower was added during the museum's major renovation. It provides incredible views of the city and serves as a luminous beacon at night.
Arctic Gallery: An immersive space that explores the vast and changing landscapes of the Canadian North through the eyes of the people who live there and the animals that call it home.
Tips and Key Information
Like many other national museums, admission to the permanent galleries is free on Thursdays from 5:00 PM to 8:00 PM. However, you still need to book a timed ticket online in advance.
It is highly recommended to reserve your tickets online, even for the free evenings, as the museum often reaches capacity during peak hours and weekends.
The museum is exceptionally kid-friendly, featuring several Nature Play areas and interactive discovery zones where children can touch specimens and engage in hands-on learning.
The entire museum is fully accessible, with elevators serving all floors and manual wheelchairs available to borrow at the welcome desk on a first-come, first-served basis.
places.note: Note that the museum is typically closed on Tuesdays during the off-peak season (September to May), so plan your visit for a different day of the week.

places.name: 8. ByWard Market
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/byward-market-in-ottawa-gm1181238381-331227799

ByWard Market is one of Ottawa’s most vibrant and historic areas, offering a blend of fresh food, local goods, and cultural experiences. Established in 1826 by Colonel John By, it has long been a hub for farmers, artisans, and locals, making it one of the oldest and most well-known public markets in Canada. The area is famous for its eclectic mix of open-air farmer stalls, artisanal boutiques, and a high concentration of some of the city's most beloved restaurants and pubs.
What to See and Do
Culinary Landmarks: No visit is complete without stopping at the original BeaverTails stand to try the world-famous cinnamon and sugar fried pastry.
Artisan Shopping: The main market building and surrounding streets are filled with local vendors selling everything from handmade jewelry and maple syrup to fresh seasonal produce and flowers.
Public Art: Look for the Ottawa sign located in the York Street Plaza, which is a popular spot for photos, and explore the various hidden courtyards like the Jeanne d'Arc Court.
Nightlife: As the sun sets, the market transforms into a nightlife hotspot with a dense array of rooftop patios, live music venues, and historic taverns.
Tips and Key Information
Many of the core streets are closed to vehicles or have widened sidewalks during the summer months, making it an ideal place to explore on foot.
While there is on-street parking, it can be very difficult to find a spot. It is highly recommended to use one of the several parking garages located on York or Clarence Streets.

The market is very safe during the day, but like any busy downtown entertainment district, it is wise to stay aware of your surroundings during the late-night hours when the bars are at their busiest.
For the best experience, visit on a weekend morning when the outdoor farmers' market is in full swing and the energy is at its peak.

places.name: 9. National War Memorial
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-national-war-memorial-in-ottawa-canada-gm481190040-69358625

The National War Memorial in Ottawa stands as a powerful tribute to Canadian soldiers who have served and sacrificed in wars and peacekeeping missions. Located in Confederation Square, it is a monumental symbol of Canada's military history and resilience. Originally built to commemorate the First World War, it was rededicated over the years to include those who served in the Second World War, the Korean War, and the war in Afghanistan.
What to See and Do

Response Statues: The memorial features 22 bronze figures representing the different branches of the Canadian forces during World War I, shown passing through a granite arch topped by the allegorical figures of Peace and Freedom.
Tomb of the Unknown Soldier: At the foot of the memorial lies the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, containing the remains of an unidentified Canadian soldier from a cemetery near Vimy Ridge, France.
Sentinels: From April to November, the tomb is guarded by sentries from the Canadian Armed Forces who stand at attention in a rotating vigil.
Remembrance Day: This is the site of Canada's national Remembrance Day ceremony every November 11, where thousands gather for two minutes of silence and the laying of wreaths.
Tips and Key Information
The site is an open public square and is accessible 24 hours a day, making it easy to visit during a morning walk or late at night when it is beautifully illuminated.
Visitors are reminded that the Tomb is a sacred site; standing on the raised granite plinth or leaving trash is strictly prohibited and monitored by security.
It is one of the most photographed spots in the city, especially with Parliament Hill visible in the background.
It is steps away from the Fairmont Château Laurier and the National Arts Centre, making it a central point for any downtown walking tour.

places.name: 10. Peace Tower
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/canadian-parliament-with-peace-tower-and-east-block-in-ottawa-canada-gm2152542178-573539014

The Peace Tower is the most iconic feature of the Canadian parliamentary complex and a national symbol of Canada. Standing at 92.2 meters (302 feet), this stone bell tower serves as a focal point of Parliament Hill and acts as a Victorian High Gothic monument to the sacrifices made by Canadians during the First World War.
What to See and Do
Memorial Chamber: Located directly above the front arch of the tower, this solemn room houses the Books of Remembrance, which list the names of every Canadian who has died in military service.

Carillon: The tower contains 53 bells of varying sizes. The Dominion Carillonneur performs regular live recitals, filling the downtown core with music that ranges from classical pieces to contemporary arrangements.
Observation Deck: Beneath the clock faces is an enclosed viewing area that offers 360-degree panoramic views of the Ottawa River, the Gatineau Hills, and the capital's skyline.
Clock Faces: Each of the four clock faces is nearly 5 meters in diameter, serving as the official timekeeper for the capital since its completion in 1927.
Tips and Key Information
Please note that because the Centre Block is undergoing a massive decade-long rehabilitation, the interior of the Peace Tower and the Observation Deck are currently closed to the public.
To see the interior while the physical tower is closed, you can visit Parliament: The Immersive Experience on Sparks Street, which uses high-definition projections to simulate the view from the top.

The Canadian flag flown atop the Peace Tower is changed every weekday (and on special occasions). These retired flags are famously given away for free to Canadians, though the current waiting list is several decades long.
For a symmetrical shot of the tower, stand directly behind the Centennial Flame at the main gates of the Hill.

places.name: 11. Fairmont Château Laurier
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/aerial-view-of-ottawas-cenotaph-and-chateau-laurier-gm909827930-250582694

Often referred to as the third chamber of Parliament, the Fairmont Château Laurier is a magnificent French Gothic Revival castle that has anchored downtown Ottawa since 1912. Built by the Grand Trunk Railway, its history is famously intertwined with the Titanic; the hotel's visionary, Charles Melville Hays, perished on the ill-fated ship just days before the scheduled grand opening. Today, it remains a focal point of Canadian political and social life, having hosted royalty, world leaders, and celebrities for over a century.
What to See and Do

Design and Materials: The castle features a limestone façade, distinctive copper roofing, and soaring turrets. Inside, you'll find Belgian marble floors, hand-moulded plaster decorations, and original Tiffany stained-glass windows.

Karsh Connection: Famed portrait photographer Yousuf Karsh lived and worked in the hotel for 18 years. Several of his world-famous portraits, including his iconic Roaring Lion photo of Winston Churchill, are displayed in the hotel's public spaces.

Presidential Suite and Renovation: Recent renovations have modernized the suites while maintaining their historic character, using a palette of antique golds, blacks, and silvers to echo early 20th-century elegance.

Zoe’s Lounge: This refined social space is the heart of the hotel’s culinary scene. It’s famous for its traditional afternoon tea service, featuring signature LOT 35 teas, English scones, and artful open-faced sandwiches. In the evening, it transforms into a sophisticated bar known for craft cocktails and live jazz on weekends.
La Terrasse: Open during the summer months, this seasonal outdoor patio offers some of the best views in the city, overlooking the Rideau Canal locks, the Ottawa River, and the Parliament Buildings.
Café Laurier: For a more casual experience, this cozy lobby-level café serves locally roasted Happy Goat Coffee and freshly baked pastries.
Tips and Key Information
One of the hotel’s hidden gems is its 60-foot indoor swimming pool, designed in a striking 1930s Art Deco style.
Visitors are often greeted in the lobby by Stewart, the hotel's friendly dog who acts as a Canine Ambassador for guests and families.
A historic tunnel beneath Rideau Street connects the hotel directly to the Senate of Canada Building (formerly Union Station), a remnant of the hotel's origins as a grand railway terminal.

places.name: 1. Canadian Museum of History
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/canadian-museum-of-history-in-gatineau-gm1248236961-363523294

The Canadian Museum of History is Canada's most visited museum, located on the Gatineau side of the Ottawa River. Its stunning architecture, designed by Douglas Cardinal, features sweeping curves inspired by the Canadian landscape. The museum is dedicated to chronicling the human history of Canada and the cultural diversity of its people.
What to See and Do
Grand Hall: This iconic space offers a breathtaking view of Parliament Hill across the river and houses the world's largest indoor collection of totem poles.
Canadian History Hall: A signature gallery that tells the story of Canada through three distinct eras, featuring over 1,500 authentic artifacts and diverse perspectives.
Canadian Children's Museum: A museum within a museum where kids can travel the world through interactive exhibits, including a bus from Pakistan and a home from Mexico.
CINÉ+ Theater: A massive screen theater (formerly IMAX) that showcases stunning documentary films and cinematic experiences.
Tips and Key Information
For the best photo opportunity, walk along the riverside path behind the museum. The view of the Ottawa River with the Parliament buildings in the background is unmatched.
While there is a fee for general admission, the museum offers free admission on Thursday evenings from 5:00 PM to 7:00 PM, though tickets must still be booked in advance.
If you are coming from downtown Ottawa, the most scenic way to arrive is by walking or cycling across the Alexandra Bridge, which leads directly to the museum's grounds.
You can often purchase a combined ticket that includes admission to the Canadian War Museum, which is located just a short distance away across the river.
The Voyageur Cafeteria on-site offers a range of options with a great view of the river, making it a convenient spot for lunch during a long visit.

places.name: 2. Diefenbunker: Canada's Cold War Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/photo-of-an-empty-underground-cement-entrance-to-a-nuclear-blast-shelter-horizonal-gm2167466216-587527725

Located in the rural village of Carp, just outside Ottawa, the Diefenbunker: Canada's Cold War Museum is a massive four-story underground bunker designed to withstand a nuclear blast. Built in secret between 1959 and 1961, it was intended to house the top officials of the Canadian government and military in the event of a nuclear war, ensuring the continuity of government. Today, the bunker serves as a haunting and fascinating museum that preserves the tension of the Cold War era.
What to See and Do
Blast Tunnel: Enter through the same 115-foot metal tunnel designed to absorb the shockwave of a nuclear explosion.
War Cabinet Room: See the nerve center where the Prime Minister and advisors would have made critical decisions during a crisis.
CBC Studio: Visit the fully equipped emergency broadcasting studio where messages would have been sent to the surviving public.
Vault: Explore the high-security area originally built to store Canada's gold reserves during a nuclear threat.
Machine Room: Marvel at the massive generators and filtration systems that made the bunker a self-sufficient underground city for 535 people.
Tips and Key Information
While you can explore with an audio guide, the guided tours (approx. 60–90 minutes) are highly recommended by visitors for the deep historical context and behind-the-scenes stories they provide.
The bunker stays a constant, chilly 18°C (65°F) year-round. Even if it is a hot summer day, you will want to bring a sweater or light jacket for your time underground.
Reservations are mandatory. You must book a specific time slot online in advance as the museum has strict capacity limits for safety.
Exploring all four levels involves a significant amount of walking and several flights of stairs. However, an elevator is available for those with mobility issues; just notify staff upon arrival.
For a unique experience, the museum hosts Escape the Diefenbunker, one of the world's largest escape rooms, which takes place across an entire floor of the facility (requires separate booking).

places.name: 3. Royal Canadian Mint
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-royal-canadian-mint-building-in-ottawa-gm1336373275-417659564

Housed in a magnificent historic Tudor-Revival building (established 1908), the Royal Canadian Mint headquarters is where Canada’s hand-crafted collector coins, gold bullion, and medals are produced. Unlike the high-speed circulation facility in Winnipeg, the Ottawa Mint is a place of artistry, precision, and immense wealth.
What to See and Do

Guided Tours: Every visit centers on a 45-minute guided tour (available in English and French) that provides a bird’s-eye view of the production floor. You’ll learn how master engravers translate art into metal and see the state-of-the-art gold refining technology.
Million Dollar Coin: Witness the Guinness World Record-breaking 100-kg coin made of 99.999% pure gold. With a face value of $1 million, it is one of the rarest and most valuable coins in the world.
Hold a Solid Gold Bar: A highlight for many is the chance to physically lift and hold a pure 400-ounce gold bar, which is currently valued at over $1.5 million (CAD). It’s surprisingly heavy.
Olympic Medals: See the precision that went into striking the 2010 Vancouver Winter Games medals, which were created right here in this facility.
Boutique: After the tour, you can visit the boutique to purchase exclusive collector coins, gift sets, and souvenirs that aren't available anywhere else.
Tips and Key Information
Admission is $12 for adults (18+), $10 for seniors (65+), and $8 for children (ages 5–17), while Indigenous Peoples and Canadian Military personnel receive free entry.
It is highly recommended to book your tour 48 to 72 hours in advance by calling 1-800-267-1871. Walk-ups are first-come, first-served and frequently sell out.
Operating hours are Tuesday to Sunday from 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM in winter, and daily from 10:00 AM to 5:00 PM in summer (Victoria Day to Labour Day).

Large bags are not permitted on the tour (lockers are available). If you plan on purchasing gold bullion in the boutique, you must bring a valid government-issued photo ID to comply with financial regulations.
Please note that tours are not guaranteed to see live coin striking, as production schedules fluctuate based on demand.

places.name: 4. Canada Aviation and Space Museum
body: https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/e/ed/BoeingVertolCH-113Labrador11301-03.JPG

Located on a former military airbase, the Canada Aviation and Space Museum is recognized as one of the finest aviation museums in the world. It houses a vast collection of more than 130 aircraft and artifacts that chronicle the history of flight, from the pioneer era to modern space exploration. The museum is famous for its Reserve Hangar, which stores many of the collection's most rare and delicate specimens in a massive, open-concept space.
What to See and Do
Avro Arrow: You can see the largest surviving pieces of the legendary Avro CF-105 Arrow, a source of enduring fascination in Canadian aviation history.
Canadarm: The museum proudly displays the original Canadarm used on the Space Shuttle Endeavour, a symbol of Canada's significant contributions to international space programs.

Flight Simulators and Rides: Visitors can experience the thrill of flight through full-motion simulators or, during the summer months, book a flight in a vintage 1939 biplane for a unique view of the capital.
Space Exhibition: Beyond atmospheric flight, the museum features life in space, including exhibits on the International Space Station and the training of Canadian astronauts.
Tips and Key Information

The museum offers free admission daily between 4:00 PM and 5:00 PM. Like other national museums, it also features free admission on Thursday evenings from 5:00 PM to 8:00 PM, though timed tickets are required.
Access to the Reserve Hangar is typically restricted to specific guided tour times. If you are a serious aviation enthusiast, check the daily schedule upon arrival so you don't miss this section.
It is situated at the Rockcliffe Airport, a bit further from the downtown core than other museums. It is best reached by car or the #7 bus, and there is ample paid parking on-site.
The museum is highly interactive for children, offering a Skyways area where kids can dress up as pilots and explore the basics of aerodynamics.

places.name: 5. Ottawa Art Gallery
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-ottawa-art-gallery-building-is-seen-in-ottawa-ontario-canada-gm1313954943-402315229

The Ottawa Art Gallery (OAG) is a contemporary cultural hub located in the heart of downtown Ottawa. Reopened in 2018 in a sleek, multi-story facility, it serves as a premier venue for the art of the Ottawa-Gatineau region while fostering connections to national and international art scenes.
What to See and Do

Diverse Collections: The gallery is home to the Firestone Collection of Canadian Art, which includes significant works by the Group of Seven, alongside rotating contemporary exhibitions featuring photography, sculpture, and new media.

Architectural Landmark: The building features stunning modern design with light-filled galleries, a rooftop terrace with views of the city, and integrated spaces that connect it to the University of Ottawa and the Rideau Centre.
Community Focused: Beyond traditional exhibits, the OAG hosts workshops, artist talks, and events that aim to make art accessible to a wide audience.
Tips and Key Information
The OAG is committed to remaining free for all visitors, making it one of the most accessible cultural institutions in the city.
The gallery is open Wednesday to Saturday from 10:00 AM to 9:00 PM, and Tuesday and Sunday from 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM (Closed Mondays).
You can visit Jackson, the on-site café and bar, which offers a sophisticated menu in a beautifully designed space that reflects the gallery's modern aesthetic.
The OAG Shop features a curated selection of unique items, many of which are produced by local artists and makers, perfect for high-quality souvenirs.
Situated at 50 Mackenzie King Bridge, it is steps away from the Rideau O-Train station and is directly connected to the historic Arts Court building.

places.name: 6. Canada Science and Technology Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/ottawa-canada-science-and-technology-museum-gm2178755495-598069818

Reopened in 2017 after a complete transformation, the Canada Science and Technology Museum is a highly interactive facility that celebrates Canada's history of innovation. It combines beloved heritage artifacts with cutting-edge digital technology to create an environment that encourages curiosity and hands-on discovery.
What to See and Do
Crazy Kitchen: One of the most famous and longest-running exhibits in Ottawa, this tilted room uses optical illusions and physical sensations to challenge your sense of balance and perception.
Locomotive Hall: This massive hall features a collection of giant steam locomotives that visitors can walk around and even climb inside, showcasing the power of early Canadian rail travel.

Artifact Alley: This central corridor features over 700 artifacts from the museum's collection, ranging from a prototype for a nuclear reactor to a collection of early bicycles and household technologies.
ZOOOM – A Children’s Innovation Zone: A dedicated, supervised play and discovery area for children aged 0 to 8, designed to foster creative problem-solving through building and experimentation.
Tips and Key Information
The museum is typically open Tuesday to Sunday, 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM (Closed on Mondays).
Like other national museums, admission is free daily between 4:00 PM and 5:00 PM. It is also free on Thursday evenings from 5:00 PM to 8:00 PM, though timed tickets must be booked online in advance.
Reservations are highly recommended, especially on weekends and during school holidays, as the museum frequently reaches its visitor capacity.
On specific Sundays, the museum offers sensory-friendly mornings with reduced lighting and noise levels for visitors who may benefit from a calmer environment.

Located at 1867 St. Laurent Blvd, it is slightly east of the downtown core. There is ample paid parking available, and it is accessible via the O-Train Line 1 (St-Laurent Station) followed by a short bus ride.

places.name: 7. Laurier House National Historic Site
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/laurier-house-national-historic-site-in-ottawa-gm1257637907-368641889

Laurier House is a stately Victorian mansion that served as the residence for two of Canada’s most important Prime Ministers: Sir Wilfrid Laurier and William Lyon Mackenzie King. This National Historic Site offers a rare, intimate look at the private lives of the leaders who shaped the country for over 50 years, preserved exactly as it was when Mackenzie King lived there.
What to See and Do

Second-Floor Library: This is the most famous room in the house, where Mackenzie King spent his evenings. It remains filled with his personal book collection, his crystal ball, and a portrait of his mother, whom he famously claimed to communicate with during spiritualist seances.

Political History: The house features original artifacts and documents that highlight key moments in Canadian history, including the development of the Commonwealth and the social reforms of the early 20th century.

Third-Floor Exhibit: A dedicated space showcases the personal belongings and legacies of both Laurier and King, providing a comparative look at their very different personalities and political styles.
Tips and Key Information
Access to the interior is by guided tour only. These tours are highly praised for their storytelling, particularly the details regarding Mackenzie King's eccentricities and spiritualism.
As a Parks Canada site, there is a small admission fee (approximately $8 for adults), though it is often free for youth under 17.
The house is typically open seasonally, usually from May to October. It is essential to check the official Parks Canada schedule before visiting, as it is often closed during the winter months.
Situated at the corner of Laurier Avenue East and Chapel Street in the Sandy Hill neighborhood, it is a pleasant 15-minute walk from the ByWard Market.

places.name: 8. Bytown Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/bytown-museum-along-the-rideau-canal-gm2182157399-601121433

The Bytown Museum is located in Ottawa's oldest stone building, originally used as a treasury and storehouse during the construction of the Rideau Canal. It sits at the dramatic meeting point of the canal and the Ottawa River, nestled right between Parliament Hill and the Fairmont Château Laurier.
What to See and Do

Historical Narrative: The museum provides a deep dive into the early years of Bytown—Ottawa's original name—covering everything from the grueling construction of the canal to the city's evolution into Canada's capital.

Unique Setting: Because it is housed in a former commissariat built in 1827, the architecture itself is a primary exhibit, featuring thick limestone walls and original wooden beams that reflect the rugged history of the region.

Diverse Exhibits: Visitors can explore a range of artifacts, including early surveying tools used by Colonel By, period clothing, and personal items belonging to the diverse laborers who built the city.
Scenic Location: Its position at the Ottawa Locks offers one of the best perspectives on the canal’s engineering, making it a perfect starting or ending point for a walk along the waterway.
Tips and Key Information

Admission is $9 for adults, $6 for seniors and students, and $3 for children under 12, while a family pass (2 adults plus kids) costs $21; seniors also get free admission on Wednesdays, in line with Ottawa’s free transit day for seniors.

Currently, the museum is typically open Tuesday to Sunday (Closed Mondays). During the deepest winter months (January–April), it is often open by appointment or has special hours for events like Winterlude, so it’s wise to call ahead at 613-234-4570.

As a 200-year-old stone building, accessibility is limited. Only two of the three floors are accessible by elevator/ramp. For those who cannot reach the top floor, a 3D virtual tour is available on-site to ensure you don't miss the exhibits.

The museum is a star attraction for the Haunted Walk of Ottawa. If you’re a fan of ghost stories, they offer special after-hours tours where you can explore the dark corners of the building by lantern light.

The museum is tucked away below the street level. You can find it by taking the stairs down from the Plaza Bridge (near the Fairmont Château Laurier) or walking down the path beside the Parliament Hill Visitor Welcome Centre.

places.name: 9. Supreme Court of Canada
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/supreme-court-of-canada-gm1441809204-481399142

The Supreme Court of Canada is the highest court in the country and a striking example of Art Deco architecture in the capital. Perched on a cliff overlooking the Ottawa River, the building's steep copper roofs and grey granite walls harmonize with the nearby Parliament Buildings, creating a powerful presence in the Judicial District.
What to See and Do
Guided Tours: Visitors can take free guided tours led by law students who explain the inner workings of the Canadian judicial system and the history of the building.
Grand Entrance Hall: The interior features a majestic Grand Entrance Hall with marble floors and walls, leading to the main courtroom where most of the country's landmark legal decisions are made.
Courtroom Access: When the court is in session, the public is often welcome to observe the proceedings from the gallery, providing a unique look at high-level legal arguments in person.
Statues of Justice: Outside the main entrance, you can see two large bronze statues representing Veritas (Truth) and Iustitia (Justice), which are popular focal points for photographers.
Tips and Key Information
Entry and guided tours are free, but it is highly recommended to book your tour in advance through their official website, especially for groups.
The building is generally open to the public from Monday to Friday, 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM. It is closed on weekends and statutory holidays.
Much like Parliament Hill, all visitors must pass through a security screening process upon entry, so allow extra time for this.
During the summer months (May to August), tours are offered more frequently and do not always require a prior reservation for individuals or small families.
Located at 301 Wellington Street, it is an easy walk from Parliament Hill and offers some of the best unobstructed views of the Ottawa River and the Gatineau Hills from its rear terrace.

places.name: 10. Watson’s Mill
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/watsons-mill-and-dam-during-winter-frozen-rideau-river-manotick-ottawa-ontario-canada-gm1749339722-543639812

Located in the charming village of Manotick, Watson's Mill (Museum/Historic Site) is one of the few remaining industrial heritage sites in Ontario that is still operating as a water-powered flour mill. Built in 1860 by Moss Kent Dickinson and Joseph Currier, it remains a centerpiece of local history and a beautiful example of mid-19th-century limestone architecture.
What to See and Do
Milling Demonstrations: During the summer months, you can watch the massive turbines and grindstones in action as they produce whole wheat flour using traditional water-power methods.
Ghost of Ann Currier: Legend has it that the mill is haunted by the ghost of Ann Currier, the wife of one of the founders, who tragically died in a milling accident just months after the mill opened.
Dickinson House: Directly across from the mill is the former home of the Dickinson family, which is also open to the public and provides a look at domestic life in the Victorian era.
Scenic Dam and Park: The mill is situated on the Rideau River, and the surrounding parkland and dam offer picturesque views, making it a popular spot for photography and picnicking.
Tips and Key Information
You can purchase stone-ground whole wheat flour directly at the mill, which is produced on-site during their milling demonstrations.
Entry to the mill and Dickinson House is by donation, making it an accessible historical outing for families.
The mill is primarily a seasonal attraction, typically open from May to October. During the winter, it often hosts special events like the Christmas Market.
The mill is a hub for community activities, including farmers' markets, antique car shows, and Haunted Mill events in October.
Manotick is about a 25-minute drive south of downtown Ottawa, offering a peaceful village atmosphere that feels worlds away from the city center.

places.name: 11. Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/canadian-tomb-of-the-unknown-soldier-in-ottawa-canada-gm480969968-69346457

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier is Canada’s most significant site of individual and collective remembrance. Located at the base of the National War Memorial in Confederation Square, it holds the remains of an unidentified Canadian soldier who died during the First World War near Vimy Ridge, France.
What to See and Do

Sarcophagus: Designed by artist Mary-Ann Liu, the tomb is made of dark Caledonia granite from Quebec, chosen to complement the National War Memorial. Its bronze relief features a medieval sword, a First World War helmet, and branches of maple and laurel leaves (signifying victory and death).
Poppies: In a spontaneous tradition that began in 2000, visitors often leave their poppies on the tomb after Remembrance Day ceremonies, covering the bronze in a sea of red.

National Sentry Program: From April to November, you can observe the Sentries—members of the Canadian Armed Forces who stand guard at the tomb daily. The sentries are changed in a small, precise ceremony every hour on the hour from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM.
National War Memorial: The tomb sits in the shadow of The Response, a massive bronze sculpture depicting 22 figures from all branches of the service passing through a granite arch.
Tips and Key Information
This is a sacred site. Visitors are asked to maintain a respectful silence and are strictly prohibited from stepping onto the granite base or touching the sarcophagus while the sentries are on duty.
This is the focal point of the National Remembrance Day Ceremony (November 11). If you plan to attend, arrive very early (by 9:00 AM) as tens of thousands of people gather in the surrounding streets.
The site is outdoors and accessible to the public 24 hours a day, free of charge. It is located at the intersection of Wellington and Elgin Streets.

places.name: 1. Major’s Hill Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/autumn-colors-at-majors-hill-park-in-ottawa-canada-gm1170225162-323742031

Major's Hill Park is a premier green space in downtown Ottawa, offering some of the most spectacular views in the city. As the site of Ottawa's first settlement, it provides a tranquil escape with rolling lawns and winding pathways, perfectly situated between the ByWard Market District and the National Gallery of Canada.
What to See and Do
Scenic Vantage Points: The park is famous for its unobstructed views of the Parliament Buildings, the Ottawa River, and the Fairmont Château Laurier.
Seasonal Displays: During the spring, it is a focal point for the Canadian Tulip Festival, while in the fall, the heritage trees provide a vibrant display of autumn colors.
Historic Foundations: You can explore the interpreted ruins of the house where Colonel John By lived during the construction of the Rideau Canal.
Event Hub: The park frequently hosts major celebrations, including outdoor concerts, Canada Day festivities, and summer garden parties.
Tips and Key Information
The park is open 24 hours a day, making it a popular spot for both early morning jogs and evening sunset strolls.
Most pathways are paved and relatively flat, though some sections near the canal cliffs have steeper inclines.
There are many benches and large shady areas under heritage trees, making it one of the best spots in the capital for a relaxed outdoor lunch.
Seasonal washrooms are typically available near the Mackenzie Avenue entrance during the warmer months.

places.name: 2. Hog’s Back Falls
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/hogs-back-falls-gm673206350-123990529

Hog's Back Park is a stunning natural retreat located where the Rideau Canal splits from the Rideau River. Known officially as Prince of Wales Falls, this site offers a dramatic display of churning water and jagged rock formations, providing a powerful contrast to the calm waters of the nearby canal.
What to See and Do
Historical Engineering: You can observe the Hog's Back Dam, a significant feat of 19th-century engineering that remains a vital part of the canal's water management system.
Hiking and Biking: The park is a major hub for Ottawa’s pathway network, with trails connecting directly to Vincent Massey Park and the Rideau Canal Eastern Pathway.
Tips and Key Information
The park and its lookout points are free to visit and generally open 24 hours a day, though they are most safely enjoyed during daylight hours.
The falls are particularly spectacular in the spring during the snowmelt when the water volume is at its peak, and in the autumn when the surrounding foliage turns vibrant colors.
The park features designated picnic areas and public washrooms (typically open seasonally from May to October).
There is a dedicated parking lot off Hog's Back Road, though it can fill up quickly on sunny weekends and during public holidays.

places.name: 3. Mer Bleue Bog
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/fall-colors-in-ottawa-canada-gm1055332906-281989921

Mer Bleue Bog is one of the most outstanding natural features of the National Capital Region. This 7,700-year-old bog provides a unique glimpse into an ecosystem more typically found in the northern Arctic. It is a designated Ramsar site, meaning it is a wetland of international importance, and it serves as a critical living laboratory for studying climate change and carbon sequestration. The bog is a favorite for nature photographers and hikers due to its stark, haunting beauty and rare flora.
What to See and Do
Boardwalk: The most popular feature is a 1.2-kilometer interpretive boardwalk that loops through the heart of the bog, allowing you to walk over the fragile peatland without damaging the ecosystem.
Unique Flora: Keep an eye out for rare plants like the carnivorous pitcher plant, bog laurel, and cottongrass, which creates a sea of white tufts in early summer.
Bird Watching: The area is a haven for birders, especially during migration seasons. You might spot sandhill cranes, northern harriers, or various species of rare dragonflies.
Trail Network: Beyond the boardwalk, there are over 20 kilometers of multi-use trails perfect for hiking, cross-country skiing, and snowshoeing in the winter.
Tips and Key Information
There is no admission fee to visit the bog or use the trails, and the parking lots are also free of charge.
Visitors must stay on the boardwalk and marked trails. The bog ecosystem is extremely sensitive, and the peat can be deceptively deep and dangerous to walk on directly.
While beautiful year-round, the bog is particularly striking in late May and June when the bog laurel blooms, and in autumn when the larch trees turn a brilliant gold.
Because it is a wetland, mosquitoes and deer flies can be very intense in the early summer months. Bringing insect repellent is highly recommended.
Dogs and other pets are not permitted on the boardwalk or many of the sensitive trails to protect the local wildlife and habitat.

places.name: 4. Petrie Island Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/petrie-island-park-gm1418285437-465027767

Petrie Island Park is a unique natural oasis situated on the Ottawa River in the city's east end. Formed by sand deposited during the last ice age, the islands offer a rare beach-and-bog environment that feels more like a coastal getaway than a typical riverside park.
What to See and Do
Sandy Beaches: The park features two main public beaches (North Beach and East Bay) with expansive sandy shores that are popular for swimming and sunbathing during the summer months.
Nature Trails: A network of low-intensity trails winds through the island’s wetlands and forests. The Turtle Pond area is particularly famous for sightings of painted and snapping turtles.

Wildflower and Interpretive Center: Run by local volunteers, this center provides information on the island’s rare plants and diverse wildlife, including its status as a significant habitat for the endangered Butternut tree.
Water Sports: The sheltered lagoons are ideal for kayaking, canoeing, and stand-up paddleboarding, while the surrounding river is a prime spot for local anglers.
Tips and Key Information
Lifeguards are generally on duty from mid-June through late August. It is always recommended to check the City of Ottawa’s water quality results before swimming.
During the summer season (typically mid-May to Labor Day), there is a paid parking system in effect ($2 per hour or $8 for the day).
Because the park is located within a wetland area, mosquitoes can be quite active, especially in the wooded trail sections. Bringing repellent is highly recommended.
As a low-lying island, the park is prone to flooding in the spring. Some trails and beach areas may be inaccessible during high-water periods in April and May.
he site includes a children's play area, volleyball nets, and a pavilion with washrooms and a small canteen that operates during the peak summer season.

places.name: 5. Ottawa Locks
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/rideau-canal-in-ottawa-canada-autumn-view-on-ottawa-river-alexandra-bridge-and-gm1367884383-438015173

The Rideau Canal, Locks 1 - 8 - Ottawa, commonly known as the Ottawa Locks, is a masterwork of 19th-century engineering located in a dramatic gorge between Parliament Hill and the Fairmont Château Laurier. These eight flight locks connect the Ottawa River to the Rideau Canal, lifting or lowering vessels a total of 24 meters (79 feet).
What to See and Do
Manual Operation: To this day, the massive wooden gates are opened and closed by hand using hand-cranked winches, exactly as they were when the canal opened in 1832.
Step-Like Design: The flight design means the locks are connected directly to one another like a giant staircase of water, providing one of the most photographed vistas in the capital.

Pathway Access: The locks are bordered by paved pathways that are part of the Trans Canada Trail, making it a primary route for cyclists and pedestrians moving between the downtown core and the river.

Historical Context: The site is adjacent to the Bytown Museum, which is housed in the canal's original stone commissariat building, offering further insight into the grueling labor required to build the waterway.
Tips and Key Information
It takes about 45 minutes to an hour for a boat to transit the entire flight of eight locks. Standing on the Plaza Bridge or the lock walls provides an excellent view of the lockmasters at work.
The locks are operational for boat traffic from mid-May to mid-October. During the winter, the water is lowered, but the surrounding pathways remain a popular spot for viewing the frozen landscape.
Walking around the locks and watching the transit process is completely free for the public.
If you are walking from the Ottawa River level up to the Parliament level, be prepared for a significant climb. There are stairs and sloped paths, but the elevation change is substantial.
The area is beautifully illuminated at night, making it a peaceful and romantic spot for an evening walk with views of the lighted Parliament buildings.

places.name: 6. Rideau Falls
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/rideau-falls-in-autumn-gm1346040980-423924913

Rideau Falls Park is a 2.89-hectare urban park where the Rideau River empties into the Ottawa River. The name Rideau (French for curtain) was coined by Samuel de Champlain in 1613, who described the twin 11-meter waterfalls as resembling a shimmering white curtain of water.
What to See and Do
Twin Falls: The waterfalls are divided by Green Island. You can view them from various angles within the park or cross the bridge on Sussex Drive to look directly down into the churning mist.
Green Island Monuments: This small island between the falls houses several significant national commemorations, including:
The Mackenzie-Papineau Monument: Honoring Canadians who fought in the Spanish Civil War.
Commonwealth Air Force Memorial: Commemorating those who died in Canada and neighboring lands during WWII.
The National Artillery Monument.

Tavern on the Falls: This popular seasonal outdoor patio sits right at the edge of the falls. It offers one of the best views in the city for a sunset drink or light snack, though it can get quite busy on warm summer evenings.
Industrial History: Look for the interpreted ruins and old dams. In the 1800s, this area was a bustling industrial hub, with the power of the falls fueled by sawmills and carding mills.
Tips and Key Information
The park is a public National Capital Commission (NCC) site and is free to visit.
The park itself is open 24 hours a day, but it is best visited during daylight hours or at sunset for the best views.

If you visit in late February or early March, you might witness the city’s annual ice blasting. Dynamite is used to break up ice at the base of the falls to prevent spring flooding—a loud and dramatic Ottawa tradition.
There is a small parking lot off Sussex Drive, but it fills up quickly. It’s often easier to walk from the nearby Rideau Hall or take the bus along Sussex Drive.
A scenic walk connects Rideau Falls to the French Embassy and the National Research Council headquarters, offering a more quiet, diplomatic side of the capital.

places.name: 7. Mooney's Bay Park and Beach
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/ottawa-parks-spring-time-gm2217551401-634133367

Mooney's Bay Park and Beach is a massive multi-use waterfront park located along the Rideau River. It is home to one of Ottawa’s most popular summer beaches and serves as a major hub for outdoor recreation and competitive water sports.
What to See and Do

Sue Holloway Fitness Park: The park features an extensive outdoor fitness circuit named after the Olympic medalist, offering various stations for strength and agility training along the scenic riverfront.

Giver 150 Playground: This is one of the largest playgrounds in Canada, built to celebrate the country's 150th anniversary. It is designed in the shape of Canada, with different play structures representing various provinces and territories.
Terry Fox Athletic Facility: Located within the park, this facility includes a professional-grade track and field stadium that hosts numerous local and national sporting events.
Beach and Bay: The expansive sandy beach is a focal point for swimming, beach volleyball, and the annual Ottawa Dragon Boat Festival, which is one of the largest events of its kind in North America.
Tips and Key Information
During the peak summer season (typically mid-May to early September), there is a paid parking requirement ($2.00 per hour or a daily max of $16.00). The lots fill up extremely early on hot weekends.

Lifeguards are generally on duty daily from 12:00 PM to 7:00 PM starting in mid-June. Always check the City of Ottawa’s daily water quality results before swimming, as the river can occasionally have high bacteria levels after heavy rain.
The park is well-equipped with public washrooms, changing rooms, and a seasonal canteen. There are also numerous picnic tables and charcoal BBQ pits available on a first-come, first-served basis.
While the park pathways are pet-friendly, dogs are strictly prohibited from the beach area and the Giver 150 playground to maintain cleanliness and safety.
The park is easily accessible via the O-Train Line 2 (Mooney's Bay Station) followed by a short walk, or by several major bus routes.

places.name: 8. Andrew Haydon Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/ottawa-andrew-hayden-park-scene-at-sunset-gm1168010904-322338592

Andrew Haydon Park is a scenic waterfront destination located along the shores of the Ottawa River in the city's west end. It is widely regarded as one of Ottawa's best spots for family gatherings and outdoor relaxation, offering a mix of manicured lawns, tranquil ponds, and river views.
What to See and Do
Acoustic Bandshell: The park features a prominent outdoor bandshell that hosts community concerts and events throughout the summer months.
Water Features: Visitors can enjoy several man-made ponds and a small waterfall, which serve as a peaceful backdrop for walks and a popular habitat for local geese and ducks.
Family Amenities: The site is well-equipped for families, featuring a large nautical-themed playground and a spacious picnic pavilion.
Birdwatching: Due to its location on the river and its interior ponds, it is a prime location for birdwatching, particularly for spotting migratory waterfowl.
Tips and Key Information
Entry to the park is free, and there are several large, free parking lots available on-site, making it very accessible for those driving.
The park is open daily from 5:00 AM to 11:00 PM.
The park is home to a very large population of Canada geese. While they are a hallmark of the park, be mindful of their presence, especially on the pathways and lawns.
It is connected to the Ottawa River Pathway, allowing for long-distance cycling or walking along the water toward downtown or further west to Britannia Park.
Public washrooms are available on-site, generally operating on a seasonal basis (typically May through October).

places.name: 9. Dows Lake Pavilion
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/dows-lake-pavilion-in-ottawa-canada-gm2153737036-574656153

Dows Lake Pavilion serves as a vibrant year-round hub for outdoor recreation and dining, located at the scenic southern end of the Rideau Canal's western section. It is a primary destination for those looking to experience Ottawa’s waterways, offering a mix of adventure and relaxation with panoramic views of the water.
What to See and Do

Year-Round Recreation: During the warmer months, the marina offers rentals for canoes, kayaks, and paddleboats. In the winter, it transforms into a major gateway for the Rideau Canal Skateway, providing skate rentals and sharpening services.

Diverse Dining: The pavilion houses several restaurants, including Lago Bar & Grill for more formal dining and Malone’s Lakeside Grill for a casual atmosphere, both of which feature patios overlooking the lake.
Tulip Festival Hub: Every May, the pavilion becomes a central site for the Canadian Tulip Festival, as it is adjacent to the Commissioners Park, where hundreds of thousands of tulips are on display.

Gateway to the Arboretum: Its location provides easy access to the Dominion Arboretum and the Ornamental Gardens, making it a perfect starting point for a day of exploring the Central Experimental Farm.
Tips and Key Information

There is a large paid parking lot located directly across from the pavilion on Preston Street. During the Tulip Festival and Winterlude, this lot fills up very early, so public transit or cycling is recommended.
The pavilion is just a short walk from the Carling O-Train station, making it easily accessible from the downtown core.
As a primary staging area for the world’s largest skating rink, the pavilion offers heated change rooms and storage lockers during the winter season.
Summer rentals typically begin in mid-May and run through early October, depending on weather and water conditions.

places.name: 10. Victoria Island
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/ottawa-river-bridges-gm528416104-92949343

Victoria Island is a place of deep historical and spiritual significance, located in the Ottawa River just below Parliament Hill. Known as Asinabka to the Algonquin Anishinaabe people, it has served as a traditional gathering place for indigenous communities for thousands of years.
What to See and Do

Indigenous Heritage: The island is a sacred site where indigenous peoples once met for trade, ceremonies, and celebrations. Today, it remains a focal point for indigenous culture and land claims within the capital.

Industrial Past: In the 19th century, the island was a major industrial hub powered by the Chaudière Falls, hosting sawmills and ironworks. You can still see the remains of heritage industrial buildings, such as the old Bronson Company structures.
Panoramic Views: It offers some of the most unique water-level views of the Parliament Buildings, the Supreme Court, and the Museum of History across the river in Gatineau.
Chaudière Falls: The island provides access to the viewing platforms for the Chaudière Falls, which were recently re-opened to the public through the Zibi development project.
Tips and Key Information

Currently, much of the island is closed to the public for a multi-year remediation and archaeological project led by the National Capital Commission (NCC). While you can walk or cycle across the Portage Bridge to see it, access to the interior of the island is limited.
The nearby Zibi development on the adjacent Chaudière and Albert Islands offers accessible parks and the O hydroelectric facility, which provides interpretive displays about the river's power.
This bridge connects Ottawa to Gatineau and passes directly over the island, making it the best route for cyclists and pedestrians to catch a glimpse of the site.
If you are interested in the falls, visit in the spring during the snowmelt to witness the full, thunderous power of the water.

places.name: 1. Alexandra Bridge
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/panorama-of-gatineau-seen-from-ottawa-gm894020676-247228037

The Alexandra Bridge is an iconic interprovincial cantilever bridge that spans the Ottawa River, connecting Ottawa, Ontario, to Gatineau, Quebec. Completed in 1901, it was once the longest cantilever bridge in Canada and remains a vital and scenic link for commuters and tourists alike.
What to See and Do

Breathtaking Panoramas: The bridge is widely considered to offer the best vantage point in the region for photographing Parliament Hill, the National Gallery of Canada, and the Canadian Museum of History.
Active Transportation Hub: It features a dedicated wooden boardwalk for pedestrians and cyclists, providing a scenic and safe route away from vehicle traffic.
Engineering Heritage: Its intricate steel truss design is a significant example of early 20th-century engineering and has been designated a National Historic Civil Engineering Site.
Sunset Destination: Because of its orientation, it is a premier spot for watching the sunset over the Ottawa River, with the light reflecting beautifully off the surrounding landmark buildings.
Tips and Key Information
The bridge is open 24 hours a day and is free for all pedestrians and cyclists to cross.
Visitors should be aware that the bridge is nearing the end of its life cycle; a major replacement project is planned to begin in the coming years, which may affect future access.
A popular loop for visitors is to cross the Alexandra Bridge from Major's Hill Park into Gatineau, walk along the river toward the Portage Bridge, and cross back into Ottawa near the Supreme Court.
The pedestrian lane is made of wooden planks, which can be slippery when wet or icy, so extra caution is advised during inclement weather.

places.name: 2. Central Experimental Farm
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/central-experimental-farm-in-ottawa-canada-gm1282375222-380127649

The Central Experimental Farm is a unique 426-hectare National Historic Site located in the heart of Ottawa. Established in 1886, it serves as a working research station and a massive urban green space that combines scientific innovation with picturesque landscapes reminiscent of a British country estate.
What to See and Do

Dominion Arboretum: This 35-hectare site features more than 2,000 varieties of trees and shrubs. It offers panoramic views of the Rideau Canal and Dow's Lake, with specific microclimates that allow for the growth of magnolias and rhododendrons.

Ornamental Gardens: An 8-acre showcase including the Macoun Sunken Garden, a rock garden, and world-renowned collections of peonies, lilies, and Preston lilacs. It is a premier destination for photographers and wedding parties.

Canada Agriculture and Food Museum: A family-favorite living museum where visitors can interact with farm animals like horses, cows, and alpacas. It features daily demonstrations, such as cow milking, and exhibitions on the science of food.
Tropical Greenhouse: Housed in a heritage octagonal building from 1928, this site contains a lush collection of tropical plants and is a warm escape during Ottawa's winter months.
Fletcher Wildlife Garden: A volunteer-run organic garden and wildlife habitat that includes a butterfly meadow, an amphibian pond, and a wildflower meadow.
Tips and Key Information
Access to the Arboretum, Ornamental Gardens, and Fletcher Wildlife Garden is free and open from dawn to dusk. The Canada Agriculture and Food Museum requires a paid ticket.
The farm is famous for developing Marquis Wheat, a strain that revolutionized agriculture in the Canadian Prairies, and the Explorer series of winter-hardy roses.
Look out for the annual Friends of the Farm Plant Sale (scheduled for May 10, 2026) and seasonal activities like horse-drawn wagon rides at the museum.
Free parking is available for visitors to the Arboretum and Ornamental Gardens, while paid parking is situated near the museum and administrative buildings.
Most areas are accessible for those with physical limitations, though some garden paths may be uneven.

places.name: 3. Lansdowne Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/aerial-photo-of-the-glebe-gm1442593025-481880162

Lansdowne Park is a 40-acre urban destination in the heart of the Glebe neighborhood. It seamlessly blends historic architecture with modern sports facilities and a vibrant retail urban village. Originally the site of the Central Canada Exhibition, it has been transformed into Ottawa's premier gathering place for sports, culture, and community events.
What to See and Do

Aberdeen Pavilion: Built in 1898, this Cattle Castle is a National Historic Site and the last remaining large-scale exhibition hall of its kind in Canada. It serves as a majestic backdrop for events and the winter farmers' market.
TD Place Stadium & Arena: The home turf for the Ottawa REDBLACKS (CFL), Atlético Ottawa (CPL), and the Ottawa 67’s (OHL). It also hosts major concerts and the popular Ottawa Charge (PWHL) games.

Ottawa Farmers' Market: Held every Sunday year-round. In the summer, the stalls line the Aberdeen Square; during winter (including right now in February), the market moves inside the historic Aberdeen Pavilion.
Great Lawn: A massive green space perfect for picnics, festivals, or just lounging. It features the Cows Fly Home on Sunday sculpture, a whimsical nod to the park's agricultural past.
Lansdowne Skating Court: In the winter, this refrigerated outdoor rink offers free skating. In the summer, it converts into basketball courts.
Tips and Key Information

As of early 2026, a major multi-year revitalization project is underway. You may notice fencing and excavation near the Great Lawn as work begins on the new Event Centre. Most shops, restaurants, and the stadium remain fully operational, but expect some noise and changes to foot traffic.

Parking can be expensive and fills up fast during games. It's best to take OC Transpo (Routes 6 or 7) or cycle via the Rideau Canal pathways. During major RedBlacks games, your game ticket often includes free transit.
The Shops at Lansdowne area features a Cineplex VIP cinema and a huge variety of dining options, from the casual Joey Lansdowne to local favorites like Beandigen Café.
The park is designed to be fully accessible, with ramps and elevators throughout the retail and stadium areas.
The public park areas are generally open from 5:00 AM to 11:00 PM daily.

places.name: 4. Canadian Tire Centre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-canadian-tire-centre-home-of-the-ottawa-senators-in-kanata-canada-gm2173571282-593297504

The Canadian Tire Centre is a premier multi-purpose arena located in Kanata, about 25 kilometers west of downtown Ottawa. Since opening in 1996, it has served as the home ice for the National Hockey League’s Ottawa Senators and is the region's primary venue for large-scale entertainment.
What to See and Do
World-Class Events: Beyond NHL hockey, the arena hosts major global touring acts, from rock concerts and pop stars to family shows like Disney on Ice and professional wrestling events.
Ottawa Hockey Hall of Fame: Located within the building, this space celebrates the rich history of hockey in the Ottawa region, featuring plaques and memorabilia from local legends.

Dining Options: The facility houses several sit-down restaurants and bars, including Bert's and the Brookstreet Lounge, alongside numerous concession stands offering standard arena fare and local favorites.
Tips and Key Information
During Senators games and major concerts, OC Transpo operates special 400-series event buses from various park-and-ride lots across the city, which is often faster than driving.
There are extensive on-site parking lots (Lots 1 through 9), but they can be slow to exit after a sold-out event. Valet parking is often available for a premium fee near the main entrance.
The venue enforces a strict bag policy; generally, only small clutches are permitted, and all guests must pass through metal detectors upon entry.
The arena offers a dedicated sensory room for guests with neurodivergent needs who may require a quiet break from the noise and lights of the main bowl.

places.name: 5. The Glebe
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-glebe-neighborhood-sign-in-ottawa-canada-gm2154798421-575648423

The Glebe is one of Ottawa’s most desirable and historic neighborhoods, offering a village-in-the-city feel just south of the downtown core. Bordered by the scenic Rideau Canal, it is a pedestrian-friendly enclave known for its high-end boutiques, lush parks, and stunning Victorian and Edwardian architecture.
What to See and Do

Bank Street Promenade: The neighborhood's main artery is lined with independent businesses. You can find everything from rare vinyl at Compact Music to artisanal kitchenware at J.D. Adam Kitchen Company.

Rideau Canal & Patterson Creek: The canal provides a scenic backdrop for year-round recreation, including skating in winter and cycling in summer. Patterson Creek Park is a local favorite for its tranquil willow-lined inlet and stone bridges.

Great Glebe Garage Sale: Held annually in late May, this massive community event attracts thousands of visitors for a neighborhood-wide treasure hunt that doubles as a fundraiser for the Ottawa Food Bank.
Lansdowne Park: While mentioned previously as a destination itself, Lansdowne Park acts as the southern anchor of the Glebe, hosting the weekly farmers' market and professional sports events.
Irene's Pub: An Ottawa institution since 1985, this cozy pub is famous for its live music, extensive whiskey collection, and intimate, wood-accented atmosphere.
Kettleman's Bagel Co.: A 24-hour favorite known for its traditional Montreal-style wood-fired bagels. You can watch the bakers in action at any time of day or night.
The Rowan: A sophisticated yet relaxed gastropub offering seasonal British-inspired dishes like fish and chips, steak frites, and savory tarts.
Erling's Variety: Perfect for groups or date nights, this spot specializes in creative small plates and shareable meals in a modern, airy setting.
Tips and Key Information

Street parking is notoriously difficult to find on weekends. Your best bet is the underground parking at Lansdowne Park or the municipal lot on Second Avenue. If you can, take the #6 or #7 bus—they run directly down Bank Street.

For the best experience, start at Bank Street and Patterson Creek, then walk south toward Lansdowne. The side streets (like Clemow and Monkland) feature some of the city's most impressive residential heritage homes.
This is arguably the most dog-friendly neighborhood in Ottawa. Many shops have water bowls outside, and you’ll find plenty of pups at the nearby Central Experimental Farm or walking along the Canal.

During the Canadian Tulip Festival (May) or Winterlude (February), the Glebe becomes extremely busy. If you’re visiting during these times, expect long wait times at popular spots like Kettleman’s or the local cafes.
If the main Bank Street cafes are too crowded, duck into Little Victory Bakery or Wild Oat for high-quality, made-from-scratch treats that locals swear by.

places.name: 6. National Arts Centre
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/nac-in-ottawa-display-work-of-metis-artist-for-indigenous-peoples-day-gm987943592-267896826

The National Arts Centre is Canada's premier bilingual performing arts hub, situated along the scenic Rideau Canal in downtown Ottawa. Since its opening in 1969 as a Centennial project, it has become a beacon for the arts, showcasing world-class theater, dance, and music across its four distinct stages.
What to See and Do

Architectural Grandeur: The building is a striking example of Brutalist architecture, recently revitalized with a magnificent glass atrium that offers panoramic views of Confederation Square and Parliament Hill.
Performance Variety: It is the home of the NAC Orchestra and hosts everything from Broadway tours and contemporary dance to indigenous theater and French-language productions.
Public Spaces: Beyond the theaters, the NAC features open public spaces perfect for working or relaxing, often hosting free community events, workshops, and pop-up performances.
Culinary Experience: The center is home to 1 Elgin, a restaurant that highlights Canadian ingredients and seasonal flavors, often featuring a rotating cast of guest chefs from across the country.
Tips and Key Information
Situated at 1 Elgin Street, the NAC is easily accessible by foot from major downtown hotels or via the Parliament or Rideau O-Train stations.
Look up at the Kipnes Lantern, the three-story glass tower that displays digital art and information about performances taking place inside and across Canada.
During the winter, the NAC provides a perfect warm-up spot for skaters on the Rideau Canal, with easy access to the ice just steps away from the building.
The box office is open daily, but it is highly recommended to book tickets for major performances in advance through their website.
The facility is fully accessible, offering elevators, accessible seating in all theaters, and assistive listening devices for patrons.

places.name: 7. Sparks Street
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sparks-street-mall-ottawa-canada-in-summer-gm852281202-140232115

Sparks Street is a historic pedestrian mall in the heart of downtown Ottawa, just a block south of Parliament Hill. Converted into a permanent outdoor mall in 1967, it was the first of its kind in Canada and remains a vibrant public space known for its heritage architecture, diverse dining, and major seasonal festivals.
What to See and Do
Iconic Landmarks: You can find the famous Ottawa Sign for a perfect photo opportunity, alongside historic buildings that house unique shops like Canada's Four Corners.

Dining and Nightlife: The mall is lined with numerous patios and restaurants, ranging from the European-inspired Bier Markt to cozy pubs and cafes, making it a popular spot for both weekday business lunches and evening socializing.
Tips and Key Information
Since the street is closed to vehicles between Elgin and Lyon Streets, it offers a relaxed walking environment, though cyclists are permitted and often share the space.
In the winter, the street is beautifully decorated with lights, and many restaurants set up heated patios. In the summer, the area is bustling with street performers and outdoor market stalls.
The mall is highly accessible by public transit, located just steps away from several O-Train Line 1 stations, including Parliament and Lyon stations.
While the street itself is always accessible, many of the independent boutiques and gift shops maintain standard business hours, often closing earlier on evenings when there are no major events.
The entire pedestrian mall is flat and paved, making it fully accessible for individuals with mobility devices or families with strollers.

places.name: 8. Winterlude
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/rideau-canal-ice-skating-rink-in-winter-ottawa-gm1129050416-298114255

Winterlude (Bal de Neige) is Ottawa’s flagship winter festival, typically held during the first three weeks of February. Established in 1979, it celebrates Canada's northern climate and culture, transforming the capital into a giant playground of ice and snow.
What to See and Do
Rideau Canal Skateway: The world’s largest skating rink is the heart of Winterlude. Stretching 7.8 kilometers, it features food kiosks selling BeaverTails and hot chocolate directly on the ice.

Snowflake Kingdom: Located across the river in Gatineau's Jacques-Cartier Park, this is a massive snow playground featuring giant slides, snow sculptures, and activities designed specifically for children and families.
