Ice Dragon Boat Festival: A unique spectacle where participants race dragon boats equipped with skates on the frozen waters of Dows Lake.
Sparks Street & Confederation Park: These areas host the International Ice Carving Challenge, where world-class artists transform massive blocks of ice into intricate, crystalline masterpieces.
Tips and Key Information
In recent years, fluctuating temperatures have affected the opening of the Skateway. Always check the NCC’s ice conditions online before heading out with your skates.
During the festival, a free shuttle service (the Sno-Bus) typically runs between the main sites (Confederation Park, Snowflake Kingdom, and the Canal), making it much easier to skip the parking hunt.

Ottawa winters are notoriously biting, especially near the river. Wear moisture-wicking base layers, wool socks, and a windproof outer shell. Hand and toe warmers are highly recommended for long days outside.
Visit the ice sculptures at night. They are professionally lit with multicolored LEDs, offering a completely different (and often more magical) experience than during the day.
Expect long lines at the kiosks on the Canal. If you want a shorter wait, try the permanent BeaverTails stand in the ByWard Market, though there's something special about eating one with skates on.

places.name: 9. Canadian Tulip Festival
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/alexandra-bridge-and-peace-tower-in-the-canadian-tulip-festival-gm145997552-6137356

The Canadian Tulip Festival is a world-renowned event held annually in May, transforming Ottawa into a sea of vibrant color. The festival is a symbol of international friendship, originating from a gift of 100,000 tulip bulbs from the Dutch Royal Family in 1945 to thank Canada for providing them refuge during WWII and for the liberation of the Netherlands.
What to See and Do
Commissioners Park: This is the festival's epicenter at Dows Lake, featuring over 300,000 tulips in dozens of garden beds. It’s the largest single display of tulips in the world.
Blacklight Boardwalk: Every evening, this boardwalk transforms into a glowing experience with ultraviolet lighting that reveals the hidden patterns on the tulips that pollinators see.
Movies in the Park: Free outdoor movie screenings are typically held daily in the afternoons and evenings at Commissioners Park.
Tulip Legacy Tour: You can take a self-guided tour using QR codes throughout the park to learn about the history of the gift and the individual varieties of tulips.
Tips and Key Information
In 2026, the festival is scheduled to run from May 8 to May 18.
Early mornings (before 10:00 AM) or weekdays are the best times to avoid massive crowds and get unobstructed photos.
Admission to Commissioners Park and most of the programming is free, though some specific guided tours or premium events may require tickets.

Parking near Dows Lake is extremely limited and strictly enforced by bylaw officers. It is highly recommended to take the O-Train Line 2 to Dows Lake Station, which is just a short walk from the main beds.
Ottawa weather in May is unpredictable. Wear layers and bring a windproof/waterproof jacket, as the lake breeze can be quite chilly even on sunny days.

places.name: 10. Gatineau Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/gatineau-national-capital-region-in-the-fall-gm1486089407-511920698

Gatineau Park is a sprawling 361-square-kilometer conservation area located just 15 minutes north of downtown Ottawa. It serves as the region's primary year-round destination for outdoor adventure, offering a rugged landscape of Precambrian hills, sparkling lakes, and dense forests that feel worlds away from the city.
What to See and Do

Scenic Lookouts: The park is famous for its panoramic views from the Eardley Escarpment. The most popular spots are Champlain Lookout, which offers a sweeping vista of the Ottawa Valley, and Pink Lake, a rare meromictic lake known for its stunning turquoise water.

Mackenzie King Estate: This historic country estate was the summer home of Canada's longest-serving Prime Minister. Visitors can explore the landscaped gardens, the charming cottages, and the Abbey Ruins—a collection of architectural fragments King gathered from various demolished buildings.

Extensive Trail Network: The park features over 183 kilometers of hiking trails and 90 kilometers of mountain bike trails. In the winter, it transforms into one of North America's premier cross-country skiing destinations, with over 200 kilometers of groomed trails and cozy heating huts.
Wolf Trail: For those seeking a more challenging hike, this trail leads to the Luskville Falls or the Tawadina Lookout, providing some of the most dramatic terrain and rewarding views in the park.
Tips and Key Information

Most of the park’s scenic parkways (Gatineau, Champlain, and Fortune Lake) are closed to motor vehicles for much of the week to prioritize cyclists and pedestrians. Always check the National Capital Commission (NCC) website for current vehicle access schedules before driving up.
While entry to the park is free, parking fees are required at popular beach areas (Meech Lake, Philippe Lake) and at the Mackenzie King Estate during the summer months.
If you plan to explore this marble cave system near Philippe Lake, bring a flashlight and be prepared for your feet to get wet, as there is often standing water inside.

The park is the busiest during the month of October when the autumn colors peak. During this time, the NCC often operates a free shuttle service from downtown Ottawa to help manage the extreme traffic volumes.

Start your visit at the Gatineau Park Visitor Centre in Chelsea. The staff can provide trail maps, up-to-date conditions, and information on the park’s unique flora and fauna, including the endangered species that live within the Eardley Escarpment.

places.name: 1. Château Frontenac
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/dufferin-terrace-boardwalk-by-the-st-lawrence-river-in-downtown-quebec-city-canada-gm1468665581-500126389

The Fairmont Le Château Frontenac is not just a hotel; it is the soul of Quebec City’s skyline. Perched dramatically on Cap Diamant, it holds the Guinness World Record as the most photographed hotel in the world.

Opened in 1893, the Château was the brainchild of William Van Horne, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway. His goal was simple: to create a destination so luxurious that wealthy travelers would take his trains just to stay there. American architect Bruce Price designed the hotel in the Châteauesque style, drawing inspiration from the castles of France’s Loire Valley. It is named after Louis de Buade, Count of Frontenac, a flamboyant governor of New France who successfully defended the colony against British attacks in the late 17th century.
What to See and Do

Take a Guided Tour: Since the hotel is private property, a guided tour is the only way to see off-limits areas like the executive boardrooms and the grand ballrooms. Tours are led by guides portraying historical figures such as Elizabeth Taylor (the guide, not the actress) or the sister of Sarah Bernhardt. Tours run roughly 60 minutes and typically start at the Frontenac kiosk on Dufferin Terrace.

Sugar Chic Experience: If you visit during the spring (late February through April), look for the Château des Sucres program. The hotel celebrates maple season with specialized mixology workshops at Bar 1608 and pastry demonstrations where you can learn the secrets of the hotel's famous desserts.
Afternoon Tea at Place Dufferin: You’ll be served a gourmet tower of sandwiches, scones with Devonshire cream, and local jams, all while looking out over the St. Lawrence River.

Cocktails at Bar 1608: Visit this circular brass bar for a mixology masterpiece. It’s famous for its cheese cellar—ask the server to pair a local Quebec cider or wine with a selection of artisanal cheeses.

Au 1884 Toboggan Slide: From mid-December to mid-March, this is the main attraction. You buy your ticket at the kiosk, drag your own wooden sled up the ramp, and plummet 250 meters at speeds reaching 70 km/h.

Saint-Louis Forts and Châteaux: Directly underneath the wooden planks of the terrace lies a hidden archaeological crypt. You can descend into the ruins of the original 1620 residence of the French and British governors. This is a Parks Canada site; guided tours are available from May to October, with self-guided options often available in the off-season.

Funicular: Located at the north end of the terrace, this cliffside elevator has been in operation since 1879. It’s the easiest (and most scenic) way to travel between the Upper Town (Château) and the Lower Town (Petit Champlain).

Quebec-Lévis Ferry: For less than $5, you can hop on the ferry at the bottom of the hill. It provides the absolute best panoramic view of the Château Frontenac towering over the cliffside. The 12-minute crossing is especially magical at night when the hotel is fully illuminated.
Tips and Key Information
You don’t need to be a guest to see the inside. Guided tours are led daily by characters in period costume who share the castle's secrets.
Named for the year Quebec City was founded, the 1608 Bar features one of the top cheese cellars in Canada. It’s the perfect spot for a cocktail by the fireplace.
The best photo of the Château isn't from the terrace, but from the Lévis Ferry or the Pierre-Dugua-de-Mons Terrace in the nearby Battlefields Park.

places.name: 2. Old Québec
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/cobblestone-roads-of-old-town-quebec-city-in-canada-gm855055012-140716605

Old Quebec (Vieux-Québec) is a UNESCO World Heritage treasure and the only fortified city in North America. Walking through its gates feels like stepping into 17th-century Europe, with narrow cobblestone streets, stone houses, and towering spires overlooking the St. Lawrence River.
What to See and Do

Walk the Fortifications: Stretching nearly 4.6 kilometers around the Upper Town, the Fortifications of Québec National Historic Site offers a unique perspective on the city's military history. You can walk along the top of the walls for great views of the surrounding neighborhoods.

Explore Place Royale: Often called the birthplace of French America, this picturesque square is where Samuel de Champlain founded the city in 1608. It is home to the Notre-Dame-des-Victoires Church, the oldest stone church in North America.

Stroll the Dufferin Terrace: This massive wooden boardwalk wraps around the Fairmont Le Château Frontenac. It’s a favorite spot for locals and tourists alike to watch street performers, enjoy the river breeze, or take a high-speed ride on the historic toboggan slide in winter.

Visit the Museum of Civilization: Located in the Lower Town, the Musée de la civilisation features immersive exhibits on Quebec’s history and culture, blending traditional artifacts with modern, interactive displays.
Tips and Key Information

The district is defined by steep hills, stairs, and uneven cobblestones. To save your legs, take the Funiculaire du Vieux-Québec to travel between the Lower Town (Petit Champlain) and Upper Town (Château Frontenac).
If you want to photograph the streets without the crowds, head to Quartier Petit Champlain before 9:00 AM. Most shops open at 10:00 AM, but the streets are beautiful and peaceful in the early light.

While there are many restaurants within the walls, they fill up quickly during peak tourist season (July–August) and the Winter Carnival. Consider making reservations at popular spots like Aux Anciens Canadiens well in advance.
Parking within Old Quebec is extremely limited and expensive. It is much easier to park in a lot outside the walls or use the RTC bus system (the 800 and 801 lines are very frequent).

Old Quebec is a year-round destination. It is famous for its elaborate Christmas decorations in December and the vibrant Quebec Winter Carnival in February, but be prepared for freezing temperatures and heavy snow.

places.name: 3. Plains of Abraham
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/martello-tower-on-plains-of-abraham-gm2237961585-653029628

The Plains of Abraham is Canada's first national historic park and one of the world's most significant urban parks. This vast green space was the site of the 1759 battle between the French and British empires that decided the fate of North America, and today it serves as a central park for Quebec City residents and visitors. The park offers a blend of heavy history and year-round outdoor recreation across its 98 hectares.
What to See and Do

Plains of Abraham Museum: This is the best starting point for visitors. It features an immersive Battles exhibition that uses 360-degree projections to put you in the middle of the historical conflict, along with archaeological artifacts found on the grounds.

Joan of Arc Garden: A masterpiece of landscape architecture, this sunken garden combines classical French and English styles. It is famous for its vibrant floral displays and the equestrian statue of Joan of Arc at its center.

Active Recreation: In the winter, the park features a refrigerated skating rink and miles of groomed cross-country skiing and snowshoeing trails. In the summer, the Great Plains host massive events like the Festival d’été de Québec (FEQ), one of the largest outdoor music festivals in North America.
Martello Towers: You can visit the historic defensive towers built by the British in the early 19th century. Tower 1 often hosts interactive exhibits about the life of a soldier during that era.
Tips and Key Information

For a classic local experience, grab some cheese and bread from a bakery in the nearby Saint-Jean-Baptiste neighborhood and head to the grassy slopes near the Cap-aux-Diamants for a picnic with views of the St. Lawrence River.
The park is massive. If you don't want to walk the entire length, the Abraham's Bus provides a seasonal shuttle service during the summer months that stops at the main points of interest.
While the museum and certain tours have admission fees, access to the park grounds, the Joan of Arc Garden, and the various walking trails is free and open 24 hours a day.
Some stairs and steep paths, like the Gilmour Hill path, may be closed or very icy during the peak winter months (January–March), so check trail conditions at the museum if you plan on hiking.

places.name: 4. Citadelle of Québechttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/fort-gm175527056-20919279
body: The Citadelle of Québec is the largest British-built fortress in North America and remains an active garrison of the Royal 22e Régiment. Perched atop Cap Diamant, this star-shaped fortification is an integral part of the city's defensive walls and offers a deep dive into Canada's military heritage.
What to See and Do
Changing of the Guard: During the summer months, visitors can witness this traditional ceremony featuring the regimental mascot, a goat named Batisse.

Royal 22e Régiment Museum: Located within the walls, the museum displays a vast collection of medals, uniforms, and artifacts that trace the history of the regiment from the 17th century to modern-day missions.

Governor General’s Residence: The fortress serves as the secondary official residence of the Governor General of Canada; guided tours often include access to the state rooms when they are not in use for official functions.
Panoramic Ramparts: A walk along the fortifications provides some of the most dramatic views of the St. Lawrence River and the rooftops of Old Quebec.
Tips and Key Information
To see the interior of the Citadelle, you must join an official guided tour, as it is still a working military base. Tours are available year-round, but schedules vary by season.
The main entrance is located at the end of Côte de la Citadelle, near the Parliament Building. It is a bit of an uphill walk from the center of Old Quebec, so plan accordingly.
During certain times of the year, special lantern-lit night tours are offered, focusing on the more eerie and mysterious legends of the fortress.
Because it is an active military site, be prepared for security screenings at the gate and follow your guide's instructions regarding photography in restricted areas.

places.name: 5. Notre Dame De Québec Basilica Cathedral
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/interior-of-notre-dame-de-quebec-basilica-cathedral-quebec-city-quebec-gm1029264920-275844461

The La Basilique-Cathédrale Notre-Dame de Québec is a monumental pillar of North American history, standing as the oldest Catholic parish in North America. Founded in 1647, this UNESCO World Heritage monument is the mother church of the first Catholic diocese in Canada and the United States, serving as the spiritual heart of Old Quebec for over 350 years.
What to See and Do

Architectural Highlights: The cathedral is a masterpiece of Neoclassical design, though its interior leans heavily into gleaming Baroque splendor. Despite enduring multiple fires and shellings throughout history, it has been faithfully restored to its mid-19th-century grandeur.
Gilded Altar: Visitors are often struck by the spectacular golden baldachin that arches over the altar, designed as a miniature homage to the one found in St. Peter’s Basilica in Rome.

Holy Door: This is one of the cathedral's most significant spiritual features; it is the only Holy Door in the Americas and only the eighth in the entire world. It was gifted by the Vatican in 2014 to mark the parish's 350th anniversary.
Casavant Organs: The church houses three impressive Casavant organs, including a massive 1927 model with 94 stops, which fills the nave with incredible sound during services.
Historic Crypt: This solemn space serves as the final resting place for nearly all the bishops of Quebec, as well as four governors of New France.

Tomb of St. François de Laval: The cathedral houses the funerary chapel and tomb of the first bishop of Quebec, who was canonized in 2014. He is a central figure in the religious history of the continent.
Tips and Key Information
The cathedral is currently open to the public on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays from 9:00 AM to 3:00 PM. It is closed to visitors from Thursday through Sunday.
Be aware that the Holy Door is traditionally sealed with a red ribbon and is only opened during Jubilee years or special occasions designated by the Pope.
Even for non-religious visitors, the cathedral is a recommended spot for its calming atmosphere and stunning stained-glass windows produced by the Meyer house of Austria.
The facility is partially accessible, offering a wheelchair-accessible entrance and restrooms for visitors with mobility needs.

places.name: 6. Terrasse Dufferin
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/terrasse-dufferin-quebec-city-gm504681439-44977486

Dufferin Terrace (Terrasse Dufferin) is a world-famous wooden boardwalk that serves as the balcony of Quebec City. Built in 1879, it wraps around the base of the Fairmont Le Château Frontenac, offering spectacular panoramic views of the St. Lawrence River, the island of Orléans, and the Lower Town.
What to See and Do

Historical Foundations: Beneath the wooden planks of the terrace lies the Saint-Louis Forts and Châteaux National Historic Site, where you can explore the archaeological remains of the residences used by French and British governors.
Iconic Recreation: During the winter months, the terrace hosts the historic Les Glissades de la Terrasse, a massive wooden toboggan slide where sleds can reach speeds of up to 70 km/h.
Atmospheric Hub: In the summer, the promenade is a lively stage for street performers, musicians, and artists, making it the perfect spot for a scenic stroll at any time of day or night.
Funicular: Located at the north end of the terrace, this cliffside elevator provides a quick and scenic link between the Upper Town and the historic Quartier Petit Champlain below.

Gazebos and Monuments: Several green-and-white roofed gazebos dot the boardwalk, providing shade and seating. You will also find the grand monument dedicated to Samuel de Champlain, the founder of Quebec City.
River Watching: Use the various binocular stations along the railing to watch the massive cruise ships and local ferries navigate the narrows of the St. Lawrence River.
Tips and Key Information
The terrace is a public space and never closes, making it a fantastic spot for sunrise photography or a quiet late-night walk to see the Château Frontenac illuminated.
If you want to visit the ruins underneath, enter through the small glass kiosks located on the terrace. Access is managed by Parks Canada and is typically available from spring through autumn.
The wind off the river can be biting in the winter. If you plan on trying the toboggan slide, make sure your hat and scarf are secured tightly.
For the best shot that includes both the boardwalk and the full height of the Château Frontenac, walk all the way to the southern end of the terrace toward the Governors' Garden.

places.name: 7. Place Royale
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/place-royale-quebec-canada-gm1428118874-471752824

Place Royale is often described as the birthplace of French America, marking the exact spot where Samuel de Champlain founded the city in 1608. This cobblestone square in the Lower Town is a living museum of 17th and 18th-century architecture, having been meticulously restored to its New France-era appearance.
What to See and Do

Notre-Dame-des-Victoires Church: The centerpiece of the square is the oldest stone church in North America. Visitors often notice the small model of a ship hanging from the ceiling, a traditional votive offering for the protection of sailors.
Bust of Louis XIV: A bronze statue of the Sun King stands in the center of the plaza, commemorating the monarch who helped the colony flourish during the 17th century.

Fresque des Québécois: Just a few steps from the main square, this massive trompe-l'œil mural depicts 400 years of Quebec's history, featuring key figures like Jacques Cartier and Lord Dufferin integrated into a realistic stone facade.
Tips and Key Information
This is one of the most picturesque spots in Canada. For shots without crowds, aim to arrive before 10:00 AM, as it is a major stop for guided walking tours.
The square is home to several cozy cafes and bistros with outdoor seating. La Maison Smith is a local favorite for grabbing a coffee or pastry while soaking in the historic atmosphere.

While the square is pedestrian-only, the cobblestones can be very uneven. Visitors with mobility concerns may find the terrain challenging, though the Funiculaire provides easy access from the Upper Town to the Lower Town nearby.

If you want to dive deeper into the archaeology of the site, this museum offers interactive exhibits that illustrate the life of the early settlers and the merchants who transformed the square into a bustling trade hub.

places.name: 8. Montmorency Falls Parkhttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/montmorency-falls-gm140377685-2586886
body: Montmorency Falls Park (Parc de la Chute-Montmorency) is a breathtaking natural monument located just 15 minutes from Old Quebec. The waterfall itself is 83 meters high—a full 30 meters taller than Niagara Falls—dominating the landscape where the Montmorency River cascades into the St. Lawrence. The park offers a variety of ways to experience the sheer power of the water, ranging from leisurely strolls to high-adrenaline activities.
What to See and Do
Suspension Bridge: A pedestrian bridge spans directly over the crest of the falls, providing a dizzying and heart-pounding view of the water plummeting into the basin below.
Panoramic Staircase: For those looking for a workout, a 487-step wooden staircase clings to the side of the cliff, offering multiple landing platforms for photography at different heights.
Cable Car: A gondola carries visitors from the base to the top of the cliff, offering a comfortable way to enjoy the sweeping views of the falls, the Île d'Orléans, and the Quebec City skyline.
Via Ferrata and Zipline: Thrill-seekers can traverse the rock face on three different climbing circuits or fly across the falls on a 300-meter double zipline.
Tips and Key Information

There are two main entry points: the Bottom of the Falls (near the boulevard) and the Top of the Falls (near Manoir Montmorency). Parking at the top is generally more convenient for accessing the bridge and cable car quickly.
In the winter, the mist from the falls freezes into a massive ice cone known as the Sugar Loaf (Pain de Sucre) at the base. It is a popular spot for winter hiking and even ice climbing.

Located at the top of the falls, this historic manor houses a gift shop and a restaurant with a terrace. It's an excellent spot for a meal with a view, though reservations are recommended during peak season.
During the summer and special events, the falls are often illuminated at night with colored lights, creating a completely different atmosphere than the daytime visit.
The cable car and the paths around the Manor and the top of the falls are wheelchair accessible, though the panoramic staircase is not.

places.name: 9. Fortifications of Québec National Historic Site
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/quebec-city-walls-gm155381114-21667596

The Fortifications of Québec National Historic Site is a massive defensive system that encircles the Upper Town of Old Quebec. As the only remaining fortified city in North America north of Mexico, these walls, gates, and bastions are a testament to nearly three centuries of military history, originally built by the French and later strengthened by the British to defend against American invasions.
What to See and Do
Scenic Ramparts: The site features 4.6 kilometers of stone walls that visitors can walk along, offering a unique birds-eye view of the historic district on one side and the modern city on the other.

Gates of the City: You can explore the iconic gates, such as Porte Saint-Louis and Porte Saint-Jean, which serve as the grand entrances to the Old City and provide excellent backdrops for photography.
Artillery Park: This sector of the fortifications includes historic barracks, a former cartridge factory, and a massive scale model of the city as it appeared in the early 19th century.
Governor's Promenade: This scenic boardwalk connects the Dufferin Terrace to the Plains of Abraham, hugging the cliffside and providing dramatic vistas of the St. Lawrence River.
Tips and Key Information
Begin your exploration at the Frontenac Kiosk on Dufferin Terrace or the Saint-Louis Gate. Parks Canada staff are often available at these locations to provide maps and historical context.
While walking the majority of the walls and ramparts is free, certain areas and specialized guided tours—such as the Fortifications and Powder Magazine tour—require a modest admission fee.
The walking paths on top of the walls are generally accessible year-round, but they can be quite slippery in the winter; sturdy footwear with good grip is highly recommended during the snowy months.
Look for the Xplorers program booklets for children, which offer fun challenges and activities to help younger visitors engage with the military history of the site.

places.name: 10. Quartier Petit Champlain
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/tourists-shopping-on-the-quartier-du-petit-champlain-street-quebec-city-old-town-in-gm1454775691-490317055

Quartier Petit Champlain is widely considered one of the most beautiful and historic commercial districts in North America. Located at the foot of the cliff beneath the Château Frontenac, this pedestrian-only neighborhood features narrow cobblestone streets lined with restored stone houses that date back to the 17th century.

Originally a small riverside village for fur traders and merchants, it has transformed into a vibrant hub for local artisans, boutique shopping, and intimate dining. The district is particularly famous for its Old World European atmosphere, which is enhanced by flowering balconies in the summer and elaborate light displays during the winter months.
What to See and Do

Breakneck Steps (Escalier Casse-Cou): These are the city's oldest stairs, built in 1635. They provide a dramatic entrance to the district from the Upper Town and offer a classic vantage point for photography of the narrow street below.

Artisanal Boutiques: The area is strictly managed to favor local talent. You can find unique Quebec-made goods, including hand-carved wooden sculptures, high-end leather products, and jewelry from local designers.

La Fresque du Petit-Champlain: This large-scale mural depicts the history of the neighborhood, including the life of the early inhabitants and the various stages of the district's development over the centuries.
Cozy Eateries: The district is home to several charming bistros and cabanes à sucre (sugar shacks) where you can sample traditional Quebecois treats like maple taffy on snow.
Tips and Key Information
For a scenic arrival that avoids the steep stairs, take the Funiculaire du Vieux-Québec from Dufferin Terrace. It drops you off directly in the heart of the Petit Champlain district.
To experience the magic of the cobblestone streets without the heavy tourist crowds, try to visit before 10:00 AM or after 7:00 PM when the day-trippers have departed.

If you visit during the holidays, this is the most decorated spot in the city. The lights and Christmas trees make it feel like a scene from a holiday film, though the cobblestones can become quite icy.
Despite its beauty, the terrain is uneven. Sturdy walking shoes are essential for navigating the cobblestones and the various sets of stairs that connect different levels of the neighborhood.

places.name: 1. Musée de la Civilisation
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/facade-of-the-museum-of-civilization-at-dawn-gm1181467919-331383031

The Museum of Civilization (Musée de la civilisation) is the most popular museum in Quebec City, known for its participatory and highly interactive approach to history and culture. Located in the heart of the Old Port, it blends sleek modern architecture by Moshe Safdie with the historic vaults of the 18th-century Maison Chevalier, creating a space where visitors literally walk over layers of the city's archaeological past. The museum typically hosts about ten original exhibitions at a time, ranging from deep historical dives to global pop culture.
What to See and Do

This Is Our Story: A major permanent exhibition that explores the history and current realities of the 11 First Nations and Inuit peoples in Quebec through 450 significant objects and personal narratives.
In Other Words, Québec: The museum's largest-ever exhibition, which uses six themed zones to tell the story of how Quebec society has evolved from its roots to the present day.

Titanic: The Human Story: A blockbuster visiting exhibition (scheduled through March 2026) that focuses on the personal lives of passengers and crew through nearly 200 authentic artifacts and room recreations.
My Place (Ma Maison): A dedicated, whimsical discovery house designed for children aged 3 to 8, featuring secret passages, a photo booth, and oversized furniture.
Grand Staircase: A signature architectural feature that acts as an urban promenade, inviting people to relax and take in the natural light and views of the river.
Tips and Key Information
The museum is a favorite retreat on rainy or snowy days, which can lead to long wait times. For the best experience, visit on a weekday morning or book your tickets online in advance.
Admission often includes access to 45-minute guided tours for specific exhibitions. Check the information desk upon arrival to register for the next available slot.
The second-floor Espace saveurs cafe offers gourmet sandwiches, pastries, and hot meals. In warmer months, the outdoor courtyard provides beautiful views of the St. Lawrence River.
The museum is fully accessible via ramps and elevators. Families can also borrow strollers or wheelchairs free of charge at the cloakroom.
Keep an eye out for the large New France-era boat integrated into the entrance floor—it was discovered during the excavation of the site before the museum was built.

places.name: 2. Musée National des Beaux-Arts du Québec (MNBAQ)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/quebec-fine-arts-museum-gm1248546887-363658642

The Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec (MNBAQ) is a world-class art complex situated on the edge of the Plains of Abraham. It consists of four distinct pavilions that represent a bridge between the city’s past and its modern artistic vision. It is the premier institution for the study and promotion of Quebec art from the 17th century to the present day.
What to See and Do

Pierre Lassonde Pavilion: The newest addition (opened in 2016), this glass-and-steel masterpiece is the museum's grand entrance. It houses contemporary art collections and features a stunning cantilevered staircase that has become a favorite spot for architecture photography.

Charles Baillairgé Pavilion: Originally built as a prison in the 19th century, this historic stone building now houses galleries. You can still see some of the original jail cells, which have been preserved to provide a hauntingly beautiful contrast to the art.
Gérard Morisset Pavilion: The first building of the complex, this pavilion focuses on historical art, featuring grand galleries dedicated to the masters of Quebecois painting and sculpture.
Central Pavilion: This serves as the glass-walled link between the various wings, offering panoramic views of the park.

Inuit Art Collection: The MNBAQ holds the Brousseau Collection, one of the most significant collections of Inuit art in the world, featuring over 2,000 works that showcase the spiritual and daily life of the North.
Sculpture Garden: Surrounding the museum are several large-scale outdoor sculptures integrated into the landscape of the Plains of Abraham, perfect for a contemplative walk.
Jean Paul Riopelle’s L'Hommage à Rosa Luxemburg: This monumental triptych, stretching over 40 meters, is one of the museum's crown jewels and a must-see for fans of abstract expressionism.
Tips and Key Information
The museum is generally closed on Mondays. On Wednesday evenings, admission is typically half-price after 5:00 PM.
Because the museum is located directly on the Plains of Abraham, it’s the perfect indoor break during a long day of hiking or cross-country skiing in the park.
Don't miss the tunnel connecting the Lassonde Pavilion to the older buildings; it often features immersive light or sound installations.

places.name: 3. Morrin Centre
body: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Morrin_Centre,_Quebec,_Canada.jpg

The Morrin Centre is one of Quebec City's most fascinating hidden gems, serving as a vibrant English-language cultural hub in a predominantly French-speaking city. This National Historic Site has lived multiple lives over its 200-year history: first as a grim public jail, then as the city's first English-language college, and finally as the home of the oldest learned society in Canada.
What to See and Do

Victorian Library: Step into a room that feels like a scene from a film, featuring floor-to-ceiling wooden bookshelves, a winding staircase, and a collection of over 27,000 books, some dating back to the 16th century.
Discovery Tour: Walk through sinister iron-barred jail cells and decipher the graffiti carved into the original floorboards by 19th-century inmates.

Chemistry Lab: Explore a remarkably preserved 19th-century science laboratory from the building's days as Morrin College, complete with original instruments, soapstone tables, and an antique darkroom.

Hanging of William Pounden Tour: Experience a specialized, immersive animated tour that retraces the tragic events of an 1823 murder and execution, using the eerie atmosphere of the old jail to tell the story.
Afternoon Teatime: Enjoy a traditional Victorian tea service in the elegant library or college hall, which includes history and etiquette lessons alongside sweet and savory snacks.
Tips and Key Information
You cannot explore the prison cells or the full history of the building on your own; access to these areas is strictly through guided tours, which are offered in both English and French.

While anyone can visit the library to browse or read, you must be a member to borrow books. However, Day Passes are available for a small fee if you wish to spend an afternoon studying or writing in this historic space.
Tours often sell out, especially during the summer and rainy days (as it’s a perfect indoor activity). It is highly recommended to book your tickets in advance on their official website.
Visitors are often asked to wear protective booties over their shoes or borrow a pair of provided Crocs to protect the historic wooden floors.
places.note: Note that some of the more graphic tours focusing on capital punishment are not recommended for children under 12.

places.name: 4. Théâtre Capitole
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/quebec-city-le-capitole-hotel-restaurant-and-theater-complex-gm1223087981-359144508

The Théâtre Capitole is a premier performing-arts landmark located in the heart of Old Quebec, right at Place d’Youville. Since its opening in 1903, this Beaux-Arts style masterpiece has served as a cultural cornerstone, hosting world-class musicians, Broadway-style musicals, and theatrical productions in a setting that evokes the glamour of the early 20th century. The theater is part of a larger complex known as Le Capitole de Québec, which offers a full evening of entertainment and luxury.
What to See and Do

Grand Theater Hall: Step inside to admire the opulent interior, featuring red velvet seating, gold leaf accents, and a majestic chandelier. It provides an intimate yet grand atmosphere for live performances.
Le Capitole Hotel: The building also houses a five-star luxury hotel, allowing guests to stay in the same historic structure where they see their shows.
Dining at Ristorante Il Teatro: This upscale on-site restaurant specializes in refined Italian cuisine. Its terrace overlooking Place d’Youville is a top spot for pre-show cocktails or dinner.
Confessions at the Theatre: In addition to major touring acts, the venue often hosts unique local productions and tribute shows that celebrate French and Quebecois musical heritage.
Tips and Key Information
Because it is a working theater, the building is primarily accessible during show times or for dining. Check their official website for a calendar of musicals and concerts during your visit.
The theater is equipped to welcome guests with reduced mobility, but it is recommended to contact the box office in advance to ensure specialized seating arrangements.

The location at Place d’Youville puts you within walking distance of the Porte Saint-Jean and the Palais Montcalm. It’s a perfect central hub for an evening stroll through the illuminated fortifications.
While the theater is in a busy pedestrian area, there is an underground public parking lot directly at Place d’Youville, making it convenient for those driving into the Old City.

places.name: 5. Musée du Fort
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/main-entrance-of-mus%C3%A9e-du-fort-quebec-city-canada-gm489433167-39690196

The Musée du Fort is a unique historical attraction located directly across from the Château Frontenac. Unlike traditional museums filled with glass cases, this venue focuses on a singular, high-impact storytelling experience that explains why Quebec City’s geography made it the most coveted strategic point in North America. The centerpiece of the museum is a massive, 400-square-foot scale model of the city and its surrounding landscape as it appeared in 1750.
What to See and Do

Sound and Light Show: Visitors watch a 30-minute immersive presentation where the scale model comes to life with lights, sound effects, and narration to depict the six major sieges of Quebec, including the famous Battle of the Plains of Abraham.

Strategic Geography: The show highlights how the Gibraltar of the Americas was defended and attacked, making it an excellent educational primer before you visit the actual battlefields or the Citadelle.
Historical Accuracy: The model is incredibly detailed, showing the original fortifications, the St. Lawrence River currents, and the difficult terrain that soldiers had to navigate centuries ago.
Tips and Key Information
The show runs multiple times a day in both English and French. It is a good idea to check the schedule upon arrival in the Upper Town so you can time your visit between outdoor strolls.
Because the presentation is fast-paced and visual, it is often more engaging for children and students than a standard walk-through museum.
Since the experience takes place in a climate-controlled theater, it is a perfect 30-minute escape from the summer heat or a winter snowstorm.

The museum sometimes offers package deals with other local attractions; ask at the front desk if there are currently any discounts for visiting nearby sites like the Morrin Centre or the Museum of Civilization.

places.name: 6. Parliament Buildinghttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/parliament-building-quebec-city-canada-gm1358679492-432229438
body: The Parliament Building in Quebec City is an architectural masterpiece and the seat of the provincial government. Its design reflects French Renaissance influences, making it one of the most stunning legislative buildings in Canada.

This location's significance stems from its role as the heart of Quebec's political life and its accessibility to the public through guided tours. The central fountain and meticulously landscaped gardens add to its charm, making it a perfect spot for both history enthusiasts and photographers.

The Parliament Building (Hôtel du Parlement) is the seat of the National Assembly of Quebec and one of the most significant architectural landmarks in the province. Completed in 1886, this Second Empire-style masterpiece was inspired by the Louvre in Paris and serves as a grand tribute to the history of the Founding Peoples of Quebec. The building is famous for its ornate facade, which functions as a stone history book of the region. While it is a working political site, the interior is open to the public and offers some of the most luxurious decor in the city.
What to See and Do

Facade Statues: The exterior is adorned with 26 bronze statues of explorers, soldiers, and politicians who shaped Quebec, including Samuel de Champlain and Frontenac. Look for the famous motto Je me souviens (I remember) carved above the main entrance.

Fontaine de Tourny: Located directly in front of the building, this massive, award-winning fountain was originally displayed at the 1855 Paris World Exhibition before being gifted to the city. It is particularly beautiful when illuminated at night.
Parliamentary Gardens: The surrounding gardens feature a wide array of native Quebec flora, as well as a vegetable garden and an apiary that highlight the province's commitment to urban biodiversity.
National Assembly Chamber: Known as the Blue Room (Salon bleu), this is where the elected members meet. It is decorated with intricate wood carvings and massive paintings depicting historic debates.
Legislative Council Chamber: Also called the Red Room, this chamber is used for formal ceremonies and features a regal design reminiscent of the British House of Lords.

Le Parlementaire Restaurant: Visitors can dine in this high-end restaurant located within the building. It offers a menu inspired by local Quebec products, served in a stunning Beaux-Arts dining hall.
Tips and Key Information
You can take a 45-minute guided tour of the building for free, but it is recommended to book your spot online in advance to ensure availability in your preferred language (English or French).
Since this is an active government building, all visitors must pass through a security screening similar to an airport. You will also need to present a piece of photo ID to enter.
If the National Assembly is in session, you can actually sit in the public gallery and watch the democratic process in action.
The building is fully accessible to people with reduced mobility, including specialized entrances and elevators.

places.name: 7. Cathedral of the Holy Trinityhttps://www.istockphoto.com/photo/cathedral-of-the-holy-trinity-quebec-city-canada-gm1290760805-386076798
body: The Cathedral of the Holy Trinity is a landmark of immense historical significance, being the first Anglican cathedral built outside the British Isles. Completed in 1804, it was modeled after London's famous St Martin-in-the-Fields and serves as a striking example of Palladian architecture in the heart of Old Quebec. This site offers a unique perspective on the British influence in Quebec following the conquest, blending religious solemnity with royal history.
What to See and Do
The Royal Gift: King George III personally donated the cathedral’s silver communion service, which is still considered a national treasure.
Architecture: The interior features magnificent box pews made of oak imported from the Royal Forests of Windsor, along with a grand organ built in London in 1804.
The Bells: It houses a ring of eight bells cast at the Whitechapel Bell Foundry—the same foundry that cast London's Big Ben and the Liberty Bell.
Monuments: The walls are lined with marble memorial plaques that tell the stories of prominent British figures and families who lived in Quebec during the 19th century.
Tips and Key Information
During the summer months, the cathedral typically offers guided tours that explain the architecture and the complex relationship between the British monarchy and the local community.
The cathedral is renowned for its acoustics and often hosts classical music concerts and choir performances. Check the local listings if you enjoy sacred or orchestral music.
It is often less crowded than the nearby Catholic Basilica, making it a peaceful place for quiet reflection or to admire the intricate stained glass.
It is situated directly across from the Place d’Armes, making it an easy stop when walking between the Fairmont Le Château Frontenac and the Hôtel de Ville (City Hall).

places.name: 8. Basilique Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/basilica-of-sainte-anne-de-beaupr%C3%A9-gm2203716101-621232300

The Basilique Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré, located about 30 kilometers east of Quebec City, is one of the eight national shrines of Canada and a world-renowned pilgrimage site. Dedicated to Saint Anne, the grandmother of Jesus, the shrine has been credited with many miracles of healing, drawing over a million visitors annually.
The current basilica is a masterpiece of Neo-Romanesque architecture, built in the early 20th century to replace a series of previous chapels and churches dating back to 1658.
What to See and Do
The Miraculous Statue: Inside the basilica, you will find the polychrome wood statue of Saint Anne, which is a focal point for pilgrims.
Stunning Mosaics and Glass: The interior is adorned with breathtaking mosaics on the ceiling and walls, along with 240 stained-glass windows that bathe the nave in colorful light.
The Commemorative Chapel: Built using the materials from the third church (1676), this smaller chapel on the grounds offers a more intimate look at the site's long history.
Way of the Cross: The hillside behind the basilica features a life-sized outdoor Way of the Cross, providing a peaceful path for reflection with views of the St. Lawrence River.
Tips and Key Information
Near the entrance, you can see columns covered in canes and crutches left behind by people who believe they were healed at the shrine.
During the summer peak season, free guided tours are often available to explain the intricate symbolism of the art and architecture.
The site includes a large shop selling religious items, books, and souvenirs related to Saint Anne.
If you don't have a car, several shuttle services operate between Old Quebec and the basilica, often stopping at Montmorency Falls Park along the way.
As an active place of worship, visitors are encouraged to dress respectfully, covering shoulders and knees.

places.name: 9. La Fresque des Québécois
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/place-royale-la-fresque-des-qu%C3%A9becois-gm621601984-108606871

La Fresque des Québécois is perhaps the most famous of Quebec City’s many "trompe-l'œil" (deceive the eye) murals. Located at the foot of Côte de la Montagne (29 Rue Notre-Dame) near Place Royale, this 420-square-meter masterpiece transforms a flat wall into a vivid, three-dimensional window into 400 years of history. The mural is designed to be explored up close, as it is packed with intricate details and hidden symbols.
What to See and Do

Identify the Legends: Look for about 15 key historical figures seamlessly integrated into the scene. You’ll see Samuel de Champlain standing proudly at the center, Jacques Cartier peeking from a third-story window, and the pioneer Louis Jolliet descending the stairs.
Cultural Icons: Modern figures are also present, including the legendary singer-songwriter Félix Leclerc and Thérèse Casgrain, a leader in the women's suffrage movement in Quebec.

Spot the Seasons: The mural subtly incorporates all four seasons. Look for children playing hockey (winter), blooming flower boxes (summer), and changing leaves to see how the artists captured Quebec’s distinct climate in a single frame.

Architectural Homage: The buildings depicted in the mural are replicas of actual historic houses in the neighborhood, and it even features the city's coat of arms and Bonhomme Carnaval, the jolly mascot of the winter festival.
Tips and Key Information
To get the best effect, stand back toward the opposite sidewalk. From the right angle, the painted stairs and balconies look so real you’ll feel like you could walk right into them.

As one of the most photographed spots in the Lower Town, it can get crowded with tour groups by mid-morning. Aim for a visit before 9:00 AM or in the early evening when the lighting on the wall is softer.
There is no cost to view the mural, and it is located in a pedestrian-friendly area. However, the street is slightly sloped, which is something to keep in mind for those with mobility aids.
There are dozens of murals across the city. Just a short walk away is the Fresque du Petit-Champlain, which focuses specifically on the working-class history of the port district.

places.name: 10. Fresque du Petit-Champlain
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/historic-wall-mural-scene-in-old-quebec-city-canada-gm1050066986-280808053

The Fresque du Petit-Champlain is a stunning mural located at the western end of the historic Quartier Petit Champlain. Painted in 2001, this massive artwork uses the trompe-l'œil technique to depict the daily life and hardships of the neighborhood’s past inhabitants, specifically focusing on the district's history as a bustling port and working-class hub.
What to See and Do

Historical Narrative: The mural illustrates key events from the waterfront's history, including the tragic 1759 fire during the Siege of Quebec and the devastating rockslides of 1889 that altered the landscape of the area.
Life at the Port: You can see depictions of sailors, longshoremen, and merchants at work, highlighting the district’s 19th-century role as one of the busiest shipping ports in North America.

Whimsical Details: Like other frescoes in the city, it features playful elements, such as a child retrieving a lost ball and laundry hanging from windows, making the stone wall appear like a living, breathing part of the street.

Visual Continuity: The artists carefully matched the colors and textures of the mural to the surrounding historic architecture, creating a seamless illusion that often makes visitors stop and double-check if the windows and figures are real.
Tips and Key Information
You will find this mural at 102 Rue du Petit-Champlain. It is located near the Breakneck Steps, making it a natural stop while exploring the shops of the Lower Town.
To capture the full scale of the mural, it is best to stand across the street near the parkette. This allows you to get the perspective needed for the three-dimensional effect to truly pop in photos.

This is one of over a dozen major murals in the city. If you enjoy this style of art, you can find a Mural Circuit map at local tourism offices that leads you to others, such as the nearby Fresque des Québécois.
The mural is well-lit at night, offering a much quieter and more atmospheric viewing experience compared to the busy midday hours.

places.name: 1. Jacques‑Cartier National Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/scenery-of-jacques-cartier-national-park-in-autumn-gm2190098260-608508346

Parc national de la Jacques-Cartier is a breathtaking 670-square-kilometer wilderness area located just 30 minutes north of Quebec City. It protects one of the province's most beautiful glacial valleys, characterized by a massive 550-meter-deep trench through which the Jacques-Cartier River winds. The park is famous for its extensive network of over 100 kilometers of hiking trails and its vibrant river-based recreation.
What to See and Do

Les Loups Trail: Widely considered the park's crown jewel, this challenging 11-kilometer round-trip hike leads to two spectacular observation decks. From the summit, you are rewarded with an iconic panoramic view of the deep fractures in the Laurentian massif and the winding river below.

River Adventures: During the warmer months, the Jacques-Cartier River becomes a playground for canoeing, kayaking, and mini-rafting. The river offers everything from calm, family-friendly stretches to thrilling Class I and II rapids for those seeking a bit more adrenaline.

Wildlife Encounters: The park's diverse ecosystems support a rich array of wildlife. Visitors frequently report sightings of moose wading in the river shallows, as well as beavers, porcupines, and even the occasional black bear or wolf in the deeper woods.

Winter Wonderland: In winter, the valley transforms into a snowy paradise. You can explore groomed trails on snowshoes, try Hok skiing (a hybrid between skiing and snowshoeing), or experience the latest craze of fatbiking on over 20 kilometers of specialized snowy paths.
Tips and Key Information

To manage crowds and protect the environment, daily access to the park now requires a mandatory online reservation via the SEPAQ website. It is highly recommended to book several days in advance, especially for weekend visits.

Located at Km 10, the Discovery and Visitors Centre is the heart of the park. It serves as a warming station in winter and offers equipment rentals, educational exhibits, and a small shop for snacks and gear.
During the peak summer season, a shuttle service is often available to transport paddlers to various launch points along the river, simplifying the logistics for those renting watercraft.
There is a daily entry fee (approximately $10 CAD for adults, while youth under 18 enter for free). Note that parking fees may be separate depending on the sector you visit.

places.name: 2. St. Lawrence River Waterfront & Promenade
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/autumn-in-quebec-city-gm1020005488-274075031

The St. Lawrence River is the lifeblood of Quebec City, and its waterfront has been transformed into a series of interconnected parks and pathways. The experience shifts from the historic, bustling atmosphere of the Vieux-Port (Old Port) to the modern, expansive natural environment of the Promenade Samuel-De Champlain. Together, they offer over 10 kilometers of continuous shoreline access for walking, cycling, and recreation.

The Vieux-Port area serves as the gateway to the river, where the city's maritime history meets modern leisure. It is a vibrant hub especially active in the summer when cruise ships dock and local festivals take over the piers. The Promenade Samuel-De Champlain is a 6.8-kilometer linear park that reclaims former industrial land for public use. It is widely praised for its award-winning architectural design and its ability to connect urban life with the coastal ecosystem.
What to See and Do
Antique District: The streets surrounding the port, particularly Rue Saint-Paul, are famous for their concentration of antique shops and art galleries.
Maritime History: You can visit the Musée naval de Québec (Naval Museum) to learn about the history of the Naval Reserve and the river’s role in wartime.
River Excursions: This is the primary departure point for boat tours, zodiac excursions, and the ferry to Lévis, which offers some of the best views of the Quebec City skyline.
Winter Ice: In the colder months, visitors often gather here to watch the powerful ice-breaking tugboats and the unique sport of ice canoeing on the frozen river.
Station de la Plage: A highlight of the newest phase, this area features a fine sandy beach, an infinity pool that overlooks the river, and a water mirror with refreshing jets for summer days.
Observation Tower: The Quai des Cageux features a 25-meter-high tower that provides a panoramic window over the St. Lawrence, the bridges, and the winding park trail.
Themed Gardens: The park is divided into four conceptual gardens—Mist, Flows, Men, and Winds—each using art and landscaping to evoke different "moods" of the river.
Active Recreation: The wide, paved multi-use trail is a favorite for runners and cyclists, stretching from the Pierre-Laporte Bridge all the way toward the city center.
Tips and Key Information
The waterfront path is part of the Route verte, a massive cycling network. You can rent a bike in the Old Port and ride the entire length of the promenade in a comfortable afternoon.
The Promenade Samuel-De Champlain is particularly famous for its sunset vistas, as the western-facing sections offer unobstructed views of the sun dipping behind the mountains.
Keep an eye out for contemporary art installations scattered throughout the park, which celebrate the 400th anniversary of the city.
While the park is free, parking can be limited at popular spots like Station de la Plage during summer weekends. Consider starting your walk at a quieter entry point like the Boisé de Tequenonday.

places.name: 3. Île d'Orléans
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/landscape-view-of-farm-in-ile-dorleans-quebec-canada-with-house-gm968626210-264078611

Often called the Garden of Quebec, Île d'Orléans is a lush island in the St. Lawrence River that serves as a living museum of French-Canadian heritage. The island is divided into six distinct parishes, each maintaining its own rural character, historic churches, and century-old stone houses. A drive along the 67-kilometer Chemin Royal (Royal Road) allows visitors to loop the entire island, stopping at roadside stands, artisanal boutiques, and picturesque villages.
What to See and Do

Paradise for Foodies: The island is a primary source of fresh produce for Quebec City, famous for its fertile soil and centuries-old farming traditions. From mid-June to mid-October, the island is at its liveliest with harvest festivals and pick-your-own activities.

Black Currant Delights: At Cassis Monna & Filles, visitors can taste award-winning black currant liqueurs and syrups, or enjoy their famous vanilla and cassis swirl soft-serve on a terrace overlooking the vineyards.
Artisanal Jams: Confiturerie Tigidou is a charming jam factory located in a repurposed barn, specializing in small-batch spreads made from organic berries grown right on the island.

Historic Treats: The Chocolaterie de l'Ile d'Orleans is housed in a building dating back to 1760; it offers handmade chocolates and is a popular stop for cyclists looking for a sweet break at the island's entrance.
Local Vineyards: Ste-Pétronille - Winery & Cidery offers tastings of organic wines and ciders with a stunning view of Montmorency Falls across the water.

Heritage and History: Stepping onto Île d'Orléans is like traveling back to the 17th century. It was one of the first areas of New France to be settled, and many residents can still trace their ancestry back to the original founding families.
Living History: The Maison Drouin is the only typical ancestral house on the island open to the public, offering a glimpse into domestic life as it was in 1730.
Scenic Views and Recreation: The island's landscape is defined by long, narrow fields that stretch from the central ridge down to the river, a traditional layout known as the seigneurial system.

Seigneurial Elegance: The Mauvide-Genest Manor is a rare example of a seigneurial manor from the French regime, once the home of a royal surgeon and later used as a military headquarters during the British conquest.

Maritime Roots: The village of Saint-Laurent was historically a hub for wooden shipbuilding; today, the Saint-Laurent Maritime Park preserves this heritage through exhibits on traditional boat construction.
Tips and Key Information
For the best view of the archipelago and the St. Lawrence estuary, climb the Parc de la Tour-du-Nordet (observation tower) at the eastern tip of the island in Saint-François.
In July, the gardens at La Seigneurie de l’Île d’Orléans come alive with rows of fragrant lavender and themed gardens that are perfect for a scenic stroll.
Many visitors choose to explore the island by bike or scooter, enjoying the gentle hills and the frequent stops for cider, cheese, and fresh strawberries.

places.name: 4. Domaine de Maizerets
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/closeup-shot-of-a-swimming-brown-mallard-duck-in-domaine-de-maizerets-quebec-gm1441583331-481244878

Domaine de Maizerets is a 27-hectare historical park that serves as a hidden oasis for both nature lovers and history buffs. Located in the Limoilou district, this sprawling estate dates back to the 17th century and offers a perfect blend of manicured gardens, wild wetlands, and heritage architecture centered around a grand historic chateau.
What to See and Do

Arboretum and Wetlands: The park features a diverse arboretum with thousands of trees and shrubs, as well as a protected marshland area where visitors can observe local bird species from specialized blinds.
Observation Tower: A multi-story wooden tower provides a tree-top view of the estate, the surrounding city, and the nearby St. Lawrence River.
A-Maze-ing Fun: One of the park's most popular family features is its large cedar hedge maze, which offers a playful challenge for children and adults alike.

Historic Manor: The main house, known as the Chateau, often hosts community workshops and exhibitions, reflecting the site's long history as a farm and later a summer retreat for the Petit Séminaire de Québec.
Tips and Key Information
In the summer, the park is a hub for cycling and picnicking; in the winter, it transforms into a snowy playground with groomed cross-country ski trails, a skating rink, and snowshoeing paths.
Entry to the park grounds is free, making it one of the most budget-friendly ways to spend a full afternoon enjoying the outdoors in Quebec City.
During the winter season, a rental pavilion on-site provides affordable access to skates, skis, and snowshoes, allowing visitors to enjoy the trails without bringing their own gear.
The majority of the primary walking paths are paved and flat, making the park highly accessible for strollers and wheelchairs, though some of the deeper wetland trails may be more rugged.

places.name: 5. Bois-de-Coulonge Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/reflecting-pond-in-bois-de-coulonge-park-gm1197356564-341829082

Bois-de-Coulonge Park is a prestigious historical estate that served as the official residence for Quebec's Lieutenant Governors for over a century. Today, it is a magnificent 24-hectare public park that blends horticultural excellence with heritage, offering some of the most refined garden landscapes in the city.
What to See and Do
Horticultural Splendor: The park is renowned for its meticulously designed flower beds, a Victorian-style greenhouse, and an arboretum that features a diverse collection of rare and centennial trees.

Historic Footprints: While the main residence was tragically destroyed by fire in 1966, several historic outbuildings remain, including the guardhouse, the stables, and the former laundry, which now serve as interpretive centers or administrative offices.
Clifftop Views: Located on the edge of the Sillery cliff, the park offers stunning panoramic views of the St. Lawrence River and the south shore from its many wooded walking trails.
Family-Friendly Amenities: In addition to its formal gardens, the park includes modern playgrounds and large open lawns that are popular for family picnics and community events.
Tips and Key Information
The park is a favorite for locals in the spring when the massive tulip displays are in bloom, and again in the fall when the old-growth trees provide a spectacular canopy of autumn colors.
Visitors can follow a series of panels throughout the park that detail the Golden Age of the estate and the lives of the prominent figures who once lived there.
Situated on the Grande Allée, the park is easily accessible by public transit or by bike via the corridor du Littoral trail. There is also a dedicated parking lot for those arriving by car.
Because it is located slightly away from the main tourist core of Old Quebec, it offers a much quieter and more local atmosphere compared to the Plains of Abraham.

places.name: 6. Chauveau Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/autumn-landscape-in-quebec-gm1435100520-476541349

Chauveau Park is a massive urban wilderness area in the Duberger-Les Saules district, serving as one of Quebec City's largest and most diverse natural escapes. Spanning over 120 hectares, the park follows the winding Saint-Charles River, providing a lush corridor for both high-energy sports and quiet nature observation.
What to See and Do

Saint-Charles River Trails: The park is a major hub for the Sentier linéaire de la rivière Saint-Charles, featuring scenic hiking and biking trails that hug the riverbanks and cross picturesque footbridges.
Soccer and Sports Hub: It is a premier destination for local athletes, boasting multiple high-quality soccer fields and a large indoor soccer stadium (Stade Chauveau) that allows for year-round play.

Canoeing and Kayaking: The calm waters of the Saint-Charles River within the park are ideal for light paddling, with easy access points for those looking to explore the city from a different perspective.

Winter Activities: During the snowy months, the park's extensive trail network is repurposed for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing, offering a peaceful forest setting right in the middle of the city.
Fishing Spots: The river within the park is known to locals as a decent spot for urban fishing, particularly for trout, provided you have the necessary provincial permits.
Tips and Key Information
While rules can vary by zone, many of the wooded trails are popular with dog walkers; just be sure to keep your pet on a leash to protect the local flora and fauna.
There are multiple entry points, but the main service pavilion on Avenue Chauveau provides the most convenient parking and access to the primary sports facilities.
Numerous shaded spots and designated picnic tables make it an excellent choice for a family afternoon out, especially near the playgrounds.

places.name: 7. Place D’Youville
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/crowd-ice-skating-on-the-youville-place-ring-seen-from-above-downtown-quebec-city-gm1088786234-292063357

Place d'Youville serves as a vibrant bridge between the historic walled city and the modern neighborhoods of Quebec. Located just outside the Porte Saint-Jean, this public square is a year-round gathering spot that hosts major festivals, open-air performances, and seasonal recreation.
What to See and Do

Public Skating Rink: During the winter months, the square features a popular refrigerated outdoor skating rink. It is renowned for its festive atmosphere, often accompanied by music and colorful light displays reflecting off the nearby fortifications.
Cultural Hub: The square is flanked by significant cultural institutions, including the Théâtre Capitole and the Palais Montcalm, making it the heart of the city's performing arts scene.
Historic Fortifications: Visitors can admire a well-preserved section of the city's defensive walls and the Artillery Park, providing a grand backdrop for photography and historical exploration.
Summer Festivals: In July, the square becomes a primary venue for the Festival d'été de Québec, hosting free concerts and street performers that draw large, energetic crowds.
Tips and Key Information
If you visit in winter, you don't need to bring your own gear; a service pavilion on the square offers affordable skate rentals and sharpening services.
Because of its proximity to the bus terminal and the busy Rue Saint-Jean, it is one of the easiest landmarks to use as a meeting spot for groups.
The area is surrounded by diverse eateries ranging from casual poutine shops to upscale Italian dining at Ristorante Il Teatro Click to open side panel for more information .
The square is flat and paved, making it easily navigable for strollers and wheelchairs, though the surrounding cobblestone streets leading into the Old City can be more challenging.

places.name: 8. Cap-Blanc Stairway
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/high-angle-view-of-cap-blanc-stairs-in-quebec-city-gm1407157588-458465509

The Cap-Blanc Stairs (Escalier du Cap-Blanc) is a legendary architectural feature of Quebec City, holding the title of the longest stairway in the city. Connecting the historic Quartier Petit Champlain area at the base of the cliff to the Plains of Abraham at the top, this wooden structure is both a vital transit link and a popular destination for fitness enthusiasts.

Originally built in the mid-19th century to allow workers living in the lower town to reach the factories and shipyards on the heights, the current wooden structure dates back to a complete reconstruction in the late 20th century. It offers a grueling but rewarding climb through a lush, forested cliffside.
What to See and Do
Impressive Scale: The stairway consists of 398 steps divided into multiple flights, spanning a significant vertical elevation that provides a intense physical challenge.

Secluded Nature: Unlike the more famous Breakneck Steps (Escalier Casse-Cou), these stairs are tucked away in a quieter, more residential area, offering a peaceful ascent surrounded by trees and the sounds of local birds.

Panoramic Landing: While the stairs themselves are enclosed by the cliff and foliage, the top of the climb opens directly onto the vast green expanses of the Plains of Abraham, offering refreshing views of the St. Lawrence River.
Training Ground: It is common to see local athletes and runners using the stairs for stair repeats, as the steep incline is considered one of the best outdoor cardiovascular workouts in the region.
Tips and Key Information
You can find the base of the stairs on Rue Champlain, while the top entrance is located near the Musée national des beaux-arts du Québec (MNBAQ) and the Citadelle.
There are several small landings along the way with benches where you can catch your breath and enjoy the greenery.
The wooden steps can become quite slippery when wet or icy. While they are usually maintained, extra caution is needed during rain or the winter months.
If you want the views without the heavy exertion, many visitors prefer to take the stairs down from the Plains of Abraham into the Lower Town as part of a scenic loop.

places.name: 9. Mont-Sainte-Anne
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/monte-sainte-anne-in-quebec-canada-gm533904342-94617051

Mont-Sainte-Anne is a world-class outdoor destination located just 40 kilometers east of Quebec City. Known as one of the most versatile mountain resorts in North America, it offers a dramatic landscape where the Laurentian Mountains meet the St. Lawrence River, providing year-round activities that range from elite-level skiing to premier mountain biking.
What to See and Do

Exceptional Skiing and Snowboarding: The resort boasts 71 trails spread across three sides of the mountain, including one of the most significant vertical drops in the region. Visitors often praise the La Crête trail for its spectacular views of the St. Lawrence River as you descend.

Mountain Biking Mecca: In the summer, the mountain transforms into a global hub for mountain biking, having hosted numerous UCI World Cups. It features an extensive network of cross-country trails and adrenaline-pumping downhill runs for all skill levels.

Summit Observation: Even for those who don't ski or bike, the panoramic gondola ride to the summit is a highlight. The observation deck at the top offers a 360-degree view of the river, Île d’Orléans, and the surrounding Laurentians.

Extensive Hiking and Snowshoeing: The base of the mountain and its slopes feature miles of wooded trails. During the winter, it becomes one of the largest cross-country skiing and snowshoeing centers in Canada, with trails that wind through beautiful maple forests.
Tips and Key Information
Mont-Sainte-Anne offers one of the highest vertical drops for night skiing in Canada. The trails are well-lit and provide a unique atmosphere with the distant lights of the Beaupré coast below.
For the best experience, consider staying at one of the ski-in/ski-out lodges or condos at the base of the mountain to maximize your time on the trails.

Because of its proximity to the river, the mountain can be susceptible to high winds which sometimes affect gondola operations. It's a good idea to check the mountain report on their website before heading out.
After a day of intense physical activity, many visitors head to the nearby Nordic spas in the Beaupré area to recover in the thermal baths.

places.name: 10. Canyon Sainte-Anne
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/view-of-waterfall-and-bridge-at-canyon-sainte-anne-in-quebec-canada-gm2152246208-573271903

Canyon Sainte-Anne is a breathtaking natural attraction carved into a 1.2-billion-year-old rock formation. Located just a few minutes past the Basilique Sainte-Anne-de-Beaupré, it features a dramatic 74-meter waterfall—higher than Niagara Falls—thundering into a narrow, rocky gorge.
The site is designed for visitors to experience the canyon from multiple heights and perspectives, making it one of the most exciting natural stops on the Beaupré Coast.
What to See and Do

Suspension Bridges: The canyon is crossed by three suspension bridges, including one that hangs 60 meters above the abyss, offering a heart-pounding view of the rushing water directly beneath your feet.

The Air Canyon: For thrill-seekers, this motorized chair flight carries two people high across the canyon at speeds of up to 50 km/h, providing a unique bird's-eye view of the falls and the forest canopy.

Via Ferrata and Giant Potholes: Visitors can explore giant potholes (geological formations carved by water) or take part in a via ferrata—a guided climbing route along the canyon walls that requires no previous experience.
Pet-Friendly Trails: The park is known for being exceptionally welcoming to pets, allowing leashed dogs to accompany their owners across the bridges and along the wooded paths.
Tips and Key Information
While there are stairs involved in reaching the lowest bridges, the upper part of the park and the first suspension bridge are accessible to strollers and those with limited mobility.

The canyon is particularly spectacular in the autumn when the surrounding Laurentian forest turns vibrant shades of red and orange, and in the spring when the snowmelt makes the waterfall exceptionally powerful.
Children can participate in the Stone Stories puzzle hunt, an interactive game that guides them through the park to discover its geological and historical secrets.
If you are planning to visit other regional sites like Mont-Sainte-Anne, check for regional tourist passes that might offer a discount on admission.

places.name: 1. Île d'Orléans Bridge
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/bridge-to-ile-dorlean-quebec-gm494290016-77365861

The Pont de l'Île-d'Orléans is the sole road link between the mainland and the pastoral paradise of Île d'Orléans. This iconic suspension bridge, which opened in 1935, is a feat of engineering that spans the North Channel of the St. Lawrence River, offering one of the most scenic (and nerve-wracking) drives in the province.
What to See and Do

Architectural Gateway: The bridge is a suspension-style structure with a central span that sits high enough to allow maritime traffic to pass underneath. Its slender, green-painted towers have become a symbol of the region.

View: As you drive toward the island, you are treated to a magnificent panorama: the Montmorency Falls thundering on your left and the silhouette of Quebec City and the Château Frontenac fading in your rearview mirror.

Transition: Crossing the bridge is often described by locals as traveling back in time. You leave the busy Highway 138 and emerge into a land of 17th-century stone houses, orchards, and rolling farmland.
Tips and Key Information

The bridge is famous for its extremely narrow lanes and lack of a shoulder. If you are driving a wide vehicle or a large RV, you’ll want to keep a steady hand and stay focused—it can feel quite tight when passing a bus or tractor.

There is a very narrow sidewalk on the bridge. While it is possible to walk or bike across, the high winds and proximity to moving cars make it a thrilling experience. Most recreational cyclists prefer to transport their bikes to the island by car and start their ride at the tourist bureau.

Because the current bridge is over 90 years old and nearing the end of its lifespan, a massive project is underway to build a new cable-stayed bridge. Construction has begun, and the new structure—slated for completion around 2028—will feature wider lanes and a dedicated path for pedestrians and cyclists.

During the autumn harvest season (especially Apple Picking weekends in September and October), the bridge can become a bottleneck. It's best to cross early in the morning or later in the evening to avoid long queues.

places.name: 2. Gare du Palais
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/gare-du-palais-in-quebec-city-gm148952969-20871210

The Gare du Palais is more than just a transit hub; it is an architectural masterpiece designated as a National Historic Site of Canada. Built in 1915 by the Canadian Pacific Railway, its design was inspired by the Châteauesque style of the nearby Château Frontenac, featuring steep turrets and grand masonry that make it one of the most beautiful train stations in North America.
The station serves as the city's primary link for VIA Rail train services and Intercar bus routes, connecting Quebec City to Montreal and beyond.
What to See and Do

Grand Architecture: The interior is just as impressive as the facade, boasting a massive stained-glass window that depicts the history of the region and a soaring waiting hall with intricate woodwork.
Heritage Significance: The building was designed to impress travelers arriving in the provincial capital, reflecting the Golden Age of rail travel with its regal stone and brickwork.
Modern Amenities: While maintaining its historic charm, the station offers modern conveniences including ticket kiosks, a small café, and comfortable waiting areas.
Strategic Location: Situated in the Lower Town (Basse-Ville), it is within easy walking distance of the Old Port, the artisanal shops of Rue Saint-Paul, and the popular Marché du Vieux-Port.
Tips and Key Information
