Unsworth Vineyards represents the region’s growing reputation for high-quality viticulture, specializing in sparkling wines and cool-climate varietals. The on-site restaurant is housed in a restored early 1900s farmhouse, offering dishes paired specifically with their estate-grown wines. The modern tasting room provides a professional environment to explore the nuances of the local terroir through guided flights.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/bamberton-beach-gm924632560-253750211
Nature and Rainforest Escapes

Goldstream Provincial Park is located about 20 minutes south and is renowned for its massive, 600-year-old Douglas fir and Western Red Cedar trees. Take a short, flat walk to see the "Niagara Falls" of the park, a 47-meter waterfall that cascades down a narrow rock canyon. If visiting in late autumn, the park is one of the best places on the island to witness the annual salmon run from the riverside observation platforms.

Bamberton Provincial Park offers a scenic coastal retreat on the Saanich Inlet, known for its warm, shallow waters and sandy beach. The terraced picnic areas provide shaded views of the water, while the beach is ideal for low-tide exploration and swimming. From the shoreline, you can see across the inlet toward the Gulf Islands and, on clear days, the distant peak of Mount Baker.

places.name: 1. The Butchart Gardens
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sunken-garden-at-butchart-gardens-gm2163292927-583648712

The Butchart Gardens is a world-renowned National Historic Site of Canada, attracting over a million visitors annually to its 22-hectare (55-acre) estate. Originally a limestone quarry, the site was transformed into a series of themed gardens by Jennie Butchart starting in 1904.
What to Do and See

The Sunken Garden: This is the most iconic part of the property. Descend the stairs to see the quarry floor, which has been reclaimed with vibrant flower beds, towering trees, and the Mound—a massive rock formation in the center that offers an elevated view of the garden floor.

The Ross Fountain: Installed in 1964 to celebrate the 60th anniversary of the gardens, this fountain features water displays that reach heights of 21 meters (70 feet). It is particularly impressive during summer evening illuminations.
Rose Garden: From June through August, this garden features thousands of roses. The Rose Carousel nearby is also a popular stop, featuring 30 hand-carved animals and chariots.
Japanese Garden: Enter through a traditional Torii gate into a tranquil space of trickling streams, bridges, and rare Himalayan Blue Poppies (typically blooming mid-May to mid-June).
Italian Garden: Formerly the Butchart family's tennis court, this formal garden is bounded by two arched entrances and features an intricate cross-shaped pond and a bronze statue of Mercury.
The Mediterranean Garden: Located near the parking area, this garden showcases drought-tolerant plants from around the world that thrive in Victoria’s temperate climate.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/fountain-at-butchart-gardens-victoria-bc-canada-gm842383158-137510059
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/butchart-gardens-sunken-garden-gm543047240-97349425
Tips & Key Information

For photography, the soft morning light or the golden hour before sunset provides the best highlights on the flower beds. In the summer (Wednesday–Sunday), the gardens stay open late for Night Illumination, where thousands of lights transform the paths into a different atmosphere entirely.
Visit early in the morning (right at opening) or later in the afternoon to avoid the mid-day tour bus peak.

Spring is peak Tulip time (April), while Autumn (October) offers striking red and gold hues from the Japanese Maples. Winter features the Magic of Christmas display with the Twelve Days of Christmas light installations.
Dining at the original Butchart family residence is a highlight for many. Reservations are highly recommended for the traditional Afternoon Tea service.
Prices vary by season. For Spring 2026, adult tickets are approximately $41.00, while Summer 2026 rates rise to roughly $44.25 (including tax). Children’s rates are significantly lower.

Generally open daily from 9:00 AM. Closing times shift from 3:30 PM in winter to as late as 10:00 PM during summer evening entertainment nights. Note that the gardens are closed for a staff holiday in late January.

Most paths are wheelchair and scooter accessible, though some older sections have steeper grades. Manual wheelchairs are available for loan at the Information Center on a first-come, first-served basis.
Dogs are welcome during most of the year if kept on a short leash (1 meter/3 feet). They are restricted during specific Christmas evening hours.
Personal photography is encouraged, but selfie sticks and drones are strictly prohibited. Professional photoshoots (weddings, graduations) are generally not permitted.

places.name: 2. Sidney Spit (part of Gulf Islands National Park Reserve)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sidney-spit-vancouver-island-bc-gm1419882080-466090025

Sidney Spit is part of the Gulf Islands National Park Reserve, located at the northern end of Sidney Island. Accessible only by boat or a seasonal passenger ferry, it is famous for its disappearing sandy spit and unique tidal ecosystem.
What to Do and See

The Sandy Spit: At low tide, a narrow finger of white sand stretches nearly two kilometers into the Salish Sea. It is a premier spot for walking between the waves, though visitors must keep an eye on the rising tide to avoid being cut off from the main island.

Birdwatching: The salt marshes and lagoons are a critical stopover for migratory shorebirds. It is one of the best locations in the region to spot Brant geese and purple martins during the spring migration.

Hiking Trails: A network of easy, level trails winds through open meadows and Douglas fir forests. These paths offer glimpses of the island’s history, including the ruins of an old brickworks factory from the early 20th century.
Backcountry Camping: The park features 29 rustic walk-in campsites nestled in the woods near the beach. It provides a true off-grid experience within sight of the Vancouver Island coastline.
Tips & Key Information
The west-facing beaches of the spit catch the full glow of the sunset over the Saanich Peninsula. This is the optimal time for postcard photography, as the light reflects off the shallow tidal pools.

The Sidney Spit Ferry departs from the Sidney Pier at the foot of Beacon Avenue. It typically runs from mid-May through Labor Day. Tickets should be booked in advance during summer weekends as they frequently sell out.

There are no trash cans on the island. Visitors must bring all their supplies and carry out all garbage. Potable water is available via a hand pump, but it can have a high mineral content, so many prefer to bring their own.
For those arriving by private vessel, there are 15 mooring buoys and a public dock. These operate on a first-come, first-served basis and require a fee for overnight stays.
While the park reserve is technically open year-round for private boaters, the passenger ferry and most visitor services only operate during the summer months.
To protect the fragile ecosystem and sensitive bird nesting areas, dogs must be kept on a leash at all times and are restricted from certain parts of the lagoon.
Pit toilets are located near the dock and the campground. There are no food services or shops on the island, so all provisions must be purchased in Sidney before departing.

places.name: 3. Whale Watching and Marine Tours
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/killer-whale-passing-by-a-nautical-vessel-gm1275975798-375877552

Sidney and the Saanich Peninsula serve as a premier gateway to the Salish Sea, offering direct access to the feeding grounds of orcas, humpbacks, and a diverse array of marine wildlife. Because these tours depart further north than those in downtown Victoria, they often reach the Gulf Islands more quickly, providing more time for actual wildlife viewing.
Whale Watching & Eco-Tours

Sidney Whale Watching is a First Nations-owned and operated company that has served the Peninsula for over 20 years. They emphasize an indigenous perspective on the local waters and the W̱SÁNEĆ peoples' connection to the land and sea.
Tour Variety: They offer standard three-hour whale watching trips with guaranteed sightings, as well as unique culinary tours and private island charters.
Wildlife Focus: Beyond whales, tours frequently stop to observe seals, sea lions, porpoises, and bald eagles.
Vessel Options: They utilize both covered vessels for comfort and open boats for a more immersive, on-the-water experience.

Prince of Whales Whale & Marine Wildlife Adventures is one of the most established operators in the region. While their main hub is in Victoria, their tours cover the same northern straits easily accessible from the Peninsula.
Educational Focus: Every tour is led by certified naturalists who provide deep insights into marine biology and conservation efforts.
The Whale Guarantee: If whales are not spotted during your tour, they provide a complimentary return trip that never expires.
Vessel Technology: They operate a fleet ranging from high-speed Zodiacs for thrill-seekers to large ocean cruisers with heated cabins and 360-degree viewing decks.
Marine Tours & Boat Charters
Port Sidney Marina acts as the primary launch point for a variety of specialty marine adventures right from the heart of downtown Sidney.
Tall Ship Sailing: Visitors can book three-hour afternoon or sunset cruises aboard traditional tall ships, which can also be chartered for private groups of up to 24 people.
Jet Ski Wildlife Tours: For a more active approach, guided jet ski tours allow for a closer look at hidden beaches and local marine life in smaller, more maneuverable groups.
Sail Training: Introduction to sailing courses are available on 40-foot sailboats, combining a scenic voyage with hands-on learning.
Canoe Cove Marina & Boatyard, located at the northern tip of the Saanich Peninsula, is a historical marine community that hosts several independent charter and tour operators.
Custom Charters: The marina is a hub for private boat charters that can be tailored for fishing, photography, or multi-day exploration of the Gulf Islands.
Kayak Rentals: For self-guided marine exploration, kayak rentals are available to explore the calmer waters of the immediate cove and nearby islets.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/orca-whale-jumping-gm90960925-4248993
Tips & Key Information
Sunset marine tours are highly recommended for photographers. The light reflecting off the Gulf Islands creates a postcard backdrop for wildlife silhouettes, especially near Sidney Spit.

Even on warm summer days, temperatures on the open water can be significantly lower than on land. Most operators recommend dressing in layers and provide windproof cruiser suits for open-vessel tours.
PWhile whales can be spotted year-round, May through October is considered the peak season with a sighting success rate often exceeding 95%.
During the summer months, tours departing from Sidney can fill up quickly due to their proximity to the Swartz Bay Ferry Terminal. Advance reservations are highly recommended.

places.name: 4. Fishing Trip
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/mount-baker-seen-from-sidney-vancouver-island-bc-canada-gm1444817974-483422320

Sidney is widely considered a premier destination for saltwater angling, offering access to some of the calmest and most productive waters on the West Coast. The region's unique geography provides year-round salmon fishing, protected from the open swells of the Pacific.
Where to Fish and What to Catch

Sidney Channel and Coal Island: These local waters are hotspots for Winter Chinook (also known as Springs). Local experts often focus on the currents around Coal Island and Fairfax Point, where the movement of water attracts baitfish and hungry salmon.

Pier Fishing at Bevan Fishing Pier: Located at the foot of Bevan Avenue in Eastview Park, this specialized pier is a popular spot for those without a boat. It is common to see anglers here targeting everything from perch and rockfish to the occasional salmon during peak runs.

Shellfishing and Prawning: The area is equally famous for its hunting and gathering opportunities. Many local boaters set traps for Dungeness crab and spot prawns in the deeper waters of Area 18, often combining a day of salmon fishing with a shellfish harvest.
Bottom Fishing: When in season, the rocky reefs near Sidney provide excellent habitat for Lingcod and various species of rockfish. These are particularly sought after for their quality as table fish.
Professional Fishing Charters

Sidney Fishing Charters - Bon Chovy: Based out of Port Sidney Marina, this operator is one of the most established in the region. They offer year-round salmon fishing on fully equipped Grady White vessels and provide all necessary gear and cleaning services for your catch.

Club SeaKing Adventures: Operating from the Resthaven area, they specialize in both fishing and marine wildlife tours. Their excursions often blend the thrill of the catch with an educational focus on the local marine ecosystem.

Storm Sport Fishing: Another highly-rated charter departing from downtown Sidney, they offer customized trips ranging from 5-hour half-days to full-day 10-hour adventures targeting the best seasonal species.
Tips and Key Information

All anglers must have a valid BC Tidal Waters Sport Fishing Licence. If you are targeting salmon, you must also purchase a salmon conservation stamp. These can be purchased online through the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) website.

Locals often say that in Sidney, the tide height matters less than the current change. Fishing is typically most productive during the hour before and after a slack tide when the water begins to move.

Regulations for Chinook, Coho, and Lingcod change frequently based on conservation efforts. It is essential to check the DFO Area 18 and Area 19 regulations on the day of your trip to confirm size limits and retention rules.

Early morning is traditionally the best time for salmon, but the late afternoon light over the Gulf Islands provides a spectacular backdrop for sunset fishing, which can be just as productive during the summer months.

places.name: 5. Sidney Waterfront
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sidney-waterfront-sidney-vancouver-island-bc-canada-gm1441498506-481183755

The Sidney Waterfront is a scenic stretch along the Salish Sea that blends public art, marine education, and nautical history. The centerpiece is a 2.5-kilometer paved walkway that is completely flat and barrier-free, offering expansive views of the Gulf Islands and Mount Baker.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/beautiful-colorful-flowers-along-the-promenade-in-sidney-waterfront-gm1433327987-475277734
What to Do and See

Shaw Centre for the Salish Sea: This award-winning aquarium focuses exclusively on the local ecosystem. Visitors often highlight the giant Pacific octopus and the unique collection of Coast Salish art integrated into the exhibits.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sidney-british-columbia-waterfront-with-hotels-and-restaurants-gm637150996-113483405

The Sidney Sculpture Walk: As you walk the shoreline, you will encounter a rotating gallery of outdoor sculptures. These range from abstract steel works to life-sized bronze figures, all positioned to use the ocean as a natural backdrop.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/views-from-along-sidney-bcs-waterfront-and-sculpture-walkway-7-gm1173410341-325911783

Beacon Park & The Pavilion: Located at the foot of Beacon Avenue, Beacon Park features a large amphitheater and a gazebo. It is the town's primary gathering spot for sunset viewing and community events.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/beacon-park-and-waterfront-in-sidney-british-columbia-gm512556602-87215687

Glass Beach: Situated just north of the main pier, Glass Beach is a local favorite for beachcombing. Over decades, the tides have deposited and smoothed fragments of sea glass and unique colorful stones along this small cove.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/glass-beach-at-the-shore-of-sidney-gm1128719494-297923920

The Sidney Pier: This working fishing pier allows visitors to walk far out over the water to watch crabbers or local boat traffic. It is also home to a popular fish market and waterfront dining options.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sidney-pier-at-sunset-gm1216966233-355047103
Tips & Key Information

Because the waterfront faces east, it is one of the best spots on the Saanich Peninsula for sunrise photography. During the late afternoon, the low sun illuminates the islands in the distance, creating a high-contrast postcard view.
Keep an eye on the kelp beds just offshore; harbor seals are frequently seen bobbing in the water, and bald eagles often perch on the lighting masts near the marinas.
The entire length of the walkway is paved and wide, making it ideal for those using wheelchairs or strollers. There are numerous benches positioned every few hundred meters for rest stops.
On Thursday evenings in the summer, the area adjacent to the waterfront becomes part of a massive night market, featuring over 100 local vendors and live music.

places.name: 6. Beacon Avenue and Downtown Sidney
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/from-the-pier-up-beacon-street-in-sidney-british-columbia-gm512556936-87216013

Beacon Avenue serves as the primary artery of downtown Sidney, sloping gently from the highway down to the Salish Sea. This tree-lined thoroughfare is the centerpiece of Canada's only Booktown, where a dense concentration of independent shops and cafes creates a nostalgic, small-town atmosphere.
What to Do and See

The Booktown Experience: You can spend hours exploring several unique bookstores within a few blocks, ranging from the multi-roomed Tanner's Books to specialty shops focusing on rare and antiquarian titles.
Artisanal Boutiques: The street is characterized by a lack of major chains, favoring local galleries, clothing boutiques, and gift shops that feature West Coast craftsmanship.
Public Art: Keep an eye out for the Sidney Murals and various bronze statues tucked into alcoves and street corners along the avenue, which depict the town's maritime and pioneer history.
Café Culture: Numerous bakeries and bistros offer sidewalk seating, making it a popular spot for a slow morning coffee or a locally sourced lunch.
The Sidney Street Market: If you visit on a Thursday evening during the summer months, the entire avenue is closed to vehicles and transformed into a massive night market with over 100 vendors.
Sidney Museum: Housed in the historic post office building, the museum explores the region’s pioneer and industrial history through rotating exhibits and a permanent collection of local artifacts.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/drone-shot-over-the-town-of-sidney-vancouver-island-bc-canada-gm1441498436-481183654
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sidney-streetview-gm935162318-255929159
Tips & Key Information
The late afternoon golden hour is particularly beautiful here, as the low sun shines directly down the length of the avenue toward the water, highlighting the colorful storefronts.
The downtown core is exceptionally flat and easy to navigate on foot, with plenty of benches for resting and clear signage pointing toward the waterfront.
While there is 1-hour and 2-hour street parking on Beacon Avenue, you can often find longer-term parking in the municipal lots just one block north or south.

places.name: 7. ȽÁU, WELṈEW̱ / John Dean Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/field-with-buildings-in-john-dean-provincial-park-bc-canada-gm1440557849-480509449

ȽÁU,WELṈEW̱/John Dean Provincial Park, situated atop Mount Newton, is a place of profound spiritual significance and natural beauty. It was the first provincial park on Vancouver Island donated from private land and holds a sacred place in the history of the W̱SÁNEĆ people, whose name for the mountain means place of refuge.
What to Do and See

Panoramic Viewpoints: The park is famous for its pick-your-own vistas. Looking east, you can see across the Saanich Peninsula toward the Gulf Islands and Mount Baker; looking west, the views stretch over the Saanich Inlet toward the Malahat and Cowichan Valley.

Old-Growth Douglas Fir: It is one of the few places on the southern peninsula where you can still walk through significant stands of old-growth forest, with some Douglas fir trees estimated to be over 400 years old.
Wildflower Displays: In the spring, the mossy bluffs and open meadows erupt with Camas lilies, chocolate lilies, and shooting stars, creating a vibrant carpet of purple and white.
Birdwatching: The varied elevations and forest types attract a wide range of avian life, from soaring turkey vultures and bald eagles to smaller woodland species like the pileated woodpecker.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/pathway-in-a-forest-at-john-dean-provincial-park-north-saanich-bc-canada-gm1446628217-484658426
Tips & Key Information

Sunset is particularly dramatic from the western viewpoints, while sunrise offers a crisp, clear light over the islands to the east. Photographers often favor the West Observation Point for capturing the silhouettes of the rugged hills across the inlet.

While the trails are well-marked, they involve significant elevation changes and rocky terrain. Sturdy footwear is highly recommended, especially after rain when the mossy sections can become slippery.

Visitors are encouraged to reflect on the mountain’s role as a sanctuary for the W̱SÁNEĆ people during the great flood. Reading the interpretive signage provides essential context for the land's heritage.
The main parking lot is at the end of John Dean Park Road. During peak summer weekends, it can fill early; visiting on a weekday morning often provides a much quieter experience.
The park features approximately 9 kilometers of hiking trails ranging from easy strolls near the parking area to more strenuous loops like the Sylvan Trail.
Pit toilets and picnic tables are available near the main trailhead. There is no potable water in the park, so be sure to bring your own.
The park is open year-round for hiking, though the vehicle access gate at the bottom of the hill may be closed during periods of heavy snow or ice in the winter.
Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a leash at all times to protect the sensitive wildflower meadows and local wildlife.

places.name: 8. Island View Beach Regional Park
body: Island View Beach Regional Park is an expansive coastal destination on the eastern shore of the Saanich Peninsula. Known for its long sandy shoreline and unique dune ecosystem, it offers some of the best unobstructed views of Haro Strait and the San Juan Islands.
What to Do and See

The Shoreline Walk: A flat, easy trail follows the coastline for several kilometers. It is a favorite for those who enjoy a mix of sandy beach walking and stabilized gravel paths, providing a constant view of the water and passing marine traffic.

Birdwatching and Wildlife: The park's diverse habitat—including salt marshes, dunes, and coastal bluffs—makes it a hotspot for birders. You can often spot bald eagles, ospreys, and various migratory shorebirds along the water's edge.

Geological Features: The beach is famous for its glacial erratic boulders and shifting sands. It is a premier location for beachcombing, especially after a winter storm when the tides reveal new treasures and reshape the shoreline.

Picnicking and Beach Use: Large open grassy areas near the parking lots are perfect for group picnics. The shallow, sloping beach is popular for kiteboarding and paddleboarding when the winds are favorable.
Tips & Key Information
Because it faces east, this is a top-tier location for sunrise photography. The light hitting the driftwood and the distant islands creates a serene, high-contrast landscape.
Check the tide tables before you go; at low tide, the beach expands significantly, revealing tide pools and long stretches of traversable sand that disappear when the water is high.

The park is very popular with dog owners. While there are off-leash areas, pay close attention to seasonal restrictions (typically between June and September) intended to protect nesting birds in the dunes.
The beach can be quite windy and exposed. Even on sunny days, bringing a windbreaker is recommended to stay comfortable during longer walks along the shore.
The main loop trail is relatively flat and surfaced with packed gravel, making it accessible for most strollers and all-terrain wheelchairs.

The park features pit toilets, seasonal drinking water stations, and several large parking areas. There are no food concessions on-site, so it is best to pack your own supplies from nearby Saanichton.
There is a seasonal RV and tent campground adjacent to the park (operated by the CRD), which is one of the few places on the peninsula where you can stay right next to the ocean.
Located at the end of Island View Road, it is about a 15-minute drive north of Victoria or 10 minutes south of Sidney.

places.name: 9. Victoria Butterfly Gardens
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/white-tree-nymph-butterfly-on-flower-in-butterfly-garden-gm1042073724-278993883

Victoria Butterfly Gardens is a vibrant, 12,000-square-foot indoor tropical jungle located in Brentwood Bay, just minutes from The Butchart Gardens. It offers a fully immersive experience where thousands of tropical butterflies fly freely among visitors in a temperature-controlled environment designed to mimic a rainforest.
What to Do and See

The Butterfly Experience: Encounter up to 70 different species of butterflies. You can observe their entire life cycle, from the pupae in the nursery to the adults feeding on fruit trays and nectar plants throughout the facility.

Tropical Inhabitants: Beyond butterflies, the gardens are home to a diverse array of tropical animals. Look for Caribbean flamingos, koi in the large pond, tropical birds like macaws and parrots, and a variety of reptiles including iguanas and tortoises.
The Insectarium: This dedicated section showcases impressive insects from around the world, such as giant walking sticks, praying mantises, and various beetle species.
Botanical Diversity: The environment is lush with hundreds of species of tropical plants, including orchids, bromeliads, and carnivorous plants, all thriving around a central waterfall.
Tips & Key Information
Many visitors find that wearing bright colors like red, orange, or pink encourages butterflies to land on them, providing excellent photography opportunities.
The facility is kept at a high temperature and humidity level to ensure the health of the tropical species, so it can feel quite warm compared to the outside air.
Use a macro lens if you have one to capture the intricate details of the butterflies. The golden hour of mid-morning light through the glass roof can create a beautiful, natural glow for wide shots.
Plan for about 60 to 90 minutes to explore the gardens at a leisurely pace. It is an excellent all-weather activity, especially on rainy days when outdoor exploration is less ideal.
The gardens are generally open daily from 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM, though it is always wise to check for any seasonal changes or private event closures before your visit.
The facility is fully wheelchair and stroller accessible, with wide, paved paths winding through the tropical foliage.
Conveniently located at the intersection of Benvenuto Avenue and West Saanich Road, it is easily combined with a trip to other nearby Saanich Peninsula attractions.

places.name: 10. BC Aviation Museum
body: The BC Aviation Museum is a premier heritage destination located on the edge of the Victoria International Airport in North Saanich. Spanning three large hangars, it preserves the rich history of flight in British Columbia through an extensive collection of over 30 aircraft and thousands of artifacts.
What to Do and See

The Lancaster Bomber: One of the museum's most significant projects is the ongoing restoration of the Avro Lancaster FM213. It is one of only a few remaining in the world, and visitors can often see volunteers actively working on its preservation.

Vickers Viscount: You can step inside this classic 1950s turboprop airliner, which served as a flagship for Trans-Canada Air Lines. The interior is meticulously maintained to reflect the golden age of commercial flight.
Early Flight & Bush Planes: Explore the roots of BC aviation with displays of early floatplanes and bush planes that were essential for connecting remote coastal and northern communities.
The Memorial Room: This quiet space is dedicated to the men and women who served in the Royal Canadian Air Force, featuring uniforms, medals, and personal stories from WWI to the present.
Tips & Key Information

While you can explore at your own pace, the museum is staffed by passionate volunteers—many of whom are retired pilots or mechanics. Striking up a conversation with them often yields fascinating first-hand stories about the planes on display.
The hangars provide unique industrial backdrops. Mid-morning light through the hangar doors can create dramatic shadows and highlights on the polished aluminum fuselages.
Check out the flight simulators and the hands-on cockpit displays, which are particularly popular with younger visitors and aspiring pilots.
The museum shop is known for its specialized collection of aviation books, model kits, and unique heritage-themed apparel.
For 2026, adult admission is approximately $15.00, with discounts available for seniors, students, and families. Children under 6 typically enter for free.
The museum is generally open daily from 10:00 AM to 4:00 PM. They are closed on major holidays like Christmas and New Year's Day.
Located at 1910 Norseman Road. There is ample free parking available directly in front of the museum entrance.
The hangars are flat and wheelchair accessible, though some aircraft interiors (like the Viscount) may have stairs or narrow aisles that are not accessible to mobility devices.

places.name: 11. Lochside Regional Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/autumn-colors-along-the-lochside-regional-trail-gm1350531855-426600157

The Lochside Regional Trail is a 29-kilometer multi-use pathway that stretches from the Swartz Bay Ferry Terminal in North Saanich to downtown Victoria. Built on a former railway line, it connects urban neighborhoods with the rolling farmland and coastal vistas of the Saanich Peninsula.
What to Do and See

The Flavour Trail Sections: As the trail winds through Central Saanich, it passes through lush agricultural land. You can stop at various farm stands, markets, and cideries located just meters off the path.
Coastal Views at Tulista Park: In Sidney, the trail runs directly along the waterfront at Tulista Park, providing clear views across the Haro Strait toward the San Juan Islands.
Birdwatching at McMinn Park: This section near the Cordova Bay area features wetlands and wooded areas where you can frequently spot local bird species and occasionally deer.
Blenkinsop Lake Trestle: A highlight of the southern section is the wooden trestle bridge crossing Blenkinsop Lake, offering a scenic perspective of the floating marsh and local waterfowl.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/lochside-trail-gm1145731633-308485345
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sidney-waterfront-walkway-sidney-vancouver-island-bc-canada-gm1441498594-481183894
Tips & Key Information
Be aware that the trail surface changes. The northern sections in Sidney and North Saanich are primarily paved, while parts of the central peninsula consist of packed gravel or shared roadways.
Cycling the northern sections toward Sidney during the late afternoon offers beautiful backlighting through the farm fields and a glowing horizon over the ocean.

At its southern end, the Lochside Trail meets the Galloping Goose Regional Trail via a signature Switchbridge. This allows for a continuous loop back toward the Western Communities or deeper into downtown Victoria.
The trail's relatively flat grade makes it excellent for e-bikes, though riders should adhere to the 20 km/h speed limit to ensure the safety of pedestrians and horses.
The majority of the trail is flat and accessible for wheelchairs and strollers, particularly the paved segments in Sidney and Saanich.
This is a multi-use trail. You will encounter cyclists, runners, walkers, and in some rural sections, equestrian riders. Always yield to pedestrians and horses.
Major trailheads with parking are located at Mitchell Farm, Cy Hampson Park, and various points along the Sidney waterfront.
Public washrooms and water fountains are spaced out at regional parks along the route, such as Tulista Park and McMinn Park.

places.name: 12. Roberts Bay and the Shoal Harbour Migratory Bird Sanctuary
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/great-blue-heron-fishing-at-roberts-bay-sidney-bc-canada-gm1473601638-503694073

The Roberts Bay - Shoal Harbour Migratory Bird Sanctuary is a vital ecological area located just north of downtown Sidney. This sheltered bay provides a tranquil environment for both wildlife and visitors, acting as a crucial wintering ground for thousands of waterfowl and shorebirds.
What to Do and See

Birdwatching: As a federally protected sanctuary, this area is a premier destination for spotting species such as Buffleheads, Harlequin Ducks, and Great Blue Herons. The intertidal mudflats are particularly active during the spring and fall migrations.

Resthaven Linear Park Walk: A well-maintained path at Resthaven Linear Park follows the shoreline, offering level walking surfaces and multiple vantage points over the harbour. It is a popular spot for those seeking a quieter alternative to the main Sidney waterfront.

Intertidal Exploration: During low tide, the bay reveals expansive mudflats and rocky pools. It’s an excellent place for gentle beachcombing and observing the small marine creatures that inhabit the Salish Sea.

Resthaven Park: Located on the western edge of the harbour, Resthaven Park features open green spaces, picnic tables, and a playground, making it a comfortable base for families exploring the shoreline.
Tips & Key Information

Visiting during the early morning or late afternoon provides the best lighting for bird photography and often coincides with increased bird activity. The low sun reflecting off the calm harbour waters creates a peaceful, high-contrast atmosphere.
Much of the sanctuary's character changes with the tides. High tide is best for seeing swimming waterfowl close to the shore, while low tide is necessary for exploring the mudflats.
Because this is a sensitive migratory area, visitors are encouraged to stay on marked paths and use binoculars to observe birds from a distance to avoid disturbing their feeding or resting patterns.
The paths around Resthaven are generally flat and paved or packed gravel, making them accessible for wheelchairs and strollers.
While dogs are permitted in nearby parks, they must be kept on a leash at all times within the migratory bird sanctuary boundaries to protect the resident and visiting bird populations.
Public washrooms and parking are available at Resthaven Park. There are no commercial services within the sanctuary itself, maintaining its natural character.

places.name: 13. Coles Bay Regional Park
body: Coles Bay Regional Park is a serene, 3.6-hectare coastal retreat located on the Saanich Inlet in North Saanich. This park is particularly valued for its quiet, woodland trails that lead to a sheltered, pebbly beach, offering a more intimate experience than the larger regional parks.
What to Do and See
The Beach: The sheltered cove is ideal for beachcombing, exploring tide pools at low tide, or simply enjoying the tranquil views across the Saanich Inlet toward the Malahat.
Forest Trails: A network of short, easy walking paths winds through a lush forest of Douglas fir, arbutus, and cedar trees, providing a cool and shaded environment even on warm days.
Birdwatching: The quiet waters and surrounding forest attract a variety of local bird life, including kingfishers, herons, and various forest-dwelling songbirds.
Intertidal Life: At low tide, the rocky shoreline reveals a wealth of marine life, such as crabs, barnacles, and sea anemones, making it a great spot for gentle nature observation.
Tips & Key Information

Because the beach faces west over the Saanich Inlet, it is one of the premier spots on the peninsula for sunset photography. The light reflecting off the calm water and the silhouettes of the arbutus trees create a classic West Coast scene.
To get the most out of the shoreline, check the tide charts. A lower tide allows for more space to walk along the beach and better access to the tide pools.
This park is generally less crowded than Island View or Sidney Spit, making it an excellent choice for those seeking a peaceful escape or a quiet spot for a picnic.
The main trail from the parking lot to the beach is relatively short and well-maintained, though it does include some gentle slopes. The beach itself is pebbly and can be uneven.
The park features a small parking lot, pit toilets, and picnic tables located near the trailhead. There is no potable water on-site.
Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a leash to protect the sensitive coastal environment and wildlife.
Situated at the end of Inverness Road in North Saanich, it is a convenient stop for those exploring the western side of the Saanich Peninsula.

places.name: 14. G.B. Church and HMCS Mackenzie
body: The waters near Sidney are home to two of British Columbia's most celebrated artificial reefs, managed by the Artificial Reef Society of BC. Both sites are accessible by boat and offer divers a chance to see significant marine colonization on historical vessels.
Artificial reef G.B. Church

The G.B. Church is a 175-foot coastal freighter that was scuttled in 1991 off the coast of Portland Island near Sidney. It was the first vessel sunk by the Artificial Reef Society and has since become one of the most popular dive sites in the region.
Marine Life: Divers frequently report seeing massive plumose anemones, rockfish, lingcod, and octopuses inhabiting the hull and deck.
Site Features: The ship sits upright on a sandy bottom at a depth of approximately 80 to 90 feet. The holds and bridge were prepared for diver access, allowing for safe penetration.
Ease of Access: Because the ship sits relatively shallow compared to other wrecks, it is often used as an introduction for divers new to wreck diving.
HMCS Mackenzie

The HMCS Mackenzie is a 366-foot decommissioned Mackenzie-class destroyer sunk in 1995 off Rum Island. Its large scale makes it an impressive site that typically requires multiple dives to fully explore.
The Structure: The ship rests at a depth of about 60 to 100 feet. The upper structures are at a more accessible depth, while the hull reaches the deeper limits.
Advanced Exploration: While the upper decks are approachable for intermediate divers, the sheer size and potential for internal exploration make certain sections better suited for advanced divers.
Natural Evolution: Much like the G.B. Church, the Mackenzie has transformed into a thriving ecosystem, completely covered in white plumose anemones and serving as a nursery for local fish species.
Tips and Key Information
Both sites are boat-access only. Most divers depart from marinas in Sidney, which are a short boat ride from the wreck locations.
Visibility is typically at its best during the winter months (November to March). While the water is colder, the lack of plankton blooms provides much clearer views of the massive structures.
These sites are part of an ongoing effort to create habitat. Divers are encouraged to practice neutral buoyancy to avoid damaging the fragile marine life growing on the metal surfaces.
Local dive shops in Sidney and the surrounding Saanich Peninsula offer regular charters to these wrecks, often providing rental gear and professional guides for those unfamiliar with the sites.

places.name: 15. Wineries, Breweries and Distilleries
body: Sidney and the surrounding Saanich Peninsula have developed a sophisticated tasting trail that ranges from waterfront distilleries to pastoral farmgate wineries. Many of these locations are easily accessible via the Lochside Regional Trail, making them popular stops for cycling-based tours.
Distilleries
Victoria Distillers is one of Canada’s oldest artisan distilleries, now operating out of a striking glass-walled facility on the Sidney waterfront.
Empress 1908 Gin: They are best known for this award-winning, indigo-colored gin, which was created in collaboration with Victoria's iconic Empress Hotel.

The Experience: While formal tours are currently paused, the retail store offers complimentary tastings where you can sample their full range, including their classic Victoria Gin and specialty spirits.
Sustainability: The distillery uses a closed-loop geothermal system to recapture heat from their stills, which is then used to warm the guest rooms at the adjacent Sidney Pier Hotel.
Breweries
Small Gods Brewing Co. is a literary-themed brewery in downtown Sidney that serves as a community third place, blending a love for craft beer with the town's Booktown identity.
Atmosphere: The tasting room is designed to feel like a modern library or bookstore, providing a relaxed environment for both social gatherings and quiet reading.
The Beer: They focus on balanced, easy-drinking styles alongside creative seasonal rotations, often named with literary references.
Beacon Brewing is a family-run, 5-barrel nanobrewery located just steps away from Small Gods, making it easy to visit both in a single afternoon.
The Vibe: Known for its cozy, local atmosphere, it features a small seating area where you can watch the brewing process through a glass partition.
Selection: They offer a diverse flight of beers, frequently featuring light-bodied ales and experimental small-batch releases.
Wineries & Cideries
Deep Cove Winery is a boutique, family-owned winery at the northern tip of the Saanich Peninsula, situated in one of the warmest microclimates in the region.
Vineyard Settings: The three-acre vineyard produces hand-crafted, cellar-aged wines, including their signature Ortega and robust reds like Alchemy.
Tastings: Their tasting room offers a tranquil setting overlooking the vines, often accompanied by local cheese boards and charcuterie.
Sea Cider Farm & Ciderhouse is a certified organic orchard and cidery in Saanichton that offers sweeping views of the Haro Strait.
Tasting Flights: They are famous for their curated cider flights, which range from bone-dry traditional styles to dessert-like infusions.
Heritage Orchard: The site features over 1,300 apple trees representing more than 50 heritage varieties, which you can explore on self-guided walks around the property.
Tips for the Best Experience
If you are planning a multi-stop tour, consider booking a tasting tour with a local shuttle service or using the Lochside Regional Trail for a scenic bike ride between locations.
While many tasting rooms accept walk-ins, popular spots like Sea Cider and Deep Cove Winery are highly recommended to be booked in advance, especially for weekend visits.
Sea Cider and Deep Cove both offer spectacular lighting during the late afternoon as the sun sets over the peninsula's ridges, making it the ideal time for vineyard photography.

places.name: 16. Golfing
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/water-hazard-gm89349434-3384302

While Sidney itself is a compact seaside town, it serves as the central hub for some of the most scenic golf courses on the Saanich Peninsula. The region's mild climate allows for year-round play, often with stunning views of the Salish Sea and the Olympic Mountains.
Premier Golf Courses Nearby

Ardmore Golf Course: A local favorite for a quicker round, this 9-hole course in North Saanich is beautifully maintained. It is particularly popular for its relaxed atmosphere and walkable flat terrain, making it ideal for a morning game before heading into downtown Sidney.

Victoria Golf Club: While a private club located further south in Oak Bay, it is often cited by visitors to Sidney due to its historic status (the oldest club in Canada in its original location) and spectacular oceanfront holes.
Mount Douglas Golf Course: For those seeking a casual or family-friendly experience, this 9-hole executive course is located on the way toward Victoria and offers a scenic, hilly landscape.
Tips and Key Information

Late afternoon tee times on the Peninsula offer spectacular lighting. At courses like Ardmore, the sun dipping behind the trees creates long, dramatic shadows across the fairways, perfect for photography.
Even on sunny days, the breeze off the Saanich Inlet or Haro Strait can be cool. It is always recommended to bring a light windbreaker or a vest to stay comfortable through 18 holes.
It is very common to share the fairways with local deer and a variety of birdlife, including bald eagles. Keep your camera ready, but remember to maintain a respectful distance from the animals.

Many golfers head back into downtown Sidney after their round to enjoy the local breweries or waterfront restaurants on Beacon Avenue, which are only a 5-to-10-minute drive from the local North Saanich courses.
Unlike many Canadian destinations, golf is a 12-month activity here. However, winter play may involve mats only on some tees or temporary greens during frost.
During the peak summer months, weekend morning tee times fill up quickly. Booking at least a week in advance is highly recommended for Glen Meadows and Ardmore.
Most courses in the area offer full club rentals, power carts, and pull carts for those traveling without their own equipment.
The courses on the Peninsula are generally well-suited for all ages and skill levels, with flat layouts at Ardmore being particularly accessible for those who prefer walking over using a cart.

places.name: Sooke Potholes Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/river-surrounded-by-rocks-and-trees-in-sooke-potholes-provincial-park-vancouver-gm1440542341-480496210

Sooke Potholes Provincial Park is a 7.3-hectare natural area on the banks of the Sooke River, famous for its unique geological formations. These potholes—deep, smooth rock pools—were carved out of volcanic rock by boulders trapped in swirling river currents over thousands of years. While the provincial park itself is smaller and less developed than the adjacent regional park, it serves as the essential southern entry point to this iconic river system.
What to See and Do

Natural Swimming Holes: The park is a premier destination for freshwater swimming. The crystal-clear emerald pools range from shallow gravel beds perfect for wading to deep basins popular with confident swimmers seeking a refreshingly cold dip.

The Riverside Trail: A well-maintained path follows the edge of the canyon, offering multiple viewpoints of the river's dramatic rock formations and cascading waterfalls. It connects directly to the larger trail network of the neighboring regional park.

Salmon Run Viewing: In the fall, the Sooke River becomes a major corridor for spawning Coho and Chinook salmon. The clear water makes it one of the best spots on the island to watch the fish battle upstream, which in turn attracts bald eagles and other wildlife.

Deertrail Resort Ruins: Visible from various vantage points along the river cliffs, these stone ruins are the remains of a failed luxury resort from the 1980s. The massive log-burning fireplace and stone walls provide a moody, lost civilization atmosphere against the forest backdrop.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/mary-vine-falls-sooke-vancouver-island-bc-gm1439276044-479580654
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sooke-river-sooke-potholes-provincial-park-vancouver-island-bc-gm1439276717-479580761
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sooke-pot-holes-gm1022477594-274508973
Tips & Key Information

The rocks around the potholes are made of polished volcanic stone which can be extremely slippery, especially when wet. Sturdy, high-traction footwear is essential for safely climbing down to the water's edge.
On hot summer weekends, the parking lots fill up very quickly. Arriving before 10:00 AM is recommended if you want to secure a spot and enjoy the quieter morning light for photography.

The water in the Sooke River stays cold year-round, even in peak summer. Additionally, the canyon is deeply shaded by tall Douglas firs, so it can feel significantly cooler than the coast; bringing layers is advised.
This is active bear and cougar country. Always pack out what you pack in, secure all food attractants, and stay on designated trails to minimize your impact on the sensitive ecosystem.
Pay parking is in effect from May 1 to September 30 in the Regional Park lots (approximately $2.25 per day). Dispensers typically accept coins and credit cards.

The park is a major highlight along the Galloping Goose Regional Trail. Cyclists can ride directly into the park from Victoria, though the provincial park section requires a short detour onto Sooke River Road.

Facilities within the Provincial Park are minimal, consisting primarily of a pit toilet at the parking lot. More extensive picnic areas and a seasonal campground are located further north in the Regional Park.
places.note: the smaller Sooke Potholes Provincial Park at the southern end and the larger Sooke Potholes Regional Park to the north. Most of the famous viewpoints and the campground are located within the Regional Park section.

places.name: East Sooke Regional Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/wild-pacific-northwest-coastline-of-east-sooke-regional-park-outside-of-victoria-gm1704591904-539078248

East Sooke Regional Park is often described as a miniature West Coast Trail, offering over 50 kilometers of trails through 1,400 hectares of rugged coastal wilderness. It is the premier destination on the southern tip of Vancouver Island for those seeking a true wilderness experience without leaving the Greater Victoria area.
What to See and Do

The Coast Trail: This challenging 10-kilometer route is the park's signature hike. It follows the jagged shoreline of the Juan de Fuca Strait, requiring some scrambling over rocky bluffs but rewarding hikers with panoramic views of the Olympic Mountains and the occasional sighting of whales or sea lions.

Aylard Farm: This is the most accessible part of the park, featuring a large open meadow and a sandy pocket beach. It is a popular spot for families, picnicking, and shorter walks to the nearby Ceepeecee Lookout.

Beechey Head: A world-renowned site for birdwatching, particularly during the autumn hawk migration. Thousands of turkey vultures and other raptors gather here before crossing the strait. It also features ancient petroglyphs carved into the rock by the Coast Salish people.

Mount Maguire: For those seeking elevation, the trail to the summit of Mount Maguire offers the highest vantage point in the park, providing a 360-degree view of the Sooke Basin, the interior hills, and the open ocean.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/coastal-trail-in-the-scenic-east-sooke-regional-park-stunning-waterscape-in-the-gm1436961492-477879655
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/beechey-head-geographic-survey-reference-marker-canada-usa-border-sooke-bc-vancouver-gm1162444151-318855409
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/a-group-of-young-people-fishing-off-the-rocks-for-salmon-by-the-kelp-beds-in-juan-de-gm1268004389-372120513
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/drone-shot-of-east-sooke-park-sooke-vancouver-island-bc-gm1439276037-479580656
Tips & Key Information
Sunset at Alldridge Point or any of the west-facing rocky outcrops is spectacular. The light catches the arbutus trees' peeling bark and turns the Olympic Peninsula across the water a deep purple.

The Coast Trail is significantly more difficult than it appears on a map. Allow at least 6 to 8 hours for the full one-way trip, wear sturdy boots, and bring plenty of water, as there are no refill stations along the shore.
Be aware that cellular reception is highly unreliable in the park's interior and along the lower coastal bluffs. It is recommended to download or carry a physical map before entering.
Bring binoculars. The deep waters close to the cliffs at Beechey Head are a frequent corridor for transient orcas and humpback whales traveling through the strait.
There are three main entrances: Aylard Farm (east), Anderson Cove (north/interior), and Pike Road (west). Most coastal hikers start at one end and arrange a vehicle shuttle at the other.
Pit toilets and picnic tables are located at the main trailheads. There is no potable water available within the park, so you must pack in all necessary supplies.
Dogs are permitted but must be kept under control at all times. They are required to be on a leash in the Aylard Farm picnic area to protect local wildlife and other visitors.
The park is characterized by its up and down nature. Even the forest trails involve frequent elevation changes over roots and rocks, making it a moderately strenuous destination for most visitors.

places.name: Whiffin Spit
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/whiffin-spit-park-sooke-british-columbia-gm2204205403-621672894

Whiffin Spit is a naturally formed gravel bar that stretches for about 1.5 kilometers into Sooke Harbour, acting as a scenic breakwater between the calm inner basin and the rugged Juan de Fuca Strait. It is a favorite for those seeking a quick, low-impact coastal walk with some of the best mountain and water views in Sooke.
What to See and Do

Coastal Stroll: The main trail is a flat, 2.7-kilometer out-and-back gravel path. It provides a unique experience of walking through the middle of the ocean, with the Olympic Mountains of Washington State looming directly ahead.

Wildlife and Birdwatching: Over 220 species of birds have been recorded here. On the seaward side, you can often spot Harlequin Ducks and Pacific Loons, while the calmer harbour side attracts Great Blue Herons and Black Oystercatchers. Keep an eye out for harbour seals, sea lions, and even orcas near the mouth of the harbour.

Driftwood and Art: The shoreline is famously piled with massive logs of West Coast driftwood. Near the end of the spit, visitors often construct elaborate driftwood forts and sculptures. You can also find commemorative carvings near the parking lot honoring the T'Sou-ke Nation and early Spanish explorers.

Navigation Aid: At the very tip of the spit sits a 6.4-meter cylindrical tower that serves as a lighted navigational aid and weather station, guiding marine traffic through the narrow entrance to Sooke Harbour.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/whiffin-spit-in-sooke-british-columbia-canada-gm180727490-24186684
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/vancouver-island-coastline-gm2160504486-581037115
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/drone-shot-of-whiffin-spit-sooke-vancouver-island-bc-gm1439276715-479580763
Tips & Key Information

Whiffin Spit is a premier location for sunset photography. The unobstructed views allow you to watch the sun dip below the horizon, casting long shadows across the driftwood and painting the Olympic Mountains in shades of purple and gold.
While the beach is accessible, many visitors stick to the main gravel path to avoid the uneven, shifting terrain of the pebbles and driftwood.

The park is exceptionally dog-friendly. There is a specialized dog fountain at the entrance, and the flat path is popular for local walkers, though leashes are required to protect the sensitive bird habitat.

Because the spit is a narrow finger of land exposed to the strait, it can be significantly windier and cooler than the Sooke town center. A windbreaker or extra layer is recommended even on sunny days.
The park is equipped with pit toilets at the parking lot and a second set about halfway down the trail. A water fountain and bottle filler are located at the entrance.
There is a free gravel parking lot at the end of Whiffin Spit Road. It can be busy on summer weekends, but the high turnover of walkers usually means a spot opens up quickly.
The trail is level and composed of packed gravel, making it accessible for strollers and most all-terrain wheelchairs.
The park is open year-round and technically accessible 24 hours a day, though there is no artificial lighting along the trail after dark.

places.name: Sheringham Point Lighthouse
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/drone-aerial-image-of-sheringham-point-lighthouse-sooke-shirley-british-columbia-gm2241296886-655827738

Sheringham Point Lighthouse is a designated National Heritage site perched on the rocky coastline of Shirley, approximately 20 minutes west of Sooke. Built in 1912 following the tragic wreck of the SS Valencia, the white hexagonal tower remains an iconic symbol of maritime history and is one of the few lighthouses on Vancouver Island accessible by land.
What to See and Do

Jennie’s Trail & Viewpoints: A short, relatively easy walking trail leads from the parking lot to the lighthouse gate. From there, you can explore several spur trails that lead to specialized viewing platforms, offering unobstructed vistas of the Juan de Fuca Strait and the Olympic Mountains.

Whale Watching: The point is a premier shore-based whale-watching spot. The preservation society has installed a speaker on the side of the engine room connected to underwater hydrophones, allowing you to listen for the vocalizations of passing orcas and humpbacks.

Heritage Exploration: While the interior of the tower is currently closed to the public, the site is filled with interpretive signage detailing the lives of the lightkeepers and the technological evolution of the station from oil lamps to automation.

Nature Photography: The rugged cliffs, wind-swept arbutus trees, and the contrasting red-and-white lighthouse provide a classic West Coast backdrop. The area is particularly popular for astrophotography due to the minimal light pollution.
Tips & Key Information

Sunset is spectacular here, as the light hits the side of the tower and the cliffs directly. For sunrise, the Eastern Spur Trail offers the best vantage point to see the sun rising over the distant peninsula.

The site is maintained by the non-profit Sheringham Point Lighthouse Preservation Society. While admission is free, there are donation tubes and QR codes on-site to help fund ongoing restoration projects.
While the initial path is groomed, the spur trails and the descent to the lighthouse base are steep and can be slippery when wet. Sturdy, closed-toe shoes are highly recommended.
There are no garbage receptacles on the property. Visitors are required to take all waste back with them to help maintain the pristine community park environment.
The park is open daily from 9:00 AM to dusk. Gates are locked in the evening; in early spring, this is typically around 6:00 PM or 7:00 PM.
A concrete path leads to a wheelchair-accessible viewing platform at the top of the site. However, the lower trails to the lighthouse base are steep and not suitable for strollers or mobility aids.

A pit toilet is available in the main parking lot at the end of Sheringham Point Road. There is no potable water or food service on-site, though the local Shirley Delicious Cafe is just a short drive away.
Use the official parking lot at the end of Sheringham Point Road. Parking along Seaside Drive or Lighthouse Road is prohibited to respect local residents.

places.name: French Beach Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/french-beach-provincial-park-woodland-gm2242072394-656468966

French Beach Provincial Park is a 59-hectare coastal destination situated along the Juan de Fuca Strait, approximately 20 kilometers west of Sooke. It is widely recognized for its long, pebble-and-sand beach and its accessibility, making it one of the most popular family destinations on the southwestern coast of Vancouver Island.
What to Do and See
Shoreline Exploration: The park features a 1,600-meter beach that is ideal for beachcombing and walking. It offers expansive views across the strait to the Olympic Mountains in Washington State.

Wildlife Viewing: The area is a prime location for spotting marine life. Gray whales can often be seen migrating past the beach in the spring, while killer whales, sea lions, and seals are frequent visitors throughout the year. Bald eagles and ospreys are also common sights in the tall trees bordering the shore.
Forest Trails: A network of short, easy trails winds through a forest of Douglas fir and Western Red cedar, connecting the campground and day-use areas to the beach.
Picnicking and Play: The large, grassy day-use area includes numerous picnic tables and a playground, providing a comfortable space for families to gather just steps from the ocean.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/french-beach-provincial-park-woodland-trail-gm1699717347-538566502
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/french-beach-provincial-park-with-the-views-of-the-strait-of-juan-de-fuca-and-the-gm927756098-254485271
Tips & Key Information

The park's westward-facing orientation makes it a top-tier location for sunset viewing. The golden hour light reflecting off the pebbles and the water provides excellent opportunities for landscape photography.
Like many coastal parks in this region, the weather can be significantly cooler and windier than in Sooke. Bringing a windbreaker or layers is recommended even on sunny days.
During the summer months and on holiday weekends, the day-use parking area and picnic spots can fill up quickly. Arriving early in the day helps ensure a prime spot near the beach.
If you are visiting during migration seasons, bring binoculars. The beach's open vista makes it easier to track the spouts and fins of passing whales from a distance.
The park offers a year-round vehicle-accessible campground with 69 campsites. Facilities include pit toilets and a sani-station, though there are no electrical hookups.
The day-use area is largely flat and features paved or packed gravel paths, making much of the park accessible for strollers and mobility aids.
Seasonal drinking water and pit toilets are available. While there are no food services on-site, the nearby communities of Shirley and Sooke offer various dining options.
Dogs are welcome but must be on a leash at all times and are restricted from the beach area to protect local wildlife and ensure a pleasant environment for all visitors.

places.name: China Beach
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/china-beach-vancouver-island-gm1465719335-498049513

China Beach is a stunning coastal destination within the Juan de Fuca Provincial Park, located roughly 35 kilometers west of Sooke. It serves as one of the major trailheads for the Juan de Fuca Marine Trail and is highly regarded for its expansive fine-sand shoreline and dramatic ocean vistas.
What to See and Do

Shoreline and Waterfall: The beach itself is a wide stretch of sand, perfect for long walks. A highlight is the small waterfall that cascades down the sandstone cliffs directly onto the beach, particularly active after a rainfall.

Juan de Fuca Marine Trail: This area serves as the eastern terminus for the 47-kilometer Juan de Fuca Marine Trail. Hikers can explore the first few kilometers of this rugged backcountry trail to get a taste of the wilderness without committing to the full multi-day trek.

Whale Watching and Marine Life: Like many spots along this coast, China Beach is an excellent vantage point for spotting migrating Gray whales in the spring and Orcas throughout the year. The tide pools at the far ends of the beach reveal a vibrant world of anemones, crabs, and sea stars at low tide.
Surfing and Storm Watching: During the winter months, the beach becomes a popular spot for cold-water surfing and observing the powerful Pacific storms that roll in from the Juan de Fuca Strait.
Tips & Key Information

Accessing the beach requires a 15-to-20-minute walk through a mature forest of Douglas fir and Sitka spruce. The trail is well-maintained but involves a steady incline on the return trip, so pace yourself accordingly.

While the beach is expansive, certain sections near the cliffs can become cut off during extremely high tides. Checking a tide table before your visit ensures you have plenty of room to explore the full length of the sands.
There are no food services at China Beach, so it is best to pack a lunch. The driftwood logs scattered along the high-tide line provide natural seating with a front-row view of the Olympic Mountains.
The misty reputation of the West Coast is often on display here. Even if it is sunny in Sooke, China Beach can be shrouded in fog or significantly cooler due to the sea breeze.
The day-use area features a large parking lot and pit toilets at the trailhead. There is no potable water available on-site, so be sure to bring enough for your hike and beach stay.
A vehicle-accessible campground is located nearby within the provincial park, offering 78 sites set in a lush forest environment. Reservations are highly recommended during the peak summer season.
The trail to the beach is wide and surfaced with gravel, but the elevation change and occasional roots make it challenging for standard strollers or wheelchairs.
Dogs are permitted in the park but must be kept on a leash at all times to protect the surrounding habitat and wildlife.

places.name: Race Rocks Ecological Reserve
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/harbor-seal-eats-chinook-king-salmon-race-rocks-ecological-reserve-vancouver-island-gm1027806846-275547140

Race Rocks Ecological Reserve is a unique marine sanctuary located at the eastern entrance of the Juan de Fuca Strait. Known for its high-current environment, it serves as a critical habitat for a diverse range of marine life and is home to one of the oldest lighthouses on the Pacific Coast.
What to See and Do

Marine Mammal Observation: This is a premier spot for viewing California and Steller sea lions, which haul out on the rocks in massive numbers. You can also frequently spot harbour seals and northern elephant seals, alongside passing orcas and humpback whales.
Birdwatching: The islands are a vital nesting and stopover site for numerous seabirds. Look for Black Oystercatchers, Pigeon Guillemots, and various species of gulls and cormorants.
Historical Lighthouse: The iconic black-and-white striped Race Rocks Lighthouse, built in 1860, still stands as a functional aid to navigation and a landmark of BC’s maritime heritage.

Underwater Life: Though primarily accessible via remote cameras or specialized diving, the surrounding waters are famous for their incredible biodiversity, including giant plumose anemones and vibrant cold-water corals fueled by the powerful tidal currents.
Tips & Key Information
The reserve is only accessible by water. Many visitors join wildlife viewing tours departing from Sooke or Victoria, which provide a safe and educational way to view the rocks from a distance.
As an ecological reserve, landing on the islands is strictly prohibited without a permit. Tour operators follow professional guidelines to ensure animals are not disturbed by the presence of vessels.
If you cannot visit in person, the Race Rocks website often hosts live webcams that allow you to watch the sea lions and birds from your own device in real-time.
The area is exceptionally exposed to wind and spray. Even on a warm day, the temperature on the water near the rocks will be significantly lower, so bring a heavy windbreaker or waterproof layer.
It was established in 1980 as the first Marine Protected Area in Canada to protect the unique high-current ecosystem and its inhabitants.
The reserve consists of a cluster of small islands and reefs located about 1.5 kilometers off the southern tip of Vancouver Island.
There are no public facilities, shops, or docks for visitors. The only residents are the ecological reserve wardens who monitor the site.
Bring a long telephoto lens. Because boats must maintain a respectful distance from the shore, high-magnification gear is essential for capturing detailed shots of the seals and birds.

places.name: Matheson Lake Regional Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/trees-and-sky-reflecting-in-a-calm-lake-on-an-autumn-day-gm1301061141-393206403

Matheson Lake Regional Park is a scenic 156-hectare park located in Metchosin, known for its tranquil freshwater lake nestled within a steep-sided forest. It is a popular destination for those seeking a peaceful alternative to the oceanfront, offering a mix of accessible recreation and rugged hiking.
What to See and Do

The Lakeside Loop: A 3.8-kilometer trail circles the entire lake. While the eastern side is relatively flat and wide, the western portion becomes more rugged, involving some scrambling over rocky outcrops and roots, providing a varied hiking experience.

Swimming and Paddling: The lake's calm, freshwater surface is ideal for swimming during the summer months. It is also a favored spot for launching kayaks, canoes, or paddleboards to explore the small islands and hidden coves along the shoreline.
Fishing: The lake is regularly stocked with Rainbow Trout. Anglers often frequent the small docks or find quiet spots along the rocky banks to cast their lines, especially during the spring and fall.

Connection to Galloping Goose: The park serves as a major access point for the Galloping Goose Regional Trail. This allows visitors to easily combine a lakeside picnic with a long-distance cycle or walk toward Sooke or Victoria.
Tips & Key Information

On hot summer weekends, the small sandy beach and parking lot can reach capacity very early. Arriving before 10:00 AM is recommended to secure a spot and enjoy the quiet morning reflections on the water.

The golden hour at Matheson Lake is particularly beautiful as the sun sets behind the western hills, casting a mirror-like glow across the water. The surrounding Douglas fir and arbutus trees provide a classic Pacific Northwest frame for landscape shots.
If you plan to hike the full loop around the lake, wear sturdy, high-traction footwear. The western sections can be slippery and uneven, even in dry weather.
For those looking for solitude, the northern end of the lake, furthest from the main parking area, tends to be much quieter and offers excellent birdwatching opportunities.
The park features a main parking lot off Matheson Lake Park Road with pit toilets and a small sandy beach area. There is no potable water available, so please bring your own.
Dogs are permitted but must be kept on a leash at all times to protect the local wildlife and ensure the comfort of other park users.

The trail from the parking lot to the main beach is relatively flat and accessible, but the loop trail around the lake is not suitable for strollers or wheelchairs due to the rugged terrain on the western side.
Situated about 30 minutes west of Victoria, it is easily accessed via Happy Valley Road and Rocky Point Road.

places.name: Roche Cove Regional Park
body: Roche Cove Regional Park is a serene 163-hectare destination that borders the Sooke Basin and the District of Metchosin. Named after Richard Roche, a 3rd Lieutenant on the HMS Satellite, the park is known for its secluded cove, lush temperate rainforest, and convenient connection to the Galloping Goose Regional Trail.
What to See and Do

The Secluded Cove: A short, easy walk from the parking area leads to the protected waters of Roche Cove. At low tide, the sandy shoreline reveals little-neck clams and barnacles, while high tide is ideal for observing sea stars and migrating waterfowl like buffleheads and mergansers.

Cedar Grove Trail: This moderate, 2.5-hour loop offers an invigorating climb through old-growth forests. A highlight of the trail is a massive fallen cedar estimated to be over 500 years old, alongside viewpoints that overlook the park and Sooke Basin.

Matheson Creek Trail: This scenic route follows a cooling creek through a forest dense with bracken ferns and western red cedars. It serves as a natural corridor connecting Roche Cove to the neighboring Matheson Lake Regional Park.
Saltwater Swimming: The eastern end of the cove features a rocky and muddy beach that is a popular local spot for a refreshing saltwater dip during the warm summer months.
Tips & Key Information
Be aware that the Matheson Creek Trail is located in a floodplain and can become extremely muddy or impassable during the rainy winter months.
The alder forest along the Cedar Grove Trail is particularly active during the spring and fall, making it an excellent spot for birdwatchers to see songbirds and raptors.

Use the park as a starting point for a day trip on the Galloping Goose Regional Trail. Cycling north from here toward Sooke offers beautiful views of the basin and accessible, flat terrain for all ages.
There are no garbage cans within the park interior. Visitors are expected to pack out all waste to help preserve the sensitive rainforest ecosystem.
The main parking lot off Gillespie Road includes an information kiosk, a bike rack, accessible pit toilets, and a picnic area.
The lot has space for approximately 12 vehicles and mid-size buses. On busy weekends, parking is permitted along Gillespie Road, provided you do not block traffic or driveways.
Dogs are welcome but must be kept under control or on a leash. They must be leashed immediately when encountering horses, as the Galloping Goose is a multi-use trail.
The park is open daily from sunrise to sunset. Motorized vehicles, camping, and open fires are strictly prohibited.

places.name: Jordan River Regional Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sandcut-beach-falls-gm1496505258-519152808

Jordan River Regional Park and Campground is a diverse 187-hectare coastal park situated about 37 kilometers west of Sooke. It is a significant hub for outdoor recreation along the Juan de Fuca Highway, offering everything from premier cold-water surfing to quiet forested campsites and unique geological formations.
What to See and Do

Surfing and Storm Watching: The park is centered around the mouth of the Jordan River, a location world-renowned for its surfing. During the winter months, large swells draw experienced surfers to the point, while the cobble beach serves as an excellent vantage point for watching powerful Pacific storms.
Sandcut Beach Access: A separate section of the park leads to Sandcut Beach, famous for its twin waterfalls that drop from a sandstone ledge directly onto the beach cobbles.

Boardwalk Trails: A series of well-maintained boardwalks and trails wind through the Sitka spruce and hemlock forest, connecting the parking areas to the shoreline while protecting the sensitive coastal undergrowth.

River and Ocean Vistas: The park provides sweeping views of the Juan de Fuca Strait and the Olympic Mountains. It is a popular spot for photographers seeking the contrast between the rugged river mouth and the open sea.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sunset-at-beautiful-sandcut-beach-sooke-vancouver-island-british-columbia-canada-gm2253190133-666588729
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sandcut-beach-vancouver-island-gm2263217192-675975360
Tips & Key Information
On weekends when the swell is up, the parking areas near the river mouth fill up very quickly with local and visiting surfers.
This area is highly exposed to the elements. Even if it is mild in Sooke, the wind off the strait at Jordan River can be biting. Heavy waterproof layers are recommended for any shoreline exploration.
The kelp beds offshore are a frequent haunt for sea otters, and gray whales are often spotted during their spring migration. Keep binoculars handy.
The nearby Shirley Delicious Cafe or the local spots in Jordan River are great for a warm meal after a cold day on the beach.

The park features a self-contained campground with 15 walk-in tent sites and 7 drive-in sites located right along the shoreline. These operate on a first-come, first-served basis, and self-registration is required.
Pit toilets are located at the main parking areas and the campground. There is no potable water available in the park, so visitors must bring their own supply.
The boardwalks near the main entrance are relatively flat, but the trails down to the beach cobbles involve stairs and uneven ground.
The park is open for day use from sunrise to sunset, while the campground is accessible year-round for overnight guests.

places.name: Galloping Goose Regional Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/autumun-landscape-on-galloping-goose-trail-victoria-bc-in-autumn-gm1301060896-393206148

The Galloping Goose Regional Trail is a picturesque 55-kilometer multi-use path that follows a decommissioned railway line from downtown Victoria to the ghost town of Leechtown. Named after the noisy rail-car that traveled the line in the 1920s, it serves as a critical artery for both commuters and recreational users, transitioning from urban pavement to rugged wilderness.
What to See and Do

The Selkirk Trestle: Located near the Victoria end, this massive wooden trestle offers spectacular views across the Upper Harbour and Gorge Waterway. It is a popular spot for watching rowing teams and sunsets over the water.

Sooke Basin Views: As the trail winds through Roche Cove Regional Park and toward Sooke, it hugs the shoreline of the basin, providing quiet vistas of the saltwater and frequent sightings of bald eagles.
The Switchbridge: This architectural landmark in Saanich connects the Galloping Goose with the Lochside Regional Trail, allowing cyclists to complete a massive loop of the peninsula.
Glen Lake and Langford Lake: The trail passes by several freshwater lakes in the Western Communities, offering easy access for a quick swim or a lakeside rest at Glen Lake Park.
Tips & Key Information

The trail is paved from Victoria through Langford but transitions to a well-maintained packed gravel surface as you head toward Sooke. Narrow road tires are fine for the urban section, but wider tires are better for the western half.
This is a very busy multi-use trail. Cyclists should use a bell or call out when passing, and all users should yield to horses, which are common in the Metchosin and Sooke sections.
The further west you travel, the more remote the trail becomes. In the Sooke and Metchosin stretches, it is common to encounter deer, and occasionally bears, so stay alert and keep pets leashed.
While the urban sections have plenty of nearby cafes and shops, water fountains become scarce west of Langford. Carry sufficient hydration if you are heading toward the Sooke Potholes.
The trail is exceptionally flat due to its railway origins, with a maximum grade of only 2%. The paved sections are fully accessible for wheelchairs and strollers.
Major staging areas with parking are located at Atkins Road in Langford, Roche Cove Regional Park, and the Sooke Potholes Regional Park.
The trail officially ends at Leechtown, an abandoned gold-rush town. Note that the area beyond the trail end is part of the Greater Victoria Water Supply Area and is closed to the public.
Kilometric markers are placed along the route to help you track your progress, starting with "0" at the Johnson Street Bridge in downtown Victoria.

places.name: Juan de Fuca Marine Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sunrise-at-mystic-beach-juan-de-fuca-trail-vancouver-island-bc-gm1437523884-478295497
