It details the moment on December 12, 1901, when Guglielmo Marconi used a kite-supported antenna near the tower to receive the first transatlantic wireless signal, proving that radio waves could travel across the ocean.

Flag Signaling Displays: Learn about the tower's original role as a marine signaling station. Until 1958, flagmen at Cabot Tower used a complex system of signal flags to communicate with ships and inform the merchants in the town below which vessels were arriving.

The Amateur Radio Station: On the second floor, you may find members of the Society of Newfoundland Radio Amateurs (SONRA) operating the VO1AA station. They continue the site's legacy by communicating with radio operators around the world from the very spot where wireless history was made.

Heritage Shopping: On the ground floor, the Heritage Shop offers high-quality, locally made Newfoundland gifts, including Marconi themed souvenirs, Labradorite jewelry, and books on local shipwrecks and legends.
Tips and Key Information

For the 2026 season (June 19 to September 7), Parks Canada is offering free admission to National Historic Sites, including Cabot Tower, for those with the Canada Strong Pass. This makes it an ideal year for a budget-friendly visit.

Because the tower sits on an exposed peak 150 meters above sea level, conditions can be extreme. Even if it is a calm day in the city, the wind can be powerful enough to make walking difficult. Always bring a wind-resistant layer.

For the best photo of the tower itself, walk a few hundred meters down the Ladies' Lookout Trail. This gives you a perspective where the tower is framed against the deep blue of the Atlantic Ocean rather than the parking lot.

While exploring, look for historical markers regarding the 1918 gunpowder explosion. A signalman’s pipe accidentally ignited gunpowder used for the noon-day gun, causing significant damage to the tower's interior which had to be completely rebuilt.

Located at the very top of Signal Hill Road. While the tower interior has seasonal hours (typically 10:00 AM to 6:00 PM, May through October), the exterior and the surrounding stone viewing platforms are accessible year-round.
While access to Signal Hill is free, there is typically a small fee (approx. $4–$6) to enter the tower’s museum and observation deck. Admission is free for youth 17 and under.

places.name: 9. Confederation building
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/confederation-building-in-st-johns-gm1004506940-271302283

The Confederation Building is the seat of the Newfoundland and Labrador House of Assembly and the headquarters of the provincial government. Situated on Confederation Hill, this 11-story high-rise and its sprawling wings overlook the city, serving as a constant reminder of the province’s 1949 entry into the Canadian Confederation. .
What to See and Do

The House of Assembly Chamber: Take a free guided tour of the legislative chamber, which features a stunning vaulted ceiling and a stained-glass rendering of the provincial Coat of Arms. The room is ringed by portraits of former Speakers, reflecting the long parliamentary history that predates the building itself.

The Harold Goodridge Mural: Located in the main lobby of the East Block, this massive allegorical mural depicts the history of Newfoundland and Labrador. It features figures like John Cabot, Sir Humphrey Gilbert, and a Beothuk person, along with hidden faces of former Prime Ministers and the province's first Premier, Joey Smallwood.

The Architecture and Dome: Admire the Beaux-Arts and Post-War Modern design of the East Block, completed in 1960. The central tower is topped by a copper-clad dome and a gilded eagle lantern that acts as a beacon for the city when illuminated at night.

The Grounds and Views: The hill offers one of the best non-coastal views of St. John’s. You can see the Basilica, The Rooms, and the harbor entrance from the front plaza, which is often used for provincial ceremonies and public gatherings.

Pippy Park Proximity: The building is located within the southern edge of Pippy Park, one of the largest urban parks in Canada. After your tour, you can easily walk to the Admiralty House Communications Museum or the Fluvarium, which are just minutes away.
Tips and Key Information

Because this is an active government facility, all visitors must enter through the dedicated Visitors' Entrance (located between the East and West Blocks). You are required to provide photo identification and pass through a security screening, including a metal detector.

Guided tours of the House of Assembly are free and typically last 45 minutes. They usually run Monday to Friday, but it is highly recommended to book in advance or check the House of Assembly website, as tours are subject to the legislative schedule.

While Halifax has its famous hill-top clock, St. John’s has the Confederation Building tower. If you see the lantern at the top of the tower lit up, it traditionally means the House of Assembly is in session.

If you choose to sit in the public gallery to watch a debate, be aware that electronic devices (phones, cameras) are strictly prohibited and must be checked with security. You must remain silent and are not permitted to applaud or display political signs.

Located at 100 Prince Philip Drive. There is designated visitor parking at the front of the East Block, but it fills up early. Public transit (Metrobus) frequently services the Confederation Stop right outside the main gates.
The building is fully accessible, featuring a modernized visitors' entrance with gradual slopes and tactile surfaces designed for those with mobility or visual impairments.

places.name: 1. The Rooms
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-rooms-st-johns-newfoundland-gm471166399-8764643

The Rooms is Newfoundland and Labrador’s largest and most important cultural space, a striking modern facility that unites the Provincial Museum, Art Gallery, and Archives under one roof. Soaring above the St. John’s skyline, its unique architecture is a bold tribute to the fishing rooms—the traditional gable-roofed sheds where generations of families processed their catch along the shoreline. It’s a definitive place to understand the province's identity, from its 9,000-year Indigenous history to its contemporary artistic soul.
What to See and Do

The Museum Galleries: Explore three floors of history that range from the natural world—featuring giant squid and Newfoundland dog exhibits—to the harrowing and heroic story of the Royal Newfoundland Regiment in the Beaumont-Hamel and First World War galleries.

The Art Gallery: With over 7,000 works in its permanent collection, the gallery showcases everything from the haunting landscapes of David Blackwood to bold, modern installations by contemporary Indigenous and local artists. Look for featured exhibits like Nasim Makaremi Nia: Entangled and Meagan Musseau: wtoqwan a'tukwaqnm.

The View from Level 4: Even if you aren't a museum buff, the top floor is a must-visit. The massive glass atrium provides an unparalleled panoramic view of the harbor, the Narrows, and Signal Hill. It is widely considered the best indoor vantage point in the city.

The Fort Townshend Ruins: The building sits on the site of an 18th-century British star-shaped citadel. Step outside to see the fort’s original footprint marked in granite pavers, allowing you to literally walk the boundaries of the military defense that once protected Britain's fishing interests.

The Rooms Café: Located on the fourth floor, this café emphasizes local food heritage. It’s the perfect spot to try traditional fare with a modern twist—like screech-infused desserts or local seafood chowder—all while overlooking the Atlantic.
Tips and Key Information

If you are visiting on a budget, admission to all exhibition galleries is free between 5:00 PM and 9:00 PM on the first Wednesday of every month. Students with a valid ID also get in free every Friday.
Check at the front desk for the 15-minute orientation tour (included with admission). It’s the fastest way to get your bearings in the massive 150,000-square-foot facility.

There are two main lots (Bonaventure Avenue and Fort Townshend). Parking is $3 per hour, 24/7. If you plan to stay more than three hours, you can obtain a parking tag from the visitor desk to simplify the process.

If you have ancestors from Newfoundland, the third-floor Archives are a goldmine. First-time researchers pay a one-time $10 fee for a permanent registration, granting access to vast records, photographs, and family histories.
Located at 9 Bonaventure Avenue, about a 15-minute uphill walk from Water Street. The building is typically closed on Mondays, with late-night hours (until 9:00 PM) on Wednesdays and Fridays.
Admission fees for adults (18+) are $13.80, seniors/students are $8.97, and youth (6-17) are $6.90. Admission is complimentary for all Indigenous Peoples.

places.name: 2. Johnson Geo Centre
body: https://www.pexels.com/photo/johnson-geo-centre-in-st-john-s-newfoundland-and-labrador-9704400/

ohnson Geo Centre is a world-class science museum with a literal twist: roughly 85% of the building is underground. Carved directly into the 550-million-year-old rock of Signal Hill, the center uses the Earth’s natural bedrock as its interior walls. It serves as the premier geological interpretation center in the province, offering an immersive journey from the cooling of the planet to the future of space exploration.
What to See and Do

The Great Rock Wall: The center’s most striking feature is its exposed 550-linear-foot interior wall of Precambrian rock. You can literally touch the ancient Gibbett Hill Formation sandstone and siltstone that forms the foundation of the city.

The Titanic Story: Explore an extensive exhibit on the world’s most famous shipwreck, which sank just 350 kilometers off the coast. The display features artifacts, passenger stories, and a deep dive into the combination of human error and environmental forces that led to the tragedy.

The Solar System Gallery: Located in the glass-encased Grand Reception Hall, this exhibit features massive, scale-model planets suspended from the ceiling. It’s one of the few parts of the building above ground, offering a transition from the stars to the subterranean world below.

Amazing Earth Theatre: Watch a high-definition multimedia show that compresses 3 billion years of geological history into a thrilling 15-minute experience, complete with special effects like rain and lightning to simulate the Earth's natural forces.

Johnson GEO-VISTA Park: Step outside to explore eight looped walking trails. These outdoor galleries feature storyboards about local botany and geology, along with replicas of traditional stone structures like root cellars and house chimneys.
Hibernia KidsPlace: A favorite for families, this interactive zone allows younger children to travel to a moon base, examine real fossils, and crawl through a Time Tunnel into the heart of a volcano.
Tips and Key Information
The building is a marvel of sustainable engineering, using a geothermal system with six wells drilled 500 feet deep to regulate the temperature naturally using the Earth's heat.
Because most of the center is indoors and underground, it is the perfect destination for the days when St. John's famous pea soup fog or rain makes coastal hiking at the summit difficult.

The glass entry pavilion provides a stunning reflection of Cabot Tower and the Narrows. For an interior shot, stand at the base of the Great Rock Wall and look up to capture the contrast between the ancient stone and modern glass architecture.

Since the center is located halfway up Signal Hill Road, it is the perfect halfway house for those hiking from downtown to the summit. You can park here for free and take the Centre to Summit Trail after your museum visit.
Located at 175 Signal Hill Road. The center is generally open daily from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM (check for seasonal variations in late autumn).

Admission rates for adults (19-59) are $15.00, seniors/students are $11.50, and youth (5-18) are $8.00. Children under 5 are free. If you are a Memorial University student or a CAA member, be sure to bring your ID for a discount.

places.name: 3. Anglican Cathedral of St. John the Baptist
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/st-john-the-baptist-anglican-cathedral-st-johns-newfoundland-canada-gm1267403833-371855365

The Anglican Cathedral of St. John the Baptist is a masterpiece of Gothic Revival architecture and the mother church of the oldest Anglican parish in Canada (founded in 1699). Designed by the world-renowned British architect Sir George Gilbert Scott, the cathedral’s austere stone exterior and soaring interior are considered among the finest examples of ecclesiastical design in North America. It’s a pillar of the city’s historic Ecclesiastical District, having been meticulously restored after the devastating Great Fire of 1892.
What to See and Do

The Gothic Revival Architecture: Admire the Gothic style of the 13th century, featuring pointed arches, ribbed vaults, and massive sandstone piers. Though Scott’s original vision for a grand central spire was never completed, the building’s cruciform (cross-shaped) layout and 80-foot roofline remain a dominant feature of the downtown landscape.

The Kempe Stained Glass: The cathedral is home to one of the largest collections of stained glass by the famous English designer C.E. Kempe. Look for his signature wheatsheaf mark hidden in the corners of the vibrant windows, which were installed during the post-fire restoration to replace those lost in 1892.

The Cathedral Crypt: Take a descent into the restored crypt to see the building’s foundations and learn about the early history of the parish. It serves as a quiet space for reflection and a window into the engineering required to build such a massive stone structure on the side of a steep hill.

The Ghost Photo Exhibit: In the cathedral’s museum area, look for the famous historical photograph taken of the stonemasons in the 1850s. Legend has it that one of the masons who fell to his death during construction appears as a ghostly figure in the background of the shot.

Candlelight Concerts: The cathedral has become a premier venue for Candlelight Concerts. These evening events feature string quartets performing everything from Vivaldi to tributes to modern artists like Adele and Coldplay, all illuminated by thousands of flickering candles.
Tips and Key Information

While the cathedral is an active place of worship open year-round, formal guided tours are available.. These tours provide deep insights into the Ecclesiological philosophy behind the building’s design.

The adjacent graveyard dates back to the late 17th century. It is a hauntingly beautiful spot for a walk, though be aware that centuries of frost and thaw on the steep slope have made the ground uneven—legend says over 20,000 people are buried here, often in tiers.

During your visit, notice the discoloration on some of the interior stonework. This is a permanent scar from the Great Fire of 1892, where the heat was so intense it melted the lead in the windows and caused the original roof to collapse.
If you visit during off-hours, the cathedral offers a Virtual Tour accessible via QR codes on-site, providing a self-guided digital experience of the Chancel, Sanctuary, and Lady Chapel.
Located at 16 Church Hill, perfectly positioned between the busy shops of Duckworth Street and the residential hills of Gower Street. It is a centerpiece of the National Historic District.

Entry for prayer and reflection is free. For sightseeing and tours, a voluntary donation (typically $5–$10) is encouraged to help with the massive ongoing costs of preserving this 180-year-old stone monument.

places.name: 4. Railway Coastal Museum
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/railway-coastal-museum-st-johns-newfoundland-canada-gm893058336-247100003

The Railway Coastal Museum is a tribute to the Iron Horse and the Coastal Boats that once served as the only lifelines for Newfoundland’s isolated outport communities. Housed in the magnificent Riverhead Station (built in 1903), the museum occupies a National Historic Site that marked Mile Zero for the trans-island journey. The museum operates as a seasonal treasure, having been revitalized through a partnership with the Memorial University-affiliated Genesis Centre to ensure the province's transportation history remains accessible to the public.
What to See and Do

The 1940s Passenger Train Diorama: Step into a 90-foot, full-scale replica of the Overland Limited. You can walk through meticulously restored sections of a 1940s train, including the Dining Car, the Pullman Sleeper, and the Mail Car, complete with costumed figures that bring the era to life.

Automated Model Railway: A highlight for families and hobbyists, this large-scale working model depicts the train’s journey across the entire island, from Port aux Basques to St. John’s. It features detailed landscapes, a busy railyard, and a functioning roundhouse.

Coastal Boat Service Exhibits: Before there were roads, there were the alphabet fleet boats. Explore murals and models of the coastal steamers that braved the North Atlantic to deliver mail, medicine, and supplies to hundreds of roadless villages.

The Riverhead Station Architecture: Admire the building itself—a fortress of Newfoundland granite and brick. It is one of the finest examples of a railway headquarters in Canada, featuring high ceilings and original woodwork that reflect the ambition of the railway era.

Outdoor Train Park: Outside the museum, you can see CN 906, a 1200-horsepower diesel-electric locomotive that served the island, along with a vintage mail car and a visitor information car once used by the city.
Tips and Key Information

The museum typically operates on a seasonal schedule (opening in late June and running through Labour Day). Always check their official website before visiting in the off-season to confirm current opening hours.

The museum is the official starting point (Mile Zero) for the Trans-Canada Trail on the island. After your museum visit, you can follow the trail along the scenic Waterford River for a peaceful walk toward Bowring Park.

You’ll learn why Newfoundland famously used a narrow gauge (1067 mm) track. While it was cheaper to build across the island's rugged bogs and mountains, it meant the trains were smaller and slower than those on the mainland, earning them the nickname The Newfie Bullet.

The upper floors of the building now house a tech incubator. This new meets old atmosphere means you might see local entrepreneurs working alongside 100-year-old railway artifacts—a true symbol of St. John’s modernization.
Located at 495 Water Street (West End). It is a short drive or a 20-minute walk from the main downtown Pedestrian Mall.
Rates are approximately $10 for adults, $7 for seniors/students/military, and $25 for a family pass (up to 3 children). Children under 5 are usually free.

places.name: 5. Colonial Building
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/colonial-building-st-johns-newfoundland-gm471078057-6125532

The Colonial Building is a neoclassical gem that served as the seat of Newfoundland’s government for over a century (1850–1959). After a massive, decade-long restoration, it reopened to the public in late 2022 as a premier provincial historic site. Tthe building stands as a masterclass in heritage conservation, featuring meticulously restored interiors that tell the complex story of Newfoundland’s journey from a self-governing Dominion to a Canadian province.
What to See and Do

The Legislative Chambers: Step into the Red Council Chamber and the Green House of Assembly. Both have been restored to their 1880s glory, featuring 30-foot ceilings and original desks. You'll notice the ruling party sits on the left of the Speaker—a local quirk dating back to the 1800s because that side of the room was closer to the heaters.

The Pindikowski Frescoes: Look up to see the breathtaking ceiling art painted in 1880 by Alexander Pindikowski. A Polish artist serving a prison sentence for forgery, he was released daily to paint these masterpieces; his work was so impressive that the government reduced his 15-month sentence by 30 days.

The 1850s Gasoliers: Admire the stunning chandeliers that were originally powered by gas (the building was the first in Newfoundland to have electricity). These were removed and restored stone-by-stone in 2022 to return them to their original bronze-and-brass finish.

Indigenous Governance Exhibits: The newly reopened site features dedicated spaces and art by Indigenous artists. These exhibits are designed to provide a more inclusive history, recognizing the forms of government that existed in the province long before the colonial era.

The Squires Staircase: On a guided tour, you’ll see the grand wooden staircase where Prime Minister Sir Richard Squires famously escaped a massive political riot in 1932. The What We Heard exhibits detail this and other colorful events, like the site of the province’s first bank robbery in 1850.
Tips and Key Information
To preserve the delicate restoration, entry is often managed via timed tickets. It is highly recommended to book your guided tour online in advance through the Provincial Historic Sites website.

While walking through the halls, you’ll notice small squares of different colors on the walls. These are conservation windows—patches left by restorers to show the various layers of historic paint used over the last 170 years.

The building is located on the edge of Bannerman Park. It’s a perfect spot to combine a historical tour with a stroll through the Victorian-style gardens or a visit to the Loop outdoor skating trail in the winter.
If you are a member of the National Trust for Canada, you can enjoy free entry to the Colonial Building as part of the Passport Places program.
Situated at the corner of Military Road and Bannerman Road. The building is fully wheelchair accessible, featuring modern elevators and ramps integrated seamlessly into the historic design.
The building typically operates seasonally from May to November, open daily from 9:30 AM to 5:00 PM. Outside of these months, access may be limited to special events or pre-booked groups.

places.name: 6. Government House
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/government-house-in-st-johns-newfoundland-canada-gm1267402577-371854228

Government House is the official residence of the Lieutenant Governor of Newfoundland and Labrador and a grand symbol of the British Crown’s historical presence in the province. Built between 1827 and 1831, this Palladian-style mansion was designed to reflect the growing status of the colony as it transitioned from naval to civilian rule. As of 2026, it remains an active vice-regal residence where dignitaries are received and provincial ceremonies are held, surrounded by some of the most beautifully manicured grounds in the city.
What to See and Do

Guided Interior Tours: Explore the main floor of the residence on a free 45-minute guided tour. You’ll see the Ballroom, the Dining Room, and the Cochrane Room, all filled with original 19th-century furnishings, grand chandeliers, and portraits of former governors that trace the province's political evolution.

The Palladian Architecture: Admire the symmetrical red sandstone exterior, which was quarried from nearby Signal Hill. The building’s austere, dignified design and English Portland stone trim were intended to project stability and authority in the early 19th-century capital.

Commemorative Trees and Gardens: The expansive 22-acre estate is open to the public from dawn to dusk. Wander the winding paths to find Commemorative Trees planted by members of the Royal Family and visiting heads of state. The gardens are particularly stunning in July and August when the flower beds are in full bloom.

The New Year’s Day Levee: If you are visiting on January 1, participate in the centuries-old tradition of the Levee. The Lieutenant Governor throws open the doors, inviting the public inside for a reception to share news and celebrate the start of the year with local refreshments.

The Lieutenant Governor’s Garden Party: Typically held in late July, this is one of the city's most beloved summer social events. It is free and open to the public, featuring live music from the Royal Newfoundland Regiment Band and light refreshments served on the sprawling back lawn.
Tips and Key Information

For most of the year, tours must be booked in advance by calling (709) 729-2669 or emailing the Government House office. However, during the peak months of July and August, walk-in tours are often available at the front entrance during weekday business hours.

If you are attending a formal ceremony or reception at Government House, pay close attention to the invitation. The dress code is strictly observed, typically requiring business or morning dress unless otherwise specified.

The estate is a premier location for wedding and graduation photos. If you plan a professional shoot, you must book your time slot in advance; however, casual tourists are welcome to take photos of the exterior and gardens without a reservation.

As a working residence and government office, security is present on the grounds 24/7. Visitors are asked to stay on the designated paths and respect the privacy of the private living quarters on the upper floors, which are not open to the public.
Located at 50 Military Road, directly across from the Colonial Building. The site is fully wheelchair accessible, with a designated accessible entrance and washroom facilities available for guests.
It is a long-standing tradition for visitors to sign the official guestbook in the front foyer. It’s a small way to leave your mark on the history of one of the oldest official residences in Canada.

places.name: 7. National War Memorial
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/war-memorial-gm1370747008-440234970

The National War Memorial is the most significant monument in the province and one of only two National War Memorials in all of Canada. Located on a sloping site between Water Street and Duckworth Street, it marks the spot where Sir Humphrey Gilbert claimed Newfoundland for England in 1583. As of 2026, the site has been completely transformed following a massive $6-million restoration and the historic 2024 centennial, which saw the repatriation and entombment of an unknown First World War soldier.
What to See and Do

The Tomb of the Unknown Soldier: This is the heart of the newly refurbished site. Added in July 2024, the tomb is the final resting place of a Royal Newfoundland Regiment soldier who was killed at Beaumont-Hamel. Crafted from black Canadian granite and blue Labradorite, it features a bronze bouquet of forget-me-nots, the traditional Newfoundland symbol of remembrance.

The Five Bronze Sculptures: Admire the intricate work of British artists Gilbert Bayes and Ferdinand Victor Blundstone. At the top stands the Spirit of Newfoundland, holding a torch for freedom and a sword for loyalty. Below her are realistic figures representing the four branches of service: a sailor (Naval Reserve), a soldier (Regiment), a fisherman (Mercantile Marine), and a lumberman (Forestry Corps).

The Whisper and Acoustic Echo: Stand on the designated echo spots on the granite plateau below the tomb. Because of the semi-circular design of the walls, your voice will echo back to you with surprising clarity, a unique architectural feature that adds to the solemnity of the space.

Memorial Day Ceremonies (July 1): In Newfoundland and Labrador, July 1 is first and foremost Memorial Day, marking the anniversary of the Battle of Beaumont-Hamel (1916). If you visit on this day, you can witness the province’s largest commemorative service, often attended by national dignitaries.

The Harbor View: Walk to the upper level of the memorial on Duckworth Street. From here, you can look out through the Narrows to the Atlantic—the exact route that thousands of young Newfoundlanders took when they sailed away to war, many never to return.
Tips and Key Information

The site was recently upgraded with new accessible walkways, stairs, and native plantings (including symbolic poppies and forget-me-nots). It is now one of the most accessible historic sites in the downtown core.

Look at the torch held by the central female figure. It was originally designed to function as a leading light to help ships navigate through the Narrows into the harbor, though it was ultimately never used for navigation.

Due to its status as a National War Grave, you will often see security or ceremonial guards posted at the tomb. It is a site of deep respect; visitors are asked to maintain a quiet demeanor and avoid stepping on the tomb itself.
While the poppy is used across Canada for Remembrance Day (Nov 11), Newfoundlanders uniquely use the tiny blue forget-me-not flower to specifically remember the losses at Beaumont-Hamel on July 1.
Situated at the foot of Duckwork Street, directly across from Harbourside Park. It is free to visit and open 24/7.
Being so close to the water and positioned on a slope, the memorial is a wind tunnel. It is often significantly colder here than just one block away on Water Street.

places.name: 1. East Coast Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/man-hiking-at-berry-head-arch-at-sunrise-along-the-east-coast-trail-of-newfoundland-gm2202618302-620205518

The East Coast Trail (ECT) is a world-class hiking network that stretches over 336 kilometers along the rugged Avalon Peninsula. Linking more than 30 historic coastal communities, it offers everything from gentle lighthouse strolls to grueling multi-day wilderness treks.The ECT has solidified its reputation as one of the premier coastal hiking destinations in North America, famous for its edge of the world views, breaching whales, and ancient geological formations.
What to See and Do

The Spout: Hike the Spout Path to see a natural, wave-driven geyser that blasts seawater up to 30 meters into the air. This blowhole is a physical roar of the North Atlantic and a favorite for experienced hikers.

Berry Head Sea Arch: Located on the Spurwink Island Path, this massive, cathedral-like stone arch is one of the most photographed natural wonders in the province. Standing atop it offers a dizzying and awe-inspiring view of the surf below.

La Manche Suspension Bridge: Walk across the 50-meter-long suspension bridge that spans a dramatic ocean inlet. It stands near the ruins of La Manche, a ghost village that was abandoned after being devastated by a massive storm surge in 1966.

Whale and Iceberg Alley: Many sections of the trail, particularly the Cape Spear Path and Sugarloaf Path, offer front-row seats to Iceberg Alley. From late spring to mid-summer, you can watch 10,000-year-old icebergs drift by while humpback whales breach just offshore.

The Sugarloaf View: For a classic St. John’s experience, hike the Sugarloaf Path from Logy Bay. It provides a backdoor entrance to the city, culminating in a breathtaking 360-degree view of Quidi Vidi, Signal Hill, and the vast Atlantic.
Tips and Key Information

Newfoundland weather is famously unpredictable. Even in mid-July, a sunny morning can turn into a cold, foggy afternoon with high winds. Always hike with moisture-wicking layers and a high-quality rain shell.
These are wilderness paths, not paved walks. Expect mud, exposed roots, and jagged rocks. Sturdy, waterproof hiking boots with good ankle support are essential to prevent injury.

The cliffs along the ECT are spectacular but can be unstable. Stay on the marked trail and avoid the edges, especially in high winds or fog. Rogue waves are a real danger on lower sea ledges (the black rocks).

The ECT is maintained by a volunteer association. Hikers are expected to follow Leave No Trace principles—pack out all trash, stay on the path to prevent erosion, and remember that open fires are strictly prohibited.

Most trail sections are linear (point-to-point), not loops. Many hikers park at one end and use a local taxi service to get back to their vehicle. Several local shuttle services also operate specifically for hikers during the peak season (June–September).

Access to the trail is free, but it is highly encouraged to purchase an annual East Coast Trail Association (ECTA) membership or make a donation. These funds are critical for the ongoing maintenance and repair of the bridges and boardwalks.

places.name: 2. North Head Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/north-head-hiking-trail-at-st-johns-gm1409086543-459754007

The North Head Trail is St. John’s most iconic and adrenaline-pumping hike, a 1.7 km cliffside path that connects the summit of Signal Hill to the historic Battery neighborhood. Originally used by fishers as far back as the 1500s, this trail offers a front-row seat to the Atlantic Ocean. It’sthe ultimate city-wilderness experience, famous for its rugged terrain, steep staircases, and the thrill of walking high above the swirling waters of the Narrows.
What to See and Do

The Chains Section: The trail’s most famous feature is a narrow, rocky ledge where a heavy metal chain is anchored into the cliffside. You’ll need to grip the chain to navigate a short, airy stretch with a sheer drop to the ocean below—an exhilarating highlight for any hiker.

Ross’ Valley: Hike through this unique hanging valley, a geological remnant from the last ice age. This tucked-away meadow was once the site of Prowse's Folly, a 19th-century quarantine hospital, and still contains hidden relics like iron rings and wild apple trees.

Chain Rock and Pancake Rock: Look down at the narrowest part of the harbor entrance to see these two strategic formations. In past centuries (and as recently as WWII), a massive defensive chain was stretched between these rocks to physically block enemy ships and submarines from entering the port.

The Red Chairs Pause: Keep an eye out for the iconic Parks Canada red Adirondack chairs placed at the most scenic overlooks. These are perfectly positioned for spotting humpback whales in the summer or Iceberg Alley traffic in the spring.

The Battery Finish: The trail concludes (or begins) in the Outer Battery, a neighborhood where houses are built directly into the cliff. The path literally winds past people’s front porches and through narrow alleyways, offering an intimate look at one of the city's most resilient communities.
Tips and Key Information

The North Head Trail is typically closed during the winter and early spring (often until mid-May) due to ice hazards and the risk of rockfalls. Parks Canada advises hikers to wait for the official spring safety assessment before attempting the route.

Most hikers prefer to start at the summit (Cabot Tower) and hike downward to the Battery. This provides the best ocean views in front of you, though the final climb back up the 100+ stairs to the parking lot is a serious cardio workout.

Parks Canada classifies this trail as strenuous. It features over 1,000 stairs in total, uneven rocky paths, and steep elevation changes. It is not recommended for those with a severe fear of heights or mobility issues.

If you finish your hike at the bottom, reward yourself at the Battery Cafe. It’s the unofficial base camp for hikers, famous for its rhubarb lemonade and espresso, located right where the trail meets the city streets.
Never hike this trail in heavy fog or high winds. The cliff edges are unprotected in many sections, and the black rocks near the water level are extremely dangerous due to unpredictable rogue waves.
The trailhead is located on the ocean side of the summit parking lot at Signal Hill National Historic Site. Access to the trail is free, though it is only recommended during daylight hours.

places.name: 3. Bowring Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/ducks-on-a-pond-in-a-park-autumn-gm1198903768-342809891

Bowring Park is the emerald heart of St. John’s and one of the most scenic urban parks in Canada. Gifted to the city in 1914 by the wealthy Bowring merchant family to celebrate their 100th anniversary in business, the park was designed in the classic English landscaping tradition. It’s a sprawling 200-acre sanctuary of ancient trees, winding rivers, and world-class sculptures, offering a peaceful retreat from the rugged coastal cliffs of the Atlantic.
What to See and Do

The Fighting Newfoundlander Statue: Standing tall near the main entrance, this bronze tribute to the Royal Newfoundland Regiment of WWI is a powerful local landmark. It depicts a soldier in full marching order, poised to throw a grenade, and serves as a poignant site for local remembrance.

The Peter Pan Statue: A beloved favorite for families, this is one of only a few authorized duplicates of the original statue in London’s Kensington Gardens. It was erected by Sir Edgar Bowring in memory of a beloved goddaughter who was lost at sea when the S.S. Florizel sank in 1918.

The Duck Pond and Stone Bridge: Walk across the picturesque cantilevered stone bridge that spans the Waterford River. The duck pond is a year-round hub of activity, where locals gather to feed the resident swans and ducks against a backdrop of weeping willows.

The Caribou Statue: See the bronze Caribou, the emblem of the Royal Newfoundland Regiment. This statue is a twin to the ones found at the five Trail of the Caribou memorial sites in France and Belgium, standing as a silent guardian over the park’s south side.

The Conservatory and Bungalow: Visit the Bowring Park Conservatory, a glass-walled botanical haven featuring exotic plants and seasonal floral displays. Nearby, the historic Bungalow offers a classic tea-room atmosphere for light lunches and treats.

Modern Recreation: For those looking for activity, the park features a large outdoor swimming pool, a splash pad, tennis courts, and a high-end playground. In the winter, the loop trail is a popular spot for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing.
Tips and Key Information
While the park is beautifully maintained, some of the wilder wooded areas along the riverbanks contain native poison ivy. Stick to the paved and groomed gravel paths to ensure a rash-free visit.

Bowring Park is home to some of the oldest and rarest trees in the province, including massive European Beeches and English Oaks. You can find tree ID plaques throughout the park that detail the age and origin of these giants.

Beneath the main road (Waterford Bridge Road) lies a pedestrian tunnel decorated with local murals. It connects the upper and lower sections of the park, providing a safe and whimsical way to navigate the 200-acre site.
Keep an eye out for more than just ducks; the park is a sanctuary for local foxes, eagles, and even the occasional moose wandering down from the surrounding hills.
Located at 305 Waterford Bridge Road, about a 10-minute drive west of downtown. There is ample free parking in several lots located at the East, West, and South entrances.
Entry to the park, the conservatory, and all walking trails is free. Some small fees may apply for use of the swimming pool or for special events at the Bungalow.

places.name: 4. Quidi Vidi Lake Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/quidi-vidi-lake-trail-gm1601491682-530225613

The Quidi Vidi Lake Trail is the most popular flat walk in St. John’s, offering a scenic 3.8 km (2.4 mile) loop around the body of water known as the rower’s paradise. While the rest of the city is defined by grueling hills, this paved and gravel path provides an accessible, high-energy circuit for runners, walkers, and families. The area is buzzing with activity as it prepares for the historic 208th anniversary of the Royal St. John’s Regatta.
What to See and Do

The Royal St. John’s Regatta (August 5, 2026): If you are here on the first Wednesday of August, you are at the center of the oldest organized sporting event in North America. Known as The Largest Garden Party in the World, the lakefront transforms into a massive festival with food stalls, games of chance, and high-stakes rowing races that draw over 50,000 people.

Birdwatching and Wildlife: The lake is a year-round sanctuary for waterfowl. It’s a prime spot to see the rare Lesser Black-backed Gull and various species of ducks. In the quieter morning hours, you might even spot an eagle or an osprey diving for fish from the surrounding White Hills.

The Lake-to-Lookout Connection: For those wanting more than a flat walk, the trail connects to the Sugarloaf Path and the Lake-to-Lookout Walk, which leads you up the ridge to the Ladies’ Lookout on Signal Hill for a dramatic transition from lakeside to cliffside.

The Dog Park and Skate Park: Located at the northern end of the lake (near the Boulevard), these modern facilities are the social hubs of the trail. The fenced-in dog park is a great place for your four-legged friends to socialize while you take in the views of the surrounding hills.

Training Rowers: From late spring through July, you can watch local rowing crews practicing in their fixed-seat shells. The rhythm of the oars and the shouts of the coxswains provide a unique soundtrack to your afternoon walk.
Tips and Key Information

The Regatta is a weather dependent holiday. If it’s too windy on the first Wednesday of August, the holiday is postponed until Thursday (and so on). Locals wait by their radios at 6:00 AM on Regatta Day to hear the committee's decision: It's a Go! or It's a No-Go!
Unlike the North Head or East Coast Trails, this loop is almost entirely level and well-maintained, making it the best option in the city for those with strollers or mobility aids.
The most popular parking area is at Quidi Vidi Park off The Boulevard. On busy weekends, you can also find parking near the Carnival Station or at the Pleasantville side of the lake.

The trail ends (or begins) just steps away from the historic Quidi Vidi Village, where you can reward your 3.8 km walk with a pint of Iceberg Beer at the brewery or a Dirty Fries snack at a local food truck.
The lake is situated at the east end of the city. It is easily accessible via Metrobus from downtown, or a pleasant 20-minute walk through the historic residential streets of the East End.
places.note: Note that work began in January 2026 on the replacement of the Quidi Vidi Slipway off Cadet Road. While the main walking trail remains open, expect some minor detours and parking impacts near the Quidi Vidi Village end of the lake as the city installs a new million-dollar wooden structure.

places.name: 5. Chance Cove Coastal Hiking Trail
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/chance-cove-hiking-trail-overlooking-the-atlantic-ocean-along-canadas-east-coast-gm2168212469-588243627

The Chance Cove Coastal Hiking Trail is one of Newfoundland’s most rapidly rising Instagram stars. Located about a 90-minute drive from St. John’s on the Isthmus of the Avalon, this trail offers a dramatic tropical-meets-North-Atlantic aesthetic that was once a local secret but is now a must-visit destination. It features emerald-green waters, hidden sea caves, and secluded pebble beaches.
What to See and Do

The Money Shot Viewpoint: After a short climb through a dense, mossy forest, the trail opens up to a spectacular ridge overlooking Big Chance Cove. On a sunny day, the refraction of the water against the white limestone rocks creates a vibrant turquoise hue that looks more like the Mediterranean than the North Atlantic.

The Rope Descent to Big Cove: For the adventurous, there is a famous section where you must use a sturdy fixed rope to shimmy down a steep embankment to reach the beach. This secluded cove features a massive sea stack and deep caves that you can explore at low tide.

Island Cove Beach Stairs: If the rope descent is too daunting, continue to Island Cove. Recent infrastructure upgrades (completed in late 2024/2025) have added a safe set of wooden stairs that lead directly down to a beautiful cobblestone beach—perfect for a midpoint snack or boiling the kettle.

Green Head Lookout: This is the most exposed part of the trail. It offers a 270-degree view of Trinity Bay where you can often spot whales in the distance or watch the swirls created by the powerful coastal currents.

The Fairy Door Forest: The initial 20 minutes of the hike wind through a magical forest section. Keep an eye out for small local touches, like hand-painted fairy doors and interpretive signs that detail the history of the families who once lived in this isolated cove.
Tips and Key Information

The hike is a 3.7 km (2.3 mile) loop, often described as a figure-8. It is rated as moderate due to some steep inclines and the uneven nature of the coastal cliffs. Most hikers complete the circuit in about 1.5 to 2 hours.
Even though it’s a shorter hike, the terrain is rugged. Waterproof hiking boots are highly recommended, especially after a rainfall when the forest section can become a muddy bog.

Because of its viral popularity, the small parking lot at the trailhead (located at the end of Main Road in Chance Cove) fills up very early on weekends. To avoid the crowds, aim to arrive before 9:30 AM or visit on a weekday.

Be careful when using GPS. There is another Chance Cove Provincial Park on the Southern Shore (near Cappahayden). Make sure you are headed to Chance Cove in Trinity Bay for this specific hiking trail.
Bring a pair of binoculars. The high vantage points of this trail make it an excellent spot for land-based whale watching during the capelin roll (typically late June and July).
Located at 49-51 Main Road, Chance Cove. There is no admission fee to hike the trail, but the local community maintains a donation box at the trailhead to fund the upkeep of the ropes and stairs.

places.name: 6. Bannerman Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/bannerman-park-entrance-gm995704798-269499308

Bannerman Park is the historic centerpiece of St. John’s and a masterpiece of 19th-century Victorian landscaping. Named after Sir Alexander Bannerman, a former Governor of Newfoundland, it was established in 1864 as the city's first public park. It’s a year-round community hub, seamlessly blending its colonial history with modern amenities that serve as the setting for some of the province's most beloved festivals.
What to See and Do

The Loop: This refrigerated outdoor skating trail is the park's crown jewel during the winter months. Opened in 2015, it allows skaters of all levels to glide through the park on a winding ice path, often accompanied by festive music and holiday lights.

The Newfoundland & Labrador Folk Festival (July 2026): For over 50 years, Bannerman Park has hosted this legendary event. The park transforms into a sea of lawn chairs and blankets as world-class traditional musicians take to the main stage, while smaller workshop tents offer intimate sessions on fiddling, storytelling, and dance.

The Fighting Newfoundlander & Memorials: Beyond the famous soldier statue, look for the Homecoming bronze (dedicated in 2018), which honors the Royal Newfoundland Regiment. You’ll also find a monument to Father Michael Morris and a plaque designating Shawnadithit (the last known Beothuk) as a National Historic Person.

The Swimming Pool & Splash Pad: A summer staple for locals, the park features a heated outdoor pool and an accessible splash pad. It is one of the few places in the city to enjoy an outdoor swim during the brief but beautiful Newfoundland summer.

The Victorian Bandstand: This ornate structure serves as the heart of the park’s formal gardens. It is a popular spot for wedding photography and free summer afternoon concerts, reflecting the British park designs of the 1800s.
Tips and Key Information

Before grabbing your skates, call the Loop Line at (709) 733-5667. Because the ice is refrigerated, it can often stay open even when temperatures are slightly above freezing, but it closes periodically for Zamboni maintenance.

Every June, the park hosts a massive celebration of Indigenous culture featuring a sunrise ceremony, drumming, dancing, and traditional foods. It is a vibrant, inclusive event that has become a cornerstone of the park's annual calendar.
The park is the perfect starting point for a heritage walk. You can exit the south side of the park and be at the front doors of the Colonial Building in less than two minutes.

Bannerman Park is one of the most accessible green spaces in the city. It features accessible washrooms, a pool lift, a water wheelchair at the pool house, and sensory-friendly zones during major city-run events like New Year’s Eve.

Bounded by Military Road, Bannerman Road, and Circular Road. While there is a small parking lot on Bannerman Road, it fills up instantly during events; most locals park on the surrounding residential streets (check for permit signs!).

Held in late summer, this magical evening sees the park lit by thousands of hand-made paper lanterns. It is a quiet, ethereal experience that culminates in a lantern light-up at the center of the park.

places.name: 7. Grand Concourse
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/staircase-to-northhead-trail-signal-hill-st-johns-newfoundland-and-labrador-canada-gm692331018-127802725

The Grand Concourse is one of Canada’s most ambitious pedestrian networks, an award-winning walker's paradise that spans over 200 kilometers across the Northeast Avalon region. Managed by the Grand Concourse Authority (GCA), it links every major park, river, pond, and green space in St. John’s, Mount Pearl, and Paradise. As of 2026, the network has expanded to integrate 10 municipalities, offering a seamless blend of urban convenience and rugged Atlantic beauty.
What to See and Do

The Three Rivers System: The Concourse is anchored by three main river-valley trails: the Rennie’s River Trail, the Virginia River Trail, and the Waterford River Trail. These paths offer lush, forested escapes right in the middle of the city, perfect for spotting local brown trout or the elusive American Dipper bird.

The T'Railway (Newfoundland T'Railway): This section follows the bed of the former Newfoundland Railway. It is a major multi-use artery that allows for longer-distance trekking and cycling, connecting the downtown core to the suburban communities of Mount Pearl and Paradise.

Interpretation & Storyboards: One of the hallmarks of the Concourse is its high-quality interpretive signage. As you walk, you’ll find hundreds of Storyboards detailing local history, from 16th-century fishing lore to the geological secrets of the 550-million-year-old rock formations under your feet.

Winter Trail Grooming (2026): For the 2026 winter season, the GCA maintains several groomed sections for active winter use, including loops around Quidi Vidi Lake, Mundy Pond, and segments of the Waterford River T’Railway. In Pippy Park, these groomed trails are specifically reserved for cross-country skiing and snowshoeing.

The Trail Explorers Program: In 2026, the City of St. John’s launched an inclusive Trail Explorers initiative. These organized group walks focus on the accessible sections of the Grand Concourse, promoting community wellness and ensuring that hikers of all ability levels can enjoy the network.
Tips and Key Information

If you are a serious trekker, look for the Walker’s Handbook. This 148-page guide is the bible of the Concourse, featuring detailed maps, difficulty ratings, and specific notes on the flora and fauna found along each of the 37+ interconnected walks.

The Grand Concourse mobile app (available for iOS and Android) is the best way to navigate. It features an interactive map with real-time GPS tracking, allowing you to see exactly where you are in the 200km web of trails and even report trail maintenance issues directly to the authority.

A major focus of the 2024–2026 Accessibility Plan has been the upgrading of trail surfaces. Many sections, such as the Adams Pond Walk and Quidi Vidi Lake, now feature 3-meter wide compacted granular surfaces or pavement, making them ideal for wheelchairs, strollers, and those with limited mobility.

Most trails are dog-friendly, but they must be kept on a leash. The GCA provides dog waste bag dispensers at many trailheads, but visitors are expected to pack it in, pack it out to keep the green belts pristine.
Because it is an integrated network, you can hop on the Grand Concourse from almost anywhere in the city. Major hubs include Bannerman Park, Bowring Park, Memorial University, and Signal Hill.
While the trails are free to use, the GCA is a non-profit organization. You can support the network by purchasing a commemorative bench or plaque or by becoming a volunteer Trail Custodian.

places.name: 8. Waterford River Walk
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-waterford-river-valley-autumn-gm1358129652-431848587

The Waterford River Walk is the most extensive river-valley trail in the Grand Concourse network, a 6.2 km (3.9 mile) linear path that follows the historic Waterford River. It serves as a natural corridor connecting the industrial heritage of the downtown west end to the manicured gardens of Bowring Park and beyond into Mount Pearl. It’s a avorite for cyclists and walkers seeking a countryside feel without leaving the city limits.
What to See and Do

The Trans Canada Trail Mile 0: The walk begins at the Railway Coastal Museum (the former Riverhead Station), which is officially designated as the eastern "Mile 0" of the Trans Canada Trail. It is a bucket-list starting point for those trekking across the country.

Heritage Architecture: As you move west from the downtown core, the trail passes behind some of the city's most beautiful 19th-century estate homes along Waterford Bridge Road. These grand houses once belonged to the city's merchant elite who wanted to escape the summer fog of the harbor.

The Cascades of Mount Pearl: If you continue past Bowring Park into the Mount Pearl section (often called the Waterford Valley Linear Trail), you'll encounter a series of four bridges that offer perfect vantage points for the river's scenic rapids and small waterfalls.

Industrial History: The trail provides a unique look at the hidden side of St. John's. You’ll pass old stone bridge abutments and ruins of early 20th-century mills that once used the river’s power, juxtaposed with modern-day murals and revitalized green spaces.

Birding and Brown Trout: The river is a thriving ecosystem. The local River Watch groups have noted healthy populations of brown trout. On a quiet morning, you can often see kingfishers or even the occasional osprey hunting along the shallower banks.
Tips and Key Information

Unlike the rugged North Head Trail, this is a mostly level walk. The surface is a mix of asphalt and high-quality crushed gravel, making it ideal for road bikes, strollers, and those who prefer a less strenuous workout.

Because this is a high-traffic commuter route for cyclists and joggers, pedestrians should stay to the right. If you are cycling, it is traditional (and expected) to use a bell or a friendly on your left when passing walkers.

Many people use the Waterford River Walk as a scenic entrance to Bowring Park. Instead of driving to the park, you can park downtown, walk the 6 km to the park for a picnic, and catch a bus (Metrobus Route 11) back to your starting point.

For the 2026 winter season, the Grand Concourse Authority has increased grooming on the section between the Railway Museum and Corpus Christi Church, making it one of the most reliable ice-free walking options in the city during February and March.
The primary trailhead is at 495 Water Street (Railway Coastal Museum). Additional popular access points include the Corpus Christi Church parking lot and the Waterford Hospital grounds.
A leisurely stroll from the museum to Bowring Park typically takes about 90 to 120 minutes one-way.

places.name: 1. The Battery
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-battery-neighborhood-in-st-johns-newfoundland-and-labrador-gm1184723215-333618956

The Battery is perhaps the most photographed neighborhood in St. John’s, a cluster of brightly painted wooden houses that "cling valiantly to the steep, rocky cliffs at the entrance to the harbor. Often described as an outport within the city, this historic fishing village is famous for its narrow, winding lanes where houses are so close together that neighbors can practically shake hands from their windows. It’s a vibrant, lived-in community and the primary gateway for hikers tackling the world-renowned North Head Trail.
What to See and Do

The Jellybean Architecture: Wander through the Upper, Lower, and Outer Battery to see homes painted in vivid teals, reds, and yellows. Because of the extreme terrain, many houses are built on high stilts or shored up with massive timber cribs to stay level against the cliffside.

Chain Rock: Walk down toward the water’s edge in the Outer Battery to see the massive iron ring bolted into the rock. This is where a heavy chain was once stretched across the Narrows to Fort Amherst on the opposite side to physically block enemy ships from entering the harbor during the 1700s and both World Wars.

Fort Waldegrave Ruins: Located at the top of the neighborhood, these grassy mounds and stone remnants are all that remain of an 18th-century gun battery. It offers a spectacular, unobstructed view of the harbor mouth and the open Atlantic.

The Battery Cafe: Located at the entrance to the neighborhood on Duckworth Street, this is the community’s social hub. It’s the perfect place to grab a coffee and a local pastry before heading into the steep lanes of the village.

Photography from the Gut: For the best view of the Battery itself, look back toward the cliffs from a boat tour or from the across the harbor at Fort Amherst. The sight of the houses glowing in the golden hour light is the classic St. John's image.
Tips and Key Information

The Battery is a residential neighborhood, not a museum. The streets are often just narrow paths that feel like private driveways. Visitors are asked to stay on the designated walking paths, keep noise levels down, and avoid peering into people's windows.

There is virtually no public parking within the Battery. The streets are barely wide enough for one car, and most spaces are strictly reserved for residents. It is highly recommended to park in the lots on Signal Hill or near Duckworth Street and walk into the neighborhood.

Because it sits directly under the slopes of Signal Hill, the Battery is prone to high winds and, historically, rockfalls or avalanches during heavy winter storms. Always check for local weather advisories if visiting during the shoulder seasons (March–May).

Most visitors enter the Battery via the North Head Trail coming down from Cabot Tower. If you are doing the reverse (hiking up), be prepared for a very steep climb right from the start of the Outer Battery.
The paths through the Battery can be uneven, slippery when wet, and involve numerous sets of wooden stairs. Sturdy footwear is a must, even for a casual stroll.
The neighborhood begins where the east end of Duckworth Street turns into Signal Hill Road. Follow the lower fork to enter the Lower Battery.

places.name: 2. Iceberg Boat Cruise
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/iceberg-just-outside-the-narrows-st-johns-harbour-st-johns-newfoundland-and-labrador-gm655516138-119492925

An Iceberg Boat Cruise is the classic Newfoundland adventure, offering a front-row seat to Iceberg Alley. These 10,000-year-old glacial giants drift down from Greenland, passing the coast of St. John's and the Avalon Peninsula every spring. As of March 2026, the first icebergs of the season have already been spotted north of the Grand Banks, with the peak viewing window in St. John's expected between mid-May and late June.
What to Expect on the Water

The Triple Threat: If you time your visit for late June, you may experience the rare Newfoundland Triple Threat—seeing an iceberg, a breaching humpback whale, and thousands of Atlantic puffins all in a single 90-minute trip.

Iceberg Beer & Spirits: Many tours will harvest a small piece of bergy bit (smaller floating ice) from the water. Because this ice is composed of compressed ancient snow, it contains no salt and is filled with tiny, highly pressurized air bubbles that fizz in your drink.

Safety Distances: For safety reasons, boats must maintain a distance of at least twice the height of the iceberg (or 50 meters, whichever is greater). Icebergs are famously unstable and can roll or shed massive growlers without warning.
Top Operators Near St. John’s

Iceberg Quest Ocean Tours (St. John’s Harbour): Departing directly from the downtown waterfront, this tour offers the unique experience of sailing through the Narrows past the Battery and Signal Hill. It is the most convenient option if you are staying downtown without a vehicle.

Quidi Vidi Charters (Quidi Vidi Village): For a more intimate, small boat feel, these charters depart from the historic Gut. Captains Noel and Kevin often include a Screech-In ceremony or a chance to jig for cod if the season is right.

Gatherall’s / O’Brien’s (Bay Bulls): Located about 25 minutes south of the city, these larger catamarans head into the Witless Bay Ecological Reserve. While famous for puffins and whales, they are expertly positioned to find icebergs that get grounded in the shallower waters of the reserve.
Tips and Key Information

Even if it is 20oC on Water Street, it will feel like 5oC on the open Atlantic. Dress in layers and bring a windproof jacket, gloves, and a hat. Most operators provide blankets, but you’ll want your own gear for the best experience.
Before booking, check IcebergFinder.com. This real-time satellite and crowdsourced map shows exactly where the bergs are currently located so you can choose the tour closest to the action.
If you don't have a car, both Gatherall’s and O’Brien’s offer daily shuttle pick-ups from major St. John’s hotels for a fee (typically $30–$35).
Expect to pay between $90 and $110 CAD per adult for a standard 2-hour tour. Discounts are almost always available for seniors, students, and families.

places.name: 3. Whale and Seabird Boat Tour
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/diving-sperm-whale-in-trinity-bay-gm119816462-15095561

Whale and Seabird Boat Tours are a bucket-list experience that combines the drama of the North Atlantic with world-class wildlife sightings. Most tours head to the Witless Bay Ecological Reserve, home to North America's largest Atlantic Puffin colony (over 260,000 pairs) and a major feeding ground for humpback whales. Operators are currently accepting bookings for the upcoming season, which officially kicks off in mid-May.
What to See and When

The Atlantic Puffin (May–August): These clowns of the sea return to the islands of Witless Bay to nest in burrows. Peak viewing is in June and July, when the islands are literally swarming with hundreds of thousands of birds.

Humpback Whales (June–August): Newfoundland hosts the world’s largest gathering of humpback whales. They follow the capelin (small silver fish) toward the shore. The capelin roll is expected in late June, which usually triggers a frenzy of whale activity including spectacular breaching and tail-slapping.

Other Marine Life: Keep your eyes peeled for Minke and Fin whales, as well as Razorbills, Common Murres, Black-legged Kittiwakes, and even the occasional Bald Eagle or playful Atlantic White-sided Dolphin.
Top Boat Tour Operators
Gatherall’s (Bay Bulls): Best for stable catamarans and onboard Screech-Ins, with adult tickets around $94.00.
O’Brien’s (Bay Bulls): Best for large vessels and lively Newfoundland music/storytelling, with adult prices starting at about $90.00.
Iceberg Quest (St. John’s): Best for downtown departures and great city views from the water, with adult tickets around $112.00.
Ocean Quest (Petty Harbour): Best for fast Zodiac tours and a water-level thrill, with adult tickets around $115.00.
Tips and Key Information
July is the month where whales, puffins, and even a few late-season icebergs can often be seen on a single trip. These dates fill up months in advance.
If you are staying downtown without a car, Gatherall’s and O’Brien’s both offer shuttle services from major St. John's hotels to their docks in Bay Bulls for a small extra fee.

Even on a calm day, the Atlantic swell can be noticeable. If you're prone to motion sickness, opt for the larger catamarans (like Gatherall's) rather than a Zodiac, and consider taking a Ginger tablet or Gravol an hour before departure.
Puffins are smaller than you might think. If you're a photographer, bring a lens with at least 300mm to 400mm reach. Most captains will try to get as close as safely possible to the nesting cliffs.

It may be 25°C on the pier, but once the boat hits the open ocean and the wind picks up, the temperature drops significantly. Wear windproof layers, a hat, and even light gloves—you'll thank me when everyone else is huddled in the heated cabin.

places.name: 4. Fort Amherst Lighthouse
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/fort-amherst-lighthouse-gm2172270187-592058929

Fort Amherst Lighthouse stands as the silent sentinel on the southern jaw of the Narrows, directly across the water from the Battery. Named after Colonel William Amherst, who recaptured St. John’s from the French in 1762, this site has hosted a light station since 1810. The current structure—a square, tapered concrete tower built in 1954—continues to guide massive container ships, fishing boats, and cruise liners into the safety of the harbor.
What to See and Do

The Panoramic Gatekeeper View: This is arguably the most dramatic view of St. John’s. Looking back across the Narrows, you get a perfectly framed postcard shot of the colorful Battery houses, Cabot Tower, and the city skyline.

The World War II Gun Emplacements: Walk among the massive concrete ruins of the coastal defense batteries built during the 1940s. You can explore the old magazines and observation posts that once housed 6-inch breech-loading guns designed to protect the port from U-boat attacks.

Whale Watching from the Rocks: The deep waters immediately off the rocks at Fort Amherst are a highway for humpback and minke whales. Because the water drops off steeply, whales often swim surprisingly close to the shore, allowing you to hear their blow from the cliffs.

The Narrows Experience: Stand at the water's edge to experience the sheer scale of the cliff walls. When a large ship passes through the 180-meter-wide opening, it feels close enough to touch, and the sound of the engines echoing off the rock walls is unforgettable.
Tips and Key Information

You can drive to the small parking area at the end of Southside Road. From there, it is a short, relatively flat 10-minute walk to the lighthouse. It is a much easier alternative to the steep hiking trails on the Signal Hill side.

Like the Battery, the small cluster of houses at Fort Amherst is a private residential community. Please stay on the gravel road and public paths, and be mindful not to block residents' driveways or park in No Parking zones.

Fort Amherst is home to a powerful automated foghorn. If you visit on a typical St. John’s pea soup day, be prepared for a very loud, vibrating blast every 20 to 30 seconds. It’s atmospheric but can be startling.

The shoreline here consists of black rocks—ledges that are frequently washed over by rogue waves, even on seemingly calm days. Stay well back from the water’s edge and never turn your back on the ocean.

Drive to the very end of Fort Amherst Road (accessible via Southside Road). There is no admission fee to visit the grounds or the ruins, though the interior of the lighthouse tower itself is closed to the public.

places.name: 5. Quidi Vidi Brewery
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/lunchtime-dining-in-quidi-vidi-gm2173447398-593176544

Quidi Vidi Brewery is Newfoundland and Labrador’s largest craft brewery, famously housed in a former fish plant in the heart of the historic Quidi Vidi Gut. Known for its blue bottle flagship and its stunning waterfront taproom, it has become a cultural landmark where industrial heritage meets modern hospitality. The brewery is a focal point of local life, currently serving as a major hub for the 2026 Montana's Brier curling festivities.
What to See and Do

The Iceberg Beer Experience: This is the brewery's claim to fame. The light, golden lager is brewed using 20,000-year-old iceberg water harvested from the North Atlantic. Because the water is so pure and devoid of minerals, it produces a crispness that is virtually impossible to replicate with tap water.

The Taproom View: Often cited as one of the most beautiful taprooms in the world, the space features massive windows and an outdoor deck that look directly out onto the cliffs and the narrow harbor entrance. It’s the perfect spot to watch small fishing boats return with their catch while you sample a flight.
Live Music & Battle of the Bands: The brewery is a champion of the local music scene. They are hosting regular concerts to keep the space lively well into the night.
Popular Brews:
1892 Traditional Ale: An award-winning amber ale that has been a staple since the brewery opened in 1996.
Sours and Seasonals: Keep an eye out for their Newfermenters series, featuring rotating small-batch experiments like the Sofa Sour or the Chocolate Cherry Bight imperial stout.
Non-Alcoholic Options:The brewery has expanded its line to include Non-Alcoholic Iceberg Beer, allowing everyone to enjoy the iceberg water experience.
Tips and Key Information

If you want to take beer to go, visit the Hops Shop (located nearby at 16 Harbour View Avenue). It is typically open Tuesday–Saturday, 12:00 PM to 6:00 PM, while the main taproom at 35 Barrows Road is open 7 days a week.

For general visits, the taproom operates on a first-come, first-served basis. However, during major events like the Brier or the Regatta, it reaches capacity very early—aim for a mid-afternoon off-peak visit for the best chance at a window seat.
For a perfect afternoon, walk the Quidi Vidi Lake Trail or the Signal Hill North Head Trail, both of which culminate just steps away from the brewery’s front door.

Parking in the Gut is extremely limited and strictly monitored. It is highly recommended to park at the Quidi Vidi Lake lot and walk the short 5-minute path into the village to avoid a ticket or a tow.

places.name: 6. Harbourside Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/harbourside-park-gm1369395470-439165696

Harbourside Park is a small but powerful urban park that serves as the front porch of downtown St. John’s. Located directly across from the National War Memorial, it marks the exact spot where Sir Humphrey Gilbert stood in 1583 to claim Newfoundland for the British Crown. The park is a bustling transit point for cruise ship passengers and a beloved lunch-break sanctuary for locals, known for its iconic bronze statues and unobstructed harbor views.
What to See and Do

Our Dogs Statues: This is the park's most famous feature—two larger-than-life bronze sculptures by artist Luben Boykov. One depicts a powerful Newfoundland dog and the other a sleek Labrador Retriever. These statues celebrate the two world-famous breeds that originated in the province.The statues are designed so that their backs form comfortable benches, making them a favorite spot for children and tourists to sit for a photo.

Sir Humphrey Gilbert Tablet: Find the stone monument commemorating the birth of the British Empire. In 1583, Gilbert performed a cut and turf ceremony here, making this site one of the most historically significant locations in North America.

Music @ Harbourside: If you are visiting on a Friday at 12:30 PM during the summer months (June–September), the park hosts a free lunchtime concert series. It features everything from traditional folk and accordion music to modern rock, providing a perfect soundtrack for a picnic by the water.

Ship Spotting: Because the park sits directly on the water’s edge at Queens Cove, it is the best place in the city to watch vessel traffic. You can see pilot boats, massive Coast Guard cutters, and luxury cruise liners like the Volendam or Celebrity Silhouette docking just meters away.
Interpretation Boards: The park is lined with detailed storyboards that explain the Narrows defenses, the history of the port, and the significance of the 1583 proclamation.
Tips and Key Information

Harbourside Park is the first stop for thousands of cruise passengers. In June and August, the park can become very crowded on Ship Days. If you prefer a quiet visit, check the City of St. John's cruise schedule and visit on a day when no major vessels are in port.
The park is fully accessible, featuring a series of ramps that connect the upper level (near Water Street) to the lower waterfront level.

The park is located within a 2-minute walk of several of the city's best coffee shops and delis. Grab a sandwich from Rocket Bakery or a coffee from The Battery Cafe and head to the dog statues for an outdoor office experience.
Harbourside Park is frequently used as the starting or ending point for local community marches and rallies due to its central location and historical gravitas.
Situated at the eastern end of Water Street, nestled between the harbor and the National War Memorial. It is open 24/7 and is free to the public.

places.name: Rathtrevor Beach Provincial Park (Parksville)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/vancouver-island-british-columbia-gm1242838054-362810170

Rathtrevor Beach Provincial Park is one of the most iconic destinations on Vancouver Island. Characterized by its massive tidal range and ancient Douglas fir forests, it offers a distinct coastal experience that transitions from a woodland sanctuary to a vast sandy playground.
What to See and Do

The Tidal Flats: This is the park's most famous feature. At low tide, the ocean recedes nearly a kilometer, exposing vast sandbars and shallow pools. It is perfect for long walks, sandcastle building, and discovering marine life like sand dollars and small crabs.

Warm Water Swimming: As the tide returns over the sun-baked sand, the water warms significantly. This makes Rathtrevor home to some of the warmest ocean swimming in British Columbia during the summer months.

Old-Growth Forest Trails: The park features over 5 kilometers of easy, level trails. The Rathtrevor Beach Path loops through a mix of mature Douglas fir, cedar, and maple forests, offering frequent glimpses of the Salish Sea.

Bird Watching: In the spring (February to April), the park becomes a hotspot for viewing thousands of migrating Brant geese. The annual herring spawn also attracts a massive variety of seabirds and eagles.
The Nature House: A hub for seasonal interpretive programs and displays. It’s an excellent spot for families to learn about local ecology and participate in the Jerry’s Rangers program for kids.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/rathtrevor-beach-at-low-tide-in-parksville-bc-gm666150354-121398537
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/birds-on-vancouver-island-british-columbia-gm2225834838-641822666
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/vancouver-island-british-columbia-gm2195914358-613967113
Tips and Key Information
Your experience will change entirely depending on the water level. Check a local tide chart before you go; aim for low tide for beachcombing and high tide for swimming.
For the best lighting, visit during the golden hour just before sunset. The western-facing beach provides a postcard view of the sun dipping behind the mountains across the Strait of Georgia.
During July and August, the day-use parking lots often fill by mid-morning. Arriving before 10:00 AM ensures a spot and a prime piece of beachfront.
While the sand is soft, some areas near the forest edge can be rocky or have driftwood. Bring sandals or water shoes if you plan to explore the further reaches of the tidal flats.
Situated 3 km south of Parksville off Highway 19A (Island Highway).
Operating Season: The park is open year-round, though full services and gate access hours may vary in the winter months.
Camping Facilities: Features 226 vehicle-accessible sites and 25 walk-in tent sites. Reservations are highly recommended through the BC Parks website, especially for the peak summer season.
Day-Use Amenities: Includes a massive picnic area with over 75 tables, two large reservable picnic shelters, and abundant parking.
Accessibility: Most trails are flat and stroller-friendly. Paved roads, accessible washrooms, and seasonal Mobi-Mats (beach access mats) make it one of the most accessible parks in the province.
Pet Policy: Dogs are not permitted on the sandy day-use beach at any time. To protect migrating Brant geese, the entire beach is strictly closed to dogs from February 15 to April 30.
Park Services: On-site facilities include flush toilets, hot showers (for campers), and a sani-station.
Fire Regulations: Campfires are only allowed in designated rings within the campground. Always check for provincial fire bans before your visit.

places.name: Parksville Beach
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/wide-sandy-beach-at-low-tide-with-tidepools-in-sunny-day-gm2245187314-659224347

Parksville Community Park, often simply called Parksville Beach, is the vibrant heart of the city’s waterfront. While Rathtrevor offers a more rustic, forested escape, the Community Park is a high-energy hub designed for families, events, and active recreation.
What to See and Do

The Parksville Beach Festival (Beachfest): This premier summer event features the world-class Quality Foods Sand Sculpting Exhibition, where professional artists from across the globe compete to create massive, intricate masterpieces that remain on display for five weeks following a mid-July competition, accompanied by live music, an artisan market, and special evening light up viewings.

Lions Ventureland Playground: This is one of the largest and most comprehensive outdoor playgrounds on Vancouver Island. It features a splash park, zip lines, and inclusive equipment, making it the ultimate stop for families.
The Waterfront Boardwalk: A flat, paved 1-kilometer walkway that hugs the shoreline. It is perfect for a leisurely stroll, sunset jog, or watching the kite flyers in the adjacent open fields.

Outdoor Performance Theatre: A newer addition to the park, this amphitheater hosts the Beachfest Rocks concert series, typically takes place in August as a major weekend feature of the broader summer festival, and various free weekend performances throughout the summer.
Active Sports Hub: The park is exceptionally well-equipped for sports, featuring:
Beach volleyball courts with professional-grade sand.
A modern skateboard park and a dedicated lacrosse box.
Resurfaced tennis and pickleball courts.
An outdoor fitness gym and a labyrinth for mindful walking.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/steller-sea-lions-french-creek-parksville-vancouver-island-british-columbia-canada-gm2241296190-655827548
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/orange-and-pink-sunset-in-the-pacific-ocean-coast-in-summer-gm1534233151-525367059
Tips and Key Information

If you are visiting during Beachfest, don't miss the Light Up nights (typically held on the final weekend), where the sand sculptures are illuminated after dark for a completely different visual perspective.
The massive open green space next to the beach is famous for its steady ocean breezes. It is the best spot in the region to fly a kite or watch the Parksville Lions Kite Festival.
