During the Sand Sculpting Exhibition, the park can see upwards of 100,000 visitors. Visit on a weekday morning or a Tuesday evening to avoid the heaviest weekend foot traffic.

Head to the Arboretum and Gardens section of the park for vibrant floral shots, or use the elevated viewing platforms near the volleyball courts for action shots of the beach with the islands in the background.
Located at 193 Island Highway East, right in the center of downtown Parksville.
Entry to the sand sculpting area is by a suggested donation of $5.00, which supports local non-profit groups.
The park is highly accessible with paved pathways, a mobi-mat for wheelchair access to the sand, and a newly constructed washroom building fitted with automatic door buttons.
Dogs are welcome in the park on a leash but are not allowed in the playground or within the gated sand sculpting exhibition area.
There is a large parking lot, but it fills up fast during festival weekends. Look for overflow parking in the surrounding downtown streets, which are within easy walking distance.
Unlike the more secluded Rathtrevor, this park is within walking distance of several cafes and ice cream shops, and food trucks are frequently on-site during summer events.

places.name: Qualicum Beach
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/drone-view-over-qualicum-bay-with-denman-hornby-island-in-background-bowser-gm2246774412-660718051

The beach at Qualicum Beach offers a more tranquil, natural alternative to the bustling park in Parksville, characterized by its long, curved shoreline and panoramic views of the distant Coast Mountains.
What to See and Do
The Coastal Promenade: A 2-kilometer paved walkway runs parallel to the shoreline, offering a completely flat and accessible path for walking, cycling, or storm watching during the winter months.

Low Tide Exploration: While the upper beach is composed of smooth, colorful sea stones, the water recedes significantly at low tide to reveal wide, sandy flats. It is a premier spot for finding sand dollars and watching blue herons hunt in the shallow pools.

Swimming and Paddling: Because the shoreline is protected, the water is generally calmer than on the west coast of the island. The shallow entry makes it a favorite for paddleboarding and kayaking, especially in the early morning before the winds pick up.

The Alpenglow Views: Unlike Parksville, which faces west for the direct sunset, Qualicum Beach faces northeast. This provides a spectacular view of the alpenglow effect, where the snow-capped peaks on the mainland turn vibrant shades of pink and purple as the sun sets behind the island’s mountains.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/qualicum-beach-vancouver-island-british-columbia-gm1007458676-271833295
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/qualicum-beach-gm1349899585-426249582
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/sea-kayakers-vancouver-island-british-columbia-canada-gm1286758120-383171528
Tips and Key Information
Highway 19A runs directly alongside the beach with plenty of parallel parking. To find the quietest spots, drive toward the northern end of the promenade near the boat ramp.
To enjoy the sand, you must visit during low tide. At high tide, the water often reaches the drift logs, leaving only the pebbled upper beach accessible for sitting.
Several local landmarks are situated right on the water. These are restaurants nearby perfect for grabbing takeout fish and chips to enjoy on the beach wall.
Keep an eye on the kelp beds just offshore; they are frequent resting spots for sea otters and harbor seals.
Stretches along Highway 19A (Island Highway) for several kilometers, beginning just north of the French Creek Marina.
The promenade is fully wheelchair and stroller accessible, with multiple concrete ramps providing transition points from the sidewalk to the beach level.
Dogs are permitted on the beach but must be on a leash at all times to protect the local bird sanctuary and sensitive ecosystem.
Public washrooms, seasonal concessions, and outdoor foot-wash stations are located at the center of the promenade near the Visitor Information kiosk.
Beach fires are strictly prohibited year-round to preserve the driftwood and protect the air quality of the surrounding residential areas.
Similar to Rathtrevor, the shallow bays warm up significantly during summer afternoons, providing some of the most comfortable ocean swimming on the coast.

places.name: Whale and Wildlife Adventure
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/humpback-whale-tail-fluke-strait-of-georgia-near-texada-island-bc-canada-gm1512750821-524037277

The Parksville and Qualicum Beach region serves as a premier gateway to the Salish Sea, offering a front-row seat to some of the most diverse marine and terrestrial wildlife in North America. While the beaches are the main draw, the deeper waters and surrounding estuaries provide a sanctuary for majestic predators and migratory species alike.
What to See and Do

Whale Watching Tours: Several professional operators depart from nearby French Creek Marina and Deep Bay. These high-speed zodiac or covered vessel tours track Southern Resident and Transient (Biggs) Orcas, as well as massive Humpback whales, which are frequently seen breaching and tail-slapping in the Strait of Georgia.

The Brant Geese Migration: Every March and April, the region hosts the Brant Wildlife Festival. Thousands of these sea geese stop on the shores of Parksville and Qualicum Beach to feast on herring spawn during their long journey from Mexico to the Arctic.

Seal and Sea Lion Sightings: The rocky outcroppings of the Winchelsea Islands (visible from Nanoose Bay) are a permanent haul-out site for hundreds of Steller and California sea lions. Their barking can often be heard from the shoreline on quiet days.

North Island Wildlife Recovery Centre: Located just inland in Errington, this world-class facility rehabilitates injured black bears, eagles, and owls. It features a massive eagle flight pen and provides an up-close look at the beast side of the island's wildlife.

Eagle Watching at French Creek: The area around the French Creek Marina is one of the best spots on the island to see Bald Eagles in high concentrations, especially during the salmon runs when they perch in the tall Douglas firs overlooking the water.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/birds-on-vancouver-island-british-columbia-gm2225834844-641822668
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/brant-geese-migration-parksville-vancouver-island-british-columbia-canada-gm2269698621-682240798
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/bald-eagle-taking-off-from-tree-top-qualicum-bay-vancouver-island-british-columbia-gm2247179985-661096173
Tips and Key Information
For whale watching, the Strait of Georgia is typically calmest in the early morning. Book the morning calm. Afternoon winds can make for a bumpier ride on the open water.
Even on a hot 25°C day in Parksville, the temperature on the water can feel 10 degrees cooler. Most tour operators provide survival suits, but wearing a warm base layer and a hat is essential.
While tours get you close, many wildlife sightings (like sea otters in the kelp beds or eagles in the canopy) are best viewed through high-quality optics from the shoreline promenade.
If you are exploring by kayak or paddleboard, federal law requires you to stay at least 400 meters away from Orcas. Always give marine mammals plenty of space to ensure their safety and yours.
Humpback whales are most common from May through October, while Orcas can be spotted year-round. The peak for migratory birds is late February to April.
Most marine adventures depart from French Creek Marina (between Parksville and Qualicum) or the Deep Bay Marine Field Station.
Expect whale watching excursions to last between 3 to 4 hours depending on where the whales are located that day.
Use a fast shutter speed (at least 1/1000s) to capture whales and birds in motion from a moving boat.
Choosing operators that are members of the Pacific Whale Watch Association (PWWA) ensures your tour follows strict ethical guidelines for wildlife viewing.

places.name: French Creek Harbour: Fishing Charters and Wildlife Tours
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/french-creek-harbour-in-parksville-on-the-east-coast-of-vancouver-island-gm1802841997-548625734

French Creek Harbour serves as the premier marine gateway for the Oceanside region. Positioned perfectly between Parksville and Qualicum Beach, this active working port is the primary departure point for those looking to explore the rich waters of the Salish Sea, whether for world-class angling or spectacular wildlife encounters.
What to See and Do
The harbour hosts a professional fleet of seasoned captains and guides who specialize in navigating the local currents and secret fishing spots.

World-Class Salmon and Halibut Fishing: Charters from French Creek offer access to some of the best fishing grounds on Vancouver Island. Depending on the season, anglers can target Chinook (King) and Coho salmon, or head further out for deep-water Pacific Halibut.

Wildlife Viewing and Whale Watching: The waters surrounding French Creek are part of a vibrant migratory corridor. Tours frequently encounter Bigg’s (transient) orcas, humpback whales, and playful pods of Pacific white-sided dolphins.

The Sea Lion Spectacle: Particularly during the spring herring spawn, the breakwaters and nearby haul-outs are covered with hundreds of Steller and California sea lions. The sound and scale of this gathering are a major draw for photographers.

Birding and Marine Ecology: Many tours provide an educational component, identifying the diverse birdlife—including bald eagles and ancient murrelets—that congregate around the nearby Sangster and Winchelsea Islands.
Tips and Key Information
Fishing and wildlife tours are in high demand from June through September. It is recommended to secure your charter several weeks in advance, especially for weekend departures.
Even on a warm summer day, the temperature on the open water can be significantly cooler than on the docks. High-quality windbreakers, hats, and polarized sunglasses are essential gear.

If you are booking a fishing charter, ensure you have a valid BC Tidal Waters Sport Fishing Licence (available online) before arriving at the dock. Most charters provide all necessary tackle and bait.
Most fishing charters leave at first light when the water is often at its calmest and the bite is most active. Plan for an early start to maximize your time on the water.
Located at 1055 Access Rd, Parksville, BC. Charters typically meet their guests at the top of the ramps near the French Creek Marine Pub or the Harbour Master’s office.

Most tour vessels are accessed via floating docks. While these are stable, the ramps can be steep at low tide. If you have mobility concerns, contact your charter operator in advance to discuss boarding assistance.
There is ample public parking available near the marina, including long-term spots for those heading out on full-day excursions.
The harbour area includes a well-stocked marine store, public washrooms, and a fresh seafood market where you can have your day's catch professionally cleaned or packed.

places.name: Horne Lake Caves Provincial Park (Qualicum Beach)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/horne-lake-caves-provincial-park-on-vancouver-island-gm981323470-266525885

Horne Lake Caves Provincial Park is one of British Columbia’s most unique protected areas, designed specifically to preserve a fragile underground ecosystem while offering some of the best cave exploration in Canada. Located at the end of a gravel road about 30 minutes west of Qualicum Beach, the park transitions from a lush lakeside forest to a hidden world of crystal formations and subterranean waterfalls.
What to See and Do

Self-Guided Exploration: Visitors can explore Main Cave and Lower Main Cave at their own pace. These provide a great introduction to wild caving, though they still require sturdy footwear and a reliable light source.

Guided Adventure Tours: For those looking to go deeper, the park offers a variety of guided tours categorized by their physical demands and technical challenges, ranging from family-friendly walks to extreme
Riverbend Cave Explorer (Easy/Family)
This is the most accessible guided option, designed for families with children as young as age five or those wanting a less strenuous introduction to caving.
Physical Demand: Involves easy walking on relatively level ground with some sections of low-ceiling duck walking.
Highlights: Focuses on cave geology and seeing delicate formations like soda straws and flowstone without the need for crawling or climbing.
Duration: Approximately 2 hours.
Multi-Cave Experience (Moderate)
This tour increases the physical challenge by visiting multiple caves and introducing more varied terrain.
Physical Demand: Requires more agility as you navigate uneven floors, steep ramps, and some small crawl spaces.
Highlights: Includes a visit to the Rainy Day cave and features more diverse passages that illustrate how different cave systems form.
Duration: Approximately 3 hours.
Achilles Challenge (Challenging)
This tour is designed for adventurous visitors who are comfortable with tight spaces and more strenuous physical activity.
Physical Demand: Involves significant crawling, squeezing through narrow passages, and climbing up internal rock faces.
Highlights: Takes you into deeper, more remote sections of the cave system that are not accessible on the easier tours.
Duration: Approximately 3 to 4 hours.
Max Depth Adventure (Extreme)
This is the park's flagship technical tour, requiring a high level of physical fitness and a lack of fear regarding heights or enclosed spaces.
Physical Demand: Features a vertical element where participants must climb a seven-story underground waterfall and navigate strenuous scrambles.
Highlights: Offers the most dramatic scenery in the park, including massive crystal-lined caverns and the thrill of a vertical ascent in total darkness.
Duration: Approximately 4 to 5 hours.

The Cave Centre: This serves as the park’s educational hub, featuring geological displays, a small museum about the history of the caves, and a practice crawl-way to test your comfort level before heading underground.
Phil Whitfield Interpretive Trail: A scenic surface trail that connects the various cave entrances, providing information on how the limestone landscape (karst) was formed over millions of years.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/horne-lake-caves-provincial-park-gm948377582-258917501
Tips and Key Information
Regardless of the temperature outside, the caves remain a constant 5°C (41°F) year-round. Wear layers of synthetic or wool clothing that you don't mind getting muddy or damp.
Helmets and high-quality headlamps are mandatory for all cave entries. If you don't have your own, the park office provides rentals for a small fee.
While self-guided caves are accessible to day-use visitors, the popular guided tours often sell out weeks in advance during the summer months.
Caving is physically demanding. Be prepared for crouching, crawling, and climbing over slippery rocks; even the easy caves require a moderate level of agility.
Located at the western end of Horne Lake; access is via a 12 km gravel logging road from Highway 19 or 19A.
The park is open year-round, but guided tour schedules vary by season. Check the Horne Lake Caves website for the most current availability.
To prevent the spread of White-Nose Syndrome (a disease affecting bats), visitors must not wear any clothing or gear that has previously been used in caves outside of British Columbia.
The park features a small shop for snacks and gear, pit toilets, and a picnic area overlooking the lake. There is no running water available at the cave site.
Dogs are allowed in the provincial park on a leash but are strictly prohibited inside any of the caves or the visitor center.
While there is no camping at the cave site itself, the adjacent Horne Lake Regional Park offers lakefront campsites and boat rentals.

places.name: Cathedral Grove (MacMillan Provincial Park)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/cathedral-grove-with-boardwalk-near-port-alberni-bc-canada-gm2171381221-591243712

Cathedral Grove, located within MacMillan Provincial Park, is one of the most accessible stands of giant Douglas fir trees in British Columbia. Situated on Highway 4 between Qualicum Beach and Port Alberni, it offers a rare opportunity to walk among living monuments that have stood for over 800 years.
What to See and Do
Ancient Douglas Firs: The park is famous for its massive trees, some measuring more than 9 meters in circumference. The big tree on the southern network of trails is a primary highlight for visitors.
Western Red Cedars: While the Douglas firs dominate the skyline, the northern side of the highway features a lush grove of ancient Western Red Cedars growing along the shores of Cameron Lake.

Looping Trail Networks: The park is split by the highway into two distinct trail systems. Both sides offer short, well-maintained boardwalks and gravel paths that are easy to navigate and provide an immersive forest experience.
The Living Classroom: Interpretive signs throughout the grove explain the lifecycle of the forest, the impact of the 1997 windstorm, and how these giants survive fire and disease.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/family-admiring-the-ancient-cedar-tree-in-forest-gm1155052244-314319637
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/mother-and-child-hiking-through-ancient-forest-in-cathedral-grove-gm2252342690-665811284
Tips and Key Information
Be extremely cautious when crossing the highway between the two trail sections. Traffic moves quickly, and the parking area can be congested.
To experience the cathedral-like silence the park is named for, try to arrive before 10:00 AM or after 4:00 PM. During midday, the proximity to the highway makes it busier and noisier.
While the canopy is breathtaking, remember to look at the nurse logs on the forest floor—fallen giants that provide essential nutrients for new saplings, mosses, and ferns.
The dense canopy acts as a natural umbrella, but it also traps moisture. The trails can be damp and cooler than the surrounding area, so a light jacket and sturdy walking shoes are recommended.
Located on Highway 4, approximately 25 kilometers west of Qualicum Beach.
The main loop trails are largely flat and surfaced with gravel or wooden boardwalks, making them accessible for most strollers and wheelchairs.
Parking is limited to designated gravel shoulders along the highway. It fills up quickly during summer weekends; avoid parking in No Parking zones to ensure safety and avoid fines.
Dogs are permitted but must be kept on a leash at all times to protect the sensitive root systems and local wildlife.
Pit toilets are available at the main trailhead. There are no running water facilities or food services within the park.
Visitors are strictly required to stay on the designated paths. The root systems of these ancient trees are shallow and easily damaged by foot traffic.

places.name: Englishman River Falls Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/englishman-river-falls-provincial-park-parksville-british-columbia-canada-gm2252050109-665545416

Englishman River Falls Provincial Park is a spectacular nature reserve located near Errington, just a short drive from Parksville. It is best known for its two distinct waterfalls set within a deep, rocky canyon and surrounded by a lush forest of Douglas fir, cedar, and hemlock.
What to See and Do
The park’s primary draw is the dramatic contrast between its upper and lower falls, connected by a well-maintained trail system.

The Upper Falls: A thunderous curtain of water that drops into a narrow, vertical-walled canyon. A sturdy footbridge directly over the falls provides a pulse-racing vantage point for photography and viewing the sheer power of the river.

The Lower Falls: Located further down the trail, these falls drop into a deep, crystal-clear basin. This area is a popular destination in the summer as the pool below the falls offers a refreshing spot for swimming.

Loop Hiking Trail: A relatively easy 1.5-kilometer loop trail connects both sets of falls. The path winds through a quintessential West Coast rainforest, featuring massive trees, moss-covered rocks, and several viewpoints overlooking the river.
Picnicking and Day Use: The park features a large, forested day-use area equipped with picnic tables and a shelter, making it an ideal spot for a family lunch after exploring the canyon.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/beautiful-englishman-river-waterfalls-upper-section-parksville-british-columbia-gm1415487252-463840162
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/englishman-river-falls-provincial-park-parksville-british-columbia-canada-gm2252050121-665545418
Tips and Key Information

To make the most of your visit, consider the timing of your trip and the natural cycles of the river. For the most dramatic, thundering water, visit in the late autumn or spring during the snowmelt. In the height of summer, the water flow decreases, revealing more of the intricate rock formations within the canyon.
If you plan to swim at the lower falls, be aware that the water remains quite cold year-round and the rocks can be extremely slippery. Always supervise children closely near the water’s edge.
The deep canyon creates high-contrast shadows during midday. For the softest light on the waterfalls and forest greenery, aim to visit in the early morning or late afternoon.
Situated at the end of Englishman River Road, approximately 13 km southwest of Parksville.

The trail to the upper falls and the main bridge is wide and relatively flat, though the full loop to the lower falls involves some elevation changes and stairs that may be challenging for those with limited mobility.
Dogs are welcome in the park but must remain on a leash at all times to protect the sensitive river ecosystem and local wildlife.
The day-use area includes pit toilets and fresh water taps (seasonal). There is also a vehicle-accessible campground with 103 sites available for those looking to stay overnight.
A large paved parking lot is available at the trailhead, though it can fill up quickly on sunny weekend afternoons.

places.name: Little Qualicum Falls Provincial Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/raging-canyon-gm512683516-87257849

Little Qualicum Falls Provincial Park is a stunning natural area centered around the Little Qualicum River, where the water travels through a series of dramatic rock chasms. It is often visited alongside Cameron Lake and Cathedral Grove due to its proximity along the same highway corridor, offering a cooler, shaded environment dominated by old-growth Douglas fir and Western hemlock.
What to See and Do

Upper and Lower Falls: A loop trail connects two distinct sets of waterfalls. The Upper Falls are characterized by a powerful drop into a deep, shaded basin, while the Lower Falls offer a wider, tiered cascade over ancient rock formations.

Canyon Trail: This 6-kilometer network of well-maintained paths follows the edge of the steep-walled gorge. Multiple wooden bridges and fenced lookout points provide safe, bird's-eye views of the rushing water and deep turquoise pools below.

Swimming at Cameron Lake: Located at the western end of the park, the day-use area at Cameron Lake is a popular spot for windsurfing, fishing, and swimming, with the surrounding Beaufort Mountains providing a dramatic backdrop.
Fishing: The river and lake are known for seasonal trout fishing; however, visitors should check current BC provincial freshwater fishing regulations for specific closures and gear requirements.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/little-qualicum-falls-provincial-park-qualicum-beach-vancouver-island-british-gm2246774407-660718048
Tips and Key Information

The deep canyon and heavy forest canopy keep this park significantly cooler than the nearby beaches of Parksville. It is an excellent destination for a hike during the hottest part of a summer afternoon.

In the spring or after a heavy rainfall, the volume of water creates a fine mist in the canyon. This provides excellent opportunities for long exposure photography of the waterfalls, though you should bring a cloth to wipe your lens.

While the main paths are well-gravelled, there are several sections with significant stairs and steep grades between the upper and lower sections. Sturdy footwear with good grip is essential, especially if the rocks are damp.
Located 19 km west of Qualicum Beach on Highway 4 (toward Port Alberni).
The trail to the first lookout of the Upper Falls is relatively accessible, but the full loop involves steep stairs and uneven terrain that is not suitable for wheelchairs or strollers.
Dogs are permitted on a leash at all times. They are not allowed in the designated swimming areas at Cameron Lake to maintain water quality and bather safety.
The park features a large picnic area with a shelter, pit toilets, and a seasonal campground with 96 vehicle-accessible sites.

The river currents are extremely strong and the canyon walls are sheer. Swimming is strictly prohibited in the river and waterfall areas; stick to the designated beach at Cameron Lake for water activities.

places.name: Milner Gardens & Woodland (Qualicum Beach)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/dragonfly-at-milner-gardens-gm2217768155-634339545

Milner Gardens & Woodland is a 70-acre wild garden and forest estate that offers a rare combination of horticultural sophistication and raw coastal beauty. Once a private retreat for the Milner family, it is now a public treasure managed by Vancouver Island University, serving as a center for both conservation and education.
What to See and Do

The Heritage House: A centerpiece of the estate, this historic home once hosted members of the British Royal Family. It now serves as a quaint tea room where visitors can enjoy traditional afternoon tea with a view of the Salish Sea.

Ancient Douglas Fir Forest: The entrance to the gardens requires a walk through a majestic stand of old-growth forest, providing a dramatic transition from the outside world into the manicured garden spaces.

The Shoots Garden: This area is specifically designed to engage younger visitors, featuring interactive elements that teach children about the lifecycle of plants and the importance of forest ecosystems.

The Grand Lawn: A wide, sloping expanse of green that leads from the house toward the bluffs, offering one of the most photographed vistas in Qualicum Beach, especially when the surrounding rhododendrons are in full bloom.
Tips and Key Information
The Milner House Tea Room is incredibly popular and operates on a seasonal schedule. To ensure a table, especially during the summer months, it is highly recommended to call ahead.
While the forest is beautiful year-round, the garden is famous for its collection of over 400 rhododendrons. These typically peak in May and June, transforming the grounds into a corridor of color.
For those who may find the 10-15 minute walk from the parking lot to the house difficult, the garden often operates a golf cart shuttle service during peak hours.

The garden is at its most ethereal during the mid-morning when light filters through the ancient canopy, or during the blue hour in December when the estate is transformed by the Milner Christmas Magic light display.
Located at 2179 Island Hwy W, Qualicum Beach, BC.
As a non-profit and educational site, there is an admission fee that directly supports the maintenance of the gardens and student programs.
The gardens are seasonal, typically open from spring through early autumn, with special openings for holiday events in December.
To protect the delicate plant collections and local birdlife, pets are not permitted within the gardens or woodland trails.
There is a dedicated gravel parking lot at the entrance. It is spacious, but it can fill up during special events like the spring plant sale.

places.name: The Qualicum Beach Heritage Forest
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/fog-beams-in-the-forest-qualicum-beach-vancouver-island-british-columbia-canada-gm2260956812-673817664

The Qualicum Beach Heritage Forest is a 50-acre ecological jewel located just minutes from the town center. This rare remnant of the Coastal Douglas-fir ecosystem was saved by the community to preserve a living museum of the island’s ancient landscape, offering a cool, silent escape beneath a canopy of 400-year-old giants.
What to See and Do

Ancient Tree Canopy: The forest is dominated by massive Douglas firs, Western Red Cedars, and Sitka spruces. Walking through the grove provides a sense of the scale of Vancouver Island’s original old-growth forests.

Extensive Trail Network: Over 2 kilometers of well-maintained, wide gravel paths crisscross the property. The trails are mostly level, making them ideal for a contemplative nature walk or a gentle jog.

Birding and Wildlife: As a protected sanctuary, the forest is a haven for pileated woodpeckers, owls, and various songbirds. The dense undergrowth of sword ferns and salal also provides cover for local black-tailed deer.
Seasonal Wildflowers: In the spring, the forest floor comes alive with native species like trilliums and fawn lilies, which thrive in the filtered sunlight of the ancient canopy.
Tips and Key Information
Because the forest is tucked away from the main highway, it is one of the quietest spots in the region. Visit in the early morning to hear the wind in the high canopy without any urban distraction.

Even on the hottest summer days, the refrigerator effect of the deep shade keeps the forest significantly cooler than the nearby beach. It is the perfect place to retreat when the afternoon sun becomes too intense.

The main entrance off Crescent Road East features a flat staging area. The trails are generally stroller-friendly and accessible for those with steady mobility, though some peripheral paths may have exposed roots.

The filtered god rays that pierce the canopy in the late afternoon create dramatic lighting for forest photography. Use a tripod or a fast lens to capture the deep greens of the moss and ferns in the lower light.
Access points are located on Crescent Road East and at the end of Beach Road, within walking distance of the Qualicum Beach village.
Entry is free to the public, as the forest is maintained through a partnership between the Town of Qualicum Beach and a local preservation society.
Dogs are permitted but must be on a leash at all times to protect the nesting birds and sensitive ground cover.
his is a leave no trace wilderness area. There are no washrooms or trash cans within the forest itself, so plan accordingly before entering.
The forest is open daily from dawn until dusk. There is no lighting on the trails, so exiting before sunset is recommended.

places.name: Top Bridge Park (Parksville)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/small-but-beautiful-top-bridge-in-rathtrevor-beach-provincial-park-bc-canada-1-gm669505784-122340287

Top Bridge Community Park is a dynamic junction of nature and recreation where the Englishman River carves through a canyon of sculpted sandstone. It serves as a vital trail link between the urban seaside and the cool, shaded woodlands of the river valley, offering a raw and rugged alternative to the manicured beaches nearby.
What to See and Do
The Suspension Bridge: The iconic 81-meter pedestrian and cyclist bridge offers panoramic views of the river gorge, clear green water, and forested slopes.
Swimming and Cliff Jumping: Below the bridge, deep natural pools and smooth sandstone rock shelves create a premier secret swimming hole for locals during the summer.
Mountain Biking Trails: The park features a specialized and extensive network of mountain biking trails, ranging from gentle forest paths to technical routes for advanced riders.
First Nations Petroglyphs: One of the park's hidden treasures is a series of three distinct ancient carvings found on the rocks near the riverbank, discovered in 1940.
Fishing and Birding: The river is a productive habitat for salmon and trout, attracting both anglers and birdwatchers who come to see eagles and herons, especially during the fall salmon run.
Tips and Key Information
You can access the park from two main sides. The Chattell Road side is best for the mountain bike park, while the Allsbrook Road side provides a short, easy walk directly to the suspension bridge.
While the Nose is a popular spot for jumping into the river, always verify the water depth first, as jutting rocks and shifting river currents can be hazardous.
P For an extended adventure, follow the RDN Top Bridge Trail for a 5-kilometer hike that connects the river canyon directly to Rathtrevor Beach Provincial Park.
Much like Qualicum Beach, the elevated sections of the park provide a unique vantage point to watch the mountains glow at dusk.
The park is a natural area with limited amenities, so you should come prepared.
Access via the Allsbrook Rd Trailhead (off Highway 4) or at the end of Chattell Road (off Highway 19A near the truck scales).
Generally open daily from 7:00 AM to 11:00 PM, though gates are locked seasonally; always check the current closing time posted at the entrance to avoid being locked in.
Amenities are basic, consisting primarily of pit toilets at the parking areas and informational signage; there are no change rooms, lifeguards, or food services.
Dogs are welcome and can even be off-leash if they are well-behaved and under control, making it one of the more pet-friendly trails in the region.
The paths to the bridge are packed gravel and relatively level, though continuing along the riverbank involves stairs and rugged sections with exposed roots.

places.name: Moorecroft Regional Park
body: Moorecroft Regional Park is a serene 79-acre conservation area located in Nanoose Bay, just a short drive south of Parksville. Once a private summer camp, the park now offers a peaceful blend of secondary old-growth forest, sensitive wetlands, and a stunning cobble beach overlooking the Salish Sea.
Visitors often appreciate this park for its quiet, contemplative atmosphere and the way it preserves the nostalgic feel of its history while protecting rare plant species.
What to See and Do
Scenic Shoreline: The park features several hundred meters of waterfront with views across the Strait of Georgia toward Lasqueti and Texada Islands.
Ms. Moore Cabin: As a nod to its past as Camp Moorecroft, the historic Ms. Moore cabin remains on-site, serving as a landmark along the coastal trail.
Diverse Ecosystems: The trail network winds through Douglas-fir and Arbutus groves, leading to a unique eagle nesting site and a tranquil inland fen.
Cook Creek: A small, picturesque creek bisects the property, providing a vital habitat for local amphibians and a soothing soundtrack to your hike.
Tips and Key Information
While there are no formal picnic shelters, the large driftwood logs along the beach provide the perfect natural seating for a quiet lunch with an ocean view.
Keep your eyes on the high canopy near the shoreline; the park is well-known among locals for its active bald eagle nests.
Visit during a receding tide to explore the tide pools at the northern end of the beach, where you can often spot small crabs and sea anemones.
The twisted, orange-red bark of the Arbutus trees against the blue backdrop of the Georgia Strait offers exceptional opportunities for nature photography.
Located at the end of Stewart Road in Nanoose Bay.
The main trail from the parking lot to the beach is relatively flat and well-maintained, though some of the interior forest loops contain narrow sections and exposed roots.
Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a leash at all times to protect the park's sensitive ecosystems and wildlife.
Amenities are minimal to maintain the natural feel, consisting of a small parking area and pit toilets near the entrance; there is no potable water available.
As a regional conservation cove, visitors are asked to stay on designated trails to avoid trampling rare wildflowers and sensitive ground cover.

places.name: Town of Qualicum Beach - Waterfront Viewing Platform & Walkway
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/qualicum-beach-and-bay-gm171249703-20082349

The Qualicum Beach Waterfront Viewing Platform & Walkway is a central feature of the town’s shoreline, offering an elevated and accessible way to experience the Strait of Georgia. Unlike the rugged trails of nearby provincial parks, this infrastructure is designed for a polished, resort-style experience that emphasizes comfort and panoramic vistas.
What to See and Do

The Elevated Viewing Platform: Located near the center of the promenade, this wooden structure provides a 180-degree view of the northern Gulf Islands and the snow-capped Coast Mountains on the mainland. It is a favorite spot for whale spotting and storm watching.

The 2km Paved Walkway: This wide, flat promenade runs the length of the beach. It is separated from the road by a landscaped buffer, making it a safe and scenic corridor for walking, jogging, or pushing a stroller.

Interpretive Signage: Several stations along the walkway offer insights into the local marine life, the history of the unplugged town, and the unique microclimate that allows Mediterranean-style gardens to flourish in the area.
The Roundel & Shade Structures: Architectural seating areas along the route provide shaded spots to rest and watch the kite surfers and paddleboarders who frequent the bay.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/qualicum-beach-boardwalk-gm512172033-47307638
Tips and Key Information

Because of its northeast-facing position, the walkway is the best place in the region to see the Alpenglow. Arrive about 20 minutes before sunset to watch the mountains across the water turn deep shades of pink and orange.
Many locals start their day here with a coffee from one of the nearby cafes. The morning light is crisp and the water is usually at its calmest, perfect for spotting seals surfacing near the shore.
During the winter months (November–February), the viewing platform is a safe, elevated vantage point to watch massive waves crash against the sea wall during high-tide storms.
If you want to transition from the walkway to the sand, look for the blue mobi-mats (seasonal), which provide a firm surface for wheelchairs and strollers to reach the water's edge.
Runs parallel to Highway 19A (Island Highway West), stretching from the Visitor Centre toward the northern end of town.
This is the most accessible waterfront feature in the region. The walkway is level with the road, and there are multiple curb cuts and ramps.

Free parallel parking is available along the entire length of the walkway. During the summer, spots near the viewing platform fill quickly, but plenty of space is usually available at the northern Schooner Cove end.
Modern, accessible public washrooms and outdoor foot-wash stations are located at the midpoint of the walkway.
Dogs are welcome on the paved walkway but must be on a leash. Be mindful of the high volume of foot traffic during weekend afternoons.

places.name: Beachcomber Regional Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/stony-shoreline-of-vancouver-island-in-nanoose-at-low-tide-gm1339337923-419710035

Beachcomber Regional Park is a hidden gem tucked away at the tip of the Beachcomber peninsula in Nanoose Bay. This compact, one-hectare park is cherished for its rugged shoreline and its position as a premier vantage point for observing the marine traffic and natural beauty of the Salish Sea. Visitors frequently highlight the park's tranquil environment and its spectacular views of the neighboring islands.
What to See and Do
Coastal Vistas: The park offers clear, unobstructed views across the water to the Ballenas Islands and the distant Coast Mountains on the mainland.
Unique Shoreline: Unlike the long sandy stretches of Parksville, this beach is characterized by its sculpted sandstone formations, colorful sea stones, and plentiful driftwood.
Marine Life Hub: Because the park juts out into the strait, it is an excellent land-based spot for spotting harbor seals, sea lions, and occasionally passing orca or humpback whales.
Sunset Serenity: Its northwest-facing orientation makes it one of the most romantic and peaceful spots in the region to watch the sun dip below the horizon.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/beachcomber-regional-park-nanoose-bay-vancouver-island-british-columbia-canada-gm2267397914-680018846
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/closeup-of-a-man-fishing-from-the-huge-rocks-by-the-pacific-ocean-at-beachcomber-gm1460453102-494629429
Tips and Key Information
At low tide, the rocky crevices along the shoreline reveal miniature ecosystems filled with tiny crabs, sea snails, and anemones—perfect for quiet exploration.
There are no vendors nearby, so bring a blanket and some local snacks to enjoy on the rocks while taking in the salt air and scenery.
Because the park is quite exposed on the peninsula, it can be significantly breezier than the sheltered forests inland; a light windbreaker is often a good idea even on sunny days.
Located at the very end of Marina Way in Nanoose Bay, about a 15-minute drive south of Parksville.
The park is small with a short, relatively flat trail leading from the parking area to the shoreline, though moving across the rocky beach itself requires steady footing.
Dogs are welcome but must remain on a leash to protect the local shoreline habitat.
This is a basic neighborhood park; it includes a small parking lot and pit toilets, but no running water or picnic tables.

places.name: Hamilton Marsh
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/drone-shot-over-a-forest-with-fog-hamilton-marsh-qualicum-beach-vancouver-island-gm2248964812-662778264

Hamilton Marsh is a massive 360-hectare wetland ecosystem located south of Qualicum Beach. Recently protected in its entirety through a significant community effort, it stands as the largest body of water in the French Creek watershed and is a vital sanctuary for both migratory and resident wildlife.
What to See and Do

Birdwatching: Recognized as the most prolific waterfowl brood marsh on this part of the island, the area has recorded over 130 species of birds. It is a critical stopover for early migrant swallows and a diverse array of shorebirds.

Dragonfly Observation: The marsh is a known exceptional habitat for Odonata, with 30 species of dragonflies recorded to date. Mid-April is a peak time to witness dragonfly larvae emerging and unfurling their wings.

Wildlife Tracking: Beyond the water, the surrounding forest is home to Roosevelt elk, black bears, and even grey wolves. Smaller red and blue-listed species like the Western Screech-owl and American Bittern also depend on this habitat.
Nature Photography: The sprawling wetlands and second-growth forest provide a quiet, natural backdrop, particularly during the spring when the marsh is alive with new growth and insect life.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-dock-at-hamilton-marsh-public-park-qualicum-beach-vancouver-island-british-gm2246416279-660373007
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/the-forest-at-hamilton-marsh-public-park-qualicum-beach-vancouver-island-british-gm2246416284-660373004
Tips and Key Information
The Hamilton Marsh Nature Trail can be muddy and uneven. Wear waterproof boots or sturdy shoes that you don't mind getting dirty, especially during the spring.
Visit in late March or April to coincide with the Brant Wildlife Festival. This is when the ecosystem is most active with migrating birds and emerging insects.
Because the marsh is a sensitive breeding ground, keeping noise to a minimum will significantly increase your chances of spotting rarer birds like the Great Blue Heron or elusive mammals.
Look for seasonal guided tours hosted by the Hamilton Wetlands & Forest Preservation Society, which offer deeper ecological context than a solo walk.
Situated south of Qualicum Beach, bounded by Hilliers Road and Memorial Avenue.
The land is managed under Mosaic Forest Management and is currently accessible to the public on a use at your own risk basis.
To protect nesting birds and sensitive wildlife, dogs are strongly discouraged on the trails, especially during the spring nesting season (February to May).
This is a rugged, undeveloped nature site. There are no washrooms, trash cans, or potable water facilities on-site, so please follow leave no trace principles.
The marsh plays a crucial role in local water security, feeding into both the French Creek and Little Qualicum watersheds.

places.name: Seaside Nature Park
body: Seaside Nature Park is a tranquil hidden gem located at the far western end of Qualicum Beach’s waterfront. Dedicated to the memory of Faye Smith, a celebrated local environmentalist and salmon advocate, this park serves as a quiet sanctuary for nature lovers looking to escape the busier sections of the main promenade.
What to See and Do

Faye Smith Memorial Pavilion: The centerpiece of the park is a charming covered gazebo that provides a sheltered spot for rest and contemplation. It is surrounded by beautifully landscaped gardens maintained by local volunteers.

Elevated Bird-Watching Platform: A dedicated wooden platform offers an elevated 180-degree vantage point of the Salish Sea. This is a premier spot for photographers and birdwatchers, especially during the spring herring spawn when marine bird activity is at its peak.

Educational Interpretive Signage: The park features a series of informative storyboards that detail the local marine ecosystem, native plant species, and the significance of wild salmon to the region's heritage.

Quiet Beach Access: Unlike the central beach areas, this park offers a more secluded point of entry to the shoreline. At low tide, the receding waters reveal expansive sand flats and tide pools teeming with small marine life.
Tips and Key Information

Because it is situated at the western end of the waterfront, the park offers some of the most unobstructed views of the sunset in Qualicum Beach. The picnic tables near the pavilion are ideal for an evening meal while watching the light fade over the water.

Bring a pair of binoculars. The elevated platform is perfectly positioned for spotting eagles, herons, and various waterfowl that frequent the estuary at the mouth of the nearby Little Qualicum River.

The gardens are a labor of love by local streamkeepers and naturalists. While the landscaping can occasionally appear more wild depending on the season, the variety of native plants makes it a unique botanical stop.
If the central Qualicum Beach walkway feels too busy on a summer weekend, this is the place to go. It is generally much quieter and offers a more intimate connection with the coastal environment.
Situated on Island Highway West at the intersection with Crescent Road West, at the very end of the waterfront seawall.
The pavilion and the main viewing areas are wheelchair and stroller friendly, featuring paved or hard-packed surfaces.
There is a small, dedicated gravel parking area at the park entrance. It is more limited than the central waterfront parking, so arriving early is recommended on sunny days.
The park is designed for short visits and nature viewing; while it has picnic tables and benches, the nearest major public washrooms are located a short drive back toward the town center.
Dogs are welcome on a leash within the park and pavilion area. Be sure to check local signage for seasonal beach access rules regarding pets, particularly during bird nesting seasons.

places.name: Grandon Creek
body: Grandon Creek offers a peaceful, wooded escape that connects the upper residential areas of Qualicum Beach to the shoreline. This shaded ravine is a favorite for locals seeking a quiet nature walk, characterized by its lush ferns, ancient trees, and the gentle sound of the creek that provides a vital habitat for returning salmon.
What to See and Do

Salmon Spawning Viewing: In the late autumn, usually October and November, the lower sections of the creek become a site of intense activity as Coho and Chum salmon return to spawn. Local streamkeepers have worked extensively to install spawning pools and woody debris to help these fish navigate the current.

The Multi-Use Trail: A well-maintained trail, often referred to as the Grandon Creek / Laburnum Access, runs for approximately 1.2 kilometers through the ravine. It transitions from a wider, flatter path near the town side to a more rugged, forested singletrack as it climbs toward Laburnum Road.

Flora and Fauna: The ravine's microclimate supports a dense growth of sword ferns and moss-covered maples. It is an excellent spot for birdwatching, particularly for spotting owls and woodpeckers that nest in the high canopy of the second-growth Douglas firs.

West-End Beach Access: The trail serves as a scenic green artery, allowing hikers to walk from the upper town directly down to the western edge of the Qualicum Beach waterfront without following the main roads.
Tips and Key Information

The terrain near the creek can be persistently wet and muddy, especially in the winter and spring. Sturdy, waterproof hiking boots are highly recommended to navigate the occasionally slippery sections.
During the salmon run, it is crucial to stay on the designated paths and keep all pets out of the water. Disturbing the gravel beds can destroy thousands of salmon eggs.

On sunny mornings, the way the light filters through the deep ravine creates dramatic beams of light (often called "God rays") through the mist and cedar branches, making it a prime time for photography.
You can easily combine a walk here with a visit to the nearby Qualicum Beach Heritage Forest for a full morning of old-growth exploration.
The main trailheads are located at the foot of Beach Road (near the waterfront) and on Laburnum Road near the Qualicum Beach Civic Centre.
Rated as a moderate hike due to some elevation changes and the potential for muddy, uneven ground, though the trail is generally easy to follow.
Dogs are permitted but must be kept on a leash. This is strictly enforced during the salmon spawning season to protect the sensitive creek ecosystem.
The lower section of the trail near the beach is relatively flat, but the full route involves a steady climb and some narrow sections that are not suitable for wheelchairs or strollers.
There are no washrooms or trash cans within the ravine itself; the nearest public facilities are located at the Waterfront Viewing Platform & Walkway or in the town center.

places.name: Saahtlam Park
body: Saahtlam Park is a quiet, forested green space located on the western edge of Qualicum Beach. It serves as a vital ecological corridor, protecting a stand of second-growth Douglas fir and providing a peaceful, less-traveled alternative to the town’s more prominent parks.
What to See and Do

Forested Walking Trails: The park features a simple network of soft-surface trails that wind through a dense canopy of fir, cedar, and maple trees. It is an ideal spot for a short, meditative nature walk away from the sound of highway traffic.

Native Plant Identification: The understory is rich with native BC flora, including large sword ferns, salal, and Oregon grape. In the spring, you can often spot delicate wildflowers like trilliums emerging from the forest floor.
Birdwatching: Because the park is less frequented by large crowds, it remains a sanctuary for local birdlife. It is a common spot for hearing the distinct calls of varied thrushes and flickers.
Tips and Key Information
The park is located near the western waterfront, making it easy to pair a shaded forest stroll here with a visit to the nearby Seaside Nature Park - Faye Smith Memorial Pavilion.

This is a neighborhood-scale park, so it rarely gets busy. Visit in the early morning or late afternoon to enjoy the filtered light effect through the trees, which is particularly beautiful in this section of the coastal forest.
While the trails are relatively flat, they are natural earth paths that can become muddy after a rainfall. Sturdy walking shoes or boots are recommended during the autumn and winter months.
Located at 3319 Island Hwy W, Qualicum Beach, BC.
The trails are mostly level but consist of natural forest floor and bark mulch, which may be challenging for narrow-wheeled strollers or wheelchairs.
Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a leash to protect the local ecosystem and nesting birds.
This is a basic nature-first park; there are no public washrooms, picnic tables, or trash cans on-site. Visitors are encouraged to follow leave no trace principles.

places.name: Coombs / The Old Country Market (Goats on the Roof)
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/goats-on-the-roof-country-market-in-coombs-the-life-of-people-in-canada-during-the-gm1415406721-463791252

The Old Country Market, world-famous for its goats on the roof, is a landmark destination in the small community of Coombs. What began as a humble roadside fruit stand in the 1970s has evolved into a sprawling complex of eclectic shops and international eateries, all anchored by the sight of grazing goats atop the sod-roofed main building.
What to See and Do

The Famous Sod Roof: The main market building features a living grass roof where a resident family of goats spends the spring and summer months. This quirky architectural feature is a primary draw for photographers and families.
International Market: Inside the main building, you'll find a massive selection of gourmet imported foods, local cheeses, freshly baked breads, and unique kitchenware.

Coombs Emporium: Adjacent to the market, this area features a collection of statues—ranging from stone lions to wooden dragons—and shops selling everything from high-end clothing to international folk art.
The Donut Shop & Ice Cream Parlour: A visit is rarely complete without stopping for their famous oversized donuts or a scoop of locally made ice cream from the seasonal outdoor windows.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/coombs-country-market-gm958920532-261845863
Tips and Key Information
The goats are typically on the roof from late spring through early autumn, depending on the weather. If you visit in the winter, they are moved to a cozy barn nearby.

As one of Vancouver Island’s most popular tourist stops, it can become extremely busy between 11:00 AM and 3:00 PM on weekends. Arriving right when they open allows for a much more relaxed shopping experience.
While the market is the star, the surrounding village of Coombs is filled with antique shops and unique galleries that are often less crowded than the main complex.
Pick up some local smoked salmon, a fresh baguette, and some Okanagan fruit from the market to create a picnic to enjoy at the nearby Little Qualicum Falls Provincial Park.
Located at 2326 Alberni Hwy, Coombs, BC (approximately 10 minutes west of Qualicum Beach).
There is no fee to view the goats or enter the market area.
There is a large gravel parking lot on-site, but it can fill up entirely during peak summer months. Additional parking is often available along the neighboring side streets.
While pets are welcome in the outdoor village areas on a leash, they are strictly prohibited inside the food market and restaurant areas.
The complex includes several sit-down options, including Cuckoo in Coombs for Italian fare and a traditional Mexican cantina.

places.name: The Sandcastle Competition
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/batman-and-joker-sand-sculpture-gm534400250-94815081

The Parksville Beach Festival is a multi-week summer celebration that centers around the world-renowned Quality Foods Sand Sculpting Competition. This event transforms the waterfront of Parksville Community Park into a massive outdoor gallery, where master sculptors from around the globe compete to create intricate, gravity-defying works of art from just sand and water.
What to See and Do

The Sculpting Competition: The festival traditionally begins with a pound up and several days of intense carving. Watching the artists use specialized tools to etch fine details and textures into massive sand blocks is a highlight for early-season visitors.

The Exhibition Gallery: Following the competition, the finished sculptures remain on display for several weeks. A gated boardwalk allows for close-up viewing, providing a clear perspective on the scale and technical difficulty of each piece.

Interactive Sculpting Zone: Most years, a dedicated area offers free lessons and demonstrations. This is a popular spot for families where professional sculptors share tips on the proper sand-to-water ratios and carving techniques.

Evening Illuminations: On select nights toward the end of the festival, the sculptures are lit with colored spotlights. This creates a dramatic, nocturnal atmosphere that highlights different shadows and details than those seen during the day.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/cat-hides-from-mouse-sand-sculpture-gm534397566-94812727
Tips and Key Information

Every visitor is encouraged to participate in the People's Choice Award. Entrance to the exhibition is usually by a suggested small donation, which often benefits various local non-profit organizations.
To avoid the largest crowds and capture the best photos, aim to arrive shortly after the gates open in the morning or during the quiet hours of a weekday evening.
The festival typically provides mobility aids like scooters or specialized wheelchairs for use within the exhibition area, as navigating the sand can be difficult for some.
The event often coincides with a free summer concert series at the nearby Parksville Outdoor Theatre, allowing visitors to enjoy live music alongside the art.
The festival usually runs from mid-July through mid-August each year. Specific dates are announced annually on the official festival website.
Held at the Parksville Community Park, located at 193 Island Highway East.
The gated exhibition typically opens in the morning and closes in the late evening, offering ample time for viewing under different lighting conditions.
Due to the fragile nature of the sand art, pets are generally not allowed inside the gated sculpture area, though they are welcome in the surrounding community park on a leash.
Amateur photography is highly encouraged, but visitors are reminded to stay on the designated boardwalks to ensure the preservation of the art until the end of the season.

places.name: Paradise Fun Park
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/paradise-mini-golf-and-fun-park-in-parksville-on-vancouver-island-gm1818727868-549867534

Paradise Fun Park is a long-standing family entertainment center in Parksville, known for its colorful, whimsical atmosphere and its prominent location near the waterfront. It serves as a classic stop for those looking for lighthearted competition and traditional seaside amusements.
What to See and Do
The park is designed around two primary 18-year-old mini-golf courses that offer distinct visual themes.

Two Miniature Golf Courses: Visitors can choose between the Turf 'n Surf course, which features water hazards and a nautical theme, or the Treasure Island course, which is filled with pirate-themed obstacles, caves, and a large Victorian-style castle.
Bumper Boats: A dedicated pond allows guests to pilot motorized bumper boats equipped with water cannons, providing a popular way to cool off during the summer months.
Amusement Arcade: The on-site arcade features a mix of classic redemption games and modern video simulators, where players can win tickets to trade for prizes.
Ice Cream and Snacks: A seasonal concession stand serves traditional park treats, including a wide variety of hard-scoop ice cream flavors and cold beverages.
Tips and Key Information

During the peak summer season, the park is illuminated with neon lights and colorful spotlights. Playing mini-golf in the evening offers a cooler temperature and a more vibrant, fairground-like atmosphere.
If you plan on doing both golf courses and the bumper boats, look for combo passes which typically offer a discount over purchasing individual tickets.

As one of the most visible attractions in Parksville, the park can become quite crowded mid-afternoon. Arriving closer to opening time usually ensures shorter wait times for the bumper boats and a faster pace on the golf courses.

Because the park is located near the open water, it can be quite breezy. If you are playing mini-golf, be prepared for the wind to occasionally affect the trajectory of your ball on the more exposed holes.
Located at 375 Island Hwy W, Parksville, BC.

The park typically opens for the season in the spring and runs through early autumn. Hours are significantly extended during the summer months; it is recommended to check the current closing time as it can vary based on weather conditions.

The main walkways and the Turf 'n Surf course are generally accessible, though some holes on the Treasure Island course involve stairs and narrow passages through caves that may be difficult for those with limited mobility.
For the safety and comfort of all guests, pets are generally not permitted within the attractions or the miniature golf courses.
There is a dedicated paved parking lot on-site, though it can fill up quickly during holiday weekends.

places.name: Qualicum Beach Farmers’ Market
body: The Qualicum Beach Farmers' Market is a year-round community staple that transitions from a bustling outdoor street market in the summer to a cozy indoor gathering in the winter. It is widely regarded as one of the premier make, bake, or grow markets on Vancouver Island, ensuring that everything sold is produced locally by the vendors themselves.
What to See and Do
The market serves as the primary Saturday morning social hub for the region, offering a high density of local flavor and artisan craftsmanship.
Farm-Fresh Produce: Depending on the season, you’ll find everything from Nanoose Bay greens and berries to stump-grown mushrooms and organic root vegetables.
Artisanal Foods: The market is famous for its selection of high-quality prepared goods, including fresh-baked sourdough, local honey, island-made cheeses, and small-batch preserves.
Handcrafted Wares: Local artisans showcase a variety of West Coast-inspired items, such as hand-thrown pottery, woodworking, natural soaps, and jewelry.
Live Entertainment: Local musicians often perform near the seating areas, contributing to a vibrant, festive atmosphere that encourages visitors to linger.
Tips and Key Information
For the best selection of popular items like fresh croissants or specific seasonal produce, arrive as close to the opening bell as possible.
In keeping with the town’s environmental focus, most vendors do not provide plastic bags. Bringing a sturdy reusable tote or a basket is standard practice.
Many visitors skip breakfast at home and instead graze through the market's ready-to-eat stalls, which often feature hot coffee, savory pies, and fresh crepes.
During the summer months, the market takes over Veterans Way in the heart of the village. In the winter, it typically moves to the Qualicum Beach Legion or a nearby indoor community space.
Location: Summer (Outdoor) on Veterans Way; Winter (Indoor) location varies but is always within the Qualicum Beach town center.
Hours: Every Saturday, typically from 8:30 AM to 12:00 PM.
The summer outdoor market is located on a paved, flat street, making it highly accessible for wheelchairs and strollers.
While the village is very pet-friendly, dogs are generally not permitted within the actual market boundaries to ensure food safety and manage the high density of crowds.
Most vendors now accept cards, but carrying a small amount of cash is still helpful for smaller purchases or at stalls with limited connectivity.

places.name: Summer by the Sea Market (Parksville)
body: The Summer by the Sea Street Market is a vibrant Tuesday evening tradition that transforms the heart of downtown Parksville into a bustling open-air festival. Spanning four city blocks along Craig Street, it is one of the largest and most popular markets on Vancouver Island, attracting thousands of visitors each week with its eclectic mix of shopping, dining, and live entertainment.
What to See and Do

Extensive Vendor Lineup: Over 150 vendors from across the island showcase a diverse range of products, including handcrafted jewelry, local fashion, artisanal soaps, organic produce, and unique home and garden decor.
Gourmet Street Food: A wide selection of food trucks and merchants offer everything from savory international cuisine to indulgent treats like locally made donuts and fresh-baked pastries.
Live Performances: Multiple stages and busker stations are scattered throughout the market area, featuring a rotating schedule of local bands and performers that add to the festive ambiance.

Picnic in the Plaza: Visitors can grab food from the market and head to the nearby Memorial Plaza, which often hosts additional community activities, kids' games, and arts and crafts during market evenings.
Tips and Key Information
The most popular food trucks often have long lines by 7:00 PM. Arriving right at the start ensures you can secure your meal before the peak rush.
Several downtown streets are closed to traffic during the market. Look for parking in the large lots near Parksville Community Park and enjoy the short walk to Craig Street.

Due to the high volume of foot traffic and pavement heat, organizers strongly advise against bringing pets. If you must bring a dog, ensure they are comfortable in dense crowds and remain on a short leash.
The market is a committed rain or shine event. In the case of typical coastal drizzle, the festivities continue, often with shorter wait times at the most popular stalls.
The market traditionally takes place every Tuesday evening from mid-June through the end of August.
Festivities typically run from 6:00 PM to 9:00 PM, though the market often closes slightly earlier (8:30 PM) in late August as the sun sets sooner.
Centered on Craig Street in downtown Parksville, stretching between Island Highway and Jensen Avenue.
Temporary portable toilets are usually available near the market boundaries, and many downtown businesses remain open late to accommodate visitors.

places.name: Morningstar Farm: Home to Little Qualicum Cheeseworks
body: Morningstar Farm, the scenic home of Little Qualicum Cheeseworks, is a functional dairy farm and culinary destination located in Parksville. It offers a transparent look at local agriculture, where visitors can see the connection between the pasture and the finished artisanal products available in the farm gate shop.
What to See and Do
Self-Guided Farm Tours: The farm is open for public exploration, allowing visitors to walk through the barns to see the dairy cows, calves, and often other farm animals like pigs and sheep.
Canada's First Milk ATM: A unique feature of the farm is the grass-fed milk dispenser, where visitors can purchase reusable glass bottles and fill them with fresh, cold milk directly from the source.
Artisanal Cheese Tasting: The farm shop features the full lineup of Little Qualicum Cheeseworks products, ranging from their famous Island Bries and Verdelait to squeaky cheese curds.
Seasonal Fruit Wines: In addition to dairy, the farm is home to MooBerry Winery, which produces a variety of fruit wines made from locally grown berries, available for tasting and purchase.
Tips and Key Information
Timing your visit for the afternoon often allows you to witness the automated milking process, a fascinating look at how modern technology is integrated into traditional farming.

The farm features several outdoor tables with views of the Beaufort Mountains. It is common practice to assemble a picnic from the farm shop’s selection of cheese, crackers, and preserves to enjoy on-site.
Depending on the time of year, the farm hosts various community events, such as Calf Days in the spring or harvest celebrations in the autumn, which feature additional family activities.
The rustic red barns and the mountain backdrop provide a quintessential Vancouver Island farm setting, especially during the soft light of the late afternoon.
Located at 403 Lowry's Rd, Parksville, BC.
Entry to the farm grounds and the self-guided tour areas is free to the public.
Due to the presence of livestock and food production facilities, pets are not permitted on the farm grounds; however, there are occasionally shaded spots in the parking area for short waits.
The farm shop includes a small cafe area with coffee and snacks, and public washrooms are available for visitors.
The farm gate shop and grounds are typically open daily year-round, though hours may be slightly reduced during the winter months.

places.name: Qualicum Beach Downtown
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/qualicum-beach-main-street-on-vancouver-island-canada-gm997986624-269992197

The Qualicum Beach Downtown area, often referred to by locals as “The Village”, is characterized by its walkable, pedestrian-friendly streets and a distinct lack of franchise stores. The town has maintained a village atmosphere through careful planning, resulting in a charming commercial core filled with unique boutiques, galleries, and garden-lined sidewalks.
What to See and Do
The downtown core is designed for slow-paced exploration, with a high concentration of independent businesses.

Unplugged Shopping Experience: The village is famous for its independent retailers. You won't find major big-box stores here; instead, the streets are lined with curated bookstores, high-end toy shops, and clothing boutiques.

Art Galleries and Studios: Qualicum Beach has a high population of resident artists. Several downtown galleries showcase local pottery, West Coast paintings, and glasswork, often reflecting the natural beauty of the surrounding island.

Garden Culture: The town takes its Britain in Bloom heritage seriously. Even in the downtown core, you’ll find elaborate hanging baskets, manicured public planters, and the Town Square which serves as a central gathering point with benches and shade trees.

Tigh-Na-Mara Toy Drive & Events: Throughout the year, the downtown streets host various community events, including car shows, seasonal festivals, and the popular Saturday morning farmers' market just a block away from the main intersection.
https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/qualicum-beach-main-street-gm171274571-20088666
Tips and Key Information
Many local shops close earlier than those in larger cities, often around 5:00 PM. Plan your shopping for the morning or early afternoon to ensure you have plenty of time to browse.
The entire downtown core is relatively compact. You can park your car once and easily reach all the main shops, cafes, and even the Qualicum Beach Heritage Forest on foot.
The village has a strong cafe culture. It is a local ritual to grab a coffee and a treat from a bakery and find a bench in the Town Square to watch the world go by.
The downtown area features wide, level sidewalks with plenty of curb cuts, making it one of the most accessible shopping districts for those using mobility aids or strollers.
The layout of the town center makes navigation straightforward for first-time visitors.
The primary commercial area is centered around the intersection of Memorial Avenue and Primrose Street.
Free angled street parking is available throughout the village, along with several public lots behind the main shops. There are no parking meters in downtown Qualicum Beach.
Clean, accessible public restrooms are located near the Town Square and within the Qualicum Beach Commons.
The village is exceptionally dog-friendly; many shops place water bowls outside their doors, and there are numerous hitching posts for pets while you pop inside.

places.name: Parksville Downtown
body: https://www.istockphoto.com/photo/parksville-main-street-gm512127583-47391712

The Parksville Downtown core serves as the commercial heart of the Oceanside region, blending a traditional main street feel with modern amenities. Unlike the strictly boutique nature of neighboring Qualicum Beach, Parksville’s downtown offers a mix of essential services, large retailers, and a growing collection of independent creative spaces.
What to See and Do
The downtown area is characterized by its accessibility to the shoreline and its diverse range of local businesses.

The Creative District: Recent years have seen a surge in artisan studios and galleries along the side streets, where visitors can find everything from custom jewelry and West Coast photography to locally made textiles.

A Foodie Corridor: The main strip features an array of dining options that reflect the island's diverse palate, including authentic Greek tavernas, modern Canadian bistros, and popular craft breweries.

Proximity to the Boardwalk: One of the greatest assets of the downtown core is its immediate connection to the Parksville Community Park. A short, five-minute walk from the main intersection leads directly to the waterfront boardwalk and the sand sculpting exhibition area.
The Mews: This charming, Tudor-style shopping alley provides a sheltered, pedestrian-only environment filled with small specialty shops, a local bookstore, and quiet courtyard seating.
Tips and Key Information
Located at the eastern edge of downtown, the Parksville & District Visitor Centre is an excellent first stop for picking up physical maps, event schedules, and local advice on hidden gems.

If you are visiting during the summer, remember that the downtown core undergoes a massive transformation for the Summer by the Sea Street Market. Arrive early in the afternoon to shop the brick-and-mortar stores before the street stalls set up.
While street parking is available, the larger lots near the Jensen Avenue civic center offer more time flexibility if you plan on spending the whole day browsing and dining.

The downtown area is home to several long-standing independent cafes. These spots are the social hubs of the community and are perfect for people-watching or planning the next leg of your island tour.
The primary downtown area is concentrated along Island Highway East and Craig Street.
The city has invested heavily in wide, smooth sidewalks and high-visibility crosswalks, making the entire downtown core very friendly for those with strollers or mobility scooters.
In addition to facilities within the Community Park, public washrooms are available at the Visitor Centre and within the Civic Centre complex.
Parksville is a very dog-friendly city; you will find many dog bars (water bowls) outside shops, though individual store policies on bringing pets inside will vary.

places.name: Mount Arrowsmith Brewing Company
body: Mount Arrowsmith Brewing Company is a multi-award-winning craft brewery located in the industrial area of Parksville. Named after the region’s most iconic mountain peak, it has quickly become a cornerstone of the local social scene, known for its commitment to high-quality ingredients and its welcoming, communal atmosphere. Visitors often highlight the brewery for its consistent quality and the lively, family-friendly vibe of its tasting room.
What to See and Do
Award-Winning Brews: The brewery is home to the "Best Beer in the World" (World Beer Awards 2017) for its Blonde Ale, alongside a diverse rotation of IPAs, stouts, and seasonal harvests.

The Arrowsmith Pizzeria: Unlike many traditional tasting rooms, this location features a full-service stone pizza oven, serving thin-crust, artisan pies that are specifically designed to pair with their beer flight.
Expansive Outdoor Patio: A large, sun-drenched patio provides plenty of seating during the warmer months and is a popular gathering spot for locals after a day at the beach or on the trails.
Brewery Culture: The interior features high ceilings and an open view of the brewing tanks, offering an authentic "behind-the-scenes" feel while you enjoy a pint.
Tips and Key Information
With a constantly rotating tap list of seasonal and experimental brews, ordering a flight is the best way to explore the full range of what the brewmasters are currently working on.
As one of the most popular evening spots in Parksville, the tasting room and patio can fill up quickly on Friday and Saturday nights. Arriving in the late afternoon is recommended to secure a table.
The brewery maintains a well-stocked retail fridge with 4-packs and growler filling stations, making it a convenient stop to pick up local refreshments for a campfire or beach day.
Look for Cask Nights or local live music sets, which are frequently hosted in the tasting room to support the regional arts scene.
Located at 425 Stanford Ave E #109, Parksville, BC.
The tasting room and patio are both ground-level and fully accessible, with wide doorways and spacious seating arrangements.
Well-behaved dogs are typically welcome on the outdoor patio area, though they are not permitted inside the production or indoor seating areas.
The brewery is a minors welcome establishment, making it a common choice for families looking for a casual dinner spot.
Modern, clean restrooms are available on-site, and there is ample free parking in the surrounding industrial complex.
